sections.heading: A Note on This Guide
sections.body:
This brief orients you to the civic and everyday culture of the United States. European American backgrounds have their own brief and Minnesota culture comes next, so this page stays with the national grammar, and it is not a civics course.

### Who this is

American culture is the civic and national grammar that people in this country live inside to different degrees. Ask which parts of this grammar a person works inside, such as English as the public language, the individual as the unit of law, medicine, and the form, time, identical process, rights language, mobility, and work, and keep in mind that race is a founding structure that is not the whole of the culture and is not optional history.

African Americans are American, and jazz, the Constitution’s unfinished business, Black churches, and the English spoken in this country are American. Yet this page does not swallow the African American brief. Somali Minnesotans live inside this grammar on Tuesday and remain Somali. The eleven nations predate the United States. When they meet this grammar in a county building, that meeting is not everyone’s immigration story.

A community portrait of Americans is not one socioeconomic slice and not one race, because scientists, clerks, farmers, soldiers, artists, nurses, truckers, attorneys, plant workers, and people on waivers are all Americans. People of color are not visitors in someone else’s nation, and dominant culture does not get to delimit who counts as American.

### Who this is not

This is not the European American brief, and it is not Minnesota culture. It is not a substitute for Somali, Hmong, African American, or the eleven nations.

All people have culture. Ask whether a form is being treated as “just how we do things,” a clock as morality, or first-middle-last as nature, and whether a household that does not fit is being called non-compliant.

### How to read this

Read it as an orientation in which regional, racial, religious, and class variation is the point, and always defer to the person in front of you. Use this page for context and questions. It does not describe the person in front of you.

If you are studying your own culture, start here, then move to Minnesota culture, then to the streams you actually come from — German, Norwegian, African American, Somali, Ojibwe. If you are studying other cultures, stay with this page too. Other cultures in the United States are in conversation with this grammar every Tuesday, and you will misread them if you think only they have culture.

The facts that follow are meant to help you meet people well — how family is named, what a greeting carries, what a form may land on. History is here so that the meeting is clearer, not so that you deliver a lecture.

sections.heading: Origins and the Founding of a People
sections.body:
Indigenous nations come first, and any American origin story that starts with a ship and no land is already a politics. The United States is a settler state on Native land, a republic that wrote equality into a document while holding people as property, and a nation of immigrants who arrived under rules that kept changing.

### Colonial and founding

Colonial British North America is not the only colonial story, since Spanish, French, Dutch, and Russian claims also sit on this map. The Revolution (1776) and the Constitution (1787) created a civic religion of documents: rights, law, amendments, courts.

Slavery was not a Southern footnote but a labor system, a legal regime, and a wealth engine. That is why the Civil War and Reconstruction are founding events as much as 1776 is. Jim Crow, the Chinese Exclusion Act, the 1924 immigration quotas, the 1965 Hart-Celler Act, and the ongoing fight over who belongs are later chapters of the same origin.

### Many origins, one civic frame

Crèvecoeur asked “What is an American?” in 1782 and answered with a melting story that erased Indigenous nations and enslaved Africans. That story still operates as common sense. Takaki’s later mirror is the correction: many origins, one civic frame, and a racial hierarchy that was built on purpose.

What people brought were languages, churches, foodways, legal ideas, capital, and labor. What they met was a state that demanded English in public, a market, a racial order, and a promise that the self could be remade. History is literacy for the meeting rather than a speech you give the family.

### The civic creed

The civic creed is a set of propositions: that persons have rights; that government is legitimate by consent; that law is written; that the self may be remade. Those propositions were never evenly applied.

Hold the creed and the record in one hand. If you drop the creed you get a cynicism that cannot work a public program, and if you drop the record you get a room that treats everyone the same and cannot see who the form was built for.

### Labor, empire, frontier

Colonial labor was Indigenous, African, European indenture, and later free European, and the nineteenth century added a continental empire (Mexico 1848; the Plains wars; Hawai‘i; the Philippines). American culture includes that expansion as “frontier” in its own hymns — Turner’s thesis — and as dispossession in Native and Mexican memory. Both are American history, but only one has usually been the school hymn.

### The twentieth century and after

The twentieth century made a mass consumer culture, a standing military, a federal administrative state (New Deal, Great Society), and a civil-rights reconstruction that is unfinished. The twenty-first opened with war, financial crisis, and a demographic shift in which the unmarked majority is no longer the future of every county, so date the Census when you cite it. A future demographic is neither a threat story nor a comfort story.

1619 and 1776 are both American origins. You do not have to pick a slogan, but you do have to know why a household might not experience a public form as a document of freedom.

sections.heading: Geography
sections.body:
The United States is not one region, and this brief treats that as a fact to work with rather than a caveat.

### Regions

New England carries a civic and Yankee residue. The South includes the Black Belt, Appalachia, the Gulf, and Texas as its own scale. The Midwest holds industrial cities and farm counties, and Minnesota sits here without being Ohio. The West is aridity, public land, and Pacific ports, and there are borderlands with Mexico. Alaska and Hawai‘i are states with different Indigenous and colonial facts. Puerto Rico and the other territories are American legal facts that the fifty-star map hides.

### Internal difference

Internal difference is culture: honor and evangelical density in much of the South; Lutheran heritage in much of the Upper Midwest (Pew, 2023-24: about 23 percent of Minnesota adults belong to Lutheran bodies, including 12 percent in the ELCA, and 29 percent are religiously unaffiliated), which some describe as shaping a conflict-avoidant style; informality and boom-bust in parts of the West. A national average does not describe a Texan or a Minnesotan.

Name the region, because a national form is not locally native. Open Minnesota culture for this state’s hymn. Rural as place is a different brief, and the eleven nations have geographies that are not states.

### Cities and suburbs

Cities and suburbs wrote a later American culture: commuting, malls, then logistics sprawl; Black urban neighborhoods shaped by the Great Migration and by highway and redline; immigrant inner-ring suburbs as the new gateway. Ask where a person lives and what that place means to them, because a suburb is a place too.

### Climate and territories

Disaster and climate are geography now, in flood, fire, and heat. When mobility hymns meet people who cannot move a grandmother, human services will meet that collision as a case.

Puerto Rico, Guam, the U.S. Virgin Islands, American Samoa, and the Northern Mariana Islands are American legal geography that the continental hymn forgets, so if a household’s kin are there, this is not foreignness.

sections.heading: Migration and Foundational Events
sections.body:
American culture is a culture of movement, both forced and chosen.

### Forced and chosen

The movements include the removal of Native nations; the Middle Passage and the domestic slave trade; European immigration in waves (colonial; 1840s–50s Irish and German; 1880–1924 southern and eastern European; post-1965 global); Chinese labor and exclusion; the Great Migration of African Americans (about six million, roughly the 1910s to the 1970s, National Archives); Bracero and later Latino labor; refugee acts after war; and internal moves toward jobs, sun, and housing.

### The mobility story

The cultural story is that you can leave and start over, a story that is real for some and a cruelty for others. Dakota exile after 1862 is not “mobility,” and Hmong resettlement after a Secret War is not “the immigrant bargain,” so open the people page.

### Civic events

There are foundational civic events you cannot skip: the Revolution; the Constitution; 1861–65; 1865–77 Reconstruction; the 19th Amendment; the 1924 and 1965 immigration regimes; the 1964 Civil Rights Act; the 1965 Voting Rights Act; the 1990 ADA. None of them is “in the past.”

### After 1965

Post-1965 immigration remade metropolitan America. Minnesota’s Somali, Hmong, Karen, Liberian, and Latino plant-town stories are American migration stories with specific wars and labor markets. They do not make those peoples “the same as Ellis Island.” When the hymn that says we are all immigrants is used that way, it skips 1862, slavery, and a Secret War.

Undocumented status is American structure, not a culture, so collect the status the work requires and not more. Fear of the lobby is an access fact, which is why you open the Latino, Mexican, and other people pages.

sections.heading: Family
sections.body:
The unmarked American household on a form is nuclear: two adults, their minor children, one address, one last name. Do not assume a household is a couple and children, or that older relatives live elsewhere. That means “just the parents” is already a design choice.

### Who is in the household

That form never described everyone, because extended kin, othermothers, mixed-status households, multi-generational immigrant homes, and Native kinship systems have always been here. The culture’s fairness story still writes the nuclear unit into waivers, taxes, and who may speak at a meeting.

Ask who should be in the room. Ask what marriage, divorce, and children mean to this family.

A scientist, a factory worker, and a grandparent raising grandchildren are the same American family landscape, and a community portrait means all of that. “Broken family” is what the English form says when the household is not nuclear.

### Childhood

Ask who decides for a child in this household, because treating children as decision-makers (“what do you want?”) may not fit every household. Using a child to translate for a parent is a gate and a burden, so book an interpreter.

### Aging

Ask what this family wants for an older relative’s care, because the form assumes a nursing home or “independence,” and neither is the only moral choice.

### Love and sex

Companionate marriage, dating as a market, later marriage, and non-marriage are all part of the picture. LGBTQ families are American families rather than a sidebar to a nuclear hymn.

sections.heading: Minnesota — open the next brief
sections.body:
This page is the national water, but it is not enough for a desk in St. Paul.

### The next brief

Minnesota culture is the drill-down: what people call Minnesota Nice; this land and the eleven nations; German-Norwegian unmarked culture plus everyone who is Minnesota; metro and Greater Minnesota; and a progressive self-image next to racial gaps; for example, the Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis found Black homeownership in the Twin Cities at 29 percent in 2024, the widest Black-white gap among comparable metros (46.9 points). Rural is place, and European American is named streams. Those three are not this chapter.

Open Minnesota culture next, and then the household’s people page, because a land acknowledgment without the Minnesota brief and without the Office of Indian Policy is still a speech.

sections.heading: Heart of the Culture
sections.body:
Ask how this person thinks about freedom, equality before the law, and responsibility for their own outcome, and ask what they mean if they say “I don’t have a culture; I’m just me.”

### Hymns of the self

Ask which of these ideas matter to this person: the American Dream, progress, equal treatment, freedom of choice, and sincerity. Bellah’s Habits of the Heart named expressive and utilitarian individualism as the common language, and Tocqueville had already seen the restlessness.

Ask whether common humanity, “we don’t see color,” a clock, or a form is being used to skip deep difference or to stand in for professionalism. Common humanity is real, and it is not the whole story.

Du Bois wrote that the American Negro wished to be both Negro and American without bleaching either. Ask whether this person wants to be seen as only American or with a hyphen. This brief names that question without mocking anyone and without canceling anyone’s belonging.

People are not asked to leave one self at the lobby, and a rule that asks them to is this heart dressed as a dress code.

### A good life, as Americans talk it

Habits of the Heart (Bellah and colleagues, 1985) remains useful because it named how Americans talk when they talk about a good life: freedom, fairness, success, and love, almost always as individual projects. Communities, traditions, and biblical or republican languages still exist, but they are often translated back into “what works for me.” A public program has to speak both languages, addressing the individual who has a case number and the household that actually lives.

### The Dream and structure

The American Dream is a hymn of mobility. When an outcome is explained by effort, choices, or “personal responsibility,” ask whether structure was checked first. Equity work in a human-services department keeps asking that question.

### Sincerity

Ask whether “be yourself” and “speak from the heart” fit this person in a meeting, and do not expect that of everyone. Ask too whether the person is carrying the fatigue of code-switching, which African American intelligence already named.

sections.heading: Core Concepts
sections.body:
These concepts recur, and they express differently by region, class, race, religion, and generation, which makes them hypotheses about the unmarked grammar rather than a script for the person in front of you.

### The individual as the unit

Law, medicine, school, and the form address one person, and family and clan are treated as “private,” so the work is seeing when the unit is actually a household.

### Identical process and fairness

Ask whether a targeted channel is being read as favoritism because identical process is the expected standard. Universal goal, targeted channel is the equity correction.

### Time and appointments

Ask what makes a time hard for this person, and do not read lateness as character. Keep medical and legal time.

### Work and rest

Ask what work and rest mean to this person, and do not treat rest, disability, or unemployment as a moral problem.

### Saying it plainly

Say what you mean and put it in writing, because email is the real meeting. Do not read a gentle or roundabout answer as evasion. Ask what the person wants to happen. What people call Minnesota Nice complicates this with its reserve and indirect no, so open that page.

### Rights and legalism

Problems become claims, forms, and due process, and the Constitution serves as civic scripture. A form is a legal object, so a person who expects to talk first can hit a wall of paper. Explain the form out loud.

### Privacy and personal space

Ask what the person is comfortable discussing in a shared lobby, whether the body, pay, family, or a diagnosis. Do not touch hair, stand close, or ask about clan unless the person invites it.

### Help and self-reliance

Ask how this person feels about asking for help, and do not assume “I don’t want charity” means they do not need the program.

### English as the public language

Other languages are treated as private, festive, or a problem to be solved with an interpreter line, and CLAS exists because this concept closes doors.

### Race as structure

Race is not the whole culture, and it is not optional. Whiteness is unmarked; Blackness is hyper-visible; Native nations are cast as mascot or past; immigrants are probationary; and a training does not cancel this.

### Informality

Ask how the person wants to be addressed. A title is not stiffness, and a first name is not always friendly.

### Volunteerism and associations

This is Tocqueville’s America of groups: boards, churches, PTAs, nonprofits. Engagement in this culture often means a meeting and a 501(c)(3), but nations and mosques are not that object by default.

### The past and the future

Ask whether the past is present for this person, and do not dismiss historical trauma as only history.

You work with these, but you do not perform a flag. “Minnesota Nice” is the local name for a stronger form of several of these, such as conflict-avoidance, sameness and reserved warmth, so open that brief.

### Conflict

Ask how this person prefers to handle disagreement in a meeting, and close each meeting by asking what was decided. Open Minnesota culture for what people call “Minnesota Nice.”

### Money

Ask what the person is comfortable discussing about pay, debt, or public benefits, and do not bring shame into the lobby.

### Gender

Ask who cares for the child, because the mother is not automatically the case.

### Disability

The ADA (1990) is American civic culture at its legal best — a rights frame — and Olmstead is living law. Ask what independence means to this person, because a waiver is not a character test.

### Generations

The American form tends to treat a working-age adult as the head of the household, so it often cannot see the grandmother as the household. Ask who is in the household and who should speak.

sections.heading: Religion and Civil Religion
sections.body:
American culture is religiously plural. Ask what faith or practice, if any, matters to this person, and do not assume belief is a personal choice for every household.

### Pluralism

Catholic, Jewish, Muslim, Buddhist, Hindu, Native traditional, and other lives are American. The unaffiliated share is large and growing, especially among the young, and since Pew gives the orders of magnitude, date the vintage you cite.

### Civil religion

Civil religion — Bellah’s term — is the civic sacred: founding documents, flags, national funerals, “God bless America,” the Super Bowl as liturgy. It is not a denomination, and it can bless a public form.

Church and state are separated in law and tangled in practice. Clergy are the case plan only when this family asked for that. Open the religion track in this program, because a mosque, a Black church, a Lutheran parish, and a lodge are not one chapter.

### Belief as choice

The First Amendment is a cultural fact: you may change churches, leave, or never go. That voluntarism is not how religion works in every people this program studies, and a Somali Muslim or a Dakota traditional household may not treat belief as a preference like a gym.

Prosperity gospel, megachurches, Black churches, Catholic parishes, mosques, gurdwaras, temples, and storefronts are all American religious geography, and the “nones” still do funerals and weddings in religious rooms. Date Pew when you cite a percentage.

sections.heading: Greetings
sections.body:
Do not treat a handshake, a smile and a quick first name as the standard for everyone. Do not read eye contact as a test of honesty.

### Titles

Ask how the person wants to be addressed, and use a title (Mr./Mrs./Dr.) until you know.

### This room

A handshake is not required. Let this person’s own greeting guide you, whatever you read on another page.

sections.heading: Naming
sections.body:
The pattern is first, middle, last, with one surname passed down or taken at marriage, because the database was built for Mary Ann Jones.

### What the form misses

Patronymics, three-part Somali names, Hmong clan names, Spanish two surnames, Native enrollment names, and no-last-name households all hit this system as error.

Ask how to say a name, because a last name is not something you invent, and a joke about a name shuts the person out. The form that only fits Mary Jones is a gate built inside this culture. That sentence belongs on every people page, because the gate is American.

sections.heading: Dates and Calendar
sections.body:
The civic year runs through New Year’s Day; MLK Day (January, federal); Washington’s and Lincoln’s Birthday (the February holiday, by that name in Minnesota law); Memorial Day; Juneteenth (federal since 2021); July 4; Labor Day; Indigenous Peoples Day (the second Monday in October; Minnesota law no longer names Columbus Day, and the state executive branch does not close that day, while other branches and local governments choose); Veterans Day; Thanksgiving (a civic harvest myth on Native land — literacy, not a speech at the table unless you are asked), with the Friday after Thanksgiving a legal holiday for the state executive branch; and Christmas as both the religious and the civic close of the year.

### Other calendars

Work and school run on this calendar, so Ramadan, Lunar New Year, Eid, Hmong New Year, and Dakota/Anishinaabe seasons have to fit it, and that fitting is a gate. A calendar click is literacy rather than engagement. Open the people page for the calendar this family actually keeps.

sections.heading: Education
sections.body:
Public school is a civic religion: the common school, the pledge, the sports Friday, the idea that education is the ladder. College is a class story and a mass expectation that is not equally funded, while standardized tests stand in for merit, and English-only is the default.

### Other schools

This is also the country of HBCUs, tribal colleges, Catholic schools, yeshivas, and Saturday language schools, even though the unmarked story hides them.

A parent who needs a language is not illiterate, and an English-only IEP is this culture’s gate. A degree is not the only intelligence, since scientists and people without diplomas are both this portrait.

### School as assimilation

The school as assimilation machine is an American project: English, punctuality, the pledge, the hidden curriculum of raising your hand. It produced literacy and it produced harm, and boarding schools for Native children are American education history. Open the eleven nations. Remember that this history is not only on the tribal page, as if the school system were innocent.

Tracking, discipline gaps, and who is called gifted are structure, and a scientist from a people of color is not an exception that proves the hymn. The community portrait includes teachers, professors, trades, and people the school failed, and all of them are American.

sections.heading: Etiquette
sections.body:
Explain which appointments have fixed times, and why. If someone misses one, first check the time, transport, interpreter and work schedule. Do not treat lateness or a raised voice as a character issue.

### Visits

If food or drink is offered, accepting a little is fine, and you can still keep to medical and legal timelines.

Keep to medical and legal timelines, and ask before taking any photograph in someone’s home.

### Food

Ask what the person eats, and do not treat one kind of meal as the standard.

### Alcohol

Alcohol is legal and commercial. Do not assume a toast at any event you plan.

sections.heading: Communication
sections.body:
Say what you mean, and put what matters in writing, in the language the person reads. Keep any disagreement to the issue.

### The real meeting

Do not rely on email or the portal alone. Do not read silence as agreement. Ask directly, and confirm what was decided.

AAVE is a systematic variety of American English, not broken English in a lobby or a case note. Spanish, Somali, Hmong, Ojibwe, and Dakota in Minnesota are not “failure to assimilate,” because they are the country’s actual linguistic life, so book what they ask for.

Whether someone answers bluntly or gently, ask whether they agree.

### Humor

Keep humor at work kind and clear, and do not repeat a joke you heard in a setting you were not part of.

### Feedback

Be plain without being cruel when you give feedback, and write what you would read aloud.

### Meetings

Ask what people need from the meeting, and leave time for introductions before the agenda. Do not force one template on a nation-to-nation consult or a mosque partnership.

sections.heading: Other Considerations
sections.body:
Class is American culture: Edina is not the Iron Range, which is not a Delta county. Region is culture and race is structure, while gender and disability sit inside the individual-as-unit and often lose.

### Not one American

Gun culture, sport culture, and military culture are civic in large parts of the country, but they are not the whole, and a coastal professional is not the only American.

Unvarnished: this culture’s fairness story has coexisted with slavery, exclusion, redlining, and mass incarceration. Naming that is literacy. Do not use it to skip a household, and do not use it to say “everyone has culture so outcomes are even.”

Follow the law, still see a person, and do not out anyone.

### Media

A common national culture was once three networks and is now fragmented feeds. People in the same building do not share a news hymn. Political disagreement in the country and disagreement about culture in a meeting are not the same object. A department has to work when staff and households do not share facts.

Conspiracy and anti-government strain are American, from the beginning. A DHS badge can activate that strain, and it can also activate histories of real harm, so listen before you lecture.

sections.heading: Health
sections.body:
Ask how this person understands illness and care, and what they expect from a visit and from mental health services.

### Insurance and disparity

Insurance tied to employment is structure, not a personality. Date disparities on the people pages — Black maternal mortality, American Indian outcomes, uninsured Latino patterns — because a national rate invented here to sound complete does not belong.

Believe reported pain for everyone. The unmarked clinic is this culture’s clinic, with English, the clock, one patient, and family in the waiting room, so ask who should be in the room.

### Population health

Opioids, alcohol, and methamphetamine are American population health, including in Greater Minnesota, so date local figures. Addiction is not a racial type, and “personal responsibility” is not the first sentence.

Maternal health, disability, and aging are where the individual-as-unit fails hardest. Ask who is actually providing care, and remember that Olmstead still applies.

sections.heading: LGBTQ
sections.body:
Legal change (Lawrence, Obergefell, state variation) and backlash both live here, with named variation by region, church, race, and generation. Use the name and pronouns, because outing someone to family is not “American culture,” and it is not anyone else’s culture either.

### Other pages

This is not the African American LGBTQ chapter and not Two-Spirit, so open those pages, and remember that the people-page rule is the workplace rule.

sections.heading: Hair and Dress
sections.body:
“Professional” hair and dress in American institutions were built on Euro-American unmarked rules: short hair or controlled hair for men; straightened or “neat” hair for women; suits; uncovered heads. CROWN Acts exist because those rules harmed Black hair, and hijab and ribbon skirts hit the same unmarked standard.

### In the room

Hair is not a professionalism test, and hair is not for touching, while a lab coat, a uniform, a ribbon skirt, and a hijab can all be American on a Tuesday.

sections.heading: Music
sections.body:
American music is one of the country’s actual gifts: spirituals, blues, jazz, country, rock and roll, hip-hop, and pop as export. Much of the global soundtrack is African American invention inside American industry, but a playlist is not engagement.

### Not one soundtrack

Country is not “real America” with hip-hop as other, and a symphony is not more cultured than a drum. Prince is Minnesota and American. Open the people pages for the rest.

sections.heading: Sports
sections.body:
Football, basketball, and baseball are civic liturgy, alongside Title IX and women’s sport, Friday night in some towns, and fandom as identity. Over-representation of Black athletes in some sports is not a personality and not the only excellence.

### Not the only excellence

The kid may not play, and sport is not the ladder story for children of color, since a scientist and a linebacker can be siblings.

sections.heading: Literature
sections.body:
Founding documents serve as civic literature, and there is a canon (Emerson, Whitman, Dickinson, Hemingway) alongside a counter-canon (Douglass, Hurston, Baldwin, Morrison, Erdrich, Anzaldúa), so this is not a people without letters.

### Who was left out

You do not need to quote in the lobby, but literacy includes who was left out. Population of a group is not culture size, and that rule applies to this page too, because American letters are not only the majority’s.

sections.heading: Art
sections.body:
Hollywood is industrial art, and there are museums, design, and the vernacular (quilts, signage, yards).

### Guest

Be a guest, and pay, because a festival is not consultation, and a design is not a logo for the unit.

sections.heading: Civil Rights Memory
sections.body:
The civic memory is a fight: 1776’s promise, 1863, 1865–77, 1954 Brown, 1964, 1965, ADA 1990, and the record that did not close. King named the Dream as a promissory note, and that is American culture rather than a minority add-on.

### The record

A DHS badge is not automatically help, and a training does not cancel the record. Civil rights statutes did not close the record for a Native household, and Floyd is not closed for a Black household, while this chapter does not replace Somali.

Amendments, courts, and statutes are this culture’s way of changing itself, and other cultures change through other means, but you still follow the statute in front of you.

### Contested memory

Memory is contested: 1619 vs 1776 as slogans; Confederate monuments; school boards; whose street name. The job in the lobby is not to win a culture war but to know that the form sits inside a country that has not agreed on its story, and that some households have bodies and kin in the part of the story the hymn skips.

King, 1963: the note was a promise to pay. Douglass, 1852: what to the slave is the Fourth of July. Those are American texts, and they belong on this page so that “American culture” cannot mean a comfortable majority memory.

sections.heading: Business and Work
sections.body:
Ask what work means to this person. At-will employment prevails in most states. The meeting and the email are common workplace routines.

### Who works here

Do not assign culture or interpreter work to staff because of who they are. A financial analyst, a scientist, a plant worker, and a county case manager are the portrait, including people of color in all of those seats.

Time at work is this culture’s time, so a plant shift, a farm season, and a Ramadan fast have to fit it, and that fitting is a gate.

### More than one economy

Corporations and small business both sit in the hymn, alongside at-will, at-shift, and gig work. Unions are American too — the Iron Range, plants, the public sector — and a coastal startup is not the economy.

Human services work is American public culture, the administrative state meeting a household. The form is a cultural object. If you cannot see that, you will call every mismatch a client problem.

sections.heading: Healthcare Encounters
sections.body:
The encounter runs on appointment, copay, consent, HIPAA, and one patient, while family may wait outside, so ask who should be in the room. Believe pain, book the language they ask for, and offer gender match if they want it.

### Help-seeking

Mandated reporting still exists, and help-seeking that becomes a child-welfare petition is a pattern some communities already know, although that fact is not a speech about “American medicine.”

sections.heading: Diaspora and Adjacent
sections.body:
This page describes the grammar inside the United States, so Americans living abroad are not its object.

### Adjacent doors

The European American streams, African American, the eleven nations, Somali, Hmong, rural place, and Minnesota culture are adjacent doors, and none of them is a synonym for this one.

This is not one diversity module, and “American” is not a mash that makes the people pages optional, so open the next brief.

sections.heading: Statistics
sections.body:
U.S. Census Bureau figures should always carry their vintage. The 2020 Census counted about 331 million residents. Race and Hispanic origin are administrative categories rather than culture. Non-Hispanic White remains the largest single category and is no longer the unmarked future of every county. Hispanic/Latino origin is an ethnicity in Census terms that people still live as culture. Black, Asian, American Indian and Alaska Native, Native Hawaiian and Other Pacific Islander, and Two or More Races are the other federal race boxes. Date any percentage you put in a report, and remember that this page is not a “white culture share.”

### Minnesota objects

Minnesota Compass cultural-community profiles are Minnesota objects that belong on the people pages, and this umbrella does not replace them.

A rate is not the person.

### Date the vintage

Date the 2020 Census and later ACS when you write a number into a report. There were about 331 million people in 2020, and Hispanic origin is ~19% (ethnicity, any race). Black alone is ~13–14% depending on vintage and on “alone or in combination.” Asian is the fastest-growing large category in many metros. American Indian and Alaska Native counts jump when “in combination” is used — Compass Minnesota Native American ~161,194 (ACS 2020–2024, Compass cultural-community table) is a Minnesota object, not this page.

The foreign-born share nationally is on the order of 14% in recent ACS vintages, and it should be dated. Minnesota’s foreign-born share is lower than some coastal states and has still remade whole neighborhoods and plant towns. Language other than English at home is on the order of one in five nationally. Minnesota Compass reports 12.3 percent (plus or minus 0.2) of Minnesotans speaking a language other than English at home for 2020 to 2024, with 4.6 percent speaking English less than “very well,” which also needs its date. CLAS exists because that 12.3% is not a rounding error at the desk.

sections.heading: Resources
sections.body:
In this program, go to Minnesota culture next; then the European American streams; the eleven nations; African American; the CLAS communities; rural as place; and the religion track.

### Public doors

The public doors are the Census, the founding documents, the National Archives, Pew on religion, and the people-page organizations.

Use these resources yourself before you ask a colleague to explain, and then open Minnesota culture.

### Read with this page

Read these with this page, not instead of it: Tocqueville, Democracy in America (selected); Bellah et al., Habits of the Heart; Takaki, A Different Mirror; Du Bois, The Souls of Black Folk (American and Negro); King, “I Have a Dream” and “Letter from Birmingham Jail”; the 1964 Civil Rights Act as a text; Pew Religious Landscape (date the wave). These are literacy, not a shrine.

Then stop reading and open Minnesota culture, then open a people page, and then go meet Tuesday.

sections.heading: How it hits DHS gates — the 40%
sections.body:
Workplace culture and service delivery are both candidates for where these gates take hold.

The packet was built inside this culture. Hour caps, exception processes, and “treat everyone the same” are not culturally empty. If the family cannot run the exception in English, the cap is the policy, which is why you name who the packet was built for.

This is a starting point for intercultural development, both personal and professional, and completing it does not mean the work is done.

Open Minnesota culture next, and then the household’s people page.

sections.heading: A Note on This Guide
sections.body:
This is Minnesota culture — and it comes after American culture, so if you have not opened that brief yet, open it first. Then read this one, and then turn to the community that matches the household in front of you.

### Who this is

What people call Minnesota Nice can show up as reserved warmth, a preference for calm, fairness understood as treating people the same, and competence as the way care often shows up. It is culture, and it is worth knowing, but it is not a tourism joke, and it is not a brand.

This land is Dakota and Anishinaabe, which means that any Minnesota hymn that starts with a lake and a settler is already a politics. The progressive self-image — we are kind, we are educated, we are not like that — sits right next to racial gaps that Minnesota’s own agencies publish, and the task is to hold both. Drop the gap and Nice becomes a lullaby; drop the hymn and you cannot hear the building.

The community portrait is broad: a scientist at 3M or Mayo, a county financial analyst, a plant worker in Worthington, a physician at a tribal clinic, a teacher in North Minneapolis, a farmer, a Somali business owner, an Ojibwe language teacher. It is not one slice, and it is not a lake postcard.

### Who this is not

Rural communities, European American backgrounds, and the eleven Tribal Nations each have their own briefs, while this page is about Minnesota as a place and a civic culture.

All people have culture. Staff who grew up inside Nice often say they do not have one, and that sentence is the reason this brief exists.

### How to read this

Read it as an orientation, and always defer to the person in front of you. Use this page for context and questions. It does not describe the person in front of you.

The facts that follow are meant to help you meet people well, and the history is here so that the meeting is clearer, not so that you deliver a lecture.

sections.heading: Origins and the Founding of a Place
sections.body:
This place begins with Dakota homeland in creation stories, and with Anishinaabe history on the lakes and in the wild rice, long before any of the later arrivals.

### What followed

The fur trade came, then U.S. territory and treaties, and in 1862 came war, internment at Fort Snelling, the Mankato executions, and exile. Homestead and railroad followed, and German and Scandinavian settlement became the unmarked later majority. The Iron Range drew Finnish, South Slavic, Italian, Cornish, and other workers, a “multiethnic regional culture” in MNopedia’s account, while timber and milling built the economy, and then a twentieth-century state sold education, cooperatives, and a progressive brand.

### Minnesota origins, not guests

Black Minnesota is not new, with roots in Near North from the 1910s, in Rondo, and then in the highway that came through. Hmong Minnesotans arrived after the Secret War and Somali Minnesotans after 1991, while Latino labor built lives in plants and dairy, and Karen and others followed. These are Minnesota origins, not guests.

History is literacy rather than a speech, and a Dakota household does not start with a lake.

sections.heading: Geography
sections.body:
The Twin Cities act as the administrative brain, but the state also includes the Iron Range, the Red River, the prairie west, southeast bluff country, the north woods, the border, and plant towns, each with its own life.

### Name the town

Rochester is a health city, and it is not rural just because it sits outside the beltway. In the same way, Duluth is not a farm, Bemidji is not Worthington, and Edina is not Phillips.

Distance is operations. The Compass people-page splits (Mexican ~39% Greater Minnesota; Somali ~22%; Hmong ~94% Twin Cities) change who this geography is, so date the vintage when you cite them (Compass profiles now use ACS 2020–2024). Use the Rural brief for infrastructure, and use this page for the hymn that still plays in a Worthington county office.

sections.heading: Migration and Foundational Events
sections.body:
Settler waves, Range labor, and the farm crisis shaped this state, as did the Great Migration into Black Minnesota. Hmong, Somali, and Latino secondary migration followed work here, and people have long left for the coasts and returned.

### Foundational events

The foundational events are 1862; I-94 construction through Rondo from 1956 to 1968, which MNopedia says “cut the neighborhood in half and fractured its identity”; AIM in Minneapolis, 1968; and Floyd, 2020.

Secondary migration is Minnesota history, and plant towns are not an afterthought. “We are all immigrants” skips nations and slavery when it is used that way, which is why the phrase hides more than it explains.

sections.heading: Family
sections.body:
The unmarked Minnesota household on a form is still the American nuclear unit, with a Lutheran-civic overlay: self-reliant, private, children in activities, elders often elsewhere.

### Who the form misses

That form has never described Ojibwe kinship, Somali households, Hmong clan, or a grandmother in North Minneapolis, so it cannot tell you who belongs at the table.

So ask who should be in the room, keeping in mind that Nice is not a family structure; it is how a meeting about family is supposed to feel — calm, brief, with no scene.

sections.heading: This is the Minnesota page
sections.body:
American culture is the water, this brief is the hymn, and the people pages are the household, which means no one page is enough on its own.

### What to open next

Keep going, and open Somali, African American, the eleven, Hmong, or European American as the person in front of you is. Open Rural if the gate is miles and broadband.

sections.heading: Heart of the Culture — Minnesota Nice
sections.body:
“Minnesota Nice” is a popular local phrase. It is not a finding about any one person, and this brief uses it so that staff can check their own habits and their own workplace. As people use the phrase, it begins with reserved warmth: you will be helped, but you may not be hugged. It includes conflict-avoidance, where disagreement goes sideways — into process, into “let’s take this offline,” into silence. It includes sameness-as-fairness, where identical treatment is the moral high ground and a targeted channel looks like playing favorites. And it includes competence as love, which means we show care by being good at the work, on time, and prepared — not by heat. Listen for the no that sounds like a yes: “That’s interesting.” “I’ll have to think about it.” “Ope.” “Not too bad.” When you hear one, ask plainly what the person wants to happen.

### What Nice oils, and what it hides

This hymn is real, and it oils a dense civic life: cooperatives, volunteering, high turnout, and public institutions that often work. It can also hide harm: a raised voice from a Black parent gets called unprofessional, a Somali mother’s directness gets called rude, and a Tribal chair who will not smile through a bad consult gets called difficult. Check whether your workplace does this, and write down what the person actually said.

Nice is not kindness as such, because kindness can be direct, whereas Nice is a regulation of affect. Intercultural work that never names this regulation will treat every other affect as excess.

### Why it frames the work

The form, the hearing, the hiring panel, and the “we treat everyone the same” all sit inside this hymn, so name it in the room. Mockery does not help, and letting it write the cap as just being adult does not help either.

sections.heading: Core Concepts
sections.body:
The concepts below are the parts of what people call Minnesota Nice that you will meet most often. See the Heart section.

### Lutheran-civic residue

Even among Catholics, evangelicals, Muslims, and the unaffiliated, there is a residue: suspicion of display, duty, committees, the sermon as civic speech, and a Jantelagen-adjacent “don’t think you’re special.” Not every Minnesotan is Lutheran, but the civic air still tastes like it.

### Lake and winter

Recreation is identity for some, and winter is a moral test (“we don’t complain”), although neither is a personality for a waiver household that cannot start a car.

### Education as civic religion

This is louder than the American average, since we are the state that ranks itself, and the achievement gaps the state publishes on itself sit next to that pride, so hold both.

### Progressive self-image

We vote (76.35 percent turnout in 2024 per the Secretary of State, second to Wisconsin’s 76.64 percent, and first among 18- to 29-year-olds at 62 percent), we volunteer, we are not Mississippi. Alongside that sit some of the widest racial disparities in the United States in income, homeownership, and criminal-legal contact — date MDH, Compass, and Council on Crime and Justice figures when you cite them. Name the gap whenever you name the self-image.

### Equal process

This is the American sameness-as-fairness concept, intensified, which means equity as a targeted channel will be felt as unfair until you can say it in this hymn’s language: universal goal, different door, same dignity.

### Conflict-avoidance as governance

It shows up as meetings without a decision, consensus as delay, and nation-to-nation consult that is actually a presentation, so close each meeting by asking: what did we decide? Who will do it by when?

### Understatement

Direct praise can embarrass some people, and direct criticism can strain a working relationship. Be plain anyway, and ask how the person wants feedback.

You work with these concepts, rather than performing a hotdish.

sections.heading: Religion and Healing
sections.body:
Lutheran is the largest single family of churches, about 23 percent of Minnesota adults in Pew’s 2023–24 Religious Landscape Study (margin of error 5.7 points), but not a majority, and the religiously unaffiliated, about 29 percent, outnumber it there. Alongside are Catholic (18 percent; Irish and German St. Paul, Latino parish), evangelical, Jewish, Muslim (including Somali civic life), wat, and Native ceremony, each with its own practice.

### Named, not mashed

Church basements as civic infrastructure — that is Minnesota. Clergy are the case plan when they asked for that, so open the religion track before you plan around faith.

sections.heading: Greetings
sections.body:
Do not read a quiet greeting as coldness or a warm one as agreement.

### Names and titles

Ask how the person wants to be addressed, and use a title until you know.

sections.heading: Naming
sections.body:
Mary Jones is the database, and plant towns and nations already know that it fails.

### Say it

Ask how to say a name, and learn to pronounce Mille Lacs, Pezihutazizi, Cansa’yapi, and Maay names, because a last name is not something you invent.

sections.heading: Dates and Calendar
sections.body:
The State Fair is civic liturgy, joined by the fishing opener, school sports, and the civic American holidays.

### Other calendars

Plus there are Ramadan, Eid, Hmong New Year, Juneteenth, Rondo Days, ricing, and powwow calendars. Other calendars fit this one at a cost, and because families pay that cost, it is a gate.

sections.heading: Education
sections.body:
Public-school pride sits beside the gaps the state publishes, tribal schools, and an English-only default that shapes who gets through.

### Who is in the portrait

A parent who needs a language is not illiterate, and scientists, teachers, and people the school failed are all the portrait.

sections.heading: Etiquette
sections.body:
Ask directly whether the person agrees, and leave room for a no.

### Time and hospitality

Keep to medical and legal timelines, and ask whether the person agrees rather than assuming silence means yes.

sections.heading: Communication
sections.body:
Say what you mean, and ask people to do the same. If you hear “That’s interesting,” ask what the person thinks of the plan.

### What a yes is not

Book Maay, Spanish, Hmong, Ojibwe, or Dakota as asked, and do not correct AAVE as broken English.

Before you write down consent, check that the person actually agreed.

sections.heading: Other Considerations
sections.body:
The progressive brand and racial disparity live in the same state, so date the figure whenever you use it. Nice does not skip the gap, and the gap does not skip the household.

### Public health in the hymn

Alcohol is a Minnesota public-health fact — date MDH. Isolation and seasonal affect are real, although they are not a personality, so follow the law while you still see a person.

sections.heading: Health
sections.body:
The default is unmarked biomedical care, and while Mayo is a global Minnesota fact, the county clinic is the actual door for most of the work here.

### Place and disparity

Rural hospital risk belongs on the rural page (about 95 rural hospitals; ~20 at risk — MinnPost April 2026), and disparities belong on the people pages. Believe pain, and remember that a missed visit may be distance, diesel, and ice.

sections.heading: LGBTQ
sections.body:
Legal and cultural variation runs by town and church, so use the name the person gives you.

### Outing is not culture

Outing someone to a small town is not culture, and two-spirit belongs on the nations page.

sections.heading: Hair and Dress
sections.body:
Unmarked professional dress here is American unmarked, sometimes louder in a county building, and CROWN applies, as do hijab and ribbon skirts.

### In the room

Hair is not a professionalism test, and hair is not for touching, whatever the room’s habits are.

sections.heading: Music
sections.body:
Prince is Minnesota — not a footnote — and so are church music, Range bars, and Somali and Hmong production.

### Not one soundtrack

There is not one soundtrack, and a playlist is not engagement, however good it is.

sections.heading: Sports
sections.body:
The state tournament is civic, professional teams are shared weather, and Friday night still matters in some towns.

### Not the only excellence

The kid may not play, and sport is not the only excellence, so look for the others.

sections.heading: Literature
sections.body:
Garrison Keillor is a hymn many Minnesotans argue with — and that argument is culture. Louise Erdrich (Turtle Mountain, Minneapolis) is world literature from this place, and she belongs in the same conversation.

### Who Lake Wobegon left out

Black Minnesota letters and immigrant letters are not empty, because literacy includes who Lake Wobegon left out.

sections.heading: Art
sections.body:
Art here runs from the Guthrie to the powwow to Cedar-Riverside galleries, and because you are a guest, pay.

### Festival is not consultation

A festival is not consultation. The State Fair is civic art, and it becomes a gate if you think it is the whole.

sections.heading: Civil Rights Memory
sections.body:
The memory here is 1862, Rondo, AIM 1968, ICWA and MIFPA, and Floyd, 25 May 2020, Minneapolis — American and Minnesota at once, which is why none of it is in the past.

### A badge is not automatically help

A DHS badge is not automatically help. A training that cannot say George Floyd’s name shuts out the people who most need that door open.

sections.heading: Business and Work
sections.body:
Cooperatives, Fortune headquarters, the public sector, plants, tribal enterprise, and farms all sit here, which means this is not one economy.

### Who is this economy

Do not assign culture or interpreter work to staff because of who they are. A Mexican scientist in a plant lab and a Somali truck owner are this economy, and so is a fourth-generation farm.

sections.heading: Healthcare Encounters
sections.body:
Care comes through Mayo, county, IHS/tribal, urban Indian, and safety-net doors, so ask which one a family uses.

### In the exam room

A reserved manner in the exam room can miss pain, so ask who should be in the room, book the language, and believe pain.

sections.heading: Diaspora and Adjacent
sections.body:
This page is not Rural, not European American, not the eleven, and not American culture as a substitute for any of them.

### Open those doors

Open those doors, because Minnesota is not one module as a people.

sections.heading: Statistics
sections.body:
The Minnesota Compass cultural-community table puts Minnesota at 5,739,445, plus or minus 7 (ACS 2020–2024), with 55.2 percent in the Twin Cities and 44.8 percent in Greater Minnesota. The Census Bureau's 2025 estimate, as summarized by USAFacts, is about 5.83 million. Date whichever you use.

### What belongs where

People-page counts (African American, Somali, Hmong, Native American, Mexican, and the rest) belong on those pages. For foreign-born and language-other-than-English, use Compass (ACS 2020–2024: 8.6% foreign-born; among people 5 and older, 12.3% speak a language other than English at home and 4.6% speak English less than “very well”) and date it, and for racial-gap figures, date MDH. A rate is not the person, and population size is not culture size.

sections.heading: Resources
sections.body:
The resources are American culture (the umbrella), the people pages, the eleven nations / Office of Indian Policy, Rural, the European American streams, Compass, MDH, and the religion track.

### How to use this

Studying this hymn is cultural self-awareness for people who live inside it, so open a people page, and then bring what you learned to Tuesday.

sections.heading: How it hits DHS gates — the 40%
sections.body:
Workplace culture and service delivery are both candidates here.

Check your own meetings, hiring, and packets for these habits. Inside these habits, a raised voice can get called “unprofessional,” an indirect no can be missed, and identical process can look like fairness while it skips Maay, ICWA, and a three-name form.

These habits frame much of the work in this department. Name them when they shape a decision, and do not ask staff of color to explain them.

Open American culture if you have not, and then open the household’s people page. Completing this is not a score, and it does not replace learning about Tribal Nations.

sections.heading: A Note on This Guide
sections.body:
This brief is about Somali people — Soomaali — a Cushitic-speaking people of the Horn of Africa and a Minnesota community made up of people with origins in Somalia and in the Somali-inhabited regions of Kenya, Ethiopia, and Djibouti. The community includes those who arrived after the 1991 collapse of the Somali state, those who came through other countries, and the large U.S.-born second generation.

### Who this is

Minnesota holds the largest Somali community in the United States, but the counts disagree, and it is worth knowing why. Minnesota Compass (ACS 2020–2024) puts Somali ancestry near 85,533 (give or take 7,711) and shows a separate 2024 total of 111,722 (give or take 20,401), which it calls the most accurate size estimate, while other ACS-based reporting in 2024–2025 has been cited near 100,000–107,000 statewide, so date whichever number you use. Within the Compass figures, about 77.3% live in the Twin Cities; 45.7% are age 17 or younger and 3.4% are age 65+; and 52.2% were foreign-born in that vintage, which means a majority of the children are U.S.-born. Cedar-Riverside and Karmel Mall are hubs, but they are not the map.

The diversity inside this people is the point. Picture a 70-year-old first-wave elder who arrived from the camps, a Maay-speaking mother in Worthington, a Benadiri family, a U.S.-born college student who uses English with friends and Somali with a grandmother, a woman who runs a mall stall and a waiver household in the same week, and a person who left the mosque and still eats halal. They share a people, and they do not share a Tuesday.

### Who this is not

This is not a Census “Black” mash, and it is not the African American cultural intelligence with a different flag. It is not Liberian, Nigerian, Ethiopian, Oromo, or Eritrean, because shared race in the United States is not shared culture, and shared Islam is not shared culture either.

### How to read this

Read this as an orientation for educators, healthcare providers, social workers, county and state staff, and anyone whose work brings them into sustained contact with Somali individuals, families, and communities. A church is not this page. Use this page for context and questions. It does not describe the person in front of you.

Always defer to the person in front of you, because this page is a hypothesis you still test with this family, and there is no single Somali household.

The facts that follow are meant to help you meet people well: how family is named, what respect looks like, what a greeting carries, and what a form may land on. Counts are dated, and history is here so that the meeting is clearer, not so that you deliver a lecture.

sections.heading: Origins and the Founding of a People
sections.body:
Somali identity is older than the 1960 republic, older than colonial borders, and older than the refugee file, because Somali people are a Cushitic-speaking nation of the Horn of Africa whose peoplehood came before any of those.

### Older than the state

Pastoral and urban life, Islam (overwhelmingly Sunni, with a long Sufi history), poetry as prestige speech, xeer (customary law), and clan genealogies all predate the Italian and British colonial administrations, and they predate the Somali Democratic Republic as well.

### Clan

Clan — qabiil — is paternal lineage, and it organizes social life and marriage and, in the homeland, political conflict. The major clan-families named in public literature include Darod, Hawiye, Dir, Isaaq, and the Digil-Mirifle (Rahanweyn) grouping associated with Maay speech in the south. That sentence is literacy for the meeting rather than something you ask about in a Minnesota lobby as an icebreaker, since the civil war was organized partly along clan lines, and many Minnesota families will not discuss clan with an outsider because it divides neighborhoods and marriages. If they name it, you listen.

### 1960 and 1991

The modern Somali state united British Somaliland and Italian Somalia in 1960. Siad Barre’s regime (1969–1991) ended in collapse, and 1991 became the foundational political event of the contemporary diaspora: state failure, civil war, famine, camps, and flight. Somaliland declared independence in 1991 and is not universally recognized, and while some Minnesota families will name Somaliland as a separate political project, a waiver meeting is not the place to referee that.

### What people brought

What people brought with them includes Standard Somali (Maxaa Tiri) and Maay, Arabic for religion, kinship obligation, oral skill and poetry, business and improvisation, Islam as daily order for many, and a living memory of a state that failed them. What they met in Minnesota was an English form, one “African” checkbox, and often one interpreter labeled “Somali.”

This is a people with a literature, a legal custom, a diaspora, and a Minnesota present, not a camp origin myth. History is literacy for the meeting rather than a speech you give the family.

sections.heading: The Geography of the Somali World
sections.body:
The Somali-inhabited Horn is not one political story, and families will name home in different ways because of it.

### Homelands

Somalia, Somaliland (which declared independence in 1991 and is not universally recognized), Puntland, and the Somali regions of Kenya and Ethiopia all matter to how families name home. Some Minnesota families will name Somaliland as a separate political project, and if they name it, listen.

### Diaspora

The diaspora is global, reaching Kenya, Ethiopia, Yemen, the Gulf, the United Kingdom, Scandinavia, Canada, and the United States. Minnesota became the largest U.S. community through refugee resettlement and secondary migration, as people who landed first in another state then moved here for work, family, mosques, and a critical mass of Somali life.

Within the United States, other significant communities exist in Columbus, Seattle, San Diego, Lewiston–Portland (Maine), and parts of the Upper Midwest. Minnesota is not “all Somalis,” and Cedar-Riverside is not all of Minnesota.

sections.heading: 1991, Camps, and Resettlement — Foundational Event
sections.body:
If the Great Migration is the foundational demographic event of modern Black America, then 1991 and what followed is the foundational event of Somali Minnesota.

### Collapse, camps, resettlement

State collapse, clan war, famine, and years in camps (Dadaab, Kakuma, and others) produced a refugee generation. U.S. resettlement and then secondary migration built this state’s community, as churches, volunteer agencies, and kin already here pulled people north.

### Who the desk meets now

The desk in 2026 does not only meet that first wave; it also meets their children, who are U.S.-born and English-dominant with peers, who are still translating for parents, and who still cannot get Maay in the lobby. If the only picture you carry is “refugee,” you will miss the 20-year-old who has never lived in Somalia and still cannot get the right interpreter for a grandmother.

Distrust of government has a source, and so does the skill of making a way through systems that were not built for you. Public attacks on this community, and politics that treat Somali Minnesotans as a threat, are current structure, which is why a DHS badge is not automatically read as help.

sections.heading: Family
sections.body:
Ask who the person wants in the room and who helps them make decisions, and hear from the person directly.

### Women and money

Civil war and resettlement also put many Somali women into work, business, and household finance. Ask who speaks first and who handles the money, and hear from the person directly.

### Care as a network

The person who cares for a disabled adult or a child may be a network rather than a single legally recognized caregiver. Hour caps and “natural supports” language can dump unpaid work onto the women in that network and then call it culture.

A nuclear two-parent English form already has a who built into it, because it was built for a different household.

sections.heading: Minnesota and Somali History
sections.body:
Minnesota holds the largest Somali community in the United States. That is not a slogan; it is the reason this page has to be as complete as the African American intelligence, because this department will meet this community on waivers, child welfare, health care, cash, food, and employment.

### Places, not a blob

Think in places. Cedar-Riverside in Minneapolis was an early hub and is still a hub, but it is not the whole map, since there are also Karmel Mall and the surrounding commercial life, Brooklyn Park and Brooklyn Center, and St. Paul. There are Rochester, St. Cloud, Willmar, Worthington, Owatonna, and other Greater Minnesota cities with work and housing, and according to Compass, about one in five Somali Minnesotans lives outside the Twin Cities.

### Institutions

Partners include the Confederation of Somali Community in Minnesota, the Somali Museum of Minnesota, mosques and Islamic civic organizations, Somali parent autism networks, and culturally specific providers, while CECLC is a department door, not the whole community.

Minnesota-specific evidence includes the 2014 MDH qualitative study conducted with the University of Minnesota, the Confederation of Somali Community, and SoLaHmo. It documented shame and blame, wait lists, doctors who said nothing was wrong, English-only meetings, fear of housing loss, and parents who wanted peers who share their language.

Somali staff are colleagues, not a stand-in for the community. A museum visit is optional professional development, and it does not make you the expert.

sections.heading: Somalinimo — the heart of a people
sections.body:
Somalinimo names peoplehood: language, genealogy, Islam for many, poetry, and the claim of a nation that outlasted a state.

### In Minnesota

In Minnesota, Somalinimo sits inside another fact: many Somali Minnesotans are Black, Muslim, and immigrants or the children of immigrants, and Minnesota writing has named that triple. Culture does not replace it, and it also does not collapse this page into the African American brief.

### Two lives in one room

Double consciousness here is not Du Bois’s sentence copied over. It is to be Somali and American at once; to be Muslim in a public institution that treats everyone the same; to be Black in a U.S. racial order that did not write this people’s history; and still to be expected to fill out an English form as if none of that were in the room.

This guide is a working orientation, and individual variation always supersedes group generalization.

sections.heading: Core Concepts
sections.body:
These concepts recur, and they express themselves differently by generation, gender, region of origin, and how this particular family lives Islam, so treat them as hypotheses rather than as a script for the person in front of you.

### Islam as daily order

For many families, though not all, prayer times, Friday jumu’ah, Ramadan, Eid, halal food, modesty (xishood), and honor (sharaf) shape daily life. Variation is the point: some are observant, some less so, there are youth, there are women who lead, and there are people who left the mosque and still eat halal. An imam is the case plan only when this family asked for that.

### Kinship and visits

Ask who the person counts as kin. If food or drink is offered, accepting a little is fine, and you can still keep to medical and legal timelines.

### Clan

Clan can matter in Somalia and in some Minnesota marriages and trust networks, and some people will not discuss it with an outsider. Do not use it as an icebreaker, and if the family names it, listen.

### Honor and modesty

Offer a private, gender-matched room for sensitive conversations.

### Nabadoonimo

Peacemaking and community dialogue are part of Somali public life. Some people distrust the state, so explain who you work for and what happens to what they tell you.

### Poetry and oral skill

A long answer is not necessarily evasion. Give the person time to answer. If you get a short yes, check that the plan was understood, and ask whether it works for them.

### Xeer

Customary law and elder mediation still matter in some disputes. They do not replace Minnesota statute, but they may explain who the family wants in the room.

### Remittance

Some people send money to relatives as an obligation. Ask about it, and do not treat it as optional in a budget.

sections.heading: Religion
sections.body:
Somali people are historically and overwhelmingly Muslim — Sunni, with a Sufi history in the Horn, and with contemporary variation that includes more conservative practice, ordinary observance, and people who are culturally Muslim without being mosque-regular.

### The mosque

The mosque is a center of prayer, information, mutual aid, and sometimes politics, but it is not “the community,” and one imam is not consultation.

### The year

Ramadan changes eating, energy, and appointment timing, and Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha are the two major festivals. Friday midday prayer matters for many men, and for many people halal is a condition of eating, not a preference sticker on a menu.

Help that looks like a report is not help. Religious framing of disability — as trial, fate, or stigma — sits next to a fierce wish for services, and you can hold both, which is why “Give it to God” is not automatically non-compliance.

sections.heading: Greetings
sections.body:
As-salāmu ʿalaykum / wa ʿalaykumu s-salām is the default Muslim greeting for many, although an English “hello” is also ordinary, especially with the second generation.

### Hands and gender

If a hand is not offered, nod and carry on.

### Elders

Ask how the person wants to be addressed, and do not use a first name just because the form printed it.

Let this person’s own greeting guide you, whatever you read on another page.

Ask before any physical contact, and let the person set the limit.

sections.heading: Naming Conventions
sections.body:
Somali names often do not match a first-middle-last pattern. A common pattern is given name, father’s name, grandfather’s name, and there may be no “family surname” as the database understands it, while women do not necessarily take a husband’s name.

### What the form invents

A form that demands a last name will invent one, and that invented name then follows the person through MHCP, child welfare, and school, which makes it a gate.

Islamic names are common (Mohamed, Ahmed, Fatima, Amina, Abdi, Hassan), and so are Somali names (Hodan, Waris, Degmo, and many others). Pronounce them and ask, because a shortened name for your own convenience shuts the person out.

Three people in one household may not share a “last name” the way a Swedish Minnesota form expects. That is a naming system, and it is not fraud until you have a reason to think so.

sections.heading: Dates of Significance
sections.body:
Ramadan is the ninth month of the Islamic calendar, a time of fasting from dawn to sunset, and its dates move each year. Schedule around it when you can, and remember that energy is not a character test.

### Eid and Mawlid

Eid al-Fitr marks the end of Ramadan with major communal prayer and visiting, while Eid al-Adha is the greater Eid, a time of sacrifice and charity for many families.

Mawlid al-Nabi marks the birth of the Prophet. It is observed by many Sunni communities, including most Somali Minnesotans, and because it is lunar it may move by a day.

### Civic dates

June 26 marks the independence of British Somaliland (1960), and July 1 marks the union and Italian Somalia’s independence. Some families mark these dates, and Somaliland politics will change what “independence” means in the room, so listen.

1991 is the collapse, and it is not a holiday but literacy.

Calendar clicks on this program are literacy for scheduling rather than community engagement.

sections.heading: Education
sections.body:
U.S.-born children sit in English-dominant schools with parents who may not be able to read the IEP in English, which is a gate, not a one-hour culture clash.

### Two schools in one week

Islamic weekend schools and Qur’an study sit beside public school, and they are not truancy by default.

Second-generation educational attainment is mixed and rising in some cohorts, so a single story does not hold, and a college student is not proof that the waiver household needs no interpreter.

Somali-language literacy and English literacy are not the same thing, so a parent who speaks fluent Somali and limited English is not “illiterate.” If anything is, it is the form that only exists in English.

sections.heading: Etiquette
sections.body:
If food or drink is offered, accepting a little is fine, and you can still keep to medical and legal timelines.

### The house

If you visit a home, look for shoes by the door or ask what the household prefers.

### Gender and dress

Offer a gender-matched interpreter for maternal and intimate care, and remember that mixed-gender small talk is not “warmth” if the room does not want it.

On dress, many women cover their hair (hijab), and some do not, while many men may not shake a woman’s hand. Covering is not oppression to be policed in the lobby, and a woman who is not covering is not “less Somali.”

### Time

Keep to clinic and court timelines. If someone is late, ask what got in the way, and record only what happened.

Visit a mosque only if you are invited, and go as a guest.

sections.heading: Communication
sections.body:
The languages here are Standard Somali (Maxaa Tiri), Maay, Benadiri and other varieties, Arabic for religion, and English among the second generation.

### Dialect is the door

An interpreter labeled “Somali” who does not speak Maay still will not work for that household, so confirm the variety before you book.

Poetry (gabay and other forms) carries prestige in Somali. Give the person time to answer. If you get a short yes, check that the plan was understood, and ask whether it works for them.

Ask directly whether the person agrees with the plan, and check back later that it still works.

Accent is not incompetence, and “Noncompliant” is the wrong word when the English exception form was never understood.

sections.heading: Other Considerations
sections.body:
Female genital cutting is widespread in Somalia, but diaspora practice and Minnesota law are not the same sentence. You follow mandated reporting and health law, and you treat the family with respect.

### Queerness, khat, trauma

Some families hold stigma around queerness. Use the person’s name and pronouns, and do not out them to family.

Khat is used in the Horn and in some diaspora settings, and it is illegal here. Do not assume it about anyone.

Some people carry mental-health stigma and war trauma together, so ask what support the person would accept.

### Structure

Poverty rates are high in Compass figures, so date them, and remember that a rate is not the person.

Islamophobia, anti-Black racism, and immigrant enforcement are structure, and triple jeopardy is not a metaphor.

Clan is real, and it is not an icebreaker.

sections.heading: Health and Mental Health
sections.body:
The MDH 2014 qualitative study (with UMN, the Confederation of Somali Community, and SoLaHmo) documented shame and blame, wait lists, doctors who said nothing was wrong, English-only meetings, fear of housing loss, and parents who wanted peers who share their language.

### Autism identification

Hewitt et al. 2016, drawing on Minneapolis surveillance, found Somali children identified with ASD at 1 in 32, similar to White children at 1 in 36 and higher than non-Somali Black and Hispanic children in that study, with later clinical diagnosis (about 5.9 vs 3.7 years). MN-ADDM (UMN, CDC-funded) reported on 26 September 2025, using 2022 data, that 1 in 12 (8.26%) 8-year-old Somali children were identified with autism in parts of Anoka, Hennepin, and Ramsey, versus 1 in 28 overall in that study. Identification is not the same as a community-wide “rate of being Somali,” so date the study. Vaccine-autism science does not support a link, while community fear has clustered around age of diagnosis, and both the fear and the system’s dismissals are real.

Disability stigma is real, and so is a parent who has already been told nothing was wrong while the child waits.

### Pain and the room

War trauma, depression, and somatic presentation exist, and a smile is not a PHQ-9.

Believe pain, and offer gender match in maternal and intimate care. Have family in the room if the person wants them there, not because you want a witness.

sections.heading: LGBTQ people
sections.body:
Queer and trans Somali people exist in Minnesota, and conservative family and mosque climates can mean silence, exile, or danger, though that is not every family.

### Duty in the room

Staff duty here is the same as on the African American page: use the name, do not share what they tell you unless a rule requires it, and know that EOAD and other doors still exist.

Do not question a household about anyone’s sexuality or gender, and take seriously that some people have reason to keep it private.

sections.heading: Dress, hair, and the body
sections.body:
This is not the CROWN Act chapter. Hijab, jilbab, and modest dress are ordinary for many Somali women, and they are not a security threat and not a consent problem, while some women do not cover, and ranking them is not the work.

### Men, celebration, the body

Men’s dress ranges from Minnesota casual to a thobe on Friday, and piety does not come off clothing alone.

Henna, gold, and Eid clothes are celebration, not a case note.

Hair and covering are not for touching and not for policing, because a covered woman can speak for herself, so ask her, with a gender-matched interpreter if she wants one.

sections.heading: Poetry, music, and voice
sections.body:
Poetry is not decoration, since gabay and related forms are prestige speech. Popular hees (songs), the oud, and diaspora pop exist alongside religious caution about some music in some families.

### Minnesota stages

Minnesota has Somali-language media, YouTube, and stage, but a playlist is not engagement. Knowing that oral art is high status will stop you from calling a long answer “rambling.”

sections.heading: Sports
sections.body:
Soccer is the default public sport for many boys and men, and increasingly for girls, while basketball shows up in the second generation, and track, wrestling, and ordinary high-school sport sit here too. The kid may not play at all, and sport is not the only excellence you can see.

### Clubs as infrastructure

Sport clubs are social infrastructure: rides, news, and who is trusted. They are not a substitute for language access on a waiver, and they are not consultation.

A scientist, a nurse, a trucker, a mall owner, and a varsity captain can all be in the same extended family, which is a reminder that the group is not the person and collective identity is not the individual.

A skipped Saturday tournament does not mean “isn’t engaged,” because Saturday may be work, mosque, or a grandmother.

sections.heading: Literature and story
sections.body:
Oral literature comes first, since gabay and related poetic forms are prestige speech, older as public art than the Latin orthography.

### Letters

Written Somali as a mass standard is young, because the Latin script was officialized in 1972, but that fact is literacy, not a claim that this is a people without letters.

Nuruddin Farah and other novelists are world literature, and diaspora memoir, journalism, and Minnesota Somali-language media all exist. Know that the record exists.

Give the person time to answer. If you get a short yes, check that the plan was understood, and ask whether it works for them. “Rambling” in a case note is the wrong word, because the grammar of prestige speech is not a bullet.

Second-generation English literature and Somali-language radio can live in the same household, so book the language the elder needs, and remember that a college essay is not proof that the IEP can stay English-only.

sections.heading: Art and public culture
sections.body:
The Somali Museum of Minnesota is a Minnesota institution. Textiles, carved headrests, and contemporary visual work all exist, and henna is both art and celebration.

### Guest

Be a guest, not a researcher, because a field trip is optional professional development rather than consultation on a form.

sections.heading: 1991, the state, and Minnesota politics
sections.body:
There is no U.S. Civil Rights Movement to copy onto this page.
