The political literacy here runs through colonial partition, 1960 independence, dictatorship, the 1991 collapse, war, camps, U.S. resettlement, and then Minnesota and federal politics that have repeatedly treated this community as suspect.

### Pattern, not paranoia

After public attacks and after years of national rhetoric, a DHS badge is not automatically help, and that is not “paranoia” but pattern.

The war being over does not make the form fair now, and 1991 is not a personality.

sections.heading: Work, business, and money
sections.body:
Entrepreneurship is a documented Minnesota pattern: mall stalls, trucking, childcare, home care, restaurants, and import. A small-business owner and a waiver recipient may belong to the same extended family.

### Obligation and staff

Some people send money to relatives as an obligation. Ask about it, and do not treat it as optional in a budget.

Book a qualified interpreter, and pay for community work. Do not assign either to staff because of who they are.

Take time to introduce yourself and explain the plan, and still give any required notice.

sections.heading: Health-care encounters
sections.body:
Confirm the language and the dialect, offer gender match, and ask who should be in the room, knowing that a handshake is not required.

### Believe the concern

Believe reported pain and developmental concern, since thin English is not a reason to close the file.

Church is not the default spiritual support here; mosque and family may be, if this family asked.

Tuskegee is African American literacy, while this community’s medical mistrust runs instead through camps, dismissals, and child-protection fear. The histories are not the same, but the pattern is: help-seeking that becomes a report.

sections.heading: Diaspora and adjacent communities
sections.body:
Oromo, Ethiopian, Eritrean, Sudanese, Liberian, Nigerian, and historic African American Minnesota are all different cultural intelligences, each with its own page.

### Not one Black module

There is never one Black module, and never one “East African” interpreter.

Some households are mixed, so ask this household, because not everyone from the Horn is Somali just because Somali is the largest community in this state.

Open the African American brief for a family from the Great Migration, open this one for a Somali household, and open the Tribal door for a Nation.

sections.heading: Numbers — date them
sections.body:
Minnesota Compass (ACS 2020–2024), dated, reports about 85,533 (give or take 7,711) people of Somali ancestry, and a separate 2024 total of 111,722 (give or take 20,401) that it calls the most accurate size estimate. Of the 2020 to 2024 group, 77.3% live in the Twin Cities; 45.7% are age 17 or younger and 3.4% are 65+; and 52.2% were foreign-born in that vintage. On language (age 5+), 82.7% speak a language other than English and 33.6% speak English less than very well. Median household income is about $49,554, 30.9% are below poverty, 84.4% rent, and average household size is about 4.07.

### Counts disagree

Counts disagree across vintages and definitions (ancestry vs. birthplace vs. language), since MinnPost 2023 cited an earlier Compass figure near 86,610, and later ACS-based journalism has cited higher statewide counts. Date the number you cite.

A rate is not the person, and child-welfare and autism identification figures are gates rather than a personality.

sections.heading: Resources
sections.body:
Sources and doors include the Confederation of Somali Community in Minnesota, the Somali Museum of Minnesota, culturally specific providers, parent autism networks, CECLC, the Minnesota Compass Somali profile, the MDH 2014 qualitative study, and MN-ADDM / UMN autism surveillance — date the release.

### Other doors

The Office of Indian Policy is not this page, and EOAD is a discrimination door, not this page.

Use these resources yourself before you ask a colleague to explain. Pay partners, and report back.

sections.heading: How it hits DHS gates — the 40%
sections.body:
Workplace culture and service delivery are both candidates here.

On language: an interpreter labeled Somali who does not speak Maay will not work, and gender match is often requested in maternal and intimate care.

On names: the database that invents a last name is a gate that follows the person.

Hour caps, exception processes, and life-sharing matches without language are not culturally neutral.

On child welfare: help-seeking that becomes a report is part of this history. Mandated reporting still exists, and so does the duty not to treat a whole community as a risk score.

On notices and comment: do not count an eList and an English PDF as reaching this community, and record who was reached and what follow-up happened. Nations are governments and are not this page, but the same comment period that BCCs a tribe and skips Maay has already chosen who counts.

On workforce: Somali staff are not the interpreter pool and not the community.

On legislation, funding, and rule: study a channel before you advocate for it. Use this page so that the 40% has a household in it.

sections.heading: A Note on This Guide
sections.body:
This brief is about Hmong people — Hmoob in White Hmong, Moob in Green Hmong / Mong Leng — a people with ancient roots in southern China, a highland life in Laos, and a Minnesota community built after 1975. The name is pronounced mung, because the H is silent, so if you say Huh-mong in a lobby, you have already told the household you did not study.

### Who this is

Minnesota Compass (ACS 2020–2024) puts Hmong ancestry near 102,500, with about 94 percent living in the Twin Cities and about 6 percent in Greater Minnesota. About 38 percent are age 17 or younger, and about 32 percent are foreign-born, which means a majority of this community was born here. Pew (May 2025, 2021–2023 ACS) put Minnesota near 95,000 on a Hmong-alone count and named it the second-largest state community after California, so date the number you use and remember that a rate is not the person.

St. Paul is a national hub, but it is not the whole map, and Frogtown, the East Side, Little Mekong on University Avenue, Hmongtown Marketplace, Hmong Village, Brooklyn Center, Maplewood, and a smaller Greater Minnesota share are not one client.

The diversity inside this people is the point. A Secret War veteran who came through Ban Vinai, a Christian grandmother, a txiv neeb (traditional healer) whose altar is in the living room, a U.S.-born nurse, a farmer at the summer market, a college student who uses English with friends and Hmong with an elder, and a person who left clan obligation and still shows up at New Year all share a people, even though they do not share a Tuesday.

### Who this is not

This is not a Census “Asian” mash, and it is not Chinese New Year. It is not Karen, Vietnamese, Lao as a synonym, Cambodian, or a generic Southeast Asian interpreter, because a shared continent is not a shared culture.

### How to read this

Read this as an orientation. Use this page for context and questions. It does not describe the person in front of you. Always defer to the person in front of you, because this page is a hypothesis that you still test with this family.

The facts that follow are meant to help you meet people well — how family is named, what respect looks like, what a greeting carries, and what a form may land on. The counts are dated, and the history is here so that the meeting is clearer, not so that you deliver a lecture.

sections.heading: Origins and the Founding of a People
sections.body:
Hmong peoplehood is older than Laos, older than the CIA file, and older than the refugee camp. Oral history and scholarship place its origin in southern China, followed by movement into the highlands of what became Laos, Vietnam, and Thailand under pressure from imperial states, which is why statelessness is a political fact rather than a personality.

### Clan, language, writing

There is no Hmong nation-state, so clan, language, agriculture, and ritual organized life without a capital city. Writing systems came late: the Romanized Popular Alphabet (RPA), developed in the 1950s in Laos, is the common Latin script in Minnesota, but historically the language was oral. Paj ntaub / paaj ntaub — story cloth and embroidery — carried memory when paper did not.

### White Hmong and Green Hmong

Two large dialect-and-dress groups live in Minnesota: White Hmong (Hmoob Dawb) and Green Hmong, also called Blue Hmong or Mong Leng (Hmoob Leeg / Moob). The names come from dress, not politics, and while the dialects are close, they are not always interchangeable in an interpreter. Green Hmong often write the people-name without the H, as Moob, which carries the same instruction as this page: say mung.

### What people brought

People brought clan, ancestor obligation, shamanic healing and Christianity both, farming knowledge, oral skill, and a memory of being recruited to fight someone else’s war and then left behind. What they met in Minnesota was an English form, one “Asian” checkbox, and often one interpreter labeled “Hmong” for a people with more than one dialect.

sections.heading: The Geography of the Hmong World
sections.body:
The homeland is not one flag. Southern China remains a Hmong (Miao) geography, while the Laos highlands — Xieng Khouang, Long Tieng, the places named in veteran stories — are the origin of most Minnesota families.

### Diaspora

There are Hmong communities in Vietnam, Thailand, and Burma/Myanmar, along with a global diaspora that reaches California, Minnesota, Wisconsin, North Carolina, France, and Australia.

Pew (May 2025) ranks California as the largest U.S. state community, Minnesota second, and Wisconsin third, and Fresno and Sacramento sit next to Minneapolis–St. Paul as sister maps. Secondary migration built Minnesota, because church sponsors scattered people and clan pulled them back together.

### In Minnesota

St. Paul is the national urban hub, with the East Side, Frogtown, University Avenue / Little Mekong, and Ramsey County at its center, along with Brooklyn Center and the inner-ring suburbs and a small Greater Minnesota share. Frogtown is not the whole, and the person in front of you may never have been to Laos, so let the family tell you where home has been.

sections.heading: The Secret War, 1975, and the Camps — Foundational Event
sections.body:
If the Great Migration is the foundational demographic event of modern Black America, and 1991 is that event for Somali Minnesota, then the Secret War and 1975 are the foundational event of Hmong Minnesota.

### The Secret War

From 1961 to 1975 the United States, through the CIA, recruited Hmong forces under General Vang Pao to fight in Laos — a war the Geneva Accords had said should not be there. Hmong soldiers blocked supply lines and died in large numbers, and boys were recruited. When the United States left in 1975, the Pathet Lao and Vietnamese forces treated Hmong allied families as the enemy.

### Airlift, walk, camps

On May 12–14, 1975, an airlift left Long Tieng carrying about 2,500 people in those days, and General Vang Pao left on May 14, a date Minnesota later marked. Most people were not on the planes; they walked, and Thai camps followed, Ban Vinai among the named ones, with years passing before resettlement.

### Minnesota

The first Hmong family in Minnesota, Dang Her and Shoua Moua, arrived in 1975: MNopedia gives November 5, 1975, and Ramsey County History gives December 1975. Both sources set this family apart from Leng Wong’s, the first refugees resettled here, in early 1976. Church and voluntary-agency sponsors (Lutheran, Catholic, and others) placed people across the country so that no one state would “take too many,” but clan and secondary migration undid that scatter, and St. Paul became a hub because people chose each other.

U.S. policy at first treated Hmong people as “too primitive” for asylum, and the Indochina Migration and Refugee Assistance Act had to be amended. That sentence is literacy for the meeting rather than a speech you give the family.

sections.heading: Family
sections.body:
Clan organizes family. About 18 clans are commonly named among Hmong from Laos now in the United States, and the clan name is the last name: Chang, Cheng, Chue, Fang, Hang, Her, Khang, Kong, Kue, Lee, Lor, Moua, Pha, Thao, Vang, Vue, Xiong, Yang, in the English spellings of Hmong names. The same last name often means the same clan, and marriage is supposed to be outside the clan.

### Household size

Households are larger than a nuclear English form, and Compass puts the average household size at about 4.3. Elders, in-laws, adult children, and clan obligation sit in the same week, which means the person who cares for the child may not match the waiver checkbox.

### Marriage and labor

Bride wealth and clan negotiation are real in some marriages. Minnesota law still stands, and so does mandated reporting, although a wedding custom is not a crime scene.

Women’s labor — market, factory, farm, and a professional second generation — sits next to a patrilineal clan, and both can be true in the same room, so ask who should be in the room.

sections.heading: Minnesota and Hmong History
sections.body:
St. Paul is one of the largest urban Hmong communities in the world. That is why this page has to be as complete as the African American and Somali intelligences, since this department will meet this community on waivers, in child welfare, in health care, in cash and food programs, in aging, and in employment.

### Places, not a blob

The places include East Side St. Paul; Frogtown; University Avenue and Little Mekong; Hmongtown Marketplace (opened 2004, a former lumberyard; as of October 2026, Stearns Bank is suing over about $6.6 million, a receiver hearing is set for Nov. 24, 2026, and the market could close); Hmong Village (2010 by Racket’s account, 2009 by MNopedia; Johnson Parkway); Brooklyn Center; Maplewood; and a small Greater Minnesota share, while Compass places about 94 percent in the Twin Cities.

### Institutions

Partners include Hmong American Partnership; Hmong Cultural Center of Minnesota; Hmong Museum; Center for Hmong Studies (Concordia); the Hmong 18 Council and the clan structures some families name; and CECLC, which is a department door but not the whole community.

On the public calendar, Hmong New Year in St. Paul falls on a weekend near the end of November, at RiverCentre in recent years, and has been held for more than 40 years (RiverCentre called 2025 the 45th). The Hmong International Freedom Festival at Como Park is sport, not consultation, and May 14, Hmong Special Guerrilla Units Remembrance Day in state law (also called Hmong American Day), is literacy, because a calendar click is not community engagement.

Hmong staff are colleagues, not a stand-in for the community. A New Year visit is optional professional development, and if you go, you go as a guest, since the visit does not make you the expert.

sections.heading: Hmoob / Moob — the heart of a people
sections.body:
Hmong people have no state of their own, and Hmong history includes being used by states.

### In Minnesota

In Minnesota that sits inside another fact. Many Hmong Minnesotans are Asian in a U.S. racial order that files them under a checkbox that also holds Chinese, Indian, and Korean histories they do not share, and they are veterans of a war the United States ran and then classified, as well as Christians and traditionalists in the same cousin-line.

### Kwvtij

Kwvtij — clan-kin — is not a metaphor, so ask who the person counts as kin.

This guide is a working orientation, and individual variation always supersedes group generalization.

sections.heading: Core Concepts
sections.body:
These concepts recur, and they express differently by clan, by church, by generation, and by how this family lives ritual, which is why they are hypotheses rather than a script for the person in front of you.

### Clan

There are about 18 clans, patrilineal and exogamous. The last name is not a decoration, and staff do not use it as an icebreaker, although if the family names it, you listen.

### Ancestors

Household ritual, soul, and funeral are not extras, and a missed funeral obligation can be a crisis in the family at the very moment the English form thinks the crisis is a missed appointment.

### Txiv neeb

A txiv neeb is a traditional healer / shaman, and an altar in a living room is not a case plan and not a museum. If they name a healer, listen, since the healer is the case plan when they asked for that; a soul-calling, however, is not DHS programming.

### Christianity

Catholic, Protestant, and evangelical streams are large in Minnesota Hmong life, and church can be the information channel, but it is not “the community.”

### Checking for agreement

Before you treat a yes as agreement, ask again, plainly and without embarrassing anyone.

### Hu plig / poob plig

Soul-calling and soul-loss are meaning systems some families use for illness, fright, and developmental difference. They can sit next to a fierce wish for services, and you can hold both at once.

### Farming and market

Garden plots, farmers markets, and the two St. Paul markets are economy and culture at once, although a food-court visit is not consultation.

sections.heading: Religion and Healing
sections.body:
Traditional Hmong religion is household-centered, built around ancestors, spirits (dab), shamanic healing, and soul, so it is not a Sunday service you can BCC. Christianity arrived through mission and camp and is now ordinary in Minnesota, sometimes in the same extended family as a traditional altar.

### Pastor and healer

A pastor or a txiv neeb is the case plan when this family asked for that. Traditional practice is not witchcraft, and church is not the evolved version.

### Funerals

Funerals can last days and gather the clan, and burial timing, animal offering in traditional practice, and who must be there are not delays for your convenience. You still keep medical and legal time, and you name the conflict instead of punishing it.

The meaning of an illness may not be the DSM sentence. MDH’s 2014 qualitative work with Hmong parents on autism found unclear meaning of the word, stigma, waiting to share concerns, and professionals who were not responsive, which is why late identification is a gate, stigma is a gate, and English-only is a gate.

sections.heading: Greetings
sections.body:
Wait to see how the person greets you, and follow their lead. Many second-generation people will shake hands in English-language rooms, so follow this room.

### Names

Nyob zoo is a common White Hmong greeting, and an English “hello” is ordinary. Say the name, and remember that the clan name is the last name and that it is not optional.

Let this person’s own greeting guide you, whatever you read on another page.

Ask before any physical contact, and let the person set the limit.

sections.heading: Naming Conventions
sections.body:
The last name is a clan name, drawn from eighteen common clans, and people who share it may be kin in a way the database cannot see — or strangers who still should not marry. Every Lee is not related, and two Lees in a household are not automatically a married couple, because they may be clan-kin of a kind your form does not have a box for.

### Given names

Given names may be Hmong, English, or both, and soul names, nicknames, and generation names exist, which is why the form that demands first-middle-last and a hyphen will invent a person.

Pronounce the name, and ask when you are unsure, and do not joke, because “Too many Vangs” can shut the person out.

Women may or may not take a husband’s clan name in U.S. records, so ask how to file, and remember that a mother and child who do not share a last name is not a fraud signal until you have a reason.

sections.heading: Dates of Significance
sections.body:
Hmong New Year traditionally follows the harvest, and in St. Paul it has been a public weekend near the end of November for more than 40 years (RiverCentre called 2025 the 45th). The courtship ball-toss (pov pob) is public history at the celebration, not a file, so be a guest, not a researcher.

### May 14 and public life

May 14 marks General Vang Pao’s 1975 departure from Laos. Minnesota law names it Hmong Special Guerrilla Units Remembrance Day (first enacted in 2019 and amended in 2023): the governor issues a proclamation, flags fly at half-staff on Capitol grounds, schools are encouraged to teach Hmong history, businesses may close, and an employee may request the day off. St. Paul Public Schools separately uses the name Hmong American Day and says the state recognized that name in 2013. That makes it literacy for the desk.

Freedom Festival soccer and sport at Como Park, held the last weekend of June in 2024, 2025 and 2026, are community public life, not consultation. Hmong Minnesota Day at the Minnesota State Fair (Labor Day) and the Qeej and Hmong Arts Festival at Union Depot (May 10 in 2026) are also recurring public dates, and other towns hold their own New Year celebrations, such as the one in Marshall in southwest Minnesota (October 17, 2026).

Lunar and household ritual dates vary by family and by traditional versus Christian practice, so ask, and keep “Asian holiday” off the case note, where it does not belong.

sections.heading: Education
sections.body:
Compass (ACS 2020–2024) reports that among Hmong Minnesotans 25 and older, about 83 percent have a high school education or higher and about 29 percent have a bachelor’s or higher. A majority of children are U.S.-born and in English-dominant schools, and the IEP still has to reach the parent who does not read it.

### Language at the door

White Hmong and Mong Leng are not always interchangeable on an interpreter line, and English-only parent forms are a gate. A parent who speaks fluent Hmong and limited English is not illiterate.

Second-generation educational mobility is real, and so is a gap, which a room that treats everyone the same will call “culture” instead of what it is: language access plus poverty plus a school that never learned the name.

sections.heading: Etiquette
sections.body:
If you visit a home, look for shoes by the door or ask what the household prefers. In a home with an altar, ask where to sit.

### Time and the plan

If food or drink is offered, accepting a little is fine, and you can still keep to medical and legal timelines.

Ask before taking any photograph or touching any religious object, and do not ask anyone to explain their faith or history for your benefit.

If someone misses an appointment, first check the time, transport, interpreter and work schedule. Confirm the plan in the language the person uses, and ask whether it works for them.

sections.heading: Language and Communication
sections.body:
The two varieties are White Hmong and Green Hmong / Mong Leng, and you confirm which one this household speaks, because an interpreter labeled Hmong who does not speak this household’s dialect still will not work. RPA is the common written form, but many elders do not read it, while second-generation English is common. Compass reports that among those 5 and older, about 76 percent speak a language other than English and about 31 percent speak English less than “very well,” so date the number.

### Tone and yes

Hmong is tonal, and the doubled vowels in RPA mark tone rather than extra sound. You do not need to become a linguist, but you do need to put the variety on the interpreter request.

Give the person time to answer. If you get a short yes, check that the plan was understood, and ask whether it works for them.

A Hmong coworker is not the interpreter, and the interpreter line is still yours to book.

sections.heading: Other Considerations
sections.body:
This section states hard facts plainly, because treating everyone the same can hide them.

### Marriage, disability, status

Early marriage and bride-wealth patterns exist in history and in some present families. Minnesota age-of-consent and forced-marriage law still stand, and you follow the law, while still seeing a family rather than a crime scene walking in.

Disability stigma and late autism identification are documented (MDH 2014; later qualitative work). Under-identification was the Hmong pattern in Minnesota autism surveillance on the combined 2014 to 2016 data, while 2022 data show Hmong 8-year-olds identified at the same rate as children overall, and the Somali page describes a different finding, so do not mix them.

Deportation to Laos of people with final orders tied to convictions — including people born in camps and raised here since childhood — is current structure, not folklore. Laos accepted few deportees before 2025 and began accepting more in early 2025. In June 2025 agents arrested at least 15 Hmong Minnesotans, some with decades-old convictions, and the Hmong 18 Council put the number at 24 by July. Operation PARRIS began in January 2026 to reexamine refugee cases, reported as aimed at 5,600 Minnesota refugees without green cards, and a federal judge barred arrest and detention of these refugees while the lawsuit goes on (restraining order January 28, preliminary injunction February 27, 2026). No reliable total is available; Sahan Journal wrote in June 2026 that it is “unclear how many” Hmong and Southeast Asian residents have been sent to Laos. It changes who opens the door, who signs, and who will not put a relative’s name on a form, so collect the status the work requires, and not more, because fear is not noncompliance.

### History that still sits in the room

Youth violence in some St. Paul neighborhoods in the 1990s is a history some families carry, but a clan last name is not a gang file.

LGBTQ Hmong Minnesotans exist, so you use the name they use, and you remember that outing someone to kin is not culture.

sections.heading: Health
sections.body:
The MDH 2014 qualitative study with Hmong community partners found parents unclear about what autism meant, delayed in sharing concerns, facing stigma, and meeting professionals who were not responsive. Late identification is the finding, and identification is not a community personality, so date the study when you cite it.

### Under-count

Minnesota ADDM-style work on combined 2014 to 2016 data reported lower autism prevalence among Hmong children than among white and non-Somali Black children, but the 2022 data show 1 in 28 (3.62 percent) of Hmong 8-year-olds identified, the same as 1 in 28 overall in that study, with 54 percent of Hmong children who had IQ tests on file having intellectual disability, against 37 percent overall, and under-count, measurement, and meaning can all sit together. Inventing a rate does not help, and skipping screening because “Hmong families don’t have that” does not help either.

Chronic disease, trauma, and aging veterans of the Secret War sit in the same clinics as U.S.-born children, and traditional healing and biomedicine are often both present in the household. Ask, and work it out together, because an altar is not a joke and a healer in the story is not a reason to skip the waiver.

Gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care, so offer it.

Believe reported pain. Ask about this person’s own experience of care.

sections.heading: LGBTQ
sections.body:
Queer and trans Hmong Minnesotans exist, and conservative clan and church climates can mean silence or exile, so some people live a public English life and a private Hmong life. Use the name the person uses, and do not share what they tell you unless a rule requires it.

### Law

Minnesota’s Human Rights Act still applies. Use the name the person uses, and do not share what they tell you unless a rule requires it.

sections.heading: Hair, Dress, and Body
sections.body:
Traditional dress is public at New Year rather than a daily uniform, and the second generation looks like Minnesota, so “Still wears the costume” is not a clinic question.

### Hair and silver

On hair and head, follow this person, and remember that hair is not for touching. Silver, embroidery, and paj ntaub are art and history, not a mascot for the unit’s Heritage Month table.

sections.heading: Music
sections.body:
The qeej (reed pipe) is both ritual and art, especially at funerals, while New Year stages hold dance, pop, and Christian music.

### Not entertainment

A playlist is not engagement, and a funeral qeej is not entertainment for staff.

sections.heading: Sports
sections.body:
Soccer and the Freedom Festival matter in public Hmong Minnesota life, while volleyball, flag football, and school sport are ordinary for the second generation.

### Not a case plan

Sport clubs are not language access, and they are not a case plan.

sections.heading: Literature
sections.body:
Oral literature came first, in proverb, funeral text, and clan narrative, and RPA then made a written public possible.

### Letters

Minnesota and U.S. Hmong writers, scholars, and journalists exist. You do not need to quote a novel, but you do need to know that this is not a people without letters.

sections.heading: Art
sections.body:
Paj ntaub / paaj ntaub — story cloth and reverse appliqué — is memory sewn when camps and exile made paper unsafe or unavailable. The Hmong Cultural Center, the Hmong Museum, and the 2025 Minnesota History Center exhibit on fifty years all hold this art.

### Guest

You are a guest, so remember that a story cloth is not a case plan and a museum visit is not consultation.

sections.heading: Conflict, War, and the State
sections.body:
The Secret War, the walk to Thailand, Ban Vinai, dispersal, secondary migration, and a United States that recruited and then delayed asylum — that is the political event. Later came policing, youth violence in some 1990s neighborhoods, and the deportation of people with records, which is why a DHS badge is not automatically help.

### Not a personality

1975 is not a personality, and a veteran is not a narrator of killing for your professional development.

sections.heading: Work, Markets, and Government
sections.body:
Hmong Minnesotans work in factory jobs, on farms, in small business, in a professional second generation, and in public employment, and Hmongtown and Hmong Village are commercial hubs. Book a qualified interpreter, and pay for community work. Do not assign either to staff because of who they are.

### Relationship and the notice

Take time to introduce yourself and explain the plan. The first visit may not be the decision, and any required notice still goes out.

sections.heading: Health-care and Human-service Encounters
sections.body:
Several things shape the encounter: language and dialect, who is in the room, gender, an altar or a pastor in the story, a late developmental concern, a deportation climate, and a nuclear form that cannot see clan.

### In the encounter

Confirm the variety, offer gender match, and ask who should hear. Staff are not the interpreter. If they name a healer, listen, while remembering that mandated reporting still exists.

sections.heading: Adjacent Peoples — Do Not Mash
sections.body:
This page is not Karen, not Lao as a synonym, not Vietnamese, and not Chinese, and it is not “Asian American” as the file.

### Open the right page

Open the Karen brief for Karen, and open this one for Hmong; some households are mixed, so ask this household.

Miao in China is a related but not identical administrative story, and a St. Paul family does not need a lecture on Chinese taxonomy.

sections.heading: Counts, Dated
sections.body:
Minnesota Compass, ACS 2020–2024, describes the Hmong cultural community this way: about 102,491 people (give or take 5,546); Twin Cities 93.8% and Greater Minnesota 6.2%; age 17 or younger 38.0%; foreign-born 31.5%; language other than English (age 5+) 75.5%; English less than “very well” 31.1%; high school or higher (25+) 82.6%; bachelor’s or higher 28.8%; median household income $92,644 (2024 dollars); poverty 10.0%; owner-occupied 62.1%; and average household size 4.27.

### Other counts

Pew, May 2025 (2021–2023 ACS / 2023), counts U.S. Hmong-alone at about 330,000 and about 360,000 including combinations, with Minnesota at about 95,000 on that count and a median age of about 26.8.

Counts disagree because definitions disagree, so date the number. A young age structure is not a personality, and a poverty rate that fell over decades is not proof the gates closed.

sections.heading: Doors and Sources
sections.body:
The sources include the Minnesota Compass Hmong profile (ACS 2020–2024); the Pew fact sheet on Hmong in the U.S. (May 2025); Minnesota Historical Society / MNHS Hmong in Minnesota and MNopedia; the Hmong Cultural Center of Minnesota; the Hmong Museum; Hmong American Partnership; the Center for Hmong Studies at Concordia University, St. Paul; the MDH 2014 qualitative autism study with community partners; Chaxiong 2022; and the EthnoMed Hmong page for clan-name spellings, which is a clinical literacy door rather than a bible.

### Where to learn more

CECLC is one door, not the whole community, so use these resources yourself before you ask a colleague to explain, and pay partners.

sections.heading: How it hits DHS gates — the 40%
sections.body:
Workplace culture and service delivery are both candidates here.

Language: an interpreter labeled Hmong who does not speak White Hmong or Mong Leng as this household speaks it will not work, and gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care.

Names: the last name is a clan name, so the database that cannot see unmatched last names without raising a fraud flag is a gate.

Hour caps, exception processes, and life-sharing matches without language are not culturally neutral.

Child welfare and disability: late identification and stigma are documented, and help-seeking that becomes a report is part of why people wait. Mandated reporting still exists, and so does the duty not to treat a whole community as a risk score.

Deportation climate: people may skip clinic, school, and waiver meetings when a relative can be moved, and that is not noncompliance, so do not collect status you do not need.

Notices and comment: do not count an eList and an English PDF as reaching this community, and record who was reached and what follow-up happened.

Workforce: Hmong staff are not the interpreter pool, and they are not the community.

Legislation, funding, rule: study a channel before you advocate for it. Use this page so that the 40% has a household in it.

sections.heading: A Note on This Guide
sections.body:
This brief is about Karen people — Kayin; pronounce kah-REN — understood as a people from the hills of what became Burma/Myanmar, with generations spent in Thai camps and a Minnesota community built from mid-2000s resettlement. It is worth saying plainly what this brief is not: this is not Burmese, it is not Hmong, and it is not a Census “Asian” mash, because a shared continent is not a shared culture. Use this page for context and questions. It does not describe the person in front of you.

### Who this is

S’gaw and Pwo are not one interpreter, and Burmese and English may also be spoken in the home, so put the dialect on the line when you make the request. An interpreter labeled Karen who does not speak this household’s variety still will not work, and literacy in the language of the form is not guaranteed either. Camp years are structure rather than background color, since camp meant school interrupted and papers that do not match.

### Who this is not

There is no Minnesota Compass “Karen” row, and the Compass Burmese figure of 19,372 (ACS 2020–2024, give or take 3,438) is not this people, so do not file them under that count. The Coalition of Asian American Leaders (CAAL) has named Karen the largest recent Southeast Asian population to arrive in Minnesota, from 2004, as political refugees. Community and media estimates have been cited near 20,000 statewide, and you should date those as estimates rather than as Compass. The pattern to follow is Karen Organization of Minnesota and school-language data (the Minnesota Department of Education counted 5,320 students with Karen as their primary home language in 2024-25, 3,419 of them English learners), which means you date counts when you have them and do not invent a rate when you do not.

This community lives in the Twin Cities AND in Greater Minnesota, and Worthington, Albert Lea, Austin, Marshall, Willmar, and other towns are not an afterthought, and the state toolkit names Freeborn, Lyon, Nobles, Kandiyohi and Mower counties. Church is often the information channel, and wherever you meet people, a smile is not consent to the plan.

The diversity inside this people is the point. A Mae La elder who does not read the English form, a Baptist deacon, a Buddhist household, a Pwo speaker who was given a S’gaw interpreter, a U.S.-born teenager, and a night-shift worker in a southern plant share a people and do not share a Tuesday.

### How to read this

Always defer to the person in front of you, because this page is a hypothesis that you still test on this family rather than a description of them.

sections.heading: Origins and the Founding of a People
sections.body:
Karen (Kayin) peoplehood is older than Burma, older than the British colonial border, and older than the camp file. Oral history and scholarship place Karen peoples in the hills of what became eastern Burma/Myanmar and adjacent Thailand, yet there is no Karen nation-state that they control. British colonial administration drew the borders and recruited from among them, and the independent Burmese states that followed continued a long conflict with Karen armed and civilian communities.

### History for the meeting

S’gaw and Pwo are the large language groups you will meet in Minnesota, and they are not always interchangeable when it comes to an interpreter. Other Karen groups exist as well, so do not flatten any of them into “Burmese,” and do not flatten them into “Asian.”

### What people brought

Baptist Christianity arrived through mission work and is now ordinary in many Minnesota Karen communities, while Buddhist and traditional/animist practice also live here. That split is a Minnesota fact rather than a ranking of one over the other.

What people brought with them was language, church or temple, agricultural knowledge, a memory of being a people inside a state that made war on them, and years of camp time. What they met in Minnesota was an English form, one “Asian” checkbox, and often one interpreter labeled “Karen” or, worse, “Burmese.”

sections.heading: The Geography of the Karen World
sections.body:
The homeland is Kayin State and the adjacent hills, not a tourism map. Thai border camps, Mae La among the named ones, were home for years or for a generation, and that geography is still in the room whenever a form assumes continuous schooling and a stable address history.

### Homeland

U.S. resettlement scattered people, and then secondary migration and church pulled some of them back together until Minnesota became a large community. St. Paul / Ramsey County is a hub, but it is not the whole map.

### Minnesota

Greater Minnesota belongs on this page, including Worthington, Albert Lea, Austin, Marshall, Willmar, and other southern and plant towns where jobs and housing pulled people out of the metro. Rural isolation is a service fact, and it can look like interpreter scarcity, little Karen-language print in the county office, or a church as the only channel. Some counties have added doors: Freeborn County Public Health hired a Karen-speaking community health worker in 2023, Albert Lea schools use Karen success coaches and interpreters, and the Minnesota Department of Health publishes S’gaw Karen fact sheets that county offices can print. Community life is there too: Albert Lea held Karen New Year gatherings in January 2018 and December 2025, the Karen Community of Worthington held one on Jan. 1, 2024, and Worthington Karen Baptist Church opened in Rushmore in November 2023. Do not assume St. Paul when the household may live in a southern town, and do not assume they have been to Mae La, since it is only one of the named camps.

sections.heading: Camps and Resettlement from 2004 — Foundational Event
sections.body:
If 1975 is Hmong Minnesota’s foundational year, Karen Minnesota’s visible U.S. chapter begins in the mid-2000s, after conflict with the Burmese state produced generations in Thai camps. Camp is not a weekend; camp is school interrupted, papers that do not match, a smile you give to authority, and a clock that is not the county’s.

### Foundational events

U.S. resettlement of Karen refugees scaled up in the mid-2000s. CAAL has named Karen the largest recent Southeast Asian population to arrive in Minnesota, from 2004, as political refugees, and you should date that claim as CAAL so that the source travels with it. Secondary migration then followed jobs and housing into Greater Minnesota.

### Who you meet

The first years were carried by voluntary agencies and churches. Karen Organization of Minnesota was founded by Karen refugees and became a national first: a social-services agency built by this people, not only for them, which is why you partner with it rather than extract from it.

Ask plainly whether the person agrees with the plan, and make it easy to say no.

sections.heading: Family
sections.body:
Do not assume a nuclear household. Elders, adult siblings, cousins, and church kin may all be involved in the same week, and the person who cares for the child may not match the waiver checkbox. Ask who should be in the room, because the form’s idea of “family” may be too small.

### Who is in the household

For some Baptist households, church is kin-like, and that is not a metaphor: a deacon or a church sister may be the person who can actually bring the child. That is still not permission to make the church the case plan unless this family asked for it.

### Who speaks

Marriage, bride arrangements, and age are matters of Minnesota law, and you follow the law while still seeing a family rather than a crime scene walking in. Do not skip mandated reporting and call it culture.

Women’s labor in plants, in churches, and in second-generation school sits right next to elder authority, and both can be true in the same room.

sections.heading: Minnesota and Karen History
sections.body:
This department will meet this community on waivers, child welfare, health care, cash, food, aging, employment, and school-linked services, in Ramsey County and in the southern towns alike.

### Places

Karen Organization of Minnesota (KOM), https://www.mnkaren.org/, is the first social-services agency in the country founded by Karen refugees from Burma, and most of its staff and board have been of this community. Pay for its time and report back rather than sending a BCC and stopping there. Do not invent a Burma briefing when KOM already exists.

### Partners

Church networks, often Baptist, may be the information channel in metro and rural sites alike. Sunday is operations for scheduling, which means a notice that lands on Saturday night in English will not work.

On the public calendar is Karen New Year, generally in late December or early January (recent gatherings ended on Dec. 31, 2023 and fell on Jan. 1, 2026, and organizers have announced Jan. 2 to 3, 2027), though you should confirm the date locally. If you go, go as a guest rather than a researcher, and remember that a New Year visit does not make you the expert. Book a qualified interpreter, and pay for community work. Do not assign either to staff because of who they are.

sections.heading: Kayin — not Burmese
sections.body:
To be Karen in Minnesota is to be a people without a state they control, filed under a checkbox that also holds Hmong, Chinese, and Korean histories they do not share, and often filed again under “Burmese” because the sending country had that name.

### In this state

Camp years sit in the body: in time, in literacy, and in trust of a badge. Ask plainly whether the person agrees with the plan, and make it easy to say no.

Baptist and Buddhist streams share a people and do not share a Sunday. Youth born here sit between camp parents and U.S. school, and that is not a personality; that is a Tuesday.

This guide is a working orientation, and individual variation always supersedes group generalization.

sections.heading: Core Concepts
sections.body:
S’gaw versus Pwo is the first distinction, so put the dialect on the line, because a “Karen interpreter” is not always the dialect in the room.

### Camp literacy

Interrupted schooling is structure. The English form is a gate, and so is a Karen written notice if this person does not read it, since speaking a language does not guarantee reading it.

### Church as channel

There is a Baptist majority in many MN communities, yet church is not the case plan unless they asked, and Sunday is operations.

### Reciprocity

Showing up, bringing food, and returning a favor are reciprocity, and they should not be read as a delay tactic.

### Checking for agreement

If you get a smile, a nod or a yes, ask again plainly whether the plan works for the person.

### Greater Minnesota

Worthington, Albert Lea, Austin, Marshall, Willmar, and other towns are part of this community, which is why print belongs in the office and why an eList will not reach them.

sections.heading: Religion
sections.body:
Baptist Christianity is the majority stream in many Minnesota Karen communities, where church is often the information channel, the mutual aid, and the Sunday calendar. Even so, it is not “the community,” and it is not the case plan unless this family asked.

### Streams

Buddhist streams live here too, and so do animist and traditional practice. Do not treat church as the evolved version, and do not treat traditional practice as folklore.

### Practice

Funerals, baptisms, and New Year gather people, and you still keep medical and legal time; when the two collide, you name the conflict instead of punishing it.

Do not make a pastor the interpreter, the case manager, or the mandated reporter’s substitute. Partner with the church if they name it, and pay and report back when you do.

sections.heading: Greetings
sections.body:
Wait to see how the person greets you, and follow their lead.

### Titles

Ask whether the person agrees with the plan rather than relying on a smile. Say the person’s name, and ask how to say it rather than assuming you already know.

### This room

Let this person’s own greeting guide you, whatever you read on another page.

Ask before any physical contact, and let the person set the limit.

sections.heading: Naming Conventions
sections.body:
Karen names may not match first-middle-last, and a person may have several given names. A family name may be absent, invented by a camp or a U.S. form, or shared in a way the database cannot see, and Burmese-style names and Karen-style names both appear, so ask how to say it and ask how to file it.

### How to file

Do not invent a last name and then flag the household when it does not match the child’s school record, and do not treat unmatched last names as fraud by default, since a camp or a form may have created the mismatch.

Pronounce kah-REN for the people, and pronounce this person’s name; do not joke about “difficult” names, because that joke shuts the person out.

Women may or may not share a last name with a spouse or child in U.S. records, so ask how to file rather than assuming.

sections.heading: Dates of Significance
sections.body:
Karen New Year falls traditionally on the lunar calendar and is generally celebrated in Minnesota in late December or early January, so confirm the date locally. Gatherings ended on Dec. 31 in 2023 and fell on Jan. 1 in 2026, and organizers have announced Jan. 2 to 3, 2027. It is a public community day where you go as a guest, not a researcher, because a tunic on a stage is not a file.

### Calendar

Karen Martyrs’ Day is August 12, marking the 1950 killing of Saw Ba U Gyi. This is literacy for the desk, which means it is not a day off the work and it is not a speech.

Christmas is operations in many Baptist streams, and Buddhist holy days are operations in Buddhist streams. Ask this family which days matter, and do not put “Asian holiday” on a case note.

A calendar click is not community engagement.

sections.heading: Education
sections.body:
Interrupted schooling in camps is structure, and literacy in English, in Burmese, or in written S’gaw or Pwo is not guaranteed. A parent who speaks fluent S’gaw and limited English is not illiterate, which is why the English-only IEP is the gate.

### School and language

U.S.-born children sit in English-dominant schools, and youth caught between camp parents and U.S. school is a documented tension in community reporting, but do not make it a personality. Put the dialect on the interpreter line for the meeting the parent has to understand.

Do not invent a Minnesota Karen attainment rate, since Compass has no Karen row; instead, date school-language data when a district has it.

Second-generation educational mobility is real. So is a gap that a room that treats everyone the same will call “culture” instead of what it is: language access plus camp years plus a rural office that never learned to say kah-REN.

sections.heading: Etiquette
sections.body:
If you visit a home, look for shoes by the door or ask what the household prefers.

### In the home

Ask about Sunday church before you schedule, and offer another waiver slot if the time conflicts.

### Time

Ask whether the person agrees, and confirm in the dialect they use. If the person has reason to be careful with officials, make it safe to say no.

Ask before taking any photograph or touching any religious object, and do not ask anyone to explain their faith or history for your benefit. Do not force first-name familiarity on an elder.

sections.heading: Language and Communication
sections.body:
S’gaw Karen and Pwo Karen are not one interpreter, so confirm the variety, since an interpreter labeled Karen who does not speak this household’s dialect will not work. Burmese may be in the home as a second language from the sending state, and it is not the same as Karen, while English may be in the home as well, although literacy in any of those written forms is not guaranteed.

### Language

Put the dialect on the request, and know that gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care. CLAS says do not use untrained people or minors, which means a child who “speaks English” is not the interpreter.

Give the person time to answer. If you get a short yes, check that the plan was understood, and ask whether it works for them.

Book a qualified interpreter, and pay for community work. Do not assign either to staff because of who they are.

sections.heading: Other Considerations
sections.body:
This section states hard facts plainly, because treating everyone the same can hide them.

### Named harms

Do not read silence or a yes as agreement, and do not call anyone an “easy client.” Ask whether the plan works, because a plan nobody follows helps no one.

Greater Minnesota isolation can look like no dialect on the county line, no print notice, and a plant shift that cannot make a 10 a.m. St. Paul appointment, which is why rural is not an afterthought.

Youth between camp parents and U.S. school are navigating language, dress, church, and a county that files the family under Burmese or Asian, so do not make the teenager the interpreter and the culture broker on top of all that.

LGBTQ Karen Minnesotans exist, so you use the name, and you do not out someone to church as culture. Do not file under Burmese or under Hmong, and do not invent a Burma briefing from a news clip.

sections.heading: Health
sections.body:
Camp and refugee health histories, including interrupted care, immunization records that do not match the form, and chronic conditions identified late, are structure. Date Minnesota rates when a professional has them, and do not invent a rate; the pattern for now is language barriers.

### Access

Literacy of the form is a health gate, because a signed English consent is not consent if they could not read it and the interpreter was the wrong dialect.

On mental health, trauma is in the history of this people, so do not skip screening, but do not make camp a personality either. Do not assume a Baptist household will refuse a counselor, and do not assume they will accept one.

Gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care, so offer it, and believe reported pain. Ask about this person’s own experience of care. If they name a healer or a pastor, listen, but do not make that person the case plan unless they asked.

sections.heading: LGBTQ
sections.body:
Queer and trans Karen Minnesotans exist. Conservative Baptist climates can mean silence or exile, while Buddhist and traditional households vary, and some people live a public English life and a private Karen life. You use the name they use and do not share what they tell you unless a rule requires it.

### This person

Minnesota’s Human Rights Act still applies. Use the name the person uses, and do not share what they tell you unless a rule requires it.

Greater Minnesota isolation can make a closed church the only room, and that is not permission to out someone, so ask this person and defer to what they tell you.

sections.heading: Hair, Dress, and Body
sections.body:
Traditional dress is public at New Year and is not a daily uniform, while the second generation looks like Minnesota, including in Worthington. For that reason, do not ask a woman in clinic whether she “still wears the costume.”

### Dress

With hair and head, follow this person; do not touch, and do not photograph a tunic as content.

Do not mash Karen dress together with Hmong paj ntaub on the unit’s Heritage Month table, since Karen is not Hmong.

sections.heading: Music
sections.body:
Church music is ordinary in Baptist streams: choir, guitar, and hymnody that is operations on Sunday. New Year stages hold dance and song, and traditional instruments exist, but none of this is a soundtrack for the unit.

### Variation

A playlist is not engagement, and a funeral or a church service is not staff entertainment.

For the same reason, do not ask a staff person to sing.

sections.heading: Sports
sections.body:
Soccer is public in some Karen Minnesota life, and ordinary school sport is ordinary for the second generation, in the metro and in Greater Minnesota alike. Neither one, however, is language access.

### Not the whole person

Sport clubs are not a case plan, and a Saturday league is not consultation.

A parent in the stands who does not read the English IEP still needs S’gaw or Pwo on the line, so book it.

sections.heading: Literature
sections.body:
S’gaw and Pwo have writing systems, and oral tradition is older than the camp school. Interrupted literacy is structure, which means a person may speak fluently and still not read the notice you printed in “their” language.

### Literacy in the lobby

Minnesota Karen students, church writers, and oral-history participants exist (MNHS Karen Community Oral History Project). You do not need to quote a text, but you do need to know that this is not a people without letters, and not a people who can all read the flyer.

Do not put a proverb on a brochure and call it CLAS.

sections.heading: Art
sections.body:
Weaving, dress, and New Year performance are public culture, and you attend them as a guest, remembering that a tunic is not a case plan and a museum visit is not consultation.

### Guest

Do not mash this with Hmong story cloth or a generic “Southeast Asian” craft table, because Karen is not Hmong and is never one Asian module.

KOM and church stages are doors if they name them, so pay for that time, and do not extract photographs.

sections.heading: Conflict, War, and the State
sections.body:
British colonial borders, a long conflict with the Burmese state, generations in Thai camps, and U.S. resettlement from the mid-2000s: that is the political event. Later comes a badge in a Minnesota lobby, and a DHS badge is not automatically help.

### The badge

Do not invent a Burma briefing from a news clip, because the news is not this family’s Tuesday. Do not use camp years as a personality, and do not ask a person to narrate killing, rape, or flight for your professional development.

Filing this household under Burmese in a database is a state act, so ask how to file it.

sections.heading: Work, Plants, and Government
sections.body:
Food processing and other Greater Minnesota work drew people to Worthington, Albert Lea, Austin, Marshall, Willmar, and other towns. Night shifts are operations, which means a 10 a.m. St. Paul appointment is a gate for a household that works through the night, while the second generation in school, college, and public employment is real as well.

### Work

KOM employment programs are a partner door, so pay for that partnership, and do not treat KOM as unpaid county staff.

### Staff

Book a qualified interpreter, and pay for community work. Do not assign either to staff because of who they are.

sections.heading: Health-care and Human-service Encounters
sections.body:
Hold these in mind together: S’gaw or Pwo, literacy of the form, who is in the room, gender, a pastor in the story, camp health history, distance from a southern town, and a smile that is not consent.

### Language

Confirm the dialect and ask whether they agree, offer gender match, and believe reported pain. Do not make staff the interpreter, and do not use a child as interpreter; mandated reporting still exists.

### The meeting

A signed English page is not consent if they could not read it, so name who the form was built for. Ask about Sunday commitments before you schedule.

sections.heading: Adjacent Peoples — Do Not Mash
sections.body:
Karen is not Hmong, not Burmese, and not Chin; it is not Karenni unless they are, and not Rohingya unless they are. It is not Vietnamese, and it is not “Asian American” as the file, so open the Hmong CI for Hmong and open this one for Karen. Some households are mixed, which is why you ask this household rather than guessing from the form.

### Adjacent doors

Compass Burmese 19,372 is a different door, so if the household needs Burmese, book Burmese, but if the household is Karen, put S’gaw or Pwo on the line, because “Burmese” on a form can erase them.

Never one Asian module.

sections.heading: Counts, Dated — and what you may not invent
sections.body:
There is no Minnesota Compass cultural-community row for Karen. Compass Burmese, ACS 2020–2024, is 19,372 (give or take 3,438), and that count is not this people, so do not file Karen under it, and do not subtract or add your way to a Karen number from that row.

### Counts

CAAL (cited 2021 in community reporting) names Karen as the largest recent Southeast Asian population to arrive in Minnesota, from 2004, as political refugees. Date that as CAAL.

### What the count is not

Community and local news accounts sometimes offer estimates, but they are not Minnesota Compass counts, so do not treat them as a confirmed count for this page. School-language counts in St. Paul and the southern districts are a pattern when a professional has them, and you should date those. Do not invent a poverty rate, an LEP rate, or an autism rate for this page.

A young school-age population is visible in classrooms, but that is not a Compass age structure, so do not invent one.

sections.heading: Doors and Sources
sections.body:
Karen Organization of Minnesota — https://www.mnkaren.org/ — is the first U.S. social-services agency founded by Karen refugees from Burma, so pay for its time, report back, and be a guest at New Year.

### Public doors

Look to CAAL reporting on Asian Minnesotans and the 2004 Karen arrival, and to the Minnesota Historical Society Karen Community Oral History Project. Karen is among the CLAS fifteen, so put S’gaw or Pwo on the line, and remember that the five standing written languages are not the ceiling, because a vital notice is still a vital notice.

### Where to learn more

CECLC is one door, not the whole community, so use these resources yourself before you ask a colleague to explain. Greater Minnesota print still matters, because an eList will not reach Worthington.

sections.heading: How it hits DHS gates — the 40%
sections.body:
Workplace culture and service delivery are both candidates.

On language, an interpreter labeled Karen who does not speak S’gaw or Pwo as this household speaks it will not work, and Burmese is not Karen. Gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care, and literacy in the form language is not guaranteed, which means a signed page is not consent.

On names, the database that invents a last name is a gate that follows the person.

Hour caps, exception processes, and life-sharing matches without the dialect and without a rural clock are not culturally neutral, which is why an English IEP will not work, and neither will a 10 a.m. metro appointment for a night-shift plant household.

In child welfare and disability, help-seeking that becomes a report is part of why people wait, and a quiet family is not proof of safety. Mandated reporting still exists, and so does the duty not to treat a whole community as a risk score.

In Greater Minnesota, print in the office still matters, because an eList and an English PDF will not reach Worthington, Albert Lea, Austin, Marshall, or Willmar. Record who was reached and what follow-up happened.

Filing under Burmese or under Asian shuts the person out.

On workforce, Karen staff are not the interpreter pool and not the community, because identity is not a staffing plan.

On legislation, funding, and rule, study a channel before you advocate for it. Use this page so that the 40% has a household in it.

sections.heading: A Note on This Guide
sections.body:
This brief is about African Americans, who are also called Black Americans. It is the cultural community whose history in this country runs through enslavement in what became the United States, Reconstruction, Jim Crow, the Great Migration, the Civil Rights Movement, and Black life in Minnesota today.

### Who this is

This community is made up of the descendants of Africans enslaved here, and of the community that grew from that history across four centuries. It numbers about 42.9 million people nationwide (U.S. Census, July 2024), or about 12.6 percent of the country.

Some people in this community use other names for the same historic lineage. This brief uses African American and Black American.

### Who this is not

This is not a brief about every Black person in Minnesota. Somali, Nigerian, Liberian, Ethiopian, Eritrean, Ghanaian, Haitian, Cuban, and other African and Afro-Caribbean communities have their own pages. The Census category “Black” mixes those stories together; this page does not.

### How to read this

Read this as an orientation rather than a profile. A church mother, a physician in St. Paul, a teenager in North Minneapolis, a producer in Atlanta, and a law professor share a history, but they do not live one life. There is no single Black culture, so always defer to the person in front of you.

The facts that follow are meant to help you meet people well: how family is named, what respect looks like, what a greeting carries, and what a form may land on. Counts are dated. History is here so that the meeting is clearer, not so that you deliver a lecture.

What shaped this culture includes West and Central African inheritances; enslavement in North America (1619–1865); Reconstruction and Jim Crow; the Great Migration (1916–1970); the Civil Rights Movement and what followed; and a cultural life of music, literature, church, food, language, and sport that has shaped the United States and the world.

sections.heading: Origins and the Founding of a People
sections.body:
African Americans came into being through one of the largest forced migrations in history, and then through a life in North America that no other large enslaved population in the Americas matched: the community grew here.

### Across the Atlantic

Between 1525 and 1866, about 12.5 million enslaved Africans were carried across the Atlantic. Of those, about 388,000 were brought directly to British North America and the United States. By 1860, on the eve of the Civil War, about four million people lived in slavery in the United States, alongside about 488,000 free Black Americans, who lived mainly in the North and in free communities in the South.

### West and Central Africa

People came mainly from West and West-Central Africa. The regions and peoples included Senegambia (Wolof, Mandinka, Fulani); Sierra Leone and the Windward Coast (Mende, Temne, Vai); the Gold Coast (Akan, Asante, Fante); the Bight of Benin (Yoruba, Fon, Ewe); the Bight of Biafra (Igbo, Ibibio, Efik); and West-Central Africa (Kongo, Mbundu, Ovimbundu, Loango). Igbo, Kongo, and Akan were among the largest groups in the British colonies.

They spoke many languages. They practiced traditional African religions, and some practiced Islam. They came from agricultural societies with music, foodways, naming traditions, craft, and knowledge that survived the Middle Passage.

### What they brought

That inheritance is not a museum label. It lives in the music, the church, the food, the names, and the way family is held. History here is literacy for the meeting; it is not a speech you give the household.

sections.heading: The Geography of African America
sections.body:
For the first 250 years of African American history, roughly 1660 to 1910, the vast majority of African Americans lived in the South: Virginia, North Carolina, South Carolina, Georgia, Florida, Alabama, Mississippi, Louisiana, Tennessee, Kentucky, Arkansas, Texas, and Maryland. They lived on plantations and in cities, and after 1865 as sharecroppers, tenant farmers, and small landowners. In 1910, about 90 percent of Black Americans lived in the South.

### After the Great Migration

Then came the Great Migration, which is taken up in the next chapter. By 1970, only about 53 percent of African Americans lived in the South. By 2020 the share had stabilized at roughly 55 percent, as the Reverse Migration (1970s–present) brought Black Americans from Northern cities back to Atlanta, Charlotte, Houston, Dallas, and other Southern metros of the New South.

### Regions now

Pew Research Center’s Facts About the U.S. Black Population lays out the regional picture.

The South holds about 55 percent, especially Atlanta, Houston, Dallas–Fort Worth, Washington, D.C., Miami, Charlotte, the Mississippi Delta, the Black Belt, the Carolinas, and the historic Tidewater.

The Midwest holds about 17 percent, in Chicago, Detroit, Cleveland, St. Louis, Milwaukee, Indianapolis, Cincinnati, Minneapolis–St. Paul, Kansas City, and Columbus.

The Northeast holds about 17 percent, in New York, Philadelphia, Baltimore, Boston, Newark, Pittsburgh, and the Hudson Valley.

The West holds about 10 percent, in Los Angeles, Oakland–San Francisco, Seattle, Las Vegas, Phoenix, Denver, San Diego, and Sacramento.

The largest concentrations include New York City (about 2 million), Atlanta (about 2 million), Chicago (about 1.5 million), Washington, D.C. (about 1.5 million), and then Miami, Dallas, Houston, Detroit, Philadelphia, Los Angeles, and Baltimore.

sections.heading: The Great Migration — Foundational Demographic Event
sections.body:
The Great Migration (1916–1970), per the National Archives, was “one of the largest movements of people in United States history. Approximately six million Black people moved from the American South to Northern, Midwestern, and Western states roughly from the 1910s until the 1970s. The driving force behind the mass movement was to escape racial violence, pursue economic and educational opportunities, and obtain freedom from the oppression of Jim Crow.”

It is the foundational demographic event of modern Black America.

### What it transformed

The Migration transformed geography, moving the community from 90 percent Southern to roughly 55 percent Southern.

It transformed urban character, from rural agrarian to urban industrial, and then to urban post-industrial.

It transformed economic structure, from sharecropping and domestic service to factory work, and later to professional, white-collar, and entrepreneurial occupations.

It transformed cultural production. The Harlem Renaissance (1920s), Chicago blues (1940s), Motown (1960s Detroit), Philly soul (1970s), New York hip-hop (1970s), Los Angeles gangsta rap (1980s), and Atlanta trap (2000s) all follow from it. Every major Black cultural movement traces to the Migration.

It transformed political power. Black voters in Northern and Midwestern cities became decisive in U.S. elections, shifting from Republican (Lincoln’s party) to Democratic (1936–present) and producing the modern civil rights coalition.

And it transformed family structure. The Migration disrupted Southern extended family networks while creating new urban kinship and community structures.

Harvard’s Great Migration in-focus piece (March 2026) puts it this way: “Between 1916 and 1970, the promise of non-agricultural work, higher wages, educational opportunities, and an escape from racial violence led six million courageous Black Americans to uproot their entire lives and migrate to industrial cities in the West and North.”

sections.heading: Family
sections.body:
The African American family has been among the most resilient and the most embattled institutions in Black America. It has survived slavery’s deliberate destruction of family bonds, Jim Crow’s economic and political subjugation, the Great Migration’s geographic dispersal, mass incarceration’s removal of millions of fathers and brothers, and persistent structural inequality. Through all of that, the Black family has continually reinvented itself in forms that have sustained the community.

### Kinship, not only biology

Niara Sudarkasa, cited in EBSCO on African American families, holds that commitment to the family is the most important factor in the socialization of African American children. Reliance on the extended family for emotional, social, and financial support is well documented, and it reflects both lasting African inheritances and the experience of slavery. The saying “It takes a village to raise a child” names this shared family and community responsibility.

Because of Them We Can, writing on Black traditions, makes the same point from inside the culture: family has nothing to do with biology alone. Black folks have a long history in kinship, and people who may not have been blood were family. In that grammar there are no such things as half-siblings or step-parents, and aunties and cousins may or may not be biologically related.

These writers describe family that can be extended, chosen, and flexible. A household may include grandparents and other generations. Some people use play cousin, play auntie, and play uncle for non-biological kin treated as family. Big Mama, Mama, or Madea may name a grandmother who anchors a family. Ask who the person counts as close family, because a cousin may be as close as a sibling. Othermothers, a term from Patricia Hill Collins, are women who take active roles in raising children not biologically theirs. Co-parenting across households means children are raised by multiple households and relatives.

All of this comes down to one working question: ask who should be in the room.

### What the numbers miss

African American families are far from homogeneous in structure. In the early twenty-first century, more African American children have been born to unwed mothers than to married women, a fact that is often misread. Many children formally counted as living with a single mother are in fact being raised by extended kinship networks that include grandmothers, aunts, fathers (even if not co-residing), godparents, and community elders.

A University of Minnesota study on African American family structure notes two distinctive features that are well known: Black children have been more likely than white children to reside without one or both parents, and Black households have had a consistently higher percentage of extended households. From 1880 through 1960, Black children were two to three times more likely to reside without one or both parents than were white children. Those patterns reflect the legacy of slavery, economic exclusion, mass incarceration, and different cultural values around extended-family commitment and shared child-rearing.

### Black matriarchs

Big Mama, Mama, Madea, Grams, Grandma, Granny, and MawMaw are names some families use for a grandmother who may raise grandchildren, hold family history, anchor Sunday dinners and holidays, and give moral and spiritual guidance. Big Mama’s house as the family gathering place appears across Black literature and film. Ask who the person relies on, and include that person if they want.

### Fatherhood

The portrayal of “absent Black fathers” is significantly misleading. CDC and academic studies, especially the 2013 NCHS report, find Black fathers more likely than white or Hispanic fathers to be involved in daily activities with their children when controlling for whether they live with the children. Many fathers who do not live with the children’s mothers maintain active involvement.

At the same time, mass incarceration of Black men has produced real father-absence at scale. The community has responded with father figures such as uncles, grandfathers, coaches, pastors, and mentors; with Black fatherhood activism, including the Million Man March (1995); and with many Black men raising children alone.

### Authority and children

Ask who in the household makes which decisions, and do not assume roles by gender. Children’s responsibilities have long been driven by age and birth order rather than gender. Shared roles in many Black households have roots in West African inheritance, in necessity, since Black women have long had to work outside the home, and in post–Civil Rights and feminist change.

Many Black writers describe child-rearing shaped by the need to survive in a hostile world, with high expectations of children. Some families use physical discipline, sometimes called a “whoopin’,” and younger parents contest it. Mandated reporters assess what happened to this child under the reporting rules, and do not infer anything from race. Many writers also describe the message “You’ll have to be twice as good,” with education held up as the path to freedom. For families in a church, upbringing may run through Sunday school, vacation Bible school, and youth choir. In some families, love is expressed through care, food, and presence as much as through words.

### Marriage and homegoing

Marriage rates among African Americans are lower than among other racial groups, for economic, demographic (a gender imbalance tied to mass incarceration), and cultural reasons. When Black couples do marry, the celebrations are often elaborate and multi-generational. Jumping the broom, a wedding ritual dating to slavery, when enslaved people could not legally marry, has been revived, and some Black couples include it. Some families co-parent across households, so ask who is raising the child.

African American funerals, the homegoing services of the Christian tradition, are among the most distinctive cultural events. As Because of Them We Can puts it, nobody does homegoing services like Black folks. In that account, a death is sacred: there is gathering and song, the service may run two to eight hours, there might be a color theme, and Black-owned funeral homes matter. Ask the family what they need, including time away from work or a program.

The sequence has its own shape. The wake or viewing, often the night before, is an open casket where the family receives mourners. The funeral itself often runs two to four hours, with multiple speakers, choirs, soloists, scripture, and eulogy. The repast follows the burial: an enormous communal meal at the church or family home. Families sometimes specify a color theme (all white, blue, the deceased’s favorite color). The obituary is often long and detailed, an act of family honor. Birthdays and death anniversaries are remembered.

### Elders

Ask how an elder wants to be addressed. Forms in use include Mother [Name], Big Mama, Granddaddy, Mr./Mrs. [Name], and the OG. A church mother may hold particular authority in her congregation. Ask who the person wants involved in their care and what they think about a nursing home, and do not assume the answer. If daughters, granddaughters, nieces, or church sisters are carrying the care, ask what help they need.

sections.heading: Minnesota and African American History
sections.body:
Minnesota’s African American population is modest in absolute terms, more than 450,000 Black Minnesotans, nearly 8 percent of the state (Minnesota Compass, March 2024), and it is culturally significant and historically deep.

### Places

Minneapolis, and especially North Minneapolis (the Near North side: Hawthorne, Jordan, Near North, Willard-Hay, Sumner-Glenwood, Harrison), has been the Black cultural and demographic heart of Minneapolis since the 1910s. MNopedia notes that the Near North community “has had a major African American presence since the early 1900s.”

South Minneapolis has historically held a smaller Black community; Bryant, Bryn Mawr, Field-Regina-Northrop, Powderhorn, Phillips, and Central have all had significant Black populations. The murder of George Floyd at 38th and Chicago in May 2020 put South Minneapolis at the global epicenter of racial justice consciousness.

In St. Paul, Rondo was the historic Black community, destroyed by I-94 construction in the 1960s. That is a generational trauma Black St. Paul still commemorates annually with Rondo Days (the third Saturday of July). Frogtown, Summit-University, and Dayton’s Bluff continue to have significant Black populations.

Brooklyn Park, Brooklyn Center, Robbinsdale, Crystal, and New Hope are rapidly diversifying first-ring northwest suburbs, now home to large and growing Black communities, both African American and East African. Eden Prairie, Plymouth, and Maple Grove are outer-ring suburbs with growing Black middle-class populations. Duluth, St. Cloud, and Rochester have smaller but distinct Black communities, often university or healthcare related.

### Minnesota’s Black history includes

Dred and Harriet Scott were enslaved by Dr. John Emerson at Fort Snelling (1830s–1840s); Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857) was a critical step toward the Civil War.

Roy Wilkins was born in St. Louis and raised in St. Paul, and became the long-time executive secretary of the NAACP.

Lena O. Smith was Minnesota’s first Black female attorney (1921) and a civil rights pioneer.

Nellie Stone Johnson was a labor and civil rights leader and the first Black person elected to a city office in Minneapolis (1945).

Prince Rogers Nelson, born in Minneapolis in 1958 and raised on the North Side, is one of the greatest musicians in American history.

August Wilson, the playwright, was raised in Pittsburgh and spent significant years in St. Paul; he won two Pulitzer Prizes.

In public office, Sharon Sayles Belton was the first Black woman mayor of Minneapolis (1994–2001). Melvin Carter III was the first Black mayor of St. Paul (2018 to January 2026); he lost to the current mayor in November 2025, and she was sworn in on January 2, 2026.
