Andrea Jenkins is the first openly transgender Black woman elected to public office in the United States (Minneapolis City Council). Minnesota's current attorney general was the first Muslim elected to Congress (elected 2006, seated 2007) and prosecuted the George Floyd case. Natalie Hudson became the first Black person to lead the Minnesota Supreme Court in October 2023 and retired on September 30, 2026. Other contemporary African American political leaders carry that line forward. East African Minnesotans in public office have their own community pages, because shared race in the United States is not shared culture.

Walter “Fritz” Mondale and Hubert Humphrey were white Minnesota political leaders whose civil-rights advocacy was profoundly shaped by Black Minnesota organizing.

The 2020 murder of George Floyd by Minneapolis police, the subsequent uprising, and the global Black Lives Matter mobilization centered Minnesota in American racial discourse. Minnesota’s racial story is now globally known. The state’s African American community navigates both the legacy of the Migration generation and the weight of being where Floyd died.

sections.heading: The Heart of the People
sections.body:
W.E.B. Du Bois, the foundational African American sociologist and intellectual (1868–1963), wrote in The Souls of Black Folk (1903):

“The history of the American Negro is the history of this strife — this longing to attain self-conscious manhood, to merge his double self into a better and truer self. In this merging he wishes neither of the older selves to be lost. He would not Africanize America, for America has too much to teach the world and Africa. He would not bleach his Negro soul in a flood of white Americanism, for he knows that Negro blood has a message for the world. He simply wishes to make it possible for a man to be both a Negro and an American.”

### Double consciousness

Du Bois treated being both Black and American, sharing in the American story while standing outside the dominant white narrative of it, as a foundation of African American identity. He called this double consciousness: the ongoing tension and synthesis between full participation in American life and the maintenance of a distinct, valued, deeply rooted Black cultural identity.

### Not one life

What follows is a generalization, and individual variation always supersedes it. Diversity within Black America is vast, running across region, class, age, education, religion, sexuality, generation, urban and rural, and political orientation. Always defer to the person in front of you.

sections.heading: Core Concepts
sections.body:
These concepts come up in African American history and public life. They express themselves differently across regions, classes, religious communities, generations, and individual circumstances. Treat them as hypotheses, not as a script for the person in front of you.

### Blackness

To be Black in America is to live in a culture where racial identity has been a central organizing fact of social existence since 1619. Blackness is several things at once. It is a racial ascription imposed by a society that categorized people of African descent as “other.” It is a self-claimed identity affirmed through Black is Beautiful (1960s), natural hair, African heritage, and distinct cultural forms. It is a political solidarity that crosses class, region, religion, and generation. And it is a cultural inheritance of music, language, food, religion, family, art, sport, and intellectual tradition.

Blackness is not monolithic. Some people describe the Black nod, the silent acknowledgment between Black strangers in white spaces, along with shared references and the touchstones of Black history.

### The race

Older Black Americans, especially those raised before the 1970s, often refer to “the race,” meaning Black people collectively. The usage carries a Du Boisian sense of collective consciousness: that one is responsible to and for the race, that individual successes and failures matter to the race, and that one carries the race into white spaces. Racial uplift, sometimes called the “talented tenth” mentality after Du Bois’s controversial term for the educated Black leadership class, shapes much Black middle-class life. It shows up in phrases like “making the race look good,” “representing,” and “lifting as we climb” (the motto of the National Association of Colored Women, 1896).

### Soul

Soul is one of the most important and least translatable Black cultural concepts. The word was coined in the 1960s but reflects a much older sensibility. Soul names distinctive emotional depth, expressive authenticity, communal feeling, and spiritual resonance. Soul food, soul music, soul brother / soul sister, having soul: the concept pervades Black self-description. To have soul is to be authentic, to feel deeply, to express truthfully, and to be in genuine connection with the community and the ancestors. To lack soul is to be cold, fake, disconnected, or assimilated past recognition.

### Respect

Treat respect as part of the work, because every person is owed it. The phrase “Respect my Black” names the demand for acknowledgment of full humanity.

Ask how the person wants to be addressed. Start with a title and last name (Mr. Johnson, Mrs. Brown, Sister, Brother) until invited otherwise, acknowledge everyone who is present, listen, and do not embarrass anyone in public. Aretha Franklin’s “Respect” (1967) became an anthem because it voiced this demand.

### Ubuntu

W.E.B. Du Bois devoted considerable time to cooperative economics, an approach rooted in African traditions such as ubuntu, often translated as “I am, because we are.” African American thinkers have taken up the South African / Bantu concept because it names individual flourishing through collective flourishing.

### Making a way out of no way

This foundational Black American expression recognizes that African Americans have survived and even thrived through 400 years of conditions designed to destroy them. The capacity to endure, adapt, improvise, and find joy in hardship is celebrated as a core cultural strength. Black resilience is not stoic suffering but creative survival: making something out of nothing, turning pain into art, dancing at the funeral, laughing through the storm. The Black church song “We’ve Come This Far by Faith” captures it, with faith understood as the lived practice of getting through what should not have been gotten through.

### Black Excellence

The term crystallized in the 2010s but expresses a much older sensibility: the celebration of Black achievement in fields where systemic barriers have made achievement extraordinarily hard. It is not assimilationist. It is affirmative, saying look what we have done despite everything. It is invoked at graduations, weddings, and professional milestones, and it is communal, meaning our excellence, not just mine.

### Code-switching

Many Black Americans describe shifting language, demeanor, accent, and presentation between Black and non-Black spaces, especially in predominantly white institutions. It can mean speaking African American Vernacular English at home and Standard American English at work, wearing professional hair in white workspaces and natural hair at home, and adjusting humor, references, tone, volume, and body language. It is a survival skill, an art form, and often a source of fatigue. Some younger people resist it and assert the right to show up as fully Black in all spaces. Do not comment on how a person talks or wears their hair.

### The hustle

Entrepreneurial, multi-job, side-business resourcefulness is a recognized cultural pattern, rooted in centuries of exclusion from mainstream employment and capital. Hustle culture is celebrated in hip-hop. The concept honors economic creativity born of necessity.

### Sankofa

The Akan (Ghanaian) word sankofa, meaning “go back and fetch it” and symbolized by a bird looking backward, has been adopted across the African American cultural community as a touchstone for knowing one’s history and honoring ancestors in order to move forward. It appears on Black cultural institutions, in HBCU graduation regalia, in Black bookstores, and in everyday discourse about heritage.

### The ancestors

Some people make a practice of honoring those who came before, particularly the enslaved generations whose labor and survival made the present possible. “The ancestors are watching” or “do it for the ancestors” invokes their moral presence. Pouring libations, a small amount of water, juice, or alcohol on the ground while naming ancestors, is observed by some at weddings, funerals, Kwanzaa, and other significant events. Visiting historic Black sites (Tuskegee, Selma, the cotton fields of the Black Belt, the African Burial Ground in New York, the Whitney Plantation, the National Museum of African American History and Culture) is a contemporary form of pilgrimage.

### Joy as resistance

Black joy, meaning celebration, pleasure, laughter, dance, beauty, and play, is increasingly named as resistance. To be joyful as a Black person in a society that has tried for centuries to make Blackness synonymous with suffering is itself a political act. The cookout, the family reunion, the wedding, the homecoming, the praise dance, and Saturday morning music are all expressions of joy as resistance.

### The Talk

The conversation Black parents have with their children, particularly Black boys, about how to interact safely with police is one many Black parents describe having. Versions include: keep your hands visible; do not run; do not reach for your wallet; address officers as Officer and Sir/Ma’am; do not argue; comply first, complain later; come home alive. That so many parents describe it is itself a commentary on the racialized texture of American life.

### The cookout

The cookout is cultural shorthand for Black community gathering and inclusion. To be “invited to the cookout” means to be accepted as a welcome guest in Black social life. As Because of Them We Can puts it, whether Labor Day, Memorial Day, or Independence Day, it means a cookout. No gathering is more sacred, and there must be a Spades table.

### The Black vote

Black Americans are the most politically cohesive racial-ethnic voting bloc in U.S. politics, voting Democratic at rates around 85–95 percent in presidential elections since 1964. That cohesion reflects the Civil Rights Movement and the Voting Rights Act (1965); the shared experience of structural racism across class; the strength of Black political institutions, including the Black church, the NAACP, the Urban League, the Congressional Black Caucus, the Divine Nine, and Black media; and a lived political consciousness around policing, housing, education, healthcare, and economic justice.

### Pride in Black institutions

These institutions were built within and against a hostile society. The HBCUs are Howard, Spelman, Morehouse, Hampton, Tuskegee, Fisk, Florida A&M, North Carolina A&T, Xavier, Dillard, and 100-plus others. Black churches are taken up in Religion. The Divine Nine, meaning Alpha Phi Alpha, Alpha Kappa Alpha, Kappa Alpha Psi, Omega Psi Phi, Delta Sigma Theta, Phi Beta Sigma, Zeta Phi Beta, Sigma Gamma Rho, and Iota Phi Theta, are central to Black professional and political life. Black-owned businesses include barbershops, beauty salons, restaurants, funeral homes, banks, newspapers, radio stations, and publishing houses. Black media includes Ebony, Jet (historic), Essence, The Root, BET, The Defender, The Amsterdam News, hundreds of Black newspapers, podcasts, and YouTube channels. And the organizations include the NAACP (1909), the National Urban League (1910), SCLC (1957), Black Lives Matter (2013), and the Movement for Black Lives.

sections.heading: Religion
sections.body:
The Black church is, per PBS American Experience: The Black Church, “a safe haven for black Christians in a nation shadowed by the legacy of slavery and a society that remains defined by race and class” — and it has been so for over 300 years.

The religious demographics of African Americans run roughly as follows: Christian about 73 percent; religiously unaffiliated (“nones”) about 22 percent; and non-Christian religious (Muslim, Buddhist, Jewish, and others) about 4 percent.

### The Black church

The Black church is the most significant institution in African American history. It was born in the Invisible Institution, the secret worship of enslaved Africans in brush arbors, slave cabins, and clearings, and formalized in the late eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. Since then it has been many things at once. It has been a spiritual center. It has been a political center; Frederick Douglass, Martin Luther King Jr., Fannie Lou Hamer, Andrew Young, Jesse Jackson, Al Sharpton, and Raphael Warnock were all Black pastors and church leaders. It has been a social-welfare institution providing food, housing assistance, childcare, and education when no one else would. It has been an economic institution through church banking, real estate, and mutual aid. It has been a cultural producer of spirituals, gospel, ring shouts, call-and-response preaching, whooping, and the praise dance. And it has been an educational institution through Sunday schools, church schools, and the founding of HBCUs by Black denominations.

### Major Black Christian denominations

The African Methodist Episcopal (AME) Church was founded by Richard Allen in 1816 in Philadelphia after Allen and other Black members of St. George’s Methodist Church walked out in protest of segregated worship. It is doctrinally Methodist, with distinctive theology and praxis, and has about 2.5–3 million members globally.

The African Methodist Episcopal Zion (AME Zion) Church was founded in 1821 in New York. Sometimes called the Freedom Church, it included Harriet Tubman, Frederick Douglass, and Sojourner Truth. It has about 1.4 million members.

The Christian Methodist Episcopal (CME) Church was founded in 1870, having split from the Methodist Episcopal Church South. It has about 800,000 members.

The National Baptist Convention, USA, Inc., founded in 1895, is the largest African American religious denomination, with about 7.5 million members. Its independent Black Baptist churches combine deep biblical preaching with Black liberation themes.

The National Baptist Convention of America, International split from NBC-USA in 1915 and has about 3.5 million members.

The Progressive National Baptist Convention was founded in 1961 in support of the Civil Rights Movement and Martin Luther King Jr., and has about 1.5 million members.

The Church of God in Christ (COGIC) was founded in 1907 in Memphis by Charles Harrison Mason. It is the largest Black Pentecostal denomination, with about 6.5 million members, and is known for fervent worship, speaking in tongues, and a strong holiness tradition. Other Pentecostal Black denominations include Apostolic, Holiness, and various COGIC offshoots.

Black members of historically white denominations are present in significant numbers in the United Methodist Church, the Episcopal Church, the Roman Catholic Church (especially in Louisiana, Maryland, parts of the Southwest, and among Caribbean-origin families), the Lutheran Church, and the Presbyterian Church (USA).

Non-denominational and megachurches are increasingly important, among them T.D. Jakes’s Potter’s House and various neo-Pentecostal churches.

### Distinctive features of Black worship

Black worship has a recognizable texture. There is call-and-response between preacher and congregation: “Can I get an Amen?” — “Amen!”; “Won’t He do it?” — “Yes He will!” There is extended preaching, with sermons of 45 minutes to 90-plus minutes being normal. There is whooping, the rhythmic, melodic, climactic preaching style. There is gospel music, with choirs, praise teams, soloists, the Hammond B3 organ, drums, and electric bass. There is the praise dance or liturgical dance. There is speaking in tongues, especially in Pentecostal and COGIC traditions, and being “slain in the spirit.” “Catching the Holy Ghost” means ecstatic worship that includes dancing, shouting, weeping, and jumping. Services can run long, often two to four hours, and longer for revivals, watch nights, and homegoing services. There is the altar call. There are tithes, offerings, and love offerings, with multiple collections per service. People wear Sunday best, including church hats, the iconic Black church crown, on older women. There is the praise leader, and there is the “First Lady,” the pastor’s wife, who is herself a significant ministry figure.

Watch Night services on New Year’s Eve are a tradition dating to 31 December 1862, the night before the Emancipation Proclamation, when enslaved people gathered to wait for freedom.

### Islam — the Black Muslim tradition

Islam has a deep history in African America. An estimated 10–20 percent of enslaved Africans brought to North America were already Muslim, coming from West African Muslim regions (Mali, Senegal, Guinea, Sierra Leone). Practice was largely suppressed, but fragments survived in names like Bilali Muhammed on Sapelo Island, Georgia; Job Ben Solomon; and Yarrow Mamout.

In the twentieth century, Islam was reclaimed and reinvented. The Moorish Science Temple (1913) was founded by Noble Drew Ali. The Nation of Islam (1930) was founded by Wallace Fard Muhammad and led by Elijah Muhammad (1934–1975), with figures like Malcolm X, Muhammad Ali, and Louis Farrakhan, combining Islamic identity with Black nationalism and a distinct theology. After Malcolm X’s pilgrimage to Mecca in 1964, he and many followers transitioned to mainstream Sunni Islam. Warith Deen Mohammed led much of the NOI into Sunni Islam in the late 1970s.

Today there are approximately 2–3 million Black Muslims in America, divided roughly between Sunni (the majority), the Nation of Islam (smaller), and other traditions. About 20 percent of all American Muslims are Black. Notable Black Muslims include Malcolm X, Muhammad Ali, Kareem Abdul-Jabbar, Mahershala Ali, Ice Cube, Lupe Fiasco, Andre 3000, and Mos Def / Yasiin Bey. Somali American Muslims in Minnesota have their own brief.

### African traditional religions and conjure

Some African Americans practice or draw on African traditional religions, particularly Yoruba Ifá, Akan religion, Vodun, and Caribbean diaspora forms like Cuban Santería, Haitian Vodou, and Brazilian Candomblé. The Ifá movement has grown, with Yoruba priests (babalawos, iyanifas) initiating American practitioners. The orishas, among them Yemoja, Oshun, Shango, Obatala, Eshu, and Ogun, are venerated.

Conjure or hoodoo, the African American folk magical-religious tradition, has been continuously practiced since slavery, often alongside Christianity. It draws on African (Kongo and West African), Indigenous American, and European folk magical traditions, and it includes herbal remedies, rootwork, mojo bags, candles, oils, prayers, and consultation with rootworkers or two-headed doctors.

### Religious “nones”

About 22 percent of African Americans are religiously unaffiliated, per Pew. Younger Black Americans are increasingly secular, which is a generational shift. Even so, culturally Christian sensibilities, such as invoking God in conversation, praying at meals, and attending church for funerals and weddings, remain widespread even among the formally unaffiliated.

sections.heading: Greetings
sections.body:
African American greetings combine mainstream American norms with distinctive Black cultural patterns, and they vary by region, age, class, gender, and context.

### Verbal greetings

Hey is a common informal greeting. Hey, sis or Hey, sister passes among Black women, especially in church and community, and Hey, bro or Hey, brother passes among Black men, carrying social and political resonance. What’s up?, What’s good?, and Wassup? are for friends, while What’s happenin’? is older and Southern. How you doin’? and How are you? are standard polite forms, and How you been? is for someone not seen recently. Greetings, family and Greetings, kings and queens belong to a politicized or Afrocentric register. Peace, or Peace, my brother or sister, is also politicized, and is heard especially among Muslim Black Americans and in older Black nationalist circles. As-salāmu ʿalaykum is used by Muslim Black Americans (Nation of Islam and Sunni). Hotep and Asé are Afrocentric / Egyptian-revival greetings in some communities. Good morning, family is heard in church and community, especially on Sunday. Hey, baby, Hey, sugar, Hey, honey, and Hey, sweetie come from older Black women to family, friends, and even strangers, especially in the South. Hey, son and Hey, daughter come from older Black adults to younger people.

### Physical greetings

Let the other person set the greeting. Offer a handshake and a spoken greeting, and wait for the person to offer a hug or any other contact. The dap is a fist bump, hand clasp, or elaborate sequence between Black men. It includes the pound (knuckle bump), the soul shake (clasping thumbs with bent fingers), and multi-step handshakes, especially between close friends, fraternity brothers, or those with a shared affiliation.

The Black nod is a quick chin-up nod between Black strangers, especially in predominantly white spaces. The nod says: I see you. We are family. We are here.

A side-hug or cheek kiss passes between close women friends, between male and female friends, and in some church communities. Ask before touching anyone during a conversation.

### Address and honorifics

Use a title and last name until the person invites you to do otherwise. Mr., Mrs., or Miss plus last name is the standard adult address, especially for elders. Mr. or Miss plus first name is an affectionate-but-respectful address often used by children for adults they know well (“Mr. James,” “Miss Tasha”), and it is a distinctively Southern Black usage. Sister or Sis plus name is used in church and between women of similar status. Brother or Bro plus name is used in church and between men, and it is also politically resonant. Mother [Name] is for elderly women, especially church mothers. Deacon, Reverend, Pastor, Bishop, Elder, and Minister are religious leaders, addressed by title. Auntie and Uncle are for older adults, whether family or family-friends. Big Mama, Mama, or Madea is for grandmothers (Madea = “Mother dear”), and Granddaddy, Granddad, Papa, or Big Daddy is for grandfathers. Cuz or Cousin is for cousins or close friends. Doctor and Professor are for credentialed professionals. Honey, Baby, Sugar, Sweetheart, Love, and Dear are used affectionately, often by women, even to strangers.

Use a title with an older person, and wait to be told “Just call me [first name].” Sidney Poitier in In the Heat of the Night (1967), with the line “They call me MISTER Tibbs!”, captured the cultural significance of proper title, especially for Black men in racially hostile contexts.

### Eye contact and body language

Do not read eye contact or body language as a sign of attitude, honesty or disrespect. If you are unsure how a conversation is going, ask.

sections.heading: Naming Conventions
sections.body:
African American names are themselves a cultural story: a story of forced renaming under slavery, of post-emancipation reclamation, of religious devotion, of the Black Power era’s African name revival, and of the contemporary creative naming tradition.

### Historical patterns

Before emancipation, enslaved African Americans were often given names by their enslavers. These were common European names (John, James, Mary, Sarah), classical names meant to be cruelly ironic (Caesar, Pompey, Hercules, Cato), or sometimes day-names from West African traditions (Quashee/Kwasi, Quamino/Kwame, Phibbi/Afua). Distinctive Black names existed even before emancipation, among them Booker, Perlie, Pres, Titus, Alzo, and Wash. Around 3 percent of Black Americans had distinctive Black names during the antebellum period, a share that mirrors the percentage observed after the Civil War.

After emancipation, freed African Americans often took surnames for the first time legally. Sometimes it was a former enslaver’s name, and sometimes a chosen name (Washington, Jefferson, Lincoln, Freeman, Freeborn). Biblical names were used widely, including Moses, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Mary, Sarah, Naomi, and Ruth, as were grand classical and aspirational names such as Imperial, Caesar, Demetrius, Aphrodite, and Cleopatra.

### The 1960s–1970s African name revival

The Black Power and Black Arts movements catalyzed a revival of African and African-inspired naming. Swahili names included Jamal (“handsome”), Aisha (“life”), Tamika, Kenyatta (after Jomo Kenyatta), Imani (“faith”), Kwame (an Akan day-name), Asante, Habari, and Salaam. Arabic names included Malik (“king”), Aaliyah (“rising”), Jamaal, Tariq, Khadijah, Ayesha, Hakeem, and Rasheed. Yoruba names were less common but present. These names spread widely in the 1970s–1990s and remain prominent.

### Distinctive Black American names

Beginning in the 1960s and accelerating in the 1980s–2010s, African Americans developed a distinctive creative naming tradition. It uses unique prefixes (La-, De-, Sha-, Ra-, Le-, Ke-, Ka-, Ja-, Ty-, Tre-) and unique suffixes (-isha, -ique, -ay, -elle, -ese). It uses apostrophes and creative spellings (D’Angelo, De’Andre, La’Quan, Mo’Nique). And it includes reclaimed and invented names (Lakeisha, Tanisha, Latasha, Shaniqua, Quentin, Quincy, Trevon, Devontae, Daquan, Aaliyah, Marquise, Tyrese).

As The Conversation observes, although the names have evolved, distinctive Black names trace to the earliest days of the United States. Since none of these Black names are derived from African languages, they constitute a unique African American cultural practice that originated during enslavement.

These names, sometimes mocked as “ghetto names,” are a creative African American cultural tradition of long standing, expressing innovation, family pride, and self-determination. They have also produced documented hiring discrimination. Bertrand and Mullainathan (2004) showed that identical résumés with names like Lakisha or Jamal received 50 percent fewer callbacks than those with names like Emily or Greg. The names are not the problem. The racism is.

### Religious names and surnames

Black Muslim Americans often use Arabic names such as Muhammad, Ali, Hassan, Hussein, Khalid, Aisha, Fatima, Khadijah, and Mariam, and many converts take new Arabic names upon embracing Islam, as did Muhammad Ali, Kareem Abdul-Jabbar, Malcolm X (rejecting “Little” as a slave name), and Yasiin Bey (formerly Mos Def).

Most African Americans bear surnames descended from English, Scotch-Irish, and other European-origin family names, which are often the names of former enslavers. Common surnames include Williams, Johnson, Brown, Jones, Davis, Miller, Wilson, Moore, Taylor, Anderson, Thomas, Jackson, White, Harris, Martin, Thompson, Robinson, Clark, Walker, Hall, Allen, Young, King, Wright, Scott, Green, Adams, Baker, Nelson, Carter, Mitchell, Roberts, Phillips, Campbell, Parker, Evans, Edwards, Collins, Stewart, Morris, Murphy, Cook, Rogers, Reed, and Cox. Some African Americans have adopted new surnames as acts of self-determination.

Most African American women adopt a husband’s surname upon marriage, though hyphenation and keeping maiden names is increasingly common, especially among professionals. Ask how to say a name. Do not Anglicize or simplify creatively spelled names. Mocking a Black name is a documented form of racism.

sections.heading: Dates of Significance
sections.body:
African American national holidays and observances sit on the civic calendar, and they also keep a memory the civic calendar did not always hold.

### The year

The year opens on 1 January with New Year’s Day; Watch Night on 31 December commemorates the 1862–63 vigil before the Emancipation Proclamation.

The third Monday in January is Martin Luther King Jr. Day, federal since 1986. It is a day of service, marked with marches, speeches, and gospel concerts.

February is Black History Month, recognized annually since 1976 (originally Negro History Week, 1926, founded by Dr. Carter G. Woodson). Schools, churches, museums, and workplaces observe it.

In March (variable) comes the Selma Bridge Crossing Jubilee, the anniversary of Bloody Sunday (7 March 1965) at the Edmund Pettus Bridge.

4 April is the anniversary of MLK’s assassination (1968), a solemn observance.

19 May is Malcolm X’s birthday, observed in Black nationalist and Muslim communities.

25 May is George Floyd Memorial Day, the anniversary of Floyd’s 2020 murder, observed in Minneapolis and beyond.

June is Black Music Month / African American Music Appreciation Month, established by President Carter in 1979 to celebrate Black musical contribution.

19 June is Juneteenth, federal since 2021.

4 July is Independence Day, celebrated with awareness of Frederick Douglass’s “What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?” (1852), and with cookouts and fireworks.

28 August is the March on Washington anniversary (1963), the day of MLK’s “I Have a Dream.”

26 December–1 January is Kwanzaa.

### Juneteenth

Juneteenth is a federal holiday commemorating the emancipation of enslaved African Americans. The name combines June and nineteenth. It is celebrated on the anniversary of General Order No. 3, issued by Major General Gordon Granger on 19 June 1865, proclaiming freedom for enslaved Africans in Texas, two and a half years after the Emancipation Proclamation of 1 January 1863.

It was made a federal holiday in 2021 after decades of advocacy. It is widely celebrated with red foods: red velvet cake, red drink (strawberry soda, hibiscus, red Kool-Aid), watermelon, red beans, and BBQ. Red symbolizes resilience and the blood of ancestors. The day brings family reunions, picnics, parades, community festivals, gospel, blues, jazz, hip-hop, and the reading of the Emancipation Proclamation and General Order No. 3.

Rondo Days in St. Paul (the third Saturday of July) is Minnesota’s most prominent African American heritage festival. It was not held from 2020 through 2023 and has since returned; in 2026 it was on July 18 at the MLK Recreation Center.

### Kwanzaa

Kwanzaa is a week-long celebration honoring African heritage and culture, held 26 December to 1 January. It was created in 1966 by Dr. Maulana Karenga and is based on seven core principles, the Nguzo Saba, one for each day:

26 December is Umoja, Unity: unity in family, community, nation, and race.

27 December is Kujichagulia, Self-Determination: to define ourselves, name ourselves, create for ourselves.

28 December is Ujima, Collective Work and Responsibility: build and maintain our community together.

29 December is Ujamaa, Cooperative Economics: build and maintain our own businesses.

30 December is Nia, Purpose: restore our people to traditional greatness.

31 December is Kuumba, Creativity: leave our community more beautiful than we found it.

1 January is Imani, Faith: believe in ourselves, our people, our struggle.

The setup includes the kinara (the seven-branched candleholder) and seven candles: one black (center, the people), three red (struggle, the blood), and three green (future, hope). It also includes mazao (fruits and vegetables, for harvest), the mkeka (a straw mat, for tradition), muhindi (ears of corn, one per child), the kikombe cha Umoja (the Unity Cup, used for libations honoring ancestors), zawadi (gifts, often educational or cultural), and the karamu (the communal feast on 31 December, with African and African American foods). Kwanzaa is not a religious holiday; Christians, Muslims, and secular Black Americans all celebrate it.

### Life-cycle events

Birth brings baby showers, often with church involvement, and baby dedication or christening is common. First steps, first words, and the first day of school are frequently celebrated. Cotillions, the formal debutante balls for young Black women, have been historically important in Black middle-class communities and are still observed in many cities. Rites of passage programs are church- or African-cultural-organization-based. Girls may have a Sweet 16. Graduations from high school and college are major family events, and HBCU graduation has special cultural significance. A wedding draws on mainstream American forms plus jumping the broom, gospel, and the wedding-day cookout vibe. For homegoing, see Family.

### Cultural festivals and Minnesota dates

The Essence Festival of Culture (New Orleans, July) is the largest African American cultural festival in the United States, founded in 1995. There is also the Afro-punk Festival (Brooklyn); Black Pride events, major in D.C., Atlanta, Philadelphia, and other cities; HBCU homecoming weekends; and the Soul Train Awards, BET Awards, and NAACP Image Awards.

In Minnesota, Rondo Days (St. Paul, the third Saturday of July) commemorates the Black St. Paul neighborhood destroyed by I-94, with a parade, music, food, and family reunion. Black History Month programming runs at the Minnesota African American Heritage Museum and Gallery, Penumbra Theatre (St. Paul), and the Hennepin History Museum. Juneteenth celebrations take place across the state; the 2026 statewide guide lists about 40 events, including Webber Natural Pool, West Broadway, Lake and Minnehaha, 315 Fisk Street, the State Capitol, and a fun run at Theodore Wirth Park. George Floyd Square, the memorial at 38th and Chicago in South Minneapolis, is a year-round gathering site. Street reconstruction began in 2026, and the city is seeking a developer for People’s Way, with a dispute over who should lead it.

sections.heading: Education
sections.body:
Educational attainment among Black Americans has risen significantly, and it still lags white attainment. About 30 percent of Black adults 25 and older have a bachelor’s degree, versus about 40 percent of white adults (Pew). The Black–white wealth gap and educational gap persist despite massive educational investment.

### HBCUs

Historically Black Colleges and Universities are a particular point of pride: Howard, Spelman, Morehouse, Hampton, Fisk, Tuskegee, Florida A&M, North Carolina A&T, Xavier, Dillard, and 100-plus others. HBCU homecoming weekends are major cultural events, and HBCU alumni networks are powerful. African American Studies / Black Studies as academic disciplines emerged in the late 1960s and have grown since.

### School as a gate and a ladder

Education as the path to freedom is a deep parental investment. “You’ll have to be twice as good” is a message many Black children still receive. At the same time, under-resourced schools, harsher discipline, and racialized tracking are structure. An English-only IEP is a gate. A parent who needs a language is not illiterate.

A degree is not exceptional in a way that implies most Black people are not capable. Scientists, teachers, tradespeople, and people the school failed are the same portrait. Athletics is not the only path.

sections.heading: Etiquette
sections.body:
Greet each person when you enter, and follow the household’s lead on a handshake, hug or nod. Ask who to greet first. If you are visiting a home, leave enough time, ask what would be welcome to bring, and look for shoes by the door or ask.

### Dining

If you are invited to share a meal, wait to see whether the household says grace, and follow the host’s lead on serving. If you are offered food or a plate to take home, accepting is fine, and you can say so if there is something you cannot eat.

### Soul food

Soul food is one of the most popular and recognizable cuisines coming out of the United States. For centuries Black Americans have passed on recipes that have marked special occasions. Its origins are mostly in Georgia, Mississippi, and Alabama, the Deep South. The term was coined in the 1960s and popularized by Malcolm X’s autobiography (1965) and the Black Power movement, which celebrated African American foodways as resistance and identity. The cuisine draws on West and Central African, European, and Indigenous American influences synthesized through slavery and Southern Black agriculture.

The major dishes make up a long table. Fried chicken is buttermilk-brined, seasoned, breaded, and fried. Collard greens are slow-cooked with smoked turkey, ham hock, or bacon, with vinegar, and the potlikker is for cornbread; mustard greens and turnip greens get a similar preparation. Cornbread is baked in an iron skillet, sweet or savory by region. Macaroni and cheese is the baked, multi-cheese, custardy Black version, often the table centerpiece. Black-eyed peas are a New Year’s Day staple for good luck, often with rice (Hoppin’ John). Sweet potato pie is the Black alternative to pumpkin pie and a Thanksgiving and special-occasion staple. There is pound cake, peach cobbler, and banana pudding (vanilla wafers, sliced bananas, vanilla custard, whipped cream), and red velvet cake, especially for Juneteenth. Catfish is cornmeal-breaded and fried. Smothered pork chops are pan-fried, then braised in onion gravy. Oxtails are slow-braised, often with rice and gravy. There are ham hocks, neck bones, and pig feet. Chitlins / chitterlings are cleaned and slow-cooked pig intestines, deeply traditional and less commonly cooked now. Red beans and rice come from Louisiana, as do gumbo, jambalaya, and étouffée from the Louisiana / Creole tradition. Grits are a breakfast and main-dish staple. There are biscuits and gravy, fried green tomatoes, and okra, which is stewed, fried, or in gumbo. BBQ means pulled pork (Carolinas), brisket (Texas), and ribs (Memphis, Kansas City); Black BBQ traditions are foundational to American BBQ. There are Cornish hens, and yams / candied yams, which are sweet potatoes baked with brown sugar, butter, and cinnamon. Hot sauce goes on nearly everything: Texas Pete, Frank’s, Crystal, Louisiana, Tabasco.

The drinks have their own place. Sweet tea, iced tea heavily sweetened, is the Southern Black staple. Red drink / Kool-Aid, strawberry or red-flavored, is a Juneteenth tradition. There is homemade lemonade, often with mint, and watermelon water. Coffee is strong, often with cream and sugar. Cognac, Hennessy, and brown liquor are culturally significant adult drinks, and champagne and sparkling wine mark celebrations.

### Personal space, time, dress, gifts

Let the person set the distance and any contact. Do not touch anyone’s hair or skin without an explicit invitation. Treating Black hair or skin as a novelty is racist objectification.

If someone arrives late or misses an appointment, first check the time, transport, interpreter and work schedule. Confirm the plan, and ask whether it works for them. Do not joke about time or write it into a case note.

Sunday best for church means suits, ties, dresses, hats, and polished shoes. Church hats / crowns are the elaborate hats worn by Black women in church, an iconic tradition. Natural hair, locs, braids, twists, weaves, and wigs are all valid; no one Black hairstyle is more authentic than another.

If you are invited to a visit, birthday, wedding or funeral, ask the host what would be welcome.

### What respect looks like here

Use Mr./Mrs./Miss plus last name with adults until invited otherwise. Listen fully, and do not rush someone’s story. Take time to build the working relationship. Know that a church may be central to a person’s life, even if you are not religious. Ask whether the person prefers Black or African American, and pronounce names correctly.

Avoid these in any setting. Do not use the n-word. “I don’t see color” lands as erasure of identity. Comparing African Americans to other communities as a lesson (“Black people should do what [another group] did”) misunderstands history. “Black-on-Black crime” as a deflection from racism conversations is a known rhetorical tactic. Tokenizing, meaning asking the Black person in the room to speak for all Black people, closes the meeting. Do not describe a Black professional’s success as “exceptional.” Do not assume a person’s interests or talents from a stereotype. Enter a church, family gathering, barbershop or salon as a guest, by invitation.

Use the resources on this page first, and do not ask a Black colleague to teach you about racism unless they have offered.

sections.heading: Communication
sections.body:
African American Vernacular English (AAVE), also called Black English Vernacular, Black Vernacular English, or, in older or politicized contexts, Ebonics, is a legitimate, systematic, rule-governed dialect of American English spoken, in varying degrees, by many African Americans. It is not “broken English,” “incorrect English,” or “slang.” Linguistically, it is as systematic as any other dialect.

### AAVE

Its features include the habitual be: “He be working” means he works regularly, which is different from “He is working” (right now). There is copula deletion: “She nice” = “She is nice.” There is multiple negation: “I ain’t never done nothing” = “I have never done anything” (standard in many world languages including French and Spanish). Pronunciation features include “th” to “d” or “f” (“dis” for “this”; “wif” for “with”). Ain’t serves as a multipurpose negative. AAVE also has a distinct vocabulary, much of which has spread into mainstream American English (cool, jazz, hip, dig, bad meaning good, fresh, slay, woke, lit, savage, the GOAT, salty, no cap, finna, on God).

Many speakers move between AAVE and Standard American English. Do not call AAVE “broken” or “wrong,” in speech or in a case note.

### In the conversation

Do not label a person’s way of talking as too loud, too emotional or too indirect. Listen to the whole message, and ask if you are not sure what the person meant or whether they agree.

### Call and response

The back-and-forth between a speaker, preacher, or performer and the audience is foundational. In church it sounds like “Can I get an Amen?” — “Amen!” In music it is the lead singer’s call and the choir’s or audience’s response. In conversation, a listener may answer with Mmm-hmm, That’s right, Sho ’nuff, Tell it, Go ahead, or Preach.

### Signifying, the dozens, roasting

Signifying is clever indirect speech, often with hidden meanings, double-entendres, or insults; it is an African American oral art form documented by Henry Louis Gates Jr. in The Signifying Monkey (1988). The dozens, also called snapping or yo mama jokes, are competitive ritual insults, traditionally between Black men, testing wit and resilience; they are not a real insult but a verbal sport. Roasting is the extended joking insult of someone in a friendly way. Reading is sharp, devastating critique, often with origins in LGBTQ+ Black ballroom culture. Shade is subtle, indirect insult.

### Storytelling and humor

Storytelling runs through African American history, from African oral tradition through enslaved narratives, sermons, blues lyrics, hip-hop, family stories at Sunday dinner, and contemporary Black literature. Leave time for a person to tell the story in full.

Black comedy has a long public history. The Apollo Theater, In Living Color, Def Comedy Jam, The Chris Rock Show, Tyler Perry’s plays, and Black Twitter form a continuous tradition. “Black don’t crack” and “the white man’s ice ain’t colder” are two of many proverbs. Do not repeat a joke you heard in a setting you were not part of.

### Silence

If someone goes quiet, do not assume you know why. Ask whether there is more they want to say, and whether they agree.

Do not assume an AAVE speaker needs an interpreter. If you are not sure you understood, ask the person to say it again, and check your understanding with them. For Black Caribbean immigrants (Haitian Creole, Jamaican Patois, and others), use professional interpreters as appropriate; those communities have their own pages.

Pronouncing African American names correctly is a basic act of respect. Ask, listen, repeat back, and get it right.

sections.heading: Other Considerations
sections.body:
Anti-Black racism remains a daily lived experience for African Americans across all classes, regions, and contexts. This is not history. It is current.

### Forms

Police violence is one form: Black Americans are killed by police at rates approximately 2.5 times white rates. Cases that have shaped contemporary consciousness include Trayvon Martin, Mike Brown, Eric Garner, Tamir Rice, Sandra Bland, Philando Castile (Falcon Heights, Minnesota), Daunte Wright (Brooklyn Center, Minnesota), George Floyd (Minneapolis), and Breonna Taylor.

Mass incarceration is another: Black Americans are about 13 percent of the population and about 38 percent of the prison population.

The wealth gap is stark, with median Black household wealth approximately one-eighth of median white household wealth.

Housing discrimination runs from redlining (historical) to continued steering, predatory lending, and gentrification.

Healthcare disparities include Black maternal mortality at about three times the white rate, lower life expectancy, under-treatment for pain, and a mistrust grounded in Tuskegee, Henrietta Lacks, and ongoing experiences.

Educational disparities take the form of under-resourced schools, harsher discipline, and racialized tracking.

Employment discrimination shows up in résumé-name studies, in the “Black tax” (the extra effort required), and in double consciousness at work.

Microaggressions are the daily slights, comments, and assumptions.

### Trauma and mental health

Racial trauma is real, accumulating, and intergenerational. There is historical trauma: slavery, Jim Crow, lynching, the Tulsa Race Massacre (1921), and countless others. There is ongoing trauma: police killings, discrimination, and anti-Black hate crimes. And there is vicarious trauma, through media exposure to anti-Black violence.

Some people, particularly older people, describe stigma around mental health: “Black people don’t go to therapy,” “give it to God,” “we got family.” Some frame depression as spiritual struggle or anxiety as faithlessness. Some distrust the healthcare system, for reasons grounded in real history, and worry about being labeled in ways that affect family, work, and custody. Others seek therapy, and there is Black mental health advocacy through organizations like the Loveland Foundation and the Boris Lawrence Henson Foundation (Taraji P. Henson).

Race is relevant to mental health, and experiences of racism are real. Black or culturally competent providers, such as Therapy for Black Girls, Therapy for Black Men, and the Association of Black Psychologists, matter when people want them. Church community, family, music, and ancestral practices are cultural strengths, and they are not a substitute for care.

Follow the law. Still see a family. Do not out anyone.

sections.heading: Health and Healthcare
sections.body:
The Michigan Department of Health and Human Services African American Culture guide notes that there is a high incidence of diabetes, hypertension, heart disease, and obesity among African Americans. African Americans account for one-third of all patients receiving dialysis in the United States, three times the rate of whites.

### Conditions

Black Americans have higher prevalence and worse outcomes in many conditions. Hypertension affects about 55 percent of Black adults, with earlier onset. Diabetes prevalence is about 13 percent, higher than the white rate. Heart disease and stroke carry higher mortality. Kidney disease shows in three times the dialysis rate. Maternal mortality is about three times the white rate; Black women die in childbirth at devastatingly high rates regardless of income or education. Sickle cell disease primarily affects the Black population and is chronic and serious. HIV/AIDS has a disproportionate impact. Cancer mortality is higher for prostate, breast, and colorectal cancers. Mental health is under-diagnosed and under-treated. Black infant mortality is about 2.3 times the white rate.

### The trust gap

Mistrust of the healthcare system is real and well documented. It is rooted in historical abuses (the Tuskegee Syphilis Study 1932–1972; Henrietta Lacks 1951; J. Marion Sims’s surgical experiments on enslaved women) and in continued differential treatment. Black pain is famously under-treated. Believe reported pain, listen to symptoms, and build trust over time. Family and faith leaders may be in the room if this family wants them. Make referrals to Black or culturally competent providers when people want them, and turn to faith-based and community resources when this family names them.

A rate is not the person. A physician, a nurse, and a patient in the same clinic can all be this page.

sections.heading: The Black LGBTQ Community
sections.body:
Black LGBTQ Americans navigate multiple, sometimes intersecting marginalizations. They face anti-Black racism, including within white-dominant LGBTQ spaces; homophobia and transphobia, including within some Black communities and some Black churches (though this is rapidly evolving); and higher rates of HIV, violence (especially against Black trans women), and economic precarity.

### Culture and gathering

There is vibrant cultural production: ballroom culture (the Houses, voguing, Paris Is Burning, Pose); Black LGBTQ writers (James Baldwin, Audre Lorde, Essex Hemphill, Roxane Gay); and artists and performers. Black Pride events exist in D.C., Atlanta, Philadelphia, Chicago, and other cities.

Use the name and pronouns. Outing someone to family or church is not culture. The people-page rule is the workplace rule.

sections.heading: Black Hair, Beauty, and Bodies
sections.body:
Black hair is a site of cultural expression, political meaning, and ongoing resistance. Its story runs from West African traditions of elaborate braiding patterns (oral tradition holds that escape-route maps were sometimes braided into hair during slavery), through the suppression of natural hair under slavery and Jim Crow, through the political statement of the 1960s–70s Afro, to the natural hair movement of the 2010s–20s. Black hair is loaded with meaning. The National Museum of African American History and Culture’s “Strands of Inspiration” is literacy here.

### Forms

Natural hair is worn in its natural texture, not chemically straightened, and the contemporary natural hair movement has grown significantly. Locs / dreadlocks are associated with Rastafarian tradition, Afrocentric identity, and increasingly mainstream Black culture. Braids, including box braids, cornrows, knotless braids, micros, Senegalese twists, and Marley twists, are protective and beautiful. Twists include Bantu knots and two-strand twists. Relaxers (perms) are chemical straighteners, widespread historically and declining as natural hair has grown. Weaves and wigs add hair extensions; they are a long tradition, legitimate, and should not be mocked. Edges are the small hair at the hairline, often laid down with edge control. Wash days are the long process of washing, conditioning, and styling Black natural hair, often weekly or every other week. Hair salons and barbershops are cultural institutions and gathering places.

The CROWN Act, state-level legislation in many states including Minnesota, protects against hair-based discrimination in employment and schools. Hair is not for touching. Hair is not a professionalism test.

### Beauty and colorism

Generations of European beauty ideals have been resisted with movements like Black is Beautiful, Black Girl Magic, and the natural hair movement. Colorism within the Black community means a historic preference for lighter skin tones, the “paper bag test,” an ongoing tension, and light-skin versus dark-skin discourse. Body diversity brings celebration of Black women’s curves and Black men’s bodies, alongside tensions with Eurocentric thin-ideal pressures.

A lawyer in a loc and a scientist in a lab coat are not opposites. They may be the same person on different Tuesdays.

sections.heading: Music — The Cultural Heartbeat
sections.body:
Per the Carnegie Hall Timeline of African American Music and the National Museum of African American History and Culture, Black American music is one of the most globally influential cultural traditions. A playlist is not engagement. The record is literacy.

### Genres and origins

The record runs in order. Spirituals came from enslaved African Christians in the eighteenth–nineteenth century, and later the Fisk Jubilee Singers. Work songs and field hollers came from enslaved labor. Blues came from the Mississippi Delta in the 1890s–early 1900s, with Robert Johnson, Bessie Smith, Ma Rainey, B.B. King, Muddy Waters, and Howlin’ Wolf. Ragtime ran from the 1890s–1910s, with Scott Joplin. Jazz came from New Orleans in the 1910s, with Louis Armstrong, Duke Ellington, Count Basie, Charlie Parker, Miles Davis, and John Coltrane. Gospel came from the 1920s urban Black church, with Thomas Dorsey, Mahalia Jackson, James Cleveland, Aretha Franklin, and Kirk Franklin. Rhythm and blues came in the 1940s, with Ruth Brown, Big Mama Thornton, Ray Charles, and Sam Cooke. Doo-wop came in the 1950s, with The Drifters, The Coasters, and The Platters. Soul came in the 1960s, with Otis Redding, Aretha Franklin, James Brown, Marvin Gaye, Stevie Wonder, Curtis Mayfield, and Al Green. Motown came from 1960s Detroit, with The Supremes, The Temptations, Smokey Robinson, Stevie Wonder, Marvin Gaye, and the Jackson 5. Funk came in the late 1960s, with James Brown, Sly and the Family Stone, Parliament-Funkadelic, and Earth, Wind & Fire. Disco came in the 1970s, with Donna Summer, Gloria Gaynor, and Chic. Hip-hop / rap came from the South Bronx, 1973–, with DJ Kool Herc, Grandmaster Flash, Run-D.M.C., Public Enemy, N.W.A., Tupac, Notorious B.I.G., Jay-Z, Nas, Outkast, Kendrick Lamar, Drake, Cardi B, and Beyoncé. Go-go came from 1970s Washington, D.C., with Chuck Brown. House came from late 1970s Chicago, with Frankie Knuckles. Techno came from 1980s Detroit, with Juan Atkins and Derrick May. New jack swing came in the late 1980s, with Teddy Riley and Bobby Brown. Neo-soul ran from the 1990s–2000s, with D’Angelo, Lauryn Hill, Erykah Badu, Maxwell, and Jill Scott. Trap came from 2000s Atlanta, with Gucci Mane, Future, Young Thug, Migos, and 21 Savage. Afrobeats and amapiano, 2010s–, are influences crossing back from African and South African scenes.

### Memory and politics

From “Lift Every Voice and Sing” (the Black national anthem, James Weldon Johnson, 1900) through Sam Cooke’s “A Change Is Gonna Come” (1964), Marvin Gaye’s What’s Going On (1971), and Public Enemy’s “Fight the Power” (1989), to Kendrick Lamar’s To Pimp a Butterfly (2015) and Beyoncé’s Lemonade (2016), Black music has been a primary art form for narrating Black experience.

### Minnesota

Prince Rogers Nelson (1958–2016), Minneapolis-born and the architect of the Minneapolis Sound, is one of the greatest musicians in American history. With The Time, Jimmy Jam and Terry Lewis, Janet Jackson (with the Minnesota production team), Morris Day, and Sheila E., Minneapolis was a major Black music center in the 1980s.

sections.heading: Sports
sections.body:
Black Americans are enormously over-represented in major American professional sports. The NBA is about 70 percent Black and the NFL about 58 percent Black. MLB has a declining Black presence, about 7 percent Black (down from about 19 percent in 1981). Track and field, boxing, tennis, and golf have a significant Black presence, with names like Tiger Woods, Serena and Venus Williams, and Simone Biles. HBCU sports, particularly football, basketball, and track, have their own standing.

Sports as a path has been both a source of opportunity and a source of myth, with an overemphasis on athletics as Black opportunity at the cost of other paths. The kid may not play. Sport is not the only excellence. A scientist and a linebacker can be siblings. Minnesota names include Andre Iguodala, Devean George, Khalid El-Amin, and Maya Moore.

sections.heading: Literature and Letters
sections.body:
The Black literary tradition is among the richest in American letters. This is not a people without letters. Know that the record exists.

### The record

The slave narratives include Frederick Douglass (Narrative of the Life, 1845), Harriet Jacobs (Incidents in the Life of a Slave Girl, 1861), and Olaudah Equiano (1789).

Reconstruction and the Harlem Renaissance gave us W.E.B. Du Bois (The Souls of Black Folk, 1903), Booker T. Washington, Langston Hughes, Zora Neale Hurston (Their Eyes Were Watching God, 1937), Claude McKay, Countee Cullen, and Jean Toomer (Cane, 1923).

The mid-twentieth century brought Richard Wright (Native Son, 1940), Ralph Ellison (Invisible Man, 1952), James Baldwin (The Fire Next Time, 1963; Go Tell It on the Mountain, 1953), and Lorraine Hansberry (A Raisin in the Sun, 1959).

The late twentieth century and the Black Arts Movement brought Toni Morrison (Nobel laureate; Beloved, Song of Solomon, Sula), Maya Angelou, Alice Walker (The Color Purple), Audre Lorde, Ntozake Shange, Gwendolyn Brooks, and Rita Dove.

The late twentieth and twenty-first century include August Wilson (Pulitzer Prize; significant years in St. Paul), Ta-Nehisi Coates, Jesmyn Ward, Colson Whitehead (multiple Pulitzers), Tracy K. Smith, Tayari Jones, Roxane Gay, N.K. Jemisin, Kiese Laymon, Imani Perry, Hanif Abdurraqib, Saeed Jones, and Jericho Brown. Haitian American and other Afro-Caribbean writers have their own pages; shared race is not shared literature.

Population size is not culture size.

sections.heading: Art and Visual Culture
sections.body:
The Harlem Renaissance visual artists include Aaron Douglas, Augusta Savage, Jacob Lawrence, and Romare Bearden. The Civil Rights era brought Charles White, Elizabeth Catlett, and Norman Lewis. Contemporary artists include Kara Walker, Kehinde Wiley, Amy Sherald, Mickalene Thomas, Mark Bradford, Theaster Gates, Hank Willis Thomas, Glenn Ligon, Carrie Mae Weems, LaToya Ruby Frazier, and Kerry James Marshall.

In film there are Spike Lee, Ava DuVernay, Barry Jenkins, Jordan Peele, Ryan Coogler, and Lena Waithe, and in television Issa Rae, Donald Glover, and Shonda Rhimes.

You are a guest, and you pay. A festival is not consultation. A design is not a logo for the department. Penumbra Theatre in St. Paul is a major Black theater.

sections.heading: The Civil Rights Movement and Beyond
sections.body:
Knowledge of this history is basic literacy. The 1619 Project, the National Museum of African American History and Culture (Smithsonian, opened 2016), and recent historical scholarship have brought this history into clearer focus. It is not “in the past.”

### Key moments

The key moments run from Brown v. Board of Education (1954) through the Montgomery Bus Boycott (1955–56) and Rosa Parks, the Little Rock Nine (1957), the Greensboro sit-ins (1960), the Freedom Rides (1961), the March on Washington (1963) and MLK’s “I Have a Dream,” the Civil Rights Act (1964), the Selma to Montgomery March (1965), the Voting Rights Act (1965), and the MLK assassination (4 April 1968). Alongside them came the Black Power Movement (1965–1975), the Black Panther Party (1966), and the Black Arts Movement (1965–1975). More recently there is the election of Barack Obama (2008), Black Lives Matter (2013–present), The 1619 Project (2019), the murder of George Floyd and the 2020 uprising, and Vice President Kamala Harris (2021).

### The record

A DHS badge is not automatically help. Civil rights statutes did not close the record, and Floyd is not closed for a Black household in this state. This chapter does not replace the Somali, Liberian, or Nigerian briefs.

sections.heading: Business and Work
sections.body:
African Americans have a long tradition of entrepreneurship despite enormous structural barriers.

### The tradition

Pre-emancipation free Black entrepreneurs worked as barbers, caterers, sailors, and craftsmen. Reconstruction and Jim Crow saw Black banks (founded after emancipation), insurance companies, newspapers, funeral homes, and beauty businesses. Madam C.J. Walker became the first self-made American female millionaire on a Black hair-care empire. Black Wall Street (Greenwood, Tulsa, Oklahoma) was destroyed in the 1921 massacre. The mid-century brought Motown Records, Johnson Publishing (Ebony, Jet), soul-food restaurants, and BET (Bob Johnson). Contemporary figures include Oprah Winfrey, Robert F. Smith, Tyler Perry, Rihanna’s Fenty, Jay-Z’s Roc Nation, and Magic Johnson’s businesses.

### Style and networks

Black American business culture varies by region, industry, and individual. Take time to build trust before you move to the task. Use titles and formal address until invited otherwise. Be direct and clear about what you need. Multiple meetings may come before commitments. Code-switching is part of predominantly white business environments. The networks are strong: the National Black MBA Association, the National Society of Black Engineers, the National Association of Black Journalists, and the Divine Nine. The Links, Incorporated is an elite Black women’s service organization, and Jack and Jill of America is a Black middle-class family organization. HBCU alumni networks are extensive and multi-generational.

Do not assign culture or interpreter work to staff because of who they are. A financial analyst, a scientist, a plant worker, and a county case manager are the portrait.

### Government and politics

African Americans are among the most politically engaged racial-ethnic groups in the United States. Turnout in presidential elections is high, and about 85–95 percent Democratic. Do not assume any person’s politics. There are about 10,000-plus Black elected officials at all levels, and a growing Congressional Black Caucus. Activism runs through the NAACP, the Urban League, Black Lives Matter, the Movement for Black Lives, SCLC, the National Action Network, and reparations advocates. The key issues are voting rights, criminal justice reform, healthcare, education, housing, and reparations.

sections.heading: Healthcare Encounters
sections.body:
Address people respectfully, using Mr./Mrs./Miss plus last name until invited otherwise. Take pain seriously; Black pain is under-treated, so believe reports. Listen. Family, meaning adult children, spouses, and faith leaders, may be involved if this family wants them. Some patients bring faith into healthcare decisions, so ask.

### Trust and maternal health

Medical mistrust is rooted in real history, so build trust over time. Be especially vigilant with Black pregnant patients, because the mortality gap is documented and lethal. Offer gender match if they want it.

Mandated reporting still exists. Help-seeking that becomes a child-welfare petition is a pattern some communities already know. Book the language they ask for, and ask who should be in the room.

sections.heading: Diaspora and Adjacent
sections.body:
While “African American” typically refers to people in the United States, the cultural community has global reach.

### In the world

Cultural exports such as jazz, hip-hop, soul food, and Black film and literature are global. African American expatriates have historically settled in Paris (Josephine Baker, James Baldwin, Richard Wright) and in Ghana (W.E.B. Du Bois moved there during Kwame Nkrumah’s presidency), and today in Berlin, Mexico City, Lisbon, and Bali. Pan-African connections run through Du Bois, Marcus Garvey, Kwame Ture / Stokely Carmichael, and Angela Davis. Family ties to Africa are growing, with DNA-based genealogy connecting African Americans to specific West African ancestries, and with Year of Return pilgrimages to Ghana (2019) and similar programs.

### Recent African immigrants

African Americans and recent African immigrants (Nigerian, Ghanaian, Senegalese, Ethiopian, Somali, and others) share race and often have distinct cultures, accents, religious traditions, and economic patterns. The tensions include competition for limited “Black opportunity” slots, cultural misunderstandings, and immigration-narrative differences. The connections include the shared experience of anti-Black racism, coalition politics, intermarriage, and Pan-African cultural events. Generational shifts are under way, as children of African immigrants growing up alongside African Americans often blend identities. Those communities have their own pages, and this page does not swallow them.

### Afro-Caribbean communities

African Americans and Afro-Caribbean immigrants (Jamaican, Haitian, Trinidadian, Cuban, Bahamian, and others) similarly share race and have distinct national-origin cultures. Long-established Afro-Caribbean communities in New York, Miami, and Boston have produced political and cultural figures who navigate both identities, among them Colin Powell (Jamaican parents), Susan Rice (Jamaican father), and Eric Holder (Barbadian father). Open those pages.

### Minnesota’s Black population

Minnesota’s Black population is more recently immigrant-heavy than the national average; Somali, Liberian, Ethiopian, Sudanese, and other African immigrant communities are significant. The historically rooted African American community in North Minneapolis, Rondo St. Paul, and South Minneapolis is distinct from these newer communities and increasingly intermingled with them. The Census category “Black” mixes those stories. This page does not.

sections.heading: Population Statistics
sections.body:
From the U.S. Census, 2024, and dated as such: the total Black population (alone or in combination) is 42,951,595, which is 12.63 percent of the country. Single-race non-Hispanic Black is about 32 million. Multiracial Black is about 5 million, and Hispanic Black about 2 million. Foreign-born Black (immigrants) is about 5 million, about 10 percent of the Black population. The median age is 35 years, and population growth since 2010 is about 15 percent.

### Geography

The South holds about 55 percent, the Northeast about 17 percent, the Midwest about 17 percent, and the West about 10 percent.

The largest metro Black populations are New York at about 3.7 million; Atlanta at about 2.1 million; Chicago at about 1.6 million; Washington, D.C. at about 1.6 million; Miami at about 1.2 million; Houston at about 1.2 million; Dallas–Fort Worth at about 1.1 million; Philadelphia at about 1.1 million; Los Angeles at about 1.0 million; and Detroit at about 1.0 million.

### Minnesota, 2024

Minnesota Compass reported more than 450,000 Black residents, nearly 8 percent of the state, in March 2024; its 2020 census figure for non-Hispanic Black Minnesotans is 7 percent. The Census Bureau (ACS 2020 to 2024) counts 206,831 Hennepin County residents (give or take 1,137) and 85,205 Ramsey County residents (give or take 1,010) who list Black alone or with another race; these totals include African-born and other Black immigrants. Minnesota Compass counts 272,870 (give or take 9,028) African American Minnesotans for 2020 to 2024. That group is defined by U.S. birth, not by descent from slavery, and it includes people of Liberian ancestry; Compass lists African-origin groups separately. The sources used here do not give a count of descendants of U.S. slavery in Minnesota. The major concentrations are Minneapolis, St. Paul, Brooklyn Park, and Brooklyn Center. Date it. The Census category “Black” is not this page’s peoplehood.

### Key indicators, national, dated

Median household income (2024) is about $53,000 for Black households and about $80,000 for white (non-Hispanic) households. The poverty rate is about 17 percent for Black Americans and about 7 percent for white Americans. A bachelor’s degree (25+) is held by about 30 percent of Black adults and about 40 percent of white adults. Homeownership is about 44 percent for Black households and about 74 percent for white households. Life expectancy is about 74 years for Black Americans and about 78 years for white Americans. Infant mortality is 10.6 per 1,000 for Black infants and 4.5 per 1,000 for white infants. Maternal mortality is about 50 per 100,000 for Black mothers and about 19 per 100,000 for white mothers. Incarceration for Black Americans is about five times the white rate.

A rate is not the person. Date the vintage you cite.

sections.heading: Recommended Resources
sections.body:
Use these resources yourself. Ask a colleague to explain only if they have offered.

### Books — foundational

The foundational books begin with W.E.B. Du Bois, The Souls of Black Folk (1903); Frederick Douglass, Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass (1845); and Harriet Jacobs, Incidents in the Life of a Slave Girl (1861). They continue with Ralph Ellison, Invisible Man (1952); James Baldwin, The Fire Next Time (1963), Notes of a Native Son (1955), and Go Tell It on the Mountain (1953); Toni Morrison, Beloved (1987), Song of Solomon (1977), and Sula (1973); Alex Haley, Roots (1976); Zora Neale Hurston, Their Eyes Were Watching God (1937); Alice Walker, The Color Purple (1982); and Maya Angelou, I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings (1969). For history and analysis there are Michelle Alexander, The New Jim Crow (2010); Isabel Wilkerson, The Warmth of Other Suns (2010), the foundational Great Migration history, and Caste (2020); Ta-Nehisi Coates, Between the World and Me (2015); Ibram X. Kendi, Stamped from the Beginning (2016) and How to Be an Antiracist (2019); Imani Perry, South to America (2022); Henry Louis Gates Jr., The Signifying Monkey (1988); Patricia Hill Collins, Black Feminist Thought (1990); and bell hooks, Ain’t I a Woman? (1981).

### Public doors

The public doors include Pew Research Center’s Facts About the U.S. Black Population; the National Museum of African American History and Culture (Smithsonian); The 1619 Project (New York Times); the National Archives and Harvard on The Great Migration; the Carnegie Hall Timeline of African American Music; NMAAHC on Kwanzaa; and PBS American Experience on The Black Church.

### Minnesota

In Minnesota, the doors include the Minnesota African American Heritage Museum and Gallery (Minneapolis); Penumbra Theatre (St. Paul); The Coalition for Black Mental Health Equity in Minnesota; Rondo Avenue, Inc., the organizers of Rondo Days; and George Floyd Square at 38th and Chicago (South Minneapolis). Liberty Community Church, Shiloh Temple, Greater Friendship Missionary Baptist, Fellowship Missionary Baptist, and St. Peter’s AME are among many key Black congregations. Minnesota Compass has a Cultural Communities page for African American. The Minnesota Spokesman-Recorder is the historic Black newspaper, and there is Insight News.

For background, see Near North African American Community, Minneapolis, from MNopedia, and North Minneapolis Houses of Worship, from the University of Minnesota.

### Black-owned media

Black-owned media includes The Root, Essence, Ebony, theGrio, NPR’s Code Switch, Capital B News, and the Black Press Association of America.

Always defer to the people in front of you over the page in front of you.

“Lift every voice and sing, till earth and heaven ring…” — James Weldon Johnson, the Black National Anthem.

sections.heading: How it hits DHS gates — the 40%
sections.body:
Workplace culture and service delivery are both candidates.

In child welfare, African American children in Minnesota have been far more likely than white peers to be placed out of home. If you work that system, active efforts are documented work with the family’s people, culture, and values, not a box after a removal. Kin search is not flavor.

In health and disability programs, the facts are under-treated pain, maternal risk, dialysis, mental-health stigma, and Tuskegee as living memory. A waiver assessment that does not believe reported pain is a structural failure. Church and family can be supports this family names, but they are not your case plan by default.

On language and ‘professionalism’: AAVE is not broken English. Black hair is protected in Minnesota by the CROWN Act. A dress and speech code that punishes locs, braids, or AAVE is not neutrality.

On workforce: do not harvest Black staff or the Black ERG as the community, the trainer, or the racial conscience of the unit. EOAD is a door for discrimination, and this page is not that door.

On notices and comment: do not count an eList and an English PDF as reaching this community, and record who was reached and what follow-up happened. Pay partners, and report back.

On legislation, funding, and rule: study a channel before you advocate for it. Use this page so that the 40% has a people in it.

sections.heading: A Note on This Guide
sections.body:
This brief is about Latino / Hispanic Minnesota as a U.S. administrative umbrella — not a people. Mexican, Guatemalan, Salvadoran, Puerto Rican, Ecuadorian, Colombian, Cuban, Honduran, Venezuelan, Nicaraguan, Dominican, and others live in this state, and they do not share a Tuesday, because Spanish is not the people. This is the CLAS Spanish line, which means you will book language access and you will still ask who is in the home. Ask whether Spanish is the language this person or family uses at home, because a Spanish interpreter may not work for everyone, and ask whether they use an Indigenous language that should be named on the request.

### Who this is

Mexican Minnesota is the largest origin. The Census Bureau’s ACS 2020–2024 origin table (B03001) counts 223,736 Mexican Minnesotans (give or take 3,903). Minnesota Compass (ACS 2020–2024), which counts differently, gives 231,993 Mexican Minnesotans, with 60.8 percent in the Twin Cities and 39.2 percent in Greater Minnesota — not an afterthought. Foreign-born is 27.5 percent, which means a majority of Mexican Minnesotans in that vintage were born here. Among those age 5+, 58.6 percent speak a language other than English, and 23.4 percent speak English less than “very well,” while poverty is 12.0 percent and median household income is about $71,697. In the Census Bureau’s ACS 2020–2024 origin table (B03001): Colombian 8,332; Cuban 6,536; Ecuadorian 15,993; Guatemalan 13,725 (nearly half Greater Minnesota); Puerto Rican 18,956 (U.S. citizens — do not run an immigration script by default); Salvadoran 14,670 (civil war and TPS history). The same table counts Honduran 8,493 (the Compass Honduran profile gives 9,409, give or take 2,059), Venezuelan 5,144, Peruvian 4,320, Dominican 4,252, Nicaraguan 3,743, and Chilean 2,013, and others live here too. Date any count you cite. Do not invent a statewide “Latino” total by adding profiles, because the profiles overlap and the umbrella is not a people. A published total does exist: 365,831, or 6.4 percent, in the ACS 2020–2024, and 388,435, or 6.7 percent, in the 2024 single-year survey. Date the number you use, and remember that a rate is not the person.

### Who this is not

Use this page for context and questions. It does not describe the person in front of you. Paternalism looks like one Latino blob, one “Spanish interpreter,” an SSN field on the first screen, and an English IEP written for a household the building never studied.

### How to read this

The diversity inside the umbrella is the point. A dairy worker in a southern county, a U.S.-born Mexican professional in a first-ring suburb, a mother in a plant town who may not use Spanish as a home language, a Puerto Rican household that has never been “immigrant,” a Salvadoran family with TPS memory, a Cuban elder, an Afro-Latino student, and a queer second-generation kid who uses English with friends and Spanish with a grandmother — all of them share a Census checkbox and do not share a case plan.

Always defer to the person in front of you, because this page is a hypothesis you still test on this family. Staff who share this community may add facts, and any correction needs a source.

sections.heading: Origins — many peoples, one checkbox
sections.body:
There is no single Latino founding. Mexico is the largest Minnesota origin, and it is itself many peoples: mestizo majority narratives, and other indigenous nations, so ask which language is spoken in the home in this state. Central America is not Mexico, because Guatemala holds Maya nations — K’iche’, Mam, Q’eqchi’ and others — whose displacement is not a Spanish-accent story. El Salvador’s civil war and TPS history is a different stream again, and Honduras and Nicaragua have their own. The Andes bring Ecuador (where indigenous languages may be in the home) and Colombia, while the Caribbean brings Puerto Rico (U.S. citizens), Cuba, and the Dominican Republic. Venezuela is present — that is pattern for now, so date it if you cite it.

### History for the meeting

Spanish colonial rule, Catholic mission, African enslavement in the Americas, indigenous survival, independence republics, and U.S. labor and foreign policy produced these streams. Shared Spanish is not shared culture, and shared Catholicism is not shared culture. “Hispanic” on a U.S. form is an ethnicity checkbox invented for administration, and people in this umbrella check white, Black, American Indian, other, two or more, which means the form that treats Hispanic as a race has already mashed.

### What people brought

People brought language (Spanish varieties and indigenous languages), kinship, parish and later evangelical church, work knowledge, and a living memory of states and borders that used them. What they met in Minnesota was an English form, one “Latino” module, often one interpreter labeled Spanish, and a rural plant town or a Minneapolis lobby that had not studied the difference.

History is literacy for the meeting rather than a speech you give the family, so do not start with food, dance, or a Heritage Month sentence.

sections.heading: The Geography of Latino Minnesota and the Americas
sections.body:
The homeland is not one flag. It is Mexico, Guatemala, El Salvador, Puerto Rico, Ecuador, Colombia, Cuba, Honduras, Nicaragua, the Dominican Republic, Venezuela — and the indigenous geographies inside those states that do not match the republic’s map.

### Homeland

The U.S. Latino map is California, Texas, Florida, New York, Illinois, and also the Upper Midwest plant and dairy counties that staff in St. Paul still treat as an afterthought.

### Minnesota

In Minnesota the split is the first operational fact. Mexican Compass ACS 2020–2024: 60.8 percent Twin Cities, 39.2 percent Greater Minnesota, while Guatemalan Minnesota is nearly half Greater Minnesota, which is not a metro leftover. Food processing, dairy, and southern and western towns built households that a Minneapolis default will miss, so Worthington, Willmar, Austin, Albert Lea, and the dairy counties are names you should be able to hold without turning them into a tour.

The metro is not one barrio. West Side St. Paul / District del Sol is historic Mexican Minnesota, not a museum, and Lake Street and Phillips in Minneapolis, first-ring suburbs, and scattered apartments near plants are not one client. Do not assume Minneapolis, and do not assume the person in front of you has been to the country on the form.

Open the rural brief beside this page when the household is Greater Minnesota, because place and people are both in the room.

sections.heading: Labor, Displacement, and Enforcement — Foundational Events
sections.body:
If the Great Migration is the foundational demographic event of modern Black America, and 1991 is that event for Somali Minnesota, Latino Minnesota is not one event, because it is stacked.

### Foundational events
