The stack includes labor recruitment into agriculture and plants; post-1990s Central American displacement; later family and work migration; Puerto Rican movement as internal U.S. migration, not immigration; and enforcement waves that reorganize who will open the door.

Mexican migrant farm labor in Minnesota — sugar beet, cannery, seasonal harvest — is older than the current plant map, and settlement followed work and church. Central American streams carry civil war, later gang and state violence, and TPS and asylum histories that are not a Mexican file. Puerto Ricans are U.S. citizens under the Jones Act (1917), so do not run an immigration script by default because the name is Spanish.

### Who you meet

Enforcement is current structure. If a household misses a clinic, school, or waiver meeting, ask what got in the way, including raids, rumors of raids, or a visible ICE climate, before calling it noncompliance. A notice mailed to a household afraid to open the door shuts the person out, so do not collect status you do not need, since the desk that asks “are you legal?” on visit one has already chosen a who.

The desk in 2026 does not only meet a first wave. Ask about the household in front of you: U.S.-born children translating for parents, mixed status, a Puerto Rican family that has never been undocumented, or a household whose language is not offered in the lobby. If you only know “immigrant,” you will miss them.

sections.heading: Family
sections.body:
Ask who counts as family and household, because an English form may not have room for them.

### Who is in the household

Grandparents may be the household, and who cares for the child may not match the waiver checkbox, so ask who should be in the room.

Mixed-status is structure: a U.S.-citizen child, a parent without status, a sibling with DACA or TPS, an aunt who works the plant. Do not collect status you do not need, and do not treat unmatched last names, a grandmother as caregiver, or a missing SSN as fraud until you have a reason, because the form’s “family” is already a design choice.

Familismo is a hypothesis, not a rule. Obligation to kin can mean fierce showing-up, and it can mean a woman who never signs for herself, and both can be true. Hour caps and “natural supports” language can dump unpaid work onto women in that network and call it culture.

Minnesota law still stands, which means domestic violence is not culture and you follow mandated reporting. You still see a family rather than a crime scene walking in, but you do not skip the report and call it respeto.

sections.heading: Minnesota and Latino History
sections.body:
Latino Minnesota is metro and Greater Minnesota at the same time, so human services will meet this community on waivers, child welfare, health care, cash, food, aging, and employment, in a plant town and on Lake Street.

### Places

West Side St. Paul / District del Sol is historic Mexican Minnesota, not a museum. The West Side Community Organization set a vote for Nov. 3, 2026, on a new name for Cesar Chavez Street, with Del Sol, West Side, El Rio Vista, La Raza and El Barrio on the list, so check the result before using the street name as an address. Add the Minneapolis corridors including Lake Street and Phillips; first-ring suburbs; Worthington, Willmar, Austin, Albert Lea, the dairy counties, and southern and western towns. Mexican Compass puts about two in five outside the Twin Cities, and Guatemalan nearly half, so a Worthington household is not a Minneapolis default, and you should not assume the person in front of you has been downtown.

### Partners

Partners include CLUES — Comunidades Latinas Unidas En Servicio (https://clues.org/); Centro Tyrone Guzmán; and rural parish and worker centers — name the local one, and do not assume Minneapolis. Churches may be the actual safe channel. CECLC is a department door, not the whole community, and an eList BCC is not a partner list.

The public calendar includes Hispanic Heritage Month (September 15–October 15) and Día de los Muertos as public history, but a calendar click is not community engagement. Book a qualified interpreter, and pay for community work. Do not assign either to staff because of who they are. A festival visit is optional professional development, and while you are a guest, that does not make you the expert.

sections.heading: Latino / Hispanic — an umbrella, not a people
sections.body:
To be filed “Latino” or “Hispanic” in Minnesota is to be placed in a U.S. checkbox that holds many nations, indigenous peoples, Afro-Latino histories, and U.S.-born lives. There is no single peoplehood word that does the work Somalinimo or Hmoob does, so the honesty of this page is the mash: the state invented a category, and you still have to meet a household.

### In this state

Mexican Minnesota is the largest origin here, and that fact becomes a harm when the building treats Mexican Spanish, Mexican parish, and Mexican food as the Latino default. A Maya household, a Puerto Rican household, an Andean household, and an Afro-Latino household are not variants of Mexico.

In the U.S. racial order, Hispanic is ethnicity, not race. People in this umbrella are racialized as white, as Black, as indigenous, as “other,” as mixed — and then treated as one client. Colorism inside the umbrella is real, and indigenous erasure under “they all speak Spanish” is real. Afro-Latino people exist, so ask, do not mash them into historic African American, and do not bleach them into a mestizo story.

This brief is a working orientation, and because individual variation always supersedes group generalization, always defer to this family.

sections.heading: Core Concepts — hypotheses, not rules
sections.body:
These concepts recur, but they are hypotheses you still test on this family rather than rules you apply to it.

### Familismo

Familismo means kin as the unit of decision and care. The hypothesis is that the person who talks in the lobby may not be the person who decides, and the caregiver on the form may not be the caregiver at 2 a.m., so ask who should be in the room. This is not a license to ignore the adult in front of you, and it is not a license to skip mandated reporting.

### Respeto

Respeto is a word for titles, elders, and register (usted). Ask how the person wants to be addressed, and start with a title and usted if you speak Spanish, because a first name or a joke may not land well. Whatever respect looks like in the room, confirm the plan directly and ask whether it works for the person.

### Personalismo

Allow time in the first visit for the person to decide whether you are safe to talk to. The clock still exists for medical and legal time, so name any conflict openly.

### Confianza

Trust is built rather than demanded on visit one. The enforcement climate, a bad interpreter, a child used as the mouth, an SSN field that feels like a trap — these spend confianza before you have it.

Variation is the point, since a U.S.-born professional, a Maya plant worker, a Puerto Rican household, and an evangelical grandmother do not share a Tuesday. You work with these hypotheses rather than performing them, and you do not write “noncompliant” when you mean “the form was a stranger.” Staff do not use familismo as an icebreaker or a risk score, but if the family names it, you listen.

sections.heading: Religion
sections.body:
Many streams have a Catholic majority — but not all, so ask rather than assume a parish.

### Streams

The parish may be the trusted channel for information, mutual aid, baptismal records, and a room people will enter when they will not enter yours. Our Lady of Guadalupe is central in many Mexican Catholic lives, while evangelical and Pentecostal churches are large, especially in some Central American and second-generation streams. Indigenous practice lives here, and it is not a souvenir. Caribbean Catholic and Afro-diasporic practice exist, so do not exoticize them, and do not assume them.

Do not make a priest, a pastor, or a curandero the case plan unless this family asked, and do not BCC one parish and call it consultation. Do not treat evangelical growth as the evolved version of Catholic, or indigenous practice as witchcraft.

### Practice

Día de los Muertos is public history — ofrendas, November 1–2 — not a file and not a personality, and Hispanic Heritage Month is not consultation. Holy Week, quinceañera as a religious-family event, and funeral obligation can collide with your calendar, so you still keep medical and legal time, and you name the conflict.

Help that looks like a report is not help. Religious framing of disability, mental health, or gender can sit next to a fierce wish for services, and you can hold both, which is why “God’s will” is not automatically non-compliance.

sections.heading: Greetings
sections.body:
Wait to see how the person greets you, and follow their lead.

### Titles

Let the other person set any greeting beyond a handshake or nod.

Use titles until invited otherwise: Señor, Señora, Don, Doña, sometimes Señorita. Use the last name you were given — and remember there may be two — and do not use a first name with an elder because the form printed it. Usted versus tú is respect in Spanish, and a qualified interpreter matches register, so you do not correct it.

### This room

Greet everyone in the room, not only the English speaker.

Let this person’s own greeting guide you, whatever you read on another page. Ask before any physical contact, and let the person set the limit.

sections.heading: Naming Conventions
sections.body:
Two surnames is the default in much of Spanish-language naming: apellido paterno, then apellido materno.

### Two surnames

José Luis García Hernández is not “José García” with leftover words. A U.S. database that keeps one surname invents a person, and that invented name then follows them through MHCP, child welfare, and school, which makes it a gate.

Ask how to file, ask how to say it, and pronounce it. Do not drop accents as a joke, and do not anglicize Jesús, Muñoz, or Ñ as a convenience. Given names may be Spanish, indigenous, English, or both, and some people use a middle given name as the call-name, so ask.

### How to file

Women may or may not take a husband’s surname in U.S. records; some add de plus the husband’s paternal surname, and some keep both family surnames. Children may carry two surnames that do not match a parent’s U.S. “last name” field, and that is not fraud until you have a reason.

Do not treat unmatched last names in a household as a fraud flag by default, and do not invent a hyphen and then punish the person when the hyphen moves.

sections.heading: Dates of Significance
sections.body:
A calendar click is literacy for scheduling, but it is not community engagement.

### Calendar

Hispanic Heritage Month runs September 15 to October 15, tied to independence days (Mexico September 16; several Central American republics September 15; Chile September 18). This is literacy for the meeting, so remember that a poster is not language access, and a Heritage Month table is not consultation.

Día de los Muertos falls on November 1–2 and is public history in Minnesota, so be a guest if you are in a public ofrenda space, since it is not a file, and it is not a costume for staff.

Our Lady of Guadalupe is December 12, and it is major for many Mexican Catholic families. Las Posadas comes in some Mexican streams (mid-December), and Día de los Reyes / Three Kings is January 6. Holy Week matters, and quinceañera is family-religious time, not a case note.

Independence days and national holidays vary by origin, and Puerto Rican households may mark distinct days, so do not put “Latino holiday” on a case note; ask.

sections.heading: Education
sections.body:
U.S.-born children in English-dominant schools with parents who may not read the IEP in English — that is a gate, not a one-hour culture clash.

### School and language

Some parents do not read Spanish either, because literacy in any language is not guaranteed, and oral Spanish is not print Spanish. An Indigenous language in the home is not a Spanish IEP.

A parent who speaks fluent Spanish, or another language fluently, and limited English is not illiterate, but the form that only exists in English is. Do not use a child as interpreter; that does harm, because it reverses respeto, it leaks adult business, and it is not CLAS.

Do not invent a dropout rate on this page. Second-generation educational mobility is real, and so is a gap that a room that treats everyone the same will call “culture” instead of language access plus poverty plus enforcement fear plus a school that never learned the second surname.

Puerto Rican, Mexican-American, and other U.S.-citizen students are not “immigrant students” by default, so do not collect status you do not need at enrollment.

sections.heading: Etiquette
sections.body:
If food or drink is offered, accepting a little is fine, and you can still keep to medical and legal timelines.

### In the home

Use titles until invited otherwise, and follow the household on shoes. Ask before taking any photograph or touching any religious object, and do not ask anyone to explain their faith or history for your benefit.

### Time

Keep to clinic and court timelines. If someone is late, ask what got in the way, and record only what happened.

Take time to introduce yourself and explain the plan, and still give any required notice. Confirm in the language they use, and ask whether they agree with the plan, rather than taking a smile as consent.

sections.heading: Language and Communication — the CLAS gate
sections.body:
This is the CLAS Spanish line — and Spanish is not the people, so booking Spanish is where the work begins, not where it ends.

### Spanish

Mexican Spanish, Central American Spanish, Caribbean Spanish, and Andean Spanish are not one interpreter accent test, so book a qualified Spanish interpreter AND ask this household. A Mexican interpreter from one region may still not work for a Salvadoran elder, a Puerto Rican parent, or a rural Guatemalan speaker. Register matters, which means usted, not a buddy tú, until the room says otherwise.

### Indigenous languages

Ask every household which language they use at home, including whether it is an Indigenous language. A Spanish interpreter may not work for everyone, so name the language on the request. A scarce interpreter is a gate, not an excuse to proceed in English only without recording the gap.

Portuguese is adjacent — Brazilian Minnesota is not this page — so do not file a Brazilian household under Latino-Spanish and call it done. Do not use a child as interpreter, and do not make a Latino coworker the interpreter. Compass (Mexican, ACS 2020–2024): among those 5 and older, 58.6 percent speak a language other than English and 23.4 percent speak English less than “very well.” Date the number, and do not invent a rate for the whole umbrella.

Give the person time to answer. If you get a short yes, check that the plan was understood, and ask whether it works for them. Ask directly whether the person agrees with the plan, and check back later that it still works. Do not write “noncompliant” when you mean “did not understand the English exception form,” because literacy in any language is not guaranteed: oral skill is not print.

sections.heading: Other Considerations
sections.body:
This section states hard facts plainly, because treating everyone the same can hide them. Staff who share this community may add facts, but they do not get to delete a fact because it is hard to say.

### Enforcement

ICE and the enforcement climate are structure. If a household misses a clinic, school, or waiver meeting, ask what got in the way before calling it noncompliance. Do not collect status you do not need, since SSN on the first screen is a gate, and because Puerto Rican is citizenship, do not run an immigration script by default.

### Named harms

Indigenous erasure under “they all speak Spanish” is a named harm. Ask which language the household uses, because a Spanish interpreter may not work for everyone. Colorism is real inside the umbrella, and intra-Latino hierarchy is real too: the Mexican default in this state will talk over a Maya or Caribbean household if you let it.

Do not joke about machismo, and do not excuse control as “that’s culture.” Who speaks in the meeting, who holds the papers, who is allowed to leave the house — ask, and follow the law. Domestic violence is not culture, so you follow mandated reporting while you still see a family.

LGBTQ Latinos exist, so you use the name, and you do not out someone to kin and call it familismo. Hispanic Heritage Month is not consultation.

sections.heading: Health
sections.body:
Uninsured and delayed-care patterns sit in this umbrella, so date Minnesota figures when you have them, and do not invent a rate on this page.

### Access

Compass Mexican poverty (ACS 2020–2024) is 12.0 percent — a poverty figure, not an uninsured rate, and not the whole umbrella. Ask whether the person has delayed care, used the emergency room as the door, or skipped follow-up, and what got in the way. MinnesotaCare ended for undocumented adults on January 1, 2026, affecting about 15,000 adults; children stay eligible.

Fear of the lobby is a health access fact. A badge, a form that asks for SSN, a child called to interpret a diagnosis, an interpreter who does not speak this Spanish or this indigenous language — these are clinical events. If someone skips clinic, ask what got in the way before calling it noncompliance.

Believe reported pain, and do not skip screening because a stereotype said this community is dramatic, or stoic, or “they take care of their own.” Do not fold this history into Tuskegee (African American literacy) or into a generic “immigrant mistrust” slide, because this community’s medical mistrust also runs through camps and war in some streams, through dismissals, and through child-protection fear.

Traditional healers, yerberías, and parish prayer can sit next to a fierce wish for biomedicine. If they name a healer, listen, but do not make the healer the case plan unless they asked. Gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care, so offer it, and do not use a child as interpreter in a health encounter.

sections.heading: LGBTQ
sections.body:
Queer and trans Latino Minnesotans exist. Conservative parish, evangelical, and family climates can mean silence, exile, or danger — and that is not every family.

### This person

Familismo can be protection, and it can be pressure, and you do not get to decide which one this household is from the doorway.

Use the name they use, and do not share what they tell you unless a rule requires it. Minnesota’s Human Rights Act still applies.

Afro-Latino and indigenous queer people exist inside this page, so do not mash them into the historic African American LGBTQ chapter, and do not bleach them. Do not question a household about anyone’s sexuality or gender, and take seriously that some people have reason to keep it private.

sections.heading: Hair, Dress, and Body
sections.body:
There is no Latino uniform, and the second generation looks like Minnesota.

### Dress

Indigenous traje and Maya dress are public at fiesta and ceremony, but they are not a daily costume, and they are not yours to request for a Heritage Month photo. Do not ask a woman in clinic whether she “still wears the costume.”

Colorism and hair texture are real inside the umbrella. Afro-Latino hair is not the CROWN Act chapter copied over — and you still do not touch, still do not police, and still do not treat tightness or looseness as a professionalism problem. Mestizo default beauty is a hierarchy, so name it if it is in the room, and do not rank.

Quinceañera dress, baptism white, funeral black, evangelical modesty, and the Catholic veil in some rooms are celebration and devotion, not a case note. Do not touch, and do not rank piety or indigeneity off clothing; instead, ask the person, with gender match if they want it.

sections.heading: Music
sections.body:
There is not one playlist, because mariachi, ranchera, norteño, banda, cumbia, salsa, merengue, bachata, vallenato, música andina, marimba, corridos, reggaeton, and church music each have an origin, and origin names the sound.

### Variation

A Mexican default playlist in a Guatemalan or Puerto Rican waiting room is the mash in speakers.

Corridos include narcocorridos in some streams, which is a named fact, not a joke and not a risk score you write on a last name.

A festival stage is not engagement, a playlist is not language access, and church music is not staff entertainment. Knowing that music is public life will not write the waiver, but it will stop you from treating one Heritage Month speaker as the community.

sections.heading: Sports
sections.body:
Fútbol is the default public sport for many boys and men, and for many girls. Boxing has prestige in some streams, baseball and softball show up especially in Caribbean households, and school sport is ordinary for the second generation.

### Not the whole person

Do not assume the kid plays, and do not make sport the only excellence you can see.

Leagues and pickup games are social infrastructure in the metro and in plant towns, but they are not a substitute for language access on a waiver, and they are not consultation.

World Cup and club fútbol are public life, yet a viewing party is not community engagement, and sport clubs are not the interpreter pool.

sections.heading: Literature
sections.body:
Spanish-language literature is world literature, although that fact does not mean the person in the lobby can read your form — in English or in Spanish.

### Literacy in the lobby

Literacy in any language is not guaranteed. Indigenous oral literature is older than the Spanish file, and it is not “no letters.”

Minnesota has Latino journalists, poets, and scholars. You do not need to quote a novel in the lobby, but you do need to know this is not a people without letters, and not a people who can all read the exception process.

Print Spanish from Spain, Mexico, or a translation produced by software is not automatically this household’s Spanish, because CLAS is qualified language — not Google, and not a child.

sections.heading: Art
sections.body:
Murals on the West Side and on Lake Street are public Minnesota art, not a booth, and ofrendas at Día de los Muertos are public history. Textiles and indigenous weaving are art and memory, not a mascot for the unit’s Heritage Month table.

### Guest

Be a guest, not a researcher, which means you do not photograph an altar because it is pretty. An ofrenda is not a case plan, and a mural tour is not consultation.

Contemporary Latino and indigenous artists work in this state. Knowing that will not write the waiver, but it will stop you from treating the umbrella as a people without a public culture — and from treating that public culture as engagement.

sections.heading: Labor, War, Enforcement, and the State
sections.body:
There is no single Civil Rights Movement to copy onto this page, because the political literacy here is stacked.

### The badge

The stack includes U.S. labor recruitment; Mexican and Central American displacement; the Salvadoran civil war and TPS; the Guatemalan war and Maya flight; Nicaraguan streams; Cuban and Venezuelan political flight (date those if you cite them); Puerto Rican colonial status and citizenship, without treating that household as foreign; and U.S. enforcement that reorganizes Tuesday.

If a household misses a clinic, school, or waiver meeting, ask what got in the way, and remember that a DHS badge is not automatically help. Do not tell people the climate is fine so the form is fair now, do not use a civil war or a raid as a personality, and do not ask a person to narrate crossing for your professional development.

Do not collect status you do not need, since SSN on the first screen is a gate, and notices to a household that will not open the door do not reach them. Mandated reporting still exists, and so does the duty not to treat a whole umbrella as a deportation score.

sections.heading: Work, Markets, and Government
sections.body:
Work here spans food processing, dairy, agriculture, construction, service, restaurants, cleaning, childcare, home care, a professional second generation, and public employment.

### Work

Rural plants and metro kitchens can sit in the same extended family, and a small-business owner and a waiver recipient may be the same household.

Worker centers and parishes may be the trusted channel in Greater Minnesota, so name the local one. Do not assume Minneapolis, and do not assume CLUES reaches a dairy county. Take time to introduce yourself and explain the plan, and still give any required notice.

### Staff

Book a qualified interpreter, and pay for community work. Do not assign either to staff because of who they are. Use these resources yourself before you ask a Latino colleague to explain.

Some people send money to relatives in another country as an obligation. Ask about it, and do not treat it as optional in a budget. Puerto Rican households may be sending money to the island after disaster — and that is still not an immigration script.

sections.heading: Health-care and Human-service Encounters
sections.body:
Language access includes indigenous languages, so book qualified Spanish AND ask.

### Language

Ask which language the household uses at home, and confirm it, including any Indigenous language, since a Spanish interpreter may not work for everyone. Do not use a child as interpreter, and do not make staff the interpreter.

### The meeting

Ask who is in the room, offer gender match in maternal and intimate care if they want it, use titles, and expect two surnames. On SSN on the first screen: if you do not need it, do not ask for it. On mixed-status, do not collect status you do not need, and ask what got in the way when an appointment is skipped.

Believe reported pain, and do not skip screening. If they name a healer or a parish, listen, but do not make either the case plan unless they asked. Mandated reporting still exists, and help-seeking that becomes a report is part of why people wait, so you follow the law, and you still see a family.

Rural access is a gate: distance, clinic hours, one interpreter contracted from the Cities who does not speak this language. Open the rural brief beside this page, and remember that a nuclear form that cannot see grandparents as the household is already a who.

sections.heading: Adjacent Peoples — Do Not Mash
sections.body:
This is not Brazilian Portuguese-only. Brazilian Minnesota is adjacent, so open a different door, and do not file Portuguese under Spanish and call it CLAS.

### Adjacent doors

Do not treat “Spanish” as indigenous, because Indigenous languages are not dialects of Spanish, and a Spanish interpreter may not work for everyone.

Puerto Rican is U.S. citizenship, so do not run an immigration script by default. Cuban, Dominican, Ecuadorian, Colombian, Salvadoran, Guatemalan, Honduran, Nicaraguan, Venezuelan, Mexican — name the origin. The Mexican default is a Minnesota fact, and it becomes a Minnesota harm when it is the only file.

This is not Somali, and it is not historic African American. Afro-Latino people exist, so ask, do not mash them into the African American brief because both are Black, and do not bleach them into a mestizo Latino blob. Filipino Spanish-colonial history is not this page, so open the people brief that matches this household. Never one Latino module.

sections.heading: Counts, Dated
sections.body:
These are Minnesota Compass figures, ACS 2020–2024, for the Mexican cultural community, and like every figure on this page they need a date when you use them.

### Counts

The Census Bureau’s ACS 2020–2024 origin table (B03001) counts 223,736 Mexican Minnesotans (give or take 3,903), while Compass, which counts differently, gives 231,993 for ACS 2020–2024, with 60.8 percent in the Twin Cities and 39.2 percent in Greater Minnesota, and foreign-born is 27.5 percent. Among those age 5+, 58.6 percent speak a language other than English and 23.4 percent speak English less than “very well.” Poverty is 12.0 percent, and median household income is about $71,697. Ask which language the household uses at home, and do not invent a count of speakers.

In the Census Bureau’s ACS 2020–2024 origin table (B03001), other origins include: Colombian 8,332; Cuban 6,536; Ecuadorian 15,993 (indigenous languages may be in the home); Guatemalan 13,725 (nearly half Greater Minnesota); Puerto Rican 18,956 (U.S. citizens); Salvadoran 14,670 (civil war and TPS history). The same table counts Honduran 8,493 (the Compass Honduran profile gives 9,409, give or take 2,059), Venezuelan 5,144, Peruvian 4,320, Dominican 4,252, Nicaraguan 3,743, and Chilean 2,013, and others live here too. Date any count you cite.

### What the count is not

Do not add these profiles into a fake “Latino Minnesota” total, because definitions overlap, people can appear in more than one story, and the umbrella is not a people. Counts disagree across ACS vintages and across Hispanic-origin versus ancestry versus language, so date the number you cite. A published total does exist: 365,831, or 6.4 percent, in the ACS 2020–2024, and 388,435, or 6.7 percent, in the 2024 single-year survey.

A rate is not the person. Poverty of 12.0 percent (Mexican, that vintage) is not the Guatemalan household in a plant town and not the Puerto Rican household in the Cities. For uninsured and delayed-care patterns, date MN figures when you have them, and do not invent a rate.

sections.heading: Doors and Sources
sections.body:
Start with CLUES — Comunidades Latinas Unidas En Servicio — https://clues.org/. It offers Twin Cities services, but it is not the whole state.

### Public doors

Centro Tyrone Guzmán serves family and youth in the metro. Rural parish and worker centers matter too, so name the local one, and do not assume Minneapolis, since the parish in a dairy county may be the actual door.

Minnesota Compass origin profiles (ACS 2020–2024) cover Mexican, Guatemalan, Puerto Rican, Salvadoran, Ecuadorian, Colombian, and Cuban — date the retrieval. CECLC is a department door, not the whole community. Open the rural brief when place is the gate, and open the African American brief for historic African American households. Open this one for a Latino household, and open an indigenous-language request when Spanish is the wrong door.

### Where to learn more

Use these resources yourself before you ask a Latino colleague to explain, and do not count a BCC to CLUES as consultation. Pay partners, and report back, because Hispanic Heritage Month is not the work.

sections.heading: How it hits DHS gates — the 40%
sections.body:
Workplace culture and service delivery are both candidates here.

Language: CLAS Spanish is not one Spanish. Ask which language the household uses at home, because a Spanish interpreter may not work for everyone, and still book a qualified interpreter, and do not use a child. Gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care.

Names: there are two surnames, and the database that keeps one invents a person, while unmatched last names are not fraud by default.

Hour caps, exception processes, SSN on the first screen, and life-sharing matches without language are not culturally neutral. Ask whether the first field feels like enforcement to the household, and do not collect status you do not need.

Child welfare and disability: help-seeking that becomes a report is part of why people wait. Mandated reporting still exists, and so does the duty not to treat a whole community as a risk score. Domestic violence is not culture, so you follow the law.

Enforcement climate: if a household misses a clinic, school, or waiver meeting, ask what got in the way before calling it noncompliance. Do not collect status you do not need, and because Puerto Rican is citizenship, do not run an immigration script by default.

Notices and comment: do not count an eList and an English PDF as reaching this community, and record who was reached and what follow-up happened. Greater Minnesota is part of this picture, so a St. Paul meeting is not the whole channel.

Workforce: Latino staff are not the interpreter pool, not the indigenous-language pool, and not the community, because staff are colleagues, not the curriculum, so do not treat them as either.

The Latino mash: opening one blob, or Mexican as the only file, because the checkbox says Hispanic shuts the person out.

Legislation, funding, rule: study a channel before you advocate for it. Use this page so that the 40% has a household in it.

sections.heading: A Note on This Guide
sections.body:
This brief is about the eleven federally recognized Tribal Nations in Minnesota — seven Anishinaabe (Ojibwe) nations and four Dakota nations. They are governments, which means consultation with them is government-to-government, so a culture card is not that door, and a land acknowledgment without a call is not that door either.

### Who this is

These are the eleven nations, as named by the Minnesota Indian Affairs Council, and each one is its own government.

The Anishinaabe reservations are Grand Portage (northeast corner); Bois Forte (extreme north); Red Lake (extreme north, west of Bois Forte); White Earth (northwest); Leech Lake (north central); Fond du Lac (northeast, west of Duluth); and Mille Lacs (central, south and east of Brainerd).

The Dakota communities are Shakopee Mdewakanton (south of the Twin Cities near Prior Lake); Prairie Island (near Red Wing); Lower Sioux (near Redwood Falls); and Upper Sioux (near Granite Falls).

Ojibwe and Dakota are distinct languages, territories, legal histories, and governments. The Minnesota Chippewa Tribe is a government of six Anishinaabe reservations — Bois Forte, Fond du Lac, Grand Portage, Leech Lake, Mille Lacs, and White Earth — while Red Lake is not in that union, and the Dakota nations are not in it either. For that reason, filing all eleven as “Chippewa” closes the meeting before it starts.

Minnesota Compass’s Native American profile (ACS 2019–2023) counts about 162,216 people — Twin Cities 44.8 percent, Greater Minnesota 55.2 percent — but Compass cannot split that count by nation. The number is not enrollment, it is not the eleven, and it is not permission to skip the Office of Indian Policy, so date it if you cite it, and remember that it is not government-to-government.

Urban Native Minneapolis–St. Paul is part of this brief, because people who live off-reservation for work, school, or kinship remain citizens of nations.

A community portrait here is not one socioeconomic slice. Native Minnesotans are attorneys, physicians, scientists, teachers, nurses, people who work for tribally run health and social programs, urban Indian-health clinicians, artists, language teachers, plant and casino workers, students, and elders, and the same is true inside each nation. A casino does not make a people, and poverty on a Compass line does not make a people either.

### Who this is not

Alaska Native people have their own brief, and other U.S. tribal citizens living in Minnesota are not automatically one of the eleven. Mendota Mdewakanton and other communities seeking recognition are not a twelfth nation on this page.

This is not a mash of “communities of color,” since Rondo is African American history and Cedar-Riverside is Somali history, while Phillips, Little Earth, and the eleven governments are this page.

### How to read this

Read it as an orientation, which means naming the nation, always deferring to this family, and always deferring to the nation on who belongs to it.

The facts that follow are meant to help you meet people well — how kinship is held, what respect looks like, what a greeting carries, what a form may land on. History is here so the meeting is clearer, not so you deliver a lecture. Population size is not culture size, and eleven governments are not a small-count brochure.

sections.heading: Origins and the Founding of a People
sections.body:
Dakota and Anishinaabe peoples are older than Minnesota and older than this department. This land is Dakota homeland in creation stories, and it is also a central place in Anishinaabe history — the westward movement along the Great Lakes, wild rice, and the northern forests.

### Anishinaabe

Anishinaabe (also written Ojibwe, Ojibwa, Chippewa in U.S. legal English) is a people across the Great Lakes — Minnesota, Wisconsin, Michigan, Ontario, and beyond. Ojibwemowin is the language, and the bands in this state are nations rather than chapters of one organization.

### Dakota

Dakota (Dakhóta) is a people of this prairie and river country, related to Lakota and Nakota — and not the same as “Sioux,” a word borrowed from a nineteenth-century statute. Dakota language and Dakota nations in Minnesota survived exile, and that sentence is literacy.

### What people brought

People brought nationhood, language, kinship, land relationship, ceremony, wild rice and water as more than commodities, and a record of dealing with the United States as governments. What they met was a territory and then a state that took children, land, and language, and then wrote English forms.

History is literacy for the meeting rather than a speech you give the family. You do not narrate 1862 to a Dakota parent as an icebreaker, but you do know it, and you know that Ojibwe and Dakota are not flavors of one story.

sections.heading: Geography
sections.body:
Name the nation, because geography here is government, not scenery.

### Anishinaabe nations

The Bois Forte Band of Chippewa (Zagaakwaandagowiniwag) is in extreme northern Minnesota, at Nett Lake and Vermilion.

The Fond du Lac Band of Lake Superior Chippewa (Nagaajiwanaang) is west of Duluth, at Cloquet, and urban Duluth households remain the nation.

The Grand Portage Band of Lake Superior Chippewa (Gichi-Onigaming) sits in the northeast corner, on Lake Superior, at a border.

The Leech Lake Band of Ojibwe is north central, at Cass Lake.

The Mille Lacs Band of Ojibwe is central, south and east of Brainerd, organized in Districts I–III as the nation names them.

Red Lake Nation is in the extreme north, west of Bois Forte, and it is not in the Minnesota Chippewa Tribe union, since it has a distinct land and legal history.

White Earth Nation is in the northwest, where allotment and land restoration are living politics, not a museum.

### Dakota nations

The Lower Sioux Indian Community (Cansa’yapi) is near Redwood Falls.

The Prairie Island Indian Community is near Red Wing, next to a nuclear generating plant.

The Shakopee Mdewakanton Sioux Community is south of the Twin Cities near Prior Lake. Its economic position is real, but it is not the Dakota story copied onto the others.

The Upper Sioux Community (Pezihutazizi Oyate) is near Granite Falls.

### Cities and off-reservation life

Urban Native Minneapolis–St. Paul includes Phillips, Little Earth, and the metro as a whole. There are off-reservation towns near each nation, and there are people who live in Duluth, Bemidji, Cloquet, Onamia, Prior Lake, Redwood Falls, Granite Falls, Red Wing, and ordinary suburbs.

A reservation address is not the only address, and Minneapolis is not the only address. Compass Native American: 55.2 percent Greater Minnesota, 44.8 percent Twin Cities (ACS 2019–2023), a split that is the opposite of Hmong Minnesota (about 94 percent Twin Cities). Distance, broadband, and county lines are how the work actually runs, while nationhood is not a ZIP code.

A physician enrolled at White Earth who works in Minneapolis is still of that nation. A scientist at a tribal natural-resources office and a student at a tribal college are the same peoplehood as a household using a waiver, which is why community portrait means all of that.

sections.heading: Migration and Foundational Events
sections.body:
The foundational events are treaties and broken treaties; removal; the U.S.–Dakota War of 1862; the largest mass execution in U.S. history at Mankato on 26 December 1862; internment at Fort Snelling; the exile of Dakota people from Minnesota; allotment and the Nelson Act of 1889; boarding schools; termination-era policy and restoration; the Indian Child Welfare Act of 1978; and the Minnesota Indian Family Preservation Act. Haaland v. Brackeen (2023) did not repeal ICWA, so that law still governs the work.

### 1862 and the boarding-school system

If the Great Migration is the foundational demographic event of modern Black America, then 1862 and the boarding-school system are foundational events you cannot skip for Dakota and Anishinaabe Minnesota. They are not “in the past,” because they are why a county petition can still sound like removal.

### Ordinary movement

People also move for ordinary reasons — work, school, love, health — and remain of their nations. Urban Native Minneapolis is not a leftover, and AIM’s founding in Minneapolis in 1968 is Minnesota history.

Boarding school and removal are why mistrust is rational, which makes it structure rather than attitude. A powwow is public and also nation, but it is not the Tuesday on which a county files a petition.

sections.heading: Family
sections.body:
Kinship systems, othermothers, and extended care all shape family here, so who cares for the child may not match a nuclear English form.

### Who is family

Aunties, grandparents, clan and tiyospaye relationships, and people who are family without a blood-quantum worksheet — all of that is family. A form that only fits two legal parents in one household cannot see kin.

Ask who should be in the room, because a scientist parent, a lawyer aunt, a grandmother who harvests rice, and someone who works for a tribally run program can be the same family. “Broken family” is what the English form says when the household is not nuclear.

### ICWA and MIFPA

The Indian Child Welfare Act and the Minnesota Indian Family Preservation Act exist because the state has a record of taking children. Placement preferences, inquiry (“is this child an Indian child?”), notice to the nation, and active efforts are law. Active efforts are documented work with the family’s people, culture, and values — not a box checked after a removal — and kin search is not an optional courtesy.

### Who belongs

You do not decide who is Native; the nation does. Blood quantum is colonial technology, and enrollment versus community belonging is nation business, which is why a lobby quiz is not inquiry.

sections.heading: Minnesota
sections.body:
The Minnesota Indian Affairs Council exists to protect the sovereignty of the eleven and the well-being of American Indian citizens throughout the state — including urban citizens. The DHS Office of Indian Policy is a door inside this department, and because Tribal-State Relations Training is required for many roles, take it, knowing that a land acknowledgment is not a substitute.

### Governments, not a mailing list

Nations are seats, not a copy line, so notice to nations on the same day as an eList is not consultation, and empty follow-up cells on a tribal notice are a structural failure.

Minnesota-specific institutions are partners, not a list you copy once: each nation’s government; urban Indian organizations including Native American Community Clinic, Division of Indian Work, Ain Dah Yung, American Indian Family Center, MIGIZI; Little Earth; tribal colleges and language tables; urban Indian health. Pay them, report back, and remember you are a guest.

### Staff

Staff of this department include citizens of these nations, but they are not unpaid liaisons, unpaid interpreters, or “the community,” because identity is not a staffing plan.

Rondo is African American literacy, and Cedar-Riverside is Somali literacy, while Phillips, Little Earth, and the eleven governments are this page.

sections.heading: Heart of the People
sections.body:
Sovereignty, land, kinship, language, and holistic health — physical, mental, emotional, spiritual as one — are the heart. Nationhood is the first fact, and culture is not yours to display.

### Peoplehood older than the United States

Du Bois’s double consciousness is African American intelligence, not a universal minority sentence to copy here, since Dakota and Anishinaabe peoplehood is older than the United States. The tension here is not “how to be both Native and American without bleaching.” It is that the United States and this state made treaties, broke them, took children, and still write English forms, and you work that fact rather than performing it.

### Not a culture club

These are eleven governments, not a club, so a Heritage Month frybread lunch is not the heart of anything.

Language revitalization is nationhood, and Manoomin (wild rice) is food and law and season. Wacipi / powwow is public and also nation. Ceremony is not a training module, and you are a guest even when the meeting is in a county building.

sections.heading: Core Concepts
sections.body:
These concepts recur, but they express differently by nation, family, and generation, so treat them as hypotheses — not a script for the person in front of you.

### Sovereignty

Nations are governments, not clubs. Treaties are living legal facts, which means a nation is not a stakeholder list.

### Treaty

The United States and Minnesota still sit on treaty ground. All seven Anishinaabe reservations in Minnesota were originally established by treaty and are considered separate and distinct nations by the United States government (Minnesota Indian Affairs Council). Dakota communities in this state are nations that survived exile.

### Kinship

Who is family may not fit the form, and ICWA and MIFPA placement is the legal expression of that fact in child welfare.

### Language

Ojibwemowin and Dakota language revitalization are underway, and English is common. A word you learned in a training is not expertise, and language nests and tribal schools are nationhood, not an interpreter convenience.

### Land and water

Land and water are not a backdrop, because hunting, fishing, ricing, and treaty rights are law, not hobbies.

### Ceremony

Ceremony is nationhood, protected by the American Indian Religious Freedom Act, so it is not a team-building event, and it is not a lodge you book as department programming.

### Seven Grandfather Teachings

Wisdom, love, respect, bravery, honesty, humility, truth — these are Anishinaabe, and they do not paste onto a Dakota household as a values poster. Dakota ethics and kinship have their own names, so ask.

### Blood quantum

Blood quantum is colonial technology, and enrollment is nation business.

### Two-spirit

Native LGBTQ people exist, and the variation is named, so this is not a side note and not a branding exercise.

### Urban Native

Urban Native people are not off the list, wherever they live.

A land acknowledgment is not consultation.

sections.heading: Religion and Healing
sections.body:
Traditional practice and Christianity both live here — often in the same family.

### Missions and ceremony

Catholic missions, Episcopal missions, boarding-school Christianity, and traditional ceremony are all Minnesota facts, and the American Indian Religious Freedom Act (1978) is law. Ceremony is not a team-building event. Hmong txiv neeb is not a sweat lodge, and Dakota lodge is not Anishinaabe lodge by default.

If they name traditional healing, follow their lead and the nation’s, since a pastor, a priest, or a healer is the case plan when this family asked. Do not book a lodge as department programming, and do not photograph ceremony.

### Boarding-school harm

Spiritual harm from boarding schools is structure: language forbidden, ceremony punished, children taken. That harm sits in the same clinic as ordinary chronic disease, and you can hold both, but you do not interrogate a ceremony to complete a field.

A white convert to a lodge is not a citizen of a nation, and a Dakota person who is Catholic is still Dakota. Mixing those facts is how the meeting goes wrong.

sections.heading: Greetings
sections.body:
Follow this room. A handshake is common in many rooms, but a protocol invented from a training slide is not a greeting, so do not force a hand, and remember that a word you learned is not an icebreaker.

### Elders and titles

Elders come first, so listen longer than the form wants, use titles if they use them, and ask how to say a name.

You are a guest in nation space even when the meeting is in a county building. The Black nod is African American intelligence, and As-salāmu ʿalaykum is Somali and Muslim intelligence, which is why importing another community’s greeting is a mash.

### Silence

Silence can be thought, not refusal, and directness is not rudeness. Filling every pause because Minnesota Nice is uncomfortable is not listening.

sections.heading: Naming
sections.body:
Ask how to say a name, since English names, nation names, and language names may all sit on one person, and enrollment names are nation business.

### Not a quiz

A name is not a blood-quantum quiz, so do not joke, and do not Anglicize. The form that only fits Mary Jones is a gate.

You do not decide who is Native. A scientist named in English and a language teacher named in Ojibwemowin can be siblings, and neither is more authentic as a case note.

Pronounce Bois Forte, Mille Lacs, Shakopee, Pezihutazizi, and if you cannot, ask, because literacy includes the map.

sections.heading: Dates and Calendar
sections.body:
The calendar holds treaty dates and 1862. 26 December — the Mankato executions — is literacy, not a holiday you put on a flyer. There is boarding-school remembrance, American Indian Month in Minnesota (May, as the state has marked it), and the nation days and powwow calendars some families name, while ricing season and hunting seasons are treaty practice.

### This family’s calendar

A calendar date is literacy, but it is not consultation and not a day off the form. “Native holiday” does not belong on a case note, so ask this family and this nation.

Juneteenth is African American literacy, and Eid is not this page, because another community’s calendar is not inclusion here.

sections.heading: Education
sections.body:
Boarding-school history is structure in the school building too, and it still shapes how families meet a school.

### Schools and colleges

The educational picture includes tribal schools, public schools, language nests, tribal colleges, University of Minnesota and Minnesota State students, attorneys with JDs, physicians, scientists, and teachers.

Bachelor’s or higher among Compass Native American adults 25 and older is 22.5 percent (ACS 2019–2023), and high school graduate or higher is 88.4 percent. Date it, and remember that a rate is not the person.

A degree is not exceptional in a way that insults the rest. Athletics is not the path, and language revitalization is not extra, while English-only forms are a gate even when speech is strong.

### Teachers and scholars

Anton Treuer’s public Ojibwe-language work, tribal-college faculty, and classroom teachers in Onamia or Red Lake are the same educational story as a Ph.D., not a hierarchy of authenticity.

A parent who speaks Dakota or Ojibwe and limited English is not illiterate, which means the English-only IEP is the gate.

sections.heading: Etiquette
sections.body:
Listen, and do not photograph ceremony. Hospitality is not consent to extract, and you still keep medical and legal time.

### Guest

Do not record a lodge, and do not ask for a song as a closer, because you are a guest. A design is not a logo for the department.

Food offered in a home is courtesy, and you still keep the clock for court and clinic. Frybread is not a personality, but refusing everything as professionalism is not courtesy either.

Nation offices are not a research site, so pay, and report back.

sections.heading: Communication
sections.body:
Ojibwe and Dakota language revitalization are underway, and English is common, so both realities may sit in the same household.

### What Compass shows

Compass Native American (age 5+): 87.9 percent English only; 12.1 percent a language other than English; 3.2 percent speak English less than very well (ACS 2019–2023). Date it. Low limited-English-proficient numbers on a Compass line are not permission to skip the language an elder asks for.

Book an interpreter if they ask, since a word you learned is not expertise, and you do not correct English in the lobby.

### Silence and story

Silence can be thought, not refusal, and directness is not rudeness, while story and circular speech can be how an elder thinks in public. A short English yes may be exhaustion, so ask whether they agree, and remember that a smile is not consent.

sections.heading: Other Considerations
sections.body:
Blood quantum is colonial technology. Enrollment versus community is nation business, and so is data sovereignty, while two-spirit people exist.

### MMIW and child welfare

Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women is current structure, not a poster. The state has a record of taking children, and that is why ICWA exists.

Follow the law and still see a family, which means you do not out anyone, and mandated reporting still stands.

### Not one economy

Gaming revenue at one nation is not the Dakota story, and poverty on a Compass line is not the Anishinaabe story. Scientists, lawyers, doctors, teachers, and professionals in tribally run programs exist in the same nations as people on waivers, so community portrait means all of that, and dominant culture does not get to choose which slice is “the real Native.”

Haaland v. Brackeen (2023) upheld ICWA, and that is current law, so the Act is not optional because a commenter was uncomfortable.

sections.heading: Health
sections.body:
The pattern, dated: American Indian Minnesotans have among the worst health outcomes of any group in the state — date the specific rate when you have the controlling Minnesota Department of Health or tribal-epidemiology source. Do not invent a number here to sound complete.

### Compass

Compass Native American (ACS 2019–2023): 16.2 percent with a disability; 8.5 percent without health insurance; median household income about $58,000; 17.9 percent below poverty. Date it, and remember that a rate is not the person.

### Systems of care

Indian Health Service, tribal health, urban Indian health, and county clinics are not interchangeable. Olmstead and disability still apply, and so does nationhood. Believe reported pain, because historical trauma and ordinary chronic disease sit in the same body, and you can hold both.

A physician who is a citizen of White Earth and a patient at an urban Indian clinic are both this page, so the clinic is not the whole portrait.

sections.heading: LGBTQ
sections.body:
Two-spirit and LGBTQ Native people exist, and while there is harm in some churches and in some traditional rooms, the variation is named.

Use the name and pronouns, because outing someone to family or to a nation office is not culture, and the people-page rule is the workplace rule.

Two-spirit is not a brand you put on a Heritage Month flyer; it is people.

sections.heading: Hair and Dress
sections.body:
Hair can be spiritual, personal, or neither. Long hair, braids, a ribbon skirt, a jingle dress, a suit in a St. Paul hearing room — all of that is this people. Do not touch, and remember that locs, braids, or long hair are not unprofessional.

CROWN-adjacent harm still happens, so follow this person, and know that a ribbon skirt is not a costume you request.

A lawyer in a ribbon skirt and a scientist in a lab coat are not opposites, since they may be the same person on different Tuesdays.

sections.heading: Music
sections.body:
Drum, song, powwow as public and as nation, church music, and contemporary Minnesota work are all here. A playlist is not engagement, and you are a guest.

A colleague is not a soundtrack of their nation, and powwow is not the only music.

sections.heading: Sports
sections.body:
School sport, nation sport, hockey, basketball, and softball are all here. Over-representation in a sport is not a personality, and the kid may not play, so sport is not the only excellence you can see.

A physician, a software engineer, a language teacher, and a varsity hockey player can be in the same family, which is why the group is not the person.

sections.heading: Literature
sections.body:
Oral literature comes first, followed by contemporary Native writers in this region and language texts, so this is not a people without letters.

### Named writers

Louise Erdrich (Turtle Mountain Band of Chippewa, Minneapolis) is world literature and Minnesota literary life — not one of the eleven, not a mash, but a reminder that Native letters are not a museum. Anton Treuer’s Ojibwe-language work is Minnesota public scholarship, while nation newspapers, language curricula, and testimony at the legislature are the literature of government.

You do not need to quote a novel in the lobby, but you do need to know the record exists, because population size is not culture size.

sections.heading: Art
sections.body:
Beadwork, quill, contemporary studio work, wild rice as food and as nation, and public art are all here. You are a guest, so pay, and remember that a design is not a logo for the department.

A festival is not consultation. An artist who sells work and a chemist at a tribal environmental office are both this portrait.

sections.heading: Civil Rights Memory
sections.body:
The memory here is treaties, 1862, boarding schools, allotment, termination and restoration, AIM in Minneapolis, 1968, ICWA 1978, the Minnesota Indian Family Preservation Act, Haaland v. Brackeen 2023, and Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women, and none of it is “in the past.”

### The record

A DHS badge is not automatically help, and the movement did not succeed so that the form is fair now. Empty follow-up cells on a tribal notice are a structural failure.

There is no U.S. Civil Rights Movement to copy onto this page as a template, because the political literacy here is nation-to-nation, child welfare, land, language, and a state that still has to be made to keep its word.

sections.heading: Business and Work
sections.body:
Work here includes self-determination contracting (Public Law 93-638), gaming as nation revenue rather than a mascot, tribal employment, urban professionals, trades, teachers, health clinicians, scientists in tribal natural-resources departments, and attorneys in tribal courts and in this department. Identity is not a staffing plan.

### Nation economies

A Heritage Month frybread lunch is not consultation, because notice goes to the nation as a government.

Shakopee Mdewakanton’s economic position is real, but it is not the Dakota story copied onto Upper Sioux or Lower Sioux, and White Earth and Red Lake are not one economy. Name the nation, since “Casino Indian” is not a type.

Native staff are not unpaid liaisons, so pay the work or do not ask for it.

sections.heading: Healthcare Encounters
sections.body:
Ask where they get care, because Indian Health Service, tribal health, urban Indian health, and county clinics are not one door. Believe pain, and include family and ceremony if they want them.

Refer with competence, knowing that mandated reporting still exists and that staff are not unpaid cultural experts.

### Trust

Mistrust is historical and current, since help-seeking that becomes a child-welfare petition is a pattern families already know. Tuskegee is African American medical history — not this page — and the pattern to name here is a county file that sounds like removal.

Offer gender match if they want it, and do not force a handshake. Inquiry under ICWA and MIFPA is not optional curiosity.

sections.heading: Diaspora and Adjacent
sections.body:
Alaska Native is a different brief. Other U.S. tribal citizens living in Minnesota are not automatically one of the eleven, and First Nations from Canada are not the eleven, while urban Native is not a leftover.

### Not one Native module

There is never one Native module, and “Indigenous” is not a mash with Māori training slides. Open the Alaska Native brief for Alaska Native people, and open this one for the eleven and for urban Native Minnesota that still belongs to a nation.

Historic African American, Somali, and Hmong are different cultural intelligences, so shared “people of color” language in a training is not shared nationhood.

sections.heading: Statistics
sections.body:
Compass Native American (ACS 2019–2023), dated: about 162,216 people; Twin Cities 44.8 percent, Greater Minnesota 55.2 percent; 40.1 percent age 17 or younger; 7.0 percent 65+; 3.8 percent foreign-born.

### Language, education, income

Language (age 5+): 87.9 percent English only, 12.1 percent another language, 3.2 percent English less than very well. Education (25+): 88.4 percent high school or higher, 22.5 percent bachelor’s or higher. Median household income is about $58,000, with 17.9 percent below poverty, 54.4 percent owner-occupied, an average household size of 2.54, disability at 16.2 percent, and 8.5 percent without health insurance.

### What the count is not

Compass cannot disaggregate by tribe, and counts disagree with enrollment, with “American Indian alone,” and with “alone or in combination,” so date the number you cite, and remember that a rate is not the person.

Child-welfare disproportionality is a gate. For health outcomes, date the controlling Minnesota Department of Health or tribal-epidemiology source, and do not invent a statewide “worst” percentage if you cannot date it.

Population size is not culture size, and 162,216 is not permission to write a brochure.

sections.heading: Resources
sections.body:
The resources are each nation’s government, the Minnesota Indian Affairs Council, the DHS Office of Indian Policy, Tribal-State Relations Training, ICWA and MIFPA, Haaland v. Brackeen (2023), and the urban Indian organizations named on this page. The Compass Native American profile is administrative, not government-to-government, and a community leadership council is not a substitute for government-to-government.

### Learn on your own time

Take Tribal-State Relations Training, and remember that a Native colleague is not an unpaid tutor, so pay partners, and report back.

The Office of Equal Opportunity and Access is a discrimination door, not this page. The African American brief is not this page, and Alaska Native is not this page.

sections.heading: How it hits DHS gates — the 40%
sections.body:
Workplace culture and service delivery are both candidates here.

Child welfare: ICWA and MIFPA apply. Active efforts are documented work with the family’s people, culture, and values — not a box checked after a removal — and kin search is not flavor. If you work that system, the nation is a government, not a culture consult.

Health and disability: IHS, tribal health, urban Indian health, and county are not interchangeable, so believe reported pain. Olmstead still applies, and ceremony is not DHS programming.

Notices and comment: notice to nations on the same day as an eList is not consultation, and empty follow-up cells are a structural failure, so pay, and report back.

If you skip consultation because you “understand Native culture now,” this has failed and it may be unlawful.

sections.heading: A Note on This Guide
sections.body:
This brief is about Alaska Native peoples who live, work, study, and use services in Minnesota, and it is worth saying plainly at the start that Alaska Native is not one of the eleven Minnesota nations, nor is it a culture sticker to be placed on an Ojibwe file.

### Who this is

Iñupiaq, Yup’ik, Cup’ik, Unangax̂ (Aleut), Alutiiq / Sugpiaq, Athabascan peoples (including Gwich’in and others), Tlingit, Haida, and Tsimshian are distinct peoples, and some people from each of those nations live in Minnesota. Wherever they live, sovereignty still belongs to their nations, which is also why it helps to know that ANCSA corporations are not the same kind of thing as Bois Forte or Lower Sioux.

The community portrait is wide, taking in attorneys, physicians, scientists, teachers, military families, Mayo and university students, people who work for tribally run and corporate programs, artists, and elders. This is not one socioeconomic slice, and it is not a subsistence cartoon copied onto a St. Paul lobby.

There is no Compass cultural-community count for Alaska Native Minnesota on this page, and that absence is itself a finding. When a controlling source exists, date any Minnesota-specific number you use, and please do not invent a population by borrowing one from the eleven.

### Who this is not

This brief is not about the eleven Minnesota nations, because filing this household under “Native” next to Leech Lake closes the meeting with a polite label rather than opening it. Other U.S. tribal citizens living here are not covered by this page by default, either.

### How to read this

Read this as an orientation rather than a profile, which means asking which nation the person belongs to and always deferring to this family. The population in this state may be small, but the culture is not, and a small Minnesota count is not permission to write a brochure.

The facts that follow are meant to help you meet people well, and the history is here so that the meeting is clearer, not so that you deliver a lecture.

sections.heading: Origins and the Founding of a People
sections.body:
Alaska Native peoples are older than the Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act and older than this department, and they carry distinct languages, territories, and legal histories whose differences matter in the room.

### Named peoples

The Iñupiaq are of the north; the Yup’ik and Cup’ik of the west; the Unangax̂ of the Aleutians; the Alutiiq / Sugpiaq of Kodiak and the gulf; the Athabascan peoples of the interior; and the Tlingit, Haida, and Tsimshian of the southeast. They are not one people, and this brief does not treat them as one, since each carries its own language, territory, and history.

### Legal history

The Russian colonial period, the U.S. purchase (1867), territorial status, statehood (1959), and the Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act (1971) together make up the legal history. ANCSA created regional and village corporations, but it is important to understand that corporations are not nations by another name, because the nations remain.

### What people brought

People brought nationhood, language, kinship, a relationship with land and water, and subsistence as a structure of life in home communities. What they meet in Minnesota, by contrast, is an English form and a checkbox that already had eleven nations on it.

History is literacy for the meeting, which means it is something you carry into the room rather than a speech you give the family.

sections.heading: Geography
sections.body:
Homelands remain in Alaska, while Minnesota is where some citizens live now — in the Twin Cities, Rochester, military and health corridors, university towns, and ordinary counties. There is not a reservation of theirs in this state, so home is somewhere else.

### Name the nation

Distance to home is how the work actually runs, since it shows up as airfare, time zones, and the question of who can sit with an elder in Bethel or Nome while a form is in St. Paul. Nationhood is not a Minnesota ZIP code, so name the nation rather than the address.

### Regions are not interchangeable

Southeast (Tlingit, Haida, Tsimshian) is not North Slope Iñupiaq, and Yup’ik villages are not Anchorage by default. Because the regions differ in these ways, ask rather than assume which one a family calls home.

sections.heading: Migration and Foundational Events
sections.body:
People move for school, work, military service, and health care — including Minnesota specialty care — and they remain of their nations wherever they go, because nationhood was not left behind in Alaska.

### Boarding schools

Boarding schools in Alaska and in the Lower 48 are part of this history, which means that if all you know is a Minnesota powwow, you will misfile this household.

### ANCSA, 1971

If the Great Migration is Black America’s foundational demographic event and 1862 is Dakota Minnesota’s, then ANCSA and boarding school are the literacy here. Corporations and cash settlements did not end nationhood, which is why the nation, not the corporation, is the first question.

### Why Minnesota

Mayo, universities, military service, and ordinary jobs bring people here, so ask how they got here rather than assuming, and do not assume they are “from the eleven.”

sections.heading: Family
sections.body:
Kinship systems vary by nation, and who cares for the child may not match a nuclear English form, so ask who should be in the room before you assume.

### ICWA

ICWA still applies to Indian children as defined in federal law — and that includes Alaska Native children. Because that is statute, follow it, while still seeing a family rather than a file. Do not copy a Leech Lake script onto the wrong nation without first asking which law applies, since the eleven Minnesota nations are not this family’s nation.

### Who decides

You do not decide who is Alaska Native; the nation does, which is why the question of belonging is never yours to settle.

sections.heading: Minnesota
sections.body:
People live, work, and use services here, but the Office of Indian Policy and the eleven are not automatic doors for Alaska Native households, so do not treat them as such.

### Partners they name

Work with the partners they name, pay them, and report back. Some people use urban Indian organizations — including the Indian Health Board of Minneapolis — so ask which ones matter to this family, since copying Leech Lake and stopping there is not notice.

### Staff in the building

Staff who are Alaska Native are colleagues, not unpaid liaisons, because identity is not a staffing plan.

### Count

Date a Minnesota-specific count when you have one. For now, the pattern is what we have, and a missing cell is a finding rather than a gap to fill with a guess.

sections.heading: Heart of the People
sections.body:
Nationhood comes first, and language, land, kinship, and subsistence as a structure of life in home communities all follow from it.

### Not a copy of another page

This is not the Eleven Nations page with a different map, nor is it a Somali or African American sentence borrowed because the checkbox was “other.”

### The group is not the person

Iñupiaq is not Tlingit, and a scientist in Rochester and a hunter at home can be the same family, which is why the group never tells you who the person is.

sections.heading: Core Concepts
sections.body:
These concepts recur, but they express differently by nation and family, so treat them as hypotheses rather than as a script for the person in front of you.

### Named nations

Ask which nation, because the names on this page are not flavor; they are the point.

### Subsistence

Subsistence is a structure of life in home communities, and it may still sit in a Minnesota household as food, money, kinship, and seasonal travel, even far from Alaska.

### ANCSA

ANCSA is a legal fact, not a personality, and the corporations it created are not nations by another name.

### Language and ceremony

Language matters, and ceremony is nationhood rather than a module. Blood quantum and enrollment are nation business, not questions for staff to settle. Two-spirit people exist, and urban life in Minnesota is not assimilation by default.

sections.heading: Religion and Healing
sections.body:
Traditional practice and Christianity both live here, including Russian Orthodox in some regions, other churches, and traditional practice alongside them.

### This family, this nation

Ceremony is not department programming, and it cannot be borrowed from other communities: Hmong txiv neeb is not this page, and Dakota lodge is not this page either.

Follow this family and this nation, and treat clergy as part of the case plan when the family has asked for that.

sections.heading: Greetings
sections.body:
Follow this room, because a protocol invented from a Minnesota training slide is not a greeting, and you should not force a hand.

### Elders

Pay attention to elders, and listen longer than the form wants you to, since what an elder brings matters more than the form’s pace.

### Not borrowed from another brief

The Black nod is African American intelligence, and a Somali greeting is Somali intelligence, so neither one belongs on this page or in this meeting.

sections.heading: Naming
sections.body:
Ask how to say a name, since English names and nation names may both sit on one person.

### Enrollment is not a quiz

You do not decide who is Alaska Native; the nation does. A name is not a quiz, so take the name as it is given rather than testing it.

sections.heading: Dates and Calendar
sections.body:
Nation calendars and subsistence seasons shape time in home communities, while ordinary Minnesota school calendars shape it here.

### ANCSA anniversary

The anniversary is literacy, not a flyer.

### A date is not consultation

A calendar date is literacy, but it is not consultation, so it never replaces asking.

sections.heading: Education
sections.body:
Boarding-school history is structure, not background, and English-only forms are a gate even when someone’s speech is strong, which is why a parent who needs a language is not illiterate.

### Community portrait

University students, researchers, teachers, and physicians from these nations live in Minnesota, so the community portrait is not a dropout cartoon, and population here is not culture size.

sections.heading: Etiquette
sections.body:
You are a guest, so do not photograph ceremony, and remember that hospitality is not consent to extract.

### Time

Keep medical and legal time, while remembering that distance to an elder in Alaska is still time a family has to spend.

sections.heading: Communication
sections.body:
There are many languages, and although English is common in Minnesota, you should book what they ask for, since a word you learned is not expertise.

### Silence and directness

Directness is not rudeness, and silence can be thought, so give it room.

### Interpreters

If they name a language, book it, and do not assume an Ojibwe or Dakota interpreter covers this household, because those are the languages of other nations.

sections.heading: Other Considerations
sections.body:
Enrollment versus community is nation business, as is data sovereignty. Two-spirit people exist, so follow the law, do not out anyone, and still see a family.

### Filing

Do not file this household under the eleven, because a small Minnesota count is not permission to thin the people.

sections.heading: Health
sections.body:
Do not invent a Minnesota rate. Indian Health Service and tribal health in Alaska are not a county clinic here, so ask where they get care rather than assuming. Believe reported pain, and date a rate when you have one so that the number is never mistaken for the person.

### Community portrait

A physician who is Iñupiaq and a patient using Mayo are both this page, which is a reminder that the same community can sit on both sides of the exam table.

### Urban Indian health

Some people use urban Indian organizations in the Twin Cities, including the Indian Health Board of Minneapolis, so ask rather than assume, since that door is not automatic, and it is not the eleven.

sections.heading: LGBTQ
sections.body:
LGBTQ and two-spirit Alaska Native people exist, so use the name.

### Privacy

Outing someone to family is not culture.

sections.heading: Hair and Dress
sections.body:
Hair can be spiritual, personal, or neither, so do not touch it, and do not treat hair as a professionalism test.

### Same person, different days

A lab coat and regalia can be the same person on different days, which is why neither one tells you everything about who they are.

sections.heading: Music
sections.body:
Drum, song, and contemporary work are each named by nation rather than blended into a mash.

### Not engagement

A playlist is not engagement, however well chosen it may be.

sections.heading: Sports
sections.body:
Ordinary school sport happens here, while home-community sport is not a personality, and the kid may not play at all.

### Not the only excellence

Sport is not the only excellence, so look for the others as well.

sections.heading: Literature
sections.body:
Oral literature and written work both belong here, because this is not a people without letters.

### In the lobby

You do not need to quote in the lobby, and population in Minnesota is not culture size.

sections.heading: Art
sections.body:
Art is named by nation, and because you are a guest, pay for what you use.

### Not a logo

A design is not a logo for the department, and a festival is not consultation with the nation.

sections.heading: Civil Rights Memory
sections.body:
Boarding schools, the Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act, and federal Indian law are this memory, and none of it is “in the past.”

### A badge is not automatically help

A DHS badge is not automatically help, so follow the law that applies while you still see this family.

sections.heading: Business and Work
sections.body:
ANCSA corporations are not the eleven, and in Minnesota you will meet professionals, trades, students, military, and health workers from these nations.

### Colleagues

Staff are colleagues, not unpaid liaisons. Scientists and attorneys exist, and so do waiver households, which is why a community portrait means both.

sections.heading: Healthcare Encounters
sections.body:
Ask where they get care, because Alaska systems and Minnesota systems are not one door. Believe pain, and book the language they ask for.

### Law that still applies

Mandated reporting still exists, and ICWA may still apply, so ask which law covers this family.

sections.heading: Diaspora and Adjacent
sections.body:
This is not the eleven, and it is not a culture sticker on Ojibwe, while other U.S. tribal citizens are not this page by default.

### Never one Native module

There is never one Native module, so open the Eleven Nations brief for Minnesota nations, and open this one for Alaska Native households.

sections.heading: Statistics
sections.body:
There is no Compass Alaska Native Minnesota count on this page, so for now the pattern is what we have, and you should date a number when a controlling source exists.

### A missing cell is a finding

Do not invent a population, because a small count is not a thin culture.

sections.heading: Resources
sections.body:
Start with the nation they name. Some people use urban Indian organizations — including the Indian Health Board of Minneapolis — so ask which ones matter to them.

### Government-to-government

The Office of Indian Policy is not automatic government-to-government for the eleven in this household’s case, although ANCSA is public record you can read for yourself.

Learn on your own time rather than the family’s, pay partners, and report back.

sections.heading: How it hits DHS gates — the 40%
sections.body:
Workplace culture and service delivery are both candidates here.

Do not file this household under the eleven. Book the language they ask for, ask where they get care, and remember that OIP is not automatic.

If you skip the nation because you “already did Native training,” this has failed.

sections.heading: A Note on This Guide
sections.body:
