This page offers European American cultural intelligence for Minnesota, and it approaches its subject as a set of historic cultures rather than a single “white people” mash. Norwegian Lutheran farm culture, German civic order, Irish Catholic St. Paul, the Iron Range, Yankee New England, and the later European streams are distinct traditions that cannot be folded into one module, because treating them as one would repeat the same error we refused to make for Black and Asian communities.

### Who this is

People of color have to understand these cultures too, because they shape the rooms everyone works in, while dominant-culture staff have to learn to see these traditions as culture rather than as professionalism. None of this makes white-versus-minority the only frame, and none of it claims that racism is symmetrical, since the record still exists and nothing in this brief asks anyone to set it aside.

People could report more than one ancestry, and the 2024 ACS one-year estimates (Census Bureau, table B04006) count German at about 1,608,999 (plus or minus 22,427); Norwegian at 662,072 (12,215); Irish at 569,161 (14,439); English at 360,916 (11,988); Swedish at 354,188 (10,217); and Polish at 214,308 (8,126). English and Swedish are now about tied within their margins of error, and Irish has grown while German and Norwegian have fallen. About 1.29 million answers were unclassified or not reported, and about 206,000 people wrote “American.” The Minnesota State Demographic Center, drawing on 2018 ACS ancestry data, counted German at about 1,801,700; Norwegian at 810,300; Irish at 516,500; Swedish at 429,800; English at 290,200; and Polish at 248,000. The overlap among these groups is the point, and the figures should be dated to 2018 whenever you use them.

### Who this is not

This brief does not describe one white people, and it is not a substitute for the briefs on Somali, Hmong, and African American communities or on the eleven nations. Nor is it a claim that racism is symmetrical, a point worth repeating because a page about dominant-culture streams can easily be misread as a balancing of the record.

### How to read this

Always defer to the family in front of you, and open the people brief that matches the household you are actually meeting rather than relying on this page to describe them.

sections.heading: Origins and the Founding of Settler Cultures Here
sections.body:
The settler cultures of Minnesota arrived in layers after the Indigenous nations who were already here: first the French, then the Yankees, then the large German and Scandinavian streams, followed by Irish, Slavic, and other groups, each of which built its presence through homestead, railroad, church, and cooperative institutions.

### History for the meeting

If you believe you have no culture, you will describe your own form as “neutral,” and this brief exists to name that problem. History is literacy for the desk, and that includes staff of color who did not grow up inside this unmarked system and so have to read it from the outside.

### What people brought

The full mosaic, stream by stream, is still deepening, but it is already clear that German, Norwegian, Swedish, Finnish, Irish, Czech, and Polish are separate grammars rather than a race poster.

sections.heading: Geography
sections.body:
European American Minnesota is spread across farm counties, the Iron Range, the Irish and German civic world of St. Paul, Scandinavian towns, and the later metro suburbs, so it cannot be drawn as one map.

### Homeland

These streams came from named places in Europe rather than from a blank, which is why the first step is always to name the stream.

### Minnesota

Name the stream and the town together, since the Iron Range is not a Minneapolis suburb.

sections.heading: Migration and Foundational Events
sections.body:
Homestead and railroad brought the first waves, later European streams followed, and people have continued to leave and return ever since.

### Foundational events

Settler presence here is not empty of 1862.

### Who you meet

Do not tell a Native household that this is “everyone’s immigration story,” because their nations were already here when these streams arrived.

sections.heading: Family
sections.body:
Inviting “just the parents” is already a design choice rather than a neutral default, so ask who should be in the room.

### Who is in the household

Ask who should be in the room, and do not treat the nuclear household as professional and the extended one as a deficit, since the nuclear form is one cultural pattern among others.

### Who speaks

The person who talks in the lobby may not be the person who decides, so follow this room rather than your assumption about who holds the decision.

sections.heading: Minnesota
sections.body:
Ask where unmarked habits run through county desks and church geography in this department.

### Places

Name it without mocking it, and at the same time do not let it write the cap and call that “just being adult,” because an unmarked habit can quietly set limits on a household.

### Partners

Church geography is real, but it is not “the community,” so open the people brief that matches this household rather than treating a congregation as its voice.

sections.heading: Heart — Unmarked Grammar
sections.body:
Minnesota Nice is a popular phrase for a style of politeness. It is a label people use, not a measured trait of any group, so ask the household rather than assuming.

### In this state

When a unit says “we don’t see color, we treat everyone the same,” ask what that rule assumes about the people it serves and who it was built for.

sections.heading: Core Concepts
sections.body:
These concepts recur across the streams, but they are hypotheses rather than conclusions, and you still test them against the family in front of you.

### Identical process and fairness

Ask whether identical process is being treated as the whole meaning of fairness, even though it is a practice rather than a statute.

### Disagreement

Ask directly, and treat a gentle no as a no.

### Time and appointments

Ask what makes a time hard for this household. Other time grammars are not rudeness, and reading them that way turns a habit into a moral judgment.

### Restraint and professionalism

Ask how restraint and difference in public are understood in this household, and do not perform a lutefisk joke as the file.

sections.heading: Religion and Healing
sections.body:
Lutheran, Catholic, evangelical, and Jewish religious life are related to ethnicity here, but religion and ethnicity are not the same object and should not be read as one.

### Streams

Open the religion track for the particulars, and do not make the pastor the case plan unless the household asked for that.

### Practice

Ask whether a congregation is part of how this household’s week runs, and work with it if it is, while you still keep medical and legal time.

sections.heading: Greetings
sections.body:
Ask how this person wants to be greeted and addressed, whether with a handshake, a first name, or a title.

### Titles

Follow this room, and do not treat first-name speed as the professional standard for every household you serve.

### This room

Do not mistake closing with “have a good one” for a universal form of warmth.

sections.heading: Naming
sections.body:
Ask which name order this person uses, because first, middle, and last is one convention among many.

### How to file

Patronymics, two surnames, clan names, and three-part Somali names all hit this form as error, which means that a form that only fits Mary Jones is a gate built inside this culture.

sections.heading: Dates and Calendar
sections.body:
Which dates matter differs by household, so ask.

### Calendar

Other calendars still have to fit around the household’s own, and while knowing a date is literacy, it is not the same thing as engagement.

sections.heading: Education
sections.body:
Ask what school and college mean to this family.

### School and language

An English-only IEP is still a gate for someone else’s parent in the same building, and a degree should not be treated as the only kind of intelligence a family brings.

sections.heading: Etiquette
sections.body:
Do not treat lateness or a raised voice as a character issue.

### In the home

Follow the household’s lead on food.

### Time

Keep to medical and legal timelines. If someone misses an appointment, first check the time, transport, interpreter and work schedule.

sections.heading: Communication
sections.body:
Say what you mean, and ask directly whether the person agrees.

### Language

Whether someone answers bluntly or gently, ask whether they agree.

sections.heading: Other Considerations
sections.body:
Class runs inside these streams as much as between them, which is why the Iron Range is not Edina.

### Named harms

Racism is a structure rather than a both-sides placement-rate argument. Do not use this brief to say the placement rate is just culture, and do not conclude that white people have no culture worth studying.

sections.heading: Health
sections.body:
Do not invent a “white health” rate and treat it as a personality, because a rate is not the person.

### Access

Rural hospital facts belong on the rural page, so date whatever you cite there, and believe reported pain for everyone.

sections.heading: LGBTQ
sections.body:
LGBTQ people live in every one of these streams, and church climates vary by synod and parish.

### This person

Use the name the person gives you, and do not out someone to a congregation and call it culture.

sections.heading: Hair and Dress
sections.body:
Ask whether a “professional” hair standard is being applied to someone it was not built for, and remember that the CROWN Act still applies to others in the same building.

### Dress

Do not police dress, and do not treat the unmarked as neutral when it is one culture’s standard.

sections.heading: Music
sections.body:
Ask what music, if any, matters to this household.

### Variation

A playlist is not engagement, so do not make lutefisk the file or let a familiar song stand in for knowing the household.

sections.heading: Sports
sections.body:
Ask what sport, if any, matters to this person or family, and remember that none of it is a personality.

### Not the whole person

Do not assume the kid plays, and do not make sport the civic test of whether a family belongs.

sections.heading: Literature
sections.body:
This is a written public, carried through newspapers and church, and it is not a people without letters, and neither is anyone else on this spine.

### Literacy in the lobby

See the form itself as culture rather than as a neutral page.

sections.heading: Art
sections.body:
Art spans civic art, church art, state fair, and contemporary work.

### Guest

You are a guest in these spaces, and a festival is not consultation.

sections.heading: Civil Rights Memory
sections.body:
This is a settler state, and 1862 sits in its memory. Civil rights are something this building had to be made to keep, and none of this is a symmetry claim.

### The badge

360° does not cancel the record, and a DHS badge is not automatically help.

sections.heading: Business and Work
sections.body:
Farm, cooperative, civic club, corporation, public employment, and the union Iron Range are all part of this picture, so it cannot be described as one economy.

### Work

Staff of color still have to navigate this unmarked system simply to get a form through.

### Staff

Identity is not a staffing plan, and this unmarked system is still the system everyone works inside, whoever happens to sit at the desk.

sections.heading: Healthcare Encounters
sections.body:
Ask whether the clinic’s defaults of English, on-time, and a nuclear family work for this household.

### Language

See the default for what it is, without mocking it.

### The meeting

Do not let the default write the cap, because a habit treated as nature can quietly cap the help.

sections.heading: Diaspora and Adjacent
sections.body:
There is not one white people, and this brief does not pretend otherwise.

### Adjacent doors

If the household is not this, open the people brief that matches them, and do not use this door to skip Somali or the eleven nations.

sections.heading: Statistics
sections.body:
Using the 2024 ACS one-year estimates (Census Bureau, table B04006) count German at about 1,608,999 (plus or minus 22,427); Norwegian at 662,072 (12,215); Irish at 569,161 (14,439); English at 360,916 (11,988); Swedish at 354,188 (10,217); and Polish at 214,308 (8,126). English and Swedish are now about tied within their margins of error, and Irish has grown while German and Norwegian have fallen. About 1.29 million answers were unclassified or not reported, and about 206,000 people wrote “American.” The Minnesota State Demographic Center, using 2018 ACS ancestry data, reported German at about 1,801,700; Norwegian at 810,300; Irish at 516,500; Swedish at 429,800; English at 290,200; and Polish at 248,000. Date these figures to 2018, and remember that the overlap is the point.

### Counts

People could report more than one ancestry, which is why one person can appear in more than one of these counts. A Star Tribune chart by MaryJo Webster, using 2018 ACS data, says that about 45 percent of Minnesotans who reported more than one ancestry identified as Scandinavian, but the majority listed German ancestry, and again the overlap is the point.

### What the count is not

A rate is not the person, and there is not one white people.

sections.heading: Resources
sections.body:
Start with the Minnesota State Demographic Center ancestry tables and the Star Tribune 2020 overlap reporting, then turn to the religion track, the rural place brief, and the eleven.

### Public doors

Open the stream this household names rather than the one you assume.

### Where to learn more

Use these resources yourself, and keep the meeting focused on the household.

sections.heading: How it hits DHS gates — the 40%
sections.body:
Workplace culture and service delivery are both candidates for where this culture does its work.

360° does not cancel the record, but it does explain how a majority-white institution that treats everyone the same keeps reproducing the same gates while calling the result professionalism.

For people of color, learning this culture is not extra emotional labor performed for white comfort; it is how you legislate, supervise, and survive the building without confusing it with nature.

Do not use this page to explain away a placement rate as culture, and do not conclude that white people have no culture worth studying.

sections.heading: A Note on This Guide
sections.body:
This brief is about rural Minnesota as geography and infrastructure rather than as a racial type, and rural is not code for white.

### Who this is

A farmer and a miner are not the same person, and neither one stands for the whole of Greater Minnesota. Somali households in Worthington, Mexican households in a dairy county, Hmong households that do live outside the metro, and the eleven nations are not afterthoughts here, because they are part of who lives in these towns.

When both apply, open the people brief and this place brief together, and name the town, because Greater Minnesota is not one region and not one people.

A community portrait here is neither a pickup-truck cartoon nor a poverty poster. Financial analysts in county buildings, scientists in plant labs, physicians in critical-access hospitals, teachers, attorneys, remote professionals, farmers, miners, plant workers, dairy workers, and small Main Street owners are all Greater Minnesota. Dominant culture does not get to choose which slice is “the real rural,” and people of color in these towns are not visitors in someone else’s landscape.

A St. Paul form that only works on good broadband is a gate, which is why print in the office still matters and so does a phone that works. Population density is not culture size, and a small town is not a thin brief.

### Who this is not

Rochester is not “rural” simply because it is outside the metro, since it is a health city, just as Duluth is not a farm and Bemidji is not Worthington. This is not the European American brief, and it is not a substitute for Somali, Mexican, Hmong, or the eleven nations.

### How to read this

Read it as an orientation, and always defer to this family and this county. The facts that follow are meant to help you meet people well, and the history is here so that the meeting is clearer, not so that you deliver a lecture.

sections.heading: Origins and the Founding of a Place
sections.body:
Dakota and Anishinaabe homelands come first, and this page does not get to start with a homestead as if the land were empty. Settler agriculture, mining, timber, and railroads made the towns, but they did not unmake the nations.

### Towns on this land

Rural Minnesota is not empty of Nations or of immigrants. Worthington, Willmar, Pelican Rapids, Austin, Albert Lea, Owatonna, St. Cloud, and a dozen plant and dairy towns are Minnesota history of the last forty years as much as they are “small town,” while Iron Range labor, for its part, is not a prairie farm.

### Later chapters of the same map

1862 is Dakota literacy that sits on this ground, and boarding schools sat in this same geography. The farm crisis, mine closures, and hospital consolidation are later chapters of the same map, and that history is literacy for the meeting rather than material for a speech.

sections.heading: Geography
sections.body:
Greater Minnesota is not one region, and it helps to say so plainly before naming the parts.

### Regions

The regions include the Iron Range, the prairie, the forest, the Red River, southeast bluff country, southwest dairy, border towns, and lake country that is not a resort brochure.

Name the town, because distance is both a number of miles and a closed office day, and a 9 a.m. St. Paul hybrid meeting is already a gate for a county worker on ice.

### Who lives here

Do not assume Minneapolis, and do not assume a white census tract. The compass on the people pages reads: Mexican Minnesota about 39.2 percent (give or take 1.3 points) Greater Minnesota; Somali about 22.7 percent (give or take 3.6 points) Greater Minnesota (both ACS 2020–2024); Hmong about 94 percent Twin Cities (ACS 2020–2024) — date the people page. This page is about place, so those splits belong on those pages, even though they still change who is in this town.

Rochester is not “rural” because it is outside the metro, since it is a health city, and in the same way Duluth is not a farm and Bemidji is not Worthington.

sections.heading: Migration and Foundational Events
sections.body:
The foundational events here are the farm crisis, mine closures, hospital consolidation, and immigrant labor in plants and dairy. People leave for the metro and return, broadband is a moving fact, and COVID was a reveal of who could stay home and who had to drive.

### Work, not a festival

A skipped visit may be diesel and ice rather than refusal. Secondary migration brought Somali and Latino households here to work, not to a festival, while the eleven nations did not migrate in at all, because the towns were built on their land.

### Calendars that collide

A plant shift and a waiver recertification can land on the same day, and if you only know a county fair, you will miss that collision.

sections.heading: Family
sections.body:
Kin may live on the next section while specialists may be a long drive away, and the person in the room may be a neighbor, a grandmother, or a coworker from the plant. Rural is not code for nuclear white family.

### Who should be in the room

Ask who should be in the room, because plant-town households may be mixed-status, three-name Somali, clan-name Hmong, two-surname Latino, or Dakota/Anishinaabe kin who do not match the English form. Open the people page before you assume the shape of the household.

### Community portrait

A scientist who farms on weekends and a county financial analyst who grew up on the Range are this place, and so is a waiver household, which is why a community portrait has to mean both.

sections.heading: Minnesota
sections.body:
County human services is often the actual desk, alongside regional resource specialists, so print notice in the office still matters, and so does a phone that works.

### Access

A St. Paul design that only works on good broadband is a gate, and hybrid access is an equity condition here too, which is one more reason to name the town.

### Partners in that county

The partners are the parish, the mosque, the civic group, and the nation office, not a metro mailing list you copy once. Copying Minneapolis and stopping is not notice, so pay these partners and report back to them.

sections.heading: Heart of Place
sections.body:
Place is identity for some people and distance for others, so do not romanticize it and do not pathologize it. The group is not the person, and place is not a race.

### In a county building

Cooperatives, churches, and civic groups carry much of local life. If a meeting ends without a decision, ask what was decided and who will do it. Neighbor as infrastructure is also real, but it is not a substitute for a hospital.

### Open both pages

A Somali household down the street has a people page, so open it, while this page holds the miles, the ice, and the county hours.

sections.heading: Core Concepts
sections.body:
These concepts recur, and they express differently by county, town, and household, which means they are hypotheses rather than a script for the person in front of you.

### Distance

Distance means miles, ice, diesel, and a closed office day.

### County capacity

The actual desk may be three people covering a statute written for a metro unit.

### Neighbor as infrastructure

Neighbor as infrastructure is real, but it is not a waiver.

### Church as channel for some

Lutheran unmarked, Catholic parish, evangelical, Native ceremony, mosque, and wat each need to be named rather than mashed together.

### Plant shift as calendar

Nights, weekends, and harvest set the calendar, so the 9 a.m. appointment is already a design choice.

### Broadband

Broadband is a gate, not a personality.

### Print and phone

Both are still operations in the counties this page describes.

A pickup-truck personality is not the work, and a Somali plant worker is not an exception to “rural,” because the people who work in these towns are the town.

sections.heading: Religion and Healing
sections.body:
Spirituality is strong among some, and Lutheran unmarked, Catholic parish, evangelical, Native ceremony, mosque, and wat are each named rather than mashed together.

### Clergy

Clergy are the case plan when the household asked for that, and the religion track is the place to open for the particulars.

### Not a copy of the metro

A mosque in a prairie town is not a copy of Cedar-Riverside. A Dakota ceremony on Dakota land is not a county diversity event, and a Lutheran basement is not “no culture.”

sections.heading: Greetings
sections.body:
Follow this room, since a handshake is common in many rooms and a metro protocol is not professionalism here.

### Respect

Ask who to greet first, or follow the household’s lead. Use Mr./Mrs. until invited otherwise.

sections.heading: Naming
sections.body:
Ask how to say a name, because the form that only fits Mary Jones is a gate here too.

### Names already in these towns

Two surnames, clan names, three-part Somali names, and Dakota and Ojibwe names are already familiar in plant towns and reservation-adjacent towns, even though the database may not know them yet.

sections.heading: Dates and Calendar
sections.body:
Plant shifts, harvest, winter roads, school sports Fridays, Ramadan, Lent, and ricing all shape the calendar, so ask which ones shape this household.

### Literacy, not engagement

A calendar date is literacy, not engagement. Friday night lights are civic in some towns, but they are not language access and not the whole portrait.

sections.heading: Education
sections.body:
Consolidation and distance shape the schools here, and English-only IEPs still appear. The second generation may sit in the same building as a parent who needs a language, and a parent who needs a language is not illiterate.

### Community portrait

The portrait includes a superintendent, a tribal-college student, a plant-lab scientist, and a kid on a 40-mile bus ride, so athletics is not the only path and a small district is not no culture.

sections.heading: Etiquette
sections.body:
Build travel time into the plan, and explain county hours clearly.

### If someone misses an appointment

Keep medical and legal time. Ask before taking any photograph in someone’s home.

sections.heading: Communication
sections.body:
English is common here but not universal, and because cell gaps are real and print still matters, you book the language they ask for.

### What not to assume

Do not assume voicemail works, and do not assume broadband.

### Open the people page

Maay in Worthington is still Maay, and Mixtec in a dairy county is still Mixtec, which is why a Spanish interpreter may still not work.

sections.heading: Other Considerations
sections.body:
Isolation and distance to shelter matter here. Substance patterns exist, but date local figures when you cite them rather than inventing a statewide “rural opioid” personality, and follow the law while you still see a family.

### Rural is not code for white

LGBTQ people live here. Native nations are here, immigrant households are here, and a financial analyst in a government building in this county is here, so a community portrait is not a catalog of deficits.

sections.heading: Health
sections.body:
Hospital closure and service reduction are operations, not background.

### Dated facts

A MinnPost opinion column (Barb Stinnett, April 2026) says Minnesota has about 95 rural hospitals, with approximately 20 at risk of closing or majorly reducing services, and gives no source for the 20. The Minnesota Department of Health supports the 95 under its own definition of rural. A later MinnPost column (Aaron Wittnebel, May 2026) says 23, with nine by year’s end, and the Center for Healthcare Quality and Payment Reform reported in 2025 at least nine at immediate risk. The Department of Health counts 34 rural hospitals as financially distressed, which is a different measure, and DTN Progressive Farmer (April 2026) does not list Minnesota among the nine states it names as most at risk. Date whichever figure you use. A January 31, 2024 repost of Axios reports that an estimated 45 percent of rural hospitals in Minnesota do not offer labor and delivery; that describes hospitals without the service, not necessarily hospitals that lost it. Newer figures: the Center for Healthcare Quality and Payment Reform, via the Pennsylvania Office of Rural Health, counts 50 rural hospitals without labor and delivery in 2026 and eight closures since 2020, and the Department of Health reports 18 counties with reduced or eliminated services from 2013 to 2023. Date whichever you use. A Minnesota Compass / Minnesota Department of Health analysis reported in 2020 found that 40 percent of residents in isolated rural areas reported a chronic condition, a figure cited here as reported. A newer Minnesota Department of Health document says roughly 51 percent of rural adults have at least one chronic condition, and 64 percent counting obesity, using its own wider definition of rural and list of conditions; the two are not directly comparable, so date whichever you use.

### Getting there

A missed visit may be diesel and ice, so believe reported pain. Specialists may be hours away, EMS time is real, and telehealth needs broadband.

A rural physician, a nurse-practitioner holding a county, and a patient who drives two hours are the same place. Indian Health Service and tribal health sit on this map where the nation is, so open that page.

sections.heading: LGBTQ
sections.body:
LGBTQ people live in Greater Minnesota, and distance to affirming care is operations.

### Name and privacy

Use the name the person gives you, and remember that outing someone to a small town is not culture.

sections.heading: Hair and Dress
sections.body:
Hair is not a professionalism test. The CROWN Act still applies here, hijab in a plant town still applies, and you do not touch.

### Same place

A ribbon skirt in a county hearing and a lab coat in a processing plant are both this place.

sections.heading: Music
sections.body:
Music lives in church, school, the community hall, radio, and the named people-page music, so it is not one soundtrack.

### Not engagement

A playlist is not engagement, and Prince is Minnesota whether the Range knows it as theirs or not.

sections.heading: Sports
sections.body:
Friday night and youth sport are civic life in some towns, but they are not a personality and they are not language access, and the kid may not play.

### Not the only excellence

A scientist, a dairy worker, and a varsity captain can be in the same extended family, including in a Somali or Mexican household in this town.

sections.heading: Literature
sections.body:
Local papers, church bulletins, and people-page literatures are all read here, so print still matters and this is not a place without letters.

### Language

County board minutes are the literature of the building, and because Somali- and Spanish-language media reach some of these towns, you book the language.

sections.heading: Art
sections.body:
Art lives in county fairs, church basements, people-page arts, and tribal arts on this land.

### Guest

You are a guest in these spaces, and a festival is not consultation.

sections.heading: Civil Rights Memory
sections.body:
The farm crisis, mine closures, hospital fights, 1862 on Dakota land, and labor in plants are all part of memory here, so this is not a place empty of history.

### What still applies

Civil rights here includes language access in a plant town, ICWA in a county court, and a CROWN complaint in a school. A full portrait does not cancel the record, and a DHS badge is not automatically help.

sections.heading: Business and Work
sections.body:
Farm, mine, timber, plant, hospital, school, small Main Street, remote professional, county employment, and tribal enterprise all run here, so it is not one economy.

### Colleagues

Book a qualified interpreter, and pay for community work. Do not assign either to staff because of who they are. A Mexican scientist in a plant lab and a Somali truck owner are this economy, and so is a fourth-generation farm, which is why a community portrait means all of that.

sections.heading: Healthcare Encounters
sections.body:
Care here means the county clinic, critical access, hours away to a specialist, and telehealth that needs broadband, so ask how they get there. Believe pain, and book the language they ask for.

### Maternity

If the hospital dropped labor and delivery, paperwork that assumes a local birth is already wrong, so date the local fact before you rely on it.

sections.heading: Diaspora and Adjacent
sections.body:
Rural is not a race, so open Somali, Mexican, the eleven, Hmong, European American, or Alaska Native as the household is, and never treat one rural module as a people.

### Name the town

Worthington is not St. Paul. Leech Lake is not a farm county, and the Iron Range is not Edina, so open the people page.

sections.heading: Statistics
sections.body:
Date local facts such as miles, hospital, and broadband. The people-page Compass splits belong on those pages (Mexican about 39.2 percent, give or take 1.3 points, and Somali about 22.7 percent, give or take 3.6 points, Greater Minnesota, ACS 2020–2024; Hmong about 94 percent Twin Cities, ACS 2020–2024 — date each).

### Hospitals and health

Rural hospitals number about 95 in Minnesota (Department of Health, under its own definition); sources put the number at risk between about nine and 23, and the 20 in a MinnPost opinion column (April 2026) carried no source. On maternity, about 45 percent of rural hospitals do not offer labor and delivery (Axios repost, January 2024), and a 2026 count has 50 without it (Center for Healthcare Quality and Payment Reform). The isolated rural chronic condition figure is 40 percent (Minnesota Department of Health via Compass, 2020); a newer Department of Health document says roughly 51 percent of rural adults, on a wider definition of rural. Date each of them, because a rate is not the person, and you still name the town.

A “rural white percentage” is not the culture.

sections.heading: Resources
sections.body:
Start with county human services, regional specialists, and the partner in that town, and add the people-page organizations, along with the Eleven Nations and the Office of Indian Policy where the household is a nation. Compass people profiles give the splits, and print and phone remain resources too.

### How to use them

Pay, and report back, because copying Minneapolis and stopping is not notice. Use these resources yourself before you ask a county colleague to explain.

sections.heading: How it hits DHS gates — the 40%
sections.body:
Workplace culture and service delivery are both candidates here for where these gates take hold.

Notices that only work on good broadband are a gate, which is why print in the office still matters, and a skipped visit may be diesel and ice rather than refusal.

Open the people CI and this place CI together when both apply, and do not use rural as code for white. If the family cannot run the exception in English, the cap is the policy.

sections.heading: A Note on This Guide — a language door, not one people
sections.body:
This brief is about Russian as a language door on the department’s CLAS five-language standing written list, where it sits alongside Hmong, Somali, Spanish, and Vietnamese. It is not a brief about one people. The moment you invent a single “Russian community” from that list, you have already stepped away from the door this brief is trying to hold open, because a list is not the person in front of you and it is not their dialect. Whatever the list says, you still book a qualified interpreter.

### Who this is

Disaggregate before you open a file, because the people who share this language do not share an origin. They include ethnic Russians and Soviet Jews of the 1970s–90s refusenik / Jackson-Vanik stream. They also include Ukrainian households who use Russian, who belong to the Ukrainian people-page rather than this one; Compass Ukrainian is about 22,254 (ACS 2020–2024), and the two should not be mashed together. They include Belarusian, Central Asian, and Caucasian Russian-speakers, along with evangelical and Baptist Russians, some of them in Greater Minnesota towns. And they include recent arrivals, people who came in the 1990s, and a third generation that may not need you to speak Russian at all.

### Who this is not

Use this page for context and questions. It does not describe the person in front of you. Shared language is not shared origin, not shared religion, and not shared politics. The Ukraine war is current structure for some households, and it becomes a trap if you assume every Russian speaker is a combatant or a Putin voter.

There is no Minnesota Compass cultural-community profile titled Russian. The Compass immigration table lists 6,483 Russian immigrants without showing survey years; the Census Bureau’s ACS 2020 to 2024 table B05006 shows 6,301 (give or take 665) Minnesotans born in Russia, and the 2024 single-year table shows 4,923 (give or take 1,239). Neither is a count of speakers. ACS 2020 to 2024 table B16001 counts 13,851 (give or take 1,218) Minnesotans age 5 and older who speak Russian at home, 5,159 of whom speak English less than “very well.” The Star Tribune (31 July 2025) reported that Russian is among the languages each representing about 2% of Minnesotans who speak a language other than English at home, and Minnesota Secretary of State voter materials include Russian. Date whatever number you use, and do not invent a community population to fill the gap.

The diversity inside this language is the point. Consider a Jewish grandmother who left on an exit visa in 1989, an Orthodox parishioner, a Belarusian family that uses Russian at the table, a Ukrainian household that will not accept a “former Soviet” interpreter after 2022, a Baptist family in a Greater Minnesota town, and a professional who does not need an interpreter but whose elder does. They share a language on a form, but they do not share a Tuesday.

### How to read this

Always defer to the person in front of you, because this page is a hypothesis and you still have to test it on this household.

sections.heading: Origins — empire, Soviet, and named streams
sections.body:
There is no single founding of “Russian-speaking Minnesota.” Ethnic Russian peoplehood is older than the Soviet Union and older than this department. It is not the whole door, because other peoples used Russian as an imperial and Soviet language of school, army, and office. That history is exactly why a language list is not a census of who counts.

### History for the meeting

Late-imperial emigration included Jews fleeing pogroms and others leaving the Russian Empire. Some of that older Jewish Minnesota is English-dominant now, which means it is not this CLAS door. Be careful not to mash a 1910 synagogue story onto a 1994 arrival and call the result one community.

### What people brought

The Soviet period produced later streams. There were dissidents; there were Jews denied exit (refuseniks) until Jackson-Vanik and the years that followed opened a way; and then came the 1991 collapse of the USSR, which moved people for work, family, and survival. Evangelical Protestants, Baptists and related churches among them, left in named waves as well. Central Asian and Caucasian families may carry Russian as a public language beside another home language.

What people brought with them is not one kit, since it includes Orthodox practice, Jewish peoplehood, evangelical church life, Soviet official atheism, Cyrillic literacy, professional skill the U.S. did not always recognize, and the memory of a state that surveilled. What they met in Minnesota was an English form, a racial order that may file them as white and skip the interpreter, and often a single interpreter labeled “Russian.”

sections.heading: The Geography of Russian-Speaking Worlds
sections.body:
Homeland is not one flag. The Russian Federation is a geography some families name. Ukraine is another, although a Ukrainian household that uses Russian is still not this page’s invented people. Belarus, Kazakhstan and other Central Asian states, the Caucasus, and the Baltics all carry Russian as a Soviet-era public language that still sits in some of those rooms. None of this means you should referee borders in a waiver meeting. If a family names a place, listen to the place they name.

### Homeland

The diaspora is global, because Israel and Germany received large Jewish streams, and the United States, Canada, and Europe each hold their own. Brighton Beach is not Minnesota, and Brooklyn, northern New Jersey, and California sit on a different map. Secondary migration and church networks built some of what you will meet here.

### Minnesota

In Minnesota the picture is made of places rather than a blob: Twin Cities households, some inner-ring suburbs, Orthodox parishes and synagogues as named places, and evangelical and Baptist congregations in some towns, including in Greater Minnesota. That is why you should not assume Northeast Minneapolis, should not assume the person in front of you has ever been to Russia, and should not assume a Greater Minnesota town has no Russian-speaking church.

sections.heading: Emigration Waves — Foundational Events, Not One Flight
sections.body:
If 1975 is the foundational event of Hmong Minnesota and 1991 of Somali Minnesota, Russian-speaking Minnesota does not get one year. It gets a stack of them, and you will misread the room if you pick the wrong one.

### Foundational events

The stack begins with late-imperial flight, followed by Soviet emigration in drips and then in named openings. The 1970s–90s Jewish stream, with refuseniks, Jackson-Vanik (1974) as the U.S. law tying trade to emigration, and then the late-1980s and 1990s movement, built part of Twin Cities Jewish life. That stream is Jewish peoplehood meeting Minnesota synagogues and a JCC, which means it is not a nesting-doll exhibit. Then 1991 and the collapse of the USSR moved others, including ethnic Russians, mixed families, professionals, and people from republics that were suddenly different countries.

### Who you meet

Evangelical and Baptist Russians arrived in church-sponsored patterns that sometimes landed in Greater Minnesota, not only in Minneapolis, while later family and employment streams are ordinary immigration rather than a refugee poster.

Then there is 2022 and the war on Ukraine, which is current structure for some households in this language: relatives under fire, mixed families, and people who will not accept a Russian-language flyer that looks like it came from Moscow. It is a trap to treat every Russian speaker as a combatant or a Putin voter, and it is equally a trap to pretend the war is not in the room when a family names it. Hold this as literacy for the desk rather than as a speech you give the family.

sections.heading: Family
sections.body:
Family is not one size. Some households look nuclear on an English form and still carry obligation to a parent who does not drive and does not read the form, some are three generations in one week, and some are a single elder whose children live in another metro. Elder isolation is a named harm in this language door, and it should never be mistaken for a cultural virtue.

### Who is in the household

The patronymic, a name built from the father, is how a person is fully named in Russian, so a form that keeps only first and last has already dropped a who. Ask how to file, and ask who should be in the room.

### Who speaks

Adult children may speak for an elder in English, but treat that as a hypothesis rather than as permission to skip the interpreter or to use a child in that role. CLAS still stands, which means a sixteen-year-old in the lobby is not the qualified interpreter.

In some rooms, women’s labor and a professional second generation sit right next to older gender patterns, and both can be true at once. Minnesota law still stands on violence, neglect, and who may consent, so do not skip mandated reporting and call it culture.

sections.heading: Minnesota and Russian-Speaking History
sections.body:
Minnesota put Russian on the CLAS five because the building already knew it would meet this language on notices and in health care, cash, food, aging, and voting, not because Compass drew a people-blob titled Russian. That is the honest origin of this spine, and it is why a language list is operations rather than a census.

### Places

Think in places rather than a blob: the Twin Cities, inner-ring suburbs, and some Greater Minnesota towns with evangelical churches. Do not write “the Russian neighborhood” onto a map you do not have, because what you have is pattern for now, and you should date a geography when a controlling source exists.

### Partners

The partners vary by stream. Synagogues and Jewish Community Centers serve some of the Jewish stream, Russian Orthodox parishes are named by some families, and evangelical and Baptist churches hold others in some towns, but there is no single “Russian community center” that stands for the whole. CECLC is a department door, not the community, so pay the partner this household actually uses.

Do not extract Russian-speaking staff as the interpreter or as “the community,” since they may be Jewish, Ukrainian, Belarusian, or a third generation that has no wish to be your culture desk. A liturgy or a JCC visit is optional professional development; you attend as a guest, and attending does not make you the expert.

sections.heading: A Language Door — not a people you invented
sections.body:
The heart of this intelligence is a refusal, because Russian on the five is a door onto many peoples. Ethnic Russian peoplehood is real, with its language, its literature, Orthodox memory for some, and a state that did harm and that some people still defend, but none of that is permission to file a Ukrainian, a Tajik, or a Soviet Jew under one folk costume.

### In this state

Jewish peoplehood in the 1970s–90s stream is not “Russian culture with a menorah,” and Ukrainian households that use Russian are not a round-up for this page. Evangelical Russians may organize life around a church in a town that has never heard the word CLAS.

In Minnesota another fact sits on the same desk: many of these households are read as white. The building’s unmarked default will skip the interpreter, skip the Cyrillic notice, and call that fairness, which is exactly why that skip is the gate. White appearance is not English proficiency, and it is not the absence of a people.

This guide is a working orientation, and because individual variation always supersedes group generalization, always defer to the person in front of you.

sections.heading: Core Concepts
sections.body:
Disaggregation is the first grammar of this door, because if you cannot name the stream, you do not have a household yet.

### Patronymic

The pattern is given name, the father’s name as a middle element, then the family name. Dropping the patronymic invents a person, and filing it wrong invents a person too, so ask rather than guess.

### Formality and titles

First name plus patronymic is respectful address in Russian, while first name only can be too familiar with an elder, and an English “hi guys” is not a translation.

### Visits

If food or drink is offered, accepting a little is fine, and you can still keep to medical and legal timelines.

### State memory

For some people, a Soviet past means you do not volunteer extra facts to a government desk; for some, the Russian Federation is still the frame; and for some, 2022 ended that sentence. You do not interrogate loyalty, because your job is to do the form.

### Church, synagogue, none

A parish, a shul, or a Baptist church may be the actual information channel for a household, but it is still not “the community.” Do not make clergy the case plan unless this family asked.

### Directness

If someone tells you a hard thing plainly, thank them and take it as information.

sections.heading: Religion — Orthodox, Jewish, evangelical, none
sections.body:
Ask rather than assume Russian Orthodox because the language is Russian, since Russian Orthodox, Jewish, evangelical Protestant, and none all live in this door, and Soviet official atheism left a mark in some families that still keep a holiday table.

### Streams

The parish is a center of liturgy, memorial, and sometimes mutual aid, but it is not the community. Do not BCC one priest and call it consultation. Icons in a home are not a case plan and not a museum.

### Practice

Jewish households in the 1970s–90s stream may be secular in the Soviet sense and still Jewish in peoplehood, with synagogue, JCC, kosher as a maybe, and Hebrew school as a maybe. That is why you should not give them an Orthodox Christian flyer and call it language access, and should not give them a “Russian culture night” and call it Jewish.

Evangelical and Baptist congregations, some of them in Greater Minnesota, can be the whole public life of a household. Church English and home Russian may sit together, but even so, do not make the pastor the case plan unless they asked.

Do not rank piety, because a person who left the church or the synagogue is still this language door if Russian is the language they need.

sections.heading: Greetings
sections.body:
A handshake is common in many rooms, among men and often among women in professional space, but follow this room, because some older Orthodox or observant Jewish settings will change the rule. If a hand is not offered, nod and carry on.

### Titles

Ask how the person wants to be addressed. First name plus patronymic is the respectful Russian address for an adult you do not know well, and English Mr./Ms. plus family name is a decent substitute if you cannot produce the patronymic. Do not use a first name with an elder simply because the form printed it.

### This room

Zdravstvuyte is the formal hello, while English “hello” is ordinary, especially with the second generation. Say the name, and ask how to say it.

Let this person’s own greeting guide you, whatever you read on another page. Ask before any physical contact, and let the person set the limit.

sections.heading: Naming — given name, patronymic, family name
sections.body:
A common Russian pattern is given name, patronymic, family name. A person is Ivan Petrovich Sokolov because his father is Petr, and Maria Ivanovna Sokolova because her father is Ivan, which means the patronymic is not a middle name you may drop for convenience. Databases that drop it invent a person, and that invented person then fails a match in MHCP, child welfare, and school.

### How to file

Family names may take a gendered ending, so Sokolov / Sokolova is the same family, and a form that flags the difference as fraud has already chosen a household type. Ask how to file, and ask how this person wants the English record to read.

Jewish, Ukrainian, Belarusian, Central Asian, and Caucasian names in this language door will not all look like Ivan and Maria, so do not “correct” a name toward a Russian textbook; pronounce it, and ask.

A form that demands first-middle-last and a hyphen will invent a person, which is why you should not invent a last name or invent a middle initial from a patronymic without asking. Three people in one household may not share a “last name” the way a Swedish Minnesota form expects, and that is not fraud until you have a reason to think so.

sections.heading: Dates of Significance
sections.body:
Orthodox Nativity and Pascha follow the Julian calendar for many Russian Orthodox households, which often places them later than Western Christmas and Easter, so schedule around them when you can. They are not a day off from the work; they are literacy.

### Calendar

Jewish High Holidays, Passover, and other calendar days matter in the Jewish stream, and since they are not “Russian holidays,” open the Jewish calendar if that is the household in front of you.

9 May, Victory Day in Soviet and Russian memory of 1945, is real for some elders and a political fight for others after 2022. Listen, and rather than lecture, keep a victory parade off the case note.

1991 is literacy, not a holiday, while 24 February 2022 is current structure for some families, so do not put “Fall of Saigon party” energy, or a Ukraine-war slogan, on a case note.

New Year’s Eve (Novy God) was the large Soviet winter holiday and still is for some secular families. A calendar click on this program is literacy for scheduling, but it is not community engagement.

sections.heading: Education
sections.body:
There is no Compass education table for “Russian speakers,” so treat what you have as pattern for now, date the number when a controlling source exists, and do not invent a rate.

### School and language

Soviet and post-Soviet credentials were often high, in engineering, medicine, and teaching, and they were not always recognized here, which means a person who was a professional in 1994 and a warehouse worker in 1996 is not a personality. Children of that stream may be in English-dominant schools with a parent who still cannot run an IEP in English.

Elders may be LEP and fully literate in Cyrillic, while professionals and the U.S.-born may not need an interpreter and may still have a parent who does. Do not skip the interpreter because the adult in the lobby is white, employed, or accent-light.

A parent who speaks fluent Russian and limited English is not illiterate, because the English-only form is the gate. Put Russian on the line, and confirm that it is Russian, not Ukrainian.

sections.heading: Etiquette
sections.body:
If you visit a home, look for shoes by the door or ask what the household prefers. If food or drink is offered, accepting a little is fine, and you can still keep to medical and legal timelines.

### In the home

Ask who to greet first, or follow the household’s lead.

### Time

Ask before taking any photograph or touching any religious object, and do not ask anyone to explain their faith or history for your benefit.

If someone misses an appointment, first check the time, transport, interpreter and work schedule. Confirm the plan in the language the person uses, and ask whether it works for them.

Visit a parish, synagogue or church only if you are invited, and go as a guest.

sections.heading: Language and Communication
sections.body:
Russian is on the five, but it is not Ukrainian, it is not Belarusian, and it is not “former Soviet.” An interpreter labeled Russian who is the wrong language for this household still will not work, and after 2022 it is a political door as well, so confirm the language. CLAS still means you book a qualified interpreter, because a list is not the person and not the dialect.

### Language

Cyrillic literacy and Latin literacy are not the same thing. Many elders read Russian in Cyrillic and do not read the English PDF, while some U.S.-born adults do not read Cyrillic at all, which means a “Russian notice” in Latin transliteration may still not work. Put the language they read on the line.

Elders may be LEP while professionals may not be, and white appearance is not English, so do not take a light accent as “no interpreter needed” without asking.

A direct answer may be the point rather than rudeness. Give the person time to answer. If you get a short yes, check that the plan was understood, and ask whether it works for them.

Do not make a Russian-speaking coworker the interpreter.

sections.heading: Other Considerations
sections.body:
This section states hard facts plainly, because treating everyone the same can hide them.

### Named harms

Alcohol harm and family violence exist in some households in this language door, but they are not “the culture,” and they are not a Slavic joke. You follow the law while still seeing a household rather than a crime scene walking in, so do not skip mandated reporting and call it humility.

Elder isolation is real for some post-Soviet elders, because thin English, adult children at work, winter, and no single community center that holds everyone all add up. That is why a missed appointment can be a bus and a language rather than noncompliance.

The Russian Federation’s anti-LGBTQ legal climate is current structure for some families. Queer and trans Russian-speakers exist in Minnesota, and Minnesota’s Human Rights Act still applies. Use the name the person uses, and do not share what they tell you with relatives unless a rule requires it.

Immigration status fear is real for some recent arrivals, so do not collect status you do not need, and do not treat fear as noncompliance.

Do not treat every Russian speaker as one origin or one politics. Staff who share this community may add facts, but they do not get to delete a fact because it is hard to say.

sections.heading: Health
sections.body:
There is no Compass health profile for this language door, so what you have is pattern for now; date a rate when a controlling source exists, and do not invent one to fill the spine.

### Access

Elder isolation, depression, and alcohol harm sit in some rooms, while war and displacement sit in others. Soviet-era medical culture was biomedical and hierarchical for many people, which is why “traditional Slavic medicine” as a staff story is often tourism. Ask what this person actually uses, and work it out together from there, without mocking it and without skipping the waiver because a home remedy is part of the story.

Mental-health stigma exists in some families, so naming a counselor is not the same as a family accepting one, and a smile is not a PHQ-9.

Believe reported pain, and do not fold this door into Tuskegee or into an Asian mash.

Gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care, so offer it. Book the interpreter even if the person is white, and confirm Russian rather than a “former Soviet” default.

sections.heading: LGBTQ
sections.body:
Queer and trans Russian-speakers exist in Minnesota. Conservative Orthodox, evangelical, and some family climates can mean silence or exile. The Russian Federation’s laws targeting LGBTQ people are current structure for some households and irrelevant in others, so you do not assume either.

### This person

Staff duty is the same here as on the other spines: use the name they use, do not share what they tell you unless a rule requires it, and remember that the Minnesota Human Rights Act still applies.

Do not question a household about anyone’s sexuality or gender, and take seriously that some people have reason to keep it private. Do not treat Russian law on this as Minnesota practice.

sections.heading: Hair, Dress, and Body
sections.body:
There is no daily Russian costume in the lobby, and the second generation looks like Minnesota, so do not ask whether someone “still dresses Russian.” Head covering happens in some Orthodox churches, some Jewish settings, and some evangelical rooms, and it is not a security threat or a consent problem.

### Dress

White appearance is not the absence of a language gate, and it is not the absence of a body that staff may still other. Do not touch, and do not comment on gold, a cross, a magen david, or a headscarf as a case note.

Winter dress is Minnesota rather than ethnography.

sections.heading: Music
sections.body:
Orthodox chant is liturgy, not a playlist. Jewish music, both liturgical and popular, belongs to the Jewish stream rather than to a “Russian mix.” Bard song, Soviet-era popular music, and contemporary pop all exist, and evangelical rooms have their own hymn and chorus life.

### Variation

A playlist is not engagement, and a funeral or a liturgy is not staff entertainment. Knowing that music splits along stream will stop you from putting one YouTube mix on a Heritage Month table and calling it this door.

Named variation is the point, because an Orthodox memorial, a Jewish wedding, and a Baptist hymn night are not one “Russian culture night” you can BCC.

sections.heading: Sports
sections.body:
Hockey, soccer, figure skating, and chess carry prestige in some post-Soviet families, while ordinary school sport is simply ordinary for the second generation. Do not assume the kid plays, and do not make sport the only excellence you can see.

### Not the whole person

Sport clubs are social infrastructure for some families, but they are not language access and not a case plan. A hockey sticker on a minivan is not proof that the elder reads English.

Greater Minnesota and the Twin Cities both play, yet a club flyer in English still will not work for the parent who needs Russian on the line.

sections.heading: Literature
sections.body:
Russian is a major written language with a long literature. That fact is literacy, a reminder that this is not a people without letters, and it is not a prompt to quote Tolstoy in the lobby. Jewish, Ukrainian, and other literatures sit in some of the same households, and they should not be mashed together.

### Literacy in the lobby

Cyrillic literacy for many elders is the actual operations fact, which means a notice that exists only in English, or only in Latin letters, will not work. U.S.-born adults may not read Cyrillic and may still be the person who has to explain the form.

You do not need a novel, because what you need is the language this person reads.

sections.heading: Art
sections.body:
Icons are liturgical art in Orthodox homes and parishes, not décor for a unit bulletin board. Soviet visual culture, contemporary work, and Jewish arts in the 1970s–90s stream are not one exhibit.

### Guest

There is no single Minnesota museum that is this whole door, so you come as a guest. An icon is not a case plan and a festival is not consultation. Do not photograph a sanctuary as professional development without being asked.

Heritage Month tables that mash matryoshka, a menorah, and a Ukrainian vyshyvanka into one “Eastern European” booth have already mashed together what this brief asks you to keep apart.

sections.heading: War, the State, and the Ukraine Trap
sections.body:
Empire, Soviet surveillance, collapse, Jewish emigration under Jackson-Vanik, and later enforcement climate for some arrivals make up the political stack, which is why a DHS badge is not automatically help. For some people a government form is a thing you survive, and that is not “paranoia” but pattern.

### The badge

The war on Ukraine is current structure for some households in this language: family under fire, mixed marriages, people who left Russia, people who did not, and people who will not speak politics in a lobby. It is a trap to assume every Russian speaker is a combatant or a Putin voter, and it is also a trap to punish someone for not performing the politics you prefer.

Do not use 1991 or 2022 as a personality. Do not ask a person to narrate a war for your professional development, and do not collect status you do not need.

sections.heading: Work and Government
sections.body:
Professional work, trades, small business, public employment, and under-recognized Soviet credentials all live here, and a small-business owner and a waiver recipient may be the same extended family.

### Work

Book a qualified interpreter, and pay for community work. Do not assign either to staff because of who they are.

### Staff

Take time to introduce yourself and explain the plan. The first visit may not be the decision, and any required notice still goes out, in Russian and in a script they can read.

Do not count an English eList comment period as reaching people who use this language.

sections.heading: Health-care and Human-service Encounters
sections.body:
The themes that shape these encounters are language, the interpreter, Cyrillic, the patronymic, and who is in the room. They also include assuming English because the person is white, elder isolation, enforcement climate for some, and alcohol and family violence as facts rather than folklore.

### Language

Confirm it is Russian, and still book a qualified interpreter. Offer gender match, ask who should hear, and ask how to file the name, but do not make staff the interpreter.

### The meeting

Believe reported pain. Mandated reporting still exists, and so does the duty not to treat a whole language as a risk score, so do not collect status you do not need.

sections.heading: Adjacent Peoples — Do Not Mash
sections.body:
This door is not Ukrainian. The Compass Ukrainian cultural community is about 22,254 (ACS 2020–2024), so open that people-page for a Ukrainian household, because a Ukrainian family that uses Russian still gets to name their people. Ask, since a Russian interpreter can still be the wrong door.

### Adjacent doors

It is not a Belarusian mash, and not a “former Soviet” interpreter for a Kazakh or Georgian household that needs another language. It is not Somali, not the African American CI, and not “white = no cultural intelligence.”

Historic German- and Scandinavian-Minnesota unmarked culture is the European American door rather than this one, because a white face in the lobby does not tell you which spine to open.

Some households are mixed, so ask this household, and never reach for one East-European module.

sections.heading: Counts, Dated — no invented population
sections.body:
There is no Minnesota Compass cultural-community profile for Russian. Do not invent one to make this spine look like Hmong or Somali.

### Counts

The Minnesota Compass immigration table lists 6,483 Russian immigrants without showing survey years, while the Census Bureau’s ACS 2020 to 2024 table B05006 shows 6,301 (give or take 665) Minnesotans born in Russia, and the 2024 single-year table shows 4,923 (give or take 1,239). Neither figure is a count of Russian speakers (ACS 2020 to 2024 counts 13,851, give or take 1,218, Minnesotans age 5 and older who speak Russian at home, 5,159 of whom speak English less than “very well”), because it is not Jewish, it is not Ukrainian, and it is not the third generation born here.

### What the count is not

The Star Tribune, on 31 July 2025, reported on languages spoken at home: German, French, Chinese, Russian, and Arabic each represent about 2% of Minnesotans who speak a language other than English at home. The same reporting said Vietnamese, Chinese, and Russian home-speaker populations had stayed about the same. Date that article, and since ACS vintages disagree, date the vintage as well.

Minnesota Secretary of State voter materials include Russian. That is operations evidence that the state already treats this language as a public-contact fact, but it is not a population.

Compass Ukrainian is about 22,254 (ACS 2020–2024), so do not add it to 6,483 and call the sum “Russian-speaking Minnesota.” A rate is not the person, and this is pattern for now; date the number when a controlling source exists.

sections.heading: Doors and Sources
sections.body:
DHS Equal Opportunity and Access LEP resources name five primary written languages: Hmong, Russian, Somali, Spanish, Vietnamese. The ten-language block and the fifteen interpreter cards also include Russian, although a list is not the notice and not the interpreter.

### Public doors

The public doors are the Minnesota Compass immigration table (Russian immigrants ~6,483, survey years not shown; ACS 2020 to 2024 table B05006 shows 6,301), the Minnesota Compass Ukrainian cultural community profile, which is adjacent rather than this page, the Star Tribune of 31 July 2025 on languages at home, and the Minnesota Secretary of State multilingual voter materials.

### Where to learn more

Community doors include the synagogues and Jewish Community Centers some Jewish households name, the Orthodox parishes some families name, and the evangelical and Baptist churches in some towns. CECLC is a door rather than the community.

Use these resources yourself before you ask a Russian-speaking colleague to explain. Do not BCC one priest or one rabbi and call it consultation. Pay the partners you actually have, and report back.

sections.heading: How it hits DHS gates — the 40%
sections.body:
Workplace culture and service delivery are both candidates here.

Language: Russian is on the five, but an interpreter labeled “former Soviet” will not work, and Ukrainian is a different language and a different brief. Still book a qualified interpreter, because a list is not the person and not the dialect, and Cyrillic is not optional decoration on a notice that actually has to be read.

Names: given name, patronymic, family name. The database that drops the patronymic or flags Sokolov / Sokolova as unmatched fraud is a gate that follows the person.

Do not assume English because the person is white. Ask which language they use.

Hour caps, exception processes, and life-sharing matches without language are not culturally neutral.

Enforcement climate: some recent arrivals may skip clinic, school, and waiver meetings, and that is not noncompliance, so do not collect status you do not need.

Notices and comment: do not count an eList and an English PDF as reaching people who use this language, and record who was reached and what follow-up happened. SOS already prints Russian for voters, and the packet can too.

Workforce: Russian-speaking staff are not the interpreter pool and not the community, because staff are colleagues, not the curriculum, so do not treat them as either.

Legislation, funding, rule: study a channel before you advocate for it. Use this page so that the 40% has a household in it.

sections.heading: A Note on This Guide
sections.body:
This brief is a language door, because Arabic sits on the CLAS ten-language block and on the fifteen-language interpreter cards at this department. It is not an Arab module, and it is not a Muslim module, so if you open Somali Minnesota because Arabic is on the card, you have already closed the door.

### Who this is

Arabic is a first language in Lebanese, Iraqi, Syrian, Palestinian, Egyptian, Sudanese, Yemeni, Gulf, and Maghrebi households in this state. It is also a liturgical and religious language in some Somali, Oromo, and other Muslim households, where it is recitation rather than the interview language, so ask which language this family needs, and confirm whether Arabic is actually spoken at home.

### Who this is not

There is no single count of “Arab Minnesota,” and you should not invent one; ancestry, language, and birthplace each catch different people. ACS 2020–2024 counts 26,405 Minnesotans (give or take 2,573) who report an Arab ancestry, plus 3,017 (give or take 809) reporting Sudanese ancestry, which the Census lists outside its Arab group, and 15,208 (give or take 1,931) who speak Arabic at home, 4,869 of them English less than “very well.” Minnesota Compass (ACS 2020–2024) puts Lebanese Minnesota near 7,232 (give or take 1,225), which is one stream rather than the whole door. The Minnesota Department of Education reports Arabic as the fifth most common home language of English learners in 2025 (1,664 English learners; 3,363 students in all). Date the number you use, and remember that a language share is not a people-count.

### How to read this

Christian and Muslim Arabs both live here, and Lebanese Christian streams are real and, in some Minnesota families, older, so do not assume mosque, and do not assume hijab. For Druze there is no dated Minnesota count, so do not invent one; if this family is Druze, defer.

Always defer to the person in front of you, because this page is a hypothesis you still test with this family.

sections.heading: Origins — a language, not a people
sections.body:
Arabic is an Afro-Asiatic language with a written standard (Modern Standard Arabic / fuṣḥā) and many spoken varieties that are not interchangeable in an interpreter. The language spread with trade, empire, and Islam, and it was already present in the Levant and Egypt before that sentence began. This is literacy for the desk rather than a speech you give the family.

### History for the meeting

The peoples who use Arabic as a first language do not share one origin story. A Lebanese Maronite household, an Iraqi Chaldean household, a Palestinian family, an Egyptian Copt, a Sudanese Muslim family, a Yemeni household, and a Maghrebi household share a language family, but they do not share a Tuesday.

### What people brought

Do not found “the Arabs” in a waiver meeting, and do not lecture a Christian family about the Prophet. Do not file a Black Sudanese or Nubian Arabic speaker under a Levantine picture, because shared language is not shared culture.

What people brought with them is a dialect; a church, a mosque, or neither; kinship; and a memory of states and wars that are not one war. What they met in Minnesota was an English form, one “Arabic interpreter,” and often a Somali default, because the building already had that page.

sections.heading: The Geography of Arabic
sections.body:
The Arabic-speaking world is not one flag and not one race, since it includes the Levant (Lebanon, Syria, Palestine, Jordan), Egypt, Iraq, Sudan and the Nile, the Maghreb, the Gulf, and Yemen. Each has its own dialects, churches, mosques, and class patterns, and none of these travel as a blob.

### Homeland

In the United States, Dearborn and the Detroit metro, southern California, New York, New Jersey, and Texas hold large communities. Minnesota is not Dearborn, so do not import a Michigan picture onto a Ramsey County lobby.

### Minnesota

In Minnesota, households live in both the Twin Cities and Greater Minnesota. Compass reports Lebanese Minnesotans at 76.7 percent Twin Cities and 23.3 percent Greater Minnesota (ACS 2020–2024), while other Arabic-speaking streams are not in that profile. Anoka County has the most Arabic speakers (4,144, give or take 1,064), ahead of Hennepin (3,794), Olmsted (2,021) and Ramsey (1,605); Blaine and Rochester each have more estimated Arabic speakers than Minneapolis, though margins are wide, and Anoka County schools have the most Arabic-speaking English learners (506 in 2025). Do not assume Minneapolis, and do not assume the person in front of you has been to the country on the passport copy.

sections.heading: Many arrivals — no single foundational year
sections.body:
If 1975 is Hmong Minnesota and 1991 is Somali Minnesota, Arabic-speaking Minnesota has no single foundational year, and that is the point, because when you collapse the streams into one, that is how a module gets written.

### Foundational events

Lebanese and other Levantine Christian streams include families with deep U.S. roots; Compass puts Lebanese foreign-born at 9.2 percent (ACS 2020–2024), a dated figure for one stream. Palestinian displacement is a twentieth-century and present fact. State health data show Iraqi refugee arrivals to Minnesota were small before 2008, peaked in 2010 (234), and totaled 1,502 from 1999 to 2024, mainly in 2008 to 2016. Syrian arrival to Minnesota after 2011 was small: State Department data cited by MPR News show 20 Syrian refugees arriving in 2016. There are Sudanese streams and Yemeni streams, while Maghrebi and Gulf streams are smaller here, and secondary migration from other states adds to all of them.

### Who you meet

The desk in 2026 meets U.S.-born children in every stream, elders who need a dialect, and people who use Arabic only at church or only in Qurʾan school. If you only know “refugee” or only know “Muslim,” you will miss this room.

Distrust of government has sources that are not one source: 9/11-era surveillance, wars the United States ran, Gaza-era harassment, and ordinary ICE. That is why a DHS badge is not automatically help.

sections.heading: Family
sections.body:
Who is in the household varies by stream, class, and generation, so some rooms are extended, and some are nuclear in the English way. The Compass Lebanese average household size of about 2.12 (ACS 2020–2024) describes one stream that is often smaller, older, and more English-dominant, so do not copy it onto a Sudanese or Iraqi waiver household.

### Who is in the household

Ask who should be in the room, because a nuclear English form already has a who built into it, and elders, in-laws, and adult children may all sit in the same week.

### Who speaks

Do not invent a last name because the database wants one, and do not treat unmatched last names as fraud by default, since patronymic and three-part patterns exist in some families, while Westernized first-middle-last patterns exist in others.

Women’s labor and men’s labor both live here, and gender norms are this family’s, not “Arab,” so ask.

sections.heading: Minnesota and Arabic as a door
sections.body:
Arabic is on the language block because the department already meets these households, which makes it operations, not a festival. There is no single Cedar-Riverside of Arabic Minnesota, though Central Avenue in Northeast Minneapolis and Columbia Heights works as a commercial corridor for Palestinian, Yemeni and other Arab businesses, anchored by Holy Land since the 1980s. Named churches — Maronite (St. Maron Maronite Catholic Church, 602 University Ave. NE, Minneapolis), Antiochian and other Orthodox (St. George Antiochian Orthodox Church, West St. Paul), Coptic (St. Mary’s Coptic Orthodox Church, 501 Sixth Ave. S., South St. Paul) — and named mosques and Islamic centers are partners if this family names them, but they are not a list to extract from.

### Places

Compass Lebanese (ACS 2020–2024) reports about 7,232 people (give or take 1,225), with 76.7 percent in the Twin Cities and 23.3 percent in Greater Minnesota, and Greater Minnesota is not an afterthought. Other Arabic-speaking streams are not inside that count.

### Partners

Book a qualified interpreter, and pay for community work. Do not assign either to staff because of who they are. A Heritage Month table is not consultation, and while you may attend as a guest, that does not make you the expert.

CECLC is a door, not the whole, so pay partners, and report back.

sections.heading: A language door — not a heart to perform
sections.body:
There is no single heart of “Arab Minnesota” to put on a poster. For some people, Arabic is the language of the grandmother and the church, while for others it is the language of the Qurʾan and not of the kitchen. For some, it is the only language that reaches an elder, and for some U.S.-born children, it is a class they do not speak.

### In this state

Race in the U.S. file fails this door in more than one direction, since Levantine and Iraqi Christians have often been filed White, while Sudanese Arabic speakers have been filed Black. “MENA” as an emerging box is still not a person. Somali is a different people, so do not fold this household into Somali Minnesota because both might be Muslim.

This guide is a working orientation, and individual variation always supersedes group generalization.

sections.heading: Core Concepts
sections.body:
Dialect comes first: Levantine, Egyptian, Iraqi, Maghrebi, Sudanese, Gulf, MSA. An interpreter labeled Arabic who does not speak this household’s variety will not work, so confirm it on the line.

### Home language versus liturgy

Arabic on a Somali or Oromo Muslim card may be recitation, so book the interview language, and do not open this door and skip Somali or Oromo when those are the people.

### Christian and Muslim both

Do not assume the mosque, and do not assume the priest, because both live behind this door.

### Checking for agreement

Before you treat a yes as agreement, ask whether the person agrees.

MSA is school and media for some, but it is not the kitchen, so do not test an elder in fuṣḥā and call it language access.

sections.heading: Religion — not the language
sections.body:
Islam is not Arabic, and Arabic is not Islam. Christian Arabs — Maronite, Orthodox, Coptic, Protestant — live in this state, as do Muslim Arabs — Sunni and Shiʿa — and people who have left both. Do not make a religion the case plan unless this family asked.

### Streams

Arabic as a Qurʾanic language is liturgical, and it is used that way in some Somali, Oromo, and other Muslim households whose interview language is not Arabic. Do not book an Arabic interpreter for a Maay grandmother because the building saw “Muslim.”

### Practice

Do not assume hijab, and do not rank covering as piety or oppression, since halal matters in some rooms and not in others.

For Druze there is no dated Minnesota count, so do not invent a community, and if this family names Druze, listen and defer.

Ramadan, Eid, Friday prayer, Christmas, Easter, Coptic fasts — ask, because a calendar click is not engagement.

sections.heading: Greetings
sections.body:
Follow this room. As-salāmu ʿalaykum is ordinary in many Muslim rooms, and the reply is wa-ʿalaykumu s-salām, but it is not the default in a Christian Arab room. Marḥaban, ahlan, and an English hello are all ordinary, so say the name.

### Titles

Ask who to greet first, or follow the household’s lead. Wait to see whether a hand is offered, and if it is not, nod.

### This room

Let this person’s own greeting guide you, whatever you read on another page.
