Ask before any physical contact, and let the person set the limit.

sections.heading: Naming Conventions
sections.body:
Naming patterns vary. Some families use given name + father’s name + family name, and some three-part names look like Somali names and are not. Some Lebanese and other Christian streams use French or English given names and a family surname that the database can already see, while some people have Westernized their names on U.S. forms, so ask.

### How to file

Do not invent a last name because the screen requires one, because that invented name becomes a gate.

Pronounce the name, and ask, but do not joke about long names. Do not assume three Somali names, and do not assume a hyphen.

Women may or may not take a husband’s family name in U.S. records, so ask how to file. Do not “correct” a mother and child who do not share a last name, and do not read it as a fraud signal until you have a reason.

sections.heading: Dates of Significance
sections.body:
Ask this family, because Muslim lunar dates — Ramadan, Eid al-Fitr, Eid al-Adha, and Mawlid in some rooms — move on the Gregorian calendar, while Christmas and Easter (Western, Orthodox, Coptic) matter in Christian rooms. Some families name national days, and some refuse to.

### Calendar

11 September 2001 is structure in this country rather than a holiday or a personality, and Gaza-era harassment is current structure as well. Neither is a calendar click that makes you engaged.

Do not put “Arab holiday” or “Muslim holiday” on a case note without asking. A calendar click is literacy, but it is not community engagement.

sections.heading: Education
sections.body:
Streams differ. Compass Lebanese (ACS 2020–2024) reports that among those 25 and older, about 97.8 percent have a high school education or higher and about 50.9 percent a bachelor’s or higher, but that is one stream, and often an English-dominant one, so do not copy it onto a recently arrived Sudanese or Iraqi parent.

### School and language

A parent who speaks fluent Arabic and limited English is not illiterate, and literacy in Modern Standard Arabic is not guaranteed for every dialect speaker, which makes the English-only IEP the gate.

The child is not the interpreter, since under CLAS, untrained individuals and minors are not the plan, so put the dialect on the line.

Second-generation educational mobility is real in some streams, and so is a gap that a room treating everyone the same will call “culture” instead of language access.

sections.heading: Etiquette
sections.body:
If food or drink is offered, accepting a little is fine, and you can still keep to medical and legal timelines.

### In the home

If you visit a home, look for shoes by the door or ask what the household prefers.

### Time

Do not assume a woman will or will not cover. Ask before taking any photograph, and enter a prayer space only if you are invited.

If someone misses an appointment, first check the time, transport, interpreter and work schedule. Confirm the plan in the language the person uses, and ask whether it works for them.

sections.heading: Language and Communication
sections.body:
The varieties are Levantine, Egyptian, Iraqi, Maghrebi, Sudanese, Gulf, and Modern Standard Arabic, so confirm the variety. An interpreter labeled Arabic who does not speak this household’s dialect still will not work, because Maghrebi and Levantine are not interchangeable just because both are “Arabic.”

### Language

Confirm whether Arabic is the home language at all, since on a Somali or Oromo Muslim card it may be religion. Book the interview language rather than opening Somali Minnesota by default because Arabic is on the card.

ACS 2020–2024 counts 15,208 Arabic speakers age 5 and older in Minnesota, 4,869 of them English less than “very well.” Date that figure, and remember that it is not a people-count.

Give the person time to answer. If you get a short yes, check that the plan was understood, and ask whether it works for them. Do not make a coworker the interpreter, because the child is not the interpreter and neither is staff.

sections.heading: Other Considerations
sections.body:
This section states hard facts plainly, because treating everyone the same can hide them.

### Named harms

Islamophobia and anti-Arab racism after 11 September 2001 and after Gaza are structure in this country and in this state. They change who opens the door, who will not put a relative’s name on a form, and who reads a DHS badge as a threat, and that is not noncompliance.

Do not collect political speech as a risk score, and do not file a protest, a flag, or an opinion about Gaza or Iraq as a safety note. Enforcement climate is real for some streams, so do not collect status you do not need.

Queer and trans Arabs exist, so you use the name, and you do not out someone to kin and call it culture.

Do not assume hijab, and do not assume Muslim, but also do not skip mandated reporting and call it humility.

Staff who share this community may add facts, but they do not get to delete a fact because it is hard to say.

sections.heading: Health
sections.body:
No dated Minnesota-wide Arabic-speaking autism, diabetes, or PTSD rate belongs on this page, so do not invent one. War trauma sits in some Iraqi, Syrian, Sudanese, Palestinian, and Yemeni streams, but it is not a personality, and it is not every household.

### Access

Gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care, so offer it, and believe reported pain. Ask about this person’s own experience of care.

Mental-health stigma exists in some families, and so does a fierce wish for services, and you can hold both. The dialect on the interpreter line is a health gate.

Do not skip screening because you have no module, and remember that identification is not a community personality.

sections.heading: LGBTQ
sections.body:
Queer and trans Arabs exist in Minnesota. Conservative church, mosque, and family climates can mean silence or exile, and some people live a public English life and a private home life, so you use the name they use and do not share what they tell you unless a rule requires it.

### This person

Minnesota’s Human Rights Act still applies. Use the name the person uses, and do not share what they tell you unless a rule requires it.

Do not question a household about anyone’s sexuality or gender, and take seriously that some people have reason to keep it private.

sections.heading: Hair, Dress, and Body
sections.body:
Hijab, niqab, and modest dress are ordinary for some Muslim women and not for others, while Christian Arab dress is Minnesota dress plus, for some, church clothes. Do not assume covering, and do not rank covering as piety or oppression.

### Dress

This is not the CROWN Act chapter, and yet Sudanese and other Black Arabic speakers may also live the hair politics of anti-Blackness, so ask this person rather than mashing.

Do not touch, and do not police covering. Do not assume a covered woman cannot speak for herself — ask her, with a gender-matched interpreter if she wants one.

sections.heading: Music
sections.body:
Arabic musical life is not one playlist, because tarab, dabke, Egyptian and Levantine pop, Maghrebi music, Coptic and Orthodox hymnody, and religious caution about some music in some families all exist side by side.

### Variation

A playlist is not engagement, so do not request a dabke as an icebreaker in a waiver meeting.

Knowing that oral art and poetry carry prestige in some rooms will stop you from calling a long answer “rambling.”

sections.heading: Sports
sections.body:
Soccer is a common public sport in many streams, and basketball shows up in the second generation, but do not assume the kid plays, and do not make sport the only excellence you can see.

### Not the whole person

Sport clubs are social infrastructure, but they are not language access, and they are not a case plan.

World Cup loyalties are not a risk score, any more than a flag or an opinion is.

sections.heading: Literature
sections.body:
Arabic is one of the world’s major literary languages, and poetry is prestige in many rooms. The Qurʾan is recitation and scripture in Muslim rooms, and it is not a literacy test you give a dialect-speaking elder in the lobby.

### Literacy in the lobby

MSA and dialect are not the same skill, so a person who does not read fuṣḥā is not a person without letters.

You do not need to quote Mahfouz or a pre-Islamic ode, but you do need to know that limited English is not illiteracy.

sections.heading: Art
sections.body:
Calligraphy, geometric ornament, Levantine and Egyptian visual work, and church iconography in Christian streams are all part of this picture, as are contemporary artists in the diaspora, so be a guest, not a researcher.

### Guest

A museum visit is optional professional development, but it is not consultation.

Do not put a camel or a keffiyeh on a Heritage Month table and call it this door.

sections.heading: Conflict, War, and the State
sections.body:
There is no single civil-rights story to copy onto this page. The political literacy is plural: 11 September 2001 and what the United States did in its name; Iraq; Syria; Sudan; Yemen; Gaza; surveillance of Muslim communities; and enforcement against some immigrants. Anti-Arab racism and Islamophobia are structure, not a personality.

### The badge

Do not collect political speech as a risk score, because a flag, a protest, a sermon, or an opinion about Gaza is not a safety note.

A DHS badge is not automatically help, so do not use a war as a personality, and do not ask a person to narrate bombing for your professional development.

sections.heading: Work, Markets, and Government
sections.body:
Streams differ: small business, the professional class, public employment, and shift work all appear, so do not write one hustle onto the door.

### Work

Book a qualified interpreter, and pay for community work. Do not assign either to staff because of who they are.

### Staff

Take time to introduce yourself and explain the plan, and still give any required notice.

sections.heading: Health-care and Human-service Encounters
sections.body:
Confirm the language, confirm the dialect, and confirm whether Arabic is the home language or the liturgy. Offer gender match, ask who should hear, and do not force a handshake.

### Language

Believe reported pain, and do not close the file because English was thin, since the child is not the interpreter.

### The meeting

Do not assume Muslim, and do not assume hijab. Do not mix Tuskegee into a Levantine Christian history, or the Somali CI into a Sudanese Arabic speaker. Mandated reporting still exists, and so does the duty not to treat a whole language group as a risk score.

On enforcement climate, people may skip clinic when a relative can be moved, and that is not noncompliance, so do not collect status you do not need.

sections.heading: Adjacent Peoples — Do Not Mash
sections.body:
This door is not Somali, not Persian / Farsi, not Turkish, not Hebrew as a synonym, and not Oromo, because shared Islam is not shared culture, and a shared region is not a shared language.

### Adjacent doors

Do not open Somali Minnesota because Arabic is on the card, do not book an Arabic interpreter for a Farsi-speaking household, and do not file a Hebrew speaker here.

The Lebanese Compass profile is one stream, and Iraqi, Syrian, Palestinian, Egyptian, Sudanese, Yemeni, Gulf, and Maghrebi households are not that profile. Some households are mixed, so ask this household.

There is never one Arab module, and never one Muslim module.

sections.heading: Counts, Dated
sections.body:
There is no dated total “Arab Minnesota” population on this page, so do not invent one.

### Counts

Minnesota Compass, ACS 2020–2024, Lebanese cultural community — one stream — reports 7,232 people in the pooled estimate (give or take 1,225) and 10,066 (give or take 3,576) as the 2024 single-year total, which Compass calls the most accurate measure of size; 76.7% live in the Twin Cities and 23.3% in Greater Minnesota. Those age 17 or younger are 24.2%, those 65+ are 17.0%, and the foreign-born share is 9.2%. Among those age 5 and older, 13.9% speak a language other than English, while English less than “very well” is suppressed on that profile. Among those 25 and older, 97.8% have a high school education or higher and 50.9% a bachelor’s or higher. Median household income is $72,873 (2024 dollars; give or take $21,005), poverty is 8.8% (give or take 5.4 points), 68.6% of homes are owner-occupied, and average household size is 2.12.

### What the count is not

ACS 2020–2024 counts 15,208 Arabic speakers age 5 and older in Minnesota, 4,869 of them English less than “very well,” and the Minnesota Department of Education reports 1,664 Arabic-speaking English learners among 3,363 Arabic-speaking students in 2025. Date the vintage, and remember that a language share is not a people-count.

Counts disagree because definitions disagree (ancestry, language, birthplace), so date the number, and remember that a rate is not the person.

sections.heading: Doors and Sources
sections.body:
Start with the Minnesota Compass Lebanese profile (ACS 2020–2024), remembering that it is one stream, not the door. The Census Bureau’s ACS 2020–2024 tables on Arab ancestry and Arabic spoken at home are another source, along with the CLAS ten-language block and the fifteen-language interpreter cards, and the churches and mosques this family names.

### Public doors

CECLC is a door, not the whole, and an eList will not reach every stream, so pay partners, and report back.

### Where to learn more

Use these resources yourself before you ask an Arabic-speaking colleague to explain, and book a qualified interpreter. Confirm the dialect, and confirm whether Arabic is the home language, because the child is not the interpreter.

sections.heading: How it hits DHS gates — the 40%
sections.body:
Workplace culture and service delivery are both candidates here.

On language: an interpreter labeled Arabic who does not speak Levantine, Egyptian, Iraqi, Maghrebi, Sudanese, or Gulf as this household speaks it will not work, and MSA is not the kitchen. Arabic on a Somali or Oromo Muslim card may be recitation, so book the interview language, and know that gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care.

On names: the database that invents a last name, or that assumes three Somali names, is a gate that follows the person.

Hour caps, exception processes, and life-sharing matches without language are not culturally neutral.

Assuming Somali, assuming Muslim, and assuming hijab shut people out, even when they look like cultural competence.

On enforcement climate and post-9/11 and Gaza-era racism: people may skip clinic, school, and waiver meetings, and that is not noncompliance, so do not collect status you do not need, and do not collect political speech as a risk score.

On notices and comment: do not count an eList and an English PDF as reaching every stream, and record who was reached and what follow-up happened.

On workforce: Arabic-speaking staff are not the interpreter pool and not the community.

On legislation, funding, and rule: study a channel before you advocate for it. Use this page so that the 40% has a household in it.

sections.heading: A Note on This Guide
sections.body:
This brief is about Oromo people — Oromoo; the language is Afaan Oromoo — as a Cushitic-speaking nation of the Horn and as a Minnesota community. Oromo is not Somali, it is not Amharic, and it is not “Ethiopian” as a synonym, so if you open Somali Minnesota or book an Amharic interpreter because the building heard East Africa, you have already closed the door.

### Who this is

Minnesota Compass puts Ethiopian Minnesota at 45,159 (plus or minus 5,404) for ACS 2020–2024 and 53,754 (plus or minus 12,826) for 2024, with 89.7 percent in the Twin Cities. About 43.8 percent are age 17 or younger and 59.8 percent are foreign-born, and among those age 5 and older, 76.2 percent speak a language other than English and LEP is 30.2 percent. Compass has noted historically that respondents born in Ethiopia who list Somali ancestry are counted as Somali, not Ethiopian. Ethiopian Compass is an umbrella in which Amhara, Oromo, Tigrayan and others are not one file, so use the Ethiopian numbers as dated context, not as an Oromo census.

### Who this is not

Oromo-specific counts disagree. MinnPost (19 May 2016) reported that the Oromo Community of Minnesota estimated up to 40,000 Oromo in the state (Wilder Research and the Minnesota Daily credit that estimate to the Oromo Cultural Institute of Minnesota), while the state demographer’s office put the figure nearer 8,500 using census plus school language. The Star Tribune (31 July 2025) reported that about 8,000 Minnesotans speak Oromo at home, and the Minnesota Department of Education listed Oromo as the 8th most-common home language in K–12. The 2024–25 state report counts 3,297 students with Oromo as primary home language, 1,568 of them English learners, and Oromo is sixth in that report’s top-12 tables, which are built around English learners, so it gives no overall rank among all languages. Date the disagreement rather than inventing a midpoint, and remember that a rate is not the person.

### How to read this

Islam and Christianity (Orthodox, Protestant) and Waaqeffanna traditional practice all live here, so do not assume Muslim like Somali. Always defer to the person in front of you, because this page is a hypothesis that you still have to test on this family.

sections.heading: Origins and the Founding of a People
sections.body:
Oromo peoplehood — Oromummaa — is older than the Ethiopian empire’s file on it and older than the refugee camp. Oromo people are a Cushitic-speaking nation of the Horn, the largest nation in the region by language, and there is no Oromo nation-state. Gadaa (the generational / governance tradition) is literacy for the desk rather than a speech you give the family, and not every household still lives it.

### History for the meeting

Afaan Oromoo is not Amharic, which is a Semitic language and was the imperial state language. The Latin Qubee script, adopted in the early 1990s after the fall of the Derg, is political and educational history: a people writing itself after suppression. That sentence is literacy, not a lecture in the lobby.

### What people brought

What people brought with them was language and dialect, Islam and Christianity and Waaqeffanna, kinship, oral art, and a memory of imperial and 20th-century state violence. What they met in Minnesota was an English form, one “Ethiopian” checkbox, one “East African” interpreter, and often Somali because the building already has that page.

Do not assume Addis Ababa as identity, because many Oromo people name Oromia, a region, a village, or a lineage — not the capital of the state that ruled them.

sections.heading: The Geography of the Oromo World
sections.body:
The homeland is Oromia and Oromo-inhabited country across the Horn, a map that does not match the Ethiopian state’s ethnic-federal drawing in every family’s mouth. Oromo communities also live in Kenya, and there is a global diaspora across the Middle East, Europe, and North America. After Kenya, Minnesota has been named among the largest Oromo communities outside the homeland (MNHS / MNopedia), though the Twin Cities as Little Oromia is community naming, not a census.

### Homeland

Compass Ethiopian (current profile) puts 89.7 percent in the Twin Cities, but that is the umbrella, not an Oromo map. Do not assume Cedar-Riverside, since that sentence is Somali geography unless this family lives there, and do not assume Addis.

### Minnesota

Do not assume the person in front of you has been to Oromia, because secondary migration built parts of this map, and Greater Minnesota is still this people when they live there.

sections.heading: Imperial Violence, Struggle, and Secondary Migration — Foundational Event
sections.body:
There is no single 1975 or 1991 on this page. The foundational political literacy is longer: Ethiopian imperial incorporation of Oromo country, 20th-century state violence, the Oromo Liberation struggle as literacy for the desk and not a speech, the 1974 revolution and the Derg, flight through Sudan and Kenya and the Gulf, U.S. resettlement, secondary migration to Minnesota, and the unrest of the 2010s–2020s that sent another wave.

### Foundational events

Do not referee Ethiopian politics in a waiver meeting, and do not pick a side as DHS. Intra-Ethiopian tension in Minnesota rooms is real, so listen if they name it, and do not file it as a risk score.

### Who you meet

The desk in 2026 meets first-wave elders and U.S.-born children — English-dominant with peers, still translating for parents, and still unable to get Afaan Oromoo in a lobby that offered Somali or Amharic.

If the only phrase you know is “Ethiopian refugee,” you will miss this household.

sections.heading: Family
sections.body:
Some households are extended, and elders may hold authority in some of them. The Compass Ethiopian average household size of 3.30 (current profile) is umbrella context rather than an Oromo census, and the person who cares for the child may not match the waiver checkbox, so ask who should be in the room.

### Who is in the household

Patronymic patterns exist: a given name and the father’s name, sometimes more. Do not invent a last name because the screen requires one, and do not assume three Somali names, because Oromo names are not Amharic names.

### Who speaks

Women’s labor, men’s labor, and church or mosque obligation all live here, and both a nuclear English form and a cousin-line can be true in the same week.

Do not collect status you do not need, since mixed-status fear is structure in some rooms.

sections.heading: Minnesota and Oromo History
sections.body:
This department will meet this community on waivers, child welfare, health care, cash, food, aging, and employment. The Twin Cities as Little Oromia is community memory (MNHS / MNopedia) rather than a Compass line, and Greater Minnesota exists.

### Places

Partners include the Oromo Community of Minnesota (OCIM / OCM), historically, from the 1980s, and the churches and mosques that families name — including Our Redeemer Oromo Evangelical Church (which grew from a 1980s Bible study and was organized in 1993, per MNHS) and Tawfiq Islamic Center in Minneapolis (per MNHS the first Oromo mosque in North America, opened in 2004 as Masjid Tawfiq). Pay them and report back, and remember that CECLC is a door, not the whole.

### Partners

Book a qualified interpreter, and pay for community work. Do not assign either to staff because of who they are. A festival or Irreecha visit is optional professional development, and you attend as a guest, knowing that it does not make you the expert.

sections.heading: Oromummaa — the heart of a people
sections.body:
Oromo people are a Cushitic-speaking nation without a state, and public systems may file them under Ethiopian, East African, Black, and sometimes Somali. Ask how the person identifies. Oromummaa is peoplehood, not a poster, and because Islam, Orthodox and Protestant Christianity, and Waaqeffanna all live here, do not assume the mosque.

### In this state

Many Oromo Minnesotans are Black in a U.S. racial order that also holds Somali and historic African American histories they do not share. Shared race is not shared culture, and shared Horn geography is not shared language.

This guide is a working orientation, and because individual variation always supersedes group generalization, ask this household.

sections.heading: Core Concepts
sections.body:
Start with Afaan Oromoo and its dialects, and since Borana, Guji, Wollo, and others exist, confirm the variety. An “Ethiopian interpreter” is often Amharic, which will not work for many Oromo households.

### Qubee

Qubee is the Latin script adopted in the 1990s, and it is political and educational history. Elders may not read it while children may, so the English form is still a gate.

### Oromummaa

Oromummaa is peoplehood rather than a clan icebreaker taken from the Somali page.

### Faith is plural

Islam, Orthodox, Protestant, and Waaqeffanna are all here, so follow this room.

### Names

Names are Oromo, not Amharic, and not three Somali names, so do not invent a last name.

Do not assume Addis, and do not referee the Oromo Liberation struggle in a waiver meeting.

sections.heading: Religion and Healing
sections.body:
Islam and Christianity both live in Oromo Minnesota in large streams, with Orthodox and Protestant (including Oromo evangelical churches) both ordinary. Waaqeffanna — traditional Oromo religious practice — lives in some rooms and as public revival in others. Do not assume Muslim like Somali, and do not assume Orthodox like a mash of “Ethiopian.”

### Streams

Arabic may be religion rather than the interview, and Qurʾanic recitation is not Afaan Oromoo, so book the interview language.

### Practice

Do not import As-salāmu ʿalaykum as a default, because in a Christian Oromo room it already shuts the person out, while in a Muslim Oromo room it may be ordinary, so follow this room.

Do not make an imam or a pastor the case plan unless this family asked. Halal and fasting matter in some rooms and not in others, and illness meaning may not be the DSM sentence, so ask.

sections.heading: Greetings
sections.body:
Ask who to greet first, or follow the household’s lead. There are many Christian Oromo and many Muslim Oromo, so As-salāmu ʿalaykum is not a default, while English hello is ordinary in the second generation. Afaan Oromoo greetings exist, so ask about them.

### Titles

Wait to see whether a hand is offered, and if it is not, nod.

### This room

Let this person’s own greeting guide you, whatever you read on another page.

Ask before any physical contact, and let the person set the limit.

sections.heading: Naming Conventions
sections.body:
Oromo names are not Amharic names. Patronymic patterns exist — a given name, the father’s name, and sometimes the grandfather’s — and while that can look like a Somali three-part name, it is not. Do not assume three Somali names, and do not invent a last name because the screen requires one, since that invented name becomes a gate.

### How to file

Ask how to say the name and how to file it, and then pronounce it.

Women may or may not take a husband’s name in U.S. records, so ask how to file. Do not “correct” a mother and child who do not share a last name, and do not read it as a fraud signal until you have a reason.

Do not joke about names, and do not collect a clan list as an icebreaker, because clan as an Oromo social fact is not the Somali qabiil icebreaker and not a risk score.

sections.heading: Dates of Significance
sections.body:
Irreecha is the thanksgiving / new-year gathering, held in autumn in homeland practice and marked in the diaspora, including Minnesota. Attend as a guest rather than a researcher, since a calendar click is not community engagement.

### Calendar

Orthodox Christmas and Easter, Protestant calendars, and Ramadan and Eid in Muslim rooms are all possible, so ask this family. Do not put Somali dates on this page by default, and do not put “Ethiopian holiday” on a case note without asking.

Political commemorations are dates some families name and some refuse, so do not collect them as a risk score, and do not referee.

1974, 1991, and the 2010s protests are literacy for the desk, not holidays.

sections.heading: Education
sections.body:
Qubee in the 1990s is why a mass written Afaan Oromoo public exists, which makes it political history and school history. Many elders still do not read it, while many children in Minnesota schools do, and the English IEP still has to reach the parent.

### School and language

Compass Ethiopian (ACS 2020–2024) reports that among those 25 and older, about 79.5 percent have high school or higher and about 24.1 percent have a bachelor’s or higher — umbrella figures, not an Oromo census. The Star Tribune (31 July 2025) reported that MDE listed Oromo as the 8th most-common home language in K–12, and you should date it. The 2024–25 state report counts 3,297 students with Oromo as primary home language, 1,568 of them English learners, and ranks Oromo sixth only within its English-learner tables.

A parent who speaks fluent Afaan Oromoo and limited English is not illiterate, and the child is not the interpreter, so book Oromo, not Amharic, because an English-only form is the gate.

sections.heading: Etiquette
sections.body:
Ask who to greet first, or follow the household’s lead. If food or drink is offered, accepting a little is fine, and you can still keep to medical and legal timelines.

### In the home

If you visit a home, look for shoes by the door or ask what the household prefers. Faith practice varies — mosque, Orthodox liturgy, Protestant church, Waaqeffanna, none — so follow this room, and do not rank covering or assume covering.

### Time

Ask before taking any photograph, and enter a prayer space only if you are invited.

If someone misses an appointment, first check the time, transport, interpreter and work schedule. Confirm the plan in Afaan Oromoo if that is the language the person uses, and ask whether it works for them.

sections.heading: Language and Communication
sections.body:
The language is Afaan Oromoo, and its varieties include Borana, Guji, Wollo, and others, so confirm. An interpreter labeled Ethiopian who speaks Amharic often will not work, a Somali interpreter is the wrong door, and Arabic may be religion, not the interview.

### Language

The Star Tribune (31 July 2025) reported that about 8,000 Minnesotans speak Oromo at home, and MDE lists Oromo as the 8th most-common K–12 home language, so date it. The 2024–25 state report counts 3,297 students with Oromo as primary home language, 1,568 of them English learners. The Compass Ethiopian LEP figure of 30.2 percent is umbrella context.

Give the person time to answer. If you get a short yes, check that the plan was understood, and ask whether it works for them.

Do not make an Oromo coworker the interpreter, and remember that the child is not the interpreter.

sections.heading: Other Considerations
sections.body:
This section states hard facts plainly, because treating everyone the same can hide them.

### Named harms

Intra-Ethiopian tension in Minnesota rooms is real — Oromo, Amhara, Tigrayan, and the state’s name itself — so do not pick a side as DHS, do not referee in a waiver meeting, and do not file politics as a risk score.

FGC exists in some Horn communities, and Minnesota law stands, but this is not the Somali page, so do not invent an Oromo rate, and do not mash Somali prevalence onto this household. Follow mandated reporting, and still see a family.

Queer and trans Oromo exist, so you use the name, and you do not out someone to kin and call it culture.

Enforcement climate is structure for some, so do not collect status you do not need, and do not treat fear as noncompliance.

Staff who share this community may add facts, but they do not get to delete a fact because it is hard to say.

sections.heading: Health
sections.body:
No dated Oromo-specific Minnesota autism, diabetes, or FGC rate belongs on this page, so do not invent one. Do not mash the MDH 2014 Somali findings onto this people, and do not skip screening because you have no module.

### Access

Compass Ethiopian reports poverty at 10.9 percent and 43.8 percent age 17 or younger in its current profile (renters are 64.4 percent) — umbrella context. A young age structure is not a personality, and a rate is not the person.

Gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care, so offer it. Believe reported pain, and remember that peers who share language matter. On FGC, Minnesota law stands, this is not the Somali page, you do not invent a rate, and you do not skip care.

War, prison, and protest trauma sit in some rooms. Mental-health stigma exists in some families, and so does a fierce wish for services, and you can hold both.

sections.heading: LGBTQ
sections.body:
Queer and trans Oromo Minnesotans exist. Conservative family, church, and mosque climates can mean silence or exile, and some people live a public English life and a private Oromo life, which is why you use the name they use and do not share what they tell you unless a rule requires it.

### This person

Minnesota’s Human Rights Act still applies. Use the name the person uses, and do not share what they tell you unless a rule requires it.

Do not question a household about anyone’s sexuality or gender, and take seriously that some people have reason to keep it private.

sections.heading: Hair, Dress, and Body
sections.body:
Hijab and modest dress are worn by some Muslim Oromo women, but not all, and Christian Oromo dress is Minnesota dress plus, for some, church clothes. Do not assume covering, and do not rank covering as piety or oppression.

### Dress

This is not the CROWN Act chapter — and yet anti-Blackness still sits on Black Oromo bodies in U.S. clinics and schools, so ask this person. Do not mash historic African American hair politics onto them as a script, and do not ignore those politics either.

Do not touch, and do not police covering. Do not assume a covered woman cannot speak for herself; ask her, with a gender-matched interpreter if she wants one.

sections.heading: Music
sections.body:
Geerarsa and related oral forms are prestige speech — praise, history, sometimes resistance — and Qeerroo-generation music is public in the 2010s–2020s diaspora. Church music is here, and Islamic nasheed in some rooms, along with religious caution about some music in some families.

### Variation

A playlist is not engagement, and a long answer may be oral art, not evasion.

Do not request a political song as an icebreaker in a waiver meeting.

sections.heading: Sports
sections.body:
Soccer is a common public sport, and basketball shows up in the second generation. Distance running as a Horn stereotype is not a file, and it is not a compliment you give a child in clinic.

### Not the whole person

Do not assume the kid plays, and do not make sport the only excellence you can see.

Sport clubs are social infrastructure, but they are not language access and not a case plan.

sections.heading: Literature
sections.body:
Oral literature comes first. Qubee in the 1990s made a mass written public possible, which is political history, not a trivia fact, and Minnesota Oromo journalists, poets, and media exist.

### Literacy in the lobby

You do not need to quote a novel in the lobby, but you do need to know this is not a people without letters, and that an elder who does not read Qubee or English is not a person without language.

Do not test an elder in Amharic and call it language access.

sections.heading: Art
sections.body:
Ethiopian Orthodox church art is not a synonym for Oromo art, because dress, oral art, contemporary visual work, and diaspora stages are the public culture here. You are a guest, not a researcher.

### Guest

A visit is optional professional development rather than consultation.

Do not put a Somali poster or an Ethiopian flag mash on a Heritage Month table and call it this people.

sections.heading: Conflict, War, and the State
sections.body:
Ethiopian imperial incorporation, 20th-century state violence, the Oromo Liberation struggle as literacy for the desk and not a speech, the Derg, and the 2010s–2020s unrest — that is the political event. Do not referee it in a waiver meeting, and do not pick a side as DHS, because intra-Ethiopian tension in Minnesota rooms is real.

### The badge

A DHS badge is not automatically help. Do not use a struggle as a personality, and do not ask a person to narrate prison or killing for your professional development.

The enforcement climate in the United States is a different state, but it still keeps some people away, so do not collect status you do not need, and do not collect political speech as a risk score.

Take time to introduce yourself and explain the plan, and still give any required notice.

In child welfare, help-seeking that becomes a report is part of why people wait. Mandated reporting still exists, and so does the duty not to treat a whole community as a risk score. On FGC, Minnesota law stands, this is not the Somali page, and you do not invent a rate.

On notices and comment, do not count an eList and an English PDF as reaching this community, and record who was reached and what follow-up happened.

On workforce, Oromo staff are not the interpreter pool and not the community; staff are colleagues, not the curriculum, and you do not treat them as either.

On legislation, funding, and rule, study a channel before you advocate for it. Use this page so that the 40% has a household in it.

sections.heading: A Note on This Guide
sections.body:
This brief is about Bosniak / Bosnian Minnesota as a people-page. The older DHS 10-language list (2007) said Serbo-Croatian (Bosnian), and the DHS language block published 09/01/17 gives notice in 15 languages that do not include it, so any such label is operations, because it is how the building batches a notice rather than the name of the household in the lobby.

### Who this is

Bosniak names the Muslim peoplehood of Bosnia and Herzegovina, while Bosnian can also mean a citizen of a state that Dayton wrote as three constituent peoples — Bosniak, Croat, Serb. Croatian and Serbian households in Minnesota are adjacent, and although they may share a mutually intelligible language, they do not share this war story by default, so ask rather than filing them here because the interpreter catalog used a hyphen.

### Who this is not

This is not a Census “white” mash, and it is not a Balkan blob or Somali Islam with a different flag. It is not Russian, not Albanian, not Kosovar, and not Ukrainian, because a shared continent is not a shared culture, and a shared Islam is not a shared culture either. Use this page for context and questions. It does not describe the person in front of you.

### How to read this

There is no Minnesota Compass cultural-community count for Bosnian, and that absence is a finding, not a reason to invent 40,000. Between 1993 and 2003, 2,379 primary Bosnian refugees arrived in Minnesota, peaking at 471 in 1998 (Minnesota Department of Health, primary refugee arrivals, 1979–2025). Primary placement is not the community, because secondary migration happened, so date the number you use, and remember that a rate is not the person.

The diversity inside this people is the point. Consider a Srebrenica widow, a man who will not name the camp, a Catholic Croat neighbor who speaks the same language and not the same memory, a less-observant Bosniak who drinks coffee and does not keep Ramadan, a woman who covers, a woman who does not, and a U.S.-born nurse who uses English with friends and Bosnian with an elder. They share a language family, but they do not share a Tuesday.

Always defer to the person in front of you, since this page is a hypothesis you still test on this family.

sections.heading: Origins and the Founding of a People
sections.body:
Bosniak peoplehood is older than 1992 and older than the refugee file. South Slavic speakers in the Dinaric and Bosnian lands lived under medieval kingdoms, Ottoman centuries (from the 15th century), Austro-Hungarian rule after 1878, royal and then socialist Yugoslavia, and finally the 1992 independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Islam in this land is Ottoman-era and European, and that sentence is literacy, not a piety rank.

### History for the meeting

Bosniak, Croat, and Serb in Bosnia are not three languages you can hear from across a lobby; they are political names on a mutually intelligible South Slavic speech, and the 1990s war made those names lethal. That is why the desk that treats them as flavor has already failed the household.

### What people brought

What people brought includes family, coffee, a language with a literature, Islam as heritage for most Bosniaks (sometimes as daily order, sometimes as a name without a public mark), Catholic and Orthodox streams in adjacent households, and a memory of neighbors who became a front. What they met in Minnesota was an English form, a language block that, in its older 10-language version, said Serbo-Croatian (Bosnian), and often one interpreter labeled “former Yugoslav.”

There is no Bosniak nation-state in the simple sense the checkbox wants, because Dayton wrote a state with two entities and three constituent peoples. Do not referee that constitution in a waiver meeting; listen instead if they name home.

sections.heading: The Geography of the Bosnian World
sections.body:
The homeland is Bosnia and Herzegovina — Sarajevo, Tuzla, Zenica, Banja Luka, Mostar, Bihać, the Drina towns, and the eastern enclaves. Srebrenica is both a place-name and a crime, which is why it does not belong on a small-talk map.

### Homeland

The 1992–1995 war produced camps and exile in Croatia, Serbia, Montenegro, Germany, Austria, Scandinavia, and then the United States. St. Louis became a large Bosnian hub in the United States, while Chicago, New York, and other cities hold communities, and Minnesota received a notable resettlement in the mid and late 1990s. Minnesota is not St. Louis, though, so do not copy a Missouri story onto this desk and call it local.

### Minnesota

In Minnesota the pattern is Twin Cities and Greater Minnesota. The Islamic Community of Bosniaks in Minnesota is a registered Minneapolis religious nonprofit with a mosque at 668 Broadway St. NE (about 1,200 congregants in 2017), though its current activity and contacts are unconfirmed. Rochester has a well-documented community dating to June 1993, with local estimates of 600 to 2,000 people at different times (Post Bulletin, 2011, 2013, 2024). Pelican Rapids received Bosnian families from 1995 and a large group of Bosnian Roma in August 1996, and Moorhead schools counted 25 Bosnian-speaking students in 2017-18. The Census count of Bosnia-born residents in the Twin Cities metro (1,368, give or take 844, in 2024) is only about two-thirds of the statewide figure (2,114, give or take 964). Do not assume one neighborhood. Do not assume the person in front of you has been back, and do not assume they want to go.

sections.heading: 1992–1995, Srebrenica, Dayton — Foundational Event
sections.body:
If the Great Migration is the foundational demographic event of modern Black America, and 1991 is that event for Somali Minnesota, then 1992–1995 is the foundational event of Bosnian Minnesota.

### Foundational events

Yugoslavia broke, and Bosnia and Herzegovina declared independence. War followed: the siege of Sarajevo, ethnic cleansing, camps, mass rape as a method of war, and on 11 July 1995 the genocide at Srebrenica — more than 8,000 Bosniak men and boys killed after a UN “safe area” failed. That is public record (ICTY, International Court of Justice), and it is literacy for the desk rather than a speech you give the family, which means you never ask a survivor to narrate the pit.

### Who you meet

Dayton, in December 1995, stopped the shooting and froze a political map. For many, camps and temporary protection in Europe came first, and resettlement in the United States followed in the mid and late 1990s. Minnesota’s primary-refugee arrivals between 1993 and 2003 were 2,379 (Minnesota Department of Health), and secondary migration after that is real, even though it is not a Compass cell.

The desk in 2026 does not only meet that first wave; it meets their children — U.S.-born, English-dominant with peers, still translating for a parent who will not tell the war to a stranger, and still unable to get the right language in the lobby. If the only category you know is “refugee,” you will miss them.

sections.heading: Family
sections.body:
Ask who counts as family and household, because an English form may not have room for them. Ask whether godparent ties (kumovi) matter to this family, because the person who cares for a child, an elder, or a disabled adult may be part of a network the waiver checkbox does not have a box for.

### Who is in the household

War and exile also broke families: missing men, split siblings, a neighbor who is now the household, camp years and then an apartment in the United States. Ask who should be in the room, rather than reconstructing a family tree as an icebreaker.

### Who speaks

Women’s labor — factory, care work, a professional second generation — sits next to a household in which an elder man may still be named as head, and both can be true in the same room.

Do not use 1995 as a family personality, and do not skip mandated reporting and call it culture, because Minnesota law still stands.

sections.heading: Minnesota and Bosnian History
sections.body:
Minnesota received a notable Bosnian resettlement in the mid and late 1990s. That is why this page has to be as complete as the Hmong and Somali intelligences, since this department will meet this community on waivers, child welfare, health care, cash, food, aging, and employment, including the elder who still needs the language and the adult child who does not think of themselves as a refugee.

### Places

Think in places rather than a blob: the Twin Cities; a Minneapolis Bosniak civic and religious life that some families name; Greater Minnesota where work pulled people. Rather than inventing a Little Sarajevo on a case note, ask this family where they live.

### Partners

Partners include the Islamic Community of Bosniaks in Minnesota (current activity and contacts unconfirmed); the mosques and churches families actually name; resettlement-era voluntary agencies as history, not as a current partner list; and CECLC as a department door — not the whole community.

Book a qualified interpreter, and pay for community work. Do not assign either to staff because of who they are. A Bajram greeting is optional professional courtesy, and it does not make you the expert.

sections.heading: Bosniak / Bosnian — the heart of a people
sections.body:
Bosniaks are a European Muslim people, and the war of the 1990s, which the United States watched on television, is part of their history in Minnesota. Many Bosnian Minnesotans are white in a U.S. racial order that can erase 1995 and call them assimilated. Do not copy the Somali page onto a Bosniak family, because the covering, the mosque, and the language may all be wrong. Ask.

### In this state

Bosnian can mean the language, the passport, or the people-name, while Bosniak is the ethnic name for the Muslim peoplehood. Use what this family uses, and do not lecture them on the difference as a greeting.

This guide is a working orientation, and individual variation always supersedes group generalization.

sections.heading: Core Concepts
sections.body:
Language here is a political name, since Bosnian, Croatian, and Serbian are mutually intelligible but not interchangeable as identity. Book what they ask, because “former Yugoslav” shuts people out, even with a polite label.

### Islam as heritage for most Bosniaks

Some Bosniaks do not mark their faith publicly, so do not assume hijab, and do not assume five daily prayers in the lobby. Equally, do not assume that the absence of a mark means the absence of faith — or of trauma.

### Family and kumovi

Ask who is in the room, and ask who signs.

### Coffee

If food or drink is offered, accepting a little is fine, and you can still keep to medical and legal timelines.

### Memory

Srebrenica and the siege are in the room for some people whether they speak them or not, so you do not extract the memory, you do not deny it, and you do not platform denial.

### Checking for agreement

Before you treat a yes as agreement, ask again, plainly and without embarrassing anyone.

sections.heading: Religion and Healing
sections.body:
Islam is the faith of most Bosniaks — Sunni, Ottoman in heritage, a European Muslim history — and practice in Minnesota ranges from daily order to a name on a form. Because hijab is not the default public mark, do not copy the Somali religion chapter onto this page. Do not assume the mosque is the case plan, and do not assume Friday prayer sets the appointment grid the way it might for another household; ask.

### Streams

Catholic Croat and Orthodox Serb streams exist within the broader language, and their Christmas dates differ. A “Bosnian” interpreter for a household that names itself Croatian or Serbian may still be the wrong political door even when the words are understood, so ask.

### Practice

Do not make an imam, a priest, or a pastor the case plan unless this family asked, because a church or mosque can be the information channel without being “the community.”

Illness meaning after war may not be the DSM sentence. Ask what the person wants the team to know about their health and how they describe it, and do not interrogate the pit to complete a field.

sections.heading: Greetings
sections.body:
Ask who to greet first, or follow the household’s lead. Ask whether a handshake is welcome, and do not import a greeting rule from another community. If a hand is not offered, nod and carry on.

### Titles

Merhaba, dobro jutro, zdravo, selam — follow what they offer, and remember that an English “hello” is ordinary in the second generation. Say the name, and ask how to say the -ić.

### This room

Do not open with the war, and do not open with “I have a friend from Bosnia.” Let this person’s own greeting guide you, whatever you read on another page.

sections.heading: Naming Conventions
sections.body:
South Slavic naming runs given name, then family name, and the -ić and -vić endings are common (Hodžić, Begović, Hadžić, Petrović — examples of a pattern, not a roll call). The ć is not optional decoration, so ask how to say it, do not joke, and do not anglicize it on the file without being asked.

### How to file

Women may or may not take a husband’s family name in United States records, so ask how to file. Do not “correct” a mother and child who do not share a last name, and do not read that as a fraud signal until you have a reason.

Given names may be Bosnian, South Slavic Christian, Arabic-origin, or English in the second generation, which is why the form that demands first-middle-last and a hyphen will invent a person if you force it.

Pronounce the name, ask, and write what they say.

sections.heading: Dates of Significance
sections.body:
Ramadan and Bajram (Eid al-Fitr, Eid al-Adha) matter for many Bosniak households, and because they are lunar, date them each year. They are operations for fasting, appointments, and an elder who will not drink water in your lobby, rather than a festival you attend as consultation.

### Calendar

Catholic Christmas (December 25) and Orthodox Christmas (January 7) belong to the adjacent Croat and Serb streams — and to mixed families — so ask, and do not put “Balkan holiday” on a case note.

11 July is Srebrenica Genocide Memorial Day, which is literacy for the desk, not a day off the work, and not a prompt to ask who they lost. The U.N. General Assembly designated July 11 as an international day on May 23, 2024, and in 2025 Rochester marked the 30th anniversary with a peace march around Cascade Lake on July 11 and a soccer tournament the next day.

1 March (Independence Day) and 25 November (Statehood Day) are holidays in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and are not observed in Republika Srpska, which marks 21 November (Dayton) instead, so Dayton’s anniversary is not a greeting. A calendar click is literacy, but it is not community engagement.

sections.heading: Education
sections.body:
There is no Compass education rate on this page, and you should not invent one. Interrupted schooling from siege, flight, and camps is structure for some first-wave adults, yet it is not a personality, and it is not illiteracy in Bosnian.

### School and language

A parent who speaks fluent Bosnian and limited English is not illiterate, and the English-only IEP is the gate, so put the language they ask for on the interpreter line. Latin script is not the same as English literacy, and Cyrillic in a Serbian-identifying household is a different written door.

Second-generation educational mobility is real, and so is an elder who still cannot run an exception form in English. Date a Minnesota figure when a controlling source exists, and until then, treat this as pattern rather than a fake percent.

sections.heading: Etiquette
sections.body:
If coffee is offered, accepting a little is fine. If it runs into an appointment, say so and reschedule together.

### In the home

If you visit a home, look for shoes by the door or ask what the household prefers. However the answer is put, ask whether the person agrees with the plan, and confirm in the language they use.

### Time

Let the person decide whether to talk about the war, faith or food.

If someone misses an appointment, first check the time, transport, interpreter and work schedule. Confirm the plan in the language the person uses, and ask whether it works for them.

sections.heading: Language and Communication
sections.body:
Bosnian, Croatian, and Serbian are mutually intelligible languages with political names. The differences that matter on Tuesday are the name the household claims, the script, and whether the interpreter will walk in as “former Yugoslav,” a label that will not work with a polite hyphen.

### Language

Script runs Latin for Bosnian and Croatian, and Cyrillic for much Serbian, so book what the household asks. The older DHS 10-language list wrote Serbo-Croatian (Bosnian), and the current 15-language block (2017) does not include it, but either way that is notice, not the interpreter, which means staff who answer the number must be ready, and the interpreter request must still name the variety.

Second-generation English is common, but elders may not have it. Give the person time to answer. If you get a short yes, check that the plan was understood, and ask whether it works for them.

Do not make a Bosnian coworker the interpreter.

sections.heading: Other Considerations
sections.body:
This section states hard facts plainly, because treating everyone the same can hide them.

### Named harms

Genocide denial in Bosnia and in diaspora politics is current, not archival. Do not platform it in a lobby, and do not “both-sides” Srebrenica to keep a meeting calm, because literacy is not a debate club.

Ask what the person wants the team to know about their health. Do not assume anything about alcohol from religion or nationality: you follow the law, and you still see a person, not a bottle with an ethnicity. LGBTQ Bosnians exist, and conservative family, mosque, and church climates can mean silence, so you use the name they use, and you do not out someone to kin and call it culture.

Do not mash this page with Somali Islam, FGC, or Maay, because those are other intelligences. The second generation is American, and they may still need language for an elder, while an English IEP that never reached the parent is still a gate.

Staff who share this community may add facts, but they do not get to delete a fact because it is hard to say.

sections.heading: Health
sections.body:
War trauma is structure for some first-wave adults, and for some children who grew up inside someone else’s silence. Ask what the person wants the team to know about their health, date any figure when a controlling source exists, and do not skip screening because “they don’t talk about that.”

### Access

Offer the substance-use screen the same way to everyone, and do not treat a screen as a nationality.

Believe reported pain, without asking them to narrate the pit to make the pain credible. Gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care, so offer it.

Do not fold this history into Tuskegee, into Somali FGC, or into a generic “refugee trauma” slide that erases Srebrenica as a specific crime.

sections.heading: LGBTQ
sections.body:
Queer and trans Bosnian Minnesotans exist, and conservative family, mosque, and church climates can mean silence or exile, so some people live a public English life and a private Bosnian life.

### This person

Use the name they use, and do not share what they tell you unless a rule requires it. Minnesota’s Human Rights Act still applies.

sections.heading: Hair, Dress, and Body
sections.body:
Do not assume hijab, since many Bosniak women in Minnesota dress like other European-origin Minnesotans, and some cover. Ask the woman, with gender match if she wants it.

### Dress

Do not rank covering as piety, oppression, or assimilation. Traditional dress is public at weddings and commemorations rather than a daily uniform, so do not ask whether they “still wear the costume.”

Do not touch hair. This is not the CROWN Act chapter and not the Somali hijab chapter, so follow this person.

sections.heading: Music
sections.body:
Ask what music, if any, matters to this person or family, and do not assume a genre.

### Variation

A playlist is not engagement, and you do not ask a survivor for a soundtrack of Sarajevo under siege.

A funeral is not staff entertainment, and second-generation rooms will have American pop, so follow this room, not a souvenir.

sections.heading: Sports
sections.body:
Soccer is a visible community activity: in Rochester there is a Bosnian team, United BiH, and an annual July tournament that has run since about 2011, and club names from home can also be a war map you do not referee.

### Not the whole person

Basketball and ordinary school sport are real in the second generation, but sport clubs are not language access, and they are not a case plan.

Do not assume the kid plays, because a Saturday league is not how you reached the elder.

sections.heading: Literature
sections.body:
Written South Slavic literature is old — older than the refugee file, and older than Dayton — and the building may know some of the novels and many it has not, so ask what stories or reading matter to this person.

### Literacy in the lobby

Second-generation English is a literature too, and you do not need to quote a Nobel.

What you need to know is that this is not a people without letters, and that the name of the language is political, which is why the English form may still be unreadable to the parent who reads Latin Bosnian.

sections.heading: Art
sections.body:
Coffee culture, calligraphy, embroidery, and contemporary Minnesota work all belong here, while Stećci and mosque architecture are homeland history, not a Heritage Month table.

### Guest

Be a guest, because a festival is not consultation, and a commemorative exhibit is not a case plan.

Do not put a wedding photograph on a unit display, since this is not a souvenir people.

sections.heading: Conflict, War, and the State
sections.body:
1992–1995, Srebrenica, the camps, Dayton, dispersal, and a United States that resettled people and then mostly stopped saying the name — that is the political event.

### The badge

Genocide denial is current politics in the region and in some diaspora rooms, so do not platform it, and do not “hear both sides” of a genocide in a lobby.

A DHS badge is not automatically help, which means you do not use 1995 as a personality, and you do not ask a veteran or a widow to narrate killing for your professional development. Mandated reporting still exists, and so does the duty not to treat a whole community as a trauma score.

sections.heading: Work, Markets, and Government
sections.body:
Work here spans trades, small business, care, a professional second generation, and public employment. There is no Compass income or poverty rate on this page, and you should not invent one, because the pattern is simply that people work, and that an elder may still need the language the coworker does not get paid to provide.

### Work

Book a qualified interpreter, and pay for community work. Do not assign either to staff because of who they are.

### Staff

Take time to introduce yourself and explain the plan, and still give any required notice.

sections.heading: Health-care and Human-service Encounters
sections.body:
Ask about the language label, Latin or Cyrillic, and who should be in the room, and do not interrogate trauma. Ask whether an elder needs Bosnian even when an adult child does not think an interpreter is needed until the form gets legal.

### Language

Confirm what they ask to book, offer gender match, and ask who should hear, but do not make staff the interpreter.

### The meeting

Believe reported pain, and do not open with the war, while remembering that mandated reporting still exists.

sections.heading: Adjacent Peoples — Do Not Mash
sections.body:
This community is not Albanian, not Kosovar by default, not Macedonian, not Russian, not Ukrainian, and not Somali, and it is not “Muslim” as a file or “former Yugoslav” as a people.

### Adjacent doors

Croatian and Serbian Minnesota households are adjacent, and they may share the language and not the war story. If the household is Croatian, book Croatian and do not make them narrate Srebrenica; if Serbian, book Serbian, do not platform denial, and do not assume they want this page.

Some households are mixed, so ask this household, and never use one Balkan module.

sections.heading: Counts, Dated
sections.body:
Minnesota Compass has no Bosnian cultural-community profile, and that is a finding, so do not invent 40,000.

### Counts

The Minnesota Department of Health’s primary refugee arrivals count (1979–2025) shows 2,379 Bosnian arrivals from 1993 through 2003, peaking at 471 in 1998. Primary placement is not the community total, because secondary migration is real. The 2024 ACS ancestry table for Minnesota has no Bosnian line. Usable Census figures are place of birth (Bosnia and Herzegovina: 2,114, give or take 964) and language spoken at home (“Serbo-Croatian”: 3,503, give or take 1,642); date them before you cite one.

### What the count is not

The older DHS 10-language list (2007) included Serbo-Croatian (Bosnian), but the current DHS language block, published 09/01/17, covers 15 languages and does not, and a language list is operations volume, not a census.

A missing rate is not permission to skip language access, and a young second generation is not proof the elder can run an English exception form.

sections.heading: Doors and Sources
sections.body:
The sources are these: the older DHS 10-language list (2007), which read Serbo-Croatian (Bosnian), and the DHS language block published 09/01/17 (15 languages, not including it); the Islamic Community of Bosniaks in Minnesota (Minneapolis); the Minnesota Department of Health primary refugee arrivals count, 1979–2025 (dated); the ICTY and ICJ public record on Srebrenica; and Dayton as political fact.

### Public doors

CECLC is a door, not the whole community. Use these resources yourself before you ask a Bosnian colleague to explain.

### Where to learn more

Pay the partner this household names, report back, and be a guest.

sections.heading: How it hits DHS gates — the 40%
sections.body:
Workplace culture and service delivery are both candidates here.

Language: the older DHS 10-language list said Serbo-Croatian (Bosnian) while the current 15-language block (2017) does not include it, and either way that is notice. An interpreter labeled “former Yugoslav” who carries the wrong political name, or the wrong script, shuts people out, even with a polite label, so book what the household asks, and remember that gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care.

War as an icebreaker: never. 1995 is literacy for the desk, not a speech and not a rapport trick, so do not ask a survivor to narrate the pit.

Names: ask how to say the -ić, and do not treat a spelling variant as fraud by default.

Hour caps, exception processes, and life-sharing matches made without language are not culturally neutral, and an English IEP for an elder is a gate.

Child welfare and disability: trauma is not a risk score. Mandated reporting still exists, and so does the duty not to treat a whole community as a personality.

Notices and comment: do not count an eList and an English PDF as reaching this community, and record who was reached and what follow-up happened.

Workforce: Bosnian staff are not the interpreter pool, and they are not the community.

One Balkan blob shuts the person out, because adjacent Croatian and Serbian households are not this war story by default, and this community is not Albanian, not Kosovar, not Russian, and not Somali.

Legislation, funding, rule: study a channel before you advocate for it. Use this page so that the 40% has a household in it.

sections.heading: A Note on This Guide
sections.body:
This brief is about Amharic-speaking Minnesota — Amhara households and other households that use Amharic as a first or working language — as a people-page. Amharic is on the CLAS fifteen interpreter cards, and that is operations rather than a census of who is Ethiopian, so it is not permission to treat Ethiopia as one people.

### Who this is

Amharic is not Oromo, Amharic is not Somali, and Amharic is not Tigrinya. Amharic is a federal working language of Ethiopia, which means many non-Amhara Ethiopians speak it as a second language of school, army, and office. If the household is Oromo, open the Oromo brief and book Afaan Oromoo, and if Tigrayan, book Tigrinya. If Somali — including people born in Ethiopia who name Somali ancestry — open Somali Minnesota, since Compass counts those last households as Somali, not Ethiopian. A shared Horn is not a shared culture, and a shared Orthodox calendar is not shared politics.

### Who this is not

Minnesota Compass Ethiopian (ACS 2020–2024) counts 45,159 people in its analysis (give or take 5,404; its 2024 single-year total is 53,754, give or take 12,826), with about 89.7 percent in the Twin Cities and 10.3 percent in Greater Minnesota. About 43.8 percent are age 17 or younger, and 59.8 percent are foreign-born. Among those age 5 and older, 76.2 percent speak a language other than English and 30.2 percent speak English less than “very well”; median household income is about $63,667 (2024 dollars), poverty is 10.9 percent, and 64.4 percent are renters. Date the number, and remember that it is an umbrella, because the Census recodes some people who write Oromo into Ethiopian, which means this is not an Amharic speaker count. Minnesota Secretary of State voter materials include Amharic, but do not invent a population from that.

The diversity inside this door is the point. Consider an Amhara Orthodox grandmother who fasts more days than the clinic has slots, a Protestant professional, a Muslim Ethiopian household, a person who uses Amharic at work and Oromo at home, a U.S.-born student who uses English with friends and Amharic with an elder, and a Tigrayan family who should not have been booked here. They share a language door, but they do not share a Tuesday.

### How to read this

Always defer to the person in front of you, since this page is a hypothesis you still test on this family.

sections.heading: Origins and the Founding of a People
sections.body:
Amhara peoplehood and Amharic as a written language are older than the refugee file and older than 1974. Highland agricultural life, Ethiopian imperial history, the Orthodox Tewahedo Church, and Ge’ez as a liturgical language organized a state that was not a European colony in the way the Somali and Karen files were. That fact is literacy rather than a rank you give the family, and it is not a reason to skip language access.

### History for the meeting

Amharic became the court language and then the federal working language, which is why a non-Amhara Ethiopian may speak it and still not belong to this people-page as a first identity. The empire’s second language in a Minnesota home becomes a Tuesday question: which language does this elder actually use for a legal notice?

### What people brought

1974 ended the empire, and the Derg, the Red Terror, the 1980s famine, and 1991 are the foundational political events of much of the Minnesota first wave. The 2020–2022 war in Tigray is current structure for some households — Tigrayan, Amhara, Eritrean-adjacent, and others. Al Jazeera reports that fighting resumed in Tigray in October 2026 and that fighting between the federal army and Fano militias in the Amhara region has continued since July 2023. Do not referee it in a waiver meeting.

What people brought includes Amharic and fidel, Orthodox fasting alongside Protestant and Muslim streams, kin obligation, injera as ordinary food, honorifics, and a memory of state violence. What they met in Minnesota was an English form, one “Ethiopian” checkbox, and often one interpreter who was Somali or Oromo because the building mashed the Horn.

sections.heading: The Geography of the Amharic-speaking World
sections.body:
The homeland is not one ethnic map, because there is the Amhara region, there is Addis Ababa, and there is a country where Amharic is heard in offices far from Amhara land. Tigray, Oromia, the south, and Eritrea are adjacent geographies with different languages, so do not draw one Ethiopia on a case note.

### Homeland

The diaspora is global: Washington D.C. as a large U.S. hub, Los Angeles, Dallas, Toronto, the Gulf, and Italy. Minnesota is a real community, although it is not the U.S. capital of this diaspora, and secondary migration and church networks pulled people here.

### Minnesota

In Minnesota, Compass Ethiopian (ACS 2020–2024) is 89.7 percent Twin Cities, with Minneapolis parishes (Debre Selam Medhanealem Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church among them, which moved in April 2026 to 2601 30th Ave. S. in Seward) and inner-ring suburbs. Greater Minnesota — including Worthington, where Ethiopian Orthodox life is public — is 10.3 percent of the Compass Ethiopian umbrella. Cedar-Riverside is a Somali hub and also a long-standing Ethiopian commercial center, so do not make it the only place you think of; 2024-25 school data show the most Amharic-speaking English learners in Dakota County. Do not assume the person in front of you has been to Addis.

sections.heading: 1974, the Derg, Famine, and Tigray — Foundational Events
sections.body:
If 1991 is Somali Minnesota’s foundational political event, then 1974 and what followed is the foundational event of much of Amharic-speaking Minnesota’s first wave.

### Foundational events

The revolution overthrew Haile Selassie, and the Derg and the Red Terror killed and scattered people. The 1980s famine and resettlement brought refugees from Ethiopia to Minnesota, while others came through Sudan, Kenya, and Europe. 1991 ended the Derg and opened another politics, and family reunification and later diversity streams followed.

### Who you meet

The 2020–2022 war in Tigray is current structure, with fighting reported again in Tigray in October 2026 and in the Amhara region since July 2023 (Al Jazeera), and some Minnesota households are living it through kin, remittance, silence, or politics in the parish parking lot. Do not referee, do not pick a side, and do not make a waiver meeting a map of the front.

The desk in 2026 also meets U.S.-born children — English with peers, still translating, and still unable to get Amharic (or the actual home language) in the lobby. If the only category you know is “Ethiopian,” you will miss the Oromo mother and the Tigrayan elder you booked wrong.

sections.heading: Family
sections.body:
Ask who counts as family and household, because an English form may not have room for them. Godparent and kin ties, adult children in the same week as a waiver, and a grandmother who is the childcare all belong to the picture. Compass Ethiopian puts the average household size at 3.30 (ACS 2020–2024) — an umbrella figure, dated, and still not Mary Jones.

### Who is in the household

The person who cares for the child may not match the checkbox, and hour caps and “natural supports” can dump unpaid work onto the women in that network and then call it culture.

### Who speaks

Naming is already a question of who, since a person carries a given name plus father’s name, often with no surname, and the database that invents a last name invents a kinship the family did not file.

Ask who should be in the room, and do not skip mandated reporting and call it respect for elders, because Minnesota law still stands.

sections.heading: Minnesota and Amharic-speaking History
sections.body:
Amharic-speaking Minnesota is why this page has to be as complete as the Somali and Hmong ones, since this department will meet this community on waivers, child welfare, health care, cash, food, aging, and employment, and the building has a long habit of hearing “East African” and booking Somali.

### Places

Think in places rather than a blob: Minneapolis parishes; inner-ring suburbs; Worthington and other Greater Minnesota towns where Orthodox liturgy is public; the south-metro suburbs (2024-25 school data show the most Amharic-speaking English learners in Dakota County); and not Cedar-Riverside as the only place to think of. Compass Ethiopian puts about nine in ten in the Twin Cities.

### Partners

Partners include the Orthodox parishes families name (Debre Selam Medhanealem among them); Protestant congregations; the Ethiopian Community in Minnesota as a historical local door; SOS Amharic voter tools as proof the state already knew this language; and CECLC as a department door — not the whole community.

Book a qualified interpreter, and pay for community work. Do not assign either to staff because of who they are. A Timkat visit is optional professional development where you are a guest, and it does not make you the expert.

sections.heading: Amharic-speaking Minnesota — the heart of a people
sections.body:
To speak Amharic in Minnesota is sometimes to be Amhara, and sometimes to be a person the empire taught a second language, and both sit in this door. Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo is central for many Amhara, while Protestant and Muslim Ethiopian streams are real as well. Intra-Ethiopian politics — Amhara, Oromo, Tigrayan — live in Minnesota parking lots, and you do not pick a side.

### In this state

In this building another fact sits on top: many of these households are Black in a racial order in the United States that will file them under Somali or under historic African American and get the language, the church, and the name wrong, because shared race is not shared culture.

This guide is a working orientation, and individual variation always supersedes group generalization.

sections.heading: Core Concepts
sections.body:
Language comes first, so confirm whether Amharic is the home language or the working language, because Afaan Oromoo and Tigrinya are not dialects of Amharic.

### Orthodox fasting and calendar

There are many fast days — weekly Wednesday and Friday for some, long Lenten and Advent fasts, and other seasons. This is operations for appointments, blood draws, and medication with food, not a piety rank.

### Honorifics

Ato (Mr.), Weizero (Mrs.), and Weizerit (Miss) are the honorifics, alongside church titles and the standing of elders.

### Three names

A person carries a given name, a father’s name, and often a grandfather’s, and there is no family surname of the kind the database wants. It is the same trap as Somali with a different grammar, so do not invent a last name.

### Checking for agreement

Before you treat a yes as agreement, ask again, plainly and without embarrassing anyone.

### Injera, coffee ceremony, parish

These are ordinary life, not a festival you attend as consultation.

sections.heading: Religion and Healing
sections.body:
Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo is central for many Amhara households — one of the oldest Christian churches, with Ge’ez liturgy, icons, fasting, Timkat, Meskel, and Gena (January 7). Debtera and priest are church roles, and they are not the case plan unless this family asked, so do not book a liturgy as DHS programming.

### Streams

Protestant and evangelical Ethiopian streams are large in the diaspora, and Muslim Ethiopian streams exist as well, so ask, book the language, do not copy Somali Islam onto this page, and use lunar Islamic dates if this family is Muslim.

### Practice

Fasting calendars are operations. A missed morning appointment during a fast, a medication labeled “with food,” a blood draw — ask about each, because what looks like noncompliance may be the calendar you never learned.

Illness meaning may sit next to holy water, vow, and parish counsel, and you can hold that next to a waiver, but you do not mock it, and you do not skip the clinic.

sections.heading: Greetings
sections.body:
Ask who to greet first, or follow the household’s lead. Use Ato, Weizero, or Weizerit plus the given name until invited otherwise, and church titles for a priest, and say the name, asking how to say it.

### Titles

Shoulder bumps and cheek kisses (often two or three) happen in some rooms among people who already know each other. A hard American handshake is not universal, though some people will shake in English-language offices, so follow the room, and do not force a hand. Let this person’s own greeting guide you, whatever you read on another page.

### This room

Selam, tenastëllïn, an English hello — follow what they offer.

sections.heading: Naming Conventions
sections.body:
Names often run given name plus the father’s given name, and the second name is not a family surname as the database wants it. Children take the father’s given name as their second name, and the grandfather’s name may appear as a third. It is the same trap as Somali, with a different grammar and different people, so do not invent a last name because the screen requires one, since that invented name becomes a gate that follows the person to Medicaid, school, and a background check.

### How to file

Women do not automatically take a husband’s name, so ask how to file. Do not “correct” a mother and child who do not share a last name, and do not treat it as fraud until you have a reason.

Honorifics are Ato, Weizero, and Weizerit, so use them. Pronounce the name, and ask, because the form that demands first-middle-last and a hyphen will invent a person.

sections.heading: Dates of Significance
sections.body:
Enkutatash — Ethiopian New Year — falls on 11 September (12 September after a Gregorian leap year). It is public and parish, and it is literacy for the desk, not a day off the work unless they asked.

### Calendar

Timkat (Epiphany, 19 January). Meskel (Finding of the True Cross, late September). Gena — Orthodox Christmas, 7 January. Fasika — Easter, on the Orthodox calculation. Fasting seasons come before these, and weekly fasts for some, and all of this is operations.

Use lunar Islamic dates if this family is Muslim, and do not assume they are not.

A calendar click is literacy rather than community engagement, so do not put “African holiday” on a case note.

sections.heading: Education
sections.body:
Compass Ethiopian, for age 25 and older and as an umbrella, reports about 79.5 percent with high school or higher and about 24.1 percent with a bachelor’s or higher. Date it, and remember it is not an Amharic-only rate, because a professional class is real, and so is an elder who reads fidel and not the English IEP.

### School and language

Fidel literacy is not English literacy, so a parent who writes Amharic and cannot run an exception form in English is not illiterate, and the English-only form is the gate.
