Confirm whether Amharic is the first language, because an Oromo parent given an Amharic interpreter still will not work. Second-generation English is common, but the IEP still has to reach the parent who does not read it.

sections.heading: Etiquette
sections.body:
If you visit a home, look for shoes by the door or ask what the household prefers. If food or drink is offered, accepting a little is fine, and you can still keep to medical and legal timelines.

### In the home

Ask before taking any photograph or touching any religious object, and do not ask anyone to explain their faith or history for your benefit.

### Time

Church time can run long, and Sunday and feast-day mornings are operations, while being on time for your appointment still matters. Name the conflict, ask whether they agree with the plan, and confirm in the language they use.

sections.heading: Language and Communication
sections.body:
The language is Amharic, written in fidel (a Ge’ez-derived script), while Ge’ez itself is liturgical, not the interview language. Compass Ethiopian, as an umbrella, reports that among those 5 and older about 76.2 percent (ACS 2020–2024) speak a language other than English and about 30.2 percent speak English less than “very well,” so date it, and remember it is not an Amharic-only LEP rate.

### Language

An Oromo interpreter is the wrong door, a Somali interpreter is the wrong door, and a Tigrinya interpreter is the wrong door unless they asked for Tigrinya. Confirm whether Amharic is the first language or the empire’s second language in this home, and book what they name.

Give the person time to answer. If you get a short yes, check that the plan was understood, and ask whether it works for them.

Do not make an Amharic-speaking coworker the interpreter.

sections.heading: Other Considerations
sections.body:
This section states hard facts plainly, because treating everyone the same can hide them.

### Named harms

Intra-Ethiopian political tension in Minnesota is real — Amhara, Oromo, Tigrayan, and the Tigray war as current structure — so do not pick a side, and do not pretend the parking lot is one “Ethiopian community.” Parish and Facebook are not a case plan.

Colorism and highland/lowland hierarchy travel, so you do not audit skin, but you also do not delete the hierarchy to keep a training comfortable. LGBTQ Amharic-speaking Minnesotans exist, and conservative Orthodox, Protestant, and Muslim climates can mean silence, so you use the name they use, and you do not out someone to kin and call it culture.

FGC is not the Amhara default story, so do not paste the Somali chapter here, and if a household names it, follow the law rather than skipping mandated reporting as humility. The enforcement climate changes who opens the door, so do not collect status you do not need, and do not treat fear as noncompliance.

Staff who share this community may add facts, but they do not get to delete a fact because it is hard to say.

sections.heading: Health
sections.body:
Compass Ethiopian disability is 5.5 percent — an umbrella figure, dated. Fasting interacts with diabetes medication, pregnancy advice, and lab timing, so ask, because “noncompliance” may be the fast you never put on the appointment.

### Access

There is no Amharic-specific Minnesota autism rate on this page, and you should not invent one or paste Somali ADDM or Hmong under-identification onto this people. Screen, and date a study when a controlling source exists.

Gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care, so offer it, and believe reported pain. Do not fold this history into Tuskegee or into a generic “African immigrant” slide.

Holy water, vow, and parish counsel can sit next to biomedicine, so if they name a healer or a priest, listen, but do not make them the case plan unless they asked.

sections.heading: LGBTQ
sections.body:
Queer and trans Amharic-speaking Minnesotans exist, and conservative Orthodox, Protestant, and Muslim climates can mean silence or exile, so some people live a public English life and a private Amharic life.

### This person

Use the name they use, and do not share what they tell you unless a rule requires it. Minnesota’s Human Rights Act still applies.

sections.heading: Hair, Dress, and Body
sections.body:
The Orthodox white netela or gabi worn in church is not a daily uniform, and the second generation looks like Minnesota, so do not ask a woman in clinic whether she “still wears the shawl.”

### Dress

Hair, covering, and modest dress vary by Orthodox, Protestant, Muslim, and secular practice, so do not touch. This is not the CROWN Act chapter, and it is not the Somali hijab chapter.

Follow this person, and offer gender match if she wants it.

sections.heading: Music
sections.body:
Orthodox chant in Ge’ez, kebero drums, eskista as dance, Protestant worship music, and diaspora pop all live here.

### Variation

Liturgy is not staff entertainment, and a playlist is not engagement.

A Timkat procession is public, and you are a guest there.

sections.heading: Sports
sections.body:
Distance running is a public image of Ethiopia, but it is not a personality, and it is not a health history.

### Not the whole person

Soccer and ordinary school sport are real in the second generation, but sport clubs are not language access, and they are not a case plan.

Do not assume the kid runs.

sections.heading: Literature
sections.body:
The Ge’ez and Amharic written tradition is old — older than the refugee file — and fidel made a public possible, a public that includes newspapers, church texts, diaspora writers, and a second-generation English.

### Literacy in the lobby

You do not need to quote a novel, but you need to know that this is not a people without letters.

The English form may still be unreadable to the parent who reads fidel.

sections.heading: Art
sections.body:
Orthodox iconography, textile, and church architecture belong here, and so does injera as an ordinary table rather than a Heritage Month sample, while the parish is public art for some.

### Guest

Be a guest, because a Timkat procession is not consultation, and a museum visit is not a case plan.

Do not put an icon on a unit display.

sections.heading: Conflict, War, and the State
sections.body:
Imperial history, 1974, the Red Terror, the Derg, the 1980s famine, 1991, and the 2020–2022 Tigray war as current structure — that is the political file, and intra-Ethiopian politics in Minnesota are not folklore.

### The badge

A DHS badge is not automatically help, so do not referee the Tigray war in a waiver meeting, and do not pick a side.

Do not ask anyone to narrate killing for your professional development. Mandated reporting still exists, and so does the duty not to treat a whole community as a faction score.

sections.heading: Work, Markets, and Government
sections.body:
Compass Ethiopian, as a dated umbrella, reports a median household income of about $63,667 (2024 dollars, ACS 2020–2024), poverty of 10.9 percent, and renters at 64.4 percent. Work spans restaurants, parking, care work, a professional class, and public employment, and that is pattern, not a personality.

### Work

Book a qualified interpreter, and pay for community work. Do not assign either to staff because of who they are.

### Staff

Take time to introduce yourself and explain the plan, and still give any required notice.

sections.heading: Health-care and Human-service Encounters
sections.body:
The encounter may open through the wrong language door — Somali, Oromo, or Tigrinya when they asked for Amharic, or Amharic when the home language is not Amharic. It may involve the three-name form, fasting set against an appointment, who is in the room, intra-community tension, and the enforcement climate.

### Language

Confirm that Amharic is the home language, offer gender match, and ask who should hear, but do not make staff the interpreter.

### The meeting

If they name a priest, listen, and remember that mandated reporting still exists.

sections.heading: Adjacent Peoples — Do Not Mash
sections.body:
This page does not treat Oromo as a synonym, and it does not treat Tigrayan as a synonym. It is not Somali, and it is not Eritrean by default, since that is Tigrinya and Arabic and a different state. It is not Kenyan, not historic African American, and not an “East African interpreter.”

### Adjacent doors

Compass Ethiopian is the umbrella, and this page is the Amharic door. If the household is Oromo, open Oromo; if Tigrayan, book Tigrinya; and if Somali — including Ethiopia-born Somali ancestry — open Somali Minnesota.

Some households are mixed, so ask this household, and never use one Ethiopian module.

sections.heading: Counts, Dated
sections.body:
Minnesota Compass, drawing on ACS 2020–2024, describes the Ethiopian cultural community (an umbrella) this way: 45,159 people used in analysis (give or take 5,404; 2024 single-year total 53,754, give or take 12,826); Twin Cities 89.7%; Greater Minnesota 10.3%; age 17 or younger 43.8%; 65+ 3.5%; foreign-born 59.8%; language other than English (age 5+) 76.2%; English less than “very well” 30.2%; median household income about $63,667 (2024 dollars); poverty 10.9%; renter-occupied 64.4%; average household size 3.30; disability 5.5%. High school or higher (25+) is 79.5%, bachelor’s or higher 24.1%, and owner-occupied housing 35.6%.

### Counts

Respondents born in Ethiopia who list Somali ancestry are counted as Somali, not Ethiopian, and the Census recodes some Oromo write-ins as Ethiopian, which means this is not an Amharic speaker count, so do not invent one.

### What the count is not

Minnesota Secretary of State voter materials include Amharic, and that is operations evidence that the language is in the state, not a population.

Date the number, and remember that a young age structure is not a personality and a rate is not the person.

sections.heading: Doors and Sources
sections.body:
The sources are these: the Minnesota Compass Ethiopian profile (ACS 2020–2024); the Compass cultural-communities methodology (the Oromo recode and the Somali ancestry carve-out); the CLAS fifteen interpreter cards, which list Amharic; the Minnesota Secretary of State Amharic voter tools; the Orthodox parishes families name, including Debre Selam Medhanealem; and the Ethiopian Community in Minnesota as a historical local door. Pay the partner, and remember that identity is not a staffing plan.

### Public doors

CECLC is a door, not the whole community. Use these resources yourself before you ask an Amharic-speaking colleague to explain.

### Where to learn more

Report back, and be a guest.

sections.heading: How it hits DHS gates — the 40%
sections.body:
Workplace culture and service delivery are both candidates here.

Language: an interpreter labeled Ethiopian, Somali, or Oromo who is not Amharic as this household speaks it will not work, so confirm whether Amharic is the first language or the empire’s second language in this home. If Oromo, book Afaan Oromoo, and if Tigrayan, book Tigrinya, and remember that gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care.

Names: given name plus father’s name. The database that invents a last name is a gate that follows the person, and it is the same trap as Somali, with different people.

Fasting: Wednesday, Friday, Lent, Advent, and other seasons for many Orthodox households. Medication with food, labs, and morning appointments all depend on it, so ask about feast days before you schedule.

Hour caps, exception processes, and life-sharing matches made without language are not culturally neutral.

Notices and comment: do not count an eList and an English PDF as reaching this community, and record who was reached and what follow-up happened. SOS already prints Amharic for voters, so the packet can too.

Workforce: Amharic-speaking staff are not the interpreter pool, and they are not the community.

Legislation, funding, rule: study a channel before you advocate for it. Use this page so that the 40% has a household in it.

sections.heading: A Note on This Guide
sections.body:
This brief is a language door rather than a people, because “French-speaking Minnesota” names a CLAS fifteen line and a set of households who may use French at school, at the clinic, or with the state, and who often use another language at home. For that reason, ask which French they use and whether another language is actually the home language.

### Who this is

The streams here are not interchangeable, since the place a family comes from shapes which language lives in the kitchen and which one lives in the school. In Haiti, Kreyòl (Haitian Creole) is often the home language and French the school or official language, while in West and Central Africa, Wolof, Bambara, Lingala, Kinyarwanda, and many other languages may be home and French the colonial/school language. France, Belgium, Quebec, and other European or North American streams are smaller in Minnesota services but real, and some Somali and other Horn households have French from Djibouti or from camps, although that is not the default.

### Who this is not

This is not historic African American CI with a different flag, and it is not Somali, not one Africa, and not France. Do not assume Africa, do not assume France, and do not assume Haiti. A full mosaic is not a stereotype, because a stereotype is what happens when this page becomes the person in the lobby.

### How to read this

Minnesota Compass has no cultural-community row for “French” or “Francophone,” but Census Bureau tables give Minnesota counts to use with their margins of error: French ancestry (with income, education, poverty and disability profiles), French Canadian, Belgian, Swiss and Haitian ancestry; birthplaces for 2020 to 2024 including France 1,626, Haiti 1,653, Cameroon 4,077 and Togo 1,731; and, for 2020 to 2024, 16,918 French speakers and 1,914 Haitian Creole speakers age 5 and older. Do not invent a census beyond those. The Star Tribune (July 31, 2025) reported that among people in Minnesota who speak a language other than English at home, French is among the languages, with German, Chinese, Russian, and Arabic, that each represent about 2 percent of that group. Date it when you use it, and remember that it is a language share rather than a Haitian count, a Senegalese count, or a Québécois count.

The diversity inside the door is the point. A Kreyòl-speaking mother, a Lingala-speaking father from Kinshasa who uses French with the school, a Dakar household that wants Wolof, a Quebecois professional, a French national on a campus, and a Djiboutian elder who has French from a camp do not share a Tuesday.

Always defer to the person in front of you, because this page is a hypothesis you still test on this family.

sections.heading: Origins — several peoples, one colonial language
sections.body:
Haitian peoplehood is neither an African checkbox nor a French checkbox, because the Haitian Revolution reached independence on January 1, 1804, creating the first Black republic in the hemisphere. The U.S. occupation (1915–1934), dictatorships, the 2010 earthquake, and later TPS designations are Haitian history, and they belong to the people rather than to a form. Kreyòl is the home language of the people, while French was the colonial and school language. Book Kreyòl if that is the home language.

### History for the meeting

West and Central Africa are many nations and many peoples under a French school language left by colonization, including Senegal, Mali, Guinea, Côte d’Ivoire, Cameroon, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Congo-Brazzaville, francophone Rwanda and Burundi, and others. Because Wolof, Bambara, Lingala, Kinyarwanda, Fulani, and more may be what the grandmother actually speaks, an “African French” interpreter can still be the wrong door.

### What people brought

France, Belgium, Switzerland, and Quebec are the European and North American streams, and although they are smaller in Minnesota human services, they are real. The largest group connected to this page is Minnesotans of French and French Canadian descent: the 2025 American Community Survey counts 127,624 Minnesotans naming French ancestry and 34,940 naming French Canadian (2020 to 2024: 150,045 and 41,490). Almost all were born in the U.S., their median age is 52.7, and only 2.6 percent speak a language other than English at home. Do not assume Africa when the household is Paris, and do not assume Paris when the household is Port-au-Prince or Yaoundé.

Some Somali and other Horn households have French from Djibouti, from camps, or from a third country, but that is not the default for Somali Minnesota. Open Somali for Somali and ask about French only if they name it.

sections.heading: The Geography of French as a Door
sections.body:
Haiti is Caribbean, while Dakar, Bamako, Abidjan, Yaoundé, Kinshasa, Brazzaville, Kigali, and Bujumbura are African cities with different languages under the French door. Paris, Brussels, and Montreal are not those cities.

### Homeland

Minnesota is a present in both the Twin Cities and Greater Minnesota, so do not assume Minneapolis when plant towns, student neighborhoods, and inner-ring suburbs can all hold a household on this door.

### Minnesota

There is no Compass map for this umbrella, which means you should date any town-level school-language count when a professional has it. The pattern now is simply that people are here, so do not invent a county number to make the map look complete.

sections.heading: 1804, Occupation, Earthquake, Colonies, and TPS — Foundational Events
sections.body:
For Haiti, 1804 is peoplehood, and the U.S. occupied Haiti from 1915 to 1934. The January 12, 2010 earthquake killed on a scale this building should not turn into a speech. Temporary Protected Status for Haiti was first designated after that earthquake and has been extended, terminated, and redesignated in later years, including after the 2021 assassination of President Jovenel Moïse and another earthquake, so date the designation you mean. Do not invent this person’s status, and do not collect status you do not need.

### Foundational events

West and Central African migration into Minnesota includes students, skilled workers, family, and people displaced by conflict, and French is often the language a school left them rather than the language of the kitchen. Colonial borders and later wars are literacy for you, not a news-clip briefing you give the family.

### Who you meet

Euro-French, Belgian, and Quebec streams arrive as professionals, students, and family, and while they are smaller in the service lobby, they are real. Do not run a refugee script on a Lyon household, and do not run a Paris script on a Cap-Haïtien household.

If you only know “French,” you will miss Kreyòl, miss Lingala, and mash a people.

sections.heading: Family
sections.body:
A Haitian or West/Central African household may be extended, and godparents, church sisters, mosque kin, and cousins called “auntie” may not match the waiver checkbox. Ask who should be in the room.

### Who is in the household

Euro-French nuclear grammar is not the default for this door, so do not import it into a household that is organized another way.

### Who speaks

Who cares for the child, who holds the lease, and who can sign may not be the same adult. Mixed-status households exist in Haitian and some African streams, which is one more reason not to collect status you do not need.

Minnesota law still stands, so do not skip mandated reporting and call it culture, and do not turn a family argument into a national personality.

sections.heading: Minnesota and This Language Door
sections.body:
This department will meet these households on waivers, child welfare, health care, cash, food, aging, TPS-adjacent fear, and employment, in both the Twin Cities and Greater Minnesota. Rural is not an afterthought when the plant or the college is the draw.

### Places

Churches (Catholic and Protestant) and mosques are often the actual information channel, and although parish and mosque are not “the community,” they are a door if this family names them.

### Partners

Alliance Française and campus French clubs are Euro-French civic and student doors, which means they are not the service partner for a Haitian or Senegalese household unless that household names them. Do not BCC a conversation group and call it consultation.

Do not make Haitian, Senegalese, Congolese, or Cameroonian staff the interpreter pool or “the African voice,” since identity is not a staffing plan.

sections.heading: A language door, not a people mash
sections.body:
To be filed under French in Minnesota is often to be asked whether you are from France, or from Africa, as if those were two rooms and Haiti were in one of them.

### In this state

Anti-Blackness in this state hits Haitian and African francophone people in the lobby, the clinic, and the traffic stop. That is not a reason to open historic African American CI and stop. Open African American for a Great Migration household, open this page for a Haitian or Senegalese household, and open Somali for Somali. Shared race in the United States is not shared culture, and a shared French class in a colonial school is not shared culture either.

Colorism sits inside some Haitian and West African families and inside Minnesota’s racial order, so you do not lecture it, and you do not pretend it is absent.

This guide is a working orientation, which is why individual variation always supersedes group generalization.

sections.heading: Core Concepts
sections.body:
Home language is the first grammar, because French may be the school language while Kreyòl, Lingala, Wolof, Bambara, or Kinyarwanda may be home, so book home.

### One Francophone client is a mash

Haiti is not Senegal, DRC is not Cameroon, and Quebec is not Port-au-Prince.

### Colorism and anti-Blackness

Both can be in the room, and neither is a personality.

### Church or mosque as channel

Neither is the case plan unless they asked, even when it is where the family hears the news.

### TPS and enforcement climate

People may skip clinic and waiver meetings when a relative can be moved, and that is not noncompliance.

### Respect and titles in many streams

Use a title with an older person until you are invited to do otherwise.

sections.heading: Religion
sections.body:
Catholic Christianity is large in Haiti, in parts of West and Central Africa, and in Euro-French streams, while Protestant and evangelical churches are ordinary too. Islam is ordinary in much of West Africa and present in some Haitian households. None is real as well.

### Streams

Vodou is a Haitian religious fact in some households, so do not sensationalize it. Do not treat it as horror-film content, as witchcraft for the file, or as the “real” Haiti. Do not make a Vodou priest the case plan unless this family asked, and hold the same rule for a Catholic priest or an imam.

### Practice

Do not assume a mosque because the passport is West African, and do not assume a cathedral because the language is French, because faith in this door follows the family rather than the language.

sections.heading: Greetings
sections.body:
French vous vs tu is a formality system some Euro-French and African school-French speakers use, but Kreyòl greetings are not that system, and neither are Wolof and Lingala greetings, so follow this room.

### Titles

Elders and titles matter in many Haitian and African streams, and while a handshake is ordinary in many professional rooms, you should not force a hug.

### This room

Do not import a Paris rule onto a Haitian elder, and do not import a Port-au-Prince manner onto a Lille professional. Let this person’s own greeting guide you, whatever you read on another page.

Ask before any physical contact, and let the person set the limit.

sections.heading: Naming Conventions
sections.body:
A French-style given name plus family name appears in some streams, but Haitian naming may not match first-middle-last, and West African naming may include a day name, a Muslim name, a family name, or a French school name that is not what the grandmother uses. Ask how to say it, and ask how to file it.

### How to file

Do not invent a last name, and do not “correct” Kreyòl or Wolof spelling to Paris French, since the spelling the family uses is the record. Do not treat unmatched last names in a household as fraud by default.

A child may have a different school name than the name on the birth record, so ask, and do not humiliate the family over the difference.

sections.heading: Dates of Significance
sections.body:
January 1 is Haitian Independence Day, marking 1804, and it is literacy for you rather than a day off the work unless this family names it. It is not Bastille Day.

### Calendar

January 12, 2010 is the Haiti earthquake, and because TPS history starts here for many families, it is literacy rather than a speech.

West African independence dates vary by country (1960 is a cluster, not a single day), and Catholic calendars, Ramadan and Eid in Muslim households, and the national days this family names all matter, so ask. Do not put Bastille Day (July 14) on a Haitian or Senegalese case note, though the Alliance Française celebrates it publicly each year. Little Canada's Canadian Days, held every year since 1977, is the state's main French Canadian heritage festival, and Haitian Flag Day (May 18) was celebrated in Minneapolis in 2025.

A calendar click is not community engagement, however well it is meant.

sections.heading: Education
sections.body:
French as a school or official language does not mean French is the home language, and it does not mean the parent can run an English IEP. Literacy in any language of the form is not guaranteed. Interrupted schooling in Haiti after 2010, or in a conflict region, is structure rather than a personal failing.

### School and language

A parent who speaks fluent Kreyòl, Wolof, or Lingala and limited English is not illiterate, because the English-only form is the gate. So is a French form when the home language is Kreyòl.

Second-generation English is common, but CLAS still says do not use minors as interpreters, so book the home language.

Do not invent a Minnesota Francophone attainment rate, since Compass has no such row.

sections.heading: Etiquette
sections.body:
If food or drink is offered, accepting a little is fine, and you can still keep to medical and legal timelines.

### In the home

Do not assume a French-restaurant manner, such as wine, first names after one meeting, or cheek kisses, is the rule in this living room. Do not assume the absence of that manner is “less educated.”

### Time

Shoes, food, and Sunday church or Friday mosque will vary, so ask. Being on time for appointments is a professional default for some and a bus-and-shift problem for others, which is why lateness is not a verdict on the family.

If someone misses an appointment, first check the time, transport, interpreter and work schedule. Confirm the plan in the language the person uses, and ask whether it works for them.

sections.heading: Language and Communication
sections.body:
Ask which language is actually home, and book that language, because the language on the form is not always the language at the table.

### Language

Kreyòl is not French, and a French interpreter for a Kreyòl household will not work. In the same way, Lingala is not French, Wolof is not French, Bambara is not French, and Kinyarwanda is not French, so an interpreter billed as “African French” can still be the wrong country, the wrong register, and the wrong language.

French itself is not one French, since Haitian school French, Dakar French, Kinshasa French, and Paris French differ in accent and vocabulary. Mutual understanding is often possible but not guaranteed, so ask.

The Star Tribune (July 31, 2025) put French at about 2 percent of the non-English-at-home group in Minnesota, listed with German, Chinese, Russian, and Arabic, so date it when you cite it. That share does not tell you which French, or whether French is home.

Give the person time to answer. If you get a short yes, check that the plan was understood, and ask whether it works for them.

sections.heading: Other Considerations
sections.body:
This section states hard facts plainly, because treating everyone the same can hide them.

### Named harms

Anti-Blackness in Minnesota hits Haitian and African francophone people, and traffic stops, clinic dismissal, and “where are you really from” are structure rather than isolated moments. Do not fold this household into historic African American CI because both are Black, and do not pretend anti-Blackness is absent because the passport is Haitian or Senegalese.

Colorism inside families and in the U.S. racial order is real, so you do not lecture it, and you do not skip it when it is the harm in the room.

LGBTQ Haitian and African francophone Minnesotans exist. Enforcement and TPS climate is current structure, and because people may skip clinic, school, and waiver meetings in that climate, the absence is not noncompliance, which is also why you should not collect status you do not need.

One Francophone client is how treating everyone the same hides difference, since Haiti is not Africa, Africa is not France, and France is not Haiti.

Staff who share this community may add facts, but they do not get to delete a fact because it is hard to say.

sections.heading: Health
sections.body:
Language is the first health gate, because a French consent form for a Kreyòl speaker is not consent, and a smile is not consent.

### Access

Trauma and displacement in some Haitian and African streams are real, so do not invent a Minnesota Francophone PTSD rate, do not skip screening, and do not make an earthquake or a war a personality.

Believe reported pain, since anti-Blackness in U.S. medicine is documented. Do not mash Tuskegee onto a Port-au-Prince or Dakar history, and do not pretend the clinic is neutral either.

Gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care, so offer it. If they name a healer, a priest, or an imam, listen, but do not make that person the case plan unless they asked.

sections.heading: LGBTQ
sections.body:
Queer and trans Haitian, African francophone, and Euro-French Minnesotans exist, and conservative church, mosque, and family climates can mean silence or exile. Because some people live a public English life and a private home-language life, you use the name they use and do not share what they tell you unless a rule requires it.

### This person

Minnesota’s Human Rights Act still applies. Use the name the person uses, and do not share what they tell you unless a rule requires it.

Do not assume a Paris household is affirming, and do not assume a Port-au-Prince household is not. Ask this person rather than reading the answer off a city.

sections.heading: Hair, Dress, and Body
sections.body:
Hair is political for many Black francophone people in this state, so with natural hair, braids, locs, wraps, and wigs, follow this person. Minnesota’s CROWN Act still applies. You do not touch, you do not ask to “see it out,” and you do not treat a headwrap as a costume.

### Dress

Euro-French dress codes are not the rule on this door, so do not police “professional” hair on Haitian or African staff.

Festival dress is public on some dates and is not a daily uniform, so do not ask if they “still wear traditional clothes.”

sections.heading: Music
sections.body:
Kompa and rara live in Haitian public life, mbalax in Senegalese streams, and Congolese rumba and ndombolo alongside church music and French pop. This is not one soundtrack, and not a festival booth.

### Variation

A playlist is not engagement, so do not ask a client or a staff person to perform.

Sunday choir is operations for some Baptist and Catholic households, and although it matters to them, it is not consultation.

sections.heading: Sports
sections.body:
Soccer is public in many Haitian and African francophone communities, and ordinary school sport is ordinary for the second generation, but neither is language access.

### Not the whole person

Do not use a national-team jersey as a case plan. Sport clubs are not a substitute for an interpreter or a notice.

A Saturday league in a southern town is not consultation, so book the home language for the parent who is in the stands and cannot run the IEP.

sections.heading: Literature
sections.body:
Haitian literature in Kreyòl and French, Senegalese and Congolese and Cameroonian writing, and the French canon are not one shelf. Kreyòl literature is literature, and oral tradition is not the absence of letters.

### Literacy in the lobby

You do not need to quote Césaire, Chauvet, or a Paris syllabus, but you do need to know that this door is not a people without letters, and not one people.

Do not put a proverb on a brochure and call it CLAS, because decoration is not language access.

sections.heading: Art
sections.body:
Haitian painting, sequined flags, West and Central African cloth and carving, and Euro-French museum culture are not interchangeable. Do not mash them onto a generic “African art” Heritage Month table.

### Guest

Be a guest, because public festivals are not consultation, and do not extract a staff person’s child as entertainment.

Alliance Française gallery nights are a Euro-French civic door, which means they are not the service partner for a Haitian or Senegalese household unless that household names them.

sections.heading: Conflict, the State, and This Climate
sections.body:
1804 is Haitian peoplehood, while U.S. occupation, dictatorship, 2010, and TPS are U.S. and Haitian state history in the same file. Colonial borders and wars in West and Central Africa produced displacement and a school language, so you do not invent a briefing from a news clip.

### The badge

The enforcement climate now, with TPS uncertainty, raids in the news, and a relative who can be moved, changes who opens the door, because a DHS badge is not automatically help. Do not collect status you do not need, and do not treat fear as noncompliance.

Do not use 1804 or 2010 as a personality, and do not ask a person to narrate an earthquake or a war for your professional development.

sections.heading: Work, Business, and Government
sections.body:
Work here spans service, care work, plants in Greater Minnesota, the professional class, students, and small business. Do not invent a Minnesota Francophone occupational census, since Compass has no such row, and the pattern is simply that people work here.

### Work

Book a qualified interpreter, and pay for community work. Do not assign either to staff because of who they are.

### Staff

Take time to introduce yourself and explain the plan, and still give any required notice.

sections.heading: Health-care and Human-service Encounters
sections.body:
The encounter turns on home language versus school French, whether Kreyòl, Lingala, or Wolof, and on who is in the room, gender, the TPS climate, anti-Blackness in the clinic, and a priest, an imam, or Vodou in the story.

### Language

Confirm the home language, offer gender match, and believe reported pain. Do not collect status, and do not make staff the interpreter, while remembering that mandated reporting still exists.

### The meeting

A French consent form for a Kreyòl speaker is not consent, and a smile is not consent, so name who the form was built for.

sections.heading: Adjacent Peoples — Do Not Mash
sections.body:
This door is not historic African American, not Somali, not Oromo, not Liberian, and not Nigerian, and it is neither one Africa nor France as the default, so open those CIs for those households.

### Adjacent doors

Haitian, Senegalese, Malian, Guinean, Ivorian, Cameroonian, Congolese, Rwandan, Burundian, and Québécois households are not interchangeable. Some Somali households have French from Djibouti or camps, but because that is not the default, ask this household.

Never one Black module, and never one Francophone client.

sections.heading: Counts, Dated — and what you may not invent
sections.body:
Minnesota Compass has no cultural-community row for French, Haitian, Senegalese, or “Francophone,” but Census Bureau tables give Minnesota counts for French, French Canadian, Belgian, Swiss and Haitian ancestry, birthplaces, and home language (2020 to 2024: 16,918 French speakers and 1,914 Haitian Creole speakers age 5 and older), so use those with their margins of error and do not invent a census beyond them. Do not borrow Compass African American, Somali, or Kenyan counts and file them here.

### Counts

The Star Tribune, July 31, 2025, reporting on languages spoken at home in Minnesota, found that among people who speak a language other than English at home, German, French, Chinese, Russian, and Arabic each represent about 2 percent of that group. A January 2026 Department of Public Safety report using Census data lists 16,313 French speakers among 658,004 people speaking a language other than English, about 2.5 percent. Date it when you use it, because that is a language share: it does not tell you home language vs school language, and it does not disaggregate Kreyòl, which may be coded elsewhere or missed. Name the gap.

### What the count is not

School-language and interpreter-request data in a county are a pattern when you have them, so date them, because a rate you do not have is not a rate you may put on this page.

sections.heading: Doors and Sources
sections.body:
Start with the Star Tribune, July 31, 2025, on languages spoken at home. French is on the CLAS fifteen, but Haitian Creole is not among the 15, so book Kreyòl when Kreyòl is home, and book Lingala, Wolof, Bambara, or Kinyarwanda when that is home, because a French interpreter can still be the wrong door.

### Public doors

The doors are the Haitian, West African, and Central African associations this person names, and the churches and mosques this person names. Alliance Française is a Euro-French civic door, so use it if they name it rather than as the default partner.

### Where to learn more

CECLC is one door, not the whole community, so use these resources yourself before you ask a Haitian or Senegalese colleague to explain. Pay partners, and report back on what you did with what they shared.

sections.heading: How it hits DHS gates — the 40%
sections.body:
Workplace culture and service delivery are both candidates here, since a gate can sit in the office as easily as at the front desk.

On language, a French interpreter for a Kreyòl household will not work, and a French interpreter for a Lingala or Wolof household will not work, because “African French” is not a dialect you may invent. Gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care.

On names, the database that invents a last name or “corrects” Kreyòl spelling to Paris French is a gate.

Hour caps, exception processes, and life-sharing matches without the home language are not culturally neutral, which means an English IEP is a gate, and a French packet when home is Kreyòl is a gate.

On the one Francophone client, Haiti is not Africa, Africa is not France, and France is not Haiti, so folding a Haitian household into historic African American CI because both are Black shuts the person out. Open the right page.

On enforcement and TPS climate, people may skip clinic, school, and waiver meetings when a relative can be moved, and that is not noncompliance, so do not collect status you do not need.

On notices and comment, do not count an eList and an English PDF as reaching these households, and record who was reached and what follow-up happened.

On workforce, Haitian and African francophone staff are not the interpreter pool and not the community.

On legislation, funding, and rule, study a channel before you advocate for it. Use this page so that the 40% has a household in it.

sections.heading: A Note on This Guide
sections.body:
This brief is about Burmese Minnesota as a people-page, and it is also a warning about an umbrella. The CLAS fifteen interpreter cards say Burmese, and Minnesota Compass (ACS 2020–2024) says Burmese 19,372, give or take 3,438. Both are operations, and both rest on a U.S. administrative name, which is why neither one is a people.

### Who this is

This is not Karen as a synonym, and not Chin as a synonym, and it is not Kachin, not Mon, not Rohingya, and not “Asian.” Compass Burmese can include Bamar, the majority people of Myanmar, often called Burman, and it may overlap with or sit beside Chin, Kachin, Rohingya, Mon, and Karen. The Compass methodology matters here, because the Census recodes some people who write Karen into Burmese, with nothing left to show the original response, so ask the people. If the household is Karen, open Karen Minnesota and put S’gaw or Pwo on the line; if Chin, book Chin, whether Hakha, Falam, or the variety they name; and if Rohingya, the language may be Rohingya or Bengali. Burmese is not the default.

### Who this is not

The Compass figures (ACS 2020–2024), dated, run as follows. Twin Cities 83.0 percent and Greater Minnesota 17.0 percent; age 17 or younger 41.1 percent, and 65+ 3.4 percent; foreign-born 66.9 percent. Among those age 5+, 89.1 percent speak a language other than English, and 68.1 percent speak English less than “very well,” which is a severe language gate. Among those 25+, high school or higher is 33.0 percent and bachelor’s or higher is 11.8 percent. Median household income is $85,747 (2024 dollars), poverty is 22.2 percent, owner-occupied housing is 67.9 percent, average household size is 5.05, and disability is 13.8 percent. Date Compass when you cite it, and remember that a rate is not the person.

The diversity inside the umbrella is the point. Picture a Bamar Buddhist elder who reads Myanmar script, a Hakha Chin Christian parent, a S’gaw Karen household that should have opened the Karen page, a Rohingya family who should not have been booked Burmese, and a U.S.-born teenager who uses English with friends and still translates for a 67-percent-LEP parent. They share a country checkbox, but they do not share a Tuesday.

### How to read this

Always defer to the person in front of you, because this page is a hypothesis and you still have to test it on this family.

sections.heading: Origins and the Founding of a People
sections.body:
Bamar peoplehood on the Irrawaddy is older than the British and older than the junta. Theravada Buddhism, Burmese as a tonal language with its own script, wet-rice agriculture, and a sequence of kingdoms organized a majority that is not the whole country, because Chin, Kachin, Karen, Karenni, Mon, Rakhine, Rohingya, Shan, and others are peoples, not dialects. That is why a country checkbox that says Burma or Myanmar is already a mash.

### History for the meeting

British colonial rule, independence in 1948, and decades of military government produced the file this desk meets. The years that matter are 1988, 2007, 2017 in Rakhine, and the 2021 coup, which is current structure. Camps in Thailand and Bangladesh are not a personality, since they meant years of interrupted school, interrupted care, and a kinship the form cannot see.

### What people brought

What people brought includes language (maybe Burmese, maybe not), church or monastery or mosque, a large household, farming and plant skill, and the memory of being hunted by a state. What they met in Minnesota was an English form, one “Asian” checkbox, and often one interpreter labeled Burmese for a household that is Chin or Karen.

sections.heading: The Geography of the Burmese World
sections.body:
Homeland is Myanmar, which includes Yangon, Mandalay, the Delta, the hills, Chin State, Kachin State, Kayin, and Rakhine, so do not draw one pagoda on a case note. Camps in Thailand (Mae La and others) are the origin-of-arrival for many Karen and Karenni Minnesota families, and those camps meant years, not a layover.

### Homeland

The U.S. map is not only Minnesota, because Indiana, New York, Texas, California, and other states hold Burma-origin communities. Minnesota is a real resettlement and secondary-migration state, and that includes Greater Minnesota.

### Minnesota

In Minnesota, Compass (ACS 2020–2024) puts the Burmese umbrella at 83.0 percent Twin Cities and 17.0 percent Greater Minnesota, so name the town. Albert Lea, Austin, Marshall, and Willmar are a Karen/Burmese pattern in public telling (MSP Magazine on Minnesota’s refugee history names those towns for Karen), and other sources place Karen people in Worthington as well. Do not assume St. Paul, and do not assume the person in front of you has ever been to Yangon, because a Worthington household is not a Minneapolis default.

sections.heading: Military Rule, Camps, 2017, 2021 — Foundational Events
sections.body:
If 1975 is Hmong Minnesota and 1991 is Somali Minnesota, then military rule, the camps, and the later coups are the foundational events of Burma-origin Minnesota. They are not one event, and they are not one people.

### Foundational events

MSP Magazine’s state refugee timeline has refugees from Burma arriving in Minnesota in 1993, most of them named as Karen in that telling. Other sources date larger arrivals later: the state health department’s refugee arrival data begin in 1999 and show a few dozen first arrivals from Burma a year through 2003, about 150 to 190 a year in 2004 to 2006, and 600 or more a year from 2007 on, and the Karen Organization of Minnesota says refugees from Burma founded it in 2008. The 2017 Rohingya atrocities, mass killing, rape, and expulsion, named as genocide by the United States in 2022, produced a specific flight. The 2021 military coup is current structure, with kin still there, remittance, silence, and status anxiety here. Temporary Protected Status for Burma ended: the federal government announced the end on Nov. 24, 2025, and Sahan Journal reported that about 1,200 Minnesotans from Myanmar lost that status on Aug. 7, 2026. Starting in January 2026, federal officials also called about 5,600 refugees in Minnesota for new interviews under Operation PARRIS, and some of those notices were later canceled.

### Who you meet

Camps in Thailand and Bangladesh shaped literacy, time, and who counts as family. U.S. resettlement scattered people, and secondary migration and church networks pulled some to Minnesota, including to plant towns.

The desk in 2026 meets U.S.-born children and a parent facing a 67 percent LEP gate, which means that if all you know is “refugee,” you will miss the 18-year-old and still fail the form for the elder. Do not ask a Rohingya survivor to narrate the village for your chart.

sections.heading: Family
sections.body:
Households can be large: Compass puts the average household size at 5.05, and married couples with children under 18 make up 48.7 percent of households. Elders, in-laws, camp-made kin, and adult children may all be present, so the person who cares for the child may not match the waiver checkbox.

### Who is in the household

Camp years shape who counts as kin. There may be a cousin who is not a cousin on the English form, a missing father, or a household that formed in a camp such as Mae La, so ask who is in the room rather than reconstructing a family tree as an icebreaker.

### Who speaks

Women’s labor, in the plant, in care, and in second-generation school, sits next to a household in which an elder may still be named as head, and both can be true at once.

Do not skip mandated reporting and call it culture, because Minnesota law still stands. A nuclear two-parent English form already has a who built into it, and it was built for a different household.

sections.heading: Minnesota and Burmese History
sections.body:
Minnesota holds a Burma-origin community large enough for Compass to profile it, at 19,372 on the ACS 2020–2024 umbrella, and mixed enough that the profile becomes a gate if you treat it as one people. This department will meet these households on waivers, child welfare, health care, cash, food, aging, and employment, in St. Paul and in Worthington alike.

### Places

Think in places rather than a blob: the Twin Cities; Roseville as a Karen Organization of Minnesota address (a door for Karen, Karenni, Mon, and Chin households); and the Greater Minnesota plant towns, with Albert Lea, Austin, Marshall, and Willmar named in public Karen/Burmese telling and Worthington documented for Karen people elsewhere. Compass puts about one in six outside the Twin Cities, so name the town, and do not assume St. Paul.

### Partners

The Karen Organization of Minnesota says it serves all ethnic groups from Burma, including Karen, Karenni, Mon, and Chin, so it is a door for more than Karen households, though not automatically this page. The partners also include the Theravada Dhamma Society of Minnesota in Chisago City, a Bamar-led temple society, and the churches, monasteries, and mosques that families name, so pay the partner this household names, while remembering that CECLC is a department door, not the whole community.

Book a qualified interpreter, and pay for community work. Do not assign either to staff because of who they are. A New Year visit is optional professional development, and while you are a guest there, being one does not make you the expert.

sections.heading: Burmese Minnesota — the heart of a people
sections.body:
There is not one heart under this umbrella, because Bamar Theravada life, Chin Christian hill life, Karen Baptist or Buddhist life, and Rohingya Muslim life are peoples in their own right. A U.S. file that recodes Karen as Burmese hides who is here, so record the people and language the person names.

### In this state

In Minnesota this sits inside another fact: an Asian checkbox that also holds Hmong, Chinese, Indian, and Korean histories these families do not share, along with camp years, Greater Minnesota isolation for some, and a language gate at 67 percent LEP.

This guide is a working orientation, and because individual variation always supersedes group generalization, ask who is actually in the room.

sections.heading: Core Concepts
sections.body:
Start with who is in the room. Bamar, Chin, Karen, Rohingya, Mon, and Kachin are all possible, so ask, because the country name is not the answer.

### Language

Burmese is tonal and uses Myanmar script, while Hakha, Falam, S’gaw, Pwo, and Rohingya/Bengali are not Burmese. 67 percent LEP is the gate, and literacy in any script is not guaranteed.

### Church, monastery, mosque

These are the information channel for some families, but they are not the case plan unless the family asked, and Sunday and moon days are operations.

### Camp time

Camp time means interrupted school, interrupted care, and kin the form cannot see, which is why 67 percent less than high school among those 25+ is structure.

### Large household

The average is 5.05, so ask who should hear.

### Checking for agreement

A smile can be misread as agreement, so ask whether they agree, and do not take a smile as consent.

sections.heading: Religion and Healing
sections.body:
Among Bamar there is a Theravada Buddhist majority, with monastery, moon days (Uposatha), Thingyan, and offerings. A monk is not the case plan unless this family asked, and you do not book a monastery as DHS programming.

### Streams

Many Chin and Karen streams in Minnesota are majority Christian, Baptist and other Protestant, with some Catholic. Church is often the information channel, the English class, and the ride, which makes Sunday operations, but church is still not “the community,” and it is not automatically the Karen Organization.

### Practice

Rohingya are Muslim, with mosque, Ramadan, and halal, so do not copy Somali Islam blindly onto them, and do not assume Burmese is the language; ask.

Do not assume pagoda, and do not assume Baptist. The meaning of an illness may sit next to a blessing, a vow, or monastery counsel, and you can hold that next to a clinic, without mocking it and without skipping the waiver.

sections.heading: Greetings
sections.body:
Wait to see how the person greets you, and follow their lead. Mingalaba is a common Burmese greeting, and English hello is ordinary in many rooms and in the second generation, but Chin and Karen greetings are not Burmese, so follow this room.

### Titles

Say the name, and ask how to say it. Ask before any physical contact, and let the person set the limit.

### This room

Do not open with the junta, and do not open with “I have a Karen friend” if this household is not Karen.

sections.heading: Naming Conventions
sections.body:
Myanmar Bamar naming often has no family surname of the kind the database wants, and personal names may be one, two, or more syllables. The honorifics U (for a man) and Daw (for a woman) appear in some rooms, and they are titles, not first names. Do not invent a last name because the screen requires one, because that invented name becomes a gate.

### How to file

Chin and Karen naming differ, with clan, baptismal, and English names in those streams, while Rohingya naming may follow a different Muslim pattern, so ask how to file the name, and ask how to say it.

Do not “correct” a mother and child who do not share a last name as a fraud signal until you have a reason, since the form that demands first-middle-last and a hyphen will invent a person.

sections.heading: Dates of Significance
sections.body:
Thingyan, the Burmese New Year in mid-April, matters for many Bamar Buddhist households. It is a water festival in the homeland, and Minnesota’s Burmese temple calls its Water Festival generally the biggest Burmese festival of the year, with folk music and dance rehearsed for weeks. That is literacy, but it is not automatically this Chin or Karen family’s day.

### Calendar

Buddhist moon days are operations for some, and Sunday is operations for many Chin and Karen churches. Karen New Year belongs on the Karen page, so do not steal it as a Burmese holiday. Christmas and Easter matter for the Christian streams, and lunar Islamic dates matter if this family is Rohingya or otherwise Muslim.

A calendar click is literacy rather than community engagement, so do not put “Asian holiday” on a case note, and ask which calendar this family uses.

sections.heading: Education
sections.body:
Compass Burmese, for those age 25+, shows (ACS 2020–2024) high school or higher at 33.0 percent, bachelor’s or higher at 11.8 percent, and less than high school at 67.0 percent, so date it. Camp years and interrupted schooling are structure, not a personality and not a refusal to value school.

### School and language

A parent who speaks fluent Burmese, Hakha, or S’gaw and limited English is not illiterate, and literacy in Burmese script is not guaranteed even when Burmese is the spoken language. The English-only IEP is the gate, and so is an interpreter in the wrong language.

Second-generation children are in English-dominant schools, including in Greater Minnesota, and the form still has to reach the parent. 41.1 percent of the Compass umbrella is 17 or younger, which is a school-and-waiver fact rather than a vibe.

sections.heading: Etiquette
sections.body:
If you visit a home, look for shoes by the door or ask what the household prefers. In a home with an altar, ask where to sit, and ask before touching anyone, including a child.

### In the home

If food or drink is offered, accepting a little is fine, and you can still keep to medical and legal timelines.

### Time

Ask whether the person agrees with the plan, and confirm in the language they use.

Be on time for appointments. If someone misses an appointment, first check the time, transport, interpreter, plant shift and distance. Confirm the plan in the language the person uses, and ask whether it works for them.

sections.heading: Language and Communication
sections.body:
Burmese (the Myanmar language) is tonal and written in its own script, so confirm that this is the language. Compass reports that among those 5 and older (ACS 2020–2024), 89.1 percent speak a language other than English and 68.1 percent speak English less than “very well,” which is a severe language gate, so date it.

### Language

A “Burmese interpreter” for a Hakha Chin household will not work, and the same is true for Falam, S’gaw, Pwo, Rohingya, and Bengali, so put the language on the request. Literacy in the spoken language is not literacy in the form, since many camp-schooled adults do not read the script you assumed.

Give the person time to answer. If you get a short yes, check that the plan was understood, and ask whether it works for them.

Do not make a Burmese, Chin, or Karen coworker the interpreter.

sections.heading: Other Considerations
sections.body:
This section states hard facts plainly, because treating everyone the same can hide them.

### Named harms

Camp years and interrupted schooling are why 67.0 percent less than high school among those 25+ is structure, so do not write it as laziness or as “they don’t value education.”

The Rohingya genocide is a fact, and the United States determined in 2022 that the 2017 atrocities were genocide. Do not platform denial in a lobby, and do not book Burmese by default for a Rohingya household. LGBTQ people exist in every stream under this umbrella, and conservative church, monastery, and mosque climates can mean silence, so you use the name, and you do not out someone to kin and call it culture.

Greater Minnesota isolation is real: a plant town, few interpreters, an English IEP, and a notice that never left a St. Paul eList. Name the town, and do not file this household under Karen if they are not Karen, under Hmong, or under Asian.

Staff who share this community may add facts, but they do not get to delete a fact because it is hard to say.

sections.heading: Health
sections.body:
Compass Burmese (ACS 2020–2024) puts disability at 13.8 percent, at 11.0 percent among those under 65, and the uninsured share at 6.4 percent, so date it. Camp and interrupted-care histories, including hepatitis, anemia, dental, and immunization gaps, are patterns in refugee clinical literacy nationally, but this page does not invent a Minnesota clinic rate; date a local figure when a controlling source exists.

### Access

67 percent LEP is a health gate now, and literacy of the consent form is a health gate too, which means a Burmese-script form for a person who does not read it still will not work.

Gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care, so offer it. Believe reported pain, and do not skip developmental screening, but do not mash this page with Hmong late autism identification or Somali ADDM, because those are other intelligences.

If they name a monk, a pastor, or a healer, listen, but do not make them the case plan unless they asked.

sections.heading: LGBTQ
sections.body:
Queer and trans Burmese, Chin, Karen, and Rohingya Minnesotans exist. Conservative church, monastery, and mosque climates can mean silence or exile, and some people live a public English life alongside a private home-language life.

### This person

Use the name they use, and do not share what they tell you unless a rule requires it. Minnesota’s Human Rights Act still applies.

sections.heading: Hair, Dress, and Body
sections.body:
Longyi and thanaka appear among some Bamar, but they are not a daily uniform in a Worthington plant, and Karen and Chin traditional dress is public at New Year rather than a clinic outfit. Some Rohingya practice Muslim covering, and the second generation looks like Minnesota.

### Dress

Do not ask whether they “still wear the costume,” do not touch hair or thanaka, and do not mash this page with Hmong New Year dress or Somali hijab.

Follow this person, and offer gender match if she wants it.

sections.heading: Music
sections.body:
Church hymns carry many Chin and Karen streams, while Buddhist ritual sound carries others. The saung and classical Burmese music are homeland art, and diaspora pop lives alongside them.

### Variation

Funeral, monastery, and church are not staff entertainment, and a playlist is not engagement.

A choir is not a case plan.

sections.heading: Sports
sections.body:
Soccer and volleyball show up, chinlone is a homeland image, and ordinary school sport is ordinary in the second generation, while Greater Minnesota plant-town leagues exist as well.

### Not the whole person

Sport clubs are not language access and not a case plan.

Do not assume the kid plays.

sections.heading: Literature
sections.body:
Burmese script and its written public are old, and oral literature runs through the Chin, Karen, and Rohingya streams. Camp years interrupted schooling, while the second generation reads English.

### Literacy in the lobby

You do not need to quote a novel. You need to know that this is not a people without letters, and also that literacy in the English form, and in Burmese script, is not guaranteed.

The form has to match the person, not the country checkbox.

sections.heading: Art
sections.body:
Thanaka, textile, monastery carving, and church banners are all part of this art. Karen weaving belongs on the Karen page, so do not steal it as a Burmese souvenir, and do not mash it with Hmong paj ntaub.

### Guest

You are a guest, so a New Year is not consultation, and a display table is not a case plan.

Do not put a longyi on a Heritage Month booth.

sections.heading: Conflict, War, and the State
sections.body:
British colonial rule, independence, military government, 1988, 2007, the 2017 Rohingya atrocities, and the 2021 coup as current structure: that is the political file. It includes camps in Thailand and Bangladesh, and a United States that resettled people into plant towns and then sent them English PDFs.

### The badge

The Rohingya genocide is a fact, so do not platform denial, and do not ask a survivor to narrate the village for your professional development.

A DHS badge is not automatically help. Mandated reporting still exists, and so does the duty not to treat a whole umbrella as a risk score.

sections.heading: Work, Markets, and Government
sections.body:
Compass Burmese (ACS 2020–2024), dated, puts median household income at $85,747 (2024 dollars), poverty at 22.2 percent, owner-occupied housing at 67.9 percent, and about 69.3 percent of working-age adults (18–64) employed. Food processing and other Greater Minnesota work hold many Burma-origin households, alongside a professional second generation and public employment.

### Work

Book a qualified interpreter, and pay for community work. Do not assign either to staff because of who they are.

### Staff

Take time to introduce yourself and explain the plan. The first visit may not be the decision, and any required notice still goes out, and a notice that never left St. Paul does not reach Worthington.

sections.heading: Health-care and Human-service Encounters
sections.body:
Begin with who is actually in the room. The 67 percent LEP gate, literacy of the form, a Greater Minnesota clinic with no interpreter on site, church versus monastery versus mosque, camp health history, and Rohingya as a language that is not Burmese by default all shape the encounter.

### Language

Confirm the people and the language, offer gender match, and ask who should hear, but do not make staff the interpreter.

### The meeting

Believe reported pain, and remember that mandated reporting still exists.

sections.heading: Adjacent Peoples — Do Not Mash
sections.body:
This is not Karen as a synonym, so open Karen Minnesota for Karen and put S’gaw or Pwo on the line. It is not Chin as a synonym, so book Hakha, Falam, or the variety they name. It is not Hmong, not Vietnamese, not Chinese, and not Thai as the camp country, and it is not “Asian American” as the file.

### Adjacent doors

Rohingya is not Burmese by default. For Mon, Kachin, and Karenni, ask, because some households are mixed.

Ask this household, and never reach for one Asian module or one Burma interpreter.

sections.heading: Counts, Dated
sections.body:
Minnesota Compass, ACS 2020–2024, describes the Burmese cultural community (umbrella) as 19,372 people (give or take 3,438), with 83.0% in the Twin Cities and 17.0% in Greater Minnesota (give or take 4.9 points). Those age 17 or younger are 41.1%, those 65+ are 3.4%, and the foreign-born share is 66.9%. Among those age 5+, 89.1% speak a language other than English and 68.1% speak English less than “very well,” while among those 25+, 33.0% have high school or higher, 11.8% have a bachelor’s or higher, and 67.0% have less than high school. Median household income is $85,747 (2024 dollars, give or take $15,049), poverty is 22.2% (give or take 7.6 points), owner-occupied housing is 67.9% and renter-occupied is 32.1%, average household size is 5.05, disability is 13.8%, the uninsured share is 6.4%, and there are 3,843 households.

### Counts

The Census recodes some Karen write-ins as Burmese, so this is an administrative umbrella rather than a people-count. Date Compass.

### What the count is not

A young age structure is not a personality, and 67 percent LEP is a gate. 67 percent less than high school among those 25+ is camp years, not a character, and a rate is not the person.

sections.heading: Doors and Sources
sections.body:
The doors begin with the Minnesota Compass Burmese profile (ACS 2020–2024) and the Compass cultural-communities methodology (Karen recoded as Burmese), and the CLAS fifteen interpreter cards list Burmese. The Karen Organization of Minnesota says it serves all ethnic groups from Burma, so it is a door for more than Karen households, though not automatically this page. The churches, monasteries, and mosques families name are doors, as is the Theravada Dhamma Society of Minnesota, so pay that partner. MSP Magazine on Minnesota’s refugee history (1993 Burma-origin arrivals in that telling; Albert Lea, Austin, Marshall, and Willmar) is a public source, and the state health department’s refugee arrival data give the later counts.

### Public doors

CECLC is a door, not the whole community. Use these resources yourself before you ask a Burmese, Chin, or Karen colleague to explain.

### Where to learn more

Report back, go as a guest, and name the town.

sections.heading: How it hits DHS gates — the 40%
sections.body:
Workplace culture and service delivery are both candidates here.

Who is in the room: Bamar, Chin, Karen, Rohingya, Mon, Kachin. An interpreter labeled Burmese for a Hakha Chin household will not work, so if Karen, open Karen Minnesota, and if Rohingya, remember that Burmese is not the default language. Gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care.

67 percent LEP is the severe language gate. Literacy of the form is a second gate, because Burmese script is not guaranteed, which means an English IEP for a parent who does not read it will not work.

Greater Minnesota is 17.0 percent, in Worthington and other plant towns, so an eList and an English PDF from St. Paul will not reach this household. Record who was reached and what follow-up happened.

Hour caps, exception processes, and life-sharing matches without language are not culturally neutral.

Child welfare and disability: camp years and interrupted schooling are structure. Mandated reporting still exists, and so does the duty not to treat a whole umbrella as a risk score.

Workforce: Burmese, Chin, and Karen staff are not the interpreter pool and not the community.

The Asian mash shuts the person out, which is why this is not Hmong, and not Karen as a synonym.

Legislation, funding, rule: study a channel before you advocate for it. Use this page so that the 40% has a household in it.

sections.heading: A Note on This Guide
sections.body:
This brief is about Cambodian / Khmer people as a people with a long state history on the Mekong and a Minnesota community built after the Khmer Rouge. Start by learning to pronounce Khmer: a common English rendering is kuh-MARE, and then you ask. If you say “Cambodian” as if it were interchangeable with Hmong or Vietnamese, you have already told the household that you did not study.

### Who this is

This community is not a Census “Asian” mash, which means it is not Hmong, not Vietnamese, not Lao, and not Thai, and it is not served by a generic Southeast Asian interpreter, because a shared continent is not a shared culture. Use this page for context and questions. It does not describe the person in front of you.

### Who this is not

Minnesota Compass (ACS 2020–2024) puts the Cambodian cultural community near 11,521 (give or take 2,142), with about 72.0 percent living in the Twin Cities and 28.0 percent in Greater Minnesota. About 30.0 percent are age 17 or younger, 10.0 percent are 65 or older, and about 47.6 percent are foreign-born. Among those age 5 and older, 57.3 percent speak a language other than English and 26.6 percent speak English less than “very well.” Date the number you use, and remember that a rate is not the person.

The diversity inside this people is the point. A survivor of 1975–1979 who came through a Thai camp, a Christian grandmother, a monk whose wat is the civic center, a U.S.-born nurse, a Greater Minnesota household the building forgot, and a college student who uses English with friends and Khmer with an elder all share a people, yet they do not share a Tuesday.

### How to read this

Always defer to the person in front of you, because this page is a hypothesis and you are still testing it on this family.

sections.heading: Origins and the Founding of a People
sections.body:
Khmer peoplehood is older than the refugee file and older than the French protectorate. The Khmer Empire — Angkor, as literacy for the desk rather than a tourism sentence — is a state history with writing, irrigation, and monumental architecture, and Khmer language and Khmer script are not oral-only. That matters when an English form meets an elder who reads Khmer, and it matters just as much when the form meets an elder who does not.

### History for the meeting

French colonial rule, independence (1953), Sihanouk, Lon Nol, and then 1975 make up the modern political sequence, and while 1975–1979 is the foundational political event of Cambodian Minnesota, it is not the origin of the people.

### What people brought

What people brought with them was language and script, Theravada Buddhism and ancestor practice, farming knowledge, kinship, and the memory of a state that ate its own. What they met in Minnesota was an English form, one “Asian” checkbox, and often a single interpreter labeled anything but Khmer.

Do not start with embroidery or Angkor Wat as an icebreaker, because history is literacy for the desk rather than a speech you give the family.

sections.heading: The Geography of the Khmer World
sections.body:
The homeland is Cambodia — the Mekong, Tonle Sap, Phnom Penh, and the provinces people name. Khmer people also live in the Mekong delta and across a global diaspora that includes California (with Long Beach among the named U.S. hubs), Massachusetts, Minnesota, France, and Australia, while the Thai border camps — Khao-I-Dang and others — are exile geography, not home.

### Homeland

Compass (ACS 2020–2024) puts 72.0 percent in the Twin Cities and 28.0 percent in Greater Minnesota, and Greater Minnesota is not an afterthought. Watt Munisotaram stands in Empire Township / Hampton, Dakota County — in the Twin Cities metro, but a wat on farmland rather than a downtown festival.

### Minnesota

Do not assume Minneapolis, and do not assume the person in front of you has been to Cambodia, since secondary migration built parts of this map.

sections.heading: Khmer Rouge, 1975–1979, and the Camps — Foundational Event
sections.body:
If the Secret War is the foundational event of Hmong Minnesota and 1991 is that of Somali Minnesota, the Khmer Rouge years of 1975–1979 and the Killing Fields are the foundational event of Cambodian Minnesota, and that is why this history belongs on the desk.

### Foundational events

On 17 April 1975, Phnom Penh fell, and the Khmer Rouge emptied the cities, abolished money and schools, murdered intellectuals, monks, and anyone marked as an enemy, and worked and starved the rest. 1975–1979 is not a personality and not an icebreaker, so do not ask a survivor to narrate killing for your professional development.

### Who you meet

The Vietnamese invasion came in 1979, followed by camps in Thailand and resettlement to the United States in the late 1970s and 1980s through voluntary agencies and churches, and then secondary migration. The desk in 2026 also meets their children — U.S.-born, English-dominant with their peers, still translating for parents, and still unable to get Khmer in the lobby.

U.S. policy later deported people with certain convictions, including people who have lived here since childhood, and that is current structure, so do not collect status you do not need.

sections.heading: Family
sections.body:
Compass puts average household size at 3.08 (ACS 2020–2024), and a nuclear English form may not fit every household. Elders, adult children, and obligation sit in the same week, which means the person who cares for the child may not match the waiver checkbox.

### Who is in the household

Ask who should be in the room, because a nuclear English form has already decided who that is, and it may be wrong.

### Who speaks

Ask how the person writes and says their name, and in what order, because U.S. forms can split names wrong, and do not treat unmatched last names as fraud by default.

sections.heading: Minnesota and Cambodian History
sections.body:
This department will meet this community on waivers, child welfare, health care, cash, food, aging, and employment, both in the Twin Cities and in Greater Minnesota, where 28.0 percent is not an afterthought and deserves the same planning.

### Places

Partners include the United Cambodian Association of Minnesota; Watt Munisotaram in Empire / Hampton, Dakota County, established in 1982 and among the largest Cambodian Buddhist temples in the United States; and the other wats that families name. CECLC is a door, not the whole community.

### Partners

Ask which dates matter to this person or family, such as Khmer New Year in April, Pchum Ben, or 17 April as genocide remembrance, and remember that a calendar click is not community engagement. At the wat you are a guest, mindful of shoes, head, and altar.

Book a qualified interpreter, and pay for community work. Do not assign either to staff because of who they are. A New Year visit is optional professional development, and you attend as a guest, knowing that being there does not make you the expert.

sections.heading: Khmer — the heart of a people
sections.body:
Khmer history includes a state of its own and the catastrophe of 1975–1979. U.S. forms file Khmer people under a racial checkbox that also holds Hmong, Chinese, Indian, and Korean histories they do not share, so ask how the person identifies.

### In this state

1975–1979 sits in some rooms as living memory and in others as a school unit the grandchild studied, so do not assume which, and do not make it a personality.

This guide is a working orientation, which means individual variation always supersedes group generalization.

sections.heading: Core Concepts
sections.body:
Khmer language and Khmer script come first, and they are not Hmong, not Vietnamese, and not Lao. Literacy in Khmer is not guaranteed for every elder, which is why the English form is still a gate.

### Wat

The Theravada Buddhist temple is a civic and ritual center for many, but you should not make a monk the case plan unless this family asked.

Ancestors and spirit practice sit beside Buddhism and, in some families, beside Christianity, so an altar in a living room is not a case plan and not a museum.

### Checking for agreement

Before you treat a yes as agreement, ask again, plainly and without embarrassing anyone.

1975–1979 is living memory in some waiver meetings, and it is not an icebreaker; you do not use it, but you know it so that you do not trample it.

sections.heading: Religion and Healing
sections.body:
Theravada Buddhism is central for many Cambodian Minnesota families, and the wat is both civic and ritual. Christianity lives in some families — sometimes in the same cousin-line as a Buddhist altar — and spirit and ancestor practice are not “extra.”

### Streams

Do not make a monk the case plan unless this family asked, and do not treat Buddhism as decoration or church as the evolved version.

### Practice

If you visit a home, look for shoes by the door or ask what the household prefers. In a home with an altar, ask where to sit, and ask before touching anyone, including a child. You still keep medical and legal time, and when the two collide you name the conflict instead of punishing it.

The meaning of an illness may not be the DSM sentence, and trauma and under-identified mental health sit in this community’s U.S. literature, so date what you cite, and do not invent a rate.

sections.heading: Greetings
sections.body:
Ask who to greet first, or follow the household’s lead. Ask how this person prefers to greet and be greeted, whether with a sampeah (palms together, a slight bow), a handshake, or something else, and follow this room.

### Titles

Say the name, pronounce Khmer, and ask rather than guess.

### This room

Let this person’s own greeting guide you, whatever you read on another page.

Ask before any physical contact, and let the person set the limit.

sections.heading: Naming Conventions
sections.body:
Ask which part of the name is the family name and in what order the person says it, because the form that demands first-middle-last and a hyphen can invent a person.

### How to file

Given names may be Khmer, English, Buddhist, or both, so ask how to say it and how to file it.

Do not “correct” a mother and child who do not share a last name, and do not read it as a fraud signal until you have a reason, nor joke about names.

Pronounce Khmer, and ask, because the building that will not say kuh-MARE has already closed a door.

sections.heading: Dates of Significance
sections.body:
Khmer New Year / Choul Chnam Thmey falls in mid-April and is public at wats including Watt Munisotaram. Come as a guest, not a researcher, remembering that a calendar click is not community engagement.

### Calendar

Pchum Ben, the ancestor fortnight, usually falls in September–October. Ask whether it affects this person’s or family’s schedule, and do not read a missed appointment at that time as the whole story.

Ask whether 17 April, the day Phnom Penh fell in 1975, is a day of remembrance for this person or family. It is literacy for the desk, not an icebreaker, and not a day you ask a survivor to speak to staff for professional development.

Buddhist holy days vary, and Christian calendars matter in some families, so ask, and do not put “Asian holiday” on a case note.

sections.heading: Education
sections.body:
Compass (ACS 2020–2024) reports that among Cambodian Minnesotans 25 and older, about 73.1 percent have a high school education or higher and about 15.8 percent hold a bachelor’s or higher. Among those 5 and older, 57.3 percent speak a language other than English and 26.6 percent speak English less than “very well,” and you should date the number when you use it.

### School and language

A parent who speaks fluent Khmer and limited English is not illiterate. At the same time, literacy in Khmer script is not guaranteed for every elder, because the camps and 1975–1979 destroyed schools, so both can be true, and the English-only IEP is the gate.
