The child is not the interpreter, so put Khmer on the line. Second-generation educational mobility is real, and so is a gap that a room treating everyone the same will call “culture,” when the truth is language access plus a school that never learned the name.

sections.heading: Etiquette
sections.body:
If you visit a home, look for shoes by the door or ask what the household prefers. In a home with an altar, ask where to sit, and ask before touching anyone, including a child.

### In the home

Ask before taking any photograph or touching any religious object, and do not ask anyone to explain their faith or history for your benefit.

### Time

If food or drink is offered, accepting a little is fine, and you can still keep to medical and legal timelines.

If someone misses an appointment, first check the time, transport, interpreter and work schedule. Confirm the plan in Khmer if that is the language the person uses, and ask whether it works for them.

sections.heading: Language and Communication
sections.body:
The language is Khmer, also called Cambodian, and it is not Hmong, not Vietnamese, not Lao, and not “Asian interpreter,” so an interpreter labeled Asian or Thai or Lao will not work for this household.

### Language

Khmer script meets English forms, and literacy in Khmer is not guaranteed for every elder, just as literacy in English is not guaranteed for every parent of a U.S.-born child. Compass puts language other than English at 57.3 percent (age 5+) and LEP at 26.6 percent, so date it when you cite it.

Give the person time to answer. If you get a short yes, check that the plan was understood, and ask whether it works for them.

Do not make a Cambodian coworker the interpreter, and remember that the child is not the interpreter either.

sections.body:
This section states hard facts plainly, because treating everyone the same can hide them.

### Named harms

Intergenerational trauma and PTSD sit in this community’s U.S. health literature, and under-identified mental health is a pattern in some rooms, so do not invent a rate, and do not skip screening. Do not make 1975–79 a personality.

The deportation of Cambodians with certain convictions — including people who have lived here since childhood — is current structure, and it changes who opens the door, so do not collect status you do not need, and do not treat fear as noncompliance.

Ask what name the person uses, and do not out someone to kin and call it culture.

Staff who share this community may add facts, but they do not get to delete a fact because it is hard to say.

### This person

Minnesota’s Human Rights Act still applies. Use the name the person uses, and do not share what they tell you unless a rule requires it.

Do not question a household about anyone’s sexuality or gender, and take seriously that some people have reason to keep it private.

sections.body:
Traditional dress is public at New Year and at the wat rather than a daily uniform, and the second generation looks like Minnesota, so do not ask a woman in clinic whether she “still wears the costume.”

### Dress

In a home with an altar, ask where to sit, and ask before touching anyone, including a child. Silver, krama, and sampot are art and history, not a mascot for the unit’s Heritage Month table.

Follow this person, and do not photograph.

sections.heading: Music
sections.body:
Pinpeat and wedding music, later pop and karaoke, and Christian music in some churches are all here. The Khmer Rouge murdered artists and silenced instruments, and that is history for the desk; it is not a speech, and it is not a request that a survivor narrate the silence.

### Variation

A playlist is not engagement, and a wat ceremony is not staff entertainment. Knowing that ritual music exists will stop you from talking over it as if it were delay.

sections.heading: Sports
sections.body:
Soccer, volleyball, and ordinary school sport are part of life for the second generation, but do not assume the kid plays, and do not make sport the only excellence you can see.

### Not the whole person

Sport clubs are social infrastructure, but they are not language access and not a case plan, and a tournament at the wat is not consultation.

sections.heading: Literature
sections.body:
Khmer is a written language with a long inscriptional and literary tradition. 1975–1979 tried to end schools, so literacy in Khmer script is not guaranteed for every elder, and English is not guaranteed for every parent; both sentences are true.

### Literacy in the lobby

Minnesota and U.S. Cambodian writers and memoirists exist, although you do not need to quote them in the lobby. What you need to know is that this is not a people without letters — and that the English form may still not work, so do not test an elder in English and call it capacity.

Angkor is literacy for the desk, not a tourism poster and not Heritage Month. Classical dance, weaving, wat mural, and contemporary work are all part of this world, and Watt Munisotaram is public architecture on Dakota County farmland.

### Guest

Come as a guest, not a researcher, because Apsara is not a case plan. A temple visit is optional professional development rather than consultation, and you should not photograph monks or altars as souvenirs.

This community is not Hmong, not Vietnamese, not Lao, not Thai, and not Chinese, and “Asian American” is not the file, so open the Hmong CI for Hmong, and open this one for Khmer. Some households are mixed, so ask this household.

### Adjacent doors

Camps in Thailand are a Cambodian and Hmong and Lao story of exile, but they are not a reason to book a Thai interpreter for a Khmer elder. Never one Asian module, and never one “Southeast Asian” interpreter.

sections.heading: Counts, Dated
sections.body:
Minnesota Compass (ACS 2020–2024) describes the Cambodian cultural community as about 11,521 people (give or take 2,142), with 72.0% in the Twin Cities and 28.0% in Greater Minnesota. Those age 17 or younger are 30.0% and those 65+ are 10.0%, and 47.6% are foreign-born. Among those age 5+, 57.3% speak a language other than English and 26.6% speak English less than “very well.” Among those 25+, 73.1% have high school or higher and 15.8% hold a bachelor’s or higher. Median household income is about $80,388 (2024 dollars, give or take $10,104), poverty is 5.3%, 56.5% of homes are owner-occupied (give or take 10.8 points), average household size is 3.08, 6.2% are without health insurance, and 15.8% have a disability (give or take 3.4 points).

### Counts

Counts disagree across ACS vintages and definitions, so date the number you cite. A poverty rate of 5.3 percent is not proof the gates closed, and Greater Minnesota at 28.0 percent is not an afterthought.

### What the count is not

A young age structure is not a personality, and an owner rate is not a gate, because a rate is not the person.

sections.heading: Doors and Sources
sections.body:
Start with the Minnesota Compass Cambodian profile (ACS 2020–2024), the United Cambodian Association of Minnesota, Watt Munisotaram in Empire / Hampton, Dakota County, and the wats this family names.

### Public doors

CECLC is a door, not the whole community, and an eList is not engagement, so pay partners, and report back.

### Where to learn more

Use these resources yourself before you ask a Cambodian colleague to explain, and book a qualified Khmer interpreter, because the child is not the interpreter.

sections.heading: How it hits DHS gates — the 40%
sections.body:
Workplace culture and service delivery are both candidates here.

Language comes first. An interpreter labeled Asian, Thai, Lao, Vietnamese, or Hmong will not work, so book Khmer. Literacy in Khmer script is not guaranteed for every elder, and literacy in English is not guaranteed for every parent, which means the form itself is a gate. Ask whether the person wants a provider of a particular gender in maternal and intimate care.

Names come next: ask which name order the person uses, because the database that flags unmatched last names as fraud is a gate.

Hour caps, exception processes, and life-sharing matches offered without language are not culturally neutral.

In child welfare and disability, trauma, stigma, and under-identified mental health are documented patterns, and help-seeking that becomes a report is part of why people wait. Mandated reporting still exists, and so does the duty not to treat a whole community as a risk score, so 1975–1979 is not an icebreaker.

The deportation climate means people may skip clinic, school, and waiver meetings when a relative can be moved, and that is not noncompliance, so do not collect status you do not need.

On notices and comment, do not count an eList and an English PDF as reaching this community, and record who was reached and what follow-up happened.

In the workforce, Cambodian staff are not the interpreter pool and not the community.

On legislation, funding, and rule: study a channel before you advocate for it. Use this page so that the 40% has a household in it.

sections.heading: A Note on This Guide
sections.body:
This brief is about Chinese Minnesota as a mosaic rather than a country checkbox, since people here name the People’s Republic of China, Taiwan, Hong Kong, Macau, and Chinese communities that have lived for generations in Southeast Asia. Students, skilled professionals, restaurant and small-business households, and adoptees all sit in the same Compass row, yet they do not share a Tuesday.

### Who this is

Minnesota Compass (ACS 2020–2024) puts the Chinese community near 45,330 people (give or take 3,937), with about 81.3 percent in the Twin Cities and 18.7 percent in Greater Minnesota. About 25.9 percent are age 17 or younger, 9.5 percent are 65 and older, and roughly 56.3 percent are foreign-born. Among those 5 and older, about 62.4 percent speak a language other than English, and about 29.9 percent speak English less than “very well”; among those 25 and older, about 85.9 percent have a high school education or higher and about 61.2 percent have a bachelor’s or higher. Median household income is about $109,309 in 2024 dollars (give or take $13,183), poverty stands at 9.1 percent, about 69.6 percent of homes are owner-occupied, and the average household size is about 2.56. Taiwanese Minnesotans are counted separately in some state counts, and totals vary by method. Date the number you use, because a rate is not the person.

The CLAS fifteen includes Cantonese, and Cantonese is not Mandarin and not “Chinese” as a file. Taishanese, Hokkien, and Shanghainese exist in this country and may exist in this lobby (no Minnesota source counts their speakers, so treat them as questions to ask), which means an interpreter labeled Chinese may still not work, so book Cantonese for a Cantonese household and Mandarin for a Mandarin one, and ask.

### Who this is not

This is not a Census “Asian” mash, and it is not Hmong, not Vietnamese, not Korean, and not Japanese, because a shared continent is not a shared culture and Lunar New Year is not Hmong New Year and not Tết. Use this page for context and questions. It does not describe the person in front of you.

### How to read this

The diversity inside this Compass row is the point. A Cantonese-speaking elder, a Mandarin-speaking graduate student, a Taiwanese professional, a Hong Kong family that left after 1997 or after 2019, a Toisan restaurant household, a U.S.-born child, and a person adopted from the PRC into a white Minnesota family share a checkbox, but they do not share a language, a politics, or a church.

Always defer to the person in front of you, since this page is a hypothesis you still test on this family.

sections.heading: Origins and the Founding of a People
sections.body:
There is no single origin story that will fit the lobby. Civilizations on the Yellow and Yangtze rivers, many spoken languages, and successive states — imperial, republican, socialist, and the Republic of China on Taiwan after 1949 — are literacy for the meeting rather than a lecture you give a parent who came in for a waiver.

### History for the meeting

Overseas Chinese communities are older than Minnesota. Nineteenth-century labor in the American West, merchant networks in Southeast Asia, and later student and professional migration are different founding events, and the person in front of you may descend from one of those, from none of them, or from more than one.

Writing is not one script in practice, even though standard written Chinese can be shared across speakers who cannot understand each other’s speech. Traditional characters are ordinary in Taiwan and among many Hong Kong and diaspora readers, while simplified characters are ordinary in the PRC, which makes this a materials problem for your print job rather than trivia.

### What people brought

People brought language, family obligation, education as a mobility strategy and as pressure, foodways, ancestral rite or a secular refusal of it, and a memory of states that claimed them. What they met in Minnesota was an English form, one “Asian” checkbox, and often one interpreter labeled “Chinese.”

sections.heading: The Geography of the Chinese World
sections.body:
The People’s Republic of China, Taiwan, Hong Kong, and Macau are not interchangeable, so a household that names Taipei is not a Beijing file, and a Hong Kong family that left after 1997 or after 2019 is not a PRC student. Ask which place they name, and do not referee it.

### Homeland

Chinese communities in Southeast Asia — Vietnam, Malaysia, Singapore, and others — carry other states’ histories, which is why a Chinese Vietnamese household is not a Beijing file either. Open Vietnamese Minnesota if that is the household they name, and open this brief if they name Chinese.

The Chinese map in the United States is California and New York, and it is also this Upper Midwest university-and-restaurant state. Compass (ACS 2020–2024) puts about 81.3 percent of the community in the Twin Cities and 18.7 percent in Greater Minnesota, so date Compass, and do not invent a dialect map.

### Minnesota

Do not assume Minneapolis, and do not assume they have been to Beijing, Taipei, or Hong Kong, because a Greater Minnesota restaurant household is still this people. A university apartment is still this people, and an adoptee raised in a western Minnesota town is still this people.

sections.heading: Exclusion, 1949, and Later Streams — Foundational Events
sections.body:
Chinese Minnesota is stacked, and there is no single 1975, because labor on the American West, the Chinese Exclusion Act, the 1949 split, Hart-Celler, students, Hong Kong, and PRC-born adoptees are different doors into the same Compass row.

### Foundational events

On May 6, 1882, the Chinese Exclusion Act became law, and the Scott Act (1888) and Geary Act (1892) tightened it. The Magnuson Act repealed Exclusion in 1943 and set a tiny quota, and Hart-Celler (October 1965) opened family and skilled immigration. That is literacy for the desk about the United States, not a speech you give the family.

In 1949 came the People’s Republic of China on the mainland and the Republic of China on Taiwan, and households that name either are not a mash you referee. Students and skilled workers from the 1980s sit next to restaurant and small-business streams that are older, while Hong Kong 1997 and the 2019–20 exits are later doors. PRC-born adoptees into Minnesota families are this state’s history, not a side note.

### Who you meet

The COVID-era anti-Asian climate is current structure, and Stop Asian Hate gathered at the Minnesota State Capitol on March 28, 2021, so date that when you cite it. Do not invent this person’s story, and do not collect status you do not need.

If the only category you know is “international student,” you will miss the Cantonese elder and the adoptee who does not want a cultural volunteer at the bedside.

sections.heading: Family
sections.body:
The family name comes first, and obligation to elders is a hypothesis rather than a waiver design. Compass puts the average household size at about 2.56, which is smaller than some neighboring spines, but that still does not always mean a nuclear English form.

### Who is in the household

The person who cares for a disabled adult or a child may be a son, a daughter-in-law, or a sibling — not the legally recognized caregiver on the checkbox. Hour caps and “natural supports” language can dump unpaid work onto the women in that network and then call it culture.

Adoptee households exist, with white Minnesota parents and a Chinese-born adult child, and a kin search may point to the PRC, to a closed file, or to no one. Do not assume Chinese relatives in the metro, and do not assume the adoptive family is either the barrier or the solution, so ask this person.

### Who speaks

The person who speaks in the lobby may be a child with the best English, but that child is not the qualified interpreter, and CLAS still stands. Using a child as the go-between does harm, so book the interpreter, ask who should be in the room, and ask how to file the name.

Minnesota law still stands, which means you do not skip mandated reporting and call it culture. Do not use an adoptee’s family as a lesson about “good Minnesota parents,” and do not use an immigrant family as a lesson about “strict Asians.”

sections.heading: Minnesota and Chinese History
sections.body:
Minnesota holds a Chinese community large enough that this department will meet it on waivers, child welfare, health care, cash, food, aging, student households, and employment. Compass counts about 45,330 people (ACS 2020–2024), and Greater Minnesota is 18.7 percent of that, so do not write this people as a Minneapolis anecdote.

### Places

The community lives in university and research settings, in professional work, in restaurants and small business, in Hong Kong and Taiwan households, in the Southeast Asian Chinese diaspora, and among PRC-born adoptees, and it lives in suburbs, campus apartments, and Greater Minnesota towns. Markets and restaurants are public life, but they are not consultation, and a food-court visit does not make you the expert.

### Partners

Partners include the Chinese American Association of Minnesota, the Chinese Community Center, and the Chinese Heritage Foundation, and Chinese Dance Theater is a known Twin Cities stage, so pay the door this person names. Book a qualified interpreter, and pay for community work. Do not assign either to staff because of who they are.

Lunar New Year is optional professional development if you are invited, and you go as a guest, since attending does not make you the expert.

sections.heading: Huárén — the heart of a people
sections.body:
Huárén names a peoplehood that some people use, while Zhōngguó rén names a PRC citizenship that some refuse, and a Taiwanese household may reject both as the file. Ask how they name themselves, and do not fold this household into “Asian Pacific.”

### In this state

Forms in Minnesota file Chinese people under a checkbox that also holds Hmong, Vietnamese, Korean, and Japanese histories this household does not share. Ask plainly whether the person agrees with the plan, and make it easy to say no.

A Cantonese-speaking elder, a Mandarin-speaking graduate student, a Taiwanese professional, a Hong Kong family, a Toisan restaurant household, a U.S.-born child, and an adoptee raised in a Minnesota church do not share a Tuesday, so you do not mash them.

This brief is a working orientation, and because individual variation always supersedes group generalization, you always defer to the person in front of you.

sections.heading: Core Concepts
sections.body:
These concepts recur across the brief, and they are hypotheses you still test on this family.

### Cantonese is not Mandarin

Book the language they name, because Taishanese, Hokkien, and Shanghainese exist as well, and an interpreter labeled Chinese may still not work.

### Name order and romanization

The family name comes first, and since Wong and Wang can be the same surname written in two systems, do not “correct” it to pinyin.

### Checking for agreement

Before you treat a yes as agreement, ask again, plainly and without embarrassing anyone, while remembering that none of this is a license to skip mandated reporting.

### Education as mobility and as pressure

A 61.2 percent bachelor’s rate is an average. Do not use the model-minority story, because it hides the 14.1 percent with less than high school, the 29.9 percent LEP, the 9.1 percent in poverty, and the child who is not thriving.

### Ancestral rite and secular life

Both may be present, sometimes in the same extended family, so ask, and Qingming is not a personality.

sections.heading: Religion
sections.body:
Chinese Protestant congregations are documented in Minnesota, including the Twin City Chinese Christian Church in Roseville, with about 500 worshippers in Mandarin, Cantonese, and English, and the Rochester Chinese Christian Church. Minnesota sources do not show how common nonreligion, Buddhist, Catholic, folk, or ancestral practice is among Chinese Minnesotans, so treat each as a possibility to ask about, sometimes in the same extended family. Ask, and do not make a pastor or a temple the case plan unless they asked.

### Streams

Qingming is not a personality. An ancestral altar in a secular household can be true, and that is not a contradiction you need to fix, so do not treat folk practice as entertainment, and do not treat church as the evolved version.

### Practice

The temple and the church are centers of ritual, mutual aid, and information for some people, but they are not “the community,” so do not BCC one pastor and call it consultation. Funerals and Qingming gather family, and while you still keep medical and legal time, you name the conflict instead of punishing it. Do not photograph an altar.

sections.heading: Greetings
sections.body:
Wait to see how the person greets you, and follow their lead. Use a title with an older person until invited otherwise.

### Titles

Nǐ hǎo is Mandarin, and a Cantonese greeting is not the same sentence, so do not perform a Mandarin hello as inclusion if this household is Cantonese. Ask how the person wants to be addressed. With elders, start with Mr. or Ms. plus the family name until invited otherwise.

### This room

Let this person’s own greeting guide you, whatever you read on another page.

Ask before any physical contact, and let the person set the limit.

sections.heading: Naming Conventions
sections.body:
The family name comes first. Wong and Wang can be the same surname in two romanization systems, and so can Lee and Li, and Chang and Zhang. Forms in the United States reverse the order, so the same person can appear as Wang Wei and as Wei Wang, which is a system failure rather than a fraud signal, until you have a reason to think otherwise.

### How to file

Ask how they write the name in English, and ask how to say it, rather than “correcting” it to pinyin. Do not mash a Wong with a Korean Wang or a Vietnamese Vương unless they tell you so.

Adoptees may carry an American given name and a family name from the adoptive household, and they may or may not use a Chinese name, so ask, and do not demand the “real” name. Ask how to say a person’s name before you call it out in a waiting room.

Pronounce the name, and ask when you are unsure, but do not joke that there are “too many Wangs.”

sections.heading: Dates of Significance
sections.body:
Lunar New Year is the large annual public and family date, and it brings travel, food, elders, red envelopes in some families, and closed shops, so schedule around it when you can. It is not a day off the work; be a guest if you are invited, and remember that a calendar click is not community engagement.

### Calendar

Lunar New Year is not Hmong New Year and not Tết, and Mid-Autumn and Qingming are also on the calendar, so do not put “Asian holiday” on a case note.

The desk dates are these: May 6, 1882 — the Chinese Exclusion Act; October 1965 — Hart-Celler; July 1, 1997 — the Hong Kong handover; the 2019–20 Hong Kong exits; the 2020 COVID-era anti-Asian climate; and March 28, 2021 — Stop Asian Hate at the Minnesota State Capitol. These are literacy for the desk rather than a speech you give the family, and they are not a file.

sections.heading: Education
sections.body:
Compass (ACS 2020–2024) reports that among Chinese Minnesotans 25 and older, about 85.9 percent have high school or higher, about 61.2 percent have a bachelor’s or higher, and about 14.1 percent have less than high school. LEP is about 29.9 percent (age 5+), so date Compass, because the average is not the elder in front of you.

### School and language

A parent who reads Chinese and limited English is not illiterate. Traditional versus simplified is a real print choice, since many elders read one and not the other and the second generation may not read characters at all, which is why the English-only form is the gate.

Do not skip the interpreter because the last Chinese family was a graduate student. The model-minority story, told as a school story, hides the child who is not thriving, the 14.1 percent with less than high school, and the 29.9 percent LEP, and CLAS is clear: do not use minors.

sections.heading: Etiquette
sections.body:
If food or drink is offered, accepting a little is fine, and you can still keep to medical and legal timelines. If you visit a home, look for shoes by the door or ask what the household prefers.

### In the home

Ask before taking any photograph or touching any religious object, and do not ask anyone to explain their faith or history for your benefit. Adoptee households may run on Minnesota Lutheran or Catholic manners — shoes on, first names, a casserole — and that is culture too, so you do not correct it toward a Beijing script.

### Time

If someone misses an appointment, first check the time, transport, interpreter and work schedule. Confirm the plan in the language the person uses, and ask whether it works for them. With elders, use Mr. or Ms. plus the family name until invited otherwise.

Book a qualified interpreter instead of using a child to go between.

sections.heading: Language and Communication
sections.body:
Cantonese is not Mandarin, and Taishanese, Hokkien, and Shanghainese exist in this country and may exist in this lobby. Minnesota sources show Mandarin and Cantonese in active use, in a trilingual church and in Chinese Community Center tutoring, and one weekend school teaches traditional characters with Zhuyin, but none counts speakers of the other varieties, so ask. The CLAS fifteen names Cantonese, so book Cantonese for a Cantonese household and Mandarin for a Mandarin one, and ask, because an interpreter labeled Chinese may still not work.

### Language

Compass reports that among those 5 and older, about 62.4 percent speak a language other than English and about 29.9 percent speak English less than “very well” (ACS 2020–2024), so date the number. Traditional versus simplified is a print choice, and a flyer in the wrong script will not work.

Give the person time to answer. If you get a short yes, check that the plan was understood, and ask whether it works for them.

Do not use a child as the interpreter. Book a qualified interpreter, and pay for community work. Do not assign either to staff because of who they are.

sections.heading: Other Considerations
sections.body:
This section states hard facts plainly, because treating everyone the same can hide them.

### Named harms

Do not use the model-minority story. A 61.2 percent bachelor’s rate and a $109,309 median can be used to skip LEP elders, 9.1 percent poverty, disability, and the child who is not thriving.

CCP versus Taiwan politics sit in some rooms, and you do not referee, you do not fly a flag as inclusion, and you do not put it on a case note as color.

COVID-era anti-Asian violence is current structure, and Stop Asian Hate at the Capitol on March 28, 2021, is Minnesota history, which is part of why a government badge is not automatically help.

Undocumented Chinese people exist, so do not collect status you do not need, and do not treat fear as noncompliance.

LGBTQ Chinese Minnesotans exist, so you use the name they use, and you do not out someone to kin and call it culture.

Staff who share this community may add facts, but they do not get to delete a fact because it is hard to say.

sections.heading: Health
sections.body:
LEP is a health gate — about 29.9 percent (Compass, age 5+) — and an English consent form is not consent if they could not run it, so book the language they name.

### Access

Mental-health stigma is real in some streams, but do not invent a Minnesota rate. Do not skip screening because “they don’t talk about that” or because the last household was a graduate student, and do not make stigma a personality.

Believe reported pain, and do not fold this community into a generic Asian slide. Gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care, so offer it.

Traditional herbal practice can sit beside biomedicine, so ask about it and work it out together rather than mocking it. Do not skip a child-protection duty when the facts are the facts, and remember that an adoptee who does not want a “cultural” volunteer at the bedside is allowed that no.

sections.heading: LGBTQ
sections.body:
Queer and trans Chinese Minnesotans exist, and conservative family and some immigrant climates can mean silence or exile, while adoptees who are LGBTQ live a different map. You use the name they use and do not share what they tell you unless a rule requires it.

### This person

Minnesota’s Human Rights Act still applies. Use the name the person uses, and do not share what they tell you unless a rule requires it.

Do not assume an adoptee household is affirming because it is white and English-speaking, and do not assume an immigrant household is not; ask this person rather than mashing the two.

sections.heading: Hair, Dress, and Body
sections.body:
Festival dress is public on Lunar New Year and on some stages, but it is not a daily uniform, and the second generation looks like Minnesota. Do not ask a woman in clinic whether she “still wears the costume,” and do not dress an adoptee in festival clothing as department programming.

### Dress

With hair and head, follow this person, and do not touch.

Do not mash a qipao with a hanbok or a kimono on the unit’s Heritage Month table, because those belong to different peoples.

sections.heading: Music
sections.body:
Opera, pop from the PRC and Taiwan and Hong Kong, church music, and karaoke in some rooms all belong here, which means there is not one soundtrack.

### Variation

A playlist is not engagement, so do not assume a temple soundtrack in a Presbyterian household, and do not ask a staff person or a client to perform.

Lunar New Year stages are public life, but they are not consultation, and they are not a case plan.

sections.heading: Sports
sections.body:
Table tennis, basketball, badminton, and ordinary school sport are all here, and none of them is a national personality, so do not assume the kid plays, and do not make sport the only excellence you can see.

### Not the whole person

Sport clubs are social infrastructure for some people, but they are not language access and not a case plan, and they are not a substitute for an interpreter or a notice.

A Saturday tournament does not replace Cantonese on Monday, and a 29.9 percent LEP rate is not something you skip because the child plays varsity.

sections.heading: Literature
sections.body:
This is a written tradition older than this department, and standard written Chinese can be shared across speakers who cannot understand each other’s speech. You do not need to quote a dynasty, but you do need to know that this is not a people without letters, and also not a people who can all read the same flyer.

### Literacy in the lobby

Literacy in characters is not guaranteed for every generation. Traditional versus simplified is a real print choice, and adoptees and a U.S.-born second generation may not read either, so a notice that exists only in English will not work, and a notice in the wrong script also will not work. Ask.

sections.heading: Art
sections.body:
Calligraphy, ink painting, and Lunar New Year art are all part of this world, and the Chinese American Association of Minnesota’s Chinese Dance Theater is a known Twin Cities stage where you attend as a guest. A lion dance is not a case plan, and a museum visit is not consultation.

### Guest

Do not mash this with Hmong paj ntaub, a dragon as a mascot, or a kimono on an “Asian art” table, because a Heritage Month that mashes those has already mashed the adjacent peoples.

Pay the door this person names, and do not extract a staff person’s child as New Year entertainment.

sections.heading: Exclusion, the State, and Anti-Asian Climate
sections.body:
The political stack runs like this: the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882, Hart-Celler in 1965, the 1949 split, Hong Kong in 1997 and after 2019, COVID-era anti-Asian violence, and Stop Asian Hate at the Minnesota State Capitol on March 28, 2021. Because of that stack, a DHS badge is not automatically help.

### The badge

Do not referee the PRC and Taiwan, and do not collect immigration status you do not need. Do not use Exclusion or a 2020 assault as a personality, and do not ask a person to narrate a hate incident, a search, or a camp for your professional development.

Filing this household as Hmong or Vietnamese or Korean or Japanese is a state act, and it shuts the person out.

sections.heading: Work, Markets, and Government
sections.body:
Restaurants and small business sit next to universities, professional and technical work, and public employment. A median household income of about $109,309 (Compass, 2024 dollars) is an average, and a poverty rate of 9.1 percent sits in the same row, so do not staff a program as if every household were the average.

### Work

Markets and restaurants are both economy and culture, but a food-court visit is not consultation.

### Staff

Book a qualified interpreter, and pay for community work. Do not assign either to staff because of who they are.

Take time to introduce yourself and explain the plan, and still give any required notice.

sections.heading: Health-care and Human-service Encounters
sections.body:
The encounter may involve Cantonese or Mandarin or whatever language they name. It may involve name order on the wristband, a child pushed forward as the English speaker, a model-minority skip of pain, an adoptee who does not want a “cultural” volunteer, an altar or a pastor in the story, and pain you must believe.

### Language

Confirm the language, and still book a qualified interpreter rather than using a child. Offer gender match, ask who should hear, and ask how to say the name. Book a qualified interpreter, and pay for community work. Do not assign either to staff because of who they are.

### The meeting

If they name herbal practice, listen, and remember that mandated reporting still exists. Believe reported pain, because a smile is not consent.

sections.heading: Adjacent Peoples — Do Not Mash
sections.body:
This community is not Hmong, not Vietnamese, not Korean, not Japanese, and not “Asian American” as the file, so open those briefs for those households, and open this one for a Chinese household. Some households are mixed, and a Chinese Vietnamese household is not a Beijing file, so ask this household.

### Adjacent doors

The PRC, Taiwan, and Hong Kong are not interchangeable. Lunar New Year is not Hmong New Year and not Tết, Cantonese is not Mandarin, and traditional is not simplified.

Never one Asian module, and never one “Chinese” interpreter; ask how they name themselves, and open the people brief that matches this household.

sections.heading: Counts, Dated
sections.body:
Minnesota Compass, drawing on ACS 2020–2024, describes the Chinese cultural community this way: about 45,330 people (give or take 3,937); Twin Cities 81.3 percent; Greater Minnesota 18.7 percent; age 17 or younger 25.9 percent; 65+ about 9.5 percent; foreign-born about 56.3 percent; language other than English (age 5+) about 62.4 percent; English less than “very well” about 29.9 percent; high school or higher (25+) about 85.9 percent; bachelor’s or higher about 61.2 percent; median household income about $109,309 (2024 dollars, give or take $13,183); poverty 9.1 percent; owner-occupied about 69.6 percent; average household size about 2.56.

### Counts

The Star Tribune (July 31, 2025) places Chinese among the languages at about 2 percent of non-English-at-home, so date Compass, and date the Star Tribune. Compass does not split PRC, Taiwan, Hong Kong, students, or adoptees, so do not invent a dialect count, and because counts disagree across ACS vintages and definitions, date the number you cite. The State Demographer’s June 2026 presentation lists 48,592 Chinese and, separately, 2,545 Taiwanese Minnesotans for 2024, and the state’s 2026 economic chartbook, which puts people of more than one cultural group in a separate category, counts about 30,500 for 2019–2023, so totals vary by method.

### What the count is not

A high bachelor’s rate is not proof that the gates closed, and a poverty rate of 9.1 percent is not zero. A 29.9 percent LEP rate is a door, and a rate is not the person.

sections.heading: Doors and Sources
sections.body:
Start with the Minnesota Compass Chinese profile (ACS 2020–2024). On the CLAS fifteen, Cantonese is listed, so book Cantonese, and book Mandarin when that is the language, and put traditional or simplified on the print job when you know which one they read.

### Public doors

The public doors include the Chinese American Association of Minnesota, the Chinese Community Center, the Chinese Heritage Foundation, and Chinese Dance Theater, so pay the door this person names rather than assigning a temple or a church.

### Where to learn more

Use these resources yourself before you ask a Chinese colleague to explain. Do not count an eList and an English PDF as reaching an LEP elder. If you are invited to Lunar New Year, be a guest there, because it is not consultation.

sections.heading: How it hits DHS gates — the 40%
sections.body:
Workplace culture and service delivery are both candidates here.

Language: an interpreter labeled Chinese who does not speak this household’s language will not work, because Cantonese is not Mandarin, and Taishanese, Hokkien, and Shanghainese exist. Still book a qualified interpreter, remembering that a list is not the person and not the dialect, and do not use a child. Gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care, and traditional versus simplified is a print choice.

Names: the family name comes first. Wong and Wang can be the same surname in two systems, and the database that reverses the order or “corrects” it to pinyin invents a person, so do not demand the “real” name of an adoptee.

Hour caps, exception processes, and life-sharing matches made without the language they use are not culturally neutral, and an English IEP is a gate for the parent who does not read it.

Model-minority: 85.9 percent high school and 61.2 percent bachelor’s can be used to skip 29.9 percent LEP, 14.1 percent less than high school, 9.1 percent poverty, disability, and the child who is not thriving.

PRC and Taiwan: you do not referee. The COVID-era anti-Asian climate is current structure, so do not collect status you do not need, and do not treat fear as noncompliance.

Notices and comment: do not count an eList and an English PDF as reaching this community, and record who was reached and what follow-up happened. Greater Minnesota is 18.7 percent of this community, so a Minneapolis meeting is not the whole channel.

Workforce: Chinese staff are not the interpreter pool and not the community, because staff are colleagues, not the curriculum, and they should not be treated as one.

Asian mash: opening the Hmong or Vietnamese or Korean or Japanese brief because the checkbox says Asian will not work.

Legislation, funding, rule: study a channel before you advocate for it. Use this page so that the 40% has a household in it.

sections.heading: A Note on This Guide
sections.body:
This brief is about Colombian people as a people with a country — Andean, Caribbean, Pacific, llanos, Amazon — and about a Minnesota community that the building will mash into Mexican if you let it. This is not Mexican, and it is not Ecuadorian as a synonym. It is not one Spanish, either, because paisa, costeño, bogotano, and vallecaucano are not an accent test you run in the lobby. Afro-Colombian and indigenous peoples exist inside the republic, so ask this household rather than assuming, and do not invent a Minnesota indigenous-language speaker count.

### Who this is

Use this page for context and questions. It does not describe the person in front of you. Paternalism looks like one Latino blob, one “Spanish interpreter,” a cartel joke as an icebreaker, and an English form handed over because Compass bachelor’s attainment looks high.

### Who this is not

Minnesota Compass (ACS 2020–2024) puts the Colombian community near 9,853 (give or take 1,784), with about 65.1 percent living in the Twin Cities and about 34.9 percent in Greater Minnesota (give or take 7.2 points), which is not an afterthought. About 26.5 percent are age 17 or younger, about 6.1 percent are 65+, and about 48.8 percent are foreign-born. Among those age 5+, 43.5 percent speak a language other than English, and 18.6 percent speak English less than “very well.” High school or higher stands at 93.9 percent and bachelor’s or higher at 54.8 percent, while poverty is 6.9 percent and uninsured is 8.9 percent. These margins of error are large for a community this small. Date the number you use, and remember that a rate is not the person.

The diversity inside this people is the point. A Medellín professional, a Caribbean-coast household, an Afro-Colombian student, a U.S.-born nurse, a Greater Minnesota family, a person who left because of conflict and will not name it in the lobby, and a second-generation kid who uses English with friends and Spanish with an elder share a people, but they do not share a Tuesday.

### How to read this

Always defer to the person in front of you, because this page is a hypothesis you still test on this family rather than a description of them.

sections.heading: Origins and the Founding of a People
sections.body:
Colombia is not one people inside one flag, since it holds the Andean interior, the Caribbean coast, the Pacific, the llanos, and the Amazon. It holds Afro-Colombian nations and communities, and indigenous nations — Wayuu, Nasa, Embera, and others — inside the republic. Mestizo majority narratives do not erase those histories, and shared Spanish is not shared culture.

### History for the meeting

Spanish colonial rule, Catholic mission, African enslavement, indigenous survival, a republic, and a half-century of armed conflict produced the streams you will meet. “Hispanic” on a U.S. form is an ethnicity checkbox, which is why people in this page check white, Black, American Indian, other, and two or more.

### What people brought

People brought regional Spanish, kinship, parish and later evangelical church, professional and trade skill, and a living memory of a state and of a war that is not one war. What they met in Minnesota was an English form, one Latino module, often one interpreter labeled Spanish, a Mexican default, and a drug-war headline that someone thought was an icebreaker.

History is literacy for the desk rather than a speech you give the family, so do not start with coffee, a telenovela, or a cartel sentence.

sections.heading: The Geography of Colombia and Colombian Minnesota
sections.body:
The homeland is not one city: Bogotá is not Medellín, Cali is not Barranquilla, and the Pacific is not the Caribbean, with regional Spanish, food, and some kinship patterns shifting from one to the next. Confirm the place if they name it, but do not referee paisa versus costeño in a waiver meeting; listen instead.

### Homeland

Minnesota is not Miami, so do not import a Doral picture onto a Ramsey County lobby.

### Minnesota

In Minnesota the split is Twin Cities 65.1 percent and Greater Minnesota 34.9 percent (Compass, ACS 2020–2024), which is not an afterthought. Do not assume Minneapolis, and do not assume the person in front of you has been to Colombia.

sections.heading: Work, Conflict, and Later Streams — Not a Mexican File
sections.body:
Colombian Minnesota is not an IRCA file and not a 1975 poster. It includes professional and family streams; internal displacement as a named Colombian fact (desplazados); and later asylum as a possible U.S. path, which is a pattern now rather than a Minnesota count. For that reason, do not invent a status number, and do not collect status you do not need.

### Foundational events

Armed conflict — guerrilla, paramilitary, state, the 2016 peace, and later violence in some regions — is literacy for the desk, but it is not a speech you give the family, and it is not every household. The U.S. drug war sat on top of that stack, and because it still sits in a lobby joke, you do not make the joke.

### Who you meet

The desk in 2026 meets U.S.-born children, mixed-status households, a professional who does not need an interpreter and whose elder does, and a person who will not put a relative’s name on a form. Compass puts foreign-born at 48.8 percent (ACS 2020–2024), a figure that is dated and is not a personality.

If you only know “immigrant” or only know “cartel,” you will miss the people actually in front of you.

sections.heading: Family
sections.body:
Family is not one size. Some households look nuclear on an English form and still carry obligation to a parent who does not read the form, while others are extended. Compass puts average household size at about 2.26, with about 32.8 percent living alone, but that is an average rather than a personality, and it does not mean “they don’t do family,” so ask who should be in the room.

### Who is in the household

Mixed-status is structure for some households, which is why you do not collect status you do not need and do not treat unmatched last names or a missing SSN as fraud until you have a reason.

### Who speaks

Familismo is a hypothesis, not a rule, because hour caps and “natural supports” language can dump unpaid work onto women in that network and call it culture.

Minnesota law still stands: domestic violence is not culture, and you follow mandated reporting while you still see a family. Do not skip the report and call it respeto, and do not use a child as interpreter.

sections.heading: Minnesota and Colombian History
sections.body:
Minnesota holds a Colombian community large enough for a Compass profile — about 9,853 (ACS 2020–2024) — and large enough that this department will meet it on waivers, child welfare, health care, cash, food, aging, and employment. Greater Minnesota is 34.9 percent of it, so do not write this people as a Minneapolis anecdote.

### Places

Think in places rather than a blob, from the Twin Cities to inner-ring suburbs and Greater Minnesota towns, and do not assume Minneapolis or assume the person in front of you has been downtown.

### Partners

Partners are the parishes and civic groups this family names; no source ties a particular parish or organization to Colombian Minnesotans, and the one Colombian-identified nonprofit named here is Colombia Live. CLUES is a Latino door rather than a Colombian community, and CECLC is a department door rather than the whole, so pay the partner this household actually uses.

Book a qualified interpreter, and pay for community work. Do not assign either to staff because of who they are. Hispanic Heritage Month is not consultation, and while you are a guest, being a guest does not make you the expert.

sections.heading: Colombian — not Mexican, not a cartel file
sections.body:
To be Colombian in Minnesota is to be placed in a U.S. checkbox that holds Mexican as the default, and in a news cycle that holds a cartel as the icebreaker. There is a peoplehood here that the mash deletes: regional Spanish, Afro-Colombian and indigenous histories, professional and working-class lives, and conflict memory for some and a history class for others.

### In this state

Mexican Minnesota is the largest Latino origin in this state, and that fact becomes a harm when the building treats Mexican Spanish as the Latino default, because a costeño household, a paisa household, and an Afro-Colombian household are not variants of Mexico.

In the U.S. racial order, Hispanic is ethnicity, not race, and colorism inside this page is real. Afro-Colombian people exist, so ask rather than mashing them into historic African American or bleaching them into a mestizo story. Drug-war stigma is a named harm, and you do not write it as ethnicity.

This guide is a working orientation, and because individual variation always supersedes group generalization, you always defer to this family.

sections.heading: Core Concepts
sections.body:
Not Mexican is the first grammar, which means that if you open a Mexican default because the name is Spanish, you do not have a household yet.

### Spanish is not one Spanish

Paisa, costeño, bogotano, and vallecaucano are distinct, so book qualified Spanish AND ask.

### Two surnames

Dropping the second surname invents a person who then has to be corrected later.

### Conflict as literacy, not personality

2016 is not a speech, and you do not ask a person to narrate displacement.

### Afro-Colombian and indigenous as hypotheses you still ask

Ask rather than assume, and do not invent a Minnesota speaker count to fill the gap.

### Drug-war stigma as a named harm

You do not make the joke, and you do not write cartel on a last name. The enforcement climate also means you do not collect status you do not need.

sections.heading: Religion
sections.body:
There is a Catholic majority in many streams, though not all, and the parish may be the trusted channel, while a household may instead attend an evangelical or Pentecostal church or follow Afro-diasporic practice. Do not assume any of these, and do not exoticize them; no Minnesota source documents Colombians’ religious affiliation, so ask.

### Streams

Do not make a priest or a pastor the case plan unless this family asked, and do not BCC one parish and call it consultation.

### Practice

Holy Week, the fiestas families name, and funeral obligation can collide with your calendar, so you still keep medical and legal time, and you name the conflict when it arises.

Help that looks like a report is not help. Religious framing of disability, mental health, or gender can sit next to a fierce wish for services, and you can hold both at once.

sections.heading: Greetings
sections.body:
Wait to see how the person greets you, and follow their lead. Let the other person set any greeting beyond a handshake or nod.

### Titles

Use titles until invited otherwise: Señor, Señora, Don, Doña. Use the last name you were given, and remember there may be two. Usted versus tú varies by region, so a qualified interpreter matches the register, and you do not correct it.

### This room

Greet everyone in the room, not only the English speaker.

Let this person’s own greeting guide you, whatever you read on another page.

sections.heading: Naming Conventions
sections.body:
Two surnames is the default in much of Spanish-language naming: apellido paterno, then apellido materno. A U.S. database that keeps one surname invents a person, and because that invented name then follows them through MHCP, child welfare, and school, it is a gate.

### How to file

Ask how to file the name, ask how to say it, and pronounce it, without dropping accents as a joke. Given names may be Spanish, indigenous, English, or both, so ask.

Women may or may not take a husband’s surname in U.S. records, and children may carry two surnames that do not match a parent’s U.S. “last name” field, which is not fraud until you have a reason.

For the same reason, do not treat unmatched last names in a household as a fraud flag by default.

sections.heading: Dates of Significance
sections.body:
Independence falls on 20 July, and some families name regional fiestas. Hispanic Heritage Month is a U.S. poster rather than this people, and a poster is not language access.

### Calendar

The 2016 peace accord is literacy, not a holiday and not a personality, so do not put it on a case note as color.

Ask this family, and do not put “Latino holiday” on a case note. Calendar clicks are literacy for scheduling, but they are not community engagement and not a day off the work.

sections.heading: Education
sections.body:
Compass (ACS 2020–2024) reports that among Colombian Minnesotans 25 and older, about 93.9 percent have high school or higher and about 54.8 percent have a bachelor’s or higher, and Compass should always be dated. High attainment is not “no language gate,” because about 48.8 percent of the community is foreign-born. The IEP still has to reach the parent who does not read it.

### School and language

A parent who speaks fluent Spanish and limited English is not illiterate, since the English-only form is the gate. Do not skip the interpreter because the adult in the lobby is professional or accent-light.

Do not use a child as interpreter, and do not treat a college student as proof the waiver household needs no interpreter. Do not copy Ecuadorian attainment onto this page, and do not copy this page onto Ecuadorian, because each people has its own counts.

sections.heading: Etiquette
sections.body:
If food or drink is offered, accepting a little is fine, and you can still keep to medical and legal timelines.

### In the home

Use titles until invited otherwise, and follow the household on shoes. Ask before taking any photograph or touching any religious object, and do not ask anyone to explain their faith or history for your benefit.

### Time

Keep to clinic and court timelines. If someone is late, ask what got in the way, and record only what happened.

Take time to introduce yourself and explain the plan, and still give any required notice. Ask whether they agree with the plan, and do not take a smile as consent.

sections.heading: Language and Communication — the CLAS gate
sections.body:
This is the CLAS Spanish line, and Spanish is not the people. Paisa, costeño, bogotano, and vallecaucano are not one interpreter accent test, and none of them is Mexican Spanish by default, so book a qualified Spanish interpreter AND ask this household, because register matters.

### Language

Indigenous languages exist inside Colombia, so ask this household, and do not invent a Minnesota speaker count. If they name a language that is not Spanish, name it on the request, because a Spanish interpreter may still not work.

Compass (ACS 2020–2024) reports that among those 5 and older, 43.5 percent speak a language other than English and 18.6 percent speak English less than “very well,” and the number should be dated. High bachelor’s attainment does not close this gate, so do not use a child as interpreter, and do not make a Colombian coworker the interpreter.

Give the person time to answer. If you get a short yes, check that the plan was understood, and ask whether it works for them.

sections.heading: Other Considerations
sections.body:
This section states hard facts plainly, because treating everyone the same can hide them.

### Named harms

Drug-war stigma is a named harm, and a cartel joke, a sniffing mime, or a “where the cocaine is from” icebreaker shuts the person out. You do not write cartel as ethnicity, and you do not put it on a last name as a risk score.

ICE and the enforcement climate are structure for some. Mixed-status households may skip clinic when a relative can be moved, which is not noncompliance, and so you do not collect status you do not need.

Conflict trauma sits in some rooms, but it is not a personality and not every household. The Mexican default will talk over this page if you let it. Colorism is real, and do not excuse control as “that’s culture.” Domestic violence is not culture, and you follow mandated reporting.

LGBTQ Colombians exist, so you use the name, and you do not out someone to kin and call it familismo.

sections.heading: Health
sections.body:
Compass (ACS 2020–2024) reports about 8.9 percent without health insurance among those for whom status is determined, and that figure should be dated. Do not invent a PTSD rate from the conflict, since trauma sits in some rooms but is not every household.

### Access

Fear of the lobby is a health access fact for some mixed-status households, which means a badge, a form that asks for SSN, or a child called to interpret a diagnosis is a clinical event.

Believe reported pain, and do not skip screening. Do not fold this history into Tuskegee or into a generic “immigrant mistrust” slide. Gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care, so offer it, and do not use a child as interpreter in a health encounter.

sections.heading: LGBTQ
sections.body:
Queer and trans Colombian Minnesotans exist. Conservative parish, evangelical, and family climates can mean silence or exile, but that is not every family, and you do not get to decide which one this household is from the doorway.

### This person

Use the name they use, and do not share what they tell you unless a rule requires it. Minnesota’s Human Rights Act still applies.

Afro-Colombian and indigenous queer people exist inside this page, so do not mash them into the historic African American LGBTQ chapter, and do not bleach them. Do not question a household about anyone’s sexuality or gender.

sections.heading: Hair, Dress, and Body
sections.body:
There is no Colombian uniform, and the second generation looks like Minnesota. Regional dress is public at fiesta, but it is not a daily costume, and it is not yours to request for a Heritage Month photo.

### Dress

Colorism and hair texture are real. Afro-Colombian hair is not the CROWN Act chapter copied over, and you still do not touch and still do not police. Mestizo default beauty is a hierarchy, so name it if it is in the room.

Do not rank piety or blackness off clothing; ask the person, with gender match if they want it.

sections.heading: Music
sections.body:
There is not one playlist, since vallenato, cumbia, salsa from Cali, champeta, and bambuco each show that the region names the sound. A Mexican default playlist in a Colombian waiting room is the mash in speakers.

### Variation

A festival stage is not engagement, a playlist is not language access, and church music is not staff entertainment.

Knowing that music is public life will not write the waiver, but it will stop you from treating one Heritage Month speaker as the community.

sections.heading: Sports
sections.body:
Fútbol is the common public sport, cycling carries prestige in some rooms, and school sport is ordinary for the second generation. Do not assume the kid plays, and do not make sport the only excellence you can see.

### Not the whole person

Leagues are social infrastructure, but they are not language access and not a case plan.

World Cup loyalties are not a risk score and should never be read as one.

sections.heading: Literature
sections.body:
Spanish-language literature is world literature, and García Márquez is literacy for the desk rather than a prompt to quote Macondo in the lobby. This is not a people without letters, but that fact does not mean the person in the lobby can read your form.

### Literacy in the lobby

You do not need a novel; you need the language this person reads, because print Spanish from Spain, Mexico, or a translation produced by software is not automatically this household’s Spanish.

CLAS is qualified language, not Google and not a child.

sections.heading: Art
sections.body:
Coastal and Andean visual work, goldwork as memory, and diaspora artists are all part of the picture, but Botero is tourism if you start there, so be a guest rather than a researcher.

### Guest

A museum visit is optional professional development, and it is not consultation.

A Heritage Month that mashes this with Mexican papel picado has already mashed the adjacent peoples.

sections.heading: Conflict, the Drug War, and the State
sections.body:
Armed conflict, internal displacement, the 2016 peace, later violence in some regions, U.S. drug-war policy, and the enforcement climate for some arrivals make up the political stack. A DHS badge is not automatically help, and for some people a government form is a thing you survive, which is not “paranoia” but pattern.

### The badge

Do not use a war or a cartel headline as a personality, and do not ask a person to narrate displacement, a kidnapping, or a crossing for your professional development. Asylum is a possible path for some, a pattern now rather than a Minnesota count, so do not collect status you do not need.

Mandated reporting still exists, and so does the duty not to treat a whole people as a deportation score or a narcotics score.

sections.heading: Work, Markets, and Government
sections.body:
The community spans a professional class, trades, small business, service, and public employment. Compass bachelor’s or higher at 54.8 percent and a median household income of about $74,087 (2024 dollars, with a margin of error of about $29,000) are averages rather than this kitchen table.

### Work

Book a qualified interpreter, and pay for community work. Do not assign either to staff because of who they are.

### Staff

Take time to introduce yourself and explain the plan, and still give any required notice.

Ask whether the household sends money to relatives in Colombia, and do not assume it is optional in a budget.

sections.heading: Health-care and Human-service Encounters
sections.body:
Start with Spanish variety by booking qualified Spanish AND asking, and do not use a child as interpreter or make staff the interpreter. Ask who is in the room, offer gender match in maternal and intimate care if they want it, and remember the two surnames.

### Language

If you do not need an SSN on the first screen, do not ask for it. With mixed-status households, do not collect status you do not need, because in this enforcement climate skipped appointments are pattern. Conflict trauma in some rooms is not a personality, and drug-war stigma in the lobby is a clinical event if you let it be.

### The meeting

Believe reported pain, and do not skip screening. Mandated reporting still exists, so you follow the law while you still see a family.

sections.heading: Adjacent Peoples — Do Not Mash
sections.body:
This people is not Mexican. Mexican Minnesota is the largest Latino origin in this state, and it becomes a Minnesota harm when it is the only file. This people is also not Ecuadorian as a synonym, not a Venezuelan mash, not “the Andes” as one interpreter, and not Peruvian.

### Adjacent doors

This people is not Somali, and not historic African American. Afro-Colombian people exist, so ask rather than mashing them into the African American CI because both are Black, and do not bleach them into a mestizo Latino blob.

Open the people CI that matches this household, and open /ci/latino as the umbrella, but never rely on one Latino module.

sections.heading: Counts, Dated
sections.body:
Minnesota Compass, ACS 2020–2024, for the Colombian cultural community: about 9,853 people (give or take 1,784); Twin Cities 65.1%; Greater Minnesota 34.9% (give or take 7.2 points); age 17 or younger 26.5%; 65+ 6.1%; foreign-born 48.8%; language other than English (age 5+) 43.5%; English less than “very well” 18.6%; English only 56.5%; high school or higher (25+) 93.9%; bachelor’s or higher 54.8%; median household income about $74,087 (2024 dollars, give or take $28,936); poverty 6.9%; owner-occupied 57.3%; average household size 2.26; uninsured 8.9%.

### Counts

Date Compass, and do not invent a status count or an indigenous-language speaker count, or copy Mexican, Ecuadorian, or Cuban numbers onto this page. Compass builds cultural communities from self-reported race, ancestry, birthplace, and parents’ characteristics, not ancestry alone, and Census Hispanic-origin counts differ: 10,494 (give or take 2,420) in the 2024 single-year ACS and 8,332 (give or take 959) in ACS 2020–2024. Counts disagree across ACS vintages and definitions, so date the number you cite.

### What the count is not

High attainment is not “no language gate,” an owner rate is not proof the gates closed, and a rate is not the person.

sections.heading: Doors and Sources
sections.body:
Start with the Minnesota Compass Colombian profile (ACS 2020–2024). CLUES is a Latino door, not this people and not the whole state, so add the parishes and civic groups this family names, and remember that CECLC is a department door rather than the community.

### Public doors

CLAS Spanish is on the five, and since Spanish is not one Spanish, open /ci/latino as the umbrella and open this brief for a Colombian household.

### Where to learn more

Use these resources yourself before you ask a Colombian colleague to explain, and do not count a BCC to CLUES as consultation. Pay partners and report back, because Hispanic Heritage Month is not the work.

sections.heading: How it hits DHS gates — the 40%
sections.body:
Workplace culture and service delivery are both candidates for where these gates take hold.

Language: CLAS Spanish is not one Spanish, and Colombian regional Spanish is not a Mexican interpreter accent test. A child as interpreter does harm, gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care, and high bachelor’s attainment is not “no interpreter.”

Names: there are two surnames, so the database that keeps one invents a person, and unmatched last names are not fraud by default.

SSN on the first screen, hour caps, exception processes, and life-sharing matches without language are not culturally neutral. Mixed-status households may bounce if the first field feels like enforcement, which is why you do not collect status you do not need.

Child welfare and disability: help-seeking that becomes a report is part of why people wait. Mandated reporting still exists and domestic violence is not culture, so you follow the law.

Enforcement climate: people may skip clinic, school, and waiver meetings when a relative can be moved, and that is not noncompliance.

Drug-war stigma in the lobby is a gate, and you do not write cartel as ethnicity.

Notices and comment: do not count an eList and an English PDF as reaching this community, and because Greater Minnesota is 34.9 percent of it, a Minneapolis default is a gate.

Workforce: Colombian staff are not the interpreter pool and not the community. Staff are colleagues, not the curriculum, and you do not treat them as the curriculum.

The Mexican default is a gate, so disaggregate, or you have invented a people.

Legislation, funding, and rule: study a channel before you advocate for it. Use this page so that the 40% has a household in it.

sections.heading: A Note on This Guide
sections.body:
This brief is about Cuban people as a people with a country and a Minnesota community that the building will mash into Mexican, or into Puerto Rican, if you let it. This is not Mexican, and it is not interchangeable with Puerto Rican, because Puerto Rican is U.S. citizenship under the Jones Act (1917), and Cuban is not that file. 1959, Mariel (1980), the 1994 balseros, and the later streams are not one exile story, and the Spanish here is Caribbean Spanish, not Mexican.

### Who this is

Use this page for context and questions. It does not describe the person in front of you. Paternalism looks like one Latino blob, one “Spanish interpreter,” a 1959 speech you give a U.S.-born twenty-year-old, and collecting status because you learned the word Mariel.

### Who this is not

Minnesota Compass (ACS 2020–2024) puts the Cuban community near 8,775 (give or take 1,811), with about 69.4 percent living in the Twin Cities and about 30.6 percent in Greater Minnesota (each give or take 8.7 points), which is not an afterthought. The Census Bureau’s Hispanic-origin count for the same years is lower, 6,536 (give or take 994). About 31.6 percent are age 17 or younger and about 9.9 percent are 65+, while about 22.8 percent are foreign-born, which means a large share was born here. Among those age 5+, 36.8 percent speak a language other than English, and 11.4 percent speak English less than “very well.” Poverty is 9.4 percent, homeownership is 49.7 percent, and disability is 22.7 percent, so date the number you use, do not invent a cause for it, and remember that a rate is not the person.

The diversity inside this people is the point. Consider a 1960s exile elder, a Mariel arrival, a 1994 balsero, a later-stream parent, a U.S.-born nurse, an Afro-Cuban student, a Greater Minnesota household, and a person who left 1959 politics behind and still shows up at a parish. They share a people, but they do not share a Tuesday.

### How to read this

Always defer to the person in front of you, because this page is a hypothesis and you still have to test it on this family.

sections.heading: Origins and the Founding of a People
sections.body:
Cuban peoplehood is older than 1959 and older than Miami, because it grew on an island in the Caribbean through Spanish colonial rule, African enslavement, Chinese contract labor, a republic, and a revolution. Cubans are white Cuban, Afro-Cuban, and mixed, and mestizaje narratives do not erase Black Cuba. Shared Spanish is not shared culture with Mexico, and a shared Caribbean is not shared culture with Puerto Rico.

### History for the meeting

What people brought includes Caribbean Spanish, kinship, Catholic and Afro-Cuban religious practice, professional and trade skill, and a living memory of a state that some fled and some still argue about. What they met in Minnesota was an English form, one Latino module, often one interpreter labeled Spanish, a Mexican default, and a Miami picture that is not this map.

### What people brought

History is literacy for the desk rather than a speech you give the family, so do not start with a cigar, a classic car, or a 1959 tourism sentence.

sections.heading: The Geography of Cuba and Cuban Minnesota
sections.body:
Homeland is not one neighborhood in Havana, because across Havana, Oriente, and the central provinces, region, color, and some speech shift. If they name a place, confirm it and listen, but do not referee in a waiver meeting.

### Homeland

The U.S. map begins with Florida, where Miami-Dade holds the large community, and continues to New Jersey, New York, and elsewhere. Minnesota is not Miami, so do not import Little Havana onto a Hennepin County lobby.

### Minnesota

In Minnesota, 69.4 percent of this community lives in the Twin Cities and 30.6 percent in Greater Minnesota (Compass, ACS 2020–2024), which is not an afterthought. That is why you should not assume Minneapolis, and should not assume the person in front of you has ever been to Cuba.

sections.heading: 1959, Mariel, 1994, Later — Not One Exile Story
sections.body:
If 1975 is the foundational event of Vietnamese Minnesota, Cuban Minnesota does not get one year that covers the lobby. It gets a stack of them, and you will misread the room if you pick the wrong one.

### Foundational events

The years 1959–early 1960s brought the revolution and the first-wave exile, a group often more connected and more already professional, although that is a stream rather than a virtue ranking. The Freedom Flights followed, and then Mariel in 1980 brought a different class mix and a stigma that still sits in some rooms. Then came the 1994 balseros. Wet foot/dry foot ended in January 2017, later irregular arrivals came via other countries, and there are U.S.-born children in every stream.

### Who you meet

The Cuban Adjustment Act (1966) is literacy for the desk: a path some people can use after a year of presence. It is not a speech, it is not permission to collect status you do not need, and it is not Puerto Rican citizenship.

The desk in 2026 meets a third-generation English-dominant adult, an elder who needs Caribbean Spanish, and last year’s arrival. Compass foreign-born at 22.8 percent (ACS 2020–2024) is the dated share, and it does not mean “everyone is an exile,” which is why 1959 is literacy rather than a speech you give the family.

sections.heading: Family
sections.body:
Family is not one size. Some households look nuclear on an English form and still carry obligation to a parent who does not read the form, while some are extended, and Compass puts the average household size at about 2.80, so ask who should be in the room.

### Who is in the household

Mixed status is structure for some later streams, so do not collect status you do not need, and do not treat unmatched last names or a missing SSN as fraud until you have a reason. First-wave households may have been U.S. citizens for decades while later streams may not be, and you do not know from the name.

### Who speaks

Hour caps and “natural supports” language can dump unpaid work onto the women in that network and call it culture.

Minnesota law still stands, because domestic violence is not culture, and you follow mandated reporting while still seeing a family. Do not use a child as the interpreter.

sections.heading: Minnesota and Cuban History
sections.body:
Minnesota holds a Cuban community large enough for a Compass profile, about 8,775 (ACS 2020–2024), and large enough that this department will meet it on waivers, child welfare, health care, cash, food, aging, and employment. Because Greater Minnesota is 30.6 percent of it, do not write this people as a Minneapolis anecdote, and do not write it as a Miami satellite.

### Places

Think in places rather than a blob: the Twin Cities, inner-ring suburbs, and Greater Minnesota towns. Do not assume Minneapolis, and do not assume the person in front of you has been downtown, or to Havana.

### Partners

The partners are the parishes families name and the civic groups this family names. CLUES is a Latino door rather than a Cuban community, and CECLC is a department door rather than the whole, so pay the partner this household actually uses.

Book a qualified interpreter, and pay for community work. Do not assign either to staff because of who they are. Hispanic Heritage Month is not consultation, and while you are a guest there, being one does not make you the expert.

sections.heading: Cuban — not Mexican, not Puerto Rican, not one exile
sections.body:
To be Cuban in Minnesota is to be placed in a U.S. checkbox that holds Mexican as the default and Miami as the picture. There is a peoplehood here that the mash deletes: an island, Caribbean Spanish, Afro-Cuban histories, 1959 as memory for some and a history class for others, Mariel stigma, later streams, and U.S.-born lives.

### In this state

Puerto Rican is citizenship, and Cuban is not that file, just as Mexican Spanish is not this Spanish. Cubans are white Cuban, Afro-Cuban, and mixed, and colorism inside this page is real. Afro-Cuban people exist, so ask, rather than mashing them into historic African American or bleaching them into a first-wave exile story.

You do not referee 1959 or put a revolution on a case note as color, because your job is to meet a household.

This guide is a working orientation, and because individual variation always supersedes group generalization, always defer to this family.

sections.heading: Core Concepts
sections.body:
Not Mexican, and not Puerto Rican as a synonym: that is the first grammar, because if you open a Mexican default or run a citizenship script copied from Puerto Rico, you do not have a household yet.

### Streams are not one exile

1959, Mariel, 1994, and later are different streams, so ask, and do not give a U.S.-born adult a 1959 speech.

### Caribbean Spanish

Book qualified Spanish, and ask this household as well.

### Two surnames

Dropping the second surname invents a person.

The Cuban Adjustment Act is literacy rather than a reason to collect status, so do not collect status you do not need.

### Colorism

White Cuban is not the whole, and Afro-Cuban is not a footnote. The parish, and in some rooms Afro-Cuban religion, are real, so do not exoticize them, and do not make clergy the case plan unless they asked.

sections.heading: Religion
sections.body:
Catholics are the majority in many streams, though not all, and Protestant churches live here as well, while Santería / Regla de Ocha and related Afro-Cuban practice live in some rooms. Do not exoticize them, and do not treat an orisha as folklore, as witchcraft, or as a risk score. None is also a Tuesday, so ask.

### Streams

Do not make a priest or a santero the case plan unless this family asked, and do not BCC one parish and call it consultation.

### Practice

Holy Week, funeral obligation, and the feast days some families name can collide with your calendar, so you still keep medical and legal time, and you name the conflict when it happens.

Help that looks like a report is not help. Religious framing of disability, mental health, or gender can sit right next to a fierce wish for services, and you can hold both.

sections.heading: Greetings
sections.body:
Wait to see how the person greets you, and follow their lead. Let the other person set any greeting beyond a handshake or nod.

### Titles

Use titles until invited otherwise, and use the last name you were given, remembering there may be two. On usted versus tú, some Caribbean rooms move to tú faster and some elders do not, which is why a qualified interpreter matches the register, and you do not correct it.

### This room

Greet everyone in the room, not only the English speaker.

Let this person’s own greeting guide you, whatever you read on another page.

sections.heading: Naming Conventions
sections.body:
Two surnames is the default in much of Spanish-language naming: apellido paterno, then apellido materno. A U.S. database that keeps one surname invents a person, and because that invented name then follows them through MHCP, child welfare, and school, it is a gate.

### How to file

Ask how to file the name and how to say it, and pronounce it, rather than dropping accents as a joke. Given names may be Spanish, English, or both, so ask.

Women may or may not take a husband’s surname in U.S. records, and children may carry two surnames that do not match a parent’s U.S. “last name” field, which is not fraud until you have a reason to think so.

Do not treat unmatched last names in a household as a fraud flag by default.

sections.heading: Dates of Significance
sections.body:
1 January 1959 is the revolution or the exile, depending on the room, and in many Cuban American rooms it is grief and politics rather than a party. Do not put a slogan on a case note, and do not celebrate or condemn in the file; if they name it, listen.

### Calendar

Independence on 20 May appears in some exile calendars, and so does 10 October, so ask. Hispanic Heritage Month is a U.S. poster, not this people.

Calendar clicks are literacy for scheduling, but they are not community engagement, and they are not a day off from the work, so do not put “Latino holiday” on a case note.

sections.heading: Education
sections.body:
Compass (ACS 2020–2024) reports that among Cuban Minnesotans 25 and older, about 88.1 percent have a high school education or higher and about 35.7 percent have a bachelor’s or higher.
