Date Compass when you cite it, and remember that streams differ, since first-wave professional memory is not Mariel, and it is not last year’s arrival. About 22.8 percent of the community is foreign-born, so a large share of children are U.S.-born, but the IEP still has to reach the parent who does not read it.

### School and language

A parent who speaks fluent Spanish and limited English is not illiterate, because the English-only form is the gate. Do not skip the interpreter because a 1959 story said professional, and do not assume illiteracy because the stream is later.

Do not use a child as the interpreter, and do not treat a college student as proof that the waiver household needs no interpreter.

sections.heading: Etiquette
sections.body:
If food or drink is offered, accepting a little is fine, and you can still keep to medical and legal timelines.

### In the home

Use titles until invited otherwise, and follow the household on shoes. Ask before taking any photograph or touching any religious object, and do not ask anyone to explain their faith or history for your benefit.

### Time

Keep to clinic and court timelines. If someone is late, ask what got in the way, and record only what happened.

Take time to introduce yourself and explain the plan, and still give any required notice. Ask whether they agree with the plan, and do not take a smile as consent.

sections.heading: Language and Communication — the CLAS gate
sections.body:
This is the CLAS Spanish line, and Spanish is not the people, because Caribbean Spanish is not Mexican Spanish and not Andean Spanish. Book a qualified Spanish interpreter, and ask this household as well, since register matters.

### Language

Compass (ACS 2020–2024) reports that among those 5 and older, 36.8 percent speak a language other than English, 11.4 percent speak English less than “very well,” and 63.2 percent speak English only, so date the number. A large U.S.-born share is English-dominant, but the elder may not be, which is why you should not skip the interpreter because Compass LEP looks modest.

Do not use a child as the interpreter, and do not make a Cuban coworker the interpreter. Give the person time to answer. If you get a short yes, check that the plan was understood, and ask whether it works for them.

sections.heading: Other Considerations
sections.body:
This section states hard facts plainly, because treating everyone the same can hide them.

### Named harms

1959 intra-community politics still split some rooms, over the flag, over exile, and over later arrivals who did not come as anti-communist heroes, so you do not referee, and you do not put it on a case note as color. Mariel stigma is a named harm, and it is not a risk score.

Colorism is real, and a white Cuban default will talk over Afro-Cuban if you let it. ICE and the enforcement climate are structure for some later streams, so do not collect status you do not need, because the Cuban Adjustment Act is literacy, not a reason to collect status.

Compass puts disability at 22.7 percent (ACS 2020–2024), so date it, do not invent a cause, and do not skip screening.

LGBTQ Cubans exist, so you use the name, and you do not out someone to kin and call it culture. Domestic violence is not culture, which is why you follow mandated reporting.

sections.heading: Health
sections.body:
Compass (ACS 2020–2024) reports about 4.5 percent without health insurance, and disability at 22.7 percent among those for whom status is determined, 22.6 percent under 65, so date them. Do not invent a cause for the disability figure or a PTSD rate, and remember that an uninsured rate that looks low is not “no health gate.”

### Access

Believe reported pain, and do not skip screening. Do not fold this history into Tuskegee or into a generic “immigrant mistrust” slide, because streams differ, and an elder of 1961 and a 2022 arrival do not share a clinic story.

Gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care, so offer it, and do not use a child as the interpreter in a health encounter. Colorism in the clinic is a named harm when staff treat Afro-Cuban as a different file.

sections.heading: LGBTQ
sections.body:
Queer and trans Cuban Minnesotans exist, and conservative parish and family climates can mean silence or exile. Island history includes persecution and later legal change, which is literacy rather than a speech, and it is not this household’s Tuesday unless they name it.

### This person

Use the name they use, and do not share what they tell you unless a rule requires it. Minnesota’s Human Rights Act still applies.

Afro-Cuban queer people exist inside this page, so do not mash them into the historic African American LGBTQ chapter, and do not bleach them. Do not question a household about anyone’s sexuality or gender.

sections.heading: Hair, Dress, and Body
sections.body:
There is no Cuban uniform, and the second generation looks like Minnesota. A guayabera and white clothing at some public events are not a daily costume, and they are not yours to request for a Heritage Month photo.

### Dress

Colorism and hair texture are real across white Cuban, Afro-Cuban, and mixed people. Afro-Cuban hair is not the CROWN Act chapter copied over, and you still do not touch and still do not police, so do not rank race off skin or hair in a case note.

Do not ask whether they “still wear the costume,” but ask the person, with gender match if they want it.

sections.heading: Music
sections.body:
This is not one playlist, because son, salsa, rumba, timba, and trova each carry an origin that names the sound, and a Mexican default playlist in a Cuban waiting room is the mash coming through the speakers.

### Variation

A festival stage is not engagement, a playlist is not language access, and a rumba or a liturgy is not staff entertainment.

Knowing that music is public life will not write the waiver, but it will stop you from treating one Heritage Month speaker as the community.

sections.heading: Sports
sections.body:
Baseball has prestige in many Cuban streams, while soccer and ordinary school sport show up in the second generation, so do not assume the kid plays, and do not make sport the only excellence you can see.

### Not the whole person

Leagues are social infrastructure, but they are not language access and not a case plan.

A baseball sticker is not proof that the elder reads English.

sections.heading: Literature
sections.body:
Spanish-language literature is world literature, and Martí is literacy for the desk rather than a prompt to quote in the lobby. This is not a people without letters, but that fact does not mean the person in the lobby can read your form.

### Literacy in the lobby

You do not need a novel, because what you need is the language this person reads. Print Spanish from Spain, Mexico, or a translation produced by software is not automatically this household’s Caribbean Spanish.

CLAS means qualified language, not Google and not a child.

sections.heading: Art
sections.body:
Afro-Cuban visual and ritual art, diaspora work, and public music culture all belong here, so do not put a santo on a Heritage Month table and call it this people, and do not exoticize.

### Guest

You are a guest, not a researcher, and a museum visit is optional professional development rather than consultation.

A Heritage Month that mashes this people with Mexican papel picado has already mashed the adjacent peoples together.

sections.heading: Revolution, Adjustment, and the State
sections.body:
1959, the U.S. embargo as structure some families name, Mariel, 1994, wet foot/dry foot ending in 2017, the Cuban Adjustment Act of 1966, and the later enforcement climate for some arrivals: that is the political stack, and it is why a DHS badge is not automatically help.

### The badge

Do not use 1959 as a personality. Do not ask a person to narrate a raft or a revolution for your professional development, and do not collect status you do not need. The Cuban Adjustment Act is literacy, a path some people can use, but it is not Puerto Rican citizenship, and it is not a reason to run an ICE script on visit one.

Mandated reporting still exists, and so does the duty not to treat a whole people as a deportation score or a 1959 loyalty test.

sections.heading: Work, Markets, and Government
sections.body:
Professional work, trades, small business, service, and public employment all live here. Compass (ACS 2020–2024) puts owner-occupied housing at 49.7 percent, which means more renters than some neighboring spines, and a median household income of about $87,497 (2024 dollars, give or take $26,805) is an average rather than this kitchen table, because streams differ.

### Work

Book a qualified interpreter, and pay for community work. Do not assign either to staff because of who they are.

### Staff

Take time to introduce yourself and explain the plan, and still give any required notice.

Some people send money to relatives on the island as an obligation. Ask about it, and do not treat it as optional in a budget, and it is still not an immigration script.

sections.heading: Health-care and Human-service Encounters
sections.body:
The language is Caribbean Spanish, so book qualified Spanish, and ask this household as well. Do not use a child as the interpreter, and do not make staff the interpreter. Notice who is in the room, offer gender match in maternal and intimate care if they want it, and remember the two surnames.

### Language

Streams are not one exile, so do not give a U.S.-born adult a 1959 clinical story. Disability at 22.7 percent is dated Compass, so do not skip screening, and do not invent a cause. Enforcement climate for some later arrivals means skipped appointments are a pattern, which is why you should not collect status you do not need.

### The meeting

Believe reported pain, and remember that colorism in the clinic is a harm. Mandated reporting still exists, and you follow the law while still seeing a family.

sections.heading: Adjacent Peoples — Do Not Mash
sections.body:
This is not Mexican. Mexican Minnesota is the largest Latino origin in this state, and it becomes a Minnesota harm when it is the only file. This is not Puerto Rican as a synonym, because Puerto Rican is U.S. citizenship, so do not run that script here, and do not run an immigration script as if Cuban were Mexican.

### Adjacent doors

This is not a Dominican mash, and not “Caribbean” as one interpreter, and it is not Somali and not historic African American. Afro-Cuban people exist, so ask, rather than mashing them into the African American CI because both are Black or bleaching them into a first-wave exile story.

Open the people CI that matches this household, and open /ci/latino as the umbrella, but never one Latino module.

sections.heading: Counts, Dated
sections.body:
Minnesota Compass, ACS 2020–2024, describes the Cuban cultural community as about 8,775 people (give or take 1,811), with 69.4% in the Twin Cities and 30.6% in Greater Minnesota (each give or take 8.7 points). Those age 17 or younger are 31.6%, those 65+ are 9.9%, and the foreign-born share is 22.8%. Among those age 5+, 36.8% speak a language other than English, 11.4% speak English less than “very well,” and 63.2% speak English only, while among those 25+, 88.1% have high school or higher and 35.7% have a bachelor’s or higher. Median household income is about $87,497 (2024 dollars, give or take $26,805), poverty is 9.4%, owner-occupied housing is 49.7% and renter-occupied is 50.3%, average household size is 2.80, the uninsured share is 4.5%, and disability is 22.7%. The Census Bureau’s Hispanic-origin count for 2020 to 2024 is lower, 6,536 (give or take 994), so say which definition you use.

### Counts

Date Compass. Do not invent a cause for disability at 22.7 percent, do not invent a stream count (1959 vs Mariel vs 1994 vs later), and do not copy Mexican, Puerto Rican, or Colombian numbers onto this page.

### What the count is not

Foreign-born at 22.8 percent does not mean “everyone is an exile.” Language and child-as-interpreter are gates, and a rate is not the person.

sections.heading: Doors and Sources
sections.body:
The doors begin with the Minnesota Compass Cuban profile (ACS 2020–2024). CLUES is a Latino door, not this people and not the whole state, while the parishes and civic groups this family names are doors as well, and CECLC is a department door, not the community.

### Public doors

CLAS Spanish is on the five, and Spanish is not one Spanish. Open /ci/latino as the umbrella, open this brief for a Cuban household, and open the Puerto Rican CI if this household is Puerto Rican.

### Where to learn more

Use these resources yourself before you ask a Cuban colleague to explain, and do not count a BCC to CLUES as consultation. Pay partners, and report back, because Hispanic Heritage Month is not the work.

sections.heading: How it hits DHS gates — the 40%
sections.body:
Workplace culture and service delivery are both candidates here.

Language: CLAS Spanish is not one Spanish, and Caribbean Spanish is not a Mexican interpreter accent test. A child as interpreter does harm, and gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care. A large U.S.-born share does not mean “no interpreter” for the elder.

Names: two surnames. The database that keeps one invents a person, and unmatched last names are not fraud by default.

SSN on the first screen, hour caps, and exception processes without language are not culturally neutral. The Cuban Adjustment Act is literacy, not a reason to collect status you do not need, and because Puerto Rican is citizenship, do not copy that script here, and do not run an ICE script as if Cuban were Mexican.

Child welfare and disability: Compass disability at 22.7 percent is dated, so do not skip screening and do not invent a cause. Help-seeking that becomes a report is part of why people wait. Mandated reporting still exists, and since domestic violence is not culture, you follow the law.

Enforcement climate for some later streams: people may skip clinic when a relative can be moved, and that is not noncompliance.

Notices and comment: do not count an eList and an English PDF as reaching this community, and because Greater Minnesota is 30.6 percent, a Minneapolis default is a gate.

Workforce: Cuban staff are not the interpreter pool and not the community. Staff are colleagues, not the curriculum, and should not be treated as either.

The Mexican default and the one-exile mash are gates, so disaggregate, or you have invented a people.

Legislation, funding, rule: study a channel before you advocate for it. Use this page so that the 40% has a household in it.

sections.heading: A Note on This Guide
sections.body:
This brief is about Ecuadorian people as a people with a country — Costa, Sierra, Amazon/Oriente, Galápagos — and about a Minnesota community that the building will mash into Mexican if you let it. This is not Mexican, it is not Colombian as a synonym, and it is not one Spanish. Indigenous languages may be in the home, among them Kichwa and others. Compass does not count speakers of Indigenous languages, so do not invent that count. El Colegio charter school told Sahan Journal in March 2024 that it offers language services and preservation classes for Quichua-speaking students. A Spanish interpreter may still not work for these households.

### Who this is

Use this page for context and questions. It does not describe the person in front of you. Paternalism looks like one Latino blob, one “Spanish interpreter,” an SSN field on the first screen, and an English IEP written for a household the building never studied.

### Who this is not

Minnesota Compass (ACS 2020–2024) puts Ecuadorian ancestry near 19,484 (plus or minus 3,601), with about 95.9 percent living in the Twin Cities and about 4.1 percent in Greater Minnesota. About 45.6 percent are age 17 or younger, about 2.1 percent are 65+, and about 53.3 percent are foreign-born. Among those age 5+, 76.8 percent speak a language other than English, and 49.1 percent speak English less than “very well,” while poverty is 19.9 percent and uninsured is 24.0 percent. Date the number you use, and remember that a rate is not the person.

The diversity inside this people is the point. A Kichwa-speaking mother who does not use Spanish as a home language, an Afro-Ecuadorian student, a coastal Spanish speaker, a Sierra household that uses usted, a U.S.-born child in an English-dominant school, a professional second generation, and a mixed-status kitchen table share a Census checkbox, but they do not share a Tuesday.

### How to read this

Always defer to the person in front of you, because this page is a hypothesis you still test on this family rather than a description of them.

sections.heading: Origins and the Founding of a People
sections.body:
Ecuador is not one people inside one flag, since it holds the Costa, the Sierra, the Amazon/Oriente, and the Galápagos. Kichwa (Runa Shimi) and other indigenous nations live inside the republic, as do the Shuar and other Amazonian peoples, and there are Afro-Ecuadorian streams in Esmeraldas and the Valle del Chota. Mestizo majority narratives do not erase those histories, and shared Spanish is not shared culture.

### History for the meeting

Spanish colonial rule, Catholic mission, indigenous survival, African enslavement on the coast, a republic, and later dollarization and emigration produced the streams you will meet. “Hispanic” on a U.S. form is an ethnicity checkbox, which is why people in this page check white, Black, American Indian, other, and two or more, and a form that treats Hispanic as a race has already mashed them.

### What people brought

People brought Spanish varieties and indigenous languages, kinship, parish and later evangelical church, work knowledge, and a living memory of a state and of a crisis that moved people. What they met in Minnesota was an English form, one Latino module, often one interpreter labeled Spanish, and a Mexican default.

History is literacy for the desk rather than a speech you give the family, so do not start with food, a hat, or a Heritage Month sentence.

sections.heading: The Geography of Ecuador and Ecuadorian Minnesota
sections.body:
The homeland is not one climate: Quito and the Sierra are not Guayaquil, and the Amazon is not the coast. Galápagos is a name some families hold and most Minnesota desks will never need, and regional Spanish and indigenous languages do not travel as a blob. Do not referee Quito versus Guayaquil in a waiver meeting, but listen if they name a place.

### Homeland

In the United States, New York and New Jersey hold large Ecuadorian communities, but Minnesota is not Queens, so do not import a Roosevelt Avenue picture onto a Hennepin County lobby.

### Minnesota

In Minnesota, the Compass split puts the Twin Cities at 95.9 percent, while Greater Minnesota is 4.1 percent, which is not zero. Do not copy a Worthington plant-town default from Mexican Minnesota onto this page, and do not assume Minneapolis is every household or that the person in front of you has been to Ecuador.

sections.heading: Labor, Crisis, and Later Streams — Not a Mexican File
sections.body:
If IRCA is a foundational settlement fact of Mexican Minnesota, Ecuadorian Minnesota is not that file. Its streams are labor and family: families from Cuenca in the late 1990s, linked to El Niño storm damage to farming and crafts in southern Ecuador (Northeaster, July 21, 2026); Ss. Cyril and Methodius parish, which became mostly Hispanic from 1997 (Archdiocese of Saint Paul and Minneapolis); a volleyball group playing since 1996 (WCCO, 2024); later family reunification and work; and secondary migration from other states. The 1999–2000 banking crisis (feriado bancario) is national background, an emigration wave toward Spain and the United States.

### Foundational events

The desk in 2026 meets U.S.-born children translating for parents, mixed-status households, a Kichwa household that has been here for years and still cannot get the language in the lobby, and a professional who does not need an interpreter and whose elder does. Compass puts foreign-born at 53.3 percent (ACS 2020–2024), a figure that is dated and is not a personality.

### Who you meet

Enforcement is current structure, so when raids or a visible ICE climate spike, people may skip clinic, school, and waiver meetings, and that is not noncompliance. Dated events touched this community in 2026: an Ecuadorian father and his 5-year-old son were detained in Columbia Heights on Jan. 20 (KSTP, Jan. 22), an ICE agent was blocked from entering the Ecuadorian consulate on Jan. 27 (NBC News), about 800 of 3,400 Columbia Heights students were not attending in person during the surge (Northeaster, Feb. 17), and MinnesotaCare ended for undocumented adults on Jan. 1 (Minnesota House). Do not collect status you do not need, because the desk that asks “are you legal?” on visit one has already chosen a who.

If you only know “immigrant” or only know “Latino,” you will miss the people actually in front of you.

sections.heading: Family
sections.body:
Ask who counts as family and household, because an English form may not have room for them. Compass puts average household size at about 3.92, which is larger than some neighboring spines, but it is not a rule, so ask who should be in the room.

### Who is in the household

Mixed-status is structure: a U.S.-citizen child, a parent without status, a sibling with another path. Do not collect status you do not need, and do not treat unmatched last names, a grandmother as caregiver, or a missing SSN as fraud until you have a reason.

### Who speaks

Familismo is a hypothesis, not a rule. Obligation to kin can mean fierce showing-up, and it can mean a woman who never signs for herself, and both can be true. Hour caps and “natural supports” language can dump unpaid work onto women in that network and call it culture.

Minnesota law still stands: domestic violence is not culture, and you follow mandated reporting while you still see a family. Do not skip the report and call it respeto, and do not use a child as interpreter.

sections.heading: Minnesota and Ecuadorian History
sections.body:
Minnesota holds an Ecuadorian community large enough for a Compass profile — about 19,484 (ACS 2020–2024, plus or minus 3,601) — and large enough that this department will meet it on waivers, child welfare, health care, cash, food, aging, and employment. The Twin Cities hold 95.9 percent, but Greater Minnesota at 4.1 percent is not an afterthought, and it is not a plant-town mash with Mexican Minnesota.

### Places

Think in places rather than a blob, from Twin Cities corridors and first-ring suburbs to scattered Greater Minnesota households, and do not assume Minneapolis or assume the person in front of you has been downtown. Sahan Journal (Nov. 11, 2025) describes the community as concentrated in Northeast Minneapolis and Columbia Heights along Central Avenue. Census counts of Ecuadorian-origin residents for 2020 to 2024 are Minneapolis 6,645, Columbia Heights 1,716 (about 8 percent of the city), Fridley 1,428, Anoka County 3,850 and Ramsey County 866.

### Partners

Partners are the parishes families name and the civic groups this family names. Documented examples include Ss. Cyril and Methodius parish, which its priest said in December 2023 has the largest Ecuadorian congregation; COPAL, whose workers center says most families it serves are Ecuadorian; the Consulate of Ecuador on Central Avenue NE; and Movimiento Comunitario Minnesota. CLUES is a Latino door, not an Ecuadorian community and not Greater Minnesota, and CECLC is a department door rather than the whole, so pay the partner this household actually uses.

Book a qualified interpreter, and pay for community work. Do not assign either to staff because of who they are. Hispanic Heritage Month is not consultation, and while you are a guest, being a guest does not make you the expert.

sections.heading: Ecuadorian — not a Mexican file
sections.body:
To be Ecuadorian in Minnesota is to be placed in a U.S. checkbox that holds Mexican as the default. There is a peoplehood here that the mash deletes — Costa, Sierra, Oriente; Kichwa and other indigenous nations; Afro-Ecuadorian histories; U.S.-born lives — and Spanish is not the people.

### In this state

Mexican Minnesota is the largest Latino origin in this state, and that fact becomes a harm when the building treats Mexican Spanish, Mexican parish, and Mexican food as the Latino default, because an Andean household, a Kichwa household, and an Afro-Ecuadorian household are not variants of Mexico.

In the U.S. racial order, Hispanic is ethnicity, not race. Colorism inside this page is real, and so is indigenous erasure under “they all speak Spanish.” Afro-Ecuadorian people exist, so ask rather than mashing them into historic African American or bleaching them into a mestizo story.

This guide is a working orientation, and because individual variation always supersedes group generalization, you always defer to this family.

sections.heading: Core Concepts
sections.body:
Not Mexican is the first grammar, which means that if you open a Mexican default because the name is Spanish, you do not have a household yet.

### Spanish is not one Spanish

The Andean register (usted) is not coastal, and neither one is Mexican, so book qualified Spanish AND ask.

### Indigenous language as a possible home language

Kichwa and others may be in the home. Compass has no speaker count for Indigenous languages. El Colegio charter school told Sahan Journal in March 2024 that it offers language services and preservation classes for Quichua-speaking students. Because a Spanish interpreter may still not work, name the language on the request.

### Two surnames

Dropping the second surname invents a person who then has to be corrected later.

### Familismo as hypothesis

Ask who should be in the room, and remember that familismo is not a license to skip mandated reporting.

### Enforcement climate

Mixed-status households are real here, so do not collect status you do not need.

sections.heading: Religion
sections.body:
There is a Catholic majority in many streams, though not all, and the parish may be the trusted channel for information, mutual aid, and a room people will enter when they will not enter yours. Evangelical and Pentecostal churches are large in some rooms, and indigenous practice lives here too, which makes it something other than a souvenir.

### Streams

Do not make a priest, a pastor, or a healer the case plan unless this family asked, and do not BCC one parish and call it consultation. Do not treat evangelical growth as the evolved version of Catholic, or indigenous practice as witchcraft.

### Practice

Holy Week, the fiestas families name, and funeral obligation can collide with your calendar, so you still keep medical and legal time, and you name the conflict when it arises.

Help that looks like a report is not help. Religious framing of disability, mental health, or gender can sit next to a fierce wish for services, and you can hold both at once.

sections.heading: Greetings
sections.body:
Wait to see how the person greets you, and follow their lead. Let the other person set any greeting beyond a handshake or nod.

### Titles

Use titles until invited otherwise: Señor, Señora, Don, Doña. Use the last name you were given, and remember there may be two, and do not use a first name with an elder because the form printed it. Usted versus tú is respect in many Andean Spanish rooms, so a qualified interpreter matches the register, and you do not correct it.

### This room

Greet everyone in the room, not only the English speaker.

Let this person’s own greeting guide you, whatever you read on another page.

sections.heading: Naming Conventions
sections.body:
Two surnames is the default in much of Spanish-language naming: apellido paterno, then apellido materno. A U.S. database that keeps one surname invents a person, and because that invented name then follows them through MHCP, child welfare, and school, it is a gate.

### How to file

Ask how to file the name, ask how to say it, and pronounce it, without dropping accents as a joke. Given names may be Spanish, indigenous, English, or both, and some people use a middle given name as the call-name, so ask.

Women may or may not take a husband’s surname in U.S. records, and children may carry two surnames that do not match a parent’s U.S. “last name” field, which is not fraud until you have a reason.

Do not treat unmatched last names in a household as a fraud flag by default, and do not invent a hyphen and then punish the person when the hyphen moves.

sections.heading: Dates of Significance
sections.body:
Hispanic Heritage Month is not Ecuadorian Minnesota, since it is a U.S. poster. Independence falls on 10 August, and Minnesota celebrations are documented: an independence celebration in Columbia Heights in 2017 and EcuaFiesta in Northeast Minneapolis on Aug. 2, 2026. Some families name local fiestas. Día de los Difuntos may be kept in some homes, but no Minnesota observance is confirmed. These are literacy for the desk, and a poster is not language access.

### Calendar

Ask this family, because some families mark national days and some refuse them, and do not put “Latino holiday” on a case note.

Calendar clicks are literacy for scheduling, but they are not community engagement and not a day off the work.

sections.heading: Education
sections.body:
Compass (ACS 2020–2024) reports that among Ecuadorian Minnesotans 25 and older, about 57.7 percent have high school or higher and about 19.8 percent have a bachelor’s or higher. Date Compass, and do not copy Colombian or Lebanese attainment onto this page. About 45.6 percent of the community is age 17 or younger, which makes the IEP a gate rather than a one-hour culture clash.

### School and language

A parent who speaks fluent Spanish, or fluent Kichwa, and limited English is not illiterate. Literacy in any language is not guaranteed, and oral Spanish is not print Spanish. Mixtec is a Mexican door while Kichwa is this one, and a Spanish IEP still will not work if Spanish is not the home language.

Do not use a child as interpreter, because that does harm: it reverses respeto, it leaks adult business, and it is not CLAS. Do not invent a dropout rate on this page.

sections.heading: Etiquette
sections.body:
If food or drink is offered, accepting a little is fine, and you can still keep to medical and legal timelines.

### In the home

Use titles until invited otherwise, and follow the household on shoes. Ask before taking any photograph or touching any religious object, and do not ask anyone to explain their faith or history for your benefit.

### Time

Keep to clinic and court timelines. If someone is late, ask what got in the way, and record only what happened.

Take time to introduce yourself and explain the plan, and still give any required notice. Confirm in the language they use, ask whether they agree with the plan, and do not take a smile as consent.

sections.heading: Language and Communication — the CLAS gate
sections.body:
This is the CLAS Spanish line, and Spanish is not the people. Andean Spanish, coastal Spanish, and Mexican Spanish are not one interpreter accent test, so book a qualified Spanish interpreter AND ask this household, because register matters: usted, not a buddy tú, until the room says otherwise.

### Language

Indigenous languages may be in the home, among them Kichwa and others. Compass does not count speakers of Indigenous languages, so do not invent that count. El Colegio charter school told Sahan Journal in March 2024 that it offers language services and preservation classes for Quichua-speaking students. A Spanish interpreter for those households still will not work, which is why you name the language on the request, and a scarce interpreter is a gate rather than an excuse to proceed in English only without recording the failure.

Compass (ACS 2020–2024) reports that among those 5 and older, 76.8 percent speak a language other than English and 49.1 percent speak English less than “very well,” and the number should be dated. Do not use a child as interpreter, and do not make an Ecuadorian coworker the interpreter.

Give the person time to answer. If you get a short yes, check that the plan was understood, and ask whether it works for them. Do not write “noncompliant” when you mean “did not understand the English exception form.”

sections.heading: Other Considerations
sections.body:
This section states hard facts plainly, because treating everyone the same can hide them.

### Named harms

ICE and the enforcement climate are structure. Mixed-status households may skip clinic, school, and waiver meetings when a relative can be moved, which is not noncompliance, so do not collect status you do not need, and remember that SSN on the first screen is a gate.

Indigenous erasure under “they all speak Spanish” is a named harm, because Kichwa and Shuar are real home languages and a Spanish interpreter may still not work. Colorism is real, and the Mexican default in this state will talk over an Andean household if you let it.

Do not joke about machismo, and do not excuse control as “that’s culture.” Domestic violence is not culture, and you follow mandated reporting while you still see a family.

LGBTQ Ecuadorians exist, so you use the name, and you do not out someone to kin and call it familismo. Hispanic Heritage Month is not consultation.

sections.heading: Health
sections.body:
Compass (ACS 2020–2024) reports about 24.0 percent without health insurance among those for whom status is determined, and poverty at 19.9 percent, and both should be dated. Do not invent a diabetes or “Andean” rate, because the pattern now is that people delay, people use the emergency room as the door, and people skip follow-up when the lobby feels like enforcement.

### Access

Fear of the lobby is a health access fact, which means a badge, a form that asks for SSN, a child called to interpret a diagnosis, or an interpreter who does not speak this Spanish or this indigenous language is a clinical event. When enforcement spikes, people may skip clinic, and that is not noncompliance.

Believe reported pain, and do not skip screening. Do not fold this history into Tuskegee or into a generic “immigrant mistrust” slide. Gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care, so offer it, and do not use a child as interpreter in a health encounter.

sections.heading: LGBTQ
sections.body:
Queer and trans Ecuadorian Minnesotans exist. Conservative parish, evangelical, and family climates can mean silence, exile, or danger, but that is not every family, and you do not get to decide which one this household is from the doorway.

### This person

Use the name they use, and do not share what they tell you unless a rule requires it. Minnesota’s Human Rights Act still applies.

Afro-Ecuadorian and indigenous queer people exist inside this page, so do not mash them into the historic African American LGBTQ chapter, and do not bleach them. Do not question a household about anyone’s sexuality or gender.

sections.heading: Hair, Dress, and Body
sections.body:
There is no Ecuadorian uniform, and the second generation looks like Minnesota. Indigenous dress is public at fiesta and ceremony, but it is not a daily costume, and it is not yours to request for a Heritage Month photo, so do not ask a woman in clinic whether she “still wears the costume.”

### Dress

Colorism and hair texture are real. Afro-Ecuadorian hair is not the CROWN Act chapter copied over, and you still do not touch, still do not police, and still do not treat tightness or looseness as a professionalism problem.

Do not rank piety or indigeneity off clothing; ask the person, with gender match if they want it.

sections.heading: Music
sections.body:
There is not one playlist, since in pasillo, sanjuanito, bomba, Andean, and coastal music, origin and region name the sound. A Mexican default playlist in an Ecuadorian waiting room is the mash in speakers.

### Variation

A festival stage is not engagement, a playlist is not language access, and church music is not staff entertainment.

Knowing that music is public life will not write the waiver, but it will stop you from treating one Heritage Month speaker as the community.

sections.heading: Sports
sections.body:
Fútbol and futsal are common public sports (Liga Northeast was founded in 2005), and the most distinctive sport is ecuavóley: the Minneapolis park board built ecuavóley courts at Audubon Park after consulting the Ecuadorian community, opened in October 2025. School sport is ordinary for the second generation, so do not assume the kid plays, and do not make sport the only excellence you can see.

### Not the whole person

Leagues are social infrastructure, but they are not a substitute for language access on a waiver, and they are not consultation.

World Cup loyalties are not a risk score and should never be read as one.

sections.heading: Literature
sections.body:
Spanish-language literature is world literature, and indigenous oral literature — Kichwa and others — is older than the Spanish file and is not “no letters.” That fact does not mean the person in the lobby can read your form, in English or in Spanish, because literacy in any language is not guaranteed.

### Literacy in the lobby

You do not need to quote a novel in the lobby, but you do need to know that this is not a people without letters, and not a people who can all read the exception process.

Print Spanish from Spain, Mexico, or a translation produced by software is not automatically this household’s Spanish, and CLAS is qualified language, not Google and not a child.

sections.heading: Art
sections.body:
Textiles, indigenous weaving, and coastal and Andean visual work are all part of the picture. Otavalo is public culture some families name, but it is not consultation and not a mascot for the unit’s Heritage Month table.

### Guest

Be a guest rather than a researcher, which means you do not photograph an altar because it is pretty, and you remember that a market visit is not a case plan.

A Heritage Month that mashes this with Mexican papel picado has already mashed the adjacent peoples.

sections.heading: Crisis, Labor, Enforcement, and the State
sections.body:
There is no single Civil Rights Movement to copy onto this page, because the political literacy here is stacked: labor and family migration, including families from Cuenca in the late 1990s; the 1999–2000 banking crisis as national background; later work streams; and U.S. enforcement that reorganizes Tuesday. Indigenous erasure under Spanish is a named harm.

### The badge

When enforcement spikes, people may skip clinic, school, and waiver meetings, and a DHS badge is not automatically help, which is not paranoia but pattern. Do not use a crisis or a raid as a personality, and do not ask a person to narrate crossing for your professional development.

Do not collect status you do not need, since SSN on the first screen is a gate. Mandated reporting still exists, and so does the duty not to treat a whole people as a deportation score.

sections.heading: Work, Markets, and Government
sections.body:
Work spans service, construction, restaurants, cleaning, childcare, a professional second generation, and public employment. Compass puts median household income at $59,501 (2024 dollars) and poverty at 19.9 percent, but these are averages rather than this kitchen table, and a small-business owner and a waiver recipient may be the same household.

### Work

Parishes may be the trusted channel, so name the local one rather than assuming CLUES reaches this family. Take time to introduce yourself and explain the plan, and still give any required notice.

### Staff

Book a qualified interpreter, and pay for community work. Do not assign either to staff because of who they are.

Some people send money to relatives in Ecuador as an obligation. Ask about it, and do not treat it as optional in a budget.

sections.heading: Health-care and Human-service Encounters
sections.body:
Language here includes indigenous languages, so book qualified Spanish AND ask, and confirm Kichwa, Shuar, or another language when that is the home language, because a Spanish interpreter may still not work. Do not use a child as interpreter, and do not make staff the interpreter.

### Language

Ask who is in the room, offer gender match in maternal and intimate care if they want it, use titles, and remember the two surnames. If you do not need an SSN on the first screen, do not ask for it. With mixed-status households, do not collect status you do not need, because in this enforcement climate skipped appointments are pattern. Uninsured 24.0 percent is dated Compass, not a personality.

### The meeting

Believe reported pain, and do not skip screening. Mandated reporting still exists, and help-seeking that becomes a report is part of why people wait, so you follow the law while you still see a family.

sections.heading: Adjacent Peoples — Do Not Mash
sections.body:
This people is not Mexican. Mexican Minnesota is the largest Latino origin in this state, and it becomes a Minnesota harm when it is the only file. This people is also not Colombian as a synonym, not a Peruvian mash, and not “the Andes” as one interpreter.

### Adjacent doors

This people is not “Spanish” as indigenous, because Kichwa and Shuar are not dialects of Spanish, and a Spanish interpreter is not those languages.

This people is not Somali, and not historic African American. Afro-Ecuadorian people exist, so ask rather than mashing them into the African American CI because both are Black, and do not bleach them into a mestizo Latino blob. Open the people CI that matches this household, and never rely on one Latino module.

sections.heading: Counts, Dated
sections.body:
Minnesota Compass, ACS 2020–2024, for the Ecuadorian cultural community: about 19,484 people (plus or minus 3,601); Twin Cities 95.9%; Greater Minnesota 4.1%; age 17 or younger 45.6%; 65+ 2.1%; foreign-born 53.3%; language other than English (age 5+) 76.8%; English less than “very well” 49.1%; English only 23.2%; high school or higher (25+) 57.7%; bachelor’s or higher 19.8%; median household income $59,501 (2024 dollars, plus or minus $12,718); poverty 19.9% (plus or minus 10.3); owner-occupied 64.8%; average household size 3.92; uninsured 24.0%. The Census Bureau's Hispanic-origin table counts 15,993 (plus or minus 1,980) Ecuadorian-origin Minnesotans for 2020 to 2024 and 17,722 (plus or minus 4,752) for 2024 alone, and 9,676 Minnesotans were born in Ecuador, second only to Mexico among Latin American birthplaces. Date whichever count you cite.

### Counts

Indigenous languages may be in the home. Compass does not count speakers of Indigenous languages, so do not invent that count. El Colegio charter school told Sahan Journal in March 2024 that it offers language services and preservation classes for Quichua-speaking students. Date Compass, and do not copy Mexican, Colombian, or Cuban numbers onto this page.

### What the count is not

A young age structure is not a personality, and poverty at 19.9 percent is not the professional second generation and not a crime score. Language and child-as-interpreter are gates, and a rate is not the person.

sections.heading: Doors and Sources
sections.body:
Start with the Minnesota Compass Ecuadorian profile (ACS 2020–2024). CLUES — Comunidades Latinas Unidas En Servicio — is a Latino door, not this people and not the whole state, so add the parishes and civic groups this family names, and remember that CECLC is a department door rather than the community.

### Public doors

CLAS Spanish is on the five, and since Spanish is not one Spanish, open an indigenous-language request when Spanish is the wrong door. Open /ci/latino as the umbrella, and open this brief for an Ecuadorian household.

### Where to learn more

Use these resources yourself before you ask an Ecuadorian colleague to explain, and do not count a BCC to CLUES as consultation. Pay partners and report back, because Hispanic Heritage Month is not the work.

sections.heading: How it hits DHS gates — the 40%
sections.body:
Workplace culture and service delivery are both candidates for where these gates take hold.

Language: CLAS Spanish is not one Spanish, and Andean and coastal Spanish are not a Mexican interpreter accent test. Kichwa, Shuar, and other indigenous languages may be in the home, so a Spanish interpreter may still not work, and literacy in any language is not guaranteed. A child as interpreter does harm, and gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care.

Names: there are two surnames, so the database that keeps one invents a person, and unmatched last names are not fraud by default.

SSN on the first screen, hour caps, exception processes, and life-sharing matches without language are not culturally neutral. Mixed-status households may bounce if the first field feels like enforcement, which is why you do not collect status you do not need.

Child welfare and disability: 45.6 percent age 17 or younger is a desk fact, and help-seeking that becomes a report is part of why people wait. Mandated reporting still exists, and so does the duty not to treat a whole people as a risk score. Domestic violence is not culture, and you follow the law.

Enforcement climate: people may skip clinic, school, and waiver meetings when a relative can be moved, and that is not noncompliance.

Notices and comment: do not count an eList and an English PDF as reaching this community, and record who was reached and what follow-up happened.

Workforce: Ecuadorian staff are not the interpreter pool, not the indigenous-language pool, and not the community. Staff are colleagues, not the curriculum, and you do not treat them as the curriculum.

The Mexican default is a gate, so disaggregate, or you have invented a people.

Legislation, funding, and rule: study a channel before you advocate for it. Use this page so that the 40% has a household in it.

sections.heading: A Note on This Guide
sections.body:
This brief covers Ethiopian Minnesota as Minnesota Compass treats it, which is as an umbrella count rather than as one people, because Oromo, Amhara, Tigrayan, Gurage, Sidama, Anuak, and other peoples all sit inside that count and they do not belong in one file. The practical consequence is to let the household tell you which brief to open. If the household is Oromo, open Oromo Minnesota and book Afaan Oromoo, and if Amharic is the home language, open Amharic-speaking Minnesota. If the family is Tigrayan, book Tigrinya, because Tigrinya is not Amharic. If they name Somali ancestry, open Somali Minnesota, since Compass already counts respondents born in Ethiopia who list Somali ancestry as Somali rather than Ethiopian.

### Who this is

Minnesota Compass (ACS 2020–2024) puts Ethiopian Minnesota near 45,159 people (plus or minus 5,404; Compass's 2024-only total is 53,754, plus or minus 12,826), with about 89.7 percent living in the Twin Cities and about 10.3 percent in Greater Minnesota. The age structure is young: about 43.8 percent are age 17 or younger, while about 3.5 percent are 65 or older, and about 59.8 percent are foreign-born. Among those age 5 and older, 76.2 percent speak a language other than English, and 30.2 percent speak English less than “very well.” Date the number whenever you use it, and keep in mind that the Census recodes some people who write Oromo into Ethiopian, which produces an overcount of a state name and an undercount of a people. These numbers are useful as dated umbrella context, but they are not a personality.

### Who this is not

This community is not Somali, because a shared Horn of Africa is not a shared culture. It is also not historic African American, since shared race in the United States is not shared culture either. Use this page for context and questions. It does not describe the person in front of you.

### How to read this

The diversity inside the umbrella is the whole point. Consider an Amhara Orthodox grandmother who fasts more days than the clinic has slots, an Oromo evangelical household that does not want Amharic, a Tigrayan family living the 2020–2022 war through kin, a Muslim Ethiopian household, and a U.S.-born student who uses English with friends and another language with an elder. All of them share a Compass row, and none of them share a Tuesday.

Always defer to the person in front of you, because this page is a hypothesis that you still have to test with this particular family.

sections.heading: Origins — an Umbrella, Not a People
sections.body:
Ethiopia is a state made up of many nations, and that fact shapes everything else in this brief. Oromo peoplehood — Oromummaa — is a Cushitic nation of the Horn, the largest by language, and one with no Oromo nation-state. Amhara highland peoplehood and Amharic as a written language are both older than 1974, while Tigrayan peoplehood sits on both sides of a later border with Eritrea, and Gurage, Sidama, Anuak, and other peoples live in Minnesota as well. A 2008 estimate by Akway Cham, head of the Anywaa Community Association in North America, put Anuak Minnesotans at 2,500 to 3,000, the largest group thought to live outside Africa. The right move is simply to ask which people they are and then to resist lecturing on a taxonomy they did not ask for.

### History for the meeting

Imperial history, Orthodox Tewahedo, Islam, and a federal working language that is not everyone’s first language together organized a state that was not a European colony in the way neighboring files were. That fact is part of your literacy as a worker, but it is not a rank you give the family, and it is never a reason to skip language access.

### What people brought

What people brought with them is substantial: many languages; Orthodox fasting alongside Protestant and Muslim streams and Waaqeffanna; kin obligation; injera as ordinary food in many rooms; and a memory of empire, of a state that won and a state that lost. What they met in Minnesota was narrower: an English form, one “Ethiopian” checkbox, one “East African” interpreter, and often Somali, because the building already had that page.

Origins did not begin in 1974, although 1974 is the foundational political event for much of the first wave you will meet. Knowing that is for your own orientation rather than a speech you give the family.

sections.heading: The Geography of the Ethiopian World
sections.body:
The homeland is not one ethnic map, since Oromia, the Amhara region, Tigray, the south, Addis Ababa, and a Somali region that Compass has already carved out of this count are all distinct places with distinct meanings. Do not draw one Ethiopia on a case note, and do not assume Addis as an identity, because many Oromo people name Oromia, a region, a village, or a lineage — not the capital of the state that ruled them.

### Homeland

The diaspora is global: Washington D.C. is a large U.S. hub, and Los Angeles, Dallas, Toronto, the Gulf, and Italy all hold communities. Minnesota is a real community in its own right, but it is not the U.S. capital of this diaspora, and secondary migration, along with church and mosque networks, is what pulled people here.

### Minnesota

Within Minnesota, Compass places 89.7 percent of this community in the Twin Cities, which includes Minneapolis parishes and the inner-ring suburbs, while Greater Minnesota — including Worthington, where Ethiopian Orthodox life is public — holds 10.3 percent. Do not assume Cedar-Riverside, because that hub is primarily Somali, although the International Institute of Minnesota's guide (last updated January 2017) names Seward and Cedar-Riverside as the Minneapolis neighborhoods with the largest Ethiopian populations, and no current neighborhood count settles it, so ask where this particular family lives, and do not assume the person in front of you has ever been to Ethiopia.

sections.heading: 1974, the Derg, Famine, and Later Streams — Foundational Events
sections.body:
If 1991 is Somali Minnesota’s foundational political event, then 1974 and what followed is the foundational event for much of this Compass row’s first wave. It helps to hold two things at once: it is not the only stream of migration, and it is not one people’s story.

### Foundational events

The revolution overthrew Haile Selassie, and the Derg and the Red Terror killed and scattered people. The 1980s famine and resettlement brought some of the first African refugees whom Minnesota named as Ethiopian; the state’s own telling has Minnesota admitting refugees from Ethiopia from 1982, while others came through Sudan, Kenya, or Europe. In 1991 the Derg ended and another politics opened, and family reunification and later diversity streams followed. Unrest in the 2010s–2020s sent another Oromo wave, and the 2020–2022 war in Tigray remains current structure for some households today. Fighting resumed on Sept. 22, 2026 in Tigray, Amhara and Afar after clashes and airstrikes since August (Human Rights Watch), and on Oct. 15, 2026 Al Jazeera reported that Ethiopian and allied forces had entered Aksum and that the TPLF had withdrawn from Mekelle, with Ethiopia and Eritrea accusing each other.

### Who you meet

Do not referee this history or pick a side as DHS, even though intra-Ethiopian tension in Minnesota rooms is real. If a family names it, listen rather than filing it as a risk score.

The desk in 2026 also meets U.S.-born children who speak English with their peers, who are still translating for their families, and who still cannot get Afaan Oromoo, Amharic, or Tigrinya in a lobby that offered Somali or “Ethiopian.” If the only picture you carry is “Ethiopian refugee,” you will miss this household.

sections.heading: Family
sections.body:
Family may be larger than a nuclear English form can hold. Ask who should speak first, and hear from the person directly. Godparent and kin ties matter, adult children may appear in the same week as a waiver meeting, and a grandmother may be the childcare. Compass reports an average household size of 3.30, which is an umbrella figure, dated, and still not Mary Jones.

### Who is in the household

The person who cares for a disabled adult or a child may be a son, a daughter-in-law, or a sibling rather than the legally recognized caregiver on the checkbox. Be aware that hour caps and “natural supports” language can dump unpaid work onto the women in that network and then call it culture.

### Who speaks

Naming already tells you something about who is who, since a name is often a given name plus the father’s name, with no surname at all, and Oromo names are not Amharic names. Do not invent a last name because the screen requires one, and do not assume three Somali names.

The person who speaks in the lobby may be the child with the best English, but that child is not the qualified interpreter, and CLAS still stands. Ask who should be in the room, and remember that Minnesota law still stands as well, so do not skip mandated reporting and call it humility.

sections.heading: Minnesota and Ethiopian History
sections.body:
Minnesota holds an Ethiopian Compass community large enough that this department will meet it on waivers, child welfare, health care, cash, food, aging, and employment. It is also large enough that the building has developed a long habit of hearing “East African” and booking Somali. Compass puts the community at about 45,159 (ACS 2020–2024, plus or minus 5,404), with Greater Minnesota at 10.3 percent, so do not write this umbrella as a Minneapolis anecdote.

### Places

Think in places rather than in a blob. There are Minneapolis parishes, Debre Selam Medhanealem Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church among them, and there are the inner-ring suburbs, as well as Worthington and other Greater Minnesota towns where Orthodox liturgy is public. There is also Little Oromia, the community naming for Oromo Twin Cities life (MNHS), so open the Oromo CI for that map, and remember that Cedar-Riverside is not the default.

### Partners

Partners include the Orthodox parishes families name; Protestant congregations, including Oromo evangelical churches; and the mosques families name, including Tawfiq for some Oromo households. Ethiopian Community in Minnesota has been a historical local door, as has Oromo Community of Minnesota, so pay the door this household actually uses. The SOS Amharic voter tools are proof that the state already knew one of these languages, and CECLC is a department door, not the whole.

Book a qualified interpreter, and pay for community work. Do not assign either to staff because of who they are. A Timkat or Irreecha visit is optional professional development if you are invited, but you are a guest there, and attending does not make you the expert.

sections.heading: An umbrella is not a people
sections.body:
To be filed as Ethiopian in Minnesota is sometimes to be Amhara, sometimes Oromo, sometimes Tigrayan, and sometimes another nation the Compass row cannot see at all. A state name is not peoplehood, Oromummaa is not the empire, and highland Orthodox life is not the mosque, which is why your role is not to pick a side.

### In this state

In this building, another fact sits on top of all that: many of these households are Black in a U.S. racial order that will file them under Somali or under historic African American, and in doing so get the language, the church, and the name wrong. Shared race is not shared culture, and shared Horn geography is not shared language.

Ask plainly whether the person agrees with the plan, and make it easy to say no.

This guide is a working orientation, and because individual variation always supersedes group generalization, always defer to the person in front of you.

sections.heading: Core Concepts
sections.body:
The first question is which people: Oromo, Amhara, Tigrayan, or another. Ask, because the Compass row is not the answer.

### Which language

The second question is which language: Afaan Oromoo, Amharic, Tigrinya, or another. An “Ethiopian interpreter” is often an Amharic interpreter, which will not work for many Oromo and Tigrayan households, while a Somali interpreter is the wrong door altogether.

### Names

A name is usually a given name plus the father’s name, so do not invent a last name, and remember that Oromo names are not Amharic names, and they are not three Somali names.

### Faith is plural

Faith here may be Orthodox Tewahedo, Protestant, Islam, Waaqeffanna, or none, so follow this room and treat fasting as a matter of operations rather than folklore.

Do not assume Addis, do not referee intra-Ethiopian politics in a waiver meeting, and do not pick a side as DHS.

### Work and school

Ask who in the family works, studies, or helps, and do not assume from a rate.

sections.heading: Religion
sections.body:
Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo is central for many Amhara households and for some others, while Protestant streams, including Oromo evangelical churches, are ordinary. Islam lives in Oromo rooms, in some other Ethiopian rooms, and in adjacent Horn rooms; Waaqeffanna lives in some Oromo rooms; and having no religion — none at all — is also an ordinary Tuesday. Ask rather than assuming Muslim the way you might with a Somali file, and do not assume Orthodox as if “Ethiopian” were one mash.

### Streams

Ge’ez is a liturgical language, not the interview language, and Arabic may be the language of religion rather than the language of the interview, so for a legal notice, book the language this elder actually uses.

### Practice

For many Orthodox households, fasting calendars are operations: Wednesday, Friday, Lent, Advent, and other seasons. That touches medication with food, labs, and morning appointments, so ask about feast days before you schedule.

Do not make a priest, a debtera, a pastor, or an imam the case plan unless this family asked for that, and do not BCC one parish and call it consultation. Funerals gather family, and you still keep medical and legal time when they do. Do not photograph an iconostasis.

sections.heading: Greetings
sections.body:
Ask who to greet first, or follow the household’s lead. In some Amharic rooms, Ato, Weizero, or Weizerit is the honorific, and you use it until you are invited not to. Shoulder bumps and cheek kisses are common in some rooms, so follow this room.

### Titles

As-salāmu ʿalaykum is not the default: in a Christian Oromo or Amhara room it already shuts the person out, while in a Muslim room it may be perfectly ordinary, and an English “hello” is ordinary in the second generation.

### This room

Wait to see whether a hand is offered, and if it is not, nod.

Let this person’s own greeting guide you, whatever you read on another page. Ask before any physical contact, and let the person set the limit.

sections.heading: Naming Conventions
sections.body:
A name is often a given name plus the father’s name, and sometimes the grandfather’s, so there is no family surname of the kind the database wants. It is the same trap as with Somali names, but a different grammar and different people. Do not invent a last name because the screen requires one, because that invented name becomes a gate that follows the person through MHCP, school, and child welfare.

### How to file

Oromo names are not Amharic names, and you should not assume three Somali names, while the honorifics Ato and Weizero in some Amharic rooms are not decoration.

Ask how to say the name, ask how to file it, and then pronounce it. Women may or may not take a husband’s name in U.S. records, so mother and child may not match, which is not fraud until you have a reason to think so.

Do not joke about names, and do not collect a clan or ethnic list as an icebreaker.

sections.heading: Dates of Significance
sections.body:
Enkutatash is the Ethiopian New Year, falling in September on the Gregorian calendar, and Timkat and Meskel follow, along with Orthodox Christmas (Gena, January 7) and Easter on the Orthodox calendar. Fasting seasons change appointments and medication, so schedule around them when you can, although a calendar click is not community engagement.

### Calendar

Irreecha is the Oromo thanksgiving and new-year gathering, held in autumn in homeland practice and marked in the diaspora, including Minnesota. If this household is Oromo, that date is theirs, so do not put it on an Amhara file as color, and be a guest if you are invited.

Ramadan and Eid matter in Muslim rooms. Some families name political commemorations — 1974, 1991, Tigray, the Oromo protest years — and some refuse to, so do not collect them as a risk score, and do not referee.

Do not write “Ethiopian holiday” or “African holiday” on a case note, and do not put Somali dates on this page by default; ask this family instead.

sections.heading: Education
sections.body:
Compass (ACS 2020–2024) reports that among those 25 and older in the Ethiopian umbrella, about 79.5 percent have a high school education or higher and about 24.1 percent have a bachelor’s or higher, so date Compass when you use it. About 59.8 percent of the community is foreign-born, while a large share of children are U.S.-born and in English-dominant schools, and the IEP still has to reach the parent who does not read it.

### School and language

A parent who reads fidel, Qubee, or Tigrinya and has limited English is not illiterate. Confirm the home language, because an Oromo parent has been handed the wrong form if you only brought Amharic, and a Tigrayan elder has been handed the wrong form if you booked “Ethiopian.”

Second-generation educational mobility is real. So is a gap that a room treating everyone the same will call “culture,” when it is really language access plus a school that never learned the name. Do not treat a college student as proof that the waiver household needs no interpreter, since the child is not the interpreter.

sections.heading: Etiquette
sections.body:
If you visit a home, look for shoes by the door or ask what the household prefers. If food or drink is offered and the family is not fasting, accepting a little is fine, and you can still keep to medical and legal timelines.

### In the home

Ask before taking any photograph or touching any religious object, and do not ask anyone to explain their faith or history for your benefit.

### Time

If someone misses an appointment, first check the time, transport, interpreter work schedule and fasting calendar. Confirm the plan in the language the person uses, and ask whether it works for them.

Book a qualified interpreter instead of using a child to go between.

sections.heading: Language and Communication
sections.body:
Book the language this household names. Amharic is a Semitic language written in fidel, while Afaan Oromoo is Cushitic, and its varieties include Borana, Guji, Wollo, and others, so confirm which one. Tigrinya is not Amharic. An interpreter labeled Ethiopian who speaks Amharic often will not work, a Somali interpreter is the wrong door, and Arabic may be the language of religion rather than of the interview.

### Language

Compass reports that among those 5 and older, about 76.2 percent speak a language other than English and about 30.2 percent speak English less than “very well,” although those are umbrella figures, and they are dated. Many elders read a home script while some do not, and second-generation English is common, but the IEP still has to reach the parent.

Give the person time to answer. If you get a short yes, check that the plan was understood, and ask whether it works for them.

Do not use a child as the interpreter, and do not make an Ethiopian-identified coworker the interpreter.

sections.heading: Other Considerations
sections.body:
This section states hard facts plainly, because treating everyone the same can hide them.

### Named harms

Intra-Ethiopian tension in Minnesota rooms is real, among Oromo, Amhara, and Tigrayan people and over the state’s name itself. Do not pick a side as DHS, do not referee in a waiver meeting, and do not file politics as a risk score. The 2020–2022 war in Tigray is current structure for some households, and fighting resumed in September 2026, so if they name it, listen.

FGC exists in some Horn communities, and Minnesota law stands, but this is not the Somali page, so do not invent an Ethiopian rate, and do not mash Somali prevalence onto this household. Follow mandated reporting, and still see a family.

Colorism and highland/lowland hierarchy sit in some rooms. You do not fix them as if they were a personality, and you do not ignore them when they become a gate.

Queer and trans Ethiopian Minnesotans exist, so you use the name, and you do not out someone to kin and call it culture, while you also do not skip mandated reporting and call it humility.

Enforcement climate is structure for some households, so do not collect status you do not need, and do not treat fear as noncompliance. Staff who share this community may add facts, but they do not get to delete a fact because it is hard to say.

sections.heading: Health
sections.body:
Believe reported pain, and do not fold this history into Tuskegee or into a Somali MDH slide, because this is not the Somali page and not the historic African American page.

### Access

Hepatitis B screening for people born in Ethiopia is a U.S. public-health pattern; CDC has treated Ethiopia as a higher-prevalence birth country in its screening guidance. Date the CDC page you cite, do not invent a Minnesota rate, and do not skip screening because the person looks well.

Compass reports disability at 5.5 percent, an umbrella figure that is dated. Fasting and medication interact, so ask before you write noncompliance. Mental-health stigma is real in some families, and war trauma, depression, and somatic presentation exist, which is why a smile is not a PHQ-9.

No dated Ethiopian-specific Minnesota autism rate belongs on this page, so do not invent one, and do not mash MDH Somali findings onto this umbrella. Gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care, so offer it. On FGC, Minnesota law stands, which means you do not invent a rate and you do not skip care. Traditional medicine often sits beside biomedicine, so ask and work it out together, and do not skip a child-protection duty when the facts are the facts.

sections.heading: LGBTQ
sections.body:
Queer and trans Ethiopian Minnesotans exist — Oromo, Amhara, Tigrayan, and others. Conservative family, parish, church, and mosque climates can mean silence or exile, and some people live a public English life and a private home-language life. You use the name they use and do not share what they tell you unless a rule requires it.

### This person

Minnesota’s Human Rights Act still applies. Use the name the person uses, and do not share what they tell you unless a rule requires it. Do not question a household about anyone’s sexuality or gender, and take seriously that some people have reason to keep it private.

Intra-Ethiopian politics do not override what this person wants, so always defer to the person in front of you.

sections.heading: Hair, Dress, and Body
sections.body:
The Orthodox white netela and gabi are public at church, at Timkat, and at some weddings, but they are not a daily uniform, and the second generation looks like Minnesota. Do not ask a woman in clinic whether she “still wears the shawl.”

### Dress

Some Muslim women wear hijab and modest dress, and some do not, so do not assume covering, and do not rank covering as either piety or oppression.

This is not the CROWN Act chapter, and yet anti-Blackness still sits on Black Ethiopian bodies in U.S. clinics and schools, so ask this person. Do not mash historic African American hair politics onto them as a script, and do not ignore those politics either. Do not touch, do not police covering, and ask the woman, with gender match if she wants it.

sections.heading: Music
sections.body:
The musical landscape includes Orthodox chant in Ge’ez, kebero drums, eskista as public dance in some rooms, diaspora pop, Protestant worship music, Oromo geerarsa and qeerroo-generation music, and Islamic nasheed in some rooms. That is named variation, not a playlist, and because intra-community politics can sit inside a song, you do not put the wrong flag on a speaker.

### Variation

Liturgy is not staff entertainment, and neither is a funeral, while a playlist is not engagement.

Do not request a political song as an icebreaker in a waiver meeting, since intra-community politics can sit inside a song.

sections.heading: Sports
sections.body:
Distance running is a public image of Ethiopia, but it is not a personality, not a compliment you give a child in clinic, and not a file. Soccer shows up in public life, and school sport is ordinary for the second generation.

### Not the whole person

Do not assume the kid runs or that the kid plays, and do not make sport the only excellence you are able to see.

Sport clubs are social infrastructure for some, but they are not language access, and they are not a case plan. Greater Minnesota teams are still part of this umbrella when the family lives there.

sections.heading: Literature
sections.body:
Ge’ez and Amharic made an old written public, and Qubee in the 1990s made a mass written Afaan Oromoo public possible, which is political history rather than trivia. Tigrinya has its own script, and oral forms sit beside all of these. Minnesota and U.S. Ethiopian, Oromo, and Tigrayan writers and journalists exist, although you do not need to quote a novel in the lobby.

### Literacy in the lobby

What you do need to know is that this umbrella is not a people without letters, and that it is not one literature. An elder who does not read the script you brought, or English, is not a person without language.

A notice that exists only in English will not work, and so is a notice in Amharic that the Oromo elder cannot read, so ask, and write what they tell you.

sections.heading: Art
sections.body:
Orthodox iconography, textile, and church architecture are an Amhara and Tigrayan stream; they are not the same as Oromo art, and they are not the whole Compass row. Oromo dress, oral art, and contemporary work are a different door, so open the Oromo CI for them. Injera and the coffee ceremony are foodway in many rooms, not consultation.

### Guest

Be a guest, not a researcher, because a Timkat procession or an Irreecha gathering is optional professional development rather than consultation, and do not photograph an altar.

A Heritage Month that mashes this community with a Somali poster, a historic African American exhibit, or one Ethiopian flag for every Horn household has already mashed the adjacent peoples.

sections.heading: State Violence, War, and Intra-Community Politics
sections.body:
Imperial incorporation, 1974, the Red Terror, the Derg, the 1980s famine, 1991, the Oromo Liberation struggle as literacy for the desk rather than a speech, unrest in the 2010s–2020s, and the 2020–2022 war in Tigray — together, that is the political event. Do not referee it in a waiver meeting, and do not pick a side as DHS, because intra-Ethiopian tension in Minnesota rooms is real.

### The badge

A DHS badge is not automatically help. Do not use 1974 or Tigray as a personality, and do not ask a person to narrate prison, famine, or killing for your professional development.

Enforcement climate in the United States is a different state, and it still keeps some people away, since it changes who opens the door, who signs, and who will not put a relative’s name on a form. That is not noncompliance, so do not collect status you do not need, and do not collect political speech as a risk score.

sections.heading: Work, Markets, and Government
sections.body:
Work in this community spans restaurants, parking, care work, factories, a professional second generation, and public employment. Compass reports a median household income of $63,667 (2024 dollars), poverty at 10.9 percent, and renters at 64.4 percent, all umbrella figures and all dated, and a rate is not the person. Markets and injera houses are both economy and culture, but a food-court visit is not consultation.

### Work

Book a qualified interpreter, and pay for community work. Do not assign either to staff because of who they are. Oromo staff are not the Amharic pool.

### Staff

Take time to introduce yourself and explain the plan, and still give any required notice. Pay the partner this household names.

sections.heading: Health-care and Human-service Encounters
sections.body:
Which people and which language are the first thing to get right, because an interpreter labeled Ethiopian, Somali, or Oromo who does not speak the language this household speaks will not work. Confirm Amharic, Afaan Oromoo (and its variety), or Tigrinya as the family names it, and still book a qualified interpreter, rather than using a child or making staff the interpreter.

### Language

Family-name order is the wrong frame, because often there is no family name. Other things shape the encounter too: who is in the room, fasting versus the appointment, pain you must believe, intra-community tension in the waiting room, deportation climate, and a nuclear form that invented a last name.

### The meeting

Offer gender match, ask who should hear, and ask how to file the name. If they name traditional medicine, listen, while remembering that mandated reporting still exists. Believe reported pain, and do not mash Tuskegee or the Somali CI into this history.

sections.heading: Adjacent Peoples — Do Not Mash
sections.body:
This Compass row is an umbrella, so open Oromo Minnesota for Oromo households and open Amharic-speaking Minnesota when Amharic is the home language. Book Tigrinya for Tigrayan households, because Tigrinya is not Amharic. Open Somali Minnesota for Somali ancestry, including people born in Ethiopia, since Compass already counts them as Somali, not Ethiopian. Eritrean households are not this file by default, because Tigrinya may be shared, but the state is not.

### Adjacent doors

This community is not historic African American, not Liberian, not Kenyan, and not Nigerian. There is never one Black module, never one East African interpreter, and never one Ethiopian module.

Some households are mixed, so ask this household. A shared Orthodox calendar is not shared politics, shared Islam is not shared culture, and shared Horn geography is not shared language.

sections.heading: Counts, Dated
sections.body:
Minnesota Compass, ACS 2020–2024, Ethiopian cultural community — an umbrella, not one people — reports about 45,159 people (plus or minus 5,404; the 2024-only total is 53,754, plus or minus 12,826), of whom 89.7% live in the Twin Cities and 10.3% in Greater Minnesota. Those age 17 or younger make up 43.8%, those 65+ make up 3.5%, and the foreign-born share is 59.8%. Among those age 5 and older, 76.2% speak a language other than English, and 30.2% speak English less than “very well.” Among those 25 and older, 79.5% have a high school education or higher and 24.1% a bachelor’s or higher. Median household income is $63,667 (2024 dollars), and poverty is 10.9%. Housing is 35.6% owner-occupied and 64.4% renter-occupied, with an average household size of 3.30, and disability is 5.5%.

### Counts

Compass counts respondents born in Ethiopia who list Somali ancestry as Somali, not Ethiopian, and the Census recodes some Oromo write-ins as Ethiopian, so date the method. This is not an Oromo census and not a count of Amharic speakers, and you should not invent a midpoint.

### What the count is not

A young age structure is not a personality, and an owner rate is not proof the gates closed, since language and child-as-interpreter are gates. A rate is not the person, so date Compass, and do not invent other rates.

sections.heading: Doors and Sources
sections.body:
Start with the Minnesota Compass Ethiopian profile (ACS 2020–2024) and the Compass cultural-communities methodology, which explains the Oromo recode and the carve-out of Somali ancestry. Open the Oromo CI and the Amharic-speaking CI, because they are the people-pages this umbrella points to. The CLAS fifteen interpreter cards include Amharic, so book Afaan Oromoo or Tigrinya as named, and the Minnesota Secretary of State Amharic voter tools are another source.

### Public doors

Public doors include the Orthodox parishes families name, Debre Selam Medhanealem among them. Debre Selam opened a new building at 2601 30th Ave. S. in Seward, with an open house on April 18, 2026, at a cost of nearly $11 million including land; its old home at 4401 Minnehaha Ave. dates from 1999. Ethiopian Community in Minnesota has been a historical local door, as has Oromo Community of Minnesota, along with the churches and mosques this family names, while CECLC is a door, not the whole community.

### Where to learn more

Use these resources yourself before you ask an Ethiopian-identified colleague to explain, and do not count a BCC to a parish as consultation. Pay partners, and report back. Be a guest at Timkat or Irreecha if invited, remembering that it is not consultation.

sections.heading: How it hits DHS gates — the 40%
sections.body:
Workplace culture and service delivery are both candidates here.

On language: an interpreter labeled Ethiopian who speaks Amharic often will not work for Oromo and Tigrayan households, and a Somali interpreter is the wrong door.
