Confirm the home language and the variety, and still book a qualified interpreter rather than using a child, and know that gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care.

On names: the pattern is a given name plus the father’s name, so a database that invents a last name, or that assumes three Somali names, is a gate that follows the person.

On fasting: Wednesday, Friday, Lent, Advent, and other seasons matter for many Orthodox households, and that touches medication with food, labs, and morning appointments. Ask about feast days before you schedule.

Hour caps, exception processes, and life-sharing matches without language are not culturally neutral.

On child welfare and disability: help-seeking that becomes a report is part of why people wait. Mandated reporting still exists, and so does the duty not to treat a whole umbrella as a risk score. On FGC, Minnesota law stands, but this is not the Somali page, and you do not invent a rate.

On intra-Ethiopian politics: do not pick a side, and do not referee the Tigray war in a waiver meeting.

On deportation climate: people may skip clinic, school, and waiver meetings when a relative can be moved, and that is not noncompliance, so do not collect status you do not need. Temporary Protected Status for Ethiopia was terminated by a notice of Dec. 15, 2025; a court stay was lifted, and Fragomen reports that benefits ended Aug. 18, 2026 while a constitutional challenge continues.

On notices and comment: do not count an eList and an English PDF as reaching this community, and record who was reached and what follow-up happened. Greater Minnesota is 10.3 percent, so a Minneapolis meeting is not the whole channel, and SOS already prints Amharic for voters, which means the packet can print the language this household reads.

On workforce: Ethiopian-identified staff are not the interpreter pool and not the community; staff are colleagues, not the curriculum, so do not treat them as anything else.

On the Somali mash and the Black mash: opening Somali because of the Horn, or historic African American because both are Black, shuts the person out.

On legislation, funding, and rule: study a channel before you advocate for it. Use this page so that the 40% has a household in it.

sections.heading: A Note on This Guide
sections.body:
This brief is about Filipino people as a people of the Philippines — Luzon, Visayas, Mindanao, many languages — and as a Minnesota community that Compass counts near 26,559 (ACS 2020–2024, plus or minus 2,422). This is not Chinese, it is not Hmong, and it is not Vietnamese, because the colonial history here is Spanish and then United States, not a China mash, and a shared continent is not a shared culture. A full mosaic of a people is not a stereotype; a stereotype is what happens when this page becomes the person in the lobby.

### Who this is

Tagalog / Filipino is a language, but it is not the only language, since Cebuano and others live in this state. English is official in the Philippines, and that fact can be used to skip the 10.8 percent who are LEP, which is the gate. Book THIS language, because an interpreter labeled Asian will not work.

### Who this is not

Minnesota Compass (ACS 2020–2024) describes the community this way: about 26,559 people (plus or minus 2,422), with 71.0 percent in the Twin Cities and 29.0 percent in Greater Minnesota. Other official counts differ widely: 28,388 in the 2024 one-year survey (State Demographic Center presentation, June 2026) and 11,800 for people coded only as Filipino in 2019 to 2023 (Economic Status of Minnesotans 2026). The count depends on whether people of mixed heritage are included. About 28.4 percent are age 17 or younger and about 6.5 percent are 65+, while foreign-born is 41.6 percent. Among those 5 and older, about 58.3 percent speak English only, about 41.7 percent speak a language other than English, and about 10.8 percent speak English less than “very well.” Among those 25 and older, about 93.2 percent have high school or higher and about 52.2 percent have a bachelor’s or higher. Median household income is about $99,593 in 2024 dollars, poverty is 8.2 percent, owner-occupied housing is 57.6 percent, average household size is about 2.72, and about 23.9 percent of individuals live alone. The community is about 59.3 percent female, and whatever number you use, date it.

The diversity inside this people is the point, so consider a U.S.-trained nurse in a Greater Minnesota hospital, a Tagalog-speaking lola who does not read the English IEP, a Cebuano household, a Catholic parish household, a U.S.-born student, and a person who left during martial law and still will not talk about it in a lobby. They share a Compass row, but they do not share a Tuesday.

### How to read this

Always defer to the person in front of you, because this page is a hypothesis that you still have to test on this family.

sections.heading: Origins and the Founding of a People
sections.body:
Filipino peoplehood is older than Magellan, older than 1898, and older than the nursing file. It holds many ethnolinguistic peoples — Tagalog, Cebuano, Ilocano, Kapampangan, Waray, Bikol, and others — inside a modern republic named after a Spanish king. That sentence is literacy for the desk rather than a lecture you give a parent who came in for a waiver.

### History for the meeting

Spanish colonial rule, Catholic mission, and then the 1898 war in which the United States took the islands from Spain and fought a Philippine republic — that is the colonial stack. It is not a China mash, and it is not the Latino CI just because the surnames are Spanish. 4 July 1946 independence is a date, while 12 June is the date many Filipino Americans mark, so ask rather than assume, and do not turn it into a speech.

### What people brought

Baybayin is history, and ordinary public literacy now is Latin script in Tagalog / Filipino, English, and regional languages. Many elders read Tagalog, some do not, and the second generation may not read it at all, which is why English being official in the sending country is not a license to skip the parent who still cannot run the IEP.

What people brought with them was a language that may not be Tagalog; Catholic or another faith, or none; family obligation; English as a school language; foodways; and a memory of occupation and of a state. What they met in Minnesota was an English form, one “Asian” checkbox, and often an assumption that English official means you can skip the interpreter.

sections.heading: The Geography of the Filipino World
sections.body:
The Philippines is Luzon, the Visayas, Mindanao, and more than seven thousand islands, so Manila is not the map, and language shifts across it. Muslim Mindanao is a named geography that some families will name and some will not, and you do not referee; if they name a place, listen.

### Homeland

The diaspora is global and labor-shaped, reaching the United States, Canada, the Gulf, Hong Kong, Singapore, and Europe. Overseas Filipino Worker is a sending-country category, not a personality. California (1.6 million), Hawaii (310,000), Texas (220,000), Florida (180,000), and Nevada (180,000) hold the largest U.S. Filipino populations (Pew Research Center), and Minnesota is a present one.

### Minnesota

Compass puts about 71.0 percent of the community in the Twin Cities and 29.0 percent in Greater Minnesota, so Greater Minnesota towns, first-ring suburbs, and Minneapolis–Saint Paul are all on this page, and Greater Minnesota is not an afterthought. Do not assume they have been to Manila, because a nurse in a southern Minnesota hospital is still this people.

sections.heading: 1898, 1965, and the Nursing Pipeline — Foundational Events
sections.body:
The sequence runs from Spanish colonial rule, to the 1898 U.S. war and occupation, to the Commonwealth, to independence in 1946. U.S. Navy enlistment, bases, and pension streams moved people, and Hart-Celler (1965) opened skilled and family immigration. The U.S. nursing and health-care pipeline is a documented Filipino labor pattern, but it is work; it is not a personality, not a joke, and not the whole community.

### Foundational events

Martial law under Ferdinand Marcos (declared 1972) and the 1986 People Power / EDSA uprising are literacy for the desk rather than a speech you give the family or an icebreaker. Later streams brought family reunification, students, and ordinary immigration, and the desk in 2026 meets U.S.-born children who still cannot get Tagalog for a lola.

### Who you meet

If the only word you know is “nurse,” you will miss the elder who needs an interpreter, the Greater Minnesota household far from a parish that speaks the language, and the person whose English is excellent and whose parent’s is not.

Martial-law years and later streams do not share a Tuesday. Compass puts foreign-born at 41.6 percent, which means a large second generation was born here, and they are still this people, and so is the lola, so do not skip the page because the nurse in the room sounds like Minnesota.

sections.heading: Family
sections.body:
Utang na loob — a debt of gratitude — and bayanihan — mutual aid — are hypotheses in scholarship and in some households. They are not a waiver design, and they are not an excuse to dump remittance, elder care, and a second job onto a daughter.

### Who is in the household

Ask who should speak first, and hear from the person directly. Lola and lolo are ordinary words. Compass puts the average household size at about 2.72, and while multi-generation households exist, so do people who live alone (about 23.9 percent), so ask who should be in the room.

### Who speaks

The person who speaks in the lobby may be the child with the best English, but that child is not the qualified interpreter, and using a child as the go-between does harm, so book the interpreter.

Minnesota law still stands, so do not skip mandated reporting and call it humility. The person who holds the child’s medical decision may not match the English form, which is another reason to ask.

sections.heading: Minnesota and Filipino History
sections.body:
This department will meet this community on waivers, child welfare, health care, cash, food, aging, and employment. Compass counts about 26,559 (ACS 2020–2024, plus or minus 2,422), with 71.0 percent in the Twin Cities, and Greater Minnesota, at 29.0 percent, is not an afterthought.

### Places

The Catholic parishes that families name are civic hubs for some, carrying language, jobs, a funeral, a fiesta, but they are not “the community.” Not every family belongs to a parish, so do not send a person to a parish as programming.

### Partners

The Filipino American associations this person names are partners, so name the local one, and pay the door this household actually uses. Documented Minnesota groups include the Fil-Minnesotan Association (formed in 1953, with its Philippine Center in Maplewood), the Cultural Society of Filipino Americans (1972), the Filipino Catholic Community of Minnesota (1995), and the Philippine Study Group of Minnesota, which is behind the corrective plaque at the Capitol (2002). The chair of the Hennepin County Board and Sarah Lancaster, daughter of a Filipino immigrant mother and the 2022 Minnesota Teacher of the Year, are visible in public life. Book a qualified interpreter, and pay for community work. Do not assign either to staff because of who they are. A grocery or a fiesta is public life rather than consultation, and you are a guest if you go.

Book a qualified interpreter, and pay for community work. Do not assign either to staff because of who they are. A nurse on the unit is not unpaid interpretation and not “the Filipino community,” and with Greater Minnesota at 29.0 percent, a St. Paul fiesta is not the whole channel.

sections.heading: Kapwa — not a China mash, not a Latino mash
sections.body:
To be Filipino in Minnesota is often to be filed under a checkbox that also holds Chinese, Hmong, and Vietnamese histories this household does not share — and then to be asked, in the same week, whether the Spanish surname means Mexican, as if Santos were a Latino file, or whether they “speak Asian.”

### In this state

Kapwa — a shared personhood some people name — is a hypothesis, not an icebreaker. Ask plainly whether the person agrees with the plan, and make it easy to say no.

Do not use the model-minority story, because English official in the Philippines and 52.2 percent bachelor’s can be used to skip 10.8 percent LEP, 8.2 percent poverty, disability, and the lola who does not read the IEP.

This guide is a working orientation, and individual variation always supersedes group generalization.

sections.heading: Core Concepts
sections.body:
Start with language. Tagalog / Filipino is not the only language, since Cebuano and others are here, and English official in the Philippines is not “no LEP,” so book THIS language.

### Name

Spanish surnames are Filipino history rather than a Latino file, so ask how to file.

### Colonial stack

The stack is Spanish and then U.S., not a China mash, and 1898 is literacy, not a speech.

### Family obligation, utang na loob, bayanihan

These are hypotheses, and they are not a staffing plan for unpaid daughters.

### Parish

A Catholic majority in the sending country is not this household, so do not make a priest the case plan unless they asked.

### Model-minority

Do not use the model-minority story, because it hides LEP elders, 8.2 percent poverty, and Greater Minnesota isolation.

sections.heading: Religion
sections.body:
Catholic Christianity is the large public stream in the sending country, which is literacy rather than a Minnesota rate you invent. Nationally, about three-quarters of Filipino Americans are Christian, mostly Catholic (Pew Research Center), and no Minnesota survey exists, so ask, and do not assume a parish, and do not assume no parish.

### Streams

The parish is a center of ritual, mutual aid, and information for some families, but it is not “the community.” Do not BCC one priest and call it consultation, and do not make clergy the case plan unless this family asked.

### Practice

Holy Week and Christmas gather family, and while you still keep medical and legal time, you name the conflict instead of punishing it.

Do not treat folk practice or a home altar as a contradiction you need to fix, and do not treat Catholicism as “less Filipino” than a costume on a stage.

sections.heading: Greetings
sections.body:
Ask who to greet first, or follow the household’s lead. Mano — taking an elder’s hand to the forehead — is ordinary in some rooms, while a handshake is ordinary in many professional rooms and in much of the second generation, so follow the person’s lead.

### Titles

Po and opo mark respect in Tagalog, and you do not need to perform them; you need to book an interpreter who can. English “hello” plus the name is ordinary, so say the name.

### This room

Let this person’s own greeting guide you, whatever you read on another page.

Ask before any physical contact, and let the person set the limit.

sections.heading: Naming Conventions
sections.body:
Spanish surnames are Filipino history: Santos, Cruz, Reyes, Garcia, Ramos, de la Cruz, Mendoza. They are not a Latino file, so do not run a Mexican or Puerto Rican script because the last name looks Spanish, and do not mash with the Latino CI; open that CI when the household is that household.

### How to file

Multiple given names and a mother’s family name in Philippine records can collide with a U.S. form that wants one first name and one last, which means the same person can appear as Maria Santos, Maria Cruz Santos, and Maria C. Santos. That is a system failure, not a fraud signal until you have a reason.

Ask how to file and how to say it, because nicknames are ordinary, and do not treat unmatched names as fraud. Women may or may not take a husband’s name in U.S. records, so mother and child may not match.

sections.heading: Dates of Significance
sections.body:
Christmas and Holy Week are large in many Catholic rooms, bringing travel, food, elders, and closed shops, so schedule around them when you can. They are not a day off the work, and a calendar click is not community engagement.

### Calendar

12 June is Philippine Independence Day (from Spain, declared 1898; the date many Filipino Americans mark), and 4 July 1946 is the U.S. recognition date, both of which are literacy, not a party on a case note. People Power / EDSA, February 1986, is literacy as well, not a speech.

Parish fiestas and hometown associations may not be on your state calendar, though Minnesota has recurring public Filipino events (Philippine Day since 1987 or 1988, Simbang Gabi, Pasko sa Nayon, Paskong Pilipino), and hometown groups such as Negrenses del Oriental have received support from the Cultural Society of Filipino Americans, so ask. Do not put “Asian holiday” on a case note, and do not mash with Chinese New Year, Hmong New Year, or Tết.

sections.heading: Education
sections.body:
Compass (ACS 2020–2024) reports that among Filipino Minnesotans 25 and older, about 93.2 percent have high school or higher and about 52.2 percent have a bachelor’s or higher. Among those 5 and older, about 58.3 percent speak English only and LEP is about 10.8 percent, while foreign-born is about 41.6 percent, and you should date Compass when you cite it.

### School and language

English is official in the Philippines, and that sentence can be used to skip the interpreter, but 10.8 percent LEP is not zero. An English IEP still closes the door for the parent who reads Tagalog and limited English, and that parent is not illiterate.

Ask what this teenager wants. A nursing degree in the family is not this teenager, and it is not proof the waiver household needs no interpreter. Education pressure in some streams is a hypothesis rather than an excuse to skip mental-health screening.

sections.heading: Etiquette
sections.body:
If food or drink is offered, accepting a little is fine, and you can still keep to medical and legal timelines. If you visit a home, look for shoes by the door or ask what the household prefers.

### In the home

Ask whether the person agrees, and confirm it in the language they use. Make it easy to say no in private.

### Time

Ask before taking any photograph or touching any religious object, and do not ask anyone to explain their faith or history for your benefit. Book a qualified interpreter instead of using a child to go between.

If someone misses an appointment, first check the time, transport, interpreter and work schedule. Confirm the plan in the language the person uses, and ask whether it works for them.

sections.heading: Language and Communication
sections.body:
Tagalog / Filipino is not the only language, since Cebuano (Bisaya) and others live in this Compass row, so book THIS language. An interpreter labeled Asian, or Tagalog for a Cebuano elder, may still not work, though you still book a qualified interpreter.

### Language

Compass puts language other than English at about 41.7 percent and LEP at about 10.8 percent (age 5+), and you should date it, because English official in the Philippines is not a skip. New arrivals and elders are inside that 10.8 percent, and the English-dominant second generation is inside the 58.3 percent English-only and still on this page.

Give the person time to answer. If you get a short yes, check that the plan was understood, and ask whether it works for them. Do not make a Filipino coworker the interpreter, and do not make a nurse coworker the interpreter as the culture.

Do not use a child as the interpreter.

sections.heading: Other Considerations
sections.body:
This section states hard facts plainly, because treating everyone the same can hide them.

### Named harms

Do not use the model-minority story, because English official and 52.2 percent bachelor’s can be used to skip 10.8 percent LEP, 8.2 percent poverty, disability, and the lola who does not read the IEP.

U.S. colonial amnesia is a building problem. 1898 and occupation are literacy, not a speech, and they are a reason a government badge is not automatically help.

Remittance labor is work, not a personality. Martial-law memory still sits in some rooms, so you do not icebreak with it, and you do not put it on a case note as color.

LGBTQ Filipino Minnesotans exist, and undocumented and visa-overstay households exist, so do not collect status you do not need, and do not treat fear as noncompliance. Do not skip mandated reporting and call it humility. Staff who share this community may add facts, but they do not get to delete a fact because it is hard to say.

sections.heading: Health
sections.body:
Believe reported pain, and do not fold this people into a generic Asian slide, since nursing as a community labor pattern does not mean this person is fine.

### Access

Do not invent a Minnesota diabetes, heart, or suicide rate, and if you cite a CDC page, date it. Do not skip screening because the person is a nurse or English-dominant.

Mental-health stigma is real in some families, and naming a counselor is not the same as a family accepting one, while a smile is not a PHQ-9. Gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care, so offer it.

Hilot, herbs, and parish prayer often sit beside biomedicine, so ask and work it out together. Do not mock, and do not skip a child-protection duty when the facts are the facts. A Filipino nurse on staff is not the interpreter and not the culture unit.

sections.heading: LGBTQ
sections.body:
Queer and trans Filipino Minnesotans exist, and conservative parish climates can mean silence or exile. Bakla and trans people are not a joke, not entertainment, and not a file you invent from a TV clip, so you use the name they use and do not share what they tell you unless a rule requires it.

### This person

Minnesota’s Human Rights Act still applies. Use the name the person uses, and do not share what they tell you unless a rule requires it.

Do not assume a Catholic household is not affirming, and do not assume a secular household is; ask this person.

sections.heading: Hair, Dress, and Body
sections.body:
Barong tagalog and terno are public at weddings, independence stages, and some parish events, but they are not a daily uniform, and the second generation looks like Minnesota, so do not ask a woman in clinic whether she “still wears the costume.”

### Dress

For hair and head, follow this person, and do not touch.

Do not mash a barong with a qipao, an áo dài, or a kimono on the unit’s Heritage Month table, because Spanish-colonial dress history is not a Latino mash and not a China mash.

sections.heading: Music
sections.body:
Parish music is ordinary in Catholic streams, and karaoke is social life in some rooms, while kundiman, pop, and none at all are also here, so there is not one soundtrack.

### Variation

A playlist is not engagement, and karaoke is not consultation, so do not ask a staff person or a client to perform.

A funeral is not staff entertainment, and fiesta stages are public life, not a case plan.

sections.heading: Sports
sections.body:
Basketball is public culture for some Filipino households, but it is not the case plan and not this teenager. School sport is ordinary for the second generation, but do not assume the kid plays.

### Not the whole person

Sport clubs are not language access, because an elder in the stands who needs Tagalog still needs Tagalog, and 10.8 percent LEP is not a skip because the child plays varsity.

A Saturday tournament does not replace an interpreter on Monday.

sections.heading: Literature
sections.body:
Letters here are in Tagalog / Filipino, English, a Spanish colonial archive, and regional languages, so this is not a people without letters, though you do not need to quote a novel in the lobby.

### Literacy in the lobby

Literacy in Tagalog is not guaranteed for every generation, which means a Tagalog notice may still not work and an English notice may still not work, so ask which language they read.

Do not put a proverb on a brochure and call it language access.

sections.heading: Art
sections.body:
Parish fiesta, weaving, diaspora visual work, and the public culture of groceries and independence stages are all here, but a foodway is not consultation.

### Guest

You are a guest rather than a researcher, and a grocery visit is not a case plan. A museum visit is optional professional development rather than consultation.

A Heritage Month that mashes this people with Hmong paj ntaub or a Chinese lion dance has already mashed the adjacent peoples.

sections.heading: Occupation, Martial Law, and the State
sections.body:
Spanish colonial rule, the 1898 U.S. war and occupation, WWII, independence, Marcos martial law, U.S. bases, and a labor-export nursing pipeline — that is the political file, and it is why a DHS badge is not automatically help.

### The badge

Do not use 1898 or martial law as a personality, and do not ask a person to narrate occupation, a base, or a riot for your professional development. Do not collect immigration status you do not need, and do not treat fear as noncompliance.

Filing this household as Chinese, as Hmong, as Vietnamese, or as Latino because the surname is Spanish is a state act, and it shuts the person out.

sections.heading: Work, Parishes, and Government
sections.body:
Work here spans health-care labor, nursing, small business, a professional second generation, and public employment. Median household income of about $99,593 (Compass, 2024 dollars) is an average, and poverty at 8.2 percent sits in the same row. Female at about 59.3 percent in this Compass row is not a personality and not a reason to skip the man in the lobby.

### Work

Book a qualified interpreter, and pay for community work. Do not assign either to staff because of who they are.

### Staff

Take time to introduce yourself and explain the plan, and still give any required notice.

sections.heading: Health-care and Human-service Encounters
sections.body:
Several things arrive together in these encounters: Tagalog / Filipino or Cebuano or Ilocano on the line — not “Asian”; the English-official skip; a Spanish surname the form files as Latino; a child pushed forward as the English speaker; a priest in the story; pain you must believe; and a nurse coworker used as culture.

### Language

Ask the language and ask how to say the name, and offer gender match. Believe reported pain, and do not skip screening. Do not make staff the interpreter, and do not use a child, while remembering that mandated reporting still exists.

### The meeting

A smile is not consent, and 10.8 percent LEP is not a rounding error, so do not mash this encounter with a Chinese or Vietnamese interpreter.

sections.heading: Adjacent Peoples — Do Not Mash
sections.body:
This people is not Chinese, not Hmong, not Vietnamese, not Korean, not Japanese, and not Thai, and “Asian American” is not the file, because the colonial history is Spanish and U.S., not a China mash. Open those CIs for those households, and open this one for a Filipino household.

### Adjacent doors

It is not Latino because the surname is Santos, Cruz, or Reyes, so open the Latino CI when the household is that household, since Filipino Spanish-colonial history is not a Mexican file.

Some households are mixed, so ask this household. Never one Asian module, and never one “Asian” interpreter.

sections.heading: Counts, Dated
sections.body:
Minnesota Compass (ACS 2020–2024) describes the Filipino cultural community this way. The count is about 26,559 (plus or minus 2,422), with 71.0% in the Twin Cities and 29.0% in Greater Minnesota, and about 28.4% are age 17 or younger and about 6.5% are 65+. Foreign-born is 41.6%, and among those age 5 and older, 58.3% speak English only, 41.7% speak a language other than English, and 10.8% speak English less than “very well.” Among those 25 and older, 93.2% have high school or higher and 52.2% have a bachelor’s or higher. Median household income is about $99,593 (2024 dollars), poverty is 8.2%, owner-occupied housing is 57.6%, average household size is 2.72, and 23.9 percent of individuals live alone, while the community is about 59.3 percent female.

### Counts

Date Compass and do not invent other rates, and because counts disagree across ACS vintages and definitions, date the number you cite.

### What the count is not

An 10.8 percent LEP rate is not zero, and a 8.2 percent poverty rate is not zero. Greater Minnesota at 29.0 percent is not an afterthought, and English official in the Philippines is not a skip. A rate is not the person.

sections.heading: Doors and Sources
sections.body:
Start with the Minnesota Compass Filipino profile (ACS 2020–2024). Then turn to the Catholic parishes this person names and the Filipino American associations this person names, paying the door this person names rather than assigning a parish.

### Public doors

CECLC is a door, not the whole community. Use these resources yourself before you ask a Filipino colleague or a nurse colleague to explain. Do not count an eList and an English PDF as reaching an LEP elder. Book Tagalog / Filipino, Cebuano, Ilocano, or the language they name.

### Where to learn more

Be a guest at a fiesta if invited, knowing that it is not consultation.

sections.heading: How it hits DHS gates — the 40%
sections.body:
Workplace culture and service delivery are both candidates here.

Language comes first: 10.8 percent LEP is not “no language gate,” and English official in the Philippines is not a skip. An elder who needs Tagalog or Cebuano and gets English, or “Asian,” is not being served. Gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care, and you do not use a child.

Names come next: Spanish surnames are Filipino history, and the database that files Santos as Latino, or flattens three given names, is a gate.

Hour caps, exception processes, and life-sharing matches without this household’s language are not culturally neutral, and an English IEP is still a gate for that parent.

On model-minority, 93.2 percent high school and 52.2 percent bachelor’s can be used to skip LEP, 8.2 percent poverty, disability, and the lola.

On notices and comment, do not count an eList and an English PDF as reaching an LEP elder, and record who was reached and what follow-up happened. Greater Minnesota is 29.0 percent, so a Minneapolis meeting is not the whole channel.

On workforce, Filipino staff are not the interpreter pool, and a nurse is not the culture unit, and neither is the community.

On the Asian mash, opening Chinese or Hmong or Vietnamese because the checkbox says Asian shuts the person out, and a Latino mix-up on a Spanish surname shuts the person out as well.

On legislation, funding, and rule, study a channel before you advocate for it. Use this page so that the 40% has a household in it.

sections.heading: A Note on This Guide
sections.body:
This brief is about Guatemalan Minnesota as a people — guatemalteco, guatemalteca — and as Maya nations living inside a republic, so it is neither a brief about a Mexican variant nor a brief about the Latino / Hispanic umbrella. K’iche’ and Mam are documented in Minnesota, and other Mayan languages may also be spoken here, which means a Spanish interpreter may still not work for the family in front of you. This community is not Mexican, not Salvadoran, and not Puerto Rican, because a shared Spanish language is not a shared culture. What follows is meant to be a full mosaic rather than a stereotype, and the difference between the two is simple: a stereotype is what happens when this page becomes the person in the lobby.

### Who this is

Open the Latino umbrella brief only as an adjacent door, since that page covers the mash and the CLAS Spanish line while this page is Guatemalan. If you file the household under “Latino” or under Mexican because that is the Minnesota default, you have left this door, and the household has lost what it offers.

### Who this is not

Minnesota Compass (ACS 2020–2024) puts the Guatemalan cultural community at 17,306 people, of whom 49.1 percent live in the Twin Cities and 50.9 percent live in Greater Minnesota — about half, give or take 7.9 points. About 46.1 percent are age 17 or younger, and because Compass suppresses the 65+ figure in this vintage, please do not invent it. The community is 43.7 percent foreign-born, and among those age 5 and older, 60.2 percent speak a language other than English and 34.3 percent speak English less than “very well,” so whatever number you use, date it. Compass does not count K’iche’ or Mam speakers, and that count should not be invented either, because a rate describes a population and is never the person.

The diversity inside this people is the point of the brief, not a footnote to it. Consider a K’iche’-speaking mother in a plant town who does not use Spanish as a home language, a Mam-speaking parent, a ladino Spanish-speaking professional in the Cities, a U.S.-born child in an English school, an evangelical grandmother, and a person who left the highlands in the 1980s and still will not open the door to a badge. They share a passport word, but they do not share a Tuesday.

### How to read this

Always defer to the person in front of you, because this page is a hypothesis that you still test on this family.

sections.heading: Origins and the Founding of a People
sections.body:
Guatemalan peoplehood is not a Mexican origin story with different mountains, because the Maya nations — K’iche’, Mam, Q’eqchi’, Kaqchikel, and others — are older than the Spanish colony and older than the republic. That republic is Spanish-language and ladino-dominated, and it has both claimed those nations and hunted them. Minnesota’s community includes Maya households and ladino Spanish-speaking households, and since the only way to know which you are meeting is to ask, there is no need to lecture a Willmar family about a taxonomy they did not ask for.

### History for the meeting

Spanish colonial rule, Catholic mission, independence alongside the other Central American republics (15 September 1821), a nineteenth- and twentieth-century plantation state, and the civil war that followed — this is literacy for the desk. It is background that helps you understand the room rather than a speech you give the family, which is why a meeting should not start with a huipil, a volcano postcard, or a Heritage Month sentence.

### What people brought

Writing in Spanish is the state’s public literacy, but Mayan languages are languages in their own right, not dialects of Spanish. Some people read Spanish and some do not, and some U.S.-born adults do not read Spanish either. Oral skill is not the same as print literacy, and some Maya literacy is oral and carried in a language the building has never put on an interpreter line.

What people brought with them includes language (Spanish varieties and Mayan languages), kinship, costumbre and later the evangelical church, farm skill, a memory of a state that used them, and a memory of villages that were emptied. What they met in Minnesota was an English form, one “Latino” checkbox, often one interpreter labeled Spanish, and a plant town that had not studied Mam.

sections.heading: The Geography of the Guatemalan World
sections.body:
The homeland is not one flag on a classroom map, since there are highlands, coast, and Petén, and there is K’iche’ country, Mam country, and Q’eqchi’ country — geographies that do not match the republic’s departments as the person in the lobby may name them. If someone names a place, confirm it with them and listen, rather than refereeing Quetzaltenango versus San Marcos in a waiver meeting.

### Homeland

The Guatemalan map in the United States includes California, and it also includes the Upper Midwest plant and dairy belt that a Minneapolis default still treats as leftover. Compass puts 49.1 percent of the community in the Twin Cities and 50.9 percent in Greater Minnesota — about half, give or take 7.9 points — so Worthington, Willmar, Austin, Fairmont, St. James, and the dairy counties are names you should be able to hold in mind without turning them into a tour.

### Minnesota

Metro pockets exist, but they are not the whole picture, so do not assume Minneapolis, and do not assume the person in front of you has been to Guatemala. A Greater Minnesota household is still this people, and when place is the gate, open the rural literacy brief beside this page.

sections.heading: War, Maya Flight, and Plant Towns — Foundational Event
sections.body:
If IRCA-era settlement is a foundational stack for Mexican Minnesota, then the Guatemalan civil war (1960–1996) and the 1980s scorched-earth campaigns against Maya communities are the foundational political event for much of Guatemalan Minnesota. Knowing this is literacy for the desk rather than a speech you give the family or an icebreaker, which means you should never ask a person to narrate massacre for your professional development.

### Foundational events

Later streams of migration carry gang and state violence, family reunification, and ordinary work migration into food processing and dairy. Plant and dairy towns in southern and western Minnesota built households that a Twin Cities default will miss, and since about half of Guatemalan Minnesota lives in Greater Minnesota, that is not a metro leftover.

### Who you meet

The desk in 2026 does not only meet a 1980s arrival; it meets U.S.-born children translating for their parents, mixed-status households, and a Mam speaker who has been in a plant town for years and still cannot get Mam in the lobby. If the only category you know is “immigrant,” you will miss them, and if the only category you know is “Mexican labor,” you will mash them.

Enforcement is current structure, not history. When raids or rumored raids spike, people may skip clinic, school, and waiver meetings, and that is not noncompliance, which is one more reason not to collect status you do not need.

sections.heading: Family
sections.body:
Ask who counts as family and household, because an English form may not have room for them. Compass puts the average household size at about 3.52, and elders, in-laws, adult children, padrinos, and cousins may all be part of the household. Because the person who cares for the child may not match the waiver checkbox, ask who should be in the room.

### Who is in the household

Mixed status is structure in some households, so do not collect status you do not need, and do not treat unmatched last names, a grandmother as caregiver, or a missing SSN as fraud until you have a reason. Be aware that hour caps and “natural supports” language can dump unpaid work onto the women in that network and then call it culture.

### Who speaks

The person who speaks in the lobby may be a child with the best English — or the only Spanish — and that child is not the qualified interpreter. If the home language is K’iche’ or Mam, a Spanish-speaking child cannot interpret for them, and CLAS still stands. Using a child as the go-between is a harm, because it reverses respeto, it leaks adult business, and it is not language access.

Minnesota law still stands as well: domestic violence is not culture, so do not skip mandated reporting and call it humility.

sections.heading: Minnesota and Guatemalan History
sections.body:
Minnesota holds a Guatemalan community large enough that this department will meet it on waivers, child welfare, health care, cash, food, aging, and employment — and about half of that community lives in Greater Minnesota. Compass counts 17,306 people (ACS 2020–2024), with 50.9 percent in Greater Minnesota, so do not write this people as a Minneapolis anecdote.

### Places

Think in places rather than a blob: plant and dairy towns in southern and western Minnesota; Worthington, Willmar, Austin, Fairmont, St. James; metro pockets. Markets are public life, but they are not consultation, and a food visit does not make you the expert.

### Partners

Partners include rural parishes and community organizations, so name the local one rather than assuming Minneapolis, since CLUES has offices in St. Paul, Minneapolis, Willmar and Austin, although a metro office may still not reach every rural county. Churches may be the actual safe channel, and CECLC is a department door rather than the whole community, so pay the partner this household actually uses.

Book a qualified interpreter, and pay for community work. Do not assign either to staff because of who they are. A fiesta visit is optional professional development if you are invited, and you go as a guest, since attending does not make you the expert.

sections.heading: Guatemalteco / Maya — the heart of a people
sections.body:
Forms in Minnesota often default a Guatemalan person to Mexican, and the person may be Maya. Ask how the person identifies. Ask plainly whether the person agrees with the plan, and make it easy to say no.

### In this state

The Mexican default in this state is a count fact on another page, but on this page it is a harm, because it is what happens when staff copy Guadalupe, norteño, and “Mexican Spanish” onto a Maya household.

In the United States another fact sits on the same desk: Hispanic is an ethnicity, not a race. Maya people are indigenous, and colorism and ladino hierarchy are real, so do not bleach this household into a mestizo Latino story.

This guide is a working orientation, and because individual variation always supersedes group generalization, you always defer to the person in front of you.

sections.heading: Core Concepts
sections.body:
Mayan languages come first among these concepts. K’iche’, Mam, Q’eqchi’, and others are languages, not dialects of Spanish, which is why a Spanish interpreter may still not work. Compass does not count their speakers, so ask the family and name the language on the interpreter request.

### Traje and huipil

Traje and huipil are public at fiesta and ceremony in some rooms, but they are not a daily uniform, and they are not yours to request for Heritage Month, which is also why you should not rank anyone’s indigeneity off their clothing.

### Costumbre

Costumbre is Maya practice that lives beside the Catholic and evangelical church. Treat it as a hypothesis rather than a case plan, and do not make an ajq’ij, a priest, or a pastor the plan unless this family asked for that.

### War memory

War is part of the history many families here carry. Do not use it as an icebreaker, and do not assume it about the person in the lobby.

### Familismo and two surnames

Familismo and two surnames are hypotheses you still test with each household, and it helps to remember that a database that keeps only one surname invents a person.

### Plant-town settlement

Greater Minnesota holds 50.9 percent of this community, and a St. Paul meeting will not reach those counties.

sections.heading: Religion
sections.body:
Catholic parish life is well documented among Guatemalan Minnesotans, especially in Worthington. Evangelical and Pentecostal churches may also matter to some households, and Maya costumbre may be part of some homes, where it is not a souvenir. The parish or the iglesia may be the trusted channel for information, mutual aid, and a room people will enter when they will not enter yours. Our Lady of Guadalupe is Mexican Catholic literacy, so rather than installing it as the default on this page, ask.

### Streams

Do not make a priest, a pastor, or a traditional practitioner the case plan unless this family asked, and do not BCC one church and call it consultation. Do not treat evangelical growth as the evolved version of Catholic practice, and do not treat Maya practice as witchcraft.

### Practice

Holy Week, funerals, and fiesta obligations can collide with your calendar, and while you still keep medical and legal time, you name the conflict instead of punishing it. Do not photograph an altar or traje as a souvenir.

Help that looks like a report is not help. Religious framing of disability, mental health, or gender can sit right next to a fierce wish for services, and you can hold both at once.

sections.heading: Greetings
sections.body:
Ask who to greet first, or follow the household’s lead. Wait to see how the person greets you, and follow their lead.

### Titles

Use titles until you are invited to do otherwise — Señor, Señora, Don, Doña — and use the last name you were given, remembering that there may be two. Do not use a first name with an elder simply because the form printed it. In Spanish, usted versus tú marks respect, and a qualified interpreter matches that register; in a Maya-language room, the interpreter matches that register as well, and you do not correct it.

### This room

Let this person’s own greeting guide you, whatever you read on another page. Ask before any physical contact, and let the person set the limit.

sections.heading: Naming Conventions
sections.body:
Two surnames is the default in much of Spanish-language naming: the apellido paterno followed by the apellido materno. A United States database that keeps only one surname invents a person, and that invented name then follows them through MHCP, child welfare, and school, which makes it a gate.

### How to file

Ask how to file the name and ask how to say it, then pronounce it. Given names may be Spanish, Maya, English, or both, and some people use a middle given name as the call-name, so ask rather than guess, and do not anglicize a name as a convenience.

Women may or may not take a husband’s surname in United States records, and children may carry two surnames that do not match a parent’s “last name” field on a United States form, which is not fraud until you have a reason to think so.

Do not treat unmatched last names in a household as a fraud flag by default, and do not invent a hyphen and then punish the person when the hyphen moves.

sections.heading: Dates of Significance
sections.body:
15 September is independence day, shared with the other Central American republics, and that is literacy for the desk. It is not Mexican 16 September, and it is not Cinco de Mayo, so do not put a restaurant calendar on a case note.

### Calendar

Holy Week is large in many Catholic streams, while funerals and fiesta days will not appear on your state calendar, so ask. Maya calendar dates (Cholq’ij and related observances) may matter to some families, so ask this family about them rather than inventing them as universal, and do not put “Maya holiday” on a file as color.

Hispanic Heritage Month is the umbrella calendar, not this people’s day, and it is not consultation. A calendar click is literacy for scheduling rather than community engagement, and it is not a day off the work, so do not put “Latino holiday” on a case note.

sections.heading: Education
sections.body:
Compass (ACS 2020–2024) reports that among Guatemalan Minnesotans 25 and older, about 61.6 percent have a high school education or higher and about 15.1 percent have a bachelor’s degree or higher, so date Compass when you cite it. About 43.7 percent of the community is foreign-born, while a large share of children are U.S.-born and in English-dominant schools, which means the IEP still has to reach the parent who does not read it.

### School and language

A parent who speaks fluent K’iche’ or Mam and limited English — or limited Spanish — is not illiterate. A Spanish IEP is not a Maya-language IEP, and the English-only form is the gate, so do not use a child as the interpreter.

Second-generation educational mobility is real. So is a gap that a room that treats everyone the same will call “culture” when it is actually language access plus poverty plus enforcement fear plus a school that never learned the second surname, so do not treat a college student in the family as proof that the waiver household needs no interpreter.

sections.heading: Etiquette
sections.body:
Ask who to greet first, or follow the household’s lead. If food or drink is offered, accepting a little is fine, and you can still keep to medical and legal timelines.

### In the home

Ask before taking any photograph or touching any religious object, and do not ask anyone to explain their faith or history for your benefit.

### Time

If someone misses an appointment, first check the time, transport, interpreter and plant shift or other work schedule. Confirm the plan in the language the person uses, and ask whether it works for them.

Book a qualified interpreter instead of using a child to go between — Spanish if that is the language, K’iche’ or Mam if that is the language.

sections.heading: Language and Communication
sections.body:
This is the CLAS gate that the Mexican default will miss. K’iche’ and Mam are documented in Minnesota, other Mayan languages may also be spoken here, and a Spanish interpreter may still not work, so name the language on the request. A scarce interpreter is a gate, not an excuse to proceed in English only without recording the failure, and because Compass does not count Mayan speakers, do not invent that count.

### Language

Guatemalan Spanish is not Mexican Spanish, and it is not one interpreter accent test, so book a qualified Spanish interpreter AND ask this household what they speak. Register matters: use usted, not a buddy tú, until the room says otherwise.

Compass reports that among those 5 and older, about 60.2 percent speak a language other than English and about 34.3 percent speak English less than “very well,” so date the number. Literacy in any language is not guaranteed, since oral skill is not print.

Give the person time to answer. If you get a short yes, check that the plan was understood, and ask whether it works for them. Do not use a child as the interpreter, and do not make a Guatemalan coworker the interpreter.

sections.heading: Other Considerations
sections.body:
This section states hard facts plainly, because treating everyone the same can hide them.

### Named harms

ICE and the enforcement climate are structure. Mixed-status households may skip clinic, school, and waiver meetings when a relative can be moved, and that is not noncompliance, so do not collect status you do not need, since SSN on the first screen is a gate.

Maya erasure under “they all speak Spanish” is a named harm. K’iche’ and Mam are among the languages at stake, and a Spanish interpreter may still not work. Colorism and ladino hierarchy are real, and the Mexican default in this state will talk over this household if you let the umbrella page do this page’s job.

Do not joke about machismo, and do not excuse control as “that’s culture.” Domestic violence is not culture, so you follow mandated reporting, and you still see a family.

LGBTQ Guatemalan Minnesotans exist, so you use the name they use, and you do not out someone to kin and call it familismo. Staff who share this community may add facts, but they do not get to delete a fact because it is hard to say.

sections.heading: Health
sections.body:
Believe reported pain. War and flight trauma sit in some rooms, but they are not a personality, and they are not a reason to skip screening; they are a reason a government badge is not automatically help. Do not fold this history into Tuskegee or into a generic immigrant-mistrust slide.

### Access

Uninsured and delayed-care patterns sit here, so date Minnesota figures when you have them, and do not invent a rate. Compass (ACS 2020–2024) puts poverty at 12.8 percent, the uninsured rate at 27.0 percent (give or take 6.7), and disability at 5.4 percent (give or take 2.3); date each figure when you cite it. Do not invent a 65+ rate, because Compass suppresses it in this vintage.

Fear of the lobby is a health access fact. A badge, a form that asks for SSN, a child called in to interpret a diagnosis, an interpreter who does not speak this Spanish or this Mam — these are clinical events. When enforcement spikes, people may skip clinic, and that is not noncompliance.

Traditional healing and parish prayer can sit next to a fierce wish for biomedicine, so if they name a healer, listen, but do not make the healer the case plan unless they asked. Gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care, so offer it, and do not use a child as the interpreter.

sections.heading: LGBTQ
sections.body:
Queer and trans Guatemalan Minnesotans exist, and conservative family, parish, and evangelical climates can mean silence or exile. Maya queer people exist, and some people live a public English life and a private K’iche’ or Spanish life, so you use the name they use and do not share what they tell you unless a rule requires it.

### This person

Minnesota’s Human Rights Act still applies. Use the name the person uses, and do not share what they tell you unless a rule requires it.

Do not let concern about family reputation or parish climate override what this person wants, and always defer to the person in front of you.

sections.heading: Hair, Dress, and Body
sections.body:
Traje and huipil are public at fiesta and ceremony in some rooms, but they are not a daily uniform, and they are not yours to request for a Heritage Month photo. The second generation looks like Minnesota, so do not ask a woman in clinic whether she “still wears the costume.”

### Dress

Colorism is real, and ladino default beauty is a hierarchy, so name it if it is in the room. Do not rank indigeneity off clothing, and do not touch.

Plant and dairy work may mean stained hands, which is labor rather than a joke or a race trait. Quinceañera dress, baptism white, and evangelical modesty are celebration and devotion, not a case note.

sections.heading: Music
sections.body:
Marimba, church music, and later pop all belong here, and this is named variation, not a playlist. A Mexican mariachi default in this waiting room is the mash playing through the speakers.

### Variation

A festival stage is not engagement, a playlist is not language access, and church music is not staff entertainment.

Knowing that music is public life will not write the waiver, but what it will do is stop you from treating one Heritage Month speaker as the community.

sections.heading: Sports
sections.body:
Fútbol is the common public sport, and school sport is ordinary for the second generation. Still, do not assume the kid plays, and do not make sport the only excellence you can see.

### Not the whole person

Leagues and pickup games may matter socially, but they are not language access, and they are not a case plan, even though Greater Minnesota teams are still this people.

A Saturday tournament does not replace a Mam interpreter on Monday.

sections.heading: Literature
sections.body:
Maya oral literature is older than the Spanish file, and it is not “no letters,” while Spanish-language letters exist as well. Neither fact means the person in the lobby can read your form — in English or in Spanish — because literacy in any language is not guaranteed.

### Literacy in the lobby

Rigoberta Menchú is literacy for the desk, not a speech you give the family and not a quote for a case note. You do not need to quote a testimonio in the lobby, because what you need is the language this person hears.

Print Spanish from Mexico or a translation produced by software is not automatically this household’s Spanish, and Spanish is not K’iche’, so CLAS means qualified language — not Google and not a child.

sections.heading: Art
sections.body:
Traje, huipil, and weaving are art and memory, not a mascot for the unit’s Heritage Month table, and plant-town public life is not a West Side mural tour copied over from Mexican Minnesota.

### Guest

Be a guest, not a researcher, which means you do not photograph traje or an altar because it is pretty. A textile is not a case plan, and a market visit is not consultation.

A Heritage Month that mashes this community with mariachi or a Mexican ofrenda has already mashed the adjacent peoples.

sections.heading: War, the State, and Deportation Climate
sections.body:
The civil war (1960–1996) and the 1980s campaigns against Maya communities are the political event. Historical-record bodies named genocide, and you do not need to litigate that in a waiver meeting, because what you need to know is why a badge is not automatically help. Later came ordinary policing and the deportation of people with records, and that is current structure.

### The badge

Do not use the war as a personality, and do not ask a person to narrate dying, crossing, or a village emptying for your professional development. Intra-community ladino and Maya difference is real, and you do not referee it on a case note as color.

When enforcement spikes, people may skip clinic, school, and waiver meetings, so do not collect status you do not need, since SSN on the first screen is a gate. Mandated reporting still exists, and so does the duty not to treat a whole people as a deportation score.

sections.heading: Work, Markets, and Government
sections.body:
Work spans food processing, dairy, agriculture, construction, service, a professional second generation, and public employment. Rural plants can sit next to a metro cousin, and a small-business owner and a waiver recipient may be the same household.

### Work

Community organizations and parishes may be the trusted channel in Greater Minnesota, so name the local one rather than assuming Minneapolis or assuming any one office reaches every dairy county (CLUES has offices in Willmar and Austin as well as the Twin Cities). Take time to introduce yourself and explain the plan, and still give any required notice.

### Staff

Book a qualified interpreter, and pay for community work. Do not assign either to staff because of who they are. Use these resources yourself before you ask a Guatemalan colleague to explain.

Some people send money to relatives in Guatemala as an obligation. Ask about it, and do not treat it as optional in a budget.

sections.heading: Health-care and Human-service Encounters
sections.body:
Language comes first, and that includes Mayan languages, so book qualified Spanish AND ask. Confirm K’iche’, Mam, or Q’eqchi’ when that is the home language, because a Spanish interpreter may still not work, and do not use a child as the interpreter or make staff the interpreter.

### Language

Consider who is in the room, and offer gender match in maternal and intimate care if they want it. Use titles, and keep both surnames. On SSN at the first screen, if you do not need it, do not ask for it, and with mixed-status households, do not collect status you do not need, because in an enforcement climate, skipped appointments are a pattern.

### The meeting

Believe reported pain, and do not skip screening. If they name a healer or a church, listen, but do not make either one the case plan unless they asked, and remember that mandated reporting still exists. Rural access is a gate — distance, clinic hours, and one interpreter contracted from the Cities who does not speak this language — and Greater Minnesota at 50.9 percent is not an afterthought.

sections.heading: Adjacent Peoples — Do Not Mash
sections.body:
This community is not Mexican, not Salvadoran, not Puerto Rican, and not the Latino / Hispanic umbrella. Open that CI as adjacent — for CLAS Spanish, the mash, and the other origins as a list — while remembering that this page is Guatemalan, so do not file this household under “Latino” or under Mexican and call it done.

### Adjacent doors

K’iche’, Mam, and Q’eqchi’ are not dialects of Spanish; they are languages and peoples, and a Spanish interpreter is not those languages. This community is also not Honduran, not Nicaraguan, and not Ecuadorian, so name the origin.

It is not Somali, and it is not historic African American. Afro-Guatemalan and Garifuna people exist in the wider Central American map, so ask rather than mash, and do not invent a Minnesota count that Compass does not have, because it is never one Latino module.

sections.heading: Counts, Dated
sections.body:
Minnesota Compass, drawing on ACS 2020–2024, describes the Guatemalan cultural community this way: 17,306 people (give or take 2,627); 49.1 percent in the Twin Cities; 50.9 percent in Greater Minnesota (about half, give or take 7.9 points); 46.1 percent age 17 or younger; 65+ suppressed, so do not invent it; 43.7 percent foreign-born; 60.2 percent speaking a language other than English (age 5+); 34.3 percent speaking English less than “very well”; 61.6 percent with high school or higher (25+); 15.1 percent with a bachelor’s or higher; median household income about $59,000 (2024 dollars, give or take $9,755); poverty 12.8 percent; owner-occupied housing 47.7 percent; average household size 3.52; disability 5.4 percent (give or take 2.3); uninsured 27.0 percent (give or take 6.7).

### Counts

K’iche’, Mam, and other Mayan languages may be spoken in the home, but Compass does not count those speakers, and you should not invent that count. Date Compass when you cite it and do not invent other rates, and since counts disagree across ACS vintages and definitions, the number you cite always needs its date.

### What the count is not

A young age structure is not a personality, and language and child-as-interpreter are gates. Greater Minnesota at 50.9 percent is not an afterthought, and a rate is not the person.

sections.heading: Doors and Sources
sections.body:
Start with the Minnesota Compass Guatemalan profile (ACS 2020–2024) — https://www.mncompass.org/topics/demographics/cultural-communities/guatemalan — and date the retrieval. Rural parishes and community organizations matter too, so name the local one rather than assuming Minneapolis, since the parish in a dairy county may be the actual door. CLUES — https://clues.org/ — has offices in St. Paul, Minneapolis, Willmar and Austin, although a metro office may still not reach every rural county.

### Public doors

CECLC is a department door, not the whole community, and the Latino umbrella CI opens as adjacent, not as this page. Open the Mexican, Salvadoran, or Puerto Rican brief when that is the household, and open a K’iche’ or Mam interpreter request when Spanish is the wrong door.

### Where to learn more

Use these resources yourself before you ask a Guatemalan colleague to explain. Do not BCC a metro organization and call it consultation for a plant town; pay partners, and report back, because Hispanic Heritage Month is not the work.

sections.heading: How it hits DHS gates — the 40%
sections.body:
Workplace culture and service delivery are both candidates here.

Language: CLAS Spanish is not one Spanish. K’iche’ and Mam are documented in Minnesota, other Mayan languages may also be spoken here, and a Spanish interpreter may still not work, so still book a qualified interpreter, and name the language on the request. Do not use a child, and remember that gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care.

Names: two surnames is the pattern, and the database that keeps only one invents a person, which is why unmatched last names are not fraud by default.

Hour caps, exception processes, SSN on the first screen, and life-sharing matches made without language are not culturally neutral. Mixed-status households may bounce if the first field feels like enforcement, so do not collect status you do not need.

Child welfare and disability: help-seeking that becomes a report is part of why people wait. Mandated reporting still exists, and so does the duty not to treat a whole community as a risk score; domestic violence is not culture, and you follow the law.

Enforcement climate: people may skip clinic, school, and waiver meetings when a relative can be moved, which is not noncompliance, so do not collect status you do not need.

Notices and comment: do not count an eList and an English PDF as reaching this community, and record who was reached and what follow-up happened. Greater Minnesota is 50.9 percent of this community, so a St. Paul meeting is not the whole channel.

Workforce: Guatemalan staff are not the interpreter pool, not the Maya-language pool, and not the community, because staff are colleagues, not the curriculum, and they should not be treated as one.

Latino mash: opening the Mexican brief, or the umbrella, because the checkbox says Hispanic shuts the person out.

Legislation, funding, rule: study a channel before you advocate for it. Use this page so that the 40% has a household in it.

sections.heading: A Note on This Guide
sections.body:
This brief is about Indian (Asian Indian) Minnesota, understood both as a people of India and of a global diaspora — many languages, many religions, many states — and as a Minnesota community that Compass counts near 51,618 (ACS 2020–2024). It is worth being clear from the start about what this brief is not: it is not about Native Americans, and it is not about the Eleven Tribal Nations. The U.S. word “Indian” is already a mash of two very different peoples, so the word alone should never decide which page you open, and you should not guess from it; if the household belongs to a Tribal Nation, open that CI, and if the household is Asian Indian, this is the page.

### Who this is

This community is not a Census “Asian” mash, and it helps to say plainly what that means: it is not Chinese and it is not Hmong, Pakistani is not a synonym for it, and it does not speak one Hindi, because a shared continent is not a shared culture. In the same way, Diwali is not Chinese New Year as a file, and it is not Hmong New Year either. Use this page for context and questions. It does not describe the person in front of you.

### Who this is not

Minnesota Compass (ACS 2020–2024) gives the community’s outline in numbers: about 51,618 people (give or take 3,878), with 90.0 percent in the Twin Cities and 10.0 percent in Greater Minnesota. About 26.6 percent are age 17 or younger and about 4.7 percent are 65 or older, while some 64.4 percent are foreign-born. Among those 5 and older (ACS 2020–2024), about 31.3 percent speak English only, about 68.7 percent speak a language other than English, and about 11.7 percent speak English less than “very well.” Among those 25 and older, about 78.9 percent hold a bachelor’s degree or higher (the state chartbook gives 84 percent for ages 25 to 64, the highest share of any cultural group), and about 95.6 percent have a high school education or higher (ACS 2020–2024). Median household income is about $133,600 in 2024 dollars, poverty is 5.5 percent, and 61.8 percent of homes are owner-occupied, with an average household size of about 2.55 (ACS 2020–2024) and roughly 26 percent of households are one-person households (about 4,600 of 17,900, state chartbook). Whichever of these figures you use, date it, and remember that a rate is not the person.

The diversity inside this people is the point, not a footnote. A Telugu-speaking H-1B household in Eden Prairie, a Gujarati shop family, a Malayalam Christian nurse, a Punjabi Sikh elder who needs an interpreter, a Tamil grandmother who does not read the English IEP, a U.S.-born college student, a Muslim family that will not share a Tuesday with a Hindutva uncle, and a person who left India and still shows up at Diwali all share a single Compass row, yet they do not share a language, a religion, or a politics.

### How to read this

Always defer to the person in front of you, because this page is a hypothesis and you are still testing it on this family.

sections.heading: Origins and the Founding of a People
sections.body:
Indian peoplehood is older than the British Raj, older than 1947, and older than the H-1B file. Named kingdoms, a modern republic, many languages with their own scripts, and religions that are not interchangeable — Hindu, Muslim, Sikh, Christian, Jain, Buddhist, none — are the basic literacy this desk needs, rather than a lecture to give a parent who came in for a waiver.

### History for the meeting

The 1947 Partition of British India into India and Pakistan is the modern political break, a time when millions of people moved and there was mass violence. That line still sits in some Minnesota rooms as family memory, while in others it is a history class; either way, it is not a speech you give the family and it is not an icebreaker. Bangladesh in 1971 is a neighboring story with its own shape, so do not mash the two together.

### What people brought

Writing is not one script, since Devanagari, Tamil, Telugu, Gujarati, Malayalam, Gurmukhi, Bengali, Kannada, Arabic-based Urdu, and English all appear in this community. Many elders read a script that is not Hindi, some do not read any of them, and the second generation may not read the language of home at all, which is why a notice in the wrong script will not work.

What people brought with them was a language that may not be Hindi, a religion that may not be Hindu, a strong sense of family obligation, education as both mobility and pressure, foodways that are not one curry, and a memory of a state and of a village. What they met in Minnesota was an English form, one “Asian” checkbox, a U.S. word already in use for Native nations, and often a single interpreter labeled “Indian” or “Hindi.”

sections.heading: The Geography of the Indian World
sections.body:
India is not one region: north, south, east, and west differ, and the states people name — Kerala, Gujarat, Andhra, Telangana, Tamil Nadu, Punjab, Maharashtra, Bengal, Karnataka, and others — shift language, food, and sometimes the script that belongs on the notice. There is no need to referee Delhi versus Chennai in a waiver meeting, so when someone names a place, simply listen.

### Homeland

The diaspora is global, reaching California, New Jersey, Texas, New York, the Gulf, East Africa, the United Kingdom, Canada, and Minnesota, which means Eden Prairie is not this map. Secondary migration, university, and employer transfer built part of what you will meet here.

### Minnesota

In Minnesota, the named concentrations sit in the Twin Cities suburbs — Eden Prairie, Plymouth, Eagan, and Maple Grove among them — along with Minneapolis and a real Greater Minnesota share of 10.0 percent. For that reason, do not assume the professional corridor is the whole community, and do not assume the person in front of you has been to India. Finally, do not mash this geography with Native nations, reservations, or urban Indian organizations, because those belong to another CI.

sections.heading: 1965, H-1B, and Earlier Streams — Foundational Events
sections.body:
Hart-Celler (1965) opened skilled and family immigration and rebuilt Asian Indian America after an earlier period of exclusion, and later decades brought students, physicians, engineers, and the H-1B / L-1 employer streams that are large in this state. That is a stream rather than a virtue ranking, and it is not the whole community.

### Foundational events

The earlier U.S. streams — Punjabi farm and railroad labor on the West Coast, and a small pre-1965 professional presence — are literacy worth having, although Minnesota’s visible community is largely post-1965 and post-1990s, built around tech and health. The India Association of Minnesota dates to 1973. Family reunification brought parents, and those parents are often the LEP elders inside the 11.7 percent that a room treating everyone the same will round to zero.

### Who you meet

1947 is the political event of the subcontinent, but it is not this person’s personality. Visa status, H-1B dependency, and green-card wait times change who is willing to open the door, and that is current structure rather than history, so do not collect status you do not need, and do not treat fear as noncompliance.

If the only word you know is “IT,” you will miss the restaurant household, the student, the U.S.-born child, and the grandmother who still cannot get Telugu in the lobby.

sections.heading: Family
sections.body:
Filial obligation is a hypothesis, not a personality. Ask who should speak first, and hear from the person directly. Adult children may be carrying a waiver meeting, a shift, and a school conference in the same week. Compass puts average household size at about 2.55 (ACS 2020–2024), and the state chartbook counts roughly 26 percent of households as one-person households (about 4,600 of 17,900), which means the joint family and the nuclear household on the English form both live here, so ask who should be in the room.

### Who is in the household

The person who cares for a disabled adult or a child may be a son, a daughter-in-law, or a sibling rather than the legally recognized caregiver on the checkbox. Hour caps and “natural supports” language can quietly shift unpaid work onto the women in that network and then call the result culture.

### Who speaks

The person who speaks in the lobby may be a child with the best English in the family, but that child is not the qualified interpreter. Using a child as the go-between does harm, so book the interpreter, and ask who should be in the room.

Minnesota law still stands throughout, so do not skip mandated reporting and call it humility. In-law duty and the question of who holds the child’s medical decision may not match the English form, which is why you ask rather than assume.

sections.heading: Minnesota and Indian History
sections.body:
Minnesota holds an Asian Indian community large enough that this department will meet it across waivers, child welfare, health care, cash, food, aging, student households, and employment. Compass counts about 51,618 (ACS 2020–2024), with 90.0 percent in the Twin Cities, but the 10.0 percent in Greater Minnesota is not an afterthought, so do not write this people as an Eden Prairie anecdote.

### Places

Think in places rather than a blob: Eden Prairie, Plymouth, Eagan, Maple Grove, Minneapolis, the university areas, and the Greater Minnesota towns that offer work and housing. Groceries, temples, gurdwaras, masjids, and restaurants are public life rather than consultation, and a food-court visit does not make you the expert.

### Partners

Partners include the India Association of Minnesota, founded in 1973, and the temples, gurdwaras, masjids, and churches this household names. CECLC is a department door, not the whole community, so pay the partner this household actually uses.

Book a qualified interpreter, and pay for community work. Do not assign either to staff because of who they are. Diwali is optional professional development if you are invited, and you attend as a guest, knowing that being there does not make you the expert.

sections.heading: Not one language, not one religion — the heart of a people
sections.body:
Do not ask whether a person speaks Hindi, is Hindu, or is “from India,” as if those three were one question. The U.S. word “Indian” is also used for Native nations this household is not, and the Asian checkbox also holds Chinese, Hmong, and Korean histories they do not share.

### In this state

Do not assume Hindi, Hindu, or Patel. Ask.

Do not use the model-minority idea. A 78.9 percent bachelor’s rate and a median near $133,600 can be used to skip past the 11.7 percent who are LEP, the 5.5 percent in poverty, disability, caste harm, and the elder who does not read the IEP.

This guide is a working orientation, which means individual variation always supersedes group generalization and you always defer to the person in front of you.

sections.heading: Core Concepts
sections.body:
Language is the first grammar, and Hindi is not the default: Telugu, Tamil, Gujarati, Malayalam, Punjabi, Urdu, Kannada, Bengali, Marathi, and English all live here, so book THIS language rather than the one a label suggests.

### Religion is not Hindu by default

Hindu, Muslim, Sikh, Christian, Jain, and none are all present, so do not make clergy the case plan unless the family asked for that.

### Name

Regional surnames, South Indian patronymics, and Singh / Kaur are all ordinary, which is why you ask how to file the name and do not correct it.

### Model-minority

Do not use this idea, because it hides LEP elders, 5.5 percent poverty, disability, and youth who are not thriving behind an average that looks like success.

### Caste

Caste is a named harm in some rooms, so it is not an icebreaker, and it is not a field you collect because you are curious.

### Pressure at home and school

These are hypotheses to test with care, not a description of this teenager.

sections.heading: Religion
sections.body:
Hindu, Muslim, Sikh, Christian, Jain, Buddhist, and none all live in Indian Minnesota, so do not assume a temple. A large Hindu public life exists, and so does a large Muslim, Sikh, and Christian public life. Kerala and Goa Christian streams, Punjabi Sikh streams, Gujarati Jain streams, and Hyderabadi and other Muslim streams are literacy rather than a piety ranking, so ask which one is this family’s.

### Streams

A home shrine in a professional household can be true, and a secular household that still shows up at Diwali can be true too. Neither is a contradiction you need to fix, and Hindu practice is not “more Indian” than the masjid, the gurdwara, or the parish.

### Practice

The temple, masjid, gurdwara, and church are centers of ritual, mutual aid, and information, but even so, they are not “the community.” Do not BCC one priest and call it consultation, and do not make clergy the case plan unless this family asked.

Dietary practice is an ask, not a file, because vegetarian, halal, no beef, and no restriction all exist; follow this household rather than writing “Indian diet” on a tray.

sections.heading: Greetings
sections.body:
Ask who to greet first, or follow the household’s lead. Namaste or namaskar is used in some Hindu rooms and salaam in some Muslim rooms, while a handshake is ordinary in many professional rooms and in much of the second generation. Follow the person’s lead on greetings.

### Titles

An English “hello” plus the name is ordinary, so say the name, and ask how to say it rather than guessing.

### This room

Let this person’s own greeting guide you, whatever you read on another page.

Ask before any physical contact, and let the person set the limit.

sections.heading: Naming Conventions
sections.body:
There is no single Indian name order. North Indian family names often sit last on a U.S. form and first in some Indian documents, while South Indian systems in Tamil, Malayalam, Telugu, and Kannada households may use a patronymic — the father’s given name as the “last name” — with no family surname of the kind the form expects. That is not fraud, so ask how to file, and ask how to say it.

### How to file

Patel, Singh, Reddy, Sharma, Kumar, Shah, Rao, Nair, and Das are regional and religious markers, not a joke, so do not joke about “too many Patels” or “too many Singhs.” Sikh men may use Singh and Sikh women may use Kaur, and either can sit alongside a family name or stand as the name, while Muslim names may not match a Hindu naming script you memorized.

Women may or may not take a husband’s family name in U.S. records, which means mother and child may not match, so treat unmatched last names as a system problem until you have a reason to think they are not.

A form that guesses will invent a person, and that invented name follows them through MHCP, school, and child welfare.

sections.heading: Dates of Significance
sections.body:
Diwali is the large public date in many Hindu rooms, and in some Jain and Sikh rooms as well, while Holi, Pongal, Onam, Navaratri, Vaisakhi, Eid al-Fitr, Eid al-Adha, and Christmas may also be on this household’s calendar. Do not put “Asian holiday” or “Indian holiday” on a case note. Schedule around a named date when you can, remembering that a calendar click is not community engagement.

### Calendar
