15 August is Independence Day and 26 January is Republic Day, and both are literacy for the desk rather than a party on a case note. 15 August 1947 is Partition as well as independence, so grief and politics sit in some rooms, and you do not referee them.

Regional new years and death-anniversary household dates will not appear on your state calendar, which is why you ask. Do not mash Diwali with Chinese Lunar New Year, Hmong New Year, Tết, or Seollal.

sections.heading: Education
sections.body:
Compass (ACS 2020–2024) reports that among Indian Minnesotans 25 and older, about 78.9 percent hold a bachelor’s or higher (the state chartbook gives 84 percent for ages 25 to 64, the highest share of any cultural group), and about 95.6 percent have a high school education or higher (ACS 2020–2024), so date Compass when you cite it. About 64.4 percent are foreign-born, and LEP is about 11.7 percent among those 5 and older (ACS 2020–2024), which is a reminder that the average is not the elder in front of you.

### School and language

That 78.9 percent bachelor’s figure can be used to skip language access, and that skip is the gate. An English IEP, an English waiver exception, and an English comment PDF still close the door for the parent who reads Gujarati and limited English, and that parent is not illiterate.

Education pressure in some streams is a hypothesis in the research and in some households, but it is not this teenager, and it is not an excuse to skip mental-health screening. A U.S.-born college student is not proof that the waiver household needs no interpreter.

sections.heading: Etiquette
sections.body:
Ask who to greet first, or follow the household’s lead. If you visit a home, look for shoes by the door or ask what the household prefers.

### In the home

Ask before taking any photograph or touching any religious object, and do not ask anyone to explain their faith or history for your benefit.

### Time

Follow the household’s lead on food and greeting.

If someone misses an appointment, first check the time, transport, interpreter and work schedule. Confirm the plan in the language the person uses, and ask whether it works for them. Book a qualified interpreter instead of using a child to go between.

sections.heading: Language and Communication
sections.body:
This is not one language, and Hindi is not the default, since Telugu, Tamil, Gujarati, Malayalam, Punjabi, Urdu, Kannada, Bengali, Marathi, English, and others all live in this Compass row. An interpreter labeled Indian or Hindi who does not speak this household’s language will not work, so book THIS language, and still book a qualified interpreter.

### Language

Compass reports that among those 5 and older, about 68.7 percent speak a language other than English and about 11.7 percent speak English less than “very well,” and you should date the number when you use it. That 11.7 percent is low compared with Vietnamese or Hmong on Compass, but it is not “no language gate,” because new arrivals and elders are inside it. The English-dominant second generation is inside the 31.3 percent English-only figure and still belongs on this page.

Give the person time to answer. If you get a short yes, check that the plan was understood, and ask whether it works for them.

Do not use a child as the interpreter, and do not make an Indian coworker the interpreter or treat them as “the Indian community.”

sections.heading: Other Considerations
sections.body:
This section states hard facts plainly, because treating everyone the same can hide them.

### Named harms

Do not use the model-minority idea, since a 78.9 percent bachelor’s rate and a median near $133,600 can be used to skip LEP elders, 5.5 percent poverty, disability, caste, and youth who are not thriving. 11.7 percent LEP is a gate.

Caste is a named harm in some rooms and a word some families will never say to you, so you do not icebreak with it, you do not pretend it is over because the person is a software engineer, and you do not collect it on a form you do not need. Colorism is a named harm in some rooms, and the same rule applies.

Hindu-Muslim-Sikh politics, Hindutva, and the memory of 1947 still split some rooms, so you do not referee, and you do not put it on a case note as color.

The H-1B, visa, and green-card climate changes who opens the door, which is why you do not collect status you do not need and do not treat fear as noncompliance.

LGBTQ Indian Minnesotans exist, so you use the name, and you do not out someone to kin and call it culture; nor do you skip mandated reporting and call it humility. Staff who share this community may add facts, but they do not get to delete a fact because it is hard to say.

sections.heading: Health
sections.body:
Believe reported pain, and do not fold this history into a generic Asian slide, because this is not the Chinese page and not the Hmong page.

### Access

Do not invent a Minnesota diabetes, heart, or suicide rate. U.S. public-health patterns for South Asian cardiovascular risk exist in the literature, and if you cite them, date the CDC or AHA page you are using. Do not import an India national rate as a Minnesota rate, and do not skip screening because the person looks well or because the median household income is high.

Mental-health stigma is real in some families, and naming a counselor is not the same as a family accepting one, just as a smile is not a PHQ-9. Gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care, so offer it.

Ayurveda, homeopathy, and other traditional practice often sit beside biomedicine, so ask about it, work with it, and do not mock it. At the same time, do not skip a child-protection duty when the facts are the facts. Late help-seeking can come from language, stigma, and a lobby that already used a child as the interpreter.

sections.heading: LGBTQ
sections.body:
Queer and trans Indian Minnesotans exist. Conservative family, temple, masjid, gurdwara, and church climates can mean silence or exile, and some people live a public English life alongside a private language-of-home life, so you use the name they use and do not share what they tell you unless a rule requires it.

### This person

Minnesota’s Human Rights Act still applies. Use the name the person uses, and do not share what they tell you unless a rule requires it.

Caste, 1947 politics, and model-minority respectability do not override what this person wants, because you always defer to the person in front of you.

sections.heading: Hair, Dress, and Body
sections.body:
Sari, salwar kameez, sherwani, and kurta are public at weddings, at Diwali, and on some stages, but they are not a daily uniform, and the second generation looks like Minnesota. Do not ask a woman in clinic whether she “still wears the costume.”

### Dress

A Sikh dastar (turban) and uncut hair (kesh) are religious practice rather than a hat, so do not touch them. Do not ask a man to remove a turban for a photo unless a lawful identification process requires it and you have offered a private alternative. A hijab in some Muslim rooms follows the same rule: do not touch.

Gold, a bindi, a karha, or a cross is not a mascot for the unit’s Heritage Month table, and you should not mash this dress with a qipao or a kimono on an “Asian” table.

sections.heading: Music
sections.body:
Carnatic and Hindustani classical, film music, bhangra, qawwali, Christian lyric, and none at all — this is named variation, not a playlist. A gurdwara kirtan is not staff entertainment, and a playlist is not engagement.

### Variation

Do not ask a staff person or a client to perform, and do not use a dance video as the training, since Diwali stages are public life rather than consultation or a case plan.

sections.heading: Sports
sections.body:
Cricket is public culture for some Indian Minnesota households, but it is not the case plan and it is not this teenager. School sport is ordinary for the second generation, yet you should not assume the kid plays, and you should not make sport the only excellence you can see.

### Not the whole person

Sport clubs are social infrastructure for some, but they are not language access, because an elder in the stands who needs Gujarati still needs Gujarati, and 11.7 percent LEP is not a skip because the child plays varsity. A Saturday tournament does not replace an interpreter on Monday.

sections.heading: Literature
sections.body:
This community writes in many scripts — Devanagari, Tamil, Telugu, Gujarati, Malayalam, Kannada, Gurmukhi, Bengali, Arabic-based Urdu, and English — so this is not a people without letters, and you do not need to quote a novel in the lobby.

### Literacy in the lobby

What you do need to know is that a notice that exists only in English will not work for the elder who reads another script, and a notice in Hindi that the Tamil elder cannot read also will not work. Ask which language they read, and do not put a proverb on a brochure and call it language access.

sections.heading: Art
sections.body:
Classical dance, temple sculpture and painting, rangoli, diaspora visual work, and the public culture of Diwali and the groceries are all part of this world, although foodway is not consultation.

### Guest

Come as a guest, not a researcher, because a grocery or temple visit is not a case plan. A museum visit is optional professional development rather than consultation, and you should not photograph a shrine.

A Heritage Month display that mashes this with Hmong paj ntaub or a Chinese New Year poster has already mashed the adjacent peoples.

sections.heading: Partition, the State, and Visa Climate
sections.body:
The 1947 Partition, Hart-Celler in 1965, and a United States that rebuilt a professional stream after exclusion make up the political file. Later came the H-1B and green-card wait, the enforcement climate, and Hindu-Muslim-Sikh politics that sit in the news and in some rooms, and for all of these reasons, a DHS badge is not automatically help.

### The badge

Do not referee the subcontinent. Do not collect immigration or caste status you do not need, and do not use Partition or a visa file as a personality, nor ask a person to narrate a riot, a temple demolition, or a camp for your professional development.

Filing this household as Native American, as Pakistani, or as a Census Asian mash is a state act, and it shuts the person out.

sections.heading: Work, Temples, and Government
sections.body:
Professional and technical work, medicine, university, small business, restaurants, and public employment all appear here. Median household income of about $133,600 (Compass, 2024 dollars) is an average, poverty of 5.5 percent sits in the same row, and roughly 26 percent of households are one-person households (state chartbook), so do not staff a program as if every household were a four-person H-1B family in Eden Prairie.

### Work

Book a qualified interpreter, and pay for community work. Do not assign either to staff because of who they are.

### Staff

Take time to introduce yourself and explain the plan. The first visit may not be the decision, and any required notice still goes out.

sections.heading: Health-care and Human-service Encounters
sections.body:
Expect THIS language on the interpreter line, not Hindi by default. Expect a name grammar the form will invent, a child pushed forward as the English speaker, and a shrine, a granthi, an imam, or a priest in the story, along with pain you must believe, vegetarian as an ask, a visa climate you do not collect as status, and a nuclear form that reversed the name.

### Language

Confirm the language, and still book a qualified interpreter rather than using a child. Offer gender match, ask who should hear, and ask how to file the name, without making staff the interpreter.

### The meeting

Believe reported pain. Do not skip screening because 78.9 percent hold a bachelor’s, and remember that mandated reporting still exists.

sections.heading: Adjacent Peoples — Do Not Mash
sections.body:
This community is not Native American and not the Eleven Tribal Nations, since the U.S. word “Indian” is already a mash; open those CIs for those households, and open this one for Asian Indian Minnesota.

### Adjacent doors

It is not Pakistani, Bangladeshi, or Sri Lankan as a synonym, and it is not Nepali. It is not Chinese, Hmong, Vietnamese, or Korean, and “Asian American” is not the file. Some households are mixed and some people name South Asian, so ask this household, and do not file them under Hindi by default.

Never one Asian module, never one “Indian” interpreter, and never a Tribal consultation checklist on this desk because the checkbox said Indian.

sections.heading: Counts, Dated
sections.body:
Minnesota Compass (ACS 2020–2024) describes the Indian cultural community as about 51,618 people (give or take 3,878), with 90.0% in the Twin Cities and 10.0% in Greater Minnesota. Those age 17 or younger are 26.6% and those 65+ are about 4.7%, and 64.4% are foreign-born. Among those age 5+ (ACS 2020–2024), 31.3% speak English only, 68.7% speak a language other than English, and 11.7% speak English less than “very well.” Among those 25+, 78.9% hold a bachelor’s or higher (the state chartbook gives 84% for ages 25 to 64), and 95.6% have high school or higher (ACS 2020–2024). Median household income is about $133,600 (2024 dollars), poverty is 5.5%, and 61.8% of homes are owner-occupied, while average household size is 2.55 (ACS 2020–2024) and roughly 26 percent of households are one-person households (about 4,600 of 17,900, state chartbook).

### Counts

Date Compass, and do not invent other rates, because counts disagree across ACS vintages and definitions — ancestry vs. birthplace vs. language vs. the IAM community estimate — so the number you cite needs its date.

### What the count is not

A 11.7 percent LEP rate is not zero, and a 5.5 percent poverty rate is not zero, while a 78.9 percent bachelor’s rate is not a skip. A 4.7 percent 65+ share does not mean there is no elder who needs Malayalam, because a rate is not the person.

sections.heading: Doors and Sources
sections.body:
Start with the Minnesota Compass Indian profile (ACS 2020–2024) and the India Association of Minnesota (established 1973), along with the temples, gurdwaras, masjids, and churches this person names. Pay the door this person names rather than assigning a temple.

### Public doors

CECLC is a door, not the whole community. Use these resources yourself before you ask an Indian colleague to explain, and do not count an eList and an English PDF as reaching an LEP elder. Book the language the person names: Hindi, Telugu, Tamil, Gujarati, Malayalam, Punjabi, Urdu, or whatever language they name.

### Where to learn more

Do not BCC a priest and call it consultation. Be a guest at Diwali if you are invited, and remember that it is not consultation either.

sections.heading: How it hits DHS gates — the 40%
sections.body:
Workplace culture and service delivery are both candidates here.

Language comes first, because an 11.7 percent LEP rate is not “no language gate,” and an elder who needs Telugu or Tamil or Gujarati and gets English — or Hindi they do not use — is not being served. Gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care, so offer it, and do not use a child.

Names come next. South Indian patronymics, Singh / Kaur, and unmatched last names are all ordinary, and the database that invents a person is a gate, so do not joke about Patels.

Hour caps, exception processes, and life-sharing matches offered without this household’s language are not culturally neutral, and an English IEP is still a gate for that parent.

The model-minority idea is its own gate, since a 95.6 percent high school rate and a 78.9 percent bachelor’s rate can be used to skip LEP, 5.5 percent poverty, disability, caste, and youth who are not thriving.

Then there is the Native mash: opening a Tribal Nation file or a Native American CI because the checkbox said Indian shuts the person out and ignores Tribal sovereignty.

On notices and comment, do not count an eList and an English PDF as reaching an LEP elder, and record who was reached and what follow-up happened. Greater Minnesota is 10.0 percent, so a suburban temple meeting is not the whole channel.

In the workforce, Indian staff are not the interpreter pool and not the community, because staff are colleagues, not the curriculum, and should not be treated as either.

On legislation, funding, and rule: study a channel before you advocate for it. Use this page so that the 40% has a household in it.

sections.heading: A Note on This Guide
sections.body:
This brief is about Japanese Minnesota as a people with a country, a long literature, and a U.S. history that includes labor on the West Coast, Exclusion, internment, a Minnesota language school at Camp Savage and Fort Snelling, later-generation families, mixed households, company transferees, and newcomers. All of them share a Compass row, and they do not share a Tuesday. This community is not Chinese, it is not Korean, and it is not interchangeable with either, because a shared continent is not a shared culture. Use this page for context and questions. It does not describe the person in front of you.

### Who this is

Internment is U.S. literacy for the desk: Executive Order 9066, 19 February 1942. It is not a speech you give the family, and it is not an icebreaker in a waiver meeting, so do not skip it because a room that treats everyone the same finds it uncomfortable, and do not open with it either.

### Who this is not

Minnesota Compass (ACS 2020–2024) counts about 13,457 Japanese Minnesotans (give or take 1,823), with about 74.1 percent living in the Twin Cities and 25.9 percent in Greater Minnesota. About 29.6 percent are age 17 or younger, about 10.7 percent are 65+, and about 16.9 percent are foreign-born. Among those 5 and older, about 73.1 percent speak English only, about 26.9 percent speak a language other than English, and about 8.8 percent speak English less than “very well.” Among those 25 and older, about 97.1 percent have a high school education or higher and about 48.1 percent a bachelor’s or higher. Median household income is about $82,258 in 2024 dollars (give or take $19,418), poverty is 6.5 percent, and 63.3 percent of homes are owner-occupied, while average household size is about 2.19, about 37.0 percent of individuals live alone, and about 35.5 percent of households are cost-burdened (62.4 percent of renters). Date the number you use, and remember that a rate is not the person.

The diversity inside this Compass row is the point. A Nisei elder who remembers a camp, a Sansei who does not speak Japanese, a company-transfer family in a suburb, a student, a mixed-race child who is asked “what are you,” and a newcomer who needs Japanese in the lobby all share a checkbox, but they do not share a language, a church, or a war memory.

### How to read this

Always defer to the person in front of you, because this page is a hypothesis you still test with this family.

sections.heading: Origins and the Founding of a People
sections.body:
Japanese peoplehood is older than Meiji (1868), older than the empire, and older than the internment file. It rests on an archipelago, a language with honorific speech, three scripts in ordinary public literacy — hiragana, katakana, kanji — and a succession of states. That is literacy for the desk rather than a lecture you give a parent who came in for a waiver.

### History for the meeting

The 1868 Meiji transformation, empire, the 1945 defeat, the postwar constitution, and a U.S. occupation make up the modern political stack, and most Minnesota immigrant and transfer households name Japan as the sending country. Do not test them on any of this, and do not ask a later-generation person to narrate a war they were not asked to remember.

### What people brought

What people brought includes language; Buddhist, Shinto, or Christian faith, or none; education as mobility; foodways; and a memory of war and of a state. What they met in this country was Exclusion, a camp, a Minnesota language school that trained Nisei soldiers while their families were incarcerated, an English form, and one “Asian” checkbox. What they meet now is an assumption that 16.9 percent foreign-born means you can skip Japanese.

Issei, Nisei, Sansei, and Yonsei are generation literacy — like Vietnamese waves, they are not a personality ranking — and mixed households and company transferees sit in the same Compass row. Ask which Tuesday this is rather than lecturing a parent about a generation word they did not use.

sections.heading: The Geography of the Japanese World
sections.body:
The homeland is the archipelago, not a Tokyo tourism map, and the prefectures people name will not be on your case note unless they put them there. Okinawa is a named geography that some families will name, so you do not mash it; you listen.

### Homeland

The diaspora is global: the West Coast of the United States historically, Hawaii, Brazil, Peru, and a Minnesota present that is unusual in part because of the Military Intelligence Service Language School at Camp Savage (1942) and Fort Snelling. Compass places about 74.1 percent of the community in the Twin Cities and 25.9 percent in Greater Minnesota.

### Minnesota

Do not assume Minneapolis, and do not assume they have been to Tokyo. A later-generation household in a Greater Minnesota town is still this people, just as a company-transfer family on a three-year assignment is still this people and a mixed household is still this people.

sections.heading: Exclusion, Internment, Fort Snelling, 1965 — Foundational Events
sections.body:
Meiji-era labor moved Japanese people to Hawaii and the West Coast, and the Gentlemen’s Agreement (1907–08) and the Immigration Act of 1924 then closed the door. That is literacy for the desk, not a speech.

### Foundational events

Executive Order 9066, signed 19 February 1942, meant the United States incarcerated Japanese Americans on the West Coast. There were camps and the loss of homes and businesses, and there was the 442nd Regimental Combat Team. The Military Intelligence Service Language School trained Nisei linguists at Camp Savage, Minnesota, in 1942, and then at Fort Snelling. That is this state’s history, but it is not a Heritage Month panel unless they asked for one, and it is not an icebreaker.

### Who you meet

Hart-Celler (1965) reopened skilled and family immigration, and later came company transferees, students, marriage, and mixed families. Redress arrived with the Civil Liberties Act of 1988 (10 August), so date the law. Do not invent this person’s family file, and do not ask them to narrate a camp for your professional development.

If the only thing you know is internment, you will miss the transfer household and the LEP elder, while if you skip internment as uncomfortable, you will miss U.S. literacy.

sections.heading: Family
sections.body:
Family-name-first is the naming grammar in Japanese, and obligation to elders is a hypothesis, not a waiver design. Compass reports an average household size of about 2.19, which is among the smaller spines, and about 37.0 percent live alone, so ask who should be in the room.

### Who is in the household

Later-generation and mixed households are common in this Compass row, and kin may be in California, in Japan, or not in the story at all. Do not assume Japanese relatives in the metro, and do not assume the mixed family is “no culture”; ask this person.

### Who speaks

The person who speaks in the lobby may be a child with the best English, but that child is not the qualified interpreter, so book the interpreter.

Minnesota law still stands, so do not skip mandated reporting and call it culture. Marriage, divorce, and who holds the child’s medical decision may not match the English form.

sections.heading: Minnesota and Japanese History
sections.body:
Camp Savage and Fort Snelling’s Military Intelligence Service Language School are Minnesota history, since Nisei soldiers trained here while their families were incarcerated elsewhere, and MNHS holds that trail. This department will meet this community on waivers, child welfare, health care, aging, student households, company-transfer families, and employment. Compass places about 74.1 percent in the Twin Cities and 25.9 percent in Greater Minnesota, and Greater Minnesota is not an afterthought.

### Places

JACL and the Japan-related associations this person names are partners, so name the local one. The Buddhist temples and churches families name are not “the community,” so pay the door this household actually uses. Book a qualified interpreter, and pay for community work. Do not assign either to staff because of who they are.

### Partners

Obon and New Year are public in some rooms, and if you go, go as a guest. A restaurant visit is not consultation, and a Fort Snelling tour is optional professional development rather than an icebreaker for the person in the lobby.

Book a qualified interpreter, and pay for community work. Do not assign either to staff because of who they are. Internment literacy is for the desk, not a speech at a staff lunch, and because Greater Minnesota is 25.9 percent, a Twin Cities association meeting is not the whole channel.

sections.heading: Not Chinese, not Korean — one Compass row, many Tuesdays
sections.body:
To be Japanese in Minnesota is often to be asked whether you were interned, whether you “speak it,” or whether you are Chinese or Korean — and to be filed under a checkbox that also holds histories this household does not share.

### In this state

Issei, Nisei, Sansei, Yonsei, mixed households, company transferees, and last year’s arrival share a Compass row, and they do not share a kitchen, a language, or a war memory. Do not ask a mixed-race teenager to represent internment, and do not skip this page because the person in front of you sounds like Minnesota, since foreign-born at 16.9 percent is not “no culture.”

Ask plainly whether the person agrees with the plan, and make it easy to say no.

This guide is a working orientation, and individual variation always supersedes group generalization.

sections.heading: Core Concepts
sections.body:
Language comes first, and the language is Japanese, with honorific speech. Book Japanese for the elder who needs it, because 8.8 percent LEP is not zero.

### Name

The family name comes first, so do not “correct” it toward Chinese, and remember that -san is not a given name.

### Internment

Internment is U.S. literacy: EO 9066, 19 February 1942. It is not a speech, not an icebreaker, and not a personality.

### Oshōgatsu is 1 January

It is not Chinese Lunar New Year as a file, it is not Seollal, and it is not Hmong New Year.

### Model-minority

Do not use the model-minority idea, because it hides LEP elders, 6.5 percent poverty, 35.5 percent cost-burden, and mixed-household grief.

### Checking for agreement

Ask whether the person agrees, and do not rely on a smile.

sections.heading: Religion
sections.body:
Buddhist practice, Shinto shrine practice, Protestant and Catholic Christianity, and no religion at all all live here. Do not assume a temple, and do not assume no faith, since Obon and New Year household practice can sit comfortably in a secular family.

### Streams

A butsudan in a living room is not a case plan and not a museum, so do not photograph it, and do not make a priest or a monk the case plan unless this family asked.

### Practice

Churches are civic hubs for some later-generation and mixed families, but they are not “the community,” and you should not assign a Buddhist temple as cultural programming.

Do not treat Buddhist practice as a souvenir, and do not treat church as the evolved version.

sections.heading: Greetings
sections.body:
A bow or nod with elders is ordinary in some immigrant and transfer rooms, while a handshake is ordinary in many professional rooms and in most later-generation rooms. Follow the person’s lead on greetings.

### Titles

Honorific speech in Japanese marks age and status. You do not need to perform it; you need to book an interpreter who can, and an English “hello” plus the name is ordinary.

### This room

Let this person’s own greeting guide you, whatever you read on another page.

Ask before any physical contact, and let the person set the limit.

sections.heading: Naming Conventions
sections.body:
In Japanese the family name comes first: Satō, Suzuki, Takahashi, Tanaka, Watanabe, Itō, Yamamoto. U.S. forms reverse the order, so the same person can appear as Tanaka Yuki and as Yuki Tanaka, which is a system failure, not a fraud signal, until you have a reason to think otherwise.

### How to file

Do not “correct” a name toward a Chinese romanization, and do not mash it with Korean names. -san is an honorific rather than a first name or a joke, so do not address a person as San.

Later-generation and mixed households often carry an American given name and a Japanese family name, or the reverse, or neither, so ask. Do not demand the “real” name, and ask how to say a person’s name before you call it out in a waiting room.

Pronounce it, and ask, keeping in mind that women may or may not take a husband’s name in U.S. records.

sections.heading: Dates of Significance
sections.body:
Oshōgatsu — Japanese New Year — falls on 1 January on the solar calendar in modern practice. It is a related winter holiday but a different people from Chinese Lunar New Year, Seollal, Tết, and Hmong New Year, so do not put “Asian holiday” on a case note.

### Calendar

Obon is ancestral remembrance, often held in mid-August in this country, and it is literacy, not a file. Golden Week in Japan is operations for some transfer families rather than a day off the work.

19 February 1942 is the date of Executive Order 9066, and the Day of Remembrance in Japanese American public life, while 2 September 1945 is another date to know. These are literacy for the desk, not a speech, not a party, and not an icebreaker.

A calendar click is not community engagement.

sections.heading: Education
sections.body:
Compass (ACS 2020–2024) reports that among Japanese Minnesotans 25 and older, about 97.1 percent have a high school education or higher and about 48.1 percent a bachelor’s or higher. Among those 5 and older, about 73.1 percent speak English only, LEP is about 8.8 percent, and about 16.9 percent are foreign-born, but the average is not the elder in front of you.

### School and language

The 97.1 percent high school figure can be used to skip language access, and that skip is the gate. An English IEP still closes the door for the parent who reads Japanese and limited English, and that parent is not illiterate.

Later-generation school histories include Minnesota classrooms that had no Japanese peer, while company-transfer children may be in and out of a district in three years. Do not mash those stories together, and do not treat a college student as proof the household needs no interpreter.

sections.heading: Etiquette
sections.body:
If you visit a home, look for shoes by the door or ask what the household prefers. Follow the person’s lead.

### In the home

Later-generation households may run on Minnesota manners — shoes on, first names, a hotdish — and that is culture too, so do not correct it toward a Tokyo script.

### Time

If food or drink is offered, accepting a little is fine, and you can still keep to medical and legal timelines.

If someone misses an appointment, first check the time, transport, interpreter and work schedule. Confirm the plan in the language the person uses, and ask whether it works for them. Book a qualified interpreter instead of using a child to go between.

sections.heading: Language and Communication
sections.body:
The language is Japanese, written in hiragana, katakana, and kanji, with honorific speech. Book Japanese for the elder who needs it and for anyone who asks, and because later-generation people may want Japanese for a clinic visit with a parent, or not at all, ask. Do not assign a tutor as programming.

### Language

Compass reports that about 26.9 percent speak a language other than English and that LEP is about 8.8 percent (age 5+), so date it. A low figure compared with Vietnamese or Hmong is not a reason to skip, because newcomers and elders are inside that 8.8 percent, and the English-dominant later generation is inside the 73.1 percent English-only and still on this page.

A Chinese or Korean mix-up will not work, and neither will an interpreter labeled “Asian.”

Give the person time to answer. If you get a short yes, check that the plan was understood, and ask whether it works for them. Do not make a Japanese coworker the interpreter, and do not use a child.

sections.heading: Other Considerations
sections.body:
This section states hard facts plainly, because treating everyone the same can hide them.

### Named harms

Internment is U.S. literacy: EO 9066, 19 February 1942, the camps, the 442nd, MIS at Camp Savage and Fort Snelling, and Redress in 1988. It is not a speech, not an icebreaker, and not a personality, and skipping it because the room is uncomfortable is how treating everyone the same deletes a state act.

Do not use the model-minority idea, because the 97.1 percent high school and 48.1 percent bachelor’s figures can be used to skip 8.8 percent LEP, 6.5 percent poverty, 35.5 percent cost-burden, disability, and mixed-household grief. A median household income of about $82,258 is not the Indian or Chinese median, so do not import another Asian average onto this kitchen table.

Mixed-race Japanese Minnesotans exist, company-transfer isolation exists, LGBTQ Japanese Minnesotans exist, and mental-health stigma exists in some streams. Do not invent a Minnesota suicide rate, and do not skip screening. Do not collect status you do not need, and do not skip mandated reporting and call it humility.

sections.heading: Health
sections.body:
Book Japanese for the elder who needs it, because an 8.8 percent LEP rate (Compass, age 5+) is a gate, not a rounding error, and an English consent form is not consent if they could not run it.

### Access

Believe reported pain, and do not fold this community into a generic Asian slide. Do not skip screening because HS+ is 97.1 percent or because the person is English-dominant.

Mental-health stigma is real in some families, so do not invent a Minnesota rate, and do not import a Japan national rate as a Minnesota rate. Naming a counselor is not the same as a family accepting one, and a smile is not a PHQ-9. Gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care, so offer it.

If they name a healer, a priest, or a butsudan, listen, but do not make that the case plan unless they asked.

sections.heading: LGBTQ
sections.body:
Queer and trans Japanese Minnesotans exist — in later-generation households, in transfer families, in mixed families, in churches, and in none of those. You use the name they use and do not share what they tell you unless a rule requires it.

### This person

Minnesota’s Human Rights Act still applies. Use the name the person uses, and do not share what they tell you unless a rule requires it.

Do not assume a mixed or English-dominant household is affirming, and do not assume an immigrant household is not; ask this person.

sections.heading: Hair, Dress, and Body
sections.body:
Kimono and yukata are public at Obon, at some weddings, and on some stages, but they are not a daily uniform, and the later generation and most mixed households look like Minnesota. Do not ask a woman in clinic whether she “still wears the costume,” and do not dress a child in kimono as DHS programming.

### Dress

On hair and head, follow this person, and do not touch.

Do not mash kimono with a qipao or a hanbok on the unit’s Heritage Month table, because that mash is the adjacent-peoples failure.

sections.heading: Music
sections.body:
Gagaku, min’yō, enka, J-pop, church music, or none at all — there is not one soundtrack. J-pop is public culture, including among people with no other Japanese language, but it is not consultation.

### Variation

A playlist is not engagement, so do not ask a staff person or a client to perform, and do not use a music video as the training.

A funeral is not staff entertainment, whatever music it carries.

sections.heading: Sports
sections.body:
Baseball is public culture for some families, while judo and kendo are public for some and a stereotype if you assume them, so do not assume them. School sport is ordinary for later generations.

### Not the whole person

Sport clubs are not language access and not a case plan, and an elder in the stands who needs Japanese still needs Japanese. An 8.8 percent LEP rate is not a skip because the child plays varsity.

A Saturday tournament does not replace an interpreter on Monday.

sections.heading: Literature
sections.body:
Japanese has a long written vernacular in hiragana, katakana, and kanji. Japanese and Japanese American writers exist in both languages, and internment memoir and scholarship are a U.S. literary fact. You do not need to quote a novel, but you do need to know this is not a people without letters.

### Literacy in the lobby

Literacy in Japanese is not guaranteed for later generations or for mixed households, which means a Japanese-language notice may still not work, just as an English notice may still not work, so ask.

Do not put a proverb on a brochure and call it language access.

sections.heading: Art
sections.body:
Ceramics, ink, and woodblock are literacy, alongside Obon public art and diaspora visual work, so be a guest. A kimono on a stage is not a case plan, a museum visit is not consultation, and a tea ceremony is not a waiver design.

### Guest

Do not mash this work with Chinese calligraphy or Korean ceramics on an “Asian art” table.

Pay the door this person names, and do not extract a staff person’s child as New Year entertainment.

sections.heading: Internment, the Language School, and the State
sections.body:
Empire, 1941–45, Executive Order 9066 (19 February 1942), the camps, the 442nd, and the Military Intelligence Service Language School at Camp Savage and Fort Snelling — that is the political event, and Redress came with the Civil Liberties Act of 1988. A DHS badge is not automatically help, because a government that incarcerated families and trained their children as linguists in this state is not automatically safe in a lobby.

### The badge

Do not use internment as a personality or an icebreaker, and do not ask a person to narrate a camp, a lost farm, or a redress check for your professional development. Do not collect immigration status you do not need.

Filing this household as Chinese or Korean is a state act, and it shuts the person out.

sections.heading: Work, Transfer, and Government
sections.body:
Work here includes professional work, company transfer, small business, and public employment. Median household income of about $82,258 (Compass, 2024 dollars) is an average, while poverty at 6.5 percent sits in the same row. About 37.0 percent live alone, and about 35.5 percent of households are cost-burdened (62.4 percent of renters), so do not staff a program as if every household were a four-person professional family, and do not import an Indian or Chinese median onto this table.

### Work

Book a qualified interpreter, and pay for community work. Do not assign either to staff because of who they are.

### Staff

Take time to introduce yourself and explain the plan, and still give any required notice.

sections.heading: Health-care and Human-service Encounters
sections.body:
Several things shape this encounter: Japanese for the elder, an English-dominant later generation who still needs this page, name order on the wristband, a butsudan in the story, an internment memory you do not use as an icebreaker, pain you must believe, and a mixed child asked “what are you” in the waiting room.

### Language

Ask the language, ask how to say the name, and offer gender match. Believe reported pain, and do not skip screening. Do not make staff the interpreter, and do not use a child, while remembering that mandated reporting still exists.

### The meeting

Do not mash this encounter with a Chinese or Korean interpreter, because a smile is not consent and an 8.8 percent LEP rate is not a rounding error.

sections.heading: Adjacent Peoples — Do Not Mash
sections.body:
This community is not Chinese, not Korean, not Hmong, not Vietnamese, and not Filipino, and it is not “Asian American” as the file. Open those CIs for those households, and open this one for a Japanese household, but because some households are mixed, ask this household.

### Adjacent doors

Oshōgatsu is not Chinese New Year as a file, and it is not Seollal, just as kimono is not hanbok and not qipao. Internment is a Japanese American story, but it is not a speech you give a Korean or Chinese family, and it is not a speech you give this family either.

There is never one Asian module. Do not skip this page because the person is English-dominant, since foreign-born at 16.9 percent is not “no culture.”

sections.heading: Counts, Dated
sections.body:
Minnesota Compass, ACS 2020–2024, Japanese cultural community, reports about 13,457 people (give or take 1,823), of whom 74.1% live in the Twin Cities and 25.9% in Greater Minnesota. Those age 17 or younger are 29.6%, those 65+ about 10.7%, and the foreign-born share is 16.9%. Among those age 5 and older, 73.1% speak English only, 26.9% speak a language other than English, and 8.8% speak English less than “very well.” Among those 25 and older, 97.1% have a high school education or higher and 48.1% a bachelor’s or higher. Median household income is about $82,258 (2024 dollars, give or take $19,418), poverty is 6.5%, and 63.3% of homes are owner-occupied, while average household size is 2.19, 37.0 percent of individuals live alone, and 35.5 percent of households are cost-burdened (62.4 percent of renters).

### Counts

Date Compass, and do not invent other rates. Counts disagree across ACS vintages and definitions (ancestry vs. birthplace vs. language), so date the number you cite.

### What the count is not

An 8.8 percent LEP rate is not zero, a 6.5 percent poverty rate is not zero, and a 16.9 percent foreign-born share is not “no culture.” A 35.5 percent cost-burden rate is not a model-minority brochure, and a median of $82,258 is not another Asian spine’s median. A rate is not the person.

sections.heading: Doors and Sources
sections.body:
Start with the Minnesota Compass Japanese profile (ACS 2020–2024) and the Minnesota Historical Society’s record of the Military Intelligence Service Language School at Camp Savage and Fort Snelling. The Japanese American Citizens League and the Japan-related associations this person names are doors, as are the Buddhist temples and churches this person names, so pay the door this person names rather than assigning a temple.

### Public doors

CECLC is a door, not the whole community. Use these resources yourself before you ask a Japanese colleague to explain. Do not count an eList and an English PDF as reaching an LEP elder. Book Japanese when they need it.

### Where to learn more

A Fort Snelling visit is optional professional development, but it is not consultation, and it is not an icebreaker.

sections.heading: How it hits DHS gates — the 40%
sections.body:
Workplace culture and service delivery are both candidates here.

On language: 8.8 percent LEP is not “no language gate,” because an elder who needs Japanese and gets English — or Chinese, or Korean — is not being served. Gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care, and later-generation people may want Japanese or may not, so ask, and do not use a child.

On names: the family name comes first, and -san is not a given name, so a database that reverses the order or “corrects” toward Chinese is a gate.

Hour caps, exception processes, and life-sharing matches without Japanese for the elder who needs it are not culturally neutral, and an English IEP is still a gate for that parent.

On the model-minority idea: 97.1 percent high school and 48.1 percent bachelor’s can be used to skip LEP, 6.5 percent poverty, 35.5 percent cost-burden, disability, and mixed-household grief. Do not import an Indian or Chinese income average onto this packet.

On internment: EO 9066 is U.S. literacy. Using it as an icebreaker shuts the person out, and skipping it because the room is uncomfortable is how treating everyone the same deletes a state act, while a DHS badge is not automatically help.

On notices and comment: do not count an eList and an English PDF as reaching an LEP elder, and record who was reached and what follow-up happened, especially when Greater Minnesota is 25.9 percent.

On workforce: Japanese staff are not the interpreter pool and not the community; staff are colleagues, not the curriculum, so do not treat them as anything else.

On legislation, funding, and rule: study a channel before you advocate for it. Use this page so that the 40% has a household in it.

sections.heading: A Note on This Guide
sections.body:
This brief is about Kenyan Minnesota as a state-name community of many peoples. Kikuyu (Gikuyu / Agĩkũyũ), Luo, Luhya, Kamba, Kalenjin, Kisii, Meru, Maasai, coastal Mijikenda, Kenyan Somali, and others are not one file, and they should not be treated as one. Book the language this household names, because although English and Kiswahili are official in Kenya, neither is the home language until this family says so, and a “Kenyan interpreter” is not a language.

### Who this is

This is not Somali. If the household is Kenyan Somali and names Somali, open Somali Minnesota instead, since a shared Horn and a shared border are not shared culture. This is not Ethiopian, and it is not Oromo as a synonym; Oromo people live in Kenya, and if this household is Oromo, open Oromo Minnesota. This is not historic African American either, because shared race in the United States is not shared culture.

### Who this is not

Minnesota Compass (ACS 2020–2024) puts Kenyan Minnesota near 20,222 (give or take 3,897), with about 71.4 percent living in the Twin Cities and about 28.6 percent in Greater Minnesota (each give or take 7.9 points). About 40.8 percent are age 17 or younger, the 65+ share is too small to publish, and about 68.8 percent are foreign-born. Among those age 5+, 65.1 percent speak a language other than English, and 26.5 percent speak English less than “very well.” Date the number when you use it, and remember that a rate is not the person.

The diversity inside this state name is the point. Picture a Kikuyu Pentecostal nurse in the suburbs, a Luo Catholic household, a Luhya factory family in Greater Minnesota, a Kenyan Somali household that should have been booked Somali, a U.S.-born student who uses English with friends and Gikuyu with an elder, and a Muslim coastal family. They share a Compass row, but they do not share a Tuesday.

### How to read this

Always defer to the person in front of you, because this page is a hypothesis and you still have to test it on this family.

sections.heading: Origins and the Founding of a People
sections.body:
Kenya is a state of many nations. There is Kikuyu highland peoplehood around Mount Kenya and Luo peoplehood on Lake Victoria, and there are Luhya, Kamba, Kalenjin, Kisii, and Meru peoples, Maasai pastoral peoplehood, coastal Swahili and Mijikenda worlds, Kenyan Somali in the northeast, and others besides. Because there is no single Kenyan ethnicity, ask which people they are rather than lecturing them on a taxonomy they did not ask for.

### History for the meeting

English and Kiswahili as official languages are colonial and national history, which makes them literacy for the desk rather than permission to skip the home language. Independence in 1963 ended the British colony. Mau Mau is literacy as well, but it is not a speech you give the family, and it is not every household’s story.

### What people brought

What people brought includes ethnic language, English, Kiswahili, church and mosque, harambee as a named mutual-aid ethic in some rooms, kin obligation, and a memory of colony and of the state that followed. What they met in Minnesota was an English form, one “East African” checkbox, and often Somali, because the building already had that page.

Do not start with a safari sentence, and do not assume Nairobi as identity, since many people name a district, a people, or a village instead.

sections.heading: The Geography of the Kenyan World
sections.body:
Homeland is not one map, because Kenya includes the central highlands, Nyanza, Western, the Rift Valley, the coast, and the north, and Nairobi is not the whole of it. A person may name Kiambu, Kisumu, Kakamega, Machakos, Eldoret, or Mombasa rather than the capital. Rather than refereeing regional politics in a waiver meeting, listen when they name a place.

### Homeland

The diaspora is global, with communities in Texas, Minnesota, Washington State, Maryland and D.C., Georgia, the Gulf, and the UK. Minnesota holds a real community. By the ACS birthplace count for 2020–2024, Minnesota has 16,726 Kenya-born residents, second among states only to Texas (22,911). LeadingAge Minnesota’s workforce director told LeadingAge in 2024 that Minnesota’s Kenyan population is the largest per capita of any state; that is one person’s statement. Secondary migration, church networks, and healthcare work pulled people here.

### Minnesota

In Minnesota, Compass puts 71.4 percent of this community in the Twin Cities and 28.6 percent in Greater Minnesota, a Greater Minnesota share that is larger than the Ethiopian Compass share and larger than the Liberian Compass share. That is why you should not assume Minneapolis. Do not assume Cedar-Riverside either, because that hub is Somali unless this family happens to live there, and do not assume the person in front of you has ever been to Kenya.

sections.heading: Independence, Skilled Streams, and 2007–08 — Foundational Events
sections.body:
There is no single 1975 or 1991 on this page. Independence in 1963 is the political founding of the state, while the later Minnesota streams are mixed: students, family, diversity visas, skilled work including healthcare, and, for some households, displacement after the 2007–08 post-election violence. Because the streams are mixed, do not file every Kenyan household as refugee, and do not file every Kenyan household as a nurse.

### Foundational events

2007–08 is named memory for some, carrying killing, camps, and flight. It is literacy rather than a personality, and it is not a reason to skip screening. You do not referee Kikuyu/Luo or other ethnic politics in a waiver meeting, and you do not pick a side as DHS.

### Who you meet

Healthcare recruitment is a Minnesota labor fact in some rooms, since LeadingAge and related pipelines have named Kenya as a nursing source. That is work, though, and it is neither a personality nor the whole Compass row.

The desk in 2026 meets first-generation professionals and U.S.-born children who speak English with peers, who are still translating for family, and who still cannot get Gikuyu or Dholuo in a lobby that offered Somali or “African.” If all you know is “East African,” you will miss this household.

sections.heading: Family
sections.body:
Some households are extended, and elders may hold authority in some of them. Harambee, which means pulling together through fundraising and mutual aid, is a hypothesis in some families rather than a personality you assign. Compass puts the average household size at about 3.31, and the person who cares for a disabled adult or a child may be a brother, a cousin, or a church mother rather than the legally recognized caregiver on the checkbox. That is why hour caps and “natural supports” can dump unpaid work onto the women in that network and call it culture.

### Who is in the household

Naming is already a who, because English or Christian given names sit beside ethnic names, and Luo naming is not Kikuyu naming. Do not invent a last name because the screen requires one, and do not assume three Somali names.

### Who speaks

The person who speaks in the lobby may be a child with the best English, but that child is not the qualified interpreter, and CLAS still stands. Ask who should be in the room. Minnesota law still stands as well, so do not skip mandated reporting and call it humility.

sections.heading: Minnesota and Kenyan History
sections.body:
Minnesota holds a Kenyan Compass community large enough that this department will meet it on waivers, child welfare, health care, cash, food, aging, and employment. It is also large enough that the building has developed a habit of hearing East Africa and booking Somali. Compass counts about 20,222, give or take 3,897 (ACS 2020–2024), and because Greater Minnesota is 28.6 percent of that, do not write this people as a Minneapolis anecdote.

### Places

Think in places rather than a blob: Twin Cities suburbs, Minneapolis and St. Paul pockets, and Greater Minnesota towns with hospitals, factories, and housing. Churches, both ethnic congregations and Kenyan fellowships, are public life, but they are not consultation, and a food visit does not make you the expert.

### Partners

The partners are the churches families name; ethnic associations (Luo, Kikuyu, Luhya, and others as this household names them); professional and nursing networks as doors rather than a staffing plan; and CECLC as a department door, not the whole. Pay the partner this household actually uses.

Book a qualified interpreter, and pay for community work. Do not assign either to staff because of who they are. A Jamhuri or harambee visit is optional professional development if you are invited, and while you are a guest there, being one does not make you the expert.

sections.heading: Kenyan Minnesota — the heart of a people
sections.body:
Kenyans are people of many nations under one state name, and public systems may file them under East African, Black, and sometimes Somali. Ask how the person identifies. Peoplehood after colony and after 1963 is not a safari poster, and since Kikuyu, Luo, Luhya, and the rest do not share one Tuesday, you do not pick a side.

### In this state

In this building another fact sits on top: many of these households are Black in a U.S. racial order that can file them under Somali or under historic African American and get the language, the church, and the name wrong. Shared race is not shared culture, and shared Horn geography is not shared language.

Ask plainly whether the person agrees with the plan, and make it easy to say no.

This guide is a working orientation, and because individual variation always supersedes group generalization, always defer to the person in front of you.

sections.heading: Core Concepts
sections.body:
Start with which people. Kikuyu, Luo, Luhya, Kamba, Kalenjin, Kisii, Meru, Maasai, Kenyan Somali, and others all live in this community, so ask, because the Compass row is not the ethnic file.

### Which language

The languages include Gikuyu, Dholuo, Luhya languages, Kikamba, Kalenjin languages, Kiswahili, English, and others. A “Kenyan interpreter” is not a language, and a Somali interpreter is the wrong door unless this household is Somali.

### Harambee as hypothesis

Harambee means mutual aid, fundraising, and pulling together, and staff do not use it as a guilt tool; if the family names it, you listen.

### Faith is plural

Protestant, Pentecostal, Catholic, AIC, Islam, and none all exist here, so follow this room.

Do not referee Kikuyu/Luo or other ethnic politics in a waiver meeting, and do not assume Nairobi.

### Work and school

Nursing is a job rather than a personality, and a rate is not the person.

sections.heading: Religion
sections.body:
Christianity is the large public stream in Kenyan Minnesota, in Protestant, Pentecostal, Catholic, and African Independent / AIC churches, while Islam lives on the coast, among Kenyan Somali, and in some other families. Traditional practice sits in some rooms, and it is not a souvenir, and none is also a Tuesday. Ask, rather than assuming Muslim the way you might with Somali.

### Streams

The church is a center of ritual, mutual aid, and information, and it is often the first Minnesota network a family has, but it is still not “the community.” Do not BCC one pastor and call it consultation, and do not make clergy the case plan unless this family asked.

### Practice

Funerals gather family and can run long. You still keep medical and legal time, and when the two collide you name the conflict instead of punishing it.

In Muslim rooms, Arabic may be religion rather than the interview language, and Kiswahili may be church or market language rather than the home language, so book the interview language.

sections.heading: Greetings
sections.body:
Ask who to greet first, or follow the household’s lead. English “hello” is ordinary in many professional rooms, and Kiswahili habari and related forms live in some rooms, so ask which greeting the person prefers. Ethnic greetings exist, so ask about them.

### Titles

Wait to see whether a hand is offered, and if it is not, nod.

### This room

Let this person’s own greeting guide you, whatever you read on another page.

Ask before any physical contact, and let the person set the limit. Say the name.

sections.heading: Naming Conventions
sections.body:
English and Christian given names are common, a legacy of mission schools and the colonial record, and ethnic names sit beside them or instead of them. Kikuyu names are not Luo names, and Luo names (Ochieng, Achieng, Odhiambo, and others) are not a joke and not a clan icebreaker you pulled from a coworker. Luhya, Kamba, and Kalenjin naming each have their own grammar, so ask.

### How to file

U.S. forms want first-middle-last, and Kenyan naming may not match. Do not invent a last name because the screen requires one, since that invented name becomes a gate, and do not assume three Somali names.

Ask how to say the name, ask how to file it, and pronounce it. Women may or may not take a husband’s name in U.S. records, which means mother and child may not match, and that is not fraud until you have a reason to think so.

sections.heading: Dates of Significance
sections.body:
Jamhuri Day, 12 December, marks Independence / Republic. Madaraka Day (1 June) and Mashujaa Day (20 October) also matter, and Mazingira Day (10 October) is also a public holiday in 2026. Schedule around the ones this family names when you can, remembering that a calendar click is not community engagement and that you are a guest if invited.

### Calendar

Christmas and Easter follow church calendars, and Eid matters in Muslim rooms. Ethnic rites, Kikuyu, Luo, and others, are named by some families and not by others, so ask, and do not put them on a case note as color.

The 2007–08 post-election violence is memory for some, not a holiday, so do not put it on a file as color, and do not collect it as a risk score.

Do not put an “African holiday” or Somali dates on this page by default; ask this family.

sections.heading: Education
sections.body:
Compass (ACS 2020–2024) reports that among Kenyan Minnesotans 25 and older, about 91.5 percent have a high school education or higher and about 39.4 percent have a bachelor’s or higher. Date Compass when you cite it, and note that about 68.8 percent of the community is foreign-born. High attainment is a pattern, but it is not proof the grandmother needs no interpreter, and it is not permission to skip the IEP in the home language.

### School and language

A parent who speaks fluent Gikuyu or Dholuo and limited English is not illiterate. Many Kenyans were schooled in English and some elders were not, which is why the English-only form is still a gate. Book this language, the one the household names, because the child is not the interpreter.

Second-generation educational mobility is real, and so is a gap that a room that treats everyone the same will call “culture.” Do not treat a nurse in the family as proof that the waiver household heard the form.

sections.heading: Etiquette
sections.body:
Ask who to greet first, or follow the household’s lead. If food or drink is offered, accepting a little is fine, and you can still keep to medical and legal timelines.

### In the home

If you visit a home, look for shoes by the door or ask what the household prefers. Ask before taking any photograph, and enter a prayer space only if you are invited.

### Time

If someone misses an appointment, first check the time, transport, interpreter and work schedule. Confirm the plan in the language the person uses, and ask whether it works for them.

Book a qualified interpreter instead of using a child to go between.

sections.heading: Language and Communication
sections.body:
Book the language this household names, which may be Gikuyu (Kikuyu), Dholuo, a Luhya language, Kikamba, a Kalenjin language, Kisii, Kimeru, Kiswahili, English, or something else, because a “Kenyan interpreter” is not a language. Kiswahili is official, but it is not always the language of home. A Somali interpreter is the wrong door unless this household is Somali, and Arabic may be religion rather than the interview language.

### Language

Compass reports that among those 5 and older, about 65.1 percent speak a language other than English and about 26.5 percent speak English less than “very well,” so date the number. Many Kenyans use English at work, but the IEP still has to reach the parent who does not.

Give the person time to answer. If you get a short yes, check that the plan was understood, and ask whether it works for them.

Do not use a child as the interpreter, and do not make a Kenyan coworker the interpreter.

sections.heading: Other Considerations
sections.body:
This section states hard facts plainly, because treating everyone the same can hide them.

### Named harms

Intra-Kenyan ethnic politics are real, among Kikuyu, Luo, and others, and they include 2007–08 memory. Do not pick a side as DHS, do not referee in a waiver meeting, and do not file politics as a risk score.

FGC exists in some Kenyan communities, including some Kenyan Somali and some other groups, and Minnesota law stands. Because this is not the Somali page, do not invent a Kenyan rate, and do not mash Somali prevalence onto this household. Follow mandated reporting, and still see a family.

Queer and trans Kenyan Minnesotans exist, so you use the name, and you do not out someone to kin and call it culture. Kenya’s own law climate is not Minnesota’s, so do not skip mandated reporting and call it humility.

Enforcement climate is structure for some, so do not collect status you do not need, and do not treat fear as noncompliance. Staff who share this community may add facts, but they do not get to delete a fact because it is hard to say.

sections.heading: Health
sections.body:
Believe reported pain, and do not fold this history into Tuskegee or into a Somali MDH slide, because this is not those pages.

### Access

Hepatitis B screening for people born in Kenya is a U.S. public-health pattern, since CDC has treated Kenya as a higher-prevalence birth country in its screening guidance. Date the CDC page you cite, do not invent a Minnesota rate, and do not skip screening because the person looks well.

Compass puts disability at 5.2 percent, a dated figure. Mental-health stigma is real in some families, and 2007–08 and other trauma sit in some rooms, so remember that a smile is not a PHQ-9. No dated Kenyan-specific Minnesota autism rate belongs on this page, which means you should not invent one, and you should not mash Somali ADDM here.

Distance running as a Kenyan stereotype is not a file, not a compliment, and not a clinical assumption. Gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care, so offer it. Traditional medicine and church healing often sit beside biomedicine, so ask about them and work it out together. On FGC, Minnesota law stands, but do not invent a rate, and do not skip care.

sections.heading: LGBTQ
sections.body:
Queer and trans Kenyan Minnesotans exist. Conservative family, church, and some mosque climates can mean silence or exile, and some people live a public English life alongside a private home-language life, so you use the name they use and do not share what they tell you unless a rule requires it.

### This person

Minnesota’s Human Rights Act still applies, and Kenya’s law climate is not this state’s. Do not question a household about anyone’s sexuality or gender, and take seriously that some people have reason to keep it private.

Ethnic politics and church do not override what this person wants, so always defer to the person in front of you.

sections.heading: Hair, Dress, and Body
sections.body:
Kanga, kitenge, and Kikuyu and Luo ceremonial dress are public at weddings, at Jamhuri, and on some church stages, but they are not a daily uniform, and the second generation looks like Minnesota. Do not ask a woman in clinic whether she “still wears the costume.”

### Dress

Some Muslim women wear hijab and modest dress, and not all do, so do not assume covering, and do not rank covering.

This is not the CROWN Act chapter, and yet anti-Blackness still sits on Black Kenyan bodies in U.S. clinics, schools, and traffic stops. Ask this person rather than mashing historic African American hair politics onto them as a script, while not ignoring those politics either. Do not touch.

sections.heading: Music
sections.body:
Benga, gospel, taarab on the coast, Luo and Kikuyu popular forms, diaspora pop, and church choir are all part of this music, which is named variation rather than a playlist. Ethnic politics can sit inside a song, so you do not put the wrong anthem on a speaker.

### Variation

A funeral is not staff entertainment, and a playlist is not engagement, so do not request a political song as an icebreaker in a waiver meeting.

Jamhuri stages are public life, but they are not consultation and not a case plan.

sections.heading: Sports
sections.body:
Distance running as a public image of Kenya is not a personality, not a compliment you give a child in clinic, and not a file. Soccer shows up, basketball too, and school sport is ordinary for the second generation.

### Not the whole person

Do not assume the kid runs, and do not assume the kid plays, because sport should not be the only excellence you can see.

Sport clubs are social infrastructure for some families, but they are not language access and not a case plan, and Greater Minnesota teams are still this people when the family lives there.

sections.heading: Literature
sections.body:
English and Kiswahili made modern written publics, and Gikuyu and other ethnic literatures sit beside them, while oral forms are older than all of them. Ngũgĩ wa Thiong’o is literacy for the desk rather than a speech you give the family in the lobby, and Minnesota and U.S. Kenyan writers and journalists exist.

### Literacy in the lobby

What you do need to know is that this is not a people without letters. Many people read English while some elders read only a home language, which is why a notice that exists only in English will not work, so ask.

Tones and names are not decoration, so write what they tell you.

sections.heading: Art
sections.body:
Kanga slogans, beadwork, and wood carving are a public image of Kenya, but they are not the whole, and they are not a safari souvenir you put on a Heritage Month table. Church art and diaspora visual work belong here too, while ugali, chapati, chai, and nyama choma are foodway rather than consultation.

### Guest

You are a guest, not a researcher. A church or harambee visit is optional professional development rather than consultation, so do not photograph a family as tourism.

A Heritage Month that mashes this people with a Somali poster, an Ethiopian flag, or a historic African American exhibit has already mashed the adjacent peoples together.

sections.heading: Colony, 2007–08, and Intra-Community Politics
sections.body:
British colony, Mau Mau as literacy for the desk rather than a speech, independence in 1963, and the 2007–08 post-election violence as named memory for some: that is the political event. Intra-Kenyan ethnic politics, including Kikuyu/Luo memory, live in Minnesota rooms, so do not referee, and do not pick a side as DHS.

### The badge

A DHS badge is not automatically help, so do not use 2007 as a personality, and do not ask a person to narrate killing for your professional development.

Enforcement climate in the United States is a different state, and it still keeps some people away, because it changes who opens the door, and that is not noncompliance. Do not collect status you do not need, and do not collect ethnic or political speech as a risk score.

sections.heading: Work, Markets, and Government
sections.body:
Healthcare and nursing are a Minnesota labor pattern in some rooms, alongside a professional class, small business, factory work, and public employment. Compass puts median household income at about $92,570, poverty at 10.6 percent, renters at 59.3 percent, and about 90.9 percent of working-age adults employed, all dated figures, and a rate is not the person. Nursing is a job, which means it is not a personality and not the whole economy.

### Work

Book a qualified interpreter, and pay for community work. Do not assign either to staff because of who they are.

### Staff

Take time to introduce yourself and explain the plan. The first visit may not be the decision, and any required notice still goes out. Pay the partner this household names.

sections.heading: Health-care and Human-service Encounters
sections.body:
Which people and which language are the first thing to get right, because an interpreter labeled Kenyan, Swahili, Somali, or African who does not speak the language this household speaks will not work. Book Gikuyu, Dholuo, a Luhya language, Kiswahili, or whatever they name, and still book a qualified interpreter, but do not use a child, and do not make staff the interpreter.

### Language

Pay attention to who is in the room: a child pushed forward as the English speaker, a pastor in the story, pain you must believe, a running stereotype in the chart, intra-community tension in the waiting room, and the deportation climate.

### The meeting

Offer gender match, ask who should hear, and ask how to file the name. If they name traditional medicine or church healing, listen, while remembering that mandated reporting still exists. Believe reported pain, and do not mix Tuskegee or Somali CI into this history.

sections.heading: Adjacent Peoples — Do Not Mash
sections.body:
This is not Somali, so if this household is Kenyan Somali and names Somali, open Somali Minnesota. It is not Ethiopian, and it is not Oromo as a synonym; Oromo people live in Kenya, and if this household is Oromo, open Oromo Minnesota. It is not Ugandan and not Tanzanian, because shared Kiswahili is not shared peoplehood, and it is not historic African American, not Liberian, and not Nigerian.

### Adjacent doors

Never book one East African interpreter, never reach for one Kenyan module, and never reach for one Black module. Some households are mixed, so ask this household.

Shared Christianity is not shared culture, shared Islam is not shared culture, and shared race is not shared culture.

sections.heading: Counts, Dated
sections.body:
Minnesota Compass, ACS 2020–2024, describes the Kenyan cultural community as about 20,222 people (give or take 3,897), with 71.4% in the Twin Cities and 28.6% in Greater Minnesota (each give or take 7.9 points). Those age 17 or younger are 40.8%, the 65+ share is too small to publish, and the foreign-born share is 68.8%. Among those age 5+, 65.1% speak a language other than English and 26.5% speak English less than “very well,” while among those 25+, 91.5% have high school or higher and 39.4% have a bachelor’s or higher. Median household income is about $92,570 (2024 dollars, give or take $19,152), poverty is 10.6%, owner-occupied housing is 40.7% and renter-occupied is 59.3%, average household size is 3.31, disability is 5.8%, and working-age employment is 90.9%.

### Counts

Date Compass, and do not invent other rates. Counts disagree across ACS vintages and definitions (ancestry vs. birthplace vs. language), which is why you date the number you cite.

### What the count is not

A young age structure is not a personality, and a high bachelor’s rate is not proof the elder heard the form. Greater Minnesota at 28.6 percent is a channel, while language and child-as-interpreter are gates, and a rate is not the person.

sections.heading: Doors and Sources
sections.body:
The doors begin with the Minnesota Compass Kenyan profile (ACS 2020–2024). They include the churches and ethnic associations this family names, Luo, Kikuyu, Luhya, and others as they name them, along with professional and nursing networks as doors rather than a staffing plan, while CECLC is a door, not the whole community.

### Public doors

If this household is Somali, open Somali Minnesota, and if Oromo, open Oromo Minnesota. Book the language they name.

### Where to learn more

Use these resources yourself before you ask a Kenyan colleague to explain, and do not count a BCC to a church as consultation. Pay partners, and report back. Be a guest at Jamhuri if invited, remembering that it is not consultation.

sections.heading: How it hits DHS gates — the 40%
sections.body:
Workplace culture and service delivery are both candidates here.

Language: an interpreter labeled Kenyan, Swahili, Somali, or African who is not Gikuyu, Dholuo, a Luhya language, or whatever this household names will not work, because Kiswahili is official and is not always the language of home. Still book a qualified interpreter, and do not use a child. Gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care.

Names: English plus ethnic names. The database that invents a last name, or that assumes three Somali names, is a gate that follows the person.

Hour caps, exception processes, and life-sharing matches without language are not culturally neutral.

Child welfare and disability: help-seeking that becomes a report is part of why people wait. Mandated reporting still exists, and so does the duty not to treat a whole community as a risk score. On FGC, Minnesota law stands, but this is not the Somali page, and you do not invent a rate.

Notices and comment: do not count an eList and an English PDF as reaching this community, and record who was reached and what follow-up happened. Greater Minnesota is 28.6 percent, so a Minneapolis meeting is not the whole channel.

Workforce: Kenyan staff are not the interpreter pool and not the community. Staff are colleagues, not the curriculum, and should not be treated as either, since nursing is a job, not a staffing plan for language.

Somali mash and Black mash: opening Somali because East Africa, or historic African American because both are Black, shuts the person out.

Legislation, funding, rule: study a channel before you advocate for it. Use this page so that the 40% has a household in it.

sections.heading: A Note on This Guide
sections.body:
This brief is about Korean Minnesota as two households that share a Compass row and do not share a Tuesday. One is the immigrant Korean family, including elders who need Korean in the lobby, and the other is the Korean adoptee, a population that is itself Minnesota history. Adoptee households are often white Minnesota families with Korean-born adults in them. That is not the same as an immigrant Korean household and is not “no culture” either. For that reason, do not skip this page because the person is English-dominant, and do not ask an adoptee to represent “the Korean community.”

### Who this is

This is not a Census “Asian” mash, and it is not Chinese, Japanese, Hmong, or Vietnamese, because a shared continent is not a shared culture. In the same way, Seollal is not Chinese New Year as a file, and it is not Hmong New Year. Use this page for context and questions. It does not describe the person in front of you.

### Who this is not

Minnesota Compass (ACS 2020–2024) puts Korean ancestry near 28,180 (give or take 2,630), with about 76.2 percent living in the Twin Cities and 23.8 percent in Greater Minnesota. About 36.4 percent are age 17 or younger, while those 65 and older are only about 2.6 percent, and foreign-born is about 44.7 percent. Among those 5 and older, about 81.5 percent speak English only, about 18.5 percent speak a language other than English, and about 8.7 percent speak English less than “very well.” Among those 25 and older, about 95.9 percent have a high school diploma or higher and about 63.6 percent hold a bachelor’s or higher. Median household income is about $102,938 in 2024 dollars (give or take $20,667), and poverty is 3.7 percent. About 64.1 percent of homes are owner-occupied, the average household size is about 2.29, and about 37.4 percent of individuals live alone, so be sure to date whichever number you use.

MPR News calls Minnesota home to the largest Korean adoptee population in the U.S., and Sahan Journal (July 29, 2024) used “about 10,000-15,000” Korean adoptees in Minnesota. Date that figure as a news estimate, because Compass does not split adoptee vs immigrant. AKConnection has said Minnesota holds on the order of 10 percent of Korean adoptees worldwide, and the pattern these estimates show is that this state is a hub, although a count is never the person.

### How to read this

Always defer to the person in front of you, because this page is only a hypothesis that you still test on this family.

sections.heading: Origins and the Founding of a People
sections.body:
Korean peoplehood is older than 1945, older than the war, and older than the adoption file. Kingdoms on the peninsula, Hangul (promulgated in the fifteenth century, then suppressed and revived), honorific speech, and clan surnames are literacy for the desk, rather than a lecture you give a parent who came in for a waiver.

### History for the meeting

The Japanese occupation (1910–1945) and the Korean War (1950–1953) are the modern political break that left the peninsula divided. The Republic of Korea and the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea are not a mash you referee in a lobby, and since most Minnesota immigrant households name the South, there is no reason to test them on it. Nor should you ask an adoptee to narrate a war they were not asked to remember.

### What people brought

What people brought includes language, church or temple or neither, education as both mobility and pressure, foodways, and a memory of occupation and war. What adoptees met was a Minnesota family, often Lutheran or Catholic, along with a file and a country that later argued about whether the passport was real. What they met in this department was an English form, one “Asian” checkbox, and often an assumption that an LEP rate of 8.7 percent means you can skip Korean.

sections.heading: The Geography of the Korean World
sections.body:
The homeland is the peninsula, rather than a Seoul tourism map or Pyongyang as a personality. The Republic of Korea is the sending country for most Minnesota immigrant and adoptee files, while the North is a political fact in the news and in some families that you do not referee.

### Homeland

The global diaspora includes Los Angeles, New York, China, Central Asia, and a Minnesota concentration that is unusual because of adoption. Compass puts about 76.2 percent in the Twin Cities and 23.8 percent in Greater Minnesota.
