That means suburbs, university areas, and the Greater Minnesota church-and-farm towns that received adoptees are all on this page.

### Minnesota

Do not assume Minneapolis, and do not assume they have been to Seoul. An adoptee raised in a western Minnesota town is still this people, just as an immigrant elder in a first-ring suburb is still this people.

sections.heading: War, Church, 1965, and the Adoption Pipeline — Foundational Events
sections.body:
The Japanese occupation, and then the Korean War (1950–1953), broke families and filled GI and missionary channels. Minnesota’s Lutheran and other churches sat on those channels. The adoption of Korean children into Minnesota homes is therefore this state’s history rather than a side note, and MNopedia documents the pipeline. Peaks in the 1980s–1990s sit in today’s adult population, even though Compass does not split them out.

### Foundational events

Hart-Celler (1965) opened skilled and family immigration, and later waves brought students, professionals, and church-sponsored families. Immigrant Korean Minnesota built congregations, Presbyterian especially, that serve as civic hubs, although that hub is not the adoptee’s church unless they say so.

### Who you meet

The Child Citizenship Act of 2000 (signed October 30, 2000; effective February 27, 2001) granted automatic citizenship to certain foreign-born children, including adoptees, who were under 18 on the effective date, but it was not retroactive for people already 18. Adoptee Citizenship Act bills (introduced from 2015, and reintroduced in 2018, 2019, 2021, and 2024, with the 2025 Protect Adoptees and American Families Act in the same line) have tried to close that gap. Date the law that exists and date the advocacy separately, so that you do not invent this person’s status or collect status you do not need.

sections.heading: Family
sections.body:
In immigrant streams, family-name-first naming, generation names, and obligation to elders are a hypothesis to test rather than a rule. Households can be multi-generation or Compass-small (average size about 2.29), and about 37.4 percent live alone. Ask who should be in the room.

### Who is in the household

Adoptee households often include white Minnesota parents, siblings who may not be Korean, and an adult who is Korean-born. Kin search may point to Korea, to a closed file, or to no one. Because of that, do not assume Korean relatives in the metro, and do not assume the adoptive family is either the barrier or the solution; ask this person instead.

### Who speaks

Marriage, in-law duty, and who holds the child’s medical decision may not match the English form. Minnesota law still stands, which means you do not skip mandated reporting and call it culture.

Do not use an adoptee’s family as a lesson about “good Minnesota parents,” and do not use an immigrant family as a lesson about “strict Asians,” since neither family is a lesson.

sections.heading: Minnesota and Korean History
sections.body:
This department will meet this community on waivers, child welfare, health care, aging, adoption-adjacent adult services, student households, and employment. Compass puts about 76.2 percent in the Twin Cities and 23.8 percent in Greater Minnesota. Greater Minnesota is not an afterthought, because the adoption pipeline placed children in towns that still hold those adults.

### Places

Korean churches, Presbyterian especially but also Methodist, Catholic, and others, are civic hubs for some immigrant families, offering language, jobs, and information. Even so, they are not “the community.” Adoptees may be Minnesota Lutheran or Catholic with no Korean congregation at all, so do not send them to a Korean church as programming.

### Partners

AKConnection, established in 2000, has been a Minnesota networking organization for adult Korean adoptees. Peer adoptee-led groups and Korean Association groups exist as well. Pay the door this person names. Book a qualified interpreter, and pay for community work. Do not assign either to staff because of who they are. Do not treat an adoptee coworker as your source on adoption or Korean culture.

Seollal and Chuseok are public at events run by community organizations, such as the Korean Cultural Association and JangmiArts (Seollal, February 21, 2026) and AK Connection (Chuseok Festival, September 26, 2026), and if you go, go as a guest, remembering that a festival or a church lunch is not consultation.

sections.heading: Two households in one Compass row
sections.body:
To be Korean in Minnesota is often to be asked whether you were adopted, or whether you “speak it,” as if those were the only two rooms. It is also to be filed under a checkbox that also holds Chinese, Hmong, and Japanese histories this household does not share.

### In this state

Immigrant Korean Minnesota and Korean adoptee Minnesota share a war and a peninsula, but they do not share a kitchen, a church, or a language on Tuesday. That is why you should not ask an adoptee to represent “the Korean community,” or ask an immigrant elder to explain an adoptee’s grief. Nor should you skip this page because the person in front of you sounds like Minnesota.

Ask plainly whether the person agrees with the plan, and make it easy to say no. Adoptee grief, citizenship anxiety, and a body that does not match the family photograph travel into others.

This guide is a working orientation, and individual variation always supersedes group generalization.

sections.heading: Core Concepts
sections.body:
Language comes first: Korean, Hangul, and honorific speech. Book Korean for immigrant elders, and since adoptees may want Korean for a parent visit or may not, ask them, remembering that an LEP rate of 8.7 percent is not zero.

### Name

The family name comes first, as in Kim, Lee/Yi, Park/Pak, Choi, and Jung, so do not “correct” Lee, and treat adoptee American names as the names they are.

Adoptee is not “no culture,” and English-dominant is not a skip, which is also why an adoptee coworker should not be used as culture.

### Church as hub — some immigrant families

Some adoptees are Minnesota Lutheran/Catholic, and neither church is the case plan unless they asked.

### Model-minority

Do not use the model-minority story, because it hides LEP elders, 3.7 percent poverty, disability, and adoptee grief.

### North/South

North and South are literacy for you, not a referee job.

sections.heading: Religion
sections.body:
Protestant Christianity, especially Presbyterian, is large in the immigrant stream, and Catholic, Buddhist, and none also live here. Church can be the civic hub for Korean language, jobs, a ride, or a funeral, but because it is not “the community,” do not make a pastor the case plan unless this family asked.

### Streams

Adoptees may be Minnesota Lutheran, Catholic, evangelical, or none, with no Korean congregation, so do not assign a Korean church as cultural programming, and do not assume no faith either.

### Practice

Do not treat Buddhist practice as a souvenir, and do not treat church as the evolved version. Sunday is operations for some immigrant households, although you still keep medical and legal time.

sections.heading: Greetings
sections.body:
A bow or nod with elders is ordinary in many immigrant rooms, while a handshake is ordinary in many professional rooms and in most adoptee rooms. Follow the person’s lead on greetings.

### Titles

Honorific speech in Korean marks age and status, and you do not need to perform it yourself, because what you need is to book an interpreter who can. An English “hello” plus the name is ordinary.

### This room

Let this person’s own greeting guide you, whatever you read on another page.

Ask before any physical contact, and let the person set the limit.

sections.heading: Naming Conventions
sections.body:
In Korean the family name comes first, as in Kim, Lee (Yi / Rhee), Park (Pak), Choi, and Jung (Jeong), and generation names may sit inside a two-syllable given name. U.S. forms reverse the order, so the same person can appear as Kim Min-jun and as Minjun Kim, which is a system failure and not a fraud signal until you have a reason.

### How to file

Lee is not a misspelling, so do not “correct” it to Li or to a Chinese romanization, and do not mash it with Chinese Chen or with Japanese names.

Adoptees often carry an American given name and family name from the adoptive household, and because they may or may not use a Korean name, ask. Do not demand the “real” name, and ask how to say a person’s name before you call it out in a waiting room.

Pronounce the name, and ask how it is said rather than joking that there are “too many Kims.”

sections.heading: Dates of Significance
sections.body:
Seollal is the Korean Lunar New Year, a time of family, food, and sometimes hanbok. It shares a related lunar calendar with Chinese New Year, Hmong New Year, and Tết, but because it belongs to a different people, do not put “Asian holiday” on a case note.

### Calendar

Chuseok is the harvest and ancestral remembrance, and it is literacy for you rather than a file.

The Korean War, 1950–1953, and its memorial days are literacy for the desk, rather than a speech you give the family or a day off the work.

Adoptee gathering days, camps, and reunions are literacy, not consultation. The Child Citizenship Act, effective February 27, 2001, is law history, and it is not this person’s status unless they name it.

A calendar click is not community engagement.

sections.heading: Education
sections.body:
Compass (ACS 2020–2024) reports that among Korean Minnesotans 25 and older, about 95.9 percent have a high school diploma or higher and about 63.6 percent hold a bachelor’s or higher. Among those 5 and older, English only is about 81.5 percent and LEP is about 8.7 percent, but the average is not the elder in front of you.

### School and language

The 8.7 percent figure is low compared with Vietnamese or Hmong on Compass, but it is not “no language gate.” An English IEP, an English waiver exception, and an English comment PDF still close the door for that elder and for a new arrival.

Education pressure in some immigrant streams is a hypothesis in research and in some households. It is not this teenager, and it is not an excuse to skip mental-health screening. Adoptee school histories include Minnesota classrooms that had no Korean peer, so do not mash those stories together.

A parent who reads Hangul and limited English is not illiterate, which is why you book Korean.

sections.heading: Etiquette
sections.body:
Ask who to greet first, or follow the household’s lead. If you visit a home, look for shoes by the door or ask what the household prefers. Follow the person’s lead.

### In the home

Adoptee households may run on Minnesota Lutheran or Catholic manners, with shoes on, first names, and a casserole, and that is culture too. Do not correct it toward a Seoul script.

### Time

If food or drink is offered, accepting a little is fine, and you can still keep to medical and legal timelines.

If someone misses an appointment, first check the time, transport, interpreter and work schedule. Confirm the plan in the language the person uses, and ask whether it works for them.

sections.heading: Language and Communication
sections.body:
Korean, Hangul, and honorific speech are the language facts, so book Korean for immigrant elders and for anyone who asks. Adoptees may want Korean for a clinic visit with a parent, for a trip, or not at all, which means you should ask rather than assigning a tutor as programming.

### Language

Compass puts language other than English at about 18.5 percent and LEP at about 8.7 percent (age 5+), and you should date it. Low compared with Vietnamese or Hmong is not a skip, since new arrivals and elders are inside that 8.7 percent. English-dominant adoptees are inside the 81.5 percent English-only and are still on this page.

A Cantonese, Mandarin, Chinese, or Japanese mix-up will not work, and neither will an interpreter labeled “Asian.”

Give the person time to answer. If you get a short yes, check that the plan was understood, and ask whether it works for them. Do not make a Korean coworker the interpreter, and do not make an adoptee coworker the interpreter as the culture.

sections.heading: Other Considerations
sections.body:
This section states hard facts plainly, because treating everyone the same can hide them.

### Named harms

Adoptee citizenship gaps were a real U.S. legal harm. The Child Citizenship Act of 2000 covered qualifying children under 18 on February 27, 2001, and it was not retroactive for those already 18. Adoptee Citizenship Act advocacy (bills from 2015 through 2024, with the 2025 Protect Adoptees and American Families Act in the same line) has tried to close the gap, so date the law and date the advocacy. Korean Quarterly reported in January 2026 that three Korean adoptees who are U.S. citizens were detained and later released during the federal immigration operation in the Twin Cities, and that Adoptee Hub held rights and safety sessions. South Korea’s Truth and Reconciliation Commission opened a third round of adoption fraud investigations on February 26, 2026. Do not invent this person’s status, do not collect status you do not need, and do not treat fear as noncompliance.

North/South politics are in the news and in some rooms, which is exactly why you do not referee them and do not fly a flag as inclusion.

Mental health and suicide risk is a documented conversation in Korean and adoptee communities, so do not invent a Minnesota rate, do not skip screening, and do not make it a personality.

LGBTQ Korean Minnesotans exist. The model-minority story hides LEP elders and adoptee grief, even though a 3.7 percent poverty rate is not zero and a 8.7 percent LEP rate is a gate.

Staff who share this community may add facts, but they do not get to delete a fact because it is hard to say.

sections.heading: Health
sections.body:
Book Korean for the elder who needs it, because an LEP rate of 8.7 percent (Compass, age 5+) is a gate rather than a rounding error, and an English consent form is not consent if they could not run it.

### Access

Mental health and suicide risk is a documented Korean and adoptee conversation in research and in community advocacy. Even so, do not invent a Minnesota rate, and do not import a South Korea national rate as a Minnesota rate. Do not skip screening because “they don’t talk about that,” or because the person is high-attaining or English-dominant, and do not make it a personality.

Believe reported pain. Gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care, so offer it.

If they name a pastor, a healer, or an adoptee therapist, listen, although you should not make that person the case plan unless they asked.

sections.heading: LGBTQ
sections.body:
Queer and trans Korean Minnesotans exist in immigrant churches, in secular professional households, and in adoptee communities that have their own maps. Conservative Presbyterian and other church climates can mean silence or exile. You use the name they use and do not share what they tell you unless a rule requires it.

### This person

Minnesota’s Human Rights Act still applies. Use the name the person uses, and do not share what they tell you unless a rule requires it.

Do not assume an adoptee household is affirming because it is white and English-speaking, and do not assume an immigrant household is not affirming; ask this person instead.

sections.heading: Hair, Dress, and Body
sections.body:
Hanbok is public at Seollal and Chuseok for some immigrant families and at some adoptee cultural events, but it is not a daily uniform. The second generation and most adoptees look like Minnesota, so do not ask a woman in clinic whether she “still wears the costume,” and do not dress an adoptee in hanbok as DHS programming.

### Dress

For hair and head, follow this person’s lead, and do not touch.

Do not mash hanbok with a qipao or a kimono on the unit’s Heritage Month table.

sections.heading: Music
sections.body:
Church music is ordinary in immigrant Presbyterian streams, K-pop is public culture, including among people with no other Korean language, and pansori and traditional forms exist too, so there is not one soundtrack.

### Variation

A playlist is not engagement, and K-pop is not consultation, so do not ask a staff person or a client to perform.

Do not use a music video as the training.

sections.heading: Sports
sections.body:
Soccer, baseball, and ordinary school sport are ordinary here. Taekwondo is public culture for some families, but it becomes a stereotype if you assume it, so do not assume it.

### Not the whole person

Sport clubs are not language access and not a case plan, adoptee sports look like Minnesota high school, and immigrant church leagues are not consultation.

An elder in the stands who needs Korean still needs Korean, because a 8.7 percent LEP rate is not a skip just because the child plays varsity.

sections.heading: Literature
sections.body:
Hangul made a national written vernacular, and Korean and Korean American writers exist in both languages. Adoptee memoir and scholarship are a Minnesota literary fact (MNopedia’s trail; Winona State and other scholars). You do not need to quote a novel, but you do need to know this is not a people without letters.

### Literacy in the lobby

Literacy in Hangul is not guaranteed for adoptees or for a second generation, which means a Korean-language notice may still not work, so ask.

Do not put a proverb on a brochure and call it CLAS.

sections.heading: Art
sections.body:
Ceramics, ink, church-stage dance, Seollal public art, and adoptee-made work are public, and you should attend as a guest, since a hanbok on a stage is not a case plan and a museum visit is not consultation.

### Guest

Do not mash this with Chinese calligraphy or Japanese woodblock on an “Asian art” table.

Pay the door this person names, and do not extract a staff person’s child as New Year entertainment.

sections.heading: Conflict, War, the Church, and the State
sections.body:
The Japanese occupation, the Korean War, and division are the political event, and U.S. military and missionary presence built the adoption pipeline that made Minnesota unusual. The Child Citizenship Act of 2000 left a gap for adoptees already 18 on February 27, 2001, and advocacy to close it is current, which is one reason a DHS badge is not automatically help.

### The badge

Do not referee North and South, and do not collect immigration or citizenship status you do not need. Do not use the war or an adoption file as a personality, and do not ask a person to narrate a search, a deportation fear, or a camp for your professional development.

Filing this household as Chinese or Japanese is a state act, and it shuts the person out.

sections.heading: Work, Church, and Government
sections.body:
Work here includes small business, professional and technical work, churches as job networks, and public employment. The median household income of about $102,938 (Compass, 2024 dollars, give or take $20,667) is an average. Poverty at 3.7 percent sits in the same row, and about 37.4 percent live alone, so do not staff a program as if every household were a four-person professional family.

### Work

Book a qualified interpreter, and pay for community work. Do not assign either to staff because of who they are. Do not treat adoptee staff as the culture unit or as “the Korean community.”

### Staff

Take time to introduce yourself and explain the plan, and still give any required notice.

sections.heading: Health-care and Human-service Encounters
sections.body:
The encounter holds Korean for the elder, and an English-dominant adoptee who still needs this page. It holds the name order on the wristband, a pastor in the immigrant story and a closed adoption file in the other, mental-health screening, and a citizenship anxiety that you do not collect as status.

### Language

Ask the language and ask how to say the name, and offer gender match. Believe reported pain, and do not skip screening. Do not make staff the interpreter or use a child as interpreter, and remember that mandated reporting still exists.

### The meeting

Do not mash this encounter with a Chinese or Japanese interpreter, and do not use an adoptee coworker as culture, because a smile is not consent and a coworker is not the community.

sections.heading: Adjacent Peoples — Do Not Mash
sections.body:
This people is not Chinese, not Japanese, not Hmong, not Vietnamese, and not “Asian American” as the file. Open those CIs for those households and open this one for a Korean household. Because some households are mixed, ask this household.

### Adjacent doors

Immigrant Korean and adoptee Korean are not interchangeable. Do not ask an adoptee to represent the immigrant community, and do not skip this page because the person is English-dominant.

Seollal is not Chinese New Year as a file, and Hangul is not Chinese characters. Lee is not Li unless they say so, which is why there is never one Asian module.

sections.heading: Counts, Dated
sections.body:
Minnesota Compass (ACS 2020–2024) describes the Korean cultural community this way: about 28,180 people (give or take 2,630); Twin Cities 76.2%; Greater Minnesota 23.8%; age 17 or younger 36.4%; 65+ about 2.6%; foreign-born 44.7%. The profile also shows English only (age 5+) 81.5%; language other than English 18.5%; English less than “very well” 8.7%. For education, it shows high school or higher (25+) 95.9%; bachelor’s or higher 63.6%. It also lists median household income about $102,938 (2024 dollars, give or take $20,667); poverty 3.7%; owner-occupied 64.1%; average household size 2.29; and individuals living alone 37.4 percent.

### Counts

Compass does not split adoptee vs immigrant. Sahan Journal (July 29, 2024) used “about 10,000-15,000” Korean adoptees in Minnesota. AKConnection has cited on the order of 10 percent of Korean adoptees worldwide, so date those as news and community estimates rather than Compass figures.

### What the count is not

A 8.7 percent LEP rate is not zero, and a 3.7 percent poverty rate is not zero either. A 2.6 percent 65+ share does not mean there is no elder who needs Korean, and you should not invent a suicide rate for this page.

sections.heading: Doors and Sources
sections.body:
Start with the Minnesota Compass Korean profile (ACS 2020–2024) and MNopedia on Korean transracial adoption in Minnesota. Korean is on the CLAS fifteen, which means you book Korean.

### Public doors

AKConnection (established 2000) and peer adoptee-led organizations are doors, as are the Korean churches and the Korean Association groups this person names. Pay the door this person names rather than assigning a church.

### Where to learn more

CECLC is a door, not the whole community. Use these resources yourself before you ask a Korean colleague or an adoptee colleague to explain, and do not count an eList and an English PDF as reaching an LEP elder.

sections.heading: How it hits DHS gates — the 40%
sections.body:
Workplace culture and service delivery are both candidates here.

On language, a 8.7 percent LEP rate is not “no language gate.” An elder who needs Korean and gets English, or Chinese, or Japanese, is not being served. Gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care, and since adoptees may want Korean or may not, ask.

On names, the family name comes first and Lee is not a misspelling. The database that reverses the order or demands a “Korean name” from an adoptee is a gate.

Hour caps, exception processes, and life-sharing matches without Korean for the elder who needs it are not culturally neutral, and an English IEP is still a gate for that parent.

On the model-minority story, the figures of 95.9 percent high school and 63.6 percent bachelor’s can be used to skip LEP, 3.7 percent poverty, disability, and adoptee grief.

On adoptee citizenship, the Child Citizenship Act of 2000 left a gap, so do not collect status you do not need, and do not treat fear as noncompliance.

On mental health, screening is the duty and an invented Minnesota suicide rate is not, so do not skip screening, and do not make it a personality.

On notices and comment, do not count an eList and an English PDF as reaching an LEP elder, and record who was reached and what follow-up happened.

On workforce, Korean staff are not the interpreter pool, and adoptee staff are not the culture unit, because neither one is the community.

On legislation, funding, and rule, study a channel before you advocate for it. Use this page so that the 40% has a household in it.

sections.heading: A Note on This Guide
sections.body:
This brief is about Lao people as a people of Laos — the lowland Lao state history, the Mekong, the Theravada wats — and as a Minnesota community counted by Compass as Lao (non-Hmong), which means this is not Hmong. If the household is Hmong, open Hmong Minnesota and put White Hmong or Mong Leng on the interpreter line, and if the household is Lao, book Lao rather than guessing from the war.

### Who this is

This is not a Census “Asian” mash, and it is not Thai, not Khmer, and not Vietnamese, because a shared continent is not a shared culture. The Secret War sits next door to this page, and the Hmong alliance with the CIA is a neighboring story rather than a story in which this people becomes a footnote. Use this page for context and questions. It does not describe the person in front of you.

### Who this is not

Minnesota Compass (ACS 2020–2024) puts Lao (non-Hmong) near 14,918 people, with about 69.0 percent living in the Twin Cities and 31.0 percent in Greater Minnesota (each give or take 6.6 points). About 23.2 percent are age 17 or younger and 12.1 percent are 65+, while about 47.1 percent are foreign-born. Among those age 5 and older, 67.5 percent speak a language other than English and 31.7 percent speak English less than “very well,” so date the number you use and remember that a rate is not the person.

The diversity inside this people is the point. A person who came through the camps after 1975, a Christian family, a wat household that keeps phi, a U.S.-born nurse, a Greater Minnesota worker the building forgot, and a college student who uses English with friends and Lao with an elder all share a people, even though they do not share a Tuesday.

### How to read this

Always defer to the person in front of you, because this page is a hypothesis that you still test with this family.

sections.heading: Origins and the Founding of a People
sections.body:
Lao peoplehood is older than the refugee file. The Kingdom of Lan Xang is literacy for the desk, not a speech: a Mekong state, Theravada Buddhism, and the Lao language and script. French colonial rule made a border and a school, and independence, the American war in Laos, and 1975 make up the modern political sequence, although they are not the origin of the people.

### History for the meeting

Lao is related to Thai, but related is not interchangeable, which is why a Thai interpreter is not the default. Isan (northeastern Thai) is a neighboring variety that some families will name, so ask rather than guess.

### What people brought

Hmong people in Laos are a different people, and highland life, clan, and the CIA alliance belong to the Hmong page, so do not file Lao as the leftover of that war.

What Lao people brought with them includes the Lao language, Theravada and phi, kinship, farming, and the memory of a state that changed hands. What they met in Minnesota was an English form, one “Asian” checkbox, and often a Hmong interpreter, offered simply because the building already had that page.

sections.heading: The Geography of the Lao World
sections.body:
The homeland is Laos — Vientiane, Luang Prabang, the Mekong, the south, and the places families name — and Lao-speaking people also live in northeastern Thailand (Isan). The diaspora is global, reaching the United States, France, Australia, and Canada, which makes Minnesota one map within it rather than the map.

### Homeland

Compass (ACS 2020–2024) puts 69.0 percent of Lao Minnesotans in the Twin Cities and 31.0 percent in Greater Minnesota, and Greater Minnesota is not an afterthought. Do not assume Minneapolis, and do not assume Frogtown either, since that sentence belongs on the Hmong page unless this family actually lives there.

### Minnesota

Do not assume the person in front of you has been to Laos, because secondary migration built parts of this map and the Thai camps were exile geography rather than home.

sections.heading: 1975, the Pathet Lao, and the Camps — Foundational Event
sections.body:
The Secret War in Laos (1961–1975) is the foundational political event of Hmong Minnesota, and it sits next door to this page. Lowland Lao people lived that war differently, through a kingdom, a coalition, bombing, and then 1975. When the Pathet Lao took the country, royal and allied families, civil servants, and others fled, and the camps came next, followed by resettlement.

### Foundational events

Do not tell a Lao family the Hmong war story as if it were theirs, and do not tell a Hmong family that this page is close enough, because each people lived that war in its own way. If the household is Hmong, open Hmong Minnesota.

### Who you meet

The desk in 2026 meets the first wave and their children, who are U.S.-born, English-dominant with peers, still translating for their parents, and still unable to get Lao in a lobby that offered Hmong.

U.S. deportation of people with certain convictions is current structure for some Southeast Asian communities, so do not collect status you do not need. MPR News (April 29, 2026), citing Deportation Data Project figures, reported about 90 people born in Laos and arrested in Minnesota who were detained by ICE from Dec. 1 to mid-March, and 10 deported to Laos in October and November 2025. A coalition said 2025 had “the highest level of Hmong and Lao deportations in the last 15 years” (MPR News, February 24, 2026). The Minnesota Board of Pardons issued an emergency pardon on May 4, 2026 (KSTP). MPR News published the SEAFN 24/7 line, which answers in Lao: 1-800-251-1083. 1975 is not a personality, and it should not be handled as one in the meeting.

sections.heading: Family
sections.body:
Households are often larger than a nuclear English form, and Compass puts the average household size at 3.37 (ACS 2020–2024). Elders, adult children, and obligation sit in the same week, which means the person who cares for the child may not match the waiver checkbox.

### Who is in the household

Ask who should be in the room, since a nuclear English form has already decided who that is before the family says a word.

### Who speaks

This is not a Hmong clan system, so do not assume a clan last name. The family name is often last in U.S. files, but ask about the order, and do not treat unmatched last names as fraud by default.

Women’s labor and elder authority both live here, and both can be true in the same room at the same time.

sections.heading: Minnesota and Lao History
sections.body:
This department will meet this community on waivers, in child welfare, in health care, in cash and food programs, in aging, and in employment. The Twin Cities hold 69.0 percent and Greater Minnesota holds 31.0 percent, a share that is not an afterthought.

### Places

Partners include the Lao Assistance Center of Minnesota and the wats that families name, so pay them for their time and report back to them when the work is done. CECLC is a door, not the whole community.

### Partners

On the public calendar are Lao New Year / Pi Mai in April, Boun Pha Vet (King Pavade Heritage Day), Lao Artists Heritage Month, the Colors of Southeast Asia Fest, and the Buddhist holy days, although a calendar click is not community engagement. At the wat you are a guest, so mind your shoes, the head, and the altar.

Book a qualified interpreter, and pay for community work. Do not assign either to staff because of who they are. A New Year visit is optional professional development, and if you go, you go as a guest; the visit does not make you the expert.

sections.heading: Lao — the heart of a people
sections.body:
Lao people have a state and a language related to Thai, and public systems often mix up the Lao war history with the Hmong one. Ask plainly whether the person agrees with the plan, and make it easy to say no.

### In this state

The U.S. racial checkbox that says Asian also holds Hmong, Chinese, and Indian histories that Lao people do not share, and filing Lao under Hmong because both came from Laos is how a person gets shut out.

This guide is a working orientation, and individual variation always supersedes group generalization.

sections.heading: Core Concepts
sections.body:
The language is Lao, which is related to Thai; that relationship does not mean a Thai interpreter by default, and the language is not Hmong.

### Wat

The Theravada Buddhist temple is a civic and ritual center for many families, but do not make a monk the case plan unless this family asked.

### Phi

Spirit practice lives in some households, so do not mash the Hmong txiv neeb onto a Lao household. If they name a practice, listen with respect, but do not book it as DHS programming.

### Family name, not Hmong clan

Ask about the name rather than opening with a clan list from the other page, since a Lao family name is not a Hmong clan.

1975 is living memory in some rooms, and it is neither a personality nor an icebreaker.

sections.heading: Religion and Healing
sections.body:
Theravada Buddhism is central for many Lao Minnesota families, and the wat is both civic and ritual. Christianity lives in some families, while phi — spirit practice — lives in some households beside the wat, so do not mash Hmong household religion or a txiv neeb onto this page.

### Streams

Do not make a monk the case plan unless this family asked. Do not treat Buddhism as decoration, and do not treat church as the evolved version, since each stream is a practice in its own right.

### Practice

If you visit a home, look for shoes by the door or ask what the household prefers. In a home with an altar, ask where to sit, and ask before touching anyone, including a child.

The meaning of an illness may not be the DSM sentence, so ask and shape the plan with the family rather than inventing a rate.

sections.heading: Greetings
sections.body:
Ask who to greet first, or follow the household’s lead.

### Titles

Say the name, and ask how the person wants to be addressed.

### This room

Let this person’s own greeting guide you, whatever you read on another page.

Ask before any physical contact, and let the person set the limit.

sections.heading: Naming Conventions
sections.body:
The family name is often last in U.S. files, but ask about the order rather than assuming a Hmong clan name. Lee, Vang, or Yang on a file may be Hmong, and if so, this is the wrong page, because Lao names are not that list.

### How to file

Given names may be Lao, Pali-Sanskrit Buddhist, English, or both, which is why the form that demands first-middle-last and a hyphen will invent a person.

Ask how to say the name and how to file it, and do not “correct” a mother and child who do not share a last name or read that as a fraud signal until you have a reason.

Pronounce the name with care, ask when you are unsure, and do not joke about names.

sections.heading: Dates of Significance
sections.body:
Lao New Year / Pi Mai falls in mid-April; it is a water festival in homeland practice. In Minnesota the celebration has long been held at the wat and has also moved to community-wide events organized by more than 20 organizations (MPR News, 2013), and the Worthington temple community held it at a Legion hall on a weekend weeks after April 15 (2015), so celebrations are often on a later weekend and at community venues as well as temples. Be a guest rather than a researcher, since a calendar click is not community engagement.

### Calendar

The That Luang festival is literacy for the desk as a national Buddhist moment in Laos, but Minnesota rooms may or may not mark it, so ask.

Buddhist holy days vary, and some families keep Christian calendars. 1975 is literacy, not a holiday and not a speech.

Do not put “Asian holiday” or “Hmong New Year” on a Lao case note, because neither label describes this family’s calendar.

sections.heading: Education
sections.body:
Compass (ACS 2020–2024) reports that among Lao (non-Hmong) Minnesotans 25 and older, about 78.9 percent have a high school education or higher and about 15.7 percent have a bachelor’s or higher. Among those 5 and older, 67.5 percent speak a language other than English and 31.7 percent speak English less than “very well,” so date the number when you use it.

### School and language

A parent who speaks fluent Lao and limited English is not illiterate, and the English-only IEP is the gate that keeps that parent out. Under-identification in schools is a pattern this desk should watch, so do not invent a rate, and do not skip screening.

The child is not the interpreter, so book Lao, not Hmong. Second-generation educational mobility is real, and so is a gap that a room which treats everyone the same will call “culture.”

sections.heading: Etiquette
sections.body:
If you visit a home, look for shoes by the door or ask what the household prefers. In a home with an altar, ask where to sit, and ask before touching anyone, including a child.

### In the home

Ask before taking any photograph or touching any religious object, and do not ask anyone to explain their faith or history for your benefit.

### Time

If food or drink is offered, accepting a little is fine, and you can still keep to medical and legal timelines.

If someone misses an appointment, first check the time, transport, interpreter and work schedule. Confirm the plan in Lao if that is the language the person uses, and ask whether it works for them.

sections.heading: Language and Communication
sections.body:
The language is Lao, which is related to Thai; that does not make a Thai interpreter the default, and the language is not Hmong. An interpreter labeled Hmong, Thai, or Asian will not work for this household unless this family said otherwise.

### Language

Compass reports that among those 5 and older, 67.5 percent speak a language other than English and 31.7 percent speak English less than “very well,” so date the figure when you cite it. Lao script is not Thai script, and it cannot be treated as such in a staffing plan, so confirm the language before you book.

Give the person time to answer. If you get a short yes, check that the plan was understood, and ask whether it works for them.

Do not make a Lao coworker the interpreter, and remember that the child is not the interpreter either. If the household is Hmong, stop and open the other door.

sections.heading: Other Considerations
sections.body:
This section states hard facts plainly, because treating everyone the same can hide them.

### Named harms

War and camp trauma sit in some rooms, and under-identification in schools is a pattern to watch, so do not invent a rate and do not skip screening. Do not mash Hmong late-autism findings onto this page without a source.

Do not file this household under Asian, and do not file it under Hmong, because those mix-ups are the first mistake to avoid.

The deportation climate for some people with records is current structure, and it changes who opens the door, so do not collect status you do not need and do not treat fear as noncompliance.

LGBTQ Lao Minnesotans exist. You use the name they use, and you do not out someone to kin and call it culture.

Staff who share this community may add facts, but they do not get to delete a fact because it is hard to say.

sections.heading: Health
sections.body:
War and camp trauma sit in the same clinics as U.S.-born children. Do not invent a Minnesota PTSD or autism rate for Lao households, and do not skip screening because you have no module, since under-identification in schools is the pattern to watch.

### Access

Compass (ACS 2020–2024) puts about 6.1 percent without health insurance, and a rate is not the person.

The wat, phi practice in some rooms, and biomedicine may all be present in the household, so if they name a healer or a monk, listen. Do not mash a Hmong txiv neeb onto this family, and do not make the monk the case plan unless they asked.

Gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care, so offer it. Believe reported pain.

sections.heading: LGBTQ
sections.body:
Queer and trans Lao Minnesotans exist, and conservative family, wat, and church climates can mean silence or exile for them, while some people live a public English life and a private Lao life. You use the name they use and do not share what they tell you unless a rule requires it.

### This person

Minnesota’s Human Rights Act still applies. Use the name the person uses, and do not share what they tell you unless a rule requires it.

Do not question a household about anyone’s sexuality or gender, and take seriously that some people have reason to keep it private.

sections.heading: Hair, Dress, and Body
sections.body:
Traditional dress is public at Pi Mai and at the wat rather than a daily uniform, and the second generation looks like Minnesota. Do not ask a woman in clinic whether she “still wears the costume,” and do not mash Hmong New Year dress onto this page.

### Dress

In a home with an altar, ask where to sit, and ask before touching anyone, including a child.

Follow this person, and do not photograph monks as souvenirs.

sections.heading: Music
sections.body:
Lam, mor lam, and the khene (reed mouth organ) are Lao music, related to Thai Isan music. The khene is not the Hmong qeej, even when the instrument looks like a cousin to a desk that has not studied, and while Buddhist chant lives at the wat, pop lives in the second generation.

### Variation

A playlist is not engagement, and a funeral or a wat rite is not staff entertainment.

Knowing that ritual music exists will stop you from talking over it as if it were delay.

sections.heading: Sports
sections.body:
Soccer, volleyball, and ordinary school sport are part of life in the second generation, but do not assume the kid plays, and do not mash the Hmong Freedom Festival onto this page.

### Not the whole person

Sport clubs are social infrastructure, although they are not language access and they are not a case plan.

A tournament is not consultation.

sections.heading: Literature
sections.body:
Lao is a written language, with a script and a literary tradition that sit beside oral forms. Related to Thai is not interchangeable with Thai, and this is not Hmong oral-first as a mash, nor is it a people without letters.

### Literacy in the lobby

You do not need to quote a poem in the lobby, but you do need to know that limited English is not illiteracy and that the English form may still not work.

Do not test an elder in English and call it capacity.

sections.heading: Art
sections.body:
That Luang is literacy for the desk, not a tourism poster. Buddhist art, weaving, and wat architecture are the tradition here — not paj ntaub, and not Angkor — so be a guest, not a researcher.

### Guest

A temple visit is optional professional development, and it is not consultation.

Do not photograph monks or altars as souvenirs, and do not put a Hmong story cloth on a Lao Heritage Month table.

sections.heading: Conflict, War, and the State
sections.body:
French colonial rule, the American war in Laos, 1975 and the Pathet Lao, camps, resettlement, and a later deportation climate for some — that is the political event on this page. The Secret War as Hmong alliance is next door, so do not steal it and do not erase it; open the right intelligence instead.

### The badge

A DHS badge is not automatically help. Do not use 1975 as a personality, and do not ask a person to narrate war for your professional development.

Do not collect status you do not need, and do not treat fear as noncompliance.

sections.heading: Work, Markets, and Government
sections.body:
Lao Minnesotans work in factory jobs, in small business, in a professional second generation, and in public employment. Book a qualified interpreter, and pay for community work. Do not assign either to staff because of who they are.

### Work

The Lao Assistance Center of Minnesota is a partner, so pay, report back, and do not count a BCC to a cultural organization as consultation.

### Staff

Take time to introduce yourself and explain the plan. The first visit may not be the decision, and any required notice still goes out.

sections.heading: Health-care and Human-service Encounters
sections.body:
Lao versus Hmong is the first thing to get right, so book Lao — not Hmong, not Thai, not “Asian.” Pay attention to who is in the room, to gender, to a monk or phi in the story, to the English IEP, and to the deportation climate.

### Language

Confirm Lao, offer gender match, and ask who should hear. Do not make staff the interpreter. If they name a healer or a monk, listen, and do not mash txiv neeb onto them, while remembering that mandated reporting still exists.

### The meeting

Believe reported pain, remember that the child is not the interpreter, and keep in mind that Greater Minnesota is still this people.

sections.heading: Adjacent Peoples — Do Not Mash
sections.body:
This page is not Hmong, not Thai, not Khmer, not Vietnamese, and not Chinese, and it is not “Asian American” as the file. Open the Hmong CI for Hmong, with White Hmong or Mong Leng on the line, and open this one for Lao; some households are mixed, so ask this household.

### Adjacent doors

Related to Thai is not a Thai interpreter by default, and the camps in Thailand are exile geography rather than a reason to file this family as Thai.

Never use one Asian module, never one “Laotian” mash that eats Hmong, and never one “Southeast Asian” interpreter.

sections.heading: Counts, Dated
sections.body:
Minnesota Compass, ACS 2020–2024, describes the Lao (non-Hmong) cultural community this way: about 14,918 people; Twin Cities 69.0% and Greater Minnesota 31.0% (each give or take 6.6 points); age 17 or younger 23.2% and 65+ 12.1%; foreign-born 47.1%; language other than English (age 5+) 67.5%; English less than “very well” 31.7%; high school or higher (25+) 78.9%; bachelor’s or higher 15.7%; median household income about $82,225 (2024 dollars, give or take $12,527); poverty 7.7% (give or take 5.3 points); owner-occupied 62.3%; renter-occupied 37.7%; average household size 3.37; and without health insurance 6.1%.

### Counts

These numbers exclude Hmong, so date the number when you use it. Greater Minnesota at 31.0 percent is not an afterthought, and a poverty rate of 7.7 percent is not proof the gates closed.

### What the count is not

A 65-and-older share of 12.1 percent is older than some refugee communities on this spine, and that is structure for aging and waiver work, although a rate is still not the person.

sections.heading: Doors and Sources
sections.body:
The sources are the Minnesota Compass Lao (non-Hmong) profile (ACS 2020–2024), the Lao Assistance Center of Minnesota, and the wats this family names, while the Hmong Minnesota CI belongs here only if this household is Hmong.

### Public doors

CECLC is a door, not the whole community, and an eList is not engagement, so pay partners and report back.

### Where to learn more

Use these resources yourself before you ask a Lao colleague to explain. Book a qualified Lao interpreter, because the child is not the interpreter.

sections.heading: How it hits DHS gates — the 40%
sections.body:
Workplace culture and service delivery are both candidates here.

Language: the Lao versus Hmong mixup is the first thing to get right, and an interpreter labeled Hmong, Thai, or Asian will not work for a Lao household. Related to Thai is not a Thai default, and gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care.

Names: do not assume a Hmong clan name, because the database that flags unmatched last names as fraud is a gate.

Hour caps, exception processes, and life-sharing matches without language are not culturally neutral.

Child welfare and disability: under-identification in schools is a pattern to watch, and help-seeking that becomes a report is part of why people wait. Mandated reporting still exists, and so does the duty not to treat a whole community as a risk score, so do not mash Hmong findings onto this page.

Greater Minnesota: 31.0 percent, which means a metro default has already decided who it serves.

Deportation climate: people may skip clinic, school, and waiver meetings when a relative can be moved, and that is not noncompliance, so do not collect status you do not need.

Notices and comment: do not count an eList and an English PDF as reaching this community, and record who was reached and what follow-up happened.

Workforce: Lao staff are not the interpreter pool, and they are not the community.

Legislation, funding, rule: study a channel before you advocate for it. Use this page so that the 40% has a household in it.

sections.heading: A Note on This Guide
sections.body:
This brief is about Lebanese people — a people with a country in the Levant and a Minnesota community that is both historic and recent. It is not the Arabic language door, which is /ci/arabic, a CLAS ten- and fifteen-language line that opens onto many peoples and should not be opened as a synonym for this people-page. This is also not Somali, because shared Arabic and shared Islam are not shared culture, and Arab Minnesota is not one file.

### Who this is

Use this page for context and questions. It does not describe the person in front of you. Paternalism looks like one “Arabic interpreter” written for an English-dominant Maronite household, a mosque default, a Somali default because Arabic is on a card, and a 1975 speech delivered to a third-generation family.

### Who this is not

Minnesota Compass (ACS 2020–2024) puts Lebanese ancestry near 7,232, with about 76.7 percent living in the Twin Cities and about 23.3 percent in Greater Minnesota. About 24.2 percent are age 17 or younger, and about 17.0 percent are 65+. About 9.2 percent are foreign-born — which means a large historic, U.S.-born share. Among those age 5+, 13.9 percent speak a language other than English, but English less than “very well” is suppressed on that profile, so do not invent a LEP rate. High school or higher is 97.8 percent, bachelor’s or higher is 50.9 percent, and poverty is 8.8 percent. Date the number you use, and remember that a rate is not the person.

Maronite and Antiochian Orthodox parishes are well documented in Minnesota. Lebanese Sunni or Shiʿa Muslims, a Lebanese mosque, and Lebanese Protestant congregations are not documented in Minnesota sources, so ask rather than assume. For Druze there is no dated Minnesota count, so do not invent one, and if this family is Druze, defer to them. Do not assume mosque, and do not assume hijab, since either guess can be wrong for the family in front of you.

### How to read this

Always defer to the person in front of you, because this page is a hypothesis that you still test on this family.

sections.heading: Origins and the Founding of a People
sections.body:
Lebanese peoplehood is older than the 1943 independence, older than the 1975–1990 civil war, and older than this department. Lebanon is a Levantine country on the eastern Mediterranean, with mountains and coast, and with Maronite, Orthodox, Sunni, Shiʿa, and Druze as named streams. This is literacy for the desk rather than a speech you give the family, so do not found “the Arabs” in a waiver meeting, and do not lecture a Maronite household about the Hijaz.

### History for the meeting

What people brought was Levantine Arabic for some, French and English for others, a church or a mosque or neither, kinship, and a memory of a state that broke and a diaspora that is old in the Americas. What they met in Minnesota was an English form, a racial order that has often filed Levantine Christians as White and skipped CI, one “Arabic interpreter,” and often a Somali default because the building already has that page.

### What people brought

Do not start with hummus, a cedar, or a Phoenician tourism sentence, because a shared language family is not shared culture with Iraq, Egypt, or Somalia.

sections.heading: The Geography of Lebanon and Lebanese Minnesota
sections.body:
The homeland is not one neighborhood in Beirut, since it includes mountains, coast, the Bekaa, and the south, and church, mosque, and some speech shift with place. If they name a place, confirm it, and rather than refereeing in a waiver meeting, listen.

### Homeland

The diaspora is old in the Americas, reaching Brazil, Argentina, and the United States. Dearborn and the Detroit metro hold a large Arab American community, but Minnesota is not Dearborn, so do not import a Michigan picture onto a Ramsey County lobby.

### Minnesota

In Minnesota, 76.7 percent live in the Twin Cities and 23.3 percent in Greater Minnesota, and there is no single dense Lebanese district, but the sources point to Northeast Minneapolis around St. Maron, St. Paul's West Side (now West St. Paul and Mendota Heights) and Mankato. Do not assume Minneapolis, and do not assume the person in front of you has been to Lebanon, since many families have been here for generations.

sections.heading: Historic Streams and Later Displacement — Not One Poster
sections.body:
If 1975 is Hmong Minnesota and 1991 is Somali Minnesota, Lebanese Minnesota does not get one foundational year that covers the lobby. Late-Ottoman and early-twentieth-century Christian streams built part of U.S. Lebanese life — including families with deep Minnesota roots. Compass foreign-born 9.2 percent (ACS 2020–2024) is the dated share, and while that share reflects a historic community, it is not “no immigrant.”

### Foundational events

The 1975–1990 civil war moved some people, as did 2006, while the later economic collapse and the 4 August 2020 Beirut port explosion sit in some later rooms. There is secondary migration from other states, and there are U.S.-born children in every stream.

### Who you meet

The desk in 2026 meets an English-dominant third-generation parish household, an elder who needs Levantine Arabic, and a recent arrival, which means that if you only know “refugee” or only know “Muslim,” you will miss this room. No Minnesota source documents a particular pattern of distrust of government for this community, so ask rather than assume. A DHS badge is not automatically help. Lebanon's Temporary Protected Status was automatically extended through Nov. 27, 2026, according to the Federal Register (May 29, 2026); AP put the number of Lebanese covered nationwide at about 11,000, and no Minnesota count is available.

sections.heading: Family
sections.body:
Who is in the household varies by stream, class, and generation. The Compass average household size is about 2.12 (ACS 2020–2024) — often smaller, older, and more English-dominant than neighboring Arabic-speaking streams — so do not copy that onto a recently arrived household, and do not copy a Sudanese or Iraqi waiver household onto this page.

### Who is in the household

Ask who should be in the room, because a nuclear English form already has a who built in, and elders and adult children may sit in the same week.

### Who speaks

Do not invent a last name because the database wants one, and do not treat unmatched last names as fraud by default. Women’s labor and men’s labor both live here, and since gender norms are this family’s rather than “Arab,” ask.

Minnesota law still stands, which means domestic violence is not culture and you follow mandated reporting. Do not use a child as interpreter.

sections.heading: Minnesota and Lebanese History
sections.body:
Minnesota holds a Lebanese community large enough for a Compass profile — about 7,232 (ACS 2020–2024) — and large enough that this department will meet it. Greater Minnesota is 23.3 percent, so do not write this people as a Minneapolis anecdote, especially since there is no single dense Lebanese district, but the sources point to Northeast Minneapolis around St. Maron, St. Paul's West Side (now West St. Paul and Mendota Heights) and Mankato.

### Places

Think in places rather than a blob: the Twin Cities, inner-ring suburbs, and Greater Minnesota. There are named churches — Maronite, Antiochian and other Orthodox, other Catholic and Protestant — and named mosques if this family names them, and these are partners, not a list to extract from. CECLC is a department door, not the community, so pay the partner this household actually uses.

### Partners

Book a qualified interpreter, and pay for community work. Do not assign either to staff because of who they are. A Heritage Month table is not consultation, and while you are a guest, that does not make you the expert.

Do not BCC one priest or one imam and call it consultation.

sections.heading: Lebanese — not an Arab module, not Somali
sections.body:
To be Lebanese in Minnesota is to be a people with a country, often filed White, sometimes filed “Arab,” and sometimes filed “Muslim” by a building that did not ask. Christian and Muslim both live here. For some, Arabic is the language of the grandmother and the church; for some, it is the language of the Qurʾan and the kitchen; and for some U.S.-born adults it is a class they do not speak. Compass LOTE 13.9 percent is dated, and it is not “no language gate.”

### In this state

Do not fold this household into Somali Minnesota because both might be Muslim. Do not fold it into /ci/arabic as if a language list were a people, and do not fold it into “MENA” as a file.

Race in the U.S. file has often marked Levantine Christians White, and that skip is the gate when the elder needs Levantine. Islamophobia and anti-Arab racism still hit Christian Lebanese when the mash is “Arab.”

This guide is a working orientation, and because individual variation always supersedes group generalization, always defer to this family.

sections.heading: Core Concepts
sections.body:
This is not the Arabic language door treated as a people, so open /ci/arabic for a language request, and open this brief for a Lebanese household.

### Religion differs by family

Do not assume the mosque, do not assume the priest, and do not assume hijab.

### Confirm whether Arabic is home language

Book Levantine if it is, since Maghrebi, Egyptian, or MSA may still not work. The English-dominant historic share is real, so ask rather than guess.

### Historic versus later stream

Compass foreign-born is 9.2 percent, and a third-generation parish household and a 2020 arrival do not share a Tuesday.

### Checking for agreement

Before you treat a yes as agreement, ask again, plainly and without embarrassing anyone.

Do not collect political speech as a risk score.

sections.heading: Religion — not the people
sections.body:
Islam is not Lebanese, and Lebanese is not Islam. Maronite and Antiochian Orthodox parishes are well documented in Minnesota, while Lebanese Sunni and Shiʿa Muslims are not documented in Minnesota sources, so ask rather than assume. For Druze there is no dated Minnesota count, so do not invent a community, and if this family names Druze, listen and defer.

### Streams

Do not assume Muslim, and do not assume hijab. Do not rank covering as piety or oppression, and do not make a priest or an imam the case plan unless this family asked.

### Practice

The parish and the mosque are centers of ritual, mutual aid, and information, but they are not “the community,” so do not BCC one clergy and call it consultation.

Ramadan, Eid, Christmas, Easter, and the Maronite and Orthodox calendars all matter, so ask which ones this family keeps, while remembering that a calendar click is not engagement.

sections.heading: Greetings
sections.body:
Follow this room. As-salāmu ʿalaykum is ordinary in many Muslim rooms, and the reply is wa-ʿalaykumu s-salām, but it is not the default in a Maronite or Orthodox room. Marḥaban, ahlan, and an English hello are all ordinary, so say the name.

### Titles

Ask who to greet first, or follow the household’s lead. Wait to see whether a hand is offered, and if it is not, nod.

### This room

Let this person’s own greeting guide you, whatever you read on another page.

Ask before any physical contact, and let the person set the limit.

sections.heading: Naming Conventions
sections.body:
Naming patterns vary. Some families use given name + father’s name + family name, and some three-part names look like Somali names and are not. Some Lebanese Christian streams use French or English given names and a family surname the database can already see, and some people have Westernized on U.S. forms, so ask.

### How to file

Do not invent a last name because the screen requires one, since that invented name becomes a gate.

Pronounce it, and ask, rather than joking about long names. Do not assume three Somali names, and do not assume a hyphen.

Women may or may not take a husband’s family name in U.S. records, so ask how to file. Do not “correct” a mother and child who do not share a last name as a fraud signal until you have a reason.

sections.heading: Dates of Significance
sections.body:
Ask this family which dates matter. Christmas and Easter — Western, Maronite, Orthodox — matter in Christian rooms, while Muslim lunar dates — Ramadan, Eid al-Fitr, Eid al-Adha — matter in Muslim rooms. Independence is 22 November. 1975 is literacy, not a holiday, and 4 August 2020 is memory for some later rooms.

### Calendar

11 September 2001 is structure in this country, not a holiday and not a personality, and Gaza-era harassment is current structure. Neither is a calendar click that makes you engaged.

Do not put “Arab holiday” or “Muslim holiday” on a case note without asking, because a calendar click is literacy; it is not community engagement.

sections.heading: Education
sections.body:
Compass (ACS 2020–2024) reports that among Lebanese Minnesotans 25 and older, about 97.8 percent have high school or higher and about 50.9 percent have a bachelor’s or higher, so date Compass when you cite it. About 9.2 percent of the community is foreign-born. High attainment and a large U.S.-born share are not “no language gate” for the household that needs Levantine Arabic.

### School and language

A parent who speaks fluent Arabic and limited English is not illiterate, and literacy in Modern Standard Arabic is not guaranteed for every dialect speaker. The English-only IEP is the gate when Arabic is the home language.

The child is not the interpreter, and you should not skip the interpreter because Compass LOTE is 13.9 percent. Do not copy this attainment onto an Iraqi or Sudanese parent, and do not copy those pages onto this one.

sections.heading: Etiquette
sections.body:
If food or drink is offered, accepting a little is fine, and you can still keep to medical and legal timelines.

### In the home

If you visit a home, look for shoes by the door or ask what the household prefers.

### Time

Do not assume a woman will or will not cover. Ask before taking any photograph, and enter a prayer space only if you are invited.

If someone misses an appointment, first check the time, transport, interpreter and work schedule. Confirm the plan in the language the person uses, and ask whether it works for them.

sections.heading: Language and Communication
sections.body:
Book Levantine Arabic if Arabic is the home language, and confirm whether it is. Compass reports that among those 5 and older, about 13.9 percent speak a language other than English, but English less than “very well” is suppressed on the Compass Lebanese profile, so do not invent a LEP rate. A large historic share is English-dominant, but the elder who is not still needs the line.

### Language

An interpreter labeled Arabic who speaks Maghrebi, or who tests the elder in fuṣḥā, may still not work, so confirm the dialect. Do not open Somali Minnesota by default because Arabic is on a card, since on a Somali household Arabic may be recitation — that is the other door.

Give the person time to answer. If you get a short yes, check that the plan was understood, and ask whether it works for them. Do not make a coworker the interpreter, and remember that the child is not the interpreter.

sections.heading: Other Considerations
sections.body:
This section states hard facts plainly, because treating everyone the same can hide them.

### Named harms

Islamophobia and anti-Arab racism after 11 September 2001 and after Gaza are structure in this country and in this state. They hit Muslim Lebanese, and they hit Christian Lebanese when the mash is “Arab,” and because they change who opens the door, that hesitation is not noncompliance.

Do not collect political speech as a risk score, and do not file a protest, a flag, or an opinion about Gaza or Hezbollah as a safety note. The enforcement climate is real for some later arrivals, so do not collect status you do not need.

Queer and trans Lebanese exist, so you use the name, and you do not out someone to kin and call it culture.

Do not assume hijab, and do not assume Muslim, but do not skip mandated reporting and call it humility.

Staff who share this community may add facts, but they do not get to delete a fact because it is hard to say.

sections.heading: Health
sections.body:
No dated Minnesota-wide Lebanese autism, diabetes, or PTSD rate belongs on this page beyond Compass poverty of 8.8 percent (ACS 2020–2024), so do not invent one. War trauma sits in some later streams, but it is not a personality and it is not every household.

### Access

Gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care, so offer it, and believe reported pain. Ask about this person’s own experience of care, and do not skip screening because Compass looks English-dominant.

Mental-health stigma exists in some families, and so does a fierce wish for services, and you can hold both. Confirm the language, and remember that identification is not a community personality.

sections.heading: LGBTQ
sections.body:
Queer and trans Lebanese Minnesotans exist. No Minnesota source describes family or community climates for LGBTQ Lebanese Minnesotans, so ask the person rather than assume, and you use the name they use and do not share what they tell you unless a rule requires it.

### This person

Minnesota’s Human Rights Act still applies. Use the name the person uses, and do not share what they tell you unless a rule requires it.

Do not question a household about anyone’s sexuality or gender, and take seriously that some people have reason to keep it private.

sections.heading: Hair, Dress, and Body
sections.body:
Hijab, niqab, and modest dress are ordinary for some Muslim women and not for others, while Christian Lebanese dress is Minnesota dress plus, for some, church clothes. Do not assume covering, and do not rank covering as piety or oppression. The second generation looks like Minnesota, so do not ask whether they “still dress Lebanese.”

### Dress

This is not the CROWN Act chapter, so do not mash the two.

Do not touch, and do not police covering. Do not assume a covered woman cannot speak for herself — ask her, with a gender-matched interpreter if she wants one.

sections.heading: Music
sections.body:
Lebanese musical life is not one playlist, because Levantine pop, dabke, Fairuz as public memory in some rooms, Maronite and Orthodox hymnody, and religious caution about some music in some families all exist side by side.

### Variation

A playlist is not engagement, and you should not request a dabke as an icebreaker in a waiver meeting.

A liturgy is not staff entertainment, even when the music is beautiful.

sections.heading: Sports
sections.body:
Soccer is a common public sport in many streams, and basketball shows up in the second generation, but do not assume the kid plays, and do not make sport the only excellence you can see.

### Not the whole person

Sport clubs are social infrastructure, but they are not language access, and they are not a case plan.

World Cup loyalties are not a risk score, however loud they get.

sections.heading: Literature
sections.body:
Arabic is one of the world’s major literary languages, and French and English letters sit in Lebanese streams as well, so this is not a people without letters. Poetry is prestige in some rooms, and the Qurʾan is recitation and scripture in Muslim rooms — not a literacy test you give a dialect-speaking elder in the lobby.

### Literacy in the lobby

MSA and dialect are not the same skill, which means a person who does not read fuṣḥā is not a person without letters, and a U.S.-born adult who does not read Arabic is still this people-page.

You do not need to quote a poet, but you do need the language this person reads.

sections.heading: Art
sections.body:
Calligraphy appears in some rooms and church iconography in Christian streams, along with Levantine visual work and contemporary diaspora artists, and you meet all of it as a guest, not a researcher.

### Guest

A museum visit is optional professional development, but it is not consultation.

Do not put a camel or a keffiyeh on a Heritage Month table and call it this people, and do not mash it with a Somali table because both might be Muslim.

sections.heading: War, the State, and the Arab-Module Trap
sections.body:
The political stack is this: the 1975–1990 civil war, 2006, the 2019–present economic collapse, the 4 August 2020 port explosion, 11 September 2001 and what the United States did in its name, Gaza-era harassment, and enforcement against some later arrivals. Anti-Arab racism and Islamophobia are structure, and they hit Christian Lebanese when the mash is “Arab,” but they are not a personality.

### The badge

Do not collect political speech as a risk score, because a flag, a protest, a sermon, or an opinion about Gaza or Hezbollah is not a safety note.

A DHS badge is not automatically help. Do not use a war as a personality, and do not ask a person to narrate bombing for your professional development. Do not assume every Lebanese person is last year’s arrival, since Compass foreign-born 9.2 percent is the dated historic share.

sections.heading: Work, Markets, and Government
sections.body:
The community includes a professional class, small business, public employment, and shift work. Compass bachelor’s or higher 50.9 percent and owner-occupied 68.6 percent are averages, not this kitchen table, so do not write one hustle onto the page.

### Work

Book a qualified interpreter, and pay for community work. Do not assign either to staff because of who they are.

### Staff

Take time to introduce yourself and explain the plan, and still give any required notice. Do not count an English eList comment period as reaching every stream.

sections.heading: Health-care and Human-service Encounters
sections.body:
Confirm the language, including whether Arabic is the home language, the liturgy, or not in this house at all, and confirm Levantine if Arabic is the interview. Offer gender match, ask who should hear, and do not force a handshake.

### Language

Believe reported pain, and do not close the file because English was thin, since the child is not the interpreter.

### The meeting

Do not assume Muslim, do not assume hijab, and do not open Somali Minnesota because Arabic is on a card. Mandated reporting still exists, and so does the duty not to treat a whole people as a risk score.

The enforcement climate matters for some later arrivals, because people may skip clinic when a relative can be moved, and that is not noncompliance. Do not collect status you do not need.

sections.heading: Adjacent Peoples — Do Not Mash
sections.body:
This is not the Arabic language door treated as a people. Open /ci/arabic for a language request onto Lebanese, Iraqi, Syrian, Palestinian, Egyptian, Sudanese, Yemeni, Gulf, or Maghrebi households, and open this brief for a Lebanese household.

### Adjacent doors

This is not Somali, not Persian / Farsi, not Turkish, and not Oromo, because shared Islam is not shared culture, and shared Arabic is not shared culture. Nor is it Syrian, Iraqi, Palestinian, or Egyptian as a synonym.

Compass Lebanese is one stream of what people call Arab Minnesota, not the whole, and since some households are mixed, ask this household. Never one Arab module, never one Muslim module, and never a Somali default because Arabic is on the card.

sections.heading: Counts, Dated
sections.body:
Minnesota Compass (ACS 2020–2024) describes the Lebanese cultural community this way: about 7,232 people (plus or minus 1,225; Compass's 2024 single-year total is 10,066, which it calls its most accurate size estimate), with 76.7% in the Twin Cities and 23.3% in Greater Minnesota. About 24.2% are age 17 or younger and 17.0% are 65+. Foreign-born is 9.2%, and 13.9% of those age 5+ speak a language other than English; English less than “very well” is suppressed on that profile, so do not invent a LEP rate. Among those 25+, 97.8% have high school or higher and 50.9% a bachelor’s or higher. Median household income is about $72,873 (2024 dollars), poverty is 8.8%, 68.6% of homes are owner-occupied, and average household size is 2.12.

### Counts

Date Compass, and do not invent an “Arab Minnesota” total or add this profile to Iraqi or Syrian guesses. Counts disagree across ACS vintages and definitions (ancestry vs. birthplace vs. language), so date the number you cite.

### What the count is not

Foreign-born 9.2 percent is not “no immigrant,” and LOTE 13.9 percent is not “no language gate.” A rate is not the person, and Lebanese numbers are not Iraqi, Syrian, Palestinian, or Somali numbers.

sections.heading: Doors and Sources
sections.body:
Start with the Minnesota Compass Lebanese profile (ACS 2020–2024). Adjacent, but not this page, is /ci/arabic — the language door — and the CLAS ten-language block and fifteen-language interpreter cards include Arabic, so confirm whether Arabic is the home language, and confirm Levantine.

### Public doors

Work through the Maronite, Orthodox, and other parishes families name, and the mosques families name. CECLC is a door, not the whole, and an eList will not reach every stream, so pay partners and report back.

### Where to learn more

Use these resources yourself before you ask a Lebanese colleague to explain. Book a qualified interpreter when they need one, since the child is not the interpreter, and do not open Somali Minnesota by default.

sections.heading: How it hits DHS gates — the 40%
sections.body:
Workplace culture and service delivery are both candidates here.

Language: book Levantine Arabic if Arabic is the home language, because an interpreter labeled Arabic who does not speak this household’s variety will not work, and MSA is not the kitchen. Arabic on a Somali or Oromo Muslim card may be recitation, so book the interview language. Compass LOTE 13.9 percent is not “no gate,” and gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care.

Names: the database that invents a last name, or that assumes three Somali names, is a gate that follows the person.

Hour caps, exception processes, and life-sharing matches without language are not culturally neutral.

Assuming Somali, assuming Muslim, assuming hijab, and opening /ci/arabic as this people shut people out, even when they look like cultural competence.

The enforcement climate and post-9/11 and Gaza-era racism mean people may skip clinic, school, and waiver meetings, and that is not noncompliance. Do not collect status you do not need, and do not collect political speech as a risk score.

Notices and comment: do not count an eList and an English PDF as reaching every stream, and record who was reached and what follow-up happened. Greater Minnesota is 23.3 percent.

Workforce: Lebanese staff are not the interpreter pool and not the community, because staff are colleagues, not the curriculum, so do not treat them as either.

Legislation, funding, rule: study a channel before you advocate for it. Use this page so that the 40% has a household in it.

sections.heading: A Note on This Guide
sections.body:
This brief is about Liberian people as a West African people with a republic (1847), many ethnic nations inside it, and a Minnesota community built in large part after the civil wars. It is not about historic African American / Black American Minnesota, because English as a shared official language is not shared culture, and it is worth knowing that Compass notes a 2024 change in how ancestry is collected for Black respondents, so the Compass African American count and the Liberian count differ. That mash is not this page. This community is also not Somali, and Nigerian is not a synonym for it, since shared race in the United States is not shared culture.

### Who this is

Minnesota Compass (ACS 2020–2024) puts Liberian ancestry near 22,571 (plus or minus 4,423), with about 86.8 percent living in the Twin Cities and about 13.2 percent in Greater Minnesota. About 46.0 percent are age 17 or younger, about 4.1 percent are 65 or older, and about 59.9 percent are foreign-born. Among those age 5 and older, 83.6 percent speak English only, 16.4 percent speak a language other than English, and 7.1 percent speak English less than “very well.” Date the number you use, and remember that a rate is not the person.

### Who this is not

Brooklyn Park and Brooklyn Center are a documented concentration (ACS 2020–2024 counts 4,544 Liberia-born residents of Brooklyn Park (plus or minus 1,153) and 1,147 in Brooklyn Center, out of 15,297 statewide, and Brooklyn Park city officials put the city's Liberian population above 7,000) — in some public tellings, among the largest Liberian communities outside Liberia. Confirm that on this family rather than assuming the city, because Greater Minnesota lives here too.

The diversity inside this people is the point. A Kpelle elder who uses Kolokwa, an Americo-Liberian professional, a Mandingo Muslim household, a U.S.-born nurse, a Greater Minnesota factory household, a person who lived DED for decades and naturalized after LRIF, and a child who has never seen Monrovia all share a people, yet they do not share a Tuesday.

### How to read this

Always defer to the person in front of you, because this page is a hypothesis and you are still testing it on this family.

sections.heading: Origins and the Founding of a People
sections.body:
Liberia is older than the refugee file and older than 1989. It is a West African coast of many peoples — Kpelle, Bassa, Gio / Dan, Kru, Grebo, Vai, Mandingo, Krahn, Lorma, and others — and a republic declared in 1847 by settlers who included free Black Americans and Caribbean recaptives. That founding is literacy for the desk rather than a speech you give the family, and it is not permission to fold this household into historic African American cultural intelligence because some founders came from the United States.

### History for the meeting

Indigenous Liberian nations were not a blank coast, and mission schools, English as the official language, and a coastal/settler and hinterland split still sit in some rooms. Ask which people they are rather than lecturing on Americo-Liberian taxonomy they did not ask for.

### What people brought

What people brought with them was English and Liberian English, ethnic languages, church and mosque, rice as ordinary food, kin obligation, and the memory of a state that broke.
