What they met in Minnesota was an English form, one “Black” checkbox, and often the historic African American page, because the building heard English and assumed it knew the rest.

Origins did not begin in the civil war, and although the war is the foundational event of much of the Minnesota community you will meet, it is not a personality.

sections.heading: The Geography of the Liberian World
sections.body:
Liberia is counties and peoples, not a blob, and Monrovia is not the whole. A person may name a county, a town, or a people — Kpelle in Bong, Bassa on the coast, Gio in Nimba — rather than the capital, so confirm it if it matters, and do not referee county politics in a waiver meeting.

### Homeland

The diaspora is U.S.-heavy, reaching Minnesota, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, New York, Georgia, and others. Minnesota is a real hub, though not the only one, and secondary migration built part of what you will meet here.

### Minnesota

In Minnesota, Compass puts 86.8 percent in the Twin Cities and 13.2 percent in Greater Minnesota. Brooklyn Park and Brooklyn Center are a documented concentration (ACS 2020–2024 counts 4,544 Liberia-born residents of Brooklyn Park (plus or minus 1,153) and 1,147 in Brooklyn Center, out of 15,297 statewide, and Brooklyn Park city officials put the city's Liberian population above 7,000), so confirm it on this family rather than assuming that city is the whole, and do not assume the person in front of you has been to Liberia. Inner-ring suburbs and Greater Minnesota towns with work and housing are still this people.

sections.heading: Civil Wars, TPS, DED, and LRIF — Foundational Event
sections.body:
If 1975 is Vietnamese Minnesota’s foundational event, the Liberian civil wars are the foundational event of much of Liberian Minnesota, and that is why the names and dates belong on this page.

### Foundational events

The names and dates matter: Samuel Doe, the 1980 coup, Charles Taylor, and wars running roughly 1989–1997 and 1999–2003. The dead numbered in the hundreds of thousands, and displacement followed, with camps in Guinea, Côte d’Ivoire, Sierra Leone, and Ghana. Child soldiers sit in some rooms as history, not as a file you open as a risk score, because most people were not fighters; most people were trying to live.

### Who you meet

The United States granted Temporary Protected Status, then Deferred Enforced Departure, and left people in temporary status for decades, until Liberian Refugee Immigration Fairness (2019) opened a path that some families used. Deferred Enforced Departure was extended only through June 30, 2026, and was allowed to expire on that date; LRIF was the route to green cards for most long-term residents. That climate still shapes who opens the door, while family reunification and ordinary immigration are later streams. The desk in 2026 meets U.S.-born children who are English-dominant with their peers, still translating for a grandmother whose English is Kolokwa, and still filed under Black.

The war is literacy for the desk rather than a speech you give the family.

sections.heading: Family
sections.body:
Some households are extended, and country kin, town kin, and church kin may all be involved. Elders may hold authority in some of them. Compass puts average household size at about 3.54, and the household is not always the nuclear one on the English form, which means the person who cares for a disabled adult or a child may be a sister, a cousin, or a church mother rather than the legally recognized caregiver on the checkbox. Hour caps and “natural supports” language can quietly shift unpaid work onto the women in that network and then call it culture.

### Who is in the household

The person who speaks in the lobby may be a child with Minnesota English, but that child is not the qualified interpreter, even when Compass says 83.6 percent English only, and CLAS still stands if this elder needs Liberian English. Using a child as the go-between does harm, so book the interpreter, and ask who should be in the room.

### Who speaks

Women’s labor — care, nursing, CNA, shop, and the professional second generation — sits next to elder obligation, and both can be true in the same room. Minnesota law still stands, so do not skip mandated reporting and call it humility.

sections.heading: Minnesota and Liberian History
sections.body:
Minnesota holds a Liberian community large enough for a Compass row, and large enough that this department will meet it on waivers, child welfare, health care, cash, food, aging, and employment. Compass counts about 22,571 (plus or minus 4,423) (ACS 2020–2024), and Greater Minnesota is 13.2 percent of that, so do not write this people as a Brooklyn Park anecdote until this family lives there.

### Places

Think in places rather than a blob: Brooklyn Park and Brooklyn Center as the documented concentration (ACS 2020–2024 counts 4,544 Liberia-born residents of Brooklyn Park (plus or minus 1,153) and 1,147 in Brooklyn Center, out of 15,297 statewide, and Brooklyn Park city officials put the city's Liberian population above 7,000), which you confirm on this family; the inner-ring suburbs; Minneapolis and St. Paul pockets; and Greater Minnesota towns with work and housing. Churches are public life, but they are not consultation, and a food visit does not make you the expert.

### Partners

Partners include the Organization of Liberians in Minnesota (OLM, founded 1973 and incorporated 1979), which runs the Liberian Community/OLM Center in Brooklyn Park, the churches that families name, and CECLC as a department door — not the whole community — so pay the partner this household actually uses.

Book a qualified interpreter, and pay for community work. Do not assign either to staff because of who they are. Independence Day (26 July) is optional professional development if you are invited, and you attend as a guest, knowing that being there does not make you the expert.

sections.heading: Liberian Minnesota — the heart of a people
sections.body:
Liberia is a West African country with English as an official language. Public systems may file Liberians under Black and stop at the historic African American page, so ask how the person identifies. Ask plainly whether the person agrees with the plan, and make it easy to say no.

### In this state

The civil war sits in the room for some and is a history class for others. First-wave survivors, later arrivals, U.S.-born children, and Mandingo, Kpelle, and Americo-Liberian families do not share one Tuesday, so you do not referee, and you do not put “child soldier” on a case note as color.

In the United States another fact sits on the same desk: many Liberian Minnesotans are Black in a racial order that also holds historic African American, Somali, Nigerian, and Kenyan histories they do not share, and the mash is the gate.

This guide is a working orientation, which means individual variation always supersedes group generalization and you always defer to the person in front of you.

sections.heading: Core Concepts
sections.body:
The first question is which people inside Liberia — Kpelle, Bassa, Gio, Kru, Grebo, Vai, Mandingo, Krahn, Americo-Liberian, or others — and you ask it because the Compass row is not the ethnic file.

### English and Liberian English

Official English is not Minnesota professional English, since Kolokwa is spoken in some rooms and ethnic languages in some homes, which means “English” on the interpreter line may still not work.

### Civil war memory

The war is part of the history many families carry. Do not raise it, and do not assume it about the person in the lobby.

### Church as channel

Pentecostal, Protestant, and Catholic churches are channels here, and Islam is present in some families, so do not make clergy the case plan unless they asked.

### DED / TPS / LRIF climate

Temporary status for decades is structure rather than choice, so do not collect status you do not need.

### Not historic African American

Shared race and shared English are not shared culture.

sections.heading: Religion
sections.body:
Christianity is the large public stream in Liberian Minnesota, in Protestant, Pentecostal, and Catholic forms, while Islam lives in Mandingo and other families. Traditional practice sits in some rooms and is not a souvenir, and none at all is also an ordinary Tuesday, so ask rather than assume.

### Streams

The church is a center of ritual, mutual aid, and information, and sometimes it was the only institution that found this family after the war, but even so, it is not “the community.” Do not BCC one pastor and call it consultation, and do not make clergy the case plan unless this family asked. Do not copy historic African American church honorifics as if they were this grammar; follow this room.

### Practice

Funerals gather family and can run long, while you still keep medical and legal time, and when the two collide you name the conflict instead of punishing it.

Do not treat traditional practice as horror-film content, and do not treat a Pentecostal fast as noncompliance with a med until you have asked.

sections.heading: Greetings
sections.body:
Ask who to greet first, or follow the household’s lead. An English “hello” is ordinary, and Liberian English greetings live in some rooms, so follow the person’s lead. A handshake is common in many professional rooms, and church titles — Reverend, Deacon, Mother — are used in some rooms, so use them until you are invited not to.

### Titles

Wait to see whether a hand is offered, and if it is not, nod.

### This room

Let this person’s own greeting guide you, whatever you read on another page.

Ask before any physical contact, and let the person set the limit.

sections.heading: Naming Conventions
sections.body:
English and biblical given names are common — James, Mary, Washington, Cooper — because of mission schools, the settler republic, and English as the official language, while country names and ethnic names also live here. A person may use an English name at the desk and another name at home, so ask which name they use on this file.

### How to file

U.S. forms want first-middle-last, and Liberian naming may not match, so ask how to file, and ask how to say it. Do not “correct” a Liberian English spelling to U.S. school English, because the form that guesses will invent a person, and that invented name follows them through MHCP, school, and child welfare.

Women may or may not take a husband’s family name in U.S. records, so mother and child may not match, and that is not fraud until you have a reason to think so. Do not joke about names that sound “American,” since they are Liberian names too.

sections.heading: Dates of Significance
sections.body:
Independence Day — 26 July — is the large annual public date, with travel, food, and church. Schedule around it when you can, and be a guest if invited, remembering that a calendar click is not community engagement.

### Calendar

Church calendars — Easter, Christmas, harvest — are ordinary, and Muslim dates matter in Mandingo and other rooms, so ask which ones this family keeps.

Some families name civil-war anniversaries and some refuse to, so do not put a war date on a case note as color, and do not collect it as a risk score.

Do not put “African holiday” on a case note. Ordinary U.S. holidays are real in the second generation, which is one more reason to ask this family.

sections.heading: Education
sections.body:
Compass (ACS 2020–2024) reports that among Liberian Minnesotans 25 and older, about 92.0 percent have a high school education or higher and about 28.8 percent hold a bachelor’s or higher, so date Compass when you cite it. About 59.9 percent of the community is foreign-born, and a large share of children are U.S.-born and in English-dominant schools, but the IEP still has to reach the parent.

### School and language

A parent who speaks fluent Liberian English and limited Minnesota professional English is not illiterate, and a form written for a historic African American household, or for a white Minnesota reader, may still not work. Kolokwa in the home is not “broken English,” so put Liberian English on the interpreter line if this household needs it.

Second-generation educational mobility is real, and so is a gap that a room treating everyone the same will call “culture,” when the truth is language access plus a school that never learned the name. Do not treat a college student as proof that the waiver household needs no interpreter, because the child is not the interpreter.

sections.heading: Etiquette
sections.body:
Ask who to greet first, or follow the household’s lead. If food or drink is offered, accepting a little is fine, and you can still keep to medical and legal timelines.

### In the home

If you visit a home, look for shoes by the door or ask what the household prefers. Ask before taking any photograph, and enter a prayer space only if you are invited.

### Time

If someone misses an appointment, first check the time, transport, interpreter and work schedule. Confirm the plan in the English the person uses, and ask whether it works for them.

Book a qualified interpreter instead of using a child to go between if this elder needs Liberian English.

sections.heading: Language and Communication
sections.body:
English is Liberia’s official language, but Liberian English and Kolokwa (Liberian Kreyol) are not Minnesota professional English, so an interpreter labeled English who does not hear this elder will not work. Ethnic languages — Kpelle, Bassa, and others — live in some homes, so ask, and book the language this household names.

### Language

Compass reports that among those 5 and older, about 83.6 percent speak English only, about 16.4 percent speak a language other than English, and about 7.1 percent speak English less than “very well,” and you should date the number when you use it. An English-only figure of 83.6 percent is not proof that the form was heard, because second-generation Minnesota English is common while the IEP still has to reach the parent.

Give the person time to answer. If you get a short yes, check that the plan was understood, and ask whether it works for them.

Do not use a child as the interpreter, do not make a Liberian coworker the interpreter, and do not write “broken English” on a file.

sections.heading: Other Considerations
sections.body:
This section states hard facts plainly, because treating everyone the same can hide them.

### Named harms

Civil-war trauma is real in some rooms: killing, camps, rape as a weapon of war, and child-soldier history. It is not a personality, and it is not a reason to skip screening, but it is a reason a government badge is not automatically help. Do not put “child soldier” on a case note as color, and do not mash this into a historic African American crime narrative.

DED for Liberians ended on June 30, 2026, and TPS and the decades of temporary status are still structure for some, even after LRIF, and that changes who opens the door, so do not collect status you do not need, and do not treat fear as noncompliance.

Compass poverty of 20.4 percent is a dated figure rather than a race trait or a personality, while care-work wages and a renter rate of 63.6 percent are labor and housing facts.

LGBTQ Liberian Minnesotans exist, so you use the name, and you do not out someone to kin and call it culture. Liberia’s own law climate is not Minnesota’s, and you do not skip mandated reporting and call it humility.

Staff who share this community may add facts, but they do not get to delete a fact because it is hard to say.

sections.heading: Health
sections.body:
Believe reported pain, and do not fold this history into Tuskegee, because this is not the historic African American page, and shared race is not shared medical history.

### Access

Hepatitis B screening for people born in Liberia is a U.S. public-health pattern; CDC has treated Liberia as a higher-prevalence birth country in its screening guidance, so date the CDC page you cite. Do not invent a Minnesota rate, and do not skip screening because the person looks well.

Compass disability is 3.4 percent, a dated figure, and poverty of 20.4 percent is context for delayed care rather than a personality. War trauma, depression, and somatic presentation exist, and mental-health stigma is real in some families, which means naming a counselor is not the same as a family accepting one, and a smile is not a PHQ-9.

Traditional medicine and church healing often sit beside biomedicine, so ask, and work it out together. Gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care, so offer it. FGC exists in some Liberian ethnic communities; Minnesota law stands, and you do not invent a rate, mash the Somali page here, or skip care. Late help-seeking can come from language, stigma, the status climate, and a lobby that already used a child as the interpreter.

sections.heading: LGBTQ
sections.body:
Queer and trans Liberian Minnesotans exist. Conservative family and church climates can mean silence or exile, and some people live a public English life alongside a private Liberian life, so you use the name they use and do not share what they tell you unless a rule requires it.

### This person

Minnesota’s Human Rights Act still applies, and Liberia’s law climate is not this state’s. Do not question a household about anyone’s sexuality or gender, and take seriously that some people have reason to keep it private.

War memory and church do not override what this person wants, because you always defer to the person in front of you.

sections.heading: Hair, Dress, and Body
sections.body:
Country cloth, lappa, and formal dress are public at Independence Day, weddings, and some church stages, but they are not a daily uniform, and the second generation looks like Minnesota. Do not ask a woman in clinic whether she “still wears the costume.”

### Dress

This is not the CROWN Act chapter as the file — and yet anti-Blackness still sits on Liberian bodies in U.S. clinics, schools, and traffic stops, so ask this person. Do not mash historic African American hair politics in as a script, and do not ignore them either.

Do not touch. Gold, a church hat, or a wedding cloth is not a mascot for the unit’s Heritage Month table, and when care work and nursing mean a uniform, that is labor rather than a personality.

sections.heading: Music
sections.body:
Gospel, church choir, highlife, hipco, diaspora pop, and reggae as regional listening all appear in some rooms, and Independence stages hold more than one of them, which makes this named variation rather than a playlist.

### Variation

A funeral is not staff entertainment, and a playlist is not engagement. Knowing that war memory can sit inside a song will stop you from putting the wrong joke on a speaker, and remember that Independence stages are public life rather than consultation or a case plan.

sections.heading: Sports
sections.body:
Soccer is public Liberian life, and George Weah is a public image of the country, but he is not a personality you assign a child in clinic. School sport is ordinary for the second generation, and basketball shows up.

### Not the whole person

Do not assume the kid plays, and do not make sport the only excellence you can see, because sport clubs are social infrastructure for some, but they are not language access and not a case plan. A Saturday tournament does not replace an interpreter on Monday if this elder needs Liberian English.

sections.heading: Literature
sections.body:
English made a written public, and oral forms, church writing, and Liberian English as the literature of the everyday sit beside it. Minnesota and U.S. Liberian writers and journalists exist, although you do not need to quote a novel in the lobby.

### Literacy in the lobby

What you do need to know is that this is not a people without letters. Many elders read English and some do not, and a notice written only in Minnesota professional English may still not work for a Kolokwa speaker, so ask.

Do not write “illiterate” because the English is not yours; write what they tell you.

sections.heading: Art
sections.body:
Country cloth, carving, church pageantry, and Independence public culture are all part of this world, while rice, soup, and pepper are foodway rather than consultation.

### Guest

Come as a guest, not a researcher. A church or community-center visit is optional professional development rather than consultation, and you should not photograph a family as tourism.

A Heritage Month display that mashes this with historic African American quilts, a Somali poster, or one “African” table has already mashed the adjacent peoples.

sections.heading: War, Temporary Status, and the State
sections.body:
The 1980 coup, two civil wars running roughly 1989–2003, the camps, TPS and then DED, and a United States that left people in temporary status for decades until LRIF in 2019 — that is the political event. Later came policing, and an enforcement climate for people still without a stable status, which is why a DHS badge is not automatically help.

### The badge

Do not use the war as a personality. Do not ask a survivor to narrate killing for your professional development, and do not put child-soldier history on a case note as color. Intra-community politics about the war and about who came when are real, but you do not referee them on a file.

DED ended on June 30, 2026, but the history of DED and TPS still changes who opens the door, who signs, and who will not put a relative’s name on a form, and that is not noncompliance. Do not collect status you do not need, and do not mash this chapter into historic African American CRM because both are Black.

sections.heading: Work, Markets, and Government
sections.body:
Care work, CNA, nursing, shop, restaurant, factory, the professional second generation, and public employment all appear here. Compass puts median household income at about $67,197, poverty at 20.4 percent, and renters at 63.6 percent, all dated figures. Nursing and CNA labor is a documented Liberian American work pattern in some rooms, and it is work — not a personality, not a joke, and not the whole economy.

### Work

Book a qualified interpreter, and pay for community work. Do not assign either to staff because of who they are.

### Staff

Take time to introduce yourself and explain the plan. The first visit may not be the decision, and any required notice still goes out. Pay the partner this household names.

sections.heading: Health-care and Human-service Encounters
sections.body:
English versus Liberian English is the first failure the building will miss, because the checkbox says English. Confirm this English, and book Liberian English if this elder needs it, while still booking a qualified interpreter when language is the gate, without using a child or making staff the interpreter.

### Language

Notice who is in the room. Expect a child pushed forward as Minnesota English, a pastor in the story, pain you must believe, war trauma you do not make a personality, the DED/TPS climate, and a nuclear form that filed them under Black and opened the historic African American page.

### The meeting

Offer gender match, ask who should hear, and ask which name they use. If they name church healing or traditional medicine, listen, and remember that mandated reporting still exists. Believe reported pain, and do not mix Tuskegee into this history as the file.

sections.heading: Adjacent Peoples — Do Not Mash
sections.body:
This is not historic African American / Black American. Compass notes a 2024 change in how ancestry is collected for Black respondents, so the Compass African American count and the Liberian count differ, and that mash is not this page, so open historic African American for a Great Migration household, and open this one for Liberian.

### Adjacent doors

It is not Somali. It is not Nigerian as a synonym — a related West African coast, but a different state, a different war, and different languages. It is not Sierra Leonean as a mash, since that is a related war but a different republic, and it is not Ghanaian. Never one Black module, and never one “African” interpreter.

Some households are mixed, and some Liberian families have historic African American in-laws, so ask this household, because shared race is not shared culture, and shared English is not shared English.

sections.heading: Counts, Dated
sections.body:
Minnesota Compass (ACS 2020–2024) describes the Liberian cultural community as about 22,571 people (plus or minus 4,423; Compass's 2024 single-year total is 23,608, plus or minus 10,872, which it calls its most accurate size estimate), with 86.8% in the Twin Cities and 13.2% in Greater Minnesota. Those age 17 or younger are 46.0% and those 65+ are 4.1%, and 59.9% are foreign-born. Among those age 5+, 83.6% speak English only, 16.4% speak a language other than English, and 7.1% speak English less than “very well.” Among those 25+, 92.0% have high school or higher and 28.8% hold a bachelor’s or higher. Median household income is about $67,197 (2024 dollars), poverty is 20.4%, 36.4% of homes are owner-occupied and 63.6% renter-occupied, average household size is 3.54, and disability is 3.4%.

### Counts

Date Compass, and do not invent other rates, because counts disagree across ACS vintages and definitions (ancestry vs. birthplace vs. the Compass African American count, which is collected differently), so the number you cite needs its date. This page is Liberian Minnesota, not that mash.

### What the count is not

A young age structure is not a personality, and English-only at 83.6 percent is not proof the elder heard the form. Poverty is not a race trait, while language and child-as-interpreter are still gates, because a rate is not the person.

sections.heading: Doors and Sources
sections.body:
Start with the Minnesota Compass Liberian profile (ACS 2020–2024), keeping in mind that the Compass African American profile is a different count, and this page is not that mash. Other doors are the Organization of Liberians in Minnesota (OLM, founded 1973 and incorporated 1979), which runs the Liberian Community/OLM Center in Brooklyn Park, the churches families name, and Brooklyn Park / Brooklyn Center as a documented concentration (ACS 2020–2024 counts 4,544 Liberia-born residents of Brooklyn Park (plus or minus 1,153) and 1,147 in Brooklyn Center, out of 15,297 statewide, and Brooklyn Park city officials put the city's Liberian population above 7,000), which you confirm on this family.

### Public doors

CECLC is a door, not the whole community, and an eList is not engagement, so pay partners, and report back.

### Where to learn more

Use these resources yourself before you ask a Liberian colleague to explain, and do not count a BCC to a church as consultation. Be a guest at Independence Day if invited, remembering that it is not consultation.

sections.heading: How it hits DHS gates — the 40%
sections.body:
Workplace culture and service delivery are both candidates here.

Language comes first, because an interpreter labeled English who does not speak Liberian English as this elder speaks it will not work, and Compass English-only at 83.6 percent is not proof the packet was heard. Still book a qualified interpreter when language is the gate, do not use a child, and do not write “broken English.” Gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care.

Names come next: English names that look “American” are still Liberian names, and the database that “corrects” spelling invents a person.

Hour caps, exception processes, and life-sharing matches offered without the English this household uses are not culturally neutral.

In child welfare and disability, help-seeking that becomes a report is part of why people wait, and war trauma is not a risk score. Mandated reporting still exists, and so does the duty not to treat a whole community as a historic African American crime narrative.

DED ended on June 30, 2026, and LRIF (2019) was the route to green cards for most long-term residents, but the status climate still means people may skip clinic, school, and waiver meetings when a relative can be moved, and that is not noncompliance, so do not collect status you do not need.

On notices and comment, do not count an eList and an English PDF as reaching this community, and record who was reached and what follow-up happened. Greater Minnesota is 13.2 percent, and Brooklyn Park is not the whole channel until this family lives there.

In the workforce, Liberian staff are not the interpreter pool and not the community, because staff are colleagues, not the curriculum, and should not be treated as either.

Then there is the Black mash: opening historic African American because both are Black and both speak English shuts the person out.

On legislation, funding, and rule: study a channel before you advocate for it. Use this page so that the 40% has a household in it.

sections.heading: A Note on This Guide
sections.body:
This brief is about Mexican Minnesota — mexicano, mexicana — the largest Latino origin in this state, and it is worth saying at the outset that Mexico is many peoples. Mixtec (Ñuu Savi) and Zapotec (Benizaa) may well be the languages spoken in a Minnesota home, which means that a Spanish interpreter, however qualified, may still not work.

### Who this is

This page is about Mexican Minnesota specifically, so it is not the Latino / Hispanic umbrella, and it is not a synonym for every Spanish-surnamed household that comes through the lobby. Minnesota Compass (ACS 2020–2024) puts the Mexican cultural community at 231,993 (plus or minus 5,615) people, of whom 60.8 percent live in the Twin Cities and 39.2 percent in Greater Minnesota, which means nearly 4 in 10 live outside the Twin Cities (Compass, ACS 2020–2024). The community is young, with about 36.8 percent age 17 or younger and 4.2 percent age 65+, and about 27.5 percent are foreign-born, so a majority in that vintage were born here. Among those age 5 and older, 58.6 percent speak a language other than English at home, and 23.4 percent speak English less than “very well,” so date one of these numbers whenever you use it. Mixtec and Zapotec may be spoken in the home, but Compass does not count those speakers, so please do not invent a count that does not exist, and remember throughout that a rate describes a population rather than the person in front of you.

### Who this is not

This brief is not about Guatemalan, Salvadoran, or Puerto Rican Minnesota, because a shared Spanish language does not mean a shared culture. The Latino umbrella brief is useful, but open it only as an adjacent resource, since that page covers the mash of origins and the CLAS Spanish line, while this page is Mexican. If a household gets filed under “Latino” because the checkbox was easier, the door this brief is trying to open has already been left behind.

### How to read this

Read this as an orientation rather than a profile, and consider the range of people it covers: a Mixtec dairy worker in a southern county, a U.S.-born professional in a first-ring suburb, a West Side elder whose family has been in St. Paul longer than your unit has existed, a Jalisco restaurant household, a college student who uses English with friends and Spanish with a grandmother, and a person who will not open the door because a relative can be moved. They share a people, even though they do not share a Tuesday.

Always defer to the person in front of you. The facts that follow are meant to help you meet people well — how family is named, what respect looks like, what a greeting carries, and what a form may land on — and the history is here so that the meeting is clearer, not so that you deliver a lecture.

sections.heading: Origins and the Founding of a People
sections.body:
Mexican peoplehood is older than the Bracero program, older than IRCA, and older than the Minnesota plant, and holding that in mind keeps the history in its proper order.

### Many peoples

Mexico is a country on the land between the United States and Guatemala, and its public narratives tend to center a mestizo majority, although within it live Mixtec, Zapotec, Purépecha, Maya in the south, and other indigenous nations whose languages may be spoken in a Minnesota home. The right response is to ask, while the wrong one is to lecture a Worthington family about a taxonomy they did not ask for.

### History for the meeting

Spanish colonial rule, the Catholic mission, independence (the Grito of 16 September 1810, consummated in 1821), the Revolution after 1910, and a modern republic that has both claimed and erased its indigenous nations — this is the literacy you bring to the meeting, not a speech you give the family. Nor is food, a sombrero, or a Heritage Month sentence a good place to start.

Writing in Spanish is the ordinary public literacy of the Mexican state, but Mixtec and Zapotec are languages in their own right, not dialects of Spanish. Some elders read Spanish and some do not, and some U.S.-born adults do not read Spanish either, because oral fluency and print literacy are different things.

### What people brought

People brought language, in Spanish varieties and in indigenous languages, along with kinship, the parish and later the evangelical church, farm and trade skill, Guadalupe, and the memory of a border that used them. What they met in Minnesota was an English form, a single “Latino” checkbox, often one interpreter labeled Spanish, and a rural plant town or a St. Paul lobby that had not studied Mixtec.

sections.heading: The Geography of the Mexican World
sections.body:
Mexico is not one climate, and it is not one Spanish.

### Mexico

North, center, and south; Oaxaca, Michoacán, Jalisco, Guanajuato, the border states, Mexico City — across these places tones, food, and some vocabulary shift. If a family names a place, confirm it and hold onto it, and if they name a pueblo, listen, but do not referee Monterrey versus Oaxaca in a waiver meeting.

### United States and Minnesota

The U.S. Mexican map runs through California, Texas, Illinois, and the Southwest, and it also runs through the Upper Midwest plant and dairy counties that a Minneapolis default still treats as leftover. Compass puts 60.8 percent of Mexican Minnesotans in the Twin Cities and 39.2 percent in Greater Minnesota, which is nearly 4 in 10 (Compass, ACS 2020–2024), so Worthington, Willmar, Austin, Albert Lea, and the dairy counties are names you should be able to hold comfortably, without turning them into a tour.

### Metro

West Side St. Paul / District del Sol is historic Mexican Minnesota, and it is a living neighborhood rather than a museum, while Lake Street and Phillips, the first-ring suburbs, and scattered apartments near plants are all part of the metro picture. Even so, do not assume West Side, and do not assume the person in front of you has ever been to Mexico, because a Greater Minnesota household is every bit as much this people.

sections.heading: Labor, IRCA, and Enforcement — Foundational Events
sections.body:
If 1975 is the single foundational event of Vietnamese Minnesota, Mexican Minnesota’s foundational events are stacked one on top of another.

### Labor and settlement

The sequence begins with labor recruitment into sugar beet fields and canneries, and later into plants and dairy, and the Bracero program (1942–1964; MNopedia's Minnesotanos timeline says 1943 to 1964) belongs in your U.S. policy literacy. IRCA-era settlement followed after 1986, and later family and work streams followed that, with enforcement waves running through all of it that reorganize who will open the door. This history is its own, which means it is not a Guatemalan war file and not a Salvadoran TPS file.

Mexican migrant farm labor in Minnesota is older than the current plant map, since settlement followed work, church, and IRCA, and secondary migration then pulled kin along.

### Who you meet

The desk in 2026 does not only meet a first wave. It meets U.S.-born children — Compass puts the foreign-born share at 27.5 percent — translating for their parents, and it meets mixed-status households, as well as a Mixtec household that has been in a dairy county for years and still cannot get Mixtec in the lobby.

### Enforcement

Enforcement is current structure, not background. When raids happen, when raids are rumored, or when a visible ICE climate spikes, people may skip clinic, school, and waiver meetings, and that is not noncompliance. A notice mailed to a household afraid to open the door shuts the person out, so do not collect status you do not need, because the desk that asks “are you legal?” on visit one has already chosen a who.

If the only word you know is “immigrant,” you will miss the majority who were born here, and you will still treat the English IEP as culturally neutral.

sections.heading: Family
sections.body:
Ask who the person wants in the room, and hear from the person directly.

### Who is in the household

Adult children may fit a waiver meeting, a plant shift, and a school conference into the same week. Compass reports an average household size of about 2.99, but that does not mean the household matches a nuclear English form, since grandparents may be the household. The person who cares for a disabled adult or a child may be a son, a daughter-in-law, a sibling, or a padrino, rather than the legally recognized caregiver on the checkbox.

Hour caps and “natural supports” language can quietly dump unpaid work onto the women in that network and then call the result culture.

### Mixed-status

Mixed-status is structure: a U.S.-citizen child, a parent without status, a sibling with DACA, an aunt who works the plant. Do not collect status you do not need, and do not treat unmatched last names, a grandmother as caregiver, or a missing SSN as fraud until you have a reason.

### Who speaks

The person who speaks in the lobby may be the child with the best English, but that child is not the qualified interpreter, and CLAS still stands. Using a child as the go-between does harm, because it reverses respeto, it leaks adult business to a child, and it is not language access, so book the interpreter and ask who should be in the room.

Minnesota law still stands, which means domestic violence is not culture and skipping mandated reporting is not humility.

sections.heading: Minnesota and Mexican History
sections.body:
Minnesota holds the largest Latino-origin community in the state in its Mexican community, and Compass counts 231,993 (plus or minus 5,615) (ACS 2020–2024). Greater Minnesota accounts for 39.2 percent, nearly 4 in 10 (Compass, ACS 2020–2024), so do not write this people as a Minneapolis anecdote, since human services will meet it on waivers, in child welfare, in health care, in cash and food programs, in aging, and in employment — in a plant town and on the West Side alike.

### Places

West Side St. Paul / District del Sol is historic Mexican Minnesota, and it is not a museum. Lake Street and Phillips, the first-ring suburbs, Worthington, Willmar, Austin, Albert Lea, the dairy counties, and the southern and western towns are all part of the map. Markets and taquerías are public life, but they are not consultation, and a food-court visit does not make you the expert.

### Partners

CLUES — Comunidades Latinas Unidas En Servicio (https://clues.org/) — and Centro Tyrone Guzmán are established partners, and rural parish and worker centers matter too, so name the local one rather than assuming Minneapolis. Churches may be the actual safe channel, while CECLC is a department door, not the whole community, so pay the partner this household actually uses.

Book a qualified interpreter, and pay for community work. Do not assign either to staff because of who they are. A fiesta or a Guadalupe mass is optional professional development if you are invited, and if you go, you go as a guest, since the visit does not make you the expert.

sections.heading: Mexicano — the heart of a people
sections.body:
Mexico is a country with Indigenous nations inside it, and Mexican history in the United States includes long years of labor on other people’s harvests. Forms in Minnesota file Mexican people under Latino, so ask how the person identifies.

### Mixtec and Zapotec peoples

Ask plainly whether the person agrees with the plan, and make it easy to say no.

Mixtec and Zapotec peoplehood is not a dialect note, and a household that names Mixtec is not “Mexican Spanish with an accent.” Treating it that way is the mash, and the mash is the gate.

### Under a Latino checkbox

In the United States another fact sits on the same desk. Mexican Minnesota is the largest origin under a Latino checkbox that also holds Guatemalan, Salvadoran, Puerto Rican, and Andean histories it does not share, and while the Mexican default in this state is a count fact, it becomes a harm when the building treats this page as the only Latino file.

This brief is a working orientation. Individual variation always supersedes group generalization, and you always defer to the person in front of you.

sections.heading: Core Concepts
sections.body:
These concepts recur throughout this brief, so treat each one as a hypothesis you still test with this family.

### Familismo

Familismo names kin as the unit of decision and care, but it is a hypothesis, not a rule. The person who talks in the lobby may not be the person who decides, so ask who should be in the room, and remember that familismo is never a license to skip mandated reporting and that staff do not use it as a guilt tool.

### Respeto

Respeto is a word for titles, deference to elders, and usted. Ask how the person wants to be addressed, and start with a title and usted if you speak Spanish, because a first name or a joke may not land well. Before you treat a yes as agreement, ask again, plainly and without embarrassing anyone.

### Personalismo and confianza

Allow time in the first visit for the person to decide whether you are safe to talk to, and name any medical or legal deadline openly. An enforcement climate, a bad interpreter, a child used as the mouth, or an SSN field that feels like a trap — each of these spends confianza before you have earned it.

### Two surnames

Names carry the apellido paterno first and then the apellido materno, so a database that keeps only one invents a person.

### Mixtec and Zapotec

These are peoples and languages, and a Spanish interpreter may still not work, while Compass does not count speakers, so ask.

Work, school, faith, and mixed status may all shape daily life, and a plant shift and a second-generation degree can sit in the same household, so do not collect status you do not need.

sections.heading: Religion
sections.body:
Many Mexican Minnesota streams are Catholic-majority, but not all of them are.

### Parish and church

Our Lady of Guadalupe (12 December) is central in many Catholic lives. The parish may be the trusted channel for information, mutual aid, and baptismal records, and it may be a room people will enter when they will not enter yours. Evangelical and Pentecostal churches are large, while indigenous practice lives in some Mixtec and Zapotec homes, and it is not a souvenir.

Do not make a priest, a pastor, or a curandero the case plan unless this family asked for that, and do not BCC one parish and call it consultation. Do not treat evangelical growth as the evolved version of Catholic, and do not treat indigenous practice as witchcraft.

### Calendar and public history

Día de los Muertos is public history — ofrendas, 1–2 November — not a file and not a personality. Holy Week, the quinceañera as a religious-family event, Las Posadas, and funeral obligation can all collide with your calendar, and while you still keep medical and legal time, you name the conflict instead of punishing it. Do not photograph an ofrenda or a Guadalupe altar.

Help that looks like a report is not help. A religious framing of disability, mental health, or gender can sit right next to a fierce wish for services, and you can hold both.

sections.heading: Greetings
sections.body:
Ask who to greet first, or follow the household’s lead. Wait to see how the person greets you, and follow their lead.

### Titles

Let the other person set any greeting beyond a handshake or nod.

Use titles until invited to do otherwise: Señor, Señora, Don, Doña. Use the last name you were given, remembering there may be two, and do not use a first name with an elder because the form printed it. Usted versus tú is a matter of respect in Spanish, so a qualified interpreter matches the register, and you do not correct it.

### This room

Let this person’s own greeting guide you, whatever you read on another page. Ask before any physical contact, and let the person set the limit.

sections.heading: Naming Conventions
sections.body:
Two surnames is the default in much of Mexican Spanish-language naming, with the apellido paterno first and then the apellido materno.

### Two surnames

José Luis García Hernández is not “José García” with leftover words. A U.S. database that keeps one surname invents a person, and that invented name then follows them through MHCP, child welfare, and school, which makes it a gate.

Ask how to file the name, ask how to say it, and then pronounce it. Do not drop accents as a joke, and do not anglicize Jesús, Muñoz, or Ñ as a convenience. Given names may be Spanish, Mixtec, Zapotec, English, or both, and some people use a middle given name as the call-name, so ask.

### How to file

Women may or may not take a husband’s surname in U.S. records; some add de plus the husband’s paternal surname, and some keep both family surnames. Children may carry two surnames that do not match a parent’s U.S. “last name” field, and that is not fraud until you have a reason.

Do not treat unmatched last names in a household as a fraud flag by default, and do not invent a hyphen and then punish the person when the hyphen moves.

sections.heading: Dates of Significance
sections.body:
Knowing the calendar is literacy for scheduling, although it is not community engagement.

### Independence and Guadalupe

16 September is Mexican independence, and knowing that is literacy for the meeting. Cinco de Mayo commemorates the Battle of Puebla (1862); it is not independence, and it is not a party you put on a case note as the national day, so do not file this household under a restaurant calendar.

12 December is Our Lady of Guadalupe, major for many Mexican Catholic families, and Las Posadas falls in mid-December in some streams. Día de los Reyes / Three Kings is 6 January, and Holy Week matters as well, while a quinceañera is family-religious time, not a case note.

### Día de los Muertos

Día de los Muertos falls on 1–2 November and is public history in Minnesota. If you are in a public ofrenda space, you are a guest, because it is not a file, and it is not a costume for staff.

Hispanic Heritage Month (15 September–15 October) is the umbrella calendar, but it is not this people’s day, and it is not consultation, so do not put “Latino holiday” on a case note.

sections.heading: Education
sections.body:
Compass (ACS 2020–2024) reports that among Mexican Minnesotans 25 and older, about 73.4 percent have a high school education or higher and about 20.6 percent have a bachelor’s or higher, so date Compass when you cite it. About 27.5 percent of the community is foreign-born.

### School and language

A large share of children are U.S.-born and in English-dominant schools, and the IEP still has to reach the parent who does not read it.

A parent who speaks fluent Spanish, or fluent Mixtec, and limited English is not illiterate, and some elders read Spanish while some do not. Mixtec or Zapotec in the home is not served by a Spanish IEP, and the English-only form is the gate, so do not use a child as the interpreter.

### Mobility and gap

Second-generation educational mobility is real, and so is a gap, which a room that treats everyone the same will call “culture” instead of what it is: language access plus poverty plus enforcement fear plus a school that never learned the second surname. Do not treat a college student in the family as proof that the waiver household needs no interpreter.

sections.heading: Etiquette
sections.body:
If food or drink is offered, accepting a little is fine, and you can still keep to medical and legal timelines.

### In the home

Ask before taking any photograph or touching any religious object, and do not ask anyone to explain their faith or history for your benefit. On shoes, follow the household.

### Time

If someone misses an appointment, first check the time, transport, interpreter and plant shift or other work schedule. Confirm the plan in the language the person uses, and ask whether it works for them.

Book a qualified interpreter instead of using a child to go between.

sections.heading: Language and Communication
sections.body:
Mexican Spanish is not Salvadoran Spanish, it is not Caribbean Spanish, and it is not one interpreter accent test.

### Spanish

Book a qualified Spanish interpreter AND ask this household what they need. Register matters, so use usted, not a buddy tú, until the room says otherwise.

### Mixtec and Zapotec

Mixtec and Zapotec may be spoken in the home. Compass notes the language possibility, but that is not a count of speakers, so do not invent one, and for those households a Spanish interpreter still will not work. Name the language on the request, because a scarce interpreter is a gate, and it is not an excuse to proceed in English only without recording the gap.

### What Compass shows

Among those 5 and older, about 58.6 percent speak a language other than English, and about 23.4 percent speak English less than “very well,” so date the number. Many U.S.-born people use English with peers and Spanish with an elder, and the IEP still has to reach the parent. Literacy in any language is not guaranteed, because oral skill is not print.

Give the person time to answer. If you get a short yes, check that the plan was understood, and ask whether it works for them. Do not use a child as the interpreter, and do not make a Mexican coworker the interpreter.

sections.heading: Other Considerations
sections.body:
This section states hard facts plainly, because treating everyone the same can hide them.

### Enforcement

ICE and the enforcement climate are structure, and mixed-status households may skip clinic, school, and waiver meetings when a relative can be moved, which is not noncompliance. Do not collect status you do not need, because an SSN on the first screen is a gate.

### Named harms

Indigenous erasure under “they all speak Spanish” is a named harm. Mixtec and Zapotec are the names to remember, and a Spanish interpreter may still not work. Colorism is real, and intra-Latino hierarchy is real too: the Mexican default in this state will talk over a Maya or Caribbean household if you let the umbrella page do this page’s job — and this page will talk over Mixtec if you let mestizo Spanish be the only file.

Do not joke about machismo, and do not excuse control as “that’s culture.” Who speaks in the meeting, who holds the papers, who is allowed to leave the house — ask about these, and follow the law, because domestic violence is not culture. You follow mandated reporting, and you still see a family.

LGBTQ Mexican Minnesotans exist, so you use the name they use, and you do not out someone to kin and call it familismo. Staff who share this community may add facts, but they do not get to delete a fact because it is hard to say.

sections.heading: Health
sections.body:
Believe reported pain or “they are dramatic,” and do not fold this history into Tuskegee or into a generic immigrant-mistrust slide.

### Patterns to date

U.S. public-health literature has treated Mexican-origin adults as a higher-prevalence group for type 2 diabetes, so date the CDC page you cite. Do not invent a Minnesota rate, and do not skip screening because the person looks well. Uninsured and delayed-care patterns sit here, and Minnesota figures should be dated when you have them, while Compass poverty (ACS 2020–2024) is 12.0 percent — that is a poverty figure, not an uninsured rate.

### Access

Fear of the lobby is a health access fact. A badge, a form that asks for SSN, a child called to interpret a diagnosis, an interpreter who does not speak this Spanish or this Mixtec — these are clinical events. When enforcement spikes, people may skip clinic, and that is not noncompliance.

Traditional medicine, yerberías, and parish prayer can sit next to a fierce wish for biomedicine, so ask, work it out together, and do not mock. Gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care, so offer it, and do not use a child as the interpreter in a health encounter. Mental-health stigma is real in some families, and a smile is not a PHQ-9.

sections.heading: LGBTQ
sections.body:
Queer and trans Mexican Minnesotans exist, and conservative family, parish, and evangelical climates can mean silence or exile for them. Mixtec and Zapotec queer people exist as well.

### This person

Some people live a public English life and a private Spanish or Mixtec life, so you use the name they use and do not share what they tell you unless a rule requires it.

Minnesota’s Human Rights Act still applies. Do not question a household about anyone’s sexuality or gender, and take seriously that some people have reason to keep it private.

Do not let concern about family reputation or parish climate override what this person wants, and always defer to the person in front of you.

sections.heading: Hair, Dress, and Body
sections.body:
There is no Mexican uniform, and the second generation looks like Minnesota.

### Dress

Mixtec and Zapotec dress is public at fiesta and ceremony, but it is not a daily costume, and it is not yours to request for a Heritage Month photo. Do not ask a woman in clinic whether she “still wears the costume.”

Colorism and hair texture are real, and the mestizo default in beauty is a hierarchy, so name it if it is in the room, but do not rank, and do not touch.

Quinceañera dress, baptism white, funeral black, evangelical modesty, a Guadalupe medal — these are celebration and devotion, not a case note. Plant and dairy work may mean stained hands, and that is labor, not a joke and not a race trait.

sections.heading: Music
sections.body:
Mariachi, ranchera, norteño, banda, cumbia, corridos, and church music are all part of the picture, and this is named variation, not a playlist.

### Variation

A Mexican default playlist in a Guatemalan or Puerto Rican waiting room is the mash coming through speakers. This page is Mexican, and even so you should not assume norteño is this household.

Corridos include narcocorridos in some streams, which is a named fact, not a joke and not a risk score you write on a last name.

A festival stage is not engagement, a playlist is not language access, and a funeral is not staff entertainment. Guadalupe mañanitas are public life, but they are not consultation and not a case plan.

sections.heading: Sports
sections.body:
Fútbol is the default public sport for many boys and men, and for many girls, while boxing carries prestige in some streams and school sport is ordinary for the second generation.

### Not the whole person

Do not assume the kid plays, and do not make sport the only excellence you can see.

Leagues and pickup games are social infrastructure in the metro and in plant towns alike, although they are not language access and not a case plan. Greater Minnesota teams are still this people.

A Saturday tournament does not replace an interpreter on Monday.

sections.heading: Literature
sections.body:
Spanish-language literature is world literature, and Mixtec and Zapotec oral literature is older than the Spanish file, so it is not “no letters.”

### Literacy in the lobby

That fact does not mean the person in the lobby can read your form, in English or in Spanish, because literacy in any language is not guaranteed.

Minnesota has Mexican and Chicano journalists, poets, and scholars. You do not need to quote a novel in the lobby, but you do need to know that this is not a people without letters, and also not a people who can all read the exception process.

Print Spanish from Spain, or a machine translation, is not automatically this household’s Spanish, since CLAS means qualified language — not Google and not a child.

sections.heading: Art
sections.body:
Murals on the West Side and on Lake Street are public Minnesota art, not a booth, and ofrendas at Día de los Muertos are public history. Mixtec and Zapotec weaving are art and memory, not a mascot for the unit’s Heritage Month table.

### Guest

Be a guest, not a researcher, and do not photograph an altar because it is pretty. An ofrenda is not a case plan, a mural tour is not consultation, and markets and taquerías are foodway, not consultation.

A Heritage Month that mashes this people with a generic Latino playlist or a Guatemalan traje has already mashed the adjacent peoples.

sections.heading: Labor, Enforcement, and the State
sections.body:
The political literacy here is labor and the border, not a single civil war.

### Labor and the badge

U.S. recruitment, Bracero, IRCA 1986 and the settlement that followed, and enforcement that reorganizes Tuesday — that is the sequence. A DHS badge is not automatically help, and saying so is not paranoia; it is pattern.

When enforcement spikes, people may skip clinic, school, and waiver meetings, so do not tell people the climate is fine so that the form feels fair now. Do not use a crossing or a raid as a personality, and do not ask a person to narrate the desert for your professional development.

### Status

Do not collect status you do not need, because an SSN on the first screen is a gate, and notices sent to a household that will not open the door do not reach them. Mandated reporting still exists, and so does the duty not to treat a whole people as a deportation score.

sections.heading: Work, Markets, and Government
sections.body:
Food processing, dairy, agriculture, construction, service, restaurants, cleaning, childcare, home care, a professional second generation, and public employment — all of these are where Mexican Minnesotans work.

### Work

Rural plants and metro kitchens can sit in the same extended family, and a small-business owner and a waiver recipient may be the same household.

Worker centers and parishes may be the trusted channel in Greater Minnesota, so name the local one rather than assuming Minneapolis, and do not assume CLUES reaches a dairy county. Take time to introduce yourself and explain the plan, and still give any required notice.

### Staff

Book a qualified interpreter, and pay for community work. Do not assign either to staff because of who they are. Use these resources yourself before you ask a Mexican colleague to explain.

Some people send money to relatives in Mexico as an obligation. Ask about it, and do not treat it as optional in a budget.

sections.heading: Health-care and Human-service Encounters
sections.body:
Language here includes indigenous languages, so book qualified Spanish AND ask.

### Language

Confirm Mixtec or Zapotec when that is the home language, because a Spanish interpreter may still not work, and do not use a child as the interpreter or make staff the interpreter.

### The meeting

Ask who is in the room, and offer gender match in maternal and intimate care if they want it. Use titles and both surnames, and if you do not need an SSN on the first screen, do not ask for it. With mixed-status households, do not collect status you do not need, and remember that in an enforcement climate, skipped appointments are pattern.

Believe reported pain, and do not skip screening. If they name a healer or a parish, listen, but do not make either the case plan unless they asked, and remember that mandated reporting still exists. Rural access is a gate — distance, clinic hours, and one interpreter contracted from the Cities who does not speak this language — and Greater Minnesota at 39.2 percent is not an afterthought.

sections.heading: Adjacent Peoples — Do Not Mash
sections.body:
This page is not the Latino / Hispanic umbrella.

### Adjacent doors

Open that brief as adjacent, for the CLAS Spanish line, the mash, and the other origins as a list, because this page is Mexican, and do not file this household under “Latino” and call it done.

This is not Guatemalan, Salvadoran, or Puerto Rican, and it is not Ecuadorian, Colombian, Cuban, Honduran, Nicaraguan, Dominican, or Venezuelan, so name the origin and open the people brief that matches this household.

### Indigenous languages

Mixtec and Zapotec are not “Mexican Spanish.” They are languages and peoples, and a Spanish interpreter is not those languages. This page is not Brazilian Portuguese, not Somali, and not historic African American — though Afro-Mexican people exist, so ask rather than mash, and never use one Latino module.

sections.heading: Counts, Dated
sections.body:
The figures that follow come from Minnesota Compass, ACS 2020–2024, for the Mexican cultural community.

### Compass

Compass counts 231,993 (plus or minus 5,615) people, of whom 60.8 percent live in the Twin Cities and 39.2 percent in Greater Minnesota (nearly 4 in 10 — Compass, ACS 2020–2024). About 36.8 percent are age 17 or younger and 4.2 percent are 65+, and the foreign-born share is 27.5 percent. Among those age 5+, 58.6 percent speak a language other than English and 23.4 percent speak English less than “very well,” while among those 25+, 73.4 percent have high school or higher and 20.6 percent have a bachelor’s or higher. Median household income is about $71,697, poverty is 12.0 percent, owner-occupied housing is 53.1 percent, average household size is 2.99, and disability is 8.1 percent.

### What Compass does not count

Mixtec and Zapotec may be spoken in the home, and Compass notes the language possibility, but it is not a count of speakers, so do not invent that count. Date Compass and do not invent other rates. Counts disagree across ACS vintages and definitions (Hispanic origin vs. ancestry vs. language vs. birthplace), so date the number you cite.

A young age structure is not a personality, and an owner rate is not proof the gates closed. Language and the child-as-interpreter are gates, Greater Minnesota at 39.2 percent is not an afterthought, and a rate is not the person.

sections.heading: Doors and Sources
sections.body:
Start with the Minnesota Compass Mexican profile (ACS 2020–2024) at https://www.mncompass.org/topics/demographics/cultural-communities/mexican, and date the retrieval.

### Public doors

Compass (ACS 2020–2024) covers the Greater Minnesota share. CLUES — Comunidades Latinas Unidas En Servicio — https://clues.org/ provides Twin Cities services, but it is not the whole state, and Centro Tyrone Guzmán works with families and youth in the metro. Rural parish and worker centers matter, so name the local one and do not assume Minneapolis, because the parish in a dairy county may be the actual door.

CECLC is a department door, not the whole community. Open the Latino umbrella brief as adjacent, not as this page, and open the Guatemalan, Salvadoran, or Puerto Rican brief when that is the household. Open a Mixtec or Zapotec interpreter request when Spanish is the wrong door.

### Where to learn more

Use these resources yourself before you ask a Mexican colleague to explain, and do not count a BCC to CLUES as consultation. Pay partners and report back, since Hispanic Heritage Month is not the work.

sections.heading: How it hits DHS gates — the 40%
sections.body:
Workplace culture and service delivery are both candidates here.

Language: CLAS Spanish is not one Spanish. Mixtec and Zapotec may be spoken in the home, and a Spanish interpreter may still not work, so you still book a qualified interpreter, because a list is not the person and not the language. Do not use a child, and remember that gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care.

Names: two surnames, which means the database that keeps one invents a person, and unmatched last names are not fraud by default.

Hour caps, exception processes, an SSN on the first screen, and life-sharing matches without language are not culturally neutral. Mixed-status households may bounce if the first field feels like enforcement, so do not collect status you do not need.

Child welfare and disability: help-seeking that becomes a report is part of why people wait. Mandated reporting still exists, and so does the duty not to treat a whole community as a risk score, while domestic violence is not culture and you follow law.

Enforcement climate: people may skip clinic, school, and waiver meetings when a relative can be moved, and that is not noncompliance, so do not collect status you do not need.

Notices and comment: do not count an eList and an English PDF as reaching this community, and record who was reached and what follow-up happened. Greater Minnesota is 39.2 percent, so a St. Paul meeting is not the whole channel.

Workforce: Mexican staff are not the interpreter pool, not the Mixtec pool, and not the community. Staff are colleagues, not the curriculum, and they should not be treated as the curriculum.

Latino mash: opening the umbrella, or the Guatemalan, Salvadoran, or Puerto Rican brief, because the checkbox says Hispanic shuts the person out.

Legislation, funding, rule: study a channel before you advocate for it. Use this page so that the 40% has a household in it.

sections.heading: A Note on This Guide
sections.body:
This brief is about Nigerian Minnesota, understood as a state-name community made up of many peoples. Yoruba, Igbo, Hausa, Edo, Ijaw, Tiv, Ibibio, Fulani, and others are not one file, so book the language this household names. English is Nigeria’s official language, and Nigerian Pidgin is a language in its own right, not broken English. Yoruba is not Igbo and Hausa is not Yoruba, which is why a “Nigerian interpreter” is not a language and an “African interpreter” will not work.

### Who this is

It helps to be clear about what this page is not. It is not Somali, because shared race in the United States is not shared culture, and it is not historic African American, since the Compass African American row is a different mash altogether. It is not Liberian used as a synonym — that is a related West African coast, but a different state, a different war, and different languages — and it is not Ghanaian.

### Who this is not

Minnesota Compass (ACS 2020–2024) puts Nigerian Minnesota near 21,206 (plus or minus 3,847) people, with about 81.7 percent living in the Twin Cities and about 18.3 percent in Greater Minnesota. About 33.4 percent are age 17 or younger and about 6.8 percent are 65+, while about 59.0 percent are foreign-born. Among those age 5 and older, 59.3 percent speak a language other than English, while 11.3 percent speak English less than “very well,” and among those 25 and older, 55.3 percent hold a bachelor’s or higher. Date the number whenever you use it, and remember that a rate is not the person; high attainment, in particular, is not the interpreter.

The diversity inside this state name is the whole point. A Yoruba Pentecostal professional, an Igbo Catholic household that still names Biafra, a Hausa Muslim family, an Edo association member, a U.S.-born student who uses English with friends and Igbo with an elder, and a Greater Minnesota nurse all share a Compass row, even though they do not share a Tuesday.

### How to read this

Always defer to the person in front of you, because this page is a hypothesis that you still test with this family.

sections.heading: Origins and the Founding of a People
sections.body:
Nigeria is a state of many nations: Yoruba peoplehood in the southwest, Igbo peoplehood in the southeast, Hausa-Fulani in the north, and Edo, Ijaw, Tiv, Ibibio, and hundreds of others. Because there is no single Nigerian ethnicity, ask which people a household belongs to rather than lecturing them on a taxonomy they did not ask for.

### History for the meeting

English as the official language is colonial history, and independence came in 1960. Biafra — 1967–1970 — is foundational literacy for many Igbo households, but it is not a speech you give the family and it is not every Nigerian’s story, so do not referee it in a waiver meeting.

### What people brought

What people brought with them includes ethnic language, English, Pidgin, church and mosque, titles, kin obligation, and a memory of colony and of a civil war that some will name and some will not. What they met in Minnesota was an English form, one “African” checkbox, one “Black” mash, and often Somali, simply because the building already had that page.

Do not start with a Nollywood or jollof tourism sentence, since origins did not begin in Minneapolis.

sections.heading: The Geography of the Nigerian World
sections.body:
The homeland is not one map. It takes in Lagos and the Yoruba southwest, the Igbo southeast, the Hausa-Fulani north, the Niger Delta, and the Middle Belt, and Abuja is not the whole of it, so a person may name Ibadan, Enugu, Kano, Benin City, Port Harcourt, or a village rather than the capital. Do not referee regional politics in a waiver meeting, and if they name a place, listen.

### Homeland

The diaspora is global and large, with concentrations in Texas, New York, Maryland and D.C., Georgia, the UK, and the Gulf, which makes Minnesota a real community within that diaspora rather than the U.S. capital of it. Secondary migration, church networks, school, and professional work are what pulled people here.

### Minnesota

In Minnesota, Compass places 81.7 percent of the community in the Twin Cities and 18.3 percent in Greater Minnesota, so do not assume Minneapolis, and do not assume Cedar-Riverside. Do not assume the person in front of you has been to Nigeria either, because inner-ring suburbs and Greater Minnesota towns with hospitals and housing are still this people.

sections.heading: Independence, Biafra, and Later Streams — Foundational Events
sections.body:
There is no single 1975 or 1991 on this page. Independence in 1960 is the political founding of the state, while Biafra, 1967–1970, is the foundational political event in much of Igbo Minnesota’s first memory, with dead in the millions by some counts and famine used as a weapon. That sentence is literacy for you rather than a speech, and it is not every Nigerian household.

### Foundational events

The later Minnesota streams are mixed: students, skilled work including healthcare, family reunification, and diversity visas. Do not file every Nigerian household as refugee, and do not file every Nigerian household as a doctor, because both sit in this Compass row.

### Who you meet

The desk in 2026 meets first-generation professionals and U.S.-born children who use English with peers and are still translating for a grandmother whose Igbo or Yoruba was never booked, and who are still filed under Black or under African.

If the only word you know is “African,” you will miss this household and the language it actually needs.

sections.heading: Family
sections.body:
Family can be larger than a nuclear English form, and it can also look exactly like one. Compass puts the average household size at about 2.92 (ACS 2020–2024); that figure is dated, and it still does not make the household Mary Jones. Ask who should speak first, hear from the person directly, and ask about titles such as Chief, Obi, Igwe, Alhaji or Deacon. The person who cares for a disabled adult or a child may be a sibling, an in-law, or a church mother rather than the legally recognized caregiver on the checkbox.

### Who is in the household

Hour caps and “natural supports” language can dump unpaid work onto the women in that network and then call it culture. Naming is already a question of who — Yoruba, Igbo, Hausa, English — so do not invent a last name because the screen requires one.

### Who speaks

The person who speaks in the lobby may be a child with Minnesota English, but that child is not the qualified interpreter, even when Compass LEP is 11.3 percent. CLAS still stands if this elder needs Yoruba, Igbo, Hausa, or Pidgin, so ask who should be in the room. Minnesota law still stands as well, which means you do not skip mandated reporting and call it humility.

sections.heading: Minnesota and Nigerian History
sections.body:
Minnesota holds a Nigerian Compass community large enough that this department will meet it on waivers, in child welfare, in health care, in cash and food programs, in aging, and in employment. It is also large enough that the building has developed a habit of hearing African and booking Somali, or of opening historic African American. Compass counts about 21,206 (plus or minus 3,847) (ACS 2020–2024), with 18.3 percent in Greater Minnesota, so do not write this people as a Minneapolis anecdote.

### Places

Think in places rather than a blob: Twin Cities suburbs; Minneapolis and St. Paul pockets; Greater Minnesota towns with hospitals and housing. IgboFest is public life, including North Hennepin / Brooklyn Park in public listings, and churches are public life too, but none of these is consultation, and a jollof visit does not make you the expert.

### Partners

Among the partners are the Minnesota Institute for Nigerian Development (MIND), which calls itself the umbrella for the Nigerian community in Minnesota since 1994; Igbo associations and IgboFest; the Yoruba, Edo, and other associations that families name; the churches and mosques that families name; and CECLC, which is a department door but not the whole. Pay the partner this household actually uses.

Book a qualified interpreter, and pay for community work. Do not assign either to staff because of who they are. IgboFest or Independence Day is optional professional development if you are invited, and if you go, you go as a guest, since the visit does not make you the expert.

sections.heading: Nigerian Minnesota — the heart of a people
sections.body:
Nigerians are people of many nations under one state name, and public systems may file them under African, Black, and sometimes Somali. Ask how the person identifies. Peoplehood after colony, after Biafra for some, and after oil and military rule is not a Nollywood poster. Yoruba, Igbo, Hausa, and the rest do not share one Tuesday, and you do not pick a side.

### In this state

In this building another fact sits on top of all that. Many of these households are Black in a U.S. racial order that can file them under historic African American and get the language, the church, the title, and the name wrong, because shared race is not shared culture.

Ask plainly whether the person agrees with the plan, and make it easy to say no.

This guide is a working orientation. Individual variation always supersedes group generalization, and you always defer to the person in front of you.

sections.heading: Core Concepts
sections.body:
Start with which people: Yoruba, Igbo, Hausa, Edo, or others. Ask, because the Compass row is not the ethnic file.

### Which language

The language may be Yoruba, Igbo, Hausa, Nigerian Pidgin, English, or another. A “Nigerian interpreter” is not a language, and an “African interpreter” will not work, while Pidgin is a language, not broken English.

### Titles

Chief, Obi, Igwe, Alhaji, Deacon, Doctor — use them until you are invited not to, because they are not decoration.

### Faith is plural

Faith here may be Pentecostal, Catholic, Anglican, Islam, Ifá and Odinani in some rooms, or none at all, so follow this room.

Do not referee Biafra or north/south politics in a waiver meeting, and do not assume Lagos.

### Work and school

A high bachelor’s rate is a pattern, but it is not a model-minority speech, and it is not proof the elder heard the form.

sections.heading: Religion
sections.body:
Christianity is the large public stream in many southern Nigerian Minnesota households, whether Pentecostal, Catholic, or Anglican, while Islam lives in Hausa-Fulani rooms and in some Yoruba families. Traditional practice — Ifá, Odinani, and others — sits in some rooms, and it is neither a souvenir nor horror-film content. None is also a Tuesday, so ask rather than assuming Muslim the way you might with Somali, and do not assume Pentecostal either.

### Streams

The church is a center of ritual, mutual aid, and information, and it is often the first Minnesota network a family finds, although it is still not “the community.” Do not BCC one pastor and call it consultation, and do not make clergy or an imam the case plan unless this family asked.

### Practice

Funerals gather family and can run long, but you still keep medical and legal time, and you name the conflict instead of punishing it.

Do not treat Ifá or “juju” as a case-note joke, and do not treat a Pentecostal fast as noncompliance with a medication until you have asked.

sections.heading: Greetings
sections.body:
Ask who to greet first, or follow the household’s lead. An English “hello” is ordinary in many professional rooms, while Yoruba ẹ n lẹ, Igbo greetings, and Hausa sannu live in others, so ask, or follow the person’s lead.

### Titles

Wait to see whether a hand is offered, and if it is not, nod, and use the title until invited not to.

### This room

Let this person’s own greeting guide you, whatever you read on another page.

Ask before any physical contact, and let the person set the limit.

sections.heading: Naming Conventions
sections.body:
Yoruba names often carry a sentence — Oluwaseun, Adebola, Temitope — while Igbo names often carry Chi or Chukwu — Chukwuemeka, Chinwe, Ngozi. Hausa and Muslim names appear in northern and some Yoruba rooms, and English and biblical names sit beside all of them. A naming ceremony in some families is not folklore, so ask which name they use on this file.

### How to file

U.S. forms want first-middle-last, and they will strip tones and meaning in the process, so ask how to file the name and how to say it. Do not joke about long names, and do not “shorten” a name for the screen, because that invented name becomes a gate.

Women may or may not take a husband’s family name in U.S. records, so mother and child may not match, and that is not fraud until you have a reason. Titles are not first names, which means you do not file Chief as a given name unless they said so.

sections.heading: Dates of Significance
sections.body:
Independence Day falls on 1 October, so schedule around it when this family names it, and be a guest if invited, since a calendar click is not community engagement.

### Calendar

Follow the Yoruba, Igbo, and Hausa festival calendars this family names — New Yam in some Igbo rooms, Eid in Muslim rooms, Christmas and Easter on church calendars. IgboFest is Minnesota public life, but it is not consultation.

For some Igbo rooms, Biafra memory is grief and politics, not a party, so do not put it on a case note as color, and do not collect it as a risk score.

Do not put “African holiday” on a case note; ask this family what they actually keep.

sections.heading: Education
sections.body:
Compass (ACS 2020–2024) reports that among Nigerian Minnesotans 25 and older, about 95.8 percent have a high school education or higher and about 55.3 percent hold a bachelor’s or higher, so date Compass when you cite it. About 59.0 percent of the community is foreign-born.
