High attainment is a documented pattern, but it is not a model-minority speech, it is not proof the grandmother needs no interpreter, and it is not permission to skip the IEP in the home language.

### School and language

A parent who speaks fluent Yoruba or Igbo and limited Minnesota professional English is not illiterate, and while many Nigerians were schooled in English, some elders were not. An LEP rate of 11.3 percent is real, and the English-only form is still a gate, so book THIS language, because the child is not the interpreter.

Second-generation educational mobility is real, but do not treat a physician in the family as proof the waiver household heard the form.

sections.heading: Etiquette
sections.body:
Ask who to greet first, or follow the household’s lead. If food or drink is offered, accepting a little is fine, and you can still keep to medical and legal timelines.

### In the home

If you visit a home, look for shoes by the door or ask what the household prefers. Ask before taking any photograph, and enter a prayer space only if you are invited.

### Time

If someone misses an appointment, first check the time, transport, interpreter and work schedule. Confirm the plan in the language the person uses, and ask whether it works for them.

Book a qualified interpreter instead of using a child to go between.

sections.heading: Language and Communication
sections.body:
Book the language this household names: Yoruba, Igbo, Hausa, Edo, Nigerian Pidgin, English, or another. A “Nigerian interpreter” is not a language, an “African interpreter” will not work, and Pidgin is a language, not broken English. A Somali interpreter is the wrong door, and in Muslim rooms, Arabic may be the language of religion rather than the language of the interview.

### Language

Compass reports that among those 5 and older, about 59.3 percent speak a language other than English and about 11.3 percent speak English less than “very well,” so date the number. Low LEP is not proof the form was heard in the language the elder uses for grief and law, and although second-generation Minnesota English is common, the IEP still has to reach the parent.

Give the person time to answer. If you get a short yes, check that the plan was understood, and ask whether it works for them.

Do not use a child as the interpreter, and do not make a Nigerian coworker the interpreter. Do not write “broken English” on a file, because Pidgin is a language.

sections.heading: Other Considerations
sections.body:
This section states hard facts plainly, because treating everyone the same can hide them.

### Named harms

Intra-Nigerian politics are real — Yoruba, Igbo, Hausa, Biafra memory, north and south — so do not pick a side as DHS, do not referee in a waiver meeting, and do not file politics as a risk score.

FGC exists in some Nigerian communities, and Minnesota law stands. Do not invent a Nigerian Minnesota rate, and do not mash Somali prevalence onto this household; follow mandated reporting, and still see a family.

Colorism sits in some rooms, and you do not fix it as if it were a personality, but you do not ignore it when it becomes a gate.

Queer and trans Nigerian Minnesotans exist, so you use the name they use, and you do not out someone to kin and call it culture. Nigeria’s own law climate is not Minnesota’s, and you do not skip mandated reporting and call it humility.

The enforcement climate is structure for some households, and since Jan. 1, 2026, a Dec. 16, 2025 proclamation has placed Nigeria under a partial entry suspension for immigrant and B, F, M and J visas, following a July 2025 move to single-entry, three-month visitor visas; a Nigerian finalist for the June 2026 Great American Think-Off in New York Mills was denied entry under it, so do not collect status you do not need, and do not treat fear as noncompliance. Staff who share this community may add facts, but they do not get to delete a fact because it is hard to say.

sections.heading: Health
sections.body:
Believe reported pain, and do not fold this history into Tuskegee. This is not the historic African American page, because shared race is not shared medical history, and you do not mash Somali MDH findings onto this people.

### Access

Hepatitis B screening for people born in Nigeria is a U.S. public-health pattern, because CDC has treated Nigeria as a higher-prevalence birth country in its screening guidance, so date the CDC page you cite. Do not invent a Minnesota rate, and do not skip screening because the person looks well or holds a degree.

Compass disability is 7.3 percent, dated. Mental-health stigma is real in some families, and Biafra memory and later trauma sit in some rooms, so remember that a smile is not a PHQ-9. No dated Nigerian-specific Minnesota autism rate belongs on this page, so do not invent one.

Gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care, so offer it. Traditional medicine and church healing often sit beside biomedicine, which means you ask and work it out together. On FGC, Minnesota law stands; do not invent a rate, and do not skip care, because high education is not a clinical history.

sections.heading: LGBTQ
sections.body:
Queer and trans Nigerian Minnesotans exist, and conservative family, Pentecostal, Catholic, and mosque climates can mean silence or exile for them, while some people live a public English life and a private Yoruba or Igbo life. You use the name they use and do not share what they tell you unless a rule requires it.

### This person

Minnesota’s Human Rights Act still applies, and Nigeria’s law climate is not this state’s. Do not question a household about anyone’s sexuality or gender, and take seriously that some people have reason to keep it private.

Biafra memory and church do not override what this person wants, so always defer to the person in front of you.

sections.heading: Hair, Dress, and Body
sections.body:
Gele, iro and buba, agbada, isiagu, and other ceremonial dress are public at weddings, Independence, IgboFest, and some church stages, but they are not a daily uniform, and the second generation looks like Minnesota. Do not ask a woman in clinic whether she “still wears the costume.”

### Dress

This is not the CROWN Act chapter as the file — and yet anti-Blackness still sits on Nigerian bodies in U.S. clinics, schools, and traffic stops. Ask this person, and do not mash historic African American hair politics onto them as a script, although you should not ignore those politics either.

Do not touch, because gold, a gele, or a wedding coral is not a mascot for the unit’s Heritage Month table.

sections.heading: Music
sections.body:
Jùjú, fuji, highlife, Igbo gospel, Hausa popular forms, Afrobeats, Nollywood sound, and church choir are all part of the picture, and this is named variation, not a playlist. Ethnic and political memory can sit inside a song, so you do not put the wrong anthem on a speaker.

### Variation

A funeral is not staff entertainment, and a playlist is not engagement. Nollywood is public culture, but it is not consultation and not a case plan.

Independence and IgboFest stages are public life rather than a form.

sections.heading: Sports
sections.body:
Soccer is public Nigerian life, and the Super Eagles are a public image, but they are not a personality you assign a child in clinic. School sport is ordinary for the second generation, and basketball shows up as well.

### Not the whole person

Do not assume the kid plays, and do not make sport the only excellence you can see. Sport clubs are social infrastructure for some, although they are not language access and not a case plan.

A Saturday tournament does not replace an interpreter on Monday if this elder needs Yoruba or Igbo.

sections.heading: Literature
sections.body:
English, Yoruba, Igbo, and Hausa have all made written publics. Chinua Achebe, Wole Soyinka, and Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie are literacy for the desk, not a speech you give the family in the lobby, and oral forms sit beside the written ones. Minnesota and U.S. Nigerian writers and journalists exist.

### Literacy in the lobby

You do need to know that this is not a people without letters. Many people read English, while some elders read only a home language, which is why a notice that exists only in English will not work and a high bachelor’s rate is not proof that this elder reads the form.

Write what they tell you, and do not strip a name because the screen is impatient.

sections.heading: Art
sections.body:
Adire, bronze as the public image of a court, gele, contemporary visual work, and Nollywood are all part of Nigerian art, while jollof, pounded yam, and egusi are foodway, not consultation.

### Guest

Be a guest, not a researcher. IgboFest is optional professional development if you are invited, but it is not consultation, and you do not photograph a family as tourism.

A Heritage Month that mashes this people with historic African American quilts, a Somali poster, or one “African” table has already mashed the adjacent peoples.

sections.heading: Colony, Biafra, and Intra-Community Politics
sections.body:
British colony, independence in 1960, Biafra in 1967–1970 as Igbo literacy for the desk rather than a speech, military rule, and current Nigeria politics — that is the political event. Intra-Nigerian tension, including Yoruba / Igbo / Hausa memory, lives in Minnesota rooms, so do not referee, and do not pick a side as DHS.

### The badge

A DHS badge is not automatically help. Do not use Biafra as a personality, and do not ask a person to narrate famine or killing for your professional development.

The enforcement climate in the United States belongs to a different state, and it still keeps some people away, because it changes who opens the door, and that is not noncompliance. Do not collect status you do not need, and do not collect ethnic or political speech as a risk score.

sections.heading: Work, Markets, and Government
sections.body:
Nigerian Minnesotans work across the professional class, nursing, entrepreneurship, shops, restaurants, and public employment. Compass puts median household income at about $76,000 (2024 dollars), ownership at 45.0 percent, and bachelor’s or higher at 55.3 percent, all dated. High income and high education are patterns, but they are not a model-minority speech, they are not proof the gates closed, and they are not permission to skip language access for the elder.

### Work

Book a qualified interpreter, and pay for community work. Do not assign either to staff because of who they are.

### Staff

Take time to introduce yourself and explain the plan. The first visit may not be the decision, and any required notice still goes out. Pay the partner this household names, such as MIND, an Igbo association, a church, or whoever they actually use.

sections.heading: Health-care and Human-service Encounters
sections.body:
Which people and which language are the first thing to get right, and an interpreter labeled Nigerian, African, or Somali who is not Yoruba, Igbo, Hausa, Pidgin, or whatever this household names will not work. Pidgin is a language, and you still book a qualified interpreter rather than using a child or making staff the interpreter.

### Language

Pay attention to who is in the room: a child pushed forward as Minnesota English, a title you skipped, a pastor in the story, pain you must believe, high education in the chart used as an excuse to skip the interpreter, and a deportation climate in the background.

### The meeting

Offer gender match, ask who should hear, ask how to file the name, and use the title. If they name traditional medicine or church healing, listen, while remembering that mandated reporting still exists. Believe reported pain, and do not mix Tuskegee or Somali CI into this history.

sections.heading: Adjacent Peoples — Do Not Mash
sections.body:
This page is not Somali, and it is not Liberian used as a synonym. It is not Ghanaian as a mash — a related coast, but a different state — and it is not Kenyan, not Ethiopian, and not historic African American, since the Compass African American row is not this page. Open historic African American for a Great Migration household, and open this one for Nigerian.

### Adjacent doors

Yoruba, Igbo, Hausa, and others are not one file, so never use one African interpreter, never one Nigerian module, and never one Black module. Some households are mixed, and some Nigerian families have historic African American in-laws, so ask this household.

Shared race is not shared culture. Shared English is not shared English, shared Christianity is not shared culture, and shared Islam is not shared culture.

sections.heading: Counts, Dated
sections.body:
Minnesota Compass, ACS 2020–2024, describes the Nigerian cultural community this way: about 21,206 people (plus or minus 3,847; Compass's best estimate of size is 25,310 for 2024, plus or minus 9,024); Twin Cities 81.7% and Greater Minnesota 18.3%; age 17 or younger 33.4% and 65+ 6.8%; foreign-born 59.0%; language other than English (age 5+) 59.3%; English less than “very well” 11.3%; high school or higher (25+) 95.8%; bachelor’s or higher 55.3%; median household income about $76,000 (2024 dollars) (2022 dollars, averaged); poverty suppressed on that profile; owner-occupied 45.0%; renter-occupied 55.0%; average household size 2.92; and disability 7.3%.

### Counts

Date Compass, and do not invent other rates. Counts disagree across ACS vintages and definitions (ancestry vs. birthplace vs. language), so date the number you cite.

### What the count is not

A smaller young share than the neighboring African Compass rows is not a personality, and high bachelor’s and low LEP are not proof the elder heard the form. Language and the child-as-interpreter are still gates, and a rate is not the person.

sections.heading: Doors and Sources
sections.body:
Start with the Minnesota Compass Nigerian profile (ACS 2020–2024). The Minnesota Institute for Nigerian Development (MIND) calls itself the umbrella for the Nigerian community in Minnesota since 1994, and IgboFest is public life. Then there are the Yoruba, Igbo, Edo, and other associations this family names, and the churches and mosques this family names, while CECLC is a door, not the whole community.

### Public doors

An eList is not engagement, so pay partners, and report back.

### Where to learn more

Use these resources yourself before you ask a Nigerian colleague to explain, and do not count a BCC to a church as consultation. Be a guest at IgboFest or Independence Day if invited, remembering that it is not consultation, and book the language this household names.

sections.heading: How it hits DHS gates — the 40%
sections.body:
Workplace culture and service delivery are both candidates here.

Language: an interpreter labeled Nigerian, African, or Somali who is not Yoruba, Igbo, Hausa, Pidgin, or whatever this household names will not work. Pidgin is a language, not broken English, and you still book a qualified interpreter rather than using a child. Gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care.

Names and titles: Yoruba and Igbo names carry sentences, so the database that shortens them or invents a last name is a gate, and if you skip a title you have already closed a door.

Hour caps, exception processes, and life-sharing matches without language are not culturally neutral.

Child welfare and disability: help-seeking that becomes a report is part of why people wait. Mandated reporting still exists, and so does the duty not to treat a whole community as a risk score. On FGC, Minnesota law stands, so do not invent a rate.

Notices and comment: do not count an eList and an English PDF as reaching this community, and record who was reached and what follow-up happened. A high bachelor’s rate is not a mailing list, and Greater Minnesota is 12.4 percent.

Workforce: Nigerian staff are not the interpreter pool and not the community. Staff are colleagues, not the curriculum, and they should not be treated as the curriculum.

Somali mash and Black mash: opening Somali because Africa, or historic African American because both are Black, shuts the person out.

Legislation, funding, rule: study a channel before you advocate for it. Use this page so that the 40% has a household in it.

sections.heading: A Note on This Guide
sections.body:
This brief is about Puerto Rican Minnesota as a people — boricua, puertorriqueño, puertorriqueña — rather than as a Mexican variant, an immigrant file, or a slice of the Latino / Hispanic umbrella. Puerto Ricans have been U.S. citizens since the Jones Act (2 March 1917), so please do not run an immigration script by default, and remember that the Compass foreign-born figure is 1.3 percent precisely because ACS does not count birth on the island as foreign. Within this community you will find several Spanish varieties and many English-dominant households, yet this is not Mexican, Guatemalan, or Salvadoran Minnesota, because a shared Spanish language is not a shared culture. Use this page for context and questions. It does not describe the person in front of you.

### Who this is

Open the Latino umbrella only as an adjacent door, since that page carries the mash and the CLAS Spanish line while this page is Puerto Rican. If you leave this door and file the household under “Latino” or under Mexican, or greet them with an ICE speech because the name is Spanish, you have left this door and the people it describes.

### Who this is not

Minnesota Compass (ACS 2020 to 2024) puts the Puerto Rican cultural community at 22,925 people (plus or minus 2,722), with 67.1 percent in the Twin Cities and 32.9 percent in Greater Minnesota (plus or minus 5.0), which is far too many people to treat as an afterthought. About 38.6 percent are age 17 or younger and 4.9 percent are 65+, and among those age 5 and older, 62.0 percent speak English only, 38.0 percent speak a language other than English, and 10.7 percent (plus or minus 2.8) speak English less than “very well.” Date whichever number you use, and keep in mind that an LEP figure of 10.7 percent does not mean “no language gate,” just as a rate is never the person.

The diversity inside this people is the point. Consider an island-born elder who uses Spanish, a Minnesota-born English-dominant kid, a Nuyorican household that moved west, a person displaced after Hurricane María, an Afro-Puerto Rican student, a Greater Minnesota worker the building filed as Mexican, and a queer second-generation adult who uses English with friends and Spanish with a grandmother. They share a people, but they do not share a Tuesday.

### How to read this

Always defer to the person in front of you, because this page is a hypothesis that you still need to test with this family rather than a conclusion about them.

sections.heading: Origins and the Founding of a People
sections.body:
Puerto Rican peoplehood is older than 1917 and far older than the Minnesota file, and the island itself was Borikén. The three-root sentence — Taíno people, Spanish colonial rule, and African enslavement in the sugar and later coffee economy — is basic literacy for the desk, but it is also incomplete, and it is not a speech you give the family. For the same reason, do not start with a salsa tourism sentence or a Heritage Month flag.

### History for the meeting

In 1898 the United States took the island in the war with Spain, and Puerto Rico became a colony; the Jones Act (2 March 1917) then made Puerto Ricans U.S. citizens. Holding that citizenship in mind, and never treating the household as foreign, is the first operational fact on this desk. Puerto Ricans still cannot vote for president from the island, although they can if they reside in Minnesota, and that is colonial status offered as literacy rather than as a lecture.

### What people brought

Spanish and English are both official on the island, and writing in both exists, but reading skill varies from person to person: some elders read Spanish and not English, some Minnesota-born adults read English and not Spanish, and some read both. Ask which is true for this person, because oral skill is not the same thing as print.

What people brought with them includes language (Caribbean Spanish and English), kinship, the Catholic and later Protestant church, Afro-diasporic practice in some families, baseball, and the memory of a colony that claimed them. What they met in Minnesota was an English form, one “Latino” checkbox, often a single interpreter labeled Spanish, and a lobby that had already decided they were immigrants.

sections.heading: The Geography of the Puerto Rican World
sections.body:
The homeland is the island, and people name its municipalities: San Juan, Ponce, Mayagüez, the mountains, the coast. Vieques and Culebra are not trivia, so if someone names a place, confirm it with them, and rather than refereeing San Juan versus the west in a waiver meeting, simply listen.

### Homeland

The U.S. Puerto Rican map runs through New York (with Nuyorican as a named diaspora), Chicago, Florida, Pennsylvania, and also Minnesota, although those hubs are not this map. Secondary migration, the military, school, and work pulled people here, and Hurricane María (2017) moved people again.

### Minnesota

In Minnesota, 67.1 percent of this community lives in the Twin Cities and 32.9 percent in Greater Minnesota (Compass ACS 2020 to 2024), which means Greater Minnesota is not an afterthought. Do not assume Minneapolis, do not assume the person in front of you has been to the island, and do not assume a Spanish-surnamed household in a plant town is Mexican, because a Greater Minnesota household is still this people.

sections.heading: Citizenship, Island, and Internal Migration — Foundational Facts
sections.body:
This is internal U.S. migration, not immigration, and the Jones Act dates to 1917. In the mid-twentieth century, Operation Bootstrap pushed industrial policy on the island and pushed labor to the mainland — to New York, Chicago, and later other states — so Nuyorican is a named diaspora, and Minnesota is a later present. None of that history is a reason to run an immigration script by default just because the name is Spanish.

### Foundational events

Hurricane María (September 2017) is displacement literacy for the desk: people left a wrecked grid, and some of them came here. That is not an immigrant wave; it is citizens moving inside the United States after a disaster. PROMESA and the fiscal control board are political literacy as well, though they are not a speech you give the family.

### Who you meet

The desk in 2026 meets island-born elders, U.S.-mainland-born adults, Minnesota-born children, and mixed island–mainland households. The Compass foreign-born figure of 1.3 percent is the ACS fact at work, since birth in Puerto Rico is not foreign-born, and if the only category you know is “immigrant,” you will miss these households and you will harm them.

The enforcement climate in the wider Latino lobby still spills over, which means a Puerto Rican citizen can still be asked for papers because the building mashed the file. That is the gate, so do not collect status you do not need.

sections.heading: Family
sections.body:
Kin networks may run from the island to the mainland to Minnesota within the same month. Compass puts the average household size at about 2.39, which is smaller than some neighboring spines, but that still does not always mean a nuclear English form, since elders, adult children, and cousins who are household in practice can all sit in the same week. Because who cares for a child may not match the waiver checkbox, ask who should be in the room.

### Who is in the household

Do not treat this household as mixed-status by default, because citizenship is the fact, and for the same reason do not collect status you do not need. Do not treat unmatched last names, or a grandmother acting as caregiver, as fraud until you have a reason. Be aware, too, that hour caps and “natural supports” language can dump unpaid work onto the women in that network and then call it culture.

### Who speaks

The person who speaks in the lobby may be a child. Even in an English-dominant household, a child is not the qualified interpreter for a Spanish-speaking elder — and an English-speaking adult is not a child to be skipped. CLAS still stands when Spanish is needed, and using a child as the go-between is a harm.

Minnesota law still stands as well, and since domestic violence is not culture, do not skip mandated reporting and call it humility.

sections.heading: Minnesota and Puerto Rican History
sections.body:
Minnesota holds a Puerto Rican community large enough that this department will meet it on waivers, child welfare, health care, cash, food, aging, and employment. Compass counts 22,925 (ACS 2020 to 2024), with 67.1 percent in the Twin Cities and 32.9 percent in Greater Minnesota — again, not an afterthought — so do not write this people as a New York anecdote, and do not write them as a Mexican leftover.

### Places

Think in places rather than a blob: Twin Cities corridors and suburbs, and Greater Minnesota towns with work, school, and military ties. Public culture here is not a sombrero mash, and a festival visit does not make you the expert.

### Partners

Partners are the parishes and cultural groups that families name, and rural partners when the household is in Greater Minnesota, so name the local one rather than assuming Minneapolis. CLUES is a Twin Cities Latino door that is adjacent, not automatic reach, and not this people, while CECLC is a department door rather than the community. Pay the partner this household actually uses.

Book a qualified interpreter, and pay for community work. Do not assign either to staff because of who they are. If you are invited to a public event, you are a guest, and being there does not make you the expert.

sections.heading: Boricua — the heart of a people
sections.body:
Puerto Ricans have an island, a colonial history, and U.S. citizenship, and forms in Minnesota may default them to Mexican or to immigrant. Ask plainly whether the person agrees with the plan, and make it easy to say no.

### In this state

Afro-Puerto Rican people exist, and colorism is real, so do not bleach this household into a mestizo Latino story, and do not mash them into historic African American because both are Black; ask instead.

The Mexican default in this state is a count fact on another page, but on this one it is a harm, because staff copy Guadalupe, ICE, and “the interpreter” onto a citizen household that may well be English-dominant.

This guide is a working orientation, which means individual variation always supersedes group generalization and you always defer to the person in front of you.

sections.heading: Core Concepts
sections.body:
Citizenship comes first, through the Jones Act of 1917, so do not run an immigration script by default, and do not collect status you do not need. The 1.3 percent foreign-born figure on Compass is simply the ACS clothing of that fact.

### Boricua

Boricua is the peoplehood word, covering island and diaspora alike, and Nuyorican is a named stream within it rather than this whole map. Ask how this family names itself instead of choosing a word for them.

### Spanish and English both

English-dominant households exist (English only 62.0 percent), but an LEP rate of 10.7 percent is not zero, so ask rather than assume which language this household needs.

### Two surnames still common

The database that keeps only one surname invents a person, even though English-style single last names exist in some U.S.-born households, so ask how this person files the name rather than guessing.

### Afro-Puerto Rican peoplehood

This is not a footnote, and the African American CI is not the file for it, because Afro-Puerto Rican peoplehood belongs on this page.

### Colonial status

Colonial status is literacy for the desk rather than a speech you give the family, and María (2017) is displacement, not an immigrant wave.

sections.heading: Religion
sections.body:
Many streams are Catholic-majority, though not all, since Protestant and evangelical churches live here and Espiritismo and Santería live in some families. Do not exoticize, do not assume, and do not treat Afro-diasporic practice as folklore or as a risk note. Our Lady of Guadalupe is Mexican Catholic literacy, so do not install it as the default on this page; ask what this family practices instead.

### Streams

Do not make a priest or a pastor the case plan unless this family asked for that, and do not BCC one parish and call it consultation.

### Practice

Three Kings (6 January) is larger than Santa in some rooms, and Holy Week, funerals, and family obligation can collide with your calendar. You still keep medical and legal time, but you name the conflict instead of punishing it, and you do not photograph an altar.

Help that looks like a report is not help. A religious framing of disability, mental health, or gender can sit right next to a fierce wish for services, and you can hold both at the same time.

sections.heading: Greetings
sections.body:
Ask who to greet first, or follow the household’s lead. Ask how the person wants to be addressed, and do not use a first name just because the form printed it.

### Titles

In some Spanish rooms, titles — Señor, Señora, Don, Doña — hold until you are invited past them, while in others an English “hello” is ordinary. Say the name, remembering there may be two surnames. Do not assume a Spanish greeting is required, and do not assume that someone who speaks English has no Spanish.

### This room

Let this person’s own greeting guide you, whatever you read on another page. Ask before any physical contact, and let the person set the limit.

sections.heading: Naming Conventions
sections.body:
Two surnames remain common: the apellido paterno followed by the apellido materno. A U.S. database that keeps only one surname invents a person, and that invented name then follows them through MHCP, child welfare, and school, which makes it a gate.

### How to file

English-style single last names exist in some U.S.-born and some mainland-raised households, so ask how to file the name and how to say it, and then pronounce it. Do not drop accents as a joke. Given names may be Spanish, English, or both, and some people use a middle given name as the call-name.

Women may or may not take a husband’s surname in U.S. records, and children may carry two surnames that do not match a parent’s U.S. “last name” field, but that is not fraud until you have a reason.

Do not treat unmatched last names in a household as a fraud flag by default, and do not invent a hyphen and then punish the person when the hyphen moves.

sections.heading: Dates of Significance
sections.body:
6 January is Día de los Reyes, Three Kings, and it is larger than Santa in some Puerto Rican rooms, so treat it as literacy for scheduling rather than a costume for staff.

### Calendar

25 July is Puerto Rico Constitution Day, while 19 November is an official public holiday in Puerto Rico, Día de la Puertorriqueñidad y el Descubrimiento de Puerto Rico (Platea PR calls it Puerto Rican Heritage Day). American Citizenship Day (2 March, the 1917 Jones-Shafroth Act) and Abolition of Slavery Day (22 March) are also on Puerto Rico’s 2026 public calendar. You do not referee independence versus commonwealth versus statehood on a case note; if they name a day, listen.

Hurricane María — September 2017 — is displacement literacy, not a holiday. Hispanic Heritage Month is the umbrella calendar rather than this people’s day, and it is not consultation, any more than Cinco de Mayo or the Mexican 16 September is. Do not put “Latino holiday” on a case note, because a calendar click is not community engagement, and it is not a day off the work.

sections.heading: Education
sections.body:
Compass (ACS 2020 to 2024) reports that among Puerto Rican Minnesotans 25 and older, about 91.9 percent (plus or minus 4.0) have a high school diploma or higher and about 41.4 percent (plus or minus 6.3) hold a bachelor’s or higher, so date Compass and do not invent a dropout rate. Among those age 5 and older, 62.0 percent speak English only, and an LEP rate of 10.7 percent is not “no language gate,” which means the IEP still has to reach the parent who does not read it, whether that is in English or in Spanish.

### School and language

A parent who speaks fluent Caribbean Spanish and limited English is not illiterate, and a parent who is English-dominant is not “no culture,” nor proof that the elder in the household needs no interpreter. Ask what each person needs, and do not use a child as interpreter.

Second-generation educational mobility is real. So is a gap that a room treating everyone the same will call “culture” when the cause is a school that never learned the second surname, or that filed this student as “immigrant.” Puerto Rican students are not immigrant students by default, so do not collect status you do not need at enrollment.

sections.heading: Etiquette
sections.body:
If food or drink is offered, accepting a little is fine, and you can still keep to medical and legal timelines. Ask how the person wants to be addressed.

### In the home

Ask before taking any photograph or touching any religious object, and do not ask anyone to explain their faith or history for your benefit.

### Time

Keep to clinic and court timelines. If someone is late, ask what got in the way, and record only what happened.

Do not use a child as the go-between, and ask whether they agree with the plan rather than taking a smile as consent.

sections.heading: Language and Communication
sections.body:
Ask about language rather than assuming, because you should not assume they need a Spanish interpreter, and you should not assume they do not. Compass (ACS 2020 to 2024) reports that among those 5 and older, 62.0 percent speak English only, 38.0 percent speak a language other than English, and 10.7 percent speak English less than “very well,” so date the number. English-dominant households exist, and Spanish-dominant elders exist in the same cousin-line.

### Language

Caribbean Spanish is not Mexican Spanish, and it is not one interpreter accent test, so book a qualified Spanish interpreter if this household needs one. Spanglish is ordinary in some rooms, and register matters. Literacy in any language is not guaranteed, because oral skill is not print.

Give the person time to answer. If you get a short yes, check that the plan was understood, and ask whether it works for them.

Do not use a child as the interpreter, do not make a Puerto Rican coworker the interpreter, and do not greet this household with an immigration script.

sections.heading: Other Considerations
sections.body:
This section states hard facts plainly, because treating everyone the same can hide them.

### Named harms

Do not run an immigration script by default, since Puerto Ricans have held citizenship since 1917 and the foreign-born figure is 1.3 percent. Asking for an SSN on the first screen is a gate even for a citizen when the building has mashed Latino into ICE, so do not collect status you do not need.

The Mexican default in this state will talk over this household if you let the umbrella page do this page’s job. Colorism is real, and Afro-Puerto Rican erasure under a mestizo Latino story is a named harm, so do not mash Afro-Puerto Rican people into the historic African American CI because both are Black, and do not bleach them.

Colonial status is structure — PROMESA, the board, María, the grid — rather than a personality. Do not joke about machismo, and do not excuse control as “that’s culture,” and domestic violence is not culture either, so you follow mandated reporting while you still see a family.

LGBTQ Puerto Rican Minnesotans exist, which means you use the name and you do not out someone to kin. Staff who share this community may add facts, but they do not get to delete a fact because it is hard to say.

sections.heading: Health
sections.body:
Believe reported pain or invent “they are dramatic.” Compass (ACS 2020 to 2024) puts disability at 13.3 percent (plus or minus 3.4), which is higher than the Mexican (8.1 percent, plus or minus 0.9), Guatemalan (5.4 percent, plus or minus 2.3), and Salvadoran (3.3 percent, plus or minus 1.6) Compass profiles in the same period, so date it, do not invent a why, and do not skip screening. Do not fold this history into Tuskegee, which is African American literacy, or into a generic immigrant-mistrust slide.

### Access

For uninsured and delayed-care patterns, Compass reports that 5.7 percent (plus or minus 1.9) of Puerto Rican Minnesotans were without health insurance (ACS 2020 to 2024), so date it and do not invent other rates; Compass poverty is 10.7 percent (plus or minus 3.8), which is a poverty figure, not an uninsured rate. U.S. public-health literature has treated Puerto Rican communities on the mainland as a higher-prevalence group for asthma in some studies, so date the CDC or the study you cite, and do not invent a Minnesota rate.

Ask about language in the clinic, because an English-dominant adult and a Spanish-dominant elder can sit in the same room. Do not use a child as interpreter, and do not run an immigration script at check-in.

Gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care, so offer it. If they name a healer, a parish, or Espiritismo, listen, but do not make any of it the case plan unless they asked.

sections.heading: LGBTQ
sections.body:
Queer and trans Puerto Rican Minnesotans exist, and conservative family and parish climates can mean silence or exile, though that is not every family. Afro-Puerto Rican queer people exist, and some people live a public English life and a private Spanish life. You use the name they use and do not share what they tell you unless a rule requires it.

### This person

Minnesota’s Human Rights Act still applies. Use the name the person uses, and do not share what they tell you unless a rule requires it. Keep this section separate from the historic African American LGBTQ section. Do not question a household about anyone’s sexuality or gender, and take seriously that some people have reason to keep it private.

Do not let concern about family reputation or parish climate override what this person wants, and always defer to the person in front of you.

sections.heading: Hair, Dress, and Body
sections.body:
There is no Puerto Rican uniform, and the second generation looks like Minnesota. Fiesta and bomba dress are public at celebrations, but they are not a daily costume, and they are not yours to request for Heritage Month, so do not ask a woman in clinic whether she “still wears the costume.”

### Dress

Afro-Puerto Rican hair is not the CROWN Act chapter copied over — and you still do not touch, still do not police, and still do not treat tightness or looseness as a professionalism problem. Colorism is a hierarchy, so name it if it is in the room, and do not rank race off hair.

Do not touch. Quinceañera dress, baptism white, and funeral black are celebration and devotion, not material for a case note.

sections.heading: Music
sections.body:
Salsa, bomba, plena, reggaeton, and church music are named variation rather than a playlist, and a Mexican mariachi default in this waiting room is the mash in speakers.

### Variation

A festival stage is not engagement, and a playlist is not language access. Bomba and plena are public culture and Afro-diasporic literacy, not staff entertainment.

Knowing that music is public life will not write the waiver, but it will stop you from treating one Heritage Month speaker as the community.

sections.heading: Sports
sections.body:
Baseball and softball show up especially in Caribbean households, boxing has prestige in some streams, and basketball and fútbol are present too. School sport is ordinary for the second generation, but do not assume the kid plays, and do not make sport the only excellence you can see.

### Not the whole person

Leagues are social infrastructure rather than language access or a case plan, and Greater Minnesota teams are still this people.

A Saturday game does not replace an interpreter on Monday if the elder needs Spanish.

sections.heading: Literature
sections.body:
Spanish- and English-language letters both exist, and Nuyorican writing is a named U.S. literature, but that fact does not mean the person in the lobby can read your form, in English or in Spanish, because literacy in any language is not guaranteed. English-dominant is not “no culture,” and it is not proof that the elder can read the exception process.

### Literacy in the lobby

You do not need to quote a poet in the lobby; you need the language this person actually reads. Print Spanish from Mexico, or a machine translation, is not automatically this household’s Spanish.

CLAS is qualified language, not Google and not a child.

sections.heading: Art
sections.body:
Bomba and plena stand as public culture, alongside contemporary diaspora visual work, and none of it is a sombrero mash or a Mexican ofrenda copied over.

### Guest

Be a guest, not a researcher, because a festival is not a case plan. A Heritage Month table that mashes this people with mariachi has already mashed the adjacent peoples, and an altar is not something to photograph because it is pretty.

Knowing that this people has a public culture will not write the waiver, but it will stop you from treating Puerto Rican Minnesota as a Mexican leftover without one.

sections.heading: Colony, Citizenship, and the State
sections.body:
The political literacy here is 1898, the Jones Act (1917), commonwealth status, PROMESA, and Hurricane María (2017). This is not an ICE file by default but internal U.S. migration, and a DHS badge is not automatically help, because island experience of federal power is mixed, so you still do not greet this household with an immigration script.

### The badge

Do not use María or the colony as a personality, and do not ask a person to narrate the storm or the grid for your professional development. Status politics — commonwealth, statehood, independence — are real, and you do not referee them on a case note.

Do not collect status you do not need, since Asking for an SSN on the first screen is a gate when the building has mashed Latino into enforcement. Mandated reporting still exists, and so does the duty not to treat a whole people as a deportation score they do not belong in.

sections.heading: Work, Markets, and Government
sections.body:
Work here spans service jobs, a professional second generation, public employment, a military stream as U.S. citizens, and plants in some Greater Minnesota towns, so do not assume the worker in the plant is Mexican, and do not assume they need Spanish.

### Work

Parishes and cultural groups may be the trusted channel, so name the local one rather than assuming Minneapolis or assuming CLUES is this people. Take time to introduce yourself and explain the plan, and still give any required notice.

### Staff

Book a qualified interpreter, and pay for community work. Do not assign either to staff because of who they are. Use these resources yourself before you ask a Puerto Rican colleague to explain.

Some people send money to relatives on the island, including after a disaster as an obligation. Ask about it, and do not treat it as optional in a budget, and it is still not an immigration script.

sections.heading: Health-care and Human-service Encounters
sections.body:
Ask about language, because English-dominant households exist and Caribbean Spanish is the need when they need it, which means a Mexican interpreter may still not work. Do not use a child as interpreter, do not make staff the interpreter, and do not run an immigration script at check-in.

### Language

Know who is in the room, and offer gender match in maternal and intimate care if they want it. Use titles in some rooms, and expect two surnames. If you do not need the SSN on the first screen, do not ask for it, because citizenship is the fact and you should not collect status you do not need.

### The meeting

Believe reported pain, and do not skip screening; Compass disability is 13.3 percent (ACS 2020 to 2024), so date it. If they name a healer, a parish, or Espiritismo, listen, and do not make any of it the case plan unless they asked. Mandated reporting still exists, and Greater Minnesota at 32.9 percent is not an afterthought.

sections.heading: Adjacent Peoples — Do Not Mash
sections.body:
This people is not Mexican, not Guatemalan, not Salvadoran, and not the Latino / Hispanic umbrella. Open that CI as adjacent, for the CLAS Spanish line, the mash, and the other origins as a list, because this page is Puerto Rican. Do not file this household under “Latino” or under Mexican and call it done, and do not run an immigration script.

### Adjacent doors

They are not Cuban and not Dominican, and since Caribbean is not one file, name the origin. They are not Brazilian, and they are not Somali.

Nor are they historic African American, although Afro-Puerto Rican people exist. Ask rather than mashing them into the African American CI because both are Black, and do not bleach them into a mestizo Latino blob, because there is never one Latino module.

sections.heading: Counts, Dated
sections.body:
Minnesota Compass (ACS 2020 to 2024) describes the Puerto Rican cultural community this way: 22,925 people (plus or minus 2,722); Twin Cities 67.1 percent; Greater Minnesota 32.9 percent (plus or minus 5.0); age 17 or younger 38.6 percent (plus or minus 4.0); 65+ 4.9 percent (plus or minus 1.6); foreign-born 1.3 percent (plus or minus 0.8); English only (age 5+) 62.0 percent (plus or minus 5.1); language other than English 38.0 percent (plus or minus 5.1); English less than “very well” 10.7 percent (plus or minus 2.8); high school or higher (25+) 91.9 percent (plus or minus 4.0); bachelor’s or higher 41.4 percent (plus or minus 6.3); median household income about $61,985 in 2024 dollars (plus or minus $16,011); poverty 10.7 percent (plus or minus 3.8); owner-occupied 46.4 percent (plus or minus 7.8); average household size 2.32; without health insurance 5.7 percent (plus or minus 1.9); and disability 13.3 percent (plus or minus 3.4).

### Counts

Date Compass, and do not invent other rates. The 1.3 percent foreign-born figure is citizenship in ACS clothing, because birth on the island is not foreign-born, and since counts disagree across ACS vintages and definitions, date the number you cite.

### What the count is not

A rate is not the person, and an LEP rate of 10.7 percent is not zero. Disability at 13.3 percent is a gate, so date it, and do not invent a why. Greater Minnesota at 32.9 percent is not an afterthought, and none of these counts is a reason to run an immigration script.

sections.heading: Doors and Sources
sections.body:
Start with the Minnesota Compass Puerto Rican profile (ACS 2020 to 2024) — https://www.mncompass.org/topics/demographics/cultural-communities/puerto-rican — and date the retrieval. Then turn to the parishes and cultural groups that families name, and to rural partners when the household is in Greater Minnesota, naming the local one rather than assuming Minneapolis. CLUES — https://clues.org/ — offers adjacent Twin Cities Latino services, but it is not this people and not the whole state.

### Public doors

CECLC is a department door, not the whole community. Open the Latino umbrella CI as adjacent rather than as this page, and open Mexican, Guatemalan, or Salvadoran when that is the household. Ask about language before you book Spanish, and do not open an immigration script.

### Where to learn more

Use these resources yourself before you ask a Puerto Rican colleague to explain, and do not count a BCC to a metro org as consultation. Pay partners and report back, remembering that Hispanic Heritage Month is not the work.

sections.heading: How it hits DHS gates — the 40%
sections.body:
Workplace culture and service delivery are both candidates here.

On language, ask rather than assume, because English-dominant households exist, Caribbean Spanish is not Mexican Spanish, and CLAS Spanish is not one Spanish. An LEP rate of 10.7 percent (Compass ACS 2020 to 2024) is not zero, so still book a qualified interpreter when they need one, do not use a child, and remember that gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care.

On names, two surnames are still common, and the database that keeps one invents a person, which is why unmatched last names are not fraud by default.

On citizenship, the Jones Act dates to 1917, so do not run an immigration script by default. Asking for an SSN on the first screen is a gate when the building has mashed Latino into ICE, so do not collect status you do not need.

Hour caps, exception processes, and life-sharing matches made without asking about language are not culturally neutral.

On child welfare and disability, Compass disability is 13.3 percent (ACS 2020 to 2024), so date it, and recognize that help-seeking that becomes a report is part of why people wait. Mandated reporting still exists, and so does the duty not to treat a whole community as a risk score; domestic violence is not culture, and you follow the law.

On notices and comment, ask which language they read, because an English PDF will not reach an elder who reads Spanish and may be right for an English-dominant household. Record who was reached and what follow-up happened, and because Greater Minnesota is 32.9 percent, a St. Paul meeting is not the whole channel.

On workforce, Puerto Rican staff are not the interpreter pool and not the community; staff are colleagues, not the curriculum, and should not be treated as such.

On the Latino mash, opening Mexican, or the umbrella, because the checkbox says Hispanic shuts the person out, and so does opening an ICE script.

On legislation, funding, and rule, study a channel before you advocate for it. Use this page so that the 40% has a household in it.

sections.heading: A Note on This Guide
sections.body:
This brief is about Salvadoran Minnesota as a people — salvadoreño, salvadoreña — and not as a Mexican variant or as a slice of the Latino / Hispanic umbrella. The civil war (1980–1992) and Temporary Protected Status are literacy for the desk, meaning background you carry so that you understand the household rather than a speech you give the family. It also helps to remember that Spanish is not one Spanish, because voseo is a feature of Salvadoran Spanish generally and a Mexican interpreter, however qualified, may still not work for this household. This is not Mexican, it is not Guatemalan, and it is not Puerto Rican, since shared Spanish is not shared culture. A full mosaic of a people is not a stereotype; a stereotype is what happens when this page becomes the person in the lobby.

### Who this is

Open the Latino umbrella only as an adjacent door, because that page carries the mash and the CLAS Spanish line and has its own place, while this page is Salvadoran. If you leave this door and file the household under “Latino,” or under Mexican because that is the Minnesota default, you have left this door and lost the person.

### Who this is not

Minnesota Compass (ACS 2020–2024) puts the Salvadoran cultural community at 17,444 people (plus or minus 3,014), with 73.2 percent living in the Twin Cities and 26.8 percent living in Greater Minnesota, which is not an afterthought. About 46.5 percent are age 17 or younger, and 1.9 percent are age 65 and older (plus or minus 1.3); Compass still suppresses the separate 65-74, 75-84 and 85+ rows, so do not invent those. The community is 43.0 percent foreign-born, and among people age 5 and older, 76.8 percent speak a language other than English and 34.8 percent speak English less than “very well.” Whatever number you use, date it, and since Compass does not split out an indigenous-language count on this profile, do not invent one of those either. A rate describes a population; it is not the person in front of you.

The diversity inside this people is the point, so consider a 1980s arrival who came through the war, a TPS holder whose status is a clock, a U.S.-born nurse, a Greater Minnesota factory household, an evangelical grandmother, a college student who uses English with friends and voseo with an uncle, and a person who will not open the door because a relative can be moved. They share a people, but they do not share a Tuesday.

### How to read this

Always defer to the person in front of you, because this page is a hypothesis that you still have to test on this family.

sections.heading: Origins and the Founding of a People
sections.body:
Salvadoran peoplehood is not a Mexican origin story with a different flag. El Salvador is the smallest mainland republic in Central America, and its Pipil / Nahua history was largely mestizo-ized by the colony and by the coffee state. That history matters, but it does not license guesswork, so do not invent a Minnesota indigenous-language count that Compass does not have, and do not copy K’iche’ from the Guatemalan page onto this one; if you want to know what a household speaks, ask this household.

### History for the meeting

Spanish colonial rule, independence alongside the other Central American republics (15 September 1821), a coffee oligarchy, and the twentieth-century state that went to war with its own people — that is literacy for the desk, and it gives you context for what a family may carry. It is not a speech you give the family, which means the meeting should not start with a pupusa, a volcano, or a Heritage Month sentence.

### What people brought

Writing in Spanish is the ordinary public literacy for this community, but ordinary does not mean universal, since some elders read Spanish and some do not, and some U.S.-born adults do not read Spanish either. Oral skill is not print skill, and Salvadoran Spanish is not Mexican Spanish.

What people brought with them was language (including voseo), kinship, faith, work knowledge, and the memory of a war the United States funded. What they met in Minnesota was an English form, a single “Latino” checkbox, often one interpreter labeled Spanish — usually Mexican — and a lobby that had not studied TPS.

sections.heading: The Geography of the Salvadoran World
sections.body:
The homeland is El Salvador, and people will name their own places within it — the departments, San Salvador, the coast, the interior — so when a family names a place, confirm it and use it. Do not referee Santa Ana versus San Miguel in a waiver meeting, because your job in that room is to listen.

### Homeland

The U.S. Salvadoran map runs through California (with Los Angeles among the named hubs), the D.C.–Maryland–Virginia corridor, Texas, New York, and also Minnesota. Those larger hubs are not this map, though, since secondary migration and family ties are what pulled people here.

### Minnesota

In Minnesota, 73.2 percent of the community lives in the Twin Cities and 26.8 percent lives in Greater Minnesota (Compass ACS 2020–2024), and Greater Minnesota is not an afterthought. Do not assume Minneapolis, do not assume a plant town is Guatemalan by default, and do not assume the person in front of you has ever been to El Salvador, because a Greater Minnesota household is still this people.

sections.heading: Civil War, TPS, and Later Streams — Foundational Event
sections.body:
If 1975 is the foundational event of Vietnamese Minnesota, the Salvadoran civil war (1980–1992) is the foundational political event of Salvadoran Minnesota. Archbishop Óscar Romero was assassinated on 24 March 1980, the United States backed the government, and people fled. All of that is literacy for the desk rather than a speech you give the family or an icebreaker, and you should never ask a person to narrate killing for your professional development.

### Foundational events

The Peace Accords were signed on 16 January 1992; in January 2022 El Salvador’s Legislative Assembly renamed that day the Day of the Victims of the Armed Conflict and repealed the peace-day decrees. Later streams carry family reunification, work, disasters, and Temporary Protected Status — including after the 2001 earthquakes — as a clock that reorganizes an ordinary Tuesday. TPS is structure in a household’s life rather than a personality, and while it is not a reason to collect status you do not need, it is a reason a form that feels like enforcement will empty the lobby.

### Who you meet

The desk in 2026 does not only meet a 1980s arrival. It meets U.S.-born children — Compass puts the community at 43.0 percent foreign-born (ACS 2020–2024) — translating for their parents, and it meets mixed-status households, TPS holders, and a person who has lived here since childhood and still cannot get Salvadoran Spanish in the lobby. If the only word you know is “immigrant,” you will miss them, and if the only word you know is “Mexican,” you will mash them.

Enforcement is current structure, not history, so when TPS is threatened or raids are rumored and people may skip clinic, school, and waiver meetings, that is not noncompliance.

sections.heading: Family
sections.body:
Familismo is a hypothesis you test, not a personality you assign. Ask who should speak first, and hear from the person directly. Adult children may be holding a waiver meeting, a shift, and a school conference in the same week. Compass puts the average household size at about 3.64 (ACS 2020–2024), and even that figure does not always map onto the nuclear household an English form expects, which means the person who cares for a child may not match the waiver checkbox, so ask who should be in the room.

### Who is in the household

TPS and mixed status are structure: a U.S.-citizen child, a parent on TPS, a sibling without status, and an aunt who works in service can all live under one roof. For that reason, do not collect status you do not need, and do not treat unmatched last names, a grandmother as caregiver, or a missing SSN as fraud until you have a reason to. Be aware, too, that hour caps and “natural supports” language can dump unpaid work onto the women in that network and then call it culture.

### Who speaks

The person who speaks in the lobby may be the child with the best English, but that child is not the qualified interpreter, and CLAS still stands. Using a child as the go-between does harm, so book the interpreter and ask who should be in the room.

Minnesota law still stands as well, because domestic violence is not culture, and you should not skip mandated reporting and call it humility.

sections.heading: Minnesota and Salvadoran History
sections.body:
Minnesota holds a Salvadoran community large enough that this department will meet it on waivers, child welfare, health care, cash, food, aging, and employment. Compass counts 17,444 people (ACS 2020–2024), with 73.2 percent in the Twin Cities and 26.8 percent in Greater Minnesota — again, not an afterthought — so do not write this people as a Minneapolis anecdote, and do not write them as a Mexican leftover.

### Places

Think in places rather than a blob: Twin Cities corridors and first-ring suburbs, and Greater Minnesota towns with work and housing. Census counts by place (ACS 2020–2024) show St. Paul (3,092) far ahead of Minneapolis (815), with Greater Minnesota concentrations in Worthington (527) and Rochester (452) and smaller towns such as St. James, Madelia and Montevideo, all with wide margins of error. Pupusa shops and markets are public life and worth knowing, but they are not consultation, and a food visit does not make you the expert.

### Partners

Ask which parishes, churches, or worker centers this family uses as partners, and name the local one rather than assuming Minneapolis. CLUES is a Twin Cities door rather than the whole community, and CECLC is a department door rather than the people, which is why you pay the partner this household actually uses.

Book a qualified interpreter, and pay for community work. Do not assign either to staff because of who they are. No current Salvadoran fiesta or Romero commemoration in Minnesota is documented here; the most recent documented Minnesota Romero event was a March 2020 speaking tour by Marta Portillo, a catechist who worked with Romero, in southern Minnesota parishes. If you are invited to a fiesta or a commemoration, it is optional professional development, and you attend as a guest, knowing that it does not make you the expert.

sections.heading: Salvadoreño — the heart of a people
sections.body:
El Salvador is a small country, and a war the United States funded is part of its history. Forms in Minnesota file Salvadorans under Latino and often under Mexican. Ask plainly whether the person agrees with the plan, and make it easy to say no.

### In this state

Spanish is not one Spanish, and since voseo is a feature of Salvadoran Spanish generally, a Mexican interpreter who does not hear this household will not work.

The Mexican default in this state is a count fact on another page, but on this page it is a harm, because it is what happens when staff copy Guadalupe, norteño, and Mexican Spanish onto a Salvadoran household.

This guide is a working orientation, and because individual variation always supersedes group generalization, always defer to the person in front of you.

sections.heading: Core Concepts
sections.body:
The civil war is part of the history many families carry. Do not use it as an icebreaker, and do not assume it about the person in the lobby.

### TPS

Temporary Protected Status works as a clock in a household’s life, which makes it structure. It is not a reason to collect status you do not need, and it is a reason a badge is not automatically help.

### Voseo

Salvadoran Spanish is not Mexican Spanish, so book qualified Spanish AND ask the household what it speaks.

### Familismo and respeto as hypotheses

Ask who takes part in decisions, confirm the plan directly, and still follow mandated reporting.

### Two surnames

The database that keeps only one surname invents a person, so ask how the name should be filed.

### Remittance, church, work

Families may be Evangelical, Catholic or neither, and a plant shift and a second-generation degree can sit in the same household. Do not make a priest or a pastor the case plan unless they asked.

sections.heading: Religion
sections.body:
Salvadoran Minnesotans may be Catholic, evangelical, Pentecostal, of another faith, or of none; this page has no Minnesota figure for religion, so ask. Ask whether a parish or iglesia is a trusted channel for this family. Romero is literacy for the desk — 24 March 1980 — and not a piety ranking you assign in the lobby, while Our Lady of Guadalupe is Mexican Catholic literacy, so do not install it as the default on this page; ask instead.

### Streams

Do not make a priest or a pastor the case plan unless this family asked for that, and do not BCC one church and call it consultation. Nor should you treat evangelical growth as the evolved version of Catholic, since they are two streams, not a ladder.

### Practice

Holy Week, funerals, and fiesta obligation can collide with your calendar, and while you still keep medical and legal time, you name the conflict instead of punishing it. Do not photograph an altar.

Help that looks like a report is not help. A religious framing of disability, mental health, or gender can sit right next to a fierce wish for services, and you can hold both at once.

sections.heading: Greetings
sections.body:
Ask who to greet first, or follow the household’s lead. Wait to see how the person greets you, and follow their lead.

### Titles

Use titles until you are invited to do otherwise — Señor, Señora, Don, Doña — and use the last name you were given, remembering there may be two. Do not use a first name with an elder just because the form printed it. Usted is respect with strangers and elders, while vos is a familiar form in Salvadoran Spanish generally, and a qualified interpreter matches that register rather than having you correct it.

### This room

Let this person’s own greeting guide you, whatever you read on another page. Ask before any physical contact, and let the person set the limit.

sections.heading: Naming Conventions
sections.body:
Two surnames is the default in much of Salvadoran Spanish-language naming, with the apellido paterno first and then the apellido materno. A U.S. database that keeps only one surname invents a person, and that invented name then follows them through MHCP, child welfare, and school, which makes it a gate.

### How to file

Ask how to file the name and how to say it, and then pronounce it rather than dropping accents as a joke. Given names may be Spanish, English, or both, and some people use a middle given name as the call-name, so ask.

Women may or may not take a husband’s surname in U.S. records, and children may carry two surnames that do not match a parent’s U.S. “last name” field, but that is not fraud until you have a reason.

For the same reason, do not treat unmatched last names in a household as a fraud flag by default, and do not invent a hyphen and then punish the person when the hyphen moves.

sections.heading: Dates of Significance
sections.body:
15 September marks independence with the other Central American republics, and that is literacy for the desk. It is not Mexican 16 September and it is not Cinco de Mayo, so do not put a restaurant calendar on a case note.

### Calendar

24 March is Romero, which is literacy rather than an icebreaker, and not a day you ask a survivor to speak to staff for professional development. 16 January 1992 is the date the Peace Accords were signed; since January 2022 El Salvador has called that day the Day of the Victims of the Armed Conflict. Because Holy Week, funerals, and fiesta days will not be on your state calendar, ask.

Hispanic Heritage Month is the umbrella calendar rather than this people’s day, and it is not consultation. A calendar click is literacy for scheduling, not community engagement and not a day off the work, so do not put “Latino holiday” on a case note.

sections.heading: Education
sections.body:
Compass (ACS 2020–2024) reports that among Salvadoran Minnesotans 25 and older, about 65.3 percent have high school or higher and about 18.7 percent have a bachelor’s or higher, and you should date Compass when you cite it. About 43.0 percent of the community is foreign-born, and among those 5 and older, 76.8 percent speak a language other than English and 34.8 percent speak English less than “very well.” That is a language gate, not a culture clash, and the IEP still has to reach the parent who does not read it.

### School and language

A parent who speaks fluent Salvadoran Spanish and limited English is not illiterate, and while some elders read Spanish, some do not, which means the English-only form is the gate. A Mexican-Spanish notice is not automatically this household’s Spanish, and you should not use a child as interpreter.

Second-generation educational mobility is real, and so is a gap that a room that treats everyone the same will call “culture” when it is really language access plus enforcement fear plus a school that never learned the second surname. Do not treat a college student in the family as proof the waiver household needs no interpreter.

sections.heading: Etiquette
sections.body:
Ask who to greet first, or follow the household’s lead. If food or drink is offered, accepting a little is fine, and you can still keep to medical and legal timelines.

### In the home

Ask before taking any photograph or touching any religious object, and do not ask anyone to explain their faith or history for your benefit. For shoes, follow the household.

### Time

If someone misses an appointment, first check the time, transport, interpreter and work schedule. Confirm the plan in the language the person uses, and ask whether it works for them.

Book a qualified interpreter instead of using a child to go between.

sections.heading: Language and Communication
sections.body:
Spanish is not one Spanish, and Salvadoran Spanish is not Mexican Spanish, because voseo is a feature of Salvadoran Spanish generally. Book a qualified Spanish interpreter AND ask this household, since a Mexican interpreter from one region may still not work. Register matters, with usted for elders and strangers and vos among familiars, and the interpreter matches the room rather than you correcting it.

### Language

Compass reports that among those 5 and older (ACS 2020–2024), about 76.8 percent speak a language other than English and about 34.8 percent speak English less than “very well,” so date the number and treat it as the large language gate it is. Literacy in any language is not guaranteed, because oral skill is not print. Compass does not split out an indigenous-language count on this Salvadoran profile, so do not invent one, and do not copy Mixtec or K’iche’ onto this page unless this household names it.

Give the person time to answer. If you get a short yes, check that the plan was understood, and ask whether it works for them.

Do not use a child as the interpreter, and do not make a Salvadoran coworker the interpreter.

sections.heading: Other Considerations
sections.body:
This section states hard facts plainly, because treating everyone the same can hide them.

### Named harms

ICE, TPS, and the enforcement climate are structure. Mixed-status households may skip clinic, school, and waiver meetings when a relative can be moved or when TPS is a clock, and that is not noncompliance. Do not collect status you do not need, and know that an SSN on the first screen is a gate.

The Mexican default in this state will talk over this household if you let the umbrella page do this page’s job, because Spanish is not one Spanish.

Gang discourse in U.S. media — including MS-13 as a story that began among Salvadoran refugee youth in Los Angeles — is HISTORY, and it is a named harm in enforcement. A last name is not a gang file, so do not score a Minnesota child on a cousin’s decade or a cable-news segment; follow law, and still see a family.

Do not joke about machismo, and do not excuse control as “that’s culture,” and since domestic violence is not culture, you follow mandated reporting. LGBTQ Salvadoran Minnesotans exist, so you use the name, and you do not out someone to kin. Staff who share this community may add facts, but they do not get to delete a fact because it is hard to say.

sections.heading: Health
sections.body:
Believe reported pain. War trauma sits in some rooms, but it is not a personality and it is not a reason to skip screening; it is a reason a government badge is not automatically help. Do not fold this history into Tuskegee or into a generic immigrant-mistrust slide.

### Access

Compass (ACS 2020–2024) reports that 19.3 percent of Salvadoran Minnesotans have no health insurance (plus or minus 5.4) and that 59.1 percent of renter households are cost-burdened, so date those figures when you cite them, and do not invent a rate Compass does not publish. Compass poverty is 5.6 percent, which is a poverty figure rather than an uninsured rate, and not proof the gates closed. Disability is 3.3 percent, and you should date it too. Compass puts people 65 and older at 1.9 percent (plus or minus 1.3), but the 65-74, 75-84 and 85+ rows are suppressed, so do not invent those rates.

Fear of the lobby is a health access fact, which means a badge, a form that asks for SSN, a child called to interpret a diagnosis, and an interpreter who does not speak this Spanish are all clinical events. When TPS is threatened or enforcement spikes, people may skip clinic, and that is not noncompliance.

Parish prayer and biomedicine can both be in the household, so if they name a healer or a pastor, listen, but do not make either the case plan unless they asked. Gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care, so offer it, and do not use a child as interpreter.

sections.heading: LGBTQ
sections.body:
Queer and trans Salvadoran Minnesotans exist. Conservative family, parish, and evangelical climates can mean silence or exile, and some people live a public English life and a private Spanish life, which is why you use the name they use and do not share what they tell you unless a rule requires it.

### This person

Minnesota’s Human Rights Act still applies. Use the name the person uses, and do not share what they tell you unless a rule requires it. Do not question a household about anyone’s sexuality or gender, and take seriously that some people have reason to keep it private.

Do not let concern about family reputation or parish climate override what this person wants, and always defer to the person in front of you.

sections.heading: Hair, Dress, and Body
sections.body:
There is no Salvadoran uniform, and the second generation looks like Minnesota. Fiesta dress is public at celebration rather than a daily costume, and it is not yours to request for Heritage Month, so do not ask a woman in clinic whether she “still wears the costume.”

### Dress

Do not touch, and do not rank piety off clothing. Colorism is real inside Central American streams, so name it if it is in the room, but do not rank.

Quinceañera dress, baptism white, and evangelical modesty are celebration and devotion, not a case note. Service and plant work may mean stained hands, which is labor and not a joke.

sections.heading: Music
sections.body:
Music varies by household and generation, and a Mexican mariachi default in this waiting room is the mash coming through the speakers.

### Variation

Ask what music, if any, matters to this person or family. A festival stage is not engagement, and a playlist is not language access.

If a family mentions a Romero commemoration, ask what it means to them; it is not consultation and not a case plan.

sections.heading: Sports
sections.body:
School sport may be part of the second generation’s life, but do not assume the kid plays, and do not make sport the only excellence you can see.

### Not the whole person

Leagues and pickup games are social infrastructure rather than language access or a case plan, and Greater Minnesota teams are still this people.

A Saturday tournament does not replace an interpreter on Monday.

sections.heading: Literature
sections.body:
Spanish-language letters exist, and Roque Dalton is literacy for the desk, not a quote for a case note. That fact does not mean the person in the lobby can read your form, in English or in Spanish, because literacy in any language is not guaranteed and oral Spanish is not print Spanish.

### Literacy in the lobby

You do not need to quote a poet in the lobby; you need the language this person reads — or hears. Print Spanish from Mexico or a translation produced by software is not automatically this household’s Spanish.

CLAS means qualified language, which is not Google and is not a child.

sections.heading: Art
sections.body:
There is a public culture of markets, church, and fiesta, and pupusas are a foodway, not consultation. You are a guest rather than a researcher, a food visit is not a case plan, and you should not photograph an altar.

### Guest

A Heritage Month that mashes this people with mariachi or a Guatemalan huipil has already mashed the adjacent peoples.

Contemporary Salvadoran artists work in this country, and while knowing that will not write the waiver, it will stop you from treating this people as a Mexican leftover without a public culture.

sections.heading: Civil War, TPS, and Enforcement Climate
sections.body:
The civil war (1980–1992), Romero, U.S. backing of the government, the Peace Accords, and TPS as a later clock — that is the political event. Later came policing and the deportation of people with records, including people who have lived here since childhood, which is why a DHS badge is not automatically help.

### The badge

Do not use the war as a personality, and do not ask a person to narrate dying for your professional development. Gang discourse in U.S. enforcement — MS-13 as a Los Angeles refugee-youth story later exported — is a named fact, but it is not a last-name score, and you do not write it on a Minnesota child; follow law, and still see a family.

When TPS is threatened or enforcement spikes, people may skip clinic, school, and waiver meetings, so do not collect status you do not need, because SSN on the first screen is a gate. Mandated reporting still exists, and so does the duty not to treat a whole people as a deportation score.

sections.heading: Work, Markets, and Government
sections.body:
Minnesota sources document Salvadoran work in meat processing, landscaping on H-2B visas, food businesses, banking and communications, and a small-business owner and a waiver recipient may be the same household.

### Work

Ask whether a parish, iglesia, or worker center is a trusted channel for this household, and name the local one rather than assuming Minneapolis, and do not assume CLUES reaches a Greater Minnesota town. Take time to introduce yourself and explain the plan, and still give any required notice.

### Staff

Book a qualified interpreter, and pay for community work. Do not assign either to staff because of who they are.

Some households may send money to relatives in El Salvador. Ask about it before you build a budget.

sections.heading: Health-care and Human-service Encounters
sections.body:
Start with language. Book qualified Spanish AND ask, because this household speaks Salvadoran Spanish / voseo and a Mexican interpreter may still not work, and do not use a child as interpreter or make staff the interpreter.

### Language

Ask who is in the room, and offer gender match in maternal and intimate care if they want it. Use titles, remembering there may be two surnames. On SSN on the first screen, if you do not need it, do not ask for it, and on TPS and mixed status, do not collect status you do not need, because in an enforcement climate, skipped appointments are a pattern.

### The meeting

Believe reported pain, and do not skip screening. If they name a pastor or a parish, listen, but do not make either the case plan unless they asked, and remember that mandated reporting still exists. Greater Minnesota, at 26.8 percent, is not an afterthought, and rural access is a gate when the only interpreter is contracted from the Cities and does not speak this Spanish.

sections.heading: Adjacent Peoples — Do Not Mash
sections.body:
This people is not Mexican, not Guatemalan, not Puerto Rican, and not the Latino / Hispanic umbrella. Open that CI as adjacent — for CLAS Spanish, the mash, and the other origins as a list — while remembering that this page is Salvadoran, so do not file this household under “Latino” or under Mexican and call it done.

### Adjacent doors

K’iche’ or Mam is not a default here, since that is the Guatemalan page unless this household names it, and neither is Mixtec. Compass does not split out an indigenous-language count here, so do not invent one, and remember that Spanish is not one Spanish.

Not Honduran, not Nicaraguan, not Cuban — name the origin. Not Somali, and not historic African American, and never one Latino module.

sections.heading: Counts, Dated
sections.body:
Minnesota Compass (ACS 2020–2024) describes the Salvadoran cultural community this way.
