The count is 17,444 (plus or minus 3,014), with 73.2 percent in the Twin Cities and 26.8 percent in Greater Minnesota, and about 46.5 percent are age 17 or younger, while 1.9 percent are 65 and older (plus or minus 1.3) and the separate 65-74, 75-84 and 85+ rows are suppressed, so do not invent those. Foreign-born is 43.0 percent, and among those age 5 and older, 76.8 percent speak a language other than English and 34.8 percent speak English less than “very well.” Among those 25 and older, 65.3 percent have high school or higher and 18.7 percent have a bachelor’s or higher. Median household income is about $88,051 (plus or minus $23,118) in 2024 dollars, poverty is 5.6 percent, owner-occupied housing is 61.6 percent, average household size is 3.64, and disability is 3.3 percent. Compass also reports that 19.3 percent of Salvadoran Minnesotans have no health insurance (plus or minus 5.4) and that 59.1 percent of renter households are cost-burdened.

### Counts

Date Compass whenever you cite it, and do not invent other rates. Compass does not split out an indigenous-language count on this profile, so do not invent one, and because counts disagree across ACS vintages and definitions, date the number you cite. The Census Bureau’s Hispanic-origin question counts 14,670 Salvadorans (plus or minus 1,712) for 2020 to 2024, while Compass’s broader cultural-community method counts 17,444; the 2024 one-year estimate is 11,312 (plus or minus 3,384), and Census counts 8,255 Minnesotans born in El Salvador.

### What the count is not

A young age structure is not a personality, and poverty at 5.6 percent is not proof the gates closed. Language — 76.8 percent LOTE and 34.8 percent LEP — is a gate, and Greater Minnesota at 26.8 percent is not an afterthought. A rate is not the person.

sections.heading: Doors and Sources
sections.body:
Start with the Minnesota Compass Salvadoran profile (ACS 2020–2024) — https://www.mncompass.org/topics/demographics/cultural-communities/salvadoran — and date the retrieval. Then ask which parishes, churches, or worker centers this family uses, naming the local one rather than assuming Minneapolis, since CLUES — https://clues.org/ — provides Twin Cities services, not the whole state.

### Public doors

CECLC is a department door, not the whole community. Open the Latino umbrella CI as adjacent rather than as this page, and open Mexican, Guatemalan, or Puerto Rican when that is the household. Book Salvadoran Spanish, and do not assume a Mexican interpreter is the same door.

### Where to learn more

Use these resources yourself before you ask a Salvadoran colleague to explain, and do not count a BCC to a metro org as consultation. Pay partners and report back, because Hispanic Heritage Month is not the work.

sections.heading: How it hits DHS gates — the 40%
sections.body:
Workplace culture and service delivery are both candidates here.

Language comes first: CLAS Spanish is not one Spanish, because this household speaks Salvadoran Spanish / voseo and a Mexican interpreter may still not work, but you still book a qualified interpreter and do not use a child. Gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care. LOTE at 76.8 percent and LEP at 34.8 percent (Compass ACS 2020–2024) are gates, so date them.

Names come next: two surnames is the norm, and the database that keeps one invents a person, which is why unmatched last names are not fraud by default.

Hour caps, exception processes, SSN on the first screen, and life-sharing matches without language are not culturally neutral, and TPS and mixed-status households may bounce if the first field feels like enforcement, so do not collect status you do not need.

In child welfare and disability, help-seeking that becomes a report is part of why people wait. Mandated reporting still exists, and so does the duty not to treat a whole community as a risk score — or a last name as a gang file — while domestic violence is not culture, and you follow law.

On enforcement climate, people may skip clinic, school, and waiver meetings when TPS is a clock or a relative can be moved, and that is not noncompliance, so do not collect status you do not need.

On notices and comment, do not count an eList and an English PDF as reaching this community, and record who was reached and what follow-up happened. Greater Minnesota is 26.8 percent, so a St. Paul meeting is not the whole channel.

On workforce, Salvadoran staff are not the interpreter pool and not the community; staff are colleagues, not the curriculum, and you do not treat them as either.

On the Latino mash, opening Mexican, or the umbrella, because the checkbox says Hispanic shuts the person out.

On legislation, funding, and rule, study a channel before you advocate for it. Use this page so that the 40% has a household in it.

sections.heading: A Note on This Guide
sections.body:
This brief is about Thai people as a people of Thailand — the lowland state history, Theravada wats, and a language related to Lao but not interchangeable with it — and as a Minnesota community that the Census Bureau counts near 4,639, plus or minus 904 (ACS 2020–2024). It is not about Hmong Minnesota, and it is not about Lao Minnesota. Camps in Thailand — Ban Vinai, Mae La, and others — held Hmong and Karen families after wars this people did not fight as those files, so do not file a Thai household under that war; if the household is Hmong, open Hmong Minnesota, if the household is Lao, open Lao Minnesota, and if the household is Thai, book Thai.

### Who this is

This community is not a Census “Asian” mash, which means it is not Khmer and it is not Vietnamese, because a shared continent is not a shared culture, and Songkran is not Hmong New Year and not Tết. Use this page for context and questions. It does not describe the person in front of you.

### Who this is not

The Census Bureau counts 4,342 Minnesotans who name Thai alone or in any combination in the 2020 Census (2,239 Thai alone) and 4,639 (plus or minus 904) in the ACS 2020–2024; the State Demographer used 4,518 (ACS 2024) in June 2026. About 72 percent (3,121 of 4,342) live in the seven metro counties in the 2020 Census, and the ACS 2020–2024 puts 3,289 (plus or minus 803) of 4,639 in the Minneapolis-St. Paul metro area, about 71 percent, so Greater Minnesota is closer to 28 to 30 percent, with Olmsted County (Rochester) the largest outside the metro. In the 2020 Census, 58.7 percent of those naming Thai alone or in combination are female (2,548 of 4,342), and 67 percent of those naming Thai alone (1,503 of 2,239). Minnesota Compass does not currently list a Thai profile, and the state's 2026 economic status report counts Thai inside “Other Asian,” so no current Minnesota income, poverty, education or housing figures for Thai Minnesotans are published. About 18,819 Minnesotans (plus or minus 1,296) were born in Thailand (ACS 2020–2024), about four times the number who identify as Thai, and many of them are Hmong, Lao or Karen, so a Thailand birthplace is not a Thai identity. Whichever figure you use, date it, and remember that a rate is not the person.

The diversity inside this people is the point. A wat household in the Twin Cities, a Greater Minnesota restaurant family, an Isan speaker, a Bangkok-origin professional, a U.S.-born child translating for a parent, and a marriage-stream household far from any Thai-speaking neighbor all share one census count, yet they do not share a Tuesday.

### How to read this

Always defer to the person in front of you, because this page is a hypothesis and you are still testing it on this family.

sections.heading: Origins and the Founding of a People
sections.body:
Thai peoplehood is older than the name Thailand (1939), older than 1932, and older than the restaurant file. Siam, its kingdoms, and a modern nation that marks itself as never colonized by a European power — that national narrative is literacy for the desk, but it is not a speech you give the family, and it is not a virtue ranking against neighbors who were colonized.

### History for the meeting

The Thai language is related to Lao, but related is not interchangeable, and a Lao interpreter is not the default, while Isan (northeastern Thai) is a neighboring variety that some families will name. Ask rather than guess, and do not mash Hmong into this origin because camps sat on Thai soil.

### What people brought

What people brought with them was language, Theravada practice or none, family obligation, foodways, and the memory of a state that was not a camp. What they met in Minnesota was an English form, one “Asian” checkbox, a restaurant cliché, and often a worker who had already filed them under Hmong because the building only studied the war.

Writing is Thai script, which is related to Lao script and not interchangeable with it. Many elders read Thai and some do not, while the second generation may not read it at all, so a notice in Lao, or in English only, may still not work, and you should ask which one this family reads.

sections.heading: The Geography of the Thai World
sections.body:
Thailand is Bangkok, the north, the south, Isan, and the places families name. Isan is related to Lao language and music, but it is not identical, not a Lao file, and not a Hmong file, so do not draw one tuk-tuk on a case note. The Malay-Muslim south is a named geography that some families will name, and you do not referee it.

### Homeland

The diaspora is global, reaching the United States, Europe, the Gulf, and East Asia, which makes Minnesota one map rather than the map. The Census Bureau puts about 71 to 72 percent in the Minneapolis-St. Paul area and about 28 to 30 percent in Greater Minnesota, with Olmsted County (Rochester) the largest outside the metro, so towns with restaurants, campuses, and mixed households are on this page.

### Minnesota

Do not assume Minneapolis, and do not assume they have been to Bangkok. Do not file this household onto a Thai border-camp map, because Ban Vinai and Mae La are Hmong and Karen geographies, so open those CIs for those households.

sections.heading: Students, Marriage, Work — Not the Camp File
sections.body:
Thai Minnesota is not a 1975 airlift community, since student, marriage, restaurant and small-business, professional, and family-reunification streams built what you will meet. The Cold War U.S. presence in Thailand and the later ordinary immigration are literacy, but they are not a Hmong Secret War sentence and not a Karen camp sentence.

### Foundational events

The camps on Thai soil held other peoples. Ban Vinai, Mae La, and others are named on the Hmong and Karen spines, and filing a Thai family under that war shuts the person out, so do not ask a Thai parent to narrate a camp they did not live, and do not skip this page because the building only trained on 1975.

### Who you meet

The desk may meet a child with English and a parent who still cannot get Thai in the lobby, and limited English is the gate.

If the only word you know is “restaurant,” you will miss the wat household, the Greater Minnesota marriage-stream family, and the professional who still needs this page.

sections.heading: Family
sections.body:
Ask who the person wants in the room, and hear from the person directly. Multi-generation households exist alongside people who live alone, so ask who should be in the room rather than assuming.

### Who is in the household

The 2020 Census shows 58.7 percent female among those naming Thai alone or in combination (2,548 of 4,342) and 67 percent among those naming Thai alone (1,503 of 2,239), which is a labor and marriage-stream fact rather than a mail-order personality, a joke, or a reason to skip the man in the lobby. Hour caps and “natural supports” language can quietly shift unpaid work onto the women in that network and then call it culture.

### Who speaks

The person who speaks in the lobby may be a child with the best English in the family, but that child is not the qualified interpreter, and using a child as the go-between does harm, so book Thai.

Minnesota law still stands, so do not skip mandated reporting and call it humility. The person who holds the child’s medical decision may not match the English form, which is why you ask.

sections.heading: Minnesota and Thai History
sections.body:
Ask which services the person or family already uses: waivers, child welfare, health care, cash, food, aging, or employment. The Census Bureau counts about 4,639 (ACS 2020–2024), with about 71 percent in the Minneapolis-St. Paul area, but the roughly 28 to 30 percent in Greater Minnesota is not an afterthought, so do not write this people as a Minneapolis restaurant anecdote.

### Places

The wats that families name are centers of ritual, mutual aid, and information, but they are not “the community.” The Thai associations this person names are partners, so name the local one, and pay the door this household actually uses. Book a qualified interpreter, and pay for community work. Do not assign either to staff because of who they are.

### Partners

Restaurants are public life and a documented work pattern, but they are not consultation, and a dinner does not make you the expert. Songkran at a wat is optional professional development if you are invited, and you attend as a guest, knowing that being there does not make you the expert.

Book a qualified interpreter, and pay for community work. Do not assign either to staff because of who they are. With roughly 28 to 30 percent in Greater Minnesota, a Twin Cities wat is not the whole channel, so pay the partner this household actually uses, and report back.

sections.heading: Not Hmong, not Lao — the heart of a people
sections.body:
Forms in Minnesota file Thai people under a checkbox that also holds Hmong, Lao, Chinese, and Indian histories this household does not share. Do not ask whether they came through “the camps,” as if Thailand were only a holding country for someone else’s war.

### In this state

Ask plainly whether the person agrees with the plan, and make it easy to say no.

Limited English and distance from a Thai-speaking neighbor are gates. Do not let a restaurant cliché stand in for those facts. Roughly 28 to 30 percent in Greater Minnesota means isolation for some households far from a Thai-speaking neighbor.

This guide is a working orientation, which means individual variation always supersedes group generalization.

sections.heading: Core Concepts
sections.body:
Language comes first, and the language is Thai, related to Lao but not interchangeable with it, so book Thai, since a Lao interpreter may still not work and a Hmong interpreter is the wrong door.

### Wat and Theravada

Do not make a monk the case plan unless they asked, and do not mash Hmong txiv neeb onto this household.

### Wai

In a home with an altar, ask where to sit, and ask before touching anyone, including a child.

### Songkran

Songkran is Thai New Year in April, which means it is not Hmong New Year, and it is not Pi Mai as a mash you did not ask about.

### Not the camp file

Camps in Thailand are a Hmong and Karen story rather than this one.

Limited English and distance from a Thai-speaking neighbor are gates, not rounding errors.

sections.heading: Religion
sections.body:
Theravada Buddhism is the large public stream, and the wat is a center of ritual, mutual aid, and information, but it is not “the community.” Some Christianity, and none at all, also live here (Thai Fellowship Church, a Thai-language congregation, launched Sept. 8, 2024 in Brooklyn Park), so ask, and do not assume a wat, and do not assume no wat.

### Streams

Do not mash Hmong household religion or txiv neeb onto this page. Do not make a monk the case plan unless this family asked, and do not BCC one wat and call it consultation.

### Practice

If you visit a home, look for shoes by the door or ask what the household prefers. Funerals and holy days gather family, while you still keep medical and legal time, and when the two collide you name the conflict instead of punishing it.

Ask what religious or spiritual practice matters to this person or family, and do not treat any of it as folklore or as a case plan.

sections.heading: Greetings
sections.body:
The wai — palms together, a slight bow — is ordinary in some rooms, especially with elders, while a handshake is ordinary in many professional rooms and in much of the second generation. Follow the person’s lead on greetings.

### Titles

Ask who to greet first, or follow the household’s lead. An English “hello” plus the name is ordinary, so say the name, and ask how to say it. Nicknames are ordinary in Thai address, which means the form-name may not be the name they use.

### This room

Let this person’s own greeting guide you, whatever you read on another page.

Ask before any physical contact, and let the person set the limit.

sections.heading: Naming Conventions
sections.body:
Given names are used in address, and family names sit last in modern Thai practice; the Surname Act of 1913 is literacy for the desk, not a lecture. Family names can be long, and nicknames are ordinary and may be the only name a teacher or a nurse hears, so ask which name they use day to day, ask how to file, and ask how to say it.

### How to file

U.S. forms flatten a long given name, invent a first-last pair, and then fail to match a nickname, which is a system failure, not a fraud signal, until you have a reason to think otherwise.

Do not assume a Hmong clan name, and do not mash this with Lao naming. Women may or may not take a husband’s family name in U.S. records, so mother and child may not match.

The form that guesses will invent a person, and that invented name follows them through MHCP, school, and child welfare.

sections.heading: Dates of Significance
sections.body:
Songkran — Thai New Year — falls in April, with water, elders, the wat, and travel. It is related to the mid-April new year of Lao Pi Mai, but it belongs to a different people, so do not mash the two, and do not put “Asian holiday” on a case note. Schedule around it when you can, remembering that a calendar click is not community engagement.

### Calendar

Loy Krathong and the Buddhist holy days (including Visakha) are on the calendar, and Thai Mother’s Day and Father’s Day in sending-country public life may matter in some rooms. Household dates will not be on your state calendar, so ask.

Do not mash Songkran with Hmong New Year, Tết, Chinese Lunar New Year, or Diwali. 1975 is a neighboring people’s date, so it is not a Thai holiday and not an icebreaker for this family.

sections.heading: Education
sections.body:
No current Minnesota education or language figures for Thai Minnesotans are published, so do not invent a rate, and remember that this is not a model-minority skip community.

### School and language

A parent who speaks fluent Thai and limited English is not illiterate. The English-only IEP is the gate, and the child is not the interpreter, so book Thai, not Lao and not Hmong.

With roughly 28 to 30 percent in Greater Minnesota, some children sit in districts that have never booked Thai. Ask whether the school has identified what this child needs, and do not treat a college student as proof that the waiver household needs no interpreter.

sections.heading: Etiquette
sections.body:
Wai with elders in some rooms. In a home with an altar, ask where to sit, and ask before touching anyone, including a child. If you visit a home, look for shoes by the door or ask what the household prefers.

### In the home

If food or drink is offered, accepting a little is fine, and you can still keep to medical and legal timelines. Ask before taking any photograph or touching any religious object, and do not ask anyone to explain their faith or history for your benefit.

### Time

If someone misses an appointment, first check the time, transport, interpreter and work schedule. Confirm the plan in Thai if that is the language the person uses, and ask whether it works for them.

Book a qualified interpreter instead of using a child to go between.

sections.heading: Language and Communication
sections.body:
The language is Thai, a tonal language with its own script, and although it is related to Lao, that does not make a Lao interpreter the default. Isan speakers may name that variety, so ask, and remember that it is not Hmong. An interpreter labeled Asian, or Lao, or Hmong, will not work, so book Thai, and still book a qualified interpreter.

### Language

No current Minnesota language figure for Thai Minnesotans is published, so do not invent a rate. Limited English is still a language gate, not a rounding error.

Give the person time to answer. If you get a short yes, check that the plan was understood, and ask whether it works for them.

Do not use a child as the interpreter, and do not make a Thai coworker the interpreter.

sections.heading: Other Considerations
sections.body:
This section states hard facts plainly, because treating everyone the same can hide them.

### Named harms

The camp mash shuts the person out. Camps in Thailand are a Hmong and Karen story, and filing a Thai family under Ban Vinai or Mae La is how a building that only studied 1975 erases this people, so do not do it.

Restaurant labor is work, not a personality and not a joke, and hours, pay, and a Greater Minnesota town with one Thai family are labor facts, which is why you do not write “Thai food” as ethnicity.

No current Minnesota poverty, language or housing figures for Thai Minnesotans are published, so do not fill the gap with a model-minority brochure or a mail-order cliché, and do not invent that personality.

LGBTQ Thai Minnesotans exist, so do not import a Bangkok nightlife cliché onto a waiver meeting. The visa climate changes who opens the door, so do not collect status you do not need, and do not skip mandated reporting and call it humility. Staff who share this community may add facts, but they do not get to delete a fact because it is hard to say.

sections.heading: Health
sections.body:
Book Thai, because limited English is a gate. An English consent form is not consent if they could not follow it, and a Lao interpreter may still not work.

### Access

Believe reported pain, and do not fold this into a Hmong or Chinese slide. Do not skip screening because the person works in a restaurant or smiles.

Ask whether the person wants to talk with a counselor, and do not invent a Minnesota rate or import a Thailand national rate as one. Naming a counselor is not the same as a family accepting one, and a smile is not a PHQ-9. Ask whether the person wants a provider of a particular gender in maternal and intimate care.

If they name a monk, a healer, or a wat, listen, but do not mash a Hmong txiv neeb onto this household, and do not make clergy the case plan unless they asked.

sections.heading: LGBTQ
sections.body:
Ask what name and pronouns the person uses and who they want to know. Public Thai discourse about gender — including kathoey, a word some people use and some people refuse — is not this person’s file and not a waiting-room lesson, so you use the name they use and do not share what they tell you unless a rule requires it.

### This person

Minnesota’s Human Rights Act still applies. Use the name the person uses, and do not share what they tell you unless a rule requires it.

Do not assume a wat household is not affirming, and do not assume a restaurant household is; ask this person.

sections.heading: Hair, Dress, and Body
sections.body:
Traditional dress is public at Songkran, at some weddings, and at the wat, but it is not a daily uniform, and the second generation looks like Minnesota. Do not ask a woman in clinic whether she “still wears the costume.”

### Dress

In a home with an altar, ask where to sit, and ask before touching anyone, including a child.

Do not mash this dress with Hmong New Year clothing, with a sinh as a Lao mash you did not ask about, or with a qipao on an “Asian” table.

sections.heading: Music
sections.body:
Ask which music matters to this person or family: luk thung, mor lam (an Isan form related to Lao music, not to the Hmong qeej), pop, Buddhist chant at the wat, or something else. This is named variation rather than a playlist.

### Variation

A playlist is not engagement, and a khene is not a Hmong qeej, nor is it staff entertainment, so do not ask someone to perform. Songkran stages are public life rather than consultation or a case plan.

sections.heading: Sports
sections.body:
Muay Thai is public culture for some, and a stereotype if you assume it, so do not assume it. School sport is ordinary for the second generation, but do not assume the kid fights, and do not make sport the only excellence you can see.

### Not the whole person

Sport clubs are not language access and not a case plan, because an elder in the stands who needs Thai still needs Thai, and limited English is not a skip because the child plays. A Saturday tournament does not replace an interpreter on Monday.

sections.heading: Literature
sections.body:
Thai has its own script and a written tradition, and the script is related to Lao script but not interchangeable with it. This is not a people without letters, although you do not need to quote a poem in the lobby.

### Literacy in the lobby

What you do need to know is that a notice that exists only in English will not work for the parent who reads Thai, and a notice in Lao that the Thai elder did not ask for also will not work. Ask which language they read, and do not put a proverb on a brochure and call it language access.

sections.heading: Art
sections.body:
Wat mural and sculpture, dance, and the public culture of Songkran and restaurants are all part of this world, but foodway is not consultation, and a restaurant visit is not a case plan.

### Guest

Come as a guest, not a researcher. A wat visit is optional professional development if you are invited, but it is not consultation, and you should not photograph an altar.

A Heritage Month display that mashes this with Hmong paj ntaub or a Chinese lion dance has already mashed the adjacent peoples.

sections.heading: The State, the Camps Next Door, and This Desk
sections.body:
Never-colonized as a national narrative, 1932, the Cold War U.S. presence, and a United States that met Thai people as students, spouses, workers, and neighbors — that is this political file. Camps on Thai soil held Hmong and Karen people, and that is a neighboring story, so telling a Thai family the Secret War as if it were theirs is a state act and shuts the person out.

### The badge

A DHS badge is not automatically help, so do not collect immigration status you do not need, and do not treat fear as noncompliance. Do not use a restaurant, a marriage, or a camp as a personality.

Filing this household as Hmong, as Lao, or as a Census Asian mash shuts the person out.

sections.heading: Work, Wats, and Government
sections.body:
Restaurant and small business, professional streams, and public employment all appear here. Restaurant labor is a documented pattern, and it is work — not a personality, not a joke, and not the whole economy — so do not write “Thai food” as ethnicity.

### Work

No current Minnesota income, poverty or housing figures for Thai Minnesotans are published, and the 2020 Census shows 58.7 percent female among those naming Thai alone or in combination. Do not staff a program as if every household were a model-minority brochure, and do not staff it as if every household were a restaurant.

### Staff

Book a qualified interpreter, and pay for community work. Do not assign either to staff because of who they are. Take time to introduce yourself and explain the plan, and still give any required notice.

sections.heading: Health-care and Human-service Encounters
sections.body:
Expect Thai on the interpreter line — not Lao, not Hmong, not “Asian” — with limited English behind it. Expect a child pushed forward as the English speaker, a monk or a wat in the story, pain you must believe, a nickname the wristband does not have, and Greater Minnesota isolation.

### Language

Confirm Thai, and still book a qualified interpreter rather than using a child. Offer gender match, ask who should hear, and ask which name they use, without making staff the interpreter.

### The meeting

Believe reported pain or mash txiv neeb onto this household. Mandated reporting still exists, and a smile is not consent.

sections.heading: Adjacent Peoples — Do Not Mash
sections.body:
This community is not Hmong, not Lao, not Khmer, not Vietnamese, not Chinese, and not Karen, and “Asian American” is not the file, so open those CIs for those households, and open this one for a Thai household.

### Adjacent doors

Camps in Thailand are a Hmong and Karen story, so do not file Thai families under that war. Isan is related to Lao, but related is not interchangeable, and a Lao interpreter may still not work. Some households are mixed and some people name Isan, so ask this household.

Never one Asian module, and never one “Southeast Asian” interpreter: if Hmong, open Hmong Minnesota, if Lao, open Lao Minnesota, and if Thai, this page.

sections.heading: Counts, Dated
sections.body:
The Census Bureau counts 4,342 Minnesotans who name Thai alone or in any combination in the 2020 Census (2,239 Thai alone) and 4,639 (plus or minus 904) in the ACS 2020–2024; the State Demographer used 4,518 (ACS 2024) in June 2026. About 72 percent (3,121 of 4,342) live in the seven metro counties in the 2020 Census, and the ACS 2020–2024 puts 3,289 (plus or minus 803) of 4,639 in the Minneapolis-St. Paul metro area, about 71 percent, so Greater Minnesota is closer to 28 to 30 percent, with Olmsted County (Rochester) the largest outside the metro. In the 2020 Census, 58.7 percent of those naming Thai alone or in combination are female (2,548 of 4,342), and 67 percent of those naming Thai alone (1,503 of 2,239). Minnesota Compass does not currently list a Thai profile, and the state's 2026 economic status report counts Thai inside “Other Asian,” so no current Minnesota income, poverty, education or housing figures for Thai Minnesotans are published. About 18,819 Minnesotans (plus or minus 1,296) were born in Thailand (ACS 2020–2024), about four times the number who identify as Thai, and many of them are Hmong, Lao or Karen, so a Thailand birthplace is not a Thai identity.

### Counts

Date the count, and do not invent other rates, because counts disagree across census products and definitions, so the number you cite needs its date.

### What the count is not

Roughly 28 to 30 percent living in Greater Minnesota is not an afterthought, and a missing income or education rate is not a model-minority skip, because a rate is not the person.

sections.heading: Doors and Sources
sections.body:
Start with the Census Bureau counts for Thai Minnesotans (2020 Census and ACS 2020–2024), the wats this person names, and the Thai associations this person names, and pay the door this person names rather than assigning a wat.

### Public doors

CECLC is a door, not the whole community. Use these resources yourself before you ask a Thai colleague to explain, and do not count an eList and an English PDF as reaching an LEP elder. Book Thai. If the household is Hmong, open Hmong Minnesota; if Lao, open Lao Minnesota.

### Where to learn more

Be a guest at Songkran if invited, remembering that it is not consultation, and that a restaurant is not consultation either.

sections.heading: How it hits DHS gates — the 40%
sections.body:
Workplace culture and service delivery are both candidates here.

Language comes first, because limited English is a gate, and an elder who needs Thai and gets English — or Lao, or Hmong, or “Asian” — is not being served. Ask whether the person wants a provider of a particular gender in maternal and intimate care, and you should not use a child.

Names come next: a given name, a long family name, and ordinary nicknames. The database that invents a person is a gate, so do not assume a Hmong clan name.

Hour caps, exception processes, and life-sharing matches offered without Thai are not culturally neutral, and an English IEP is still a gate for that parent.

Poverty and housing need will be skipped if the building files this people under a model-minority Asian mash.

Then there is the camp mash: opening Hmong or Karen because the war file said Thailand shuts the person out, so do not tell a Thai family the Secret War as if it were theirs.

On notices and comment, do not count an eList and an English PDF as reaching this community, and record who was reached and what follow-up happened. Greater Minnesota is roughly 28 to 30 percent, so a Twin Cities wat meeting is not the whole channel.

In the workforce, Thai staff are not the interpreter pool and not the community, and a cook is not the culture unit, because staff are colleagues, not the curriculum, and should not be treated as either.

On legislation, funding, and rule: study a channel before you advocate for it. Use this page so that the 40% has a household in it.

sections.heading: A Note on This Guide
sections.body:
This brief is about Ukrainian people — українці — as a people with a country, a language, and a Minnesota community that is both historic and recent. It is not the Russian language door, and it is not “Russian-speaking” treated as a people, because a shared empire and a shared alphabet family are not a shared culture. Rather than opening /ci/russian as a synonym, book Ukrainian if that is the language, and book Russian only if this household asks for Russian.

### Who this is

Use this page for context and questions. It does not describe the person in front of you. Paternalism looks like one “former Soviet” interpreter, an English form handed over because the person looks white, and a 2022 speech delivered to a third-generation parish household that never asked for it.

### Who this is not

Minnesota Compass (ACS 2020–2024) puts Ukrainian ancestry near 22,254 (give or take 3,082), with about 71.9 percent living in the Twin Cities and about 28.1 percent in Greater Minnesota. About 28.8 percent are age 17 or younger and about 15.2 percent are 65+, while about 31.3 percent are foreign-born, which means a large share was born here and a large first generation was not. Date the number you use, because the 2020–2024 five-year estimate includes early 2022 and does not hold the whole post-invasion stream, so you should not invent a 2026 total. A rate is not the person.

The diversity inside this people is the point. Consider a Greek Catholic elder whose family has been in Minnesota since a mid-century parish, a 1990s professional, a 2014 arrival, a 2022 mother on humanitarian parole, a U.S.-born nurse, a Greater Minnesota household, a person who uses Ukrainian with an elder and English with friends, and a household that uses Russian at the table and still names itself Ukrainian. They share a people, although they do not share a Tuesday.

### How to read this

Always defer to the person in front of you, because this page is a hypothesis that you still test on this family rather than a conclusion you bring to the meeting.

sections.heading: Origins and the Founding of a People
sections.body:
Ukrainian peoplehood is older than the Soviet Union, older than 1991, and older than 24 February 2022. It is a country on the Black Sea and the steppe, a language, a literature, and churches for which Moscow is not the default, and its memory runs through Kyivan Rusʼ, the Cossack polities, partitions under empire, the Holodomor, and a modern nation. Minnesota’s community is Ukrainian, so ask how this family names itself rather than lecturing a St. Paul family about a taxonomy they did not ask for.

### History for the meeting

Writing in Ukrainian Cyrillic is the ordinary public literacy of the language rather than Russian with a different flag. Many elders read it and some do not, while the second generation may not read Ukrainian at all. Some households use Russian as a home language because of Soviet schooling, which is a Tuesday fact and not a reason to file this people under the Russian door.

### What people brought

What people brought includes language, parish, kinship, farming and professional skill, and a memory of famine and of a state that denied the name. What they met in Minnesota was an English form, a racial order that may file them as white and skip the interpreter, and often one interpreter labeled “Russian.”

History is literacy for the desk rather than a speech you give the family, which is why you should not start with a nesting-doll, a borscht, or a 2022 tourism sentence.

sections.heading: The Geography of the Ukrainian World
sections.body:
Ukraine has a west, a center, an east, and a south, and language, church, and some vocabulary shift across them, so Galicia and the Greek Catholic west are not Donetsk. Crimea is occupied geography that some families name, and if they name a place, confirm it. Rather than refereeing Kyiv versus Lviv versus the east in a waiver meeting, listen to how this family describes its own map.

### Homeland

The diaspora is global, with Canada (a large historic community), the United States, Poland, Germany, and elsewhere. Toronto is not this map, and Chicago and the Rust Belt sit on a different U.S. map, while secondary migration and parish networks built part of what you will meet here.

### Minnesota

In Minnesota, the community lives in the Twin Cities — including some inner-ring suburbs and named parishes — and holds a real Greater Minnesota share, which Compass puts at 71.9 percent Twin Cities and 28.1 percent Greater Minnesota (ACS 2020–2024). Because of that spread, do not assume Northeast Minneapolis is the whole, and do not assume the person in front of you has been to Ukraine.

sections.heading: Historic Streams and 2022 — Foundational Events, Not One Flight
sections.body:
If 1975 is the foundational event of Vietnamese Minnesota, Ukrainian Minnesota does not get one year; it gets a stack, and you will misread the room if you pick the wrong one.

### Foundational events

The stack begins with late-imperial and early-twentieth-century labor and farm streams, then post-WWII displaced persons, then 1991 independence and the 1990s movement. In 2014, with Crimea annexed and war in the Donbas, some families moved before the full-scale invasion, while 24 February 2022 is current structure for some households: Uniting for Ukraine humanitarian parole, relatives under fire, and a child who has never seen a Minnesota winter. It is a trap to treat every Ukrainian as last year’s arrival, and it is also a trap to pretend the war is not in the room when they name it.

### Who you meet

The desk in 2026 meets U.S.-born adults who do not need an interpreter, elders who need Ukrainian, mixed families, and people who will not accept a Russian-language flyer that looks like Moscow. The Compass foreign-born figure of 31.3 percent (ACS 2020–2024) is the dated share in that vintage rather than the whole post-2022 stream.

Because 2022 is literacy for the desk and not a speech you give the family, do not ask a person to narrate Bucha, Mariupol, or a crossing for your professional development.

sections.heading: Family
sections.body:
Family is not one size. Some households look nuclear on an English form and still carry obligation to a parent who does not drive and does not read the form, while some are three generations in one week, and some are a 2022 mother and children whose spouse is still in Ukraine. Compass puts the average household size at about 2.46, smaller than some neighboring spines, but that is still not always a nuclear English form.

### Who is in the household

The patronymic — a name built from the father — is how a person is fully named in Ukrainian, which means a form that keeps only first and last has already dropped a who. Ask how to file, and ask who should be in the room, rather than letting the form decide both questions for you.

### Who speaks

Adult children may speak for an elder in English, but that is a hypothesis rather than permission to skip the interpreter or to use a child. CLAS still stands, and a sixteen-year-old in the lobby is not the qualified interpreter.

Women’s labor and a professional second generation sit next to older gender patterns in some rooms, and both can be true. Minnesota law still stands on violence, neglect, and who may consent, so do not skip mandated reporting and call it culture.

sections.heading: Minnesota and Ukrainian History
sections.body:
Minnesota holds a Ukrainian community large enough for a Compass profile, and large enough that this department will meet it on waivers, child welfare, health care, cash, food, aging, and employment — historic parish households and recent arrivals in the same week. Compass counts about 22,254 (ACS 2020–2024), and because Greater Minnesota is 28.1 percent of that, do not write this people as a Minneapolis anecdote.

### Places

Think in places rather than a blob: the Twin Cities, inner-ring suburbs, and Greater Minnesota towns. Rather than writing “the Ukrainian neighborhood” onto a map you do not have, work from the pattern as it stands now.

### Partners

Partners are the Ukrainian Catholic parishes some families name, the Ukrainian Orthodox parishes some families name, and the civic groups this family names, since there is no single “Russian community center” that stands for this people. CECLC is a department door, not the community, so pay the partner this household actually uses.

Do not extract Ukrainian staff as the interpreter or as “the community.” A liturgy is optional professional development if you are invited, and while you are there you are a guest, which does not make you the expert.

sections.heading: Українці — not a Russian-speaking file
sections.body:
To be Ukrainian in Minnesota is to be a people with a country and a language, filed under white in a building that may skip the interpreter and skip the page. Ask plainly whether the person agrees with the plan, and make it easy to say no.

### In this state

2022 sits in the room for some and is a news cycle for others, since historic parish families, 1990s arrivals, 2014 arrivals, U.S.-born children, and last year’s parole household do not share one Tuesday. You do not referee, and you do not put a war slogan on a case note as color.

In the United States another fact sits on the same desk: many Ukrainian Minnesotans are read as white. The building’s unmarked default will skip Ukrainian, skip the patronymic, and call that fairness, but that skip is the gate, because white appearance is not English proficiency and it is not the absence of a people.

This guide is a working orientation, which means individual variation always supersedes group generalization and you always defer to the person in front of you.

sections.heading: Core Concepts
sections.body:
The first grammar is Ukrainian, not Russian as a synonym, so if you open the Russian door because the face is white and the name looks Slavic, you do not have a household yet.

### Language of the home, asked

Book Ukrainian if that is the language, and Russian only if this household asks for Russian, and confirm the choice, because after 2022 a Russian interpreter can be a political door.

### Patronymic

The pattern is given name, the father’s name as a middle element, then family name, and since dropping it invents a person and filing it wrong invents a person, ask before you enter it.

### Parish as a channel, not the community

Families may be Ukrainian Greek Catholic, Orthodox, evangelical, or none, so do not make a priest the case plan unless this family asked.

### Historic versus 2022

A third-generation English-dominant household and a parole arrival are not one file, and rather than interrogating loyalty, you do the form.

### White appearance is not English

The skip is the gate, because assuming English from appearance closes the door before the household has a chance to name its language.

sections.heading: Religion
sections.body:
Ask first, because the streams are many. Ukrainian Orthodox and Ukrainian Greek Catholic (Byzantine rite, in communion with Rome) are the two large historic public streams, while Roman Catholic, evangelical Protestant, Jewish in some families, and none all live here as well. Do not assume Moscow, and do not assume no church.

### Streams

The parish is a center of liturgy, memorial, and sometimes mutual aid, but it is not the community, so do not BCC one priest and call it consultation. Icons in a home are neither a case plan nor a museum.

### Practice

Intra-church politics after 2018 — autocephaly, the Moscow patriarchate — are real in some rooms, although you do not referee them on a case note.

Do not rank piety, since a person who left the church is still this people-page if that is the household in front of you.

sections.heading: Greetings
sections.body:
A handshake is common in many rooms — among men, and often among women in professional space — but follow this room, because some older parish settings will change the rule. If a hand is not offered, nod and carry on.

### Titles

Ask how the person wants to be addressed. Given name plus patronymic is the respectful Ukrainian address for an adult you do not know well. English Mr./Ms. plus family name is a decent substitute if you cannot produce the patronymic, but do not use a first name with an elder simply because the form printed it.

### This room

Добрий день is a common formal hello, while an English “hello” is ordinary, especially with the second generation. Say the name, and ask how to say it.

Let this person’s own greeting guide you, whatever you read on another page. Ask before any physical contact, and let the person set the limit.

sections.heading: Naming Conventions
sections.body:
A common Ukrainian pattern is given name, patronymic, family name, and the patronymic is not a middle name you may drop for convenience. Databases that drop it invent a person, and that invented person then fails a match in MHCP, child welfare, and school.

### How to file

Family names may take a gendered ending, and endings such as -enko, -uk, -chuk, and -skyi / -ska are patterns, not a joke. A form that flags the difference as fraud has already chosen a household type, so ask how to file, and ask how this person wants the English record to read.

Do not “correct” a name toward a Russian textbook. Kyiv, Kharkiv, and Lviv are place-literacy for the desk, but on the form you write what they tell you, pronounce it, and ask.

Women may or may not take a husband’s family name in U.S. records, so mother and child may not match, which is not fraud until you have a reason. Three people in one household may not share a “last name” the way a Swedish Minnesota form expects.

sections.heading: Dates of Significance
sections.body:
Orthodox Nativity and Pascha follow the Julian calendar for many Orthodox households, often falling later than Western Christmas and Easter, although some Ukrainian churches have moved Nativity to 25 December (St. Constantine Ukrainian Catholic Church in Minneapolis has used the Gregorian calendar since 1943, by its own timeline), so ask which one this family keeps. These days are not a day off the work; they are literacy.

### Calendar

Independence Day falls on 24 August, and Holodomor Remembrance is the fourth Saturday of November in many Ukrainian rooms, which is literacy rather than a file. In Minnesota, a 2023 House resolution named the last week of November Holodomor Memorial Week, and the Ukrainian American Community Center gives the memorial day as Nov. 25 on one page and Nov. 28 on another. Vyshyvanka Day exists in some public life, but a calendar click is not community engagement.

24 February 2022 is current structure for some families rather than a holiday or a personality, so do not put a war slogan, a flag lecture, or “Fall of Saigon party” energy on a case note.

Do not put “Eastern European holiday” on a case note either, because it erases the specific people this page describes.

sections.heading: Education
sections.body:
Compass (ACS 2020–2024) reports that among Ukrainian Minnesotans 25 and older, about 94.5 percent have a high school diploma or higher and about 53.2 percent hold a bachelor’s or higher. Date Compass, and remember that about 31.3 percent of the community is foreign-born, so high attainment is not “no language gate.” A large share of children are U.S.-born and in English-dominant schools, but the IEP still has to reach the parent who does not read it.

### School and language

A parent who speaks fluent Ukrainian and limited English is not illiterate, since many elders read Ukrainian Cyrillic, although some do not. Recent arrivals may hold credentials this country has not recognized, which is why the English-only form is the gate.

Do not skip the interpreter because the adult in the lobby is white, employed, or accent-light, and do not treat a college student as proof that the waiver household needs no interpreter.

sections.heading: Etiquette
sections.body:
If you visit a home, look for shoes by the door or ask what the household prefers. You still keep medical and legal time.

### In the home

Ask before taking any photograph or touching any religious object, and do not ask anyone to explain their faith or history for your benefit.

### Time

If someone misses an appointment, first check the time, transport, interpreter and work schedule. Confirm the plan in the language the person uses, and ask whether it works for them.

Book a qualified interpreter instead of using a child to go between.

sections.heading: Language and Communication
sections.body:
Ukrainian is not Russian, it is not Belarusian, and it is not “former Soviet,” which means an interpreter labeled Russian who is the wrong language for this household will not work, and after 2022 it may also feel political. Book Ukrainian if that is the language, and Russian only if this household asks for Russian. Under CLAS you still book a qualified interpreter, because a list is not the person and not the dialect.

### Language

Compass reports that among those 5 and older, about 30.0 percent speak a language other than English and about 13.7 percent speak English less than “very well,” so date the number. Many elders read Ukrainian in Cyrillic, while some U.S.-born adults do not, and a notice in Russian is not a Ukrainian notice.

White appearance is not English, so do not take a light accent as “no interpreter needed” without asking. Give the person time to answer. If you get a short yes, check that the plan was understood, and ask whether it works for them.

Do not use a child as the interpreter, and do not make a Ukrainian coworker the interpreter.

sections.heading: Other Considerations
sections.body:
This section states hard facts plainly, because treating everyone the same can hide them.

### Named harms

War trauma is real in some 2022 rooms: cities, roads, loss, a spouse still there. It is not a personality and not a reason to skip screening, but it is a reason a government badge is not automatically help, and you should not invent a Minnesota PTSD rate to describe it.

Intra-community language politics still split some rooms — Ukrainian only, Russian at the table, mixed families — and rather than refereeing, you book the language this household asks for.

Alcohol harm and family violence exist in some households, although they are not “the culture,” and they are not a Slavic joke. You follow the law and you still see a family, so do not skip mandated reporting and call it humility.

Immigration status fear is real for some recent arrivals, including those on parole that can expire, so do not collect status you do not need, and do not treat fear as noncompliance.

LGBTQ Ukrainian Minnesotans exist, which means you use the name and you do not out someone to kin and call it culture. Staff who share this community may add facts, but they do not get to delete a fact because it is hard to say.

sections.heading: Health
sections.body:
Compass (ACS 2020–2024) reports about 5.3 percent without health insurance among those for whom status is determined. Date it, remembering that this vintage is not the whole 2022 stream, and do not invent a PTSD rate to fill this chapter, since trauma sits in some rooms but not in every household.

### Access

Believe reported pain. Do not fold this history into Tuskegee or into a generic refugee module.

Mental-health stigma exists in some families, and naming a counselor is not the same as a family accepting one, just as a smile is not a PHQ-9. War does not make screening optional, and it does not make every person a case study.

Gender match may be requested in maternal and intimate care, so offer it. Book the language they name even if the person is white, and confirm Ukrainian rather than a “former Soviet” default.

sections.heading: LGBTQ
sections.body:
Queer and trans Ukrainian Minnesotans exist, although conservative Orthodox, Greek Catholic, and some family climates can mean silence or exile. The war does not erase this person, and it does not change the name they use.

### This person

Staff duty is the same as on the other spines: use the name they use, do not share what they tell you unless a rule requires it, and remember that the Minnesota Human Rights Act still applies.

Do not question a household about anyone’s sexuality or gender, and take seriously that some people have reason to keep it private. Follow the person’s lead.

sections.heading: Hair, Dress, and Body
sections.body:
The vyshyvanka is public at festivals, Independence Day tables, and some church days, but it is not a daily uniform, and the second generation looks like Minnesota. For that reason, do not ask a woman in clinic whether she “still wears the costume.”

### Dress

Head covering happens in some parish rooms, and it is neither a security threat nor a consent problem. Do not touch, and do not comment on gold, a cross, or embroidery as a case note.

Winter dress is Minnesota, not ethnography, and Heritage Month tables that mash this with a matryoshka have already failed the adjacent-peoples chapter.

sections.heading: Music
sections.body:
Church chant is liturgy, not a playlist, while Kobzar and folk forms, popular song, and wartime music exist in some rooms. This is named variation rather than a “Slavic mix.”

### Variation

A playlist is not engagement, and a funeral or a liturgy is not staff entertainment. Knowing that 2022 can sit inside a song will stop you from putting the wrong flag on a speaker.

Festival stages are public life, which means they are not consultation and not a case plan.

sections.heading: Sports
sections.body:
Soccer shows up in public Ukrainian Minnesota life, and school sport is ordinary for the second generation, but do not assume the kid plays, and do not make sport the only excellence you can see.

### Not the whole person

Sport clubs are social infrastructure for some, although they are not language access and not a case plan. A club flyer in English still will not work for the parent who needs Ukrainian on the line.

Greater Minnesota and the Twin Cities both play, so the club scene is not only a metro story.

sections.heading: Literature
sections.body:
Ukrainian is a major written language with a long literature, and Shevchenko is literacy for the desk rather than a prompt to quote Кобзар in the lobby. This is not a people without letters, and it is not Russian literature with a different flag.

### Literacy in the lobby

Cyrillic literacy for many elders is the actual operations fact, which means a notice that exists only in English, or only in Russian, will not work. U.S.-born adults may not read Cyrillic and may still be the person who has to explain the form.

You do not need a novel, because what you need is the language this person reads.

sections.heading: Art
sections.body:
Pysanky, vyshyvanka embroidery, icons, and diaspora visual work are the public art here, and none of it is matryoshka, a nesting-doll exhibit, or a Russian folk-costume mash.

### Guest

Be a guest rather than a researcher, since an icon is not a case plan and a festival is not consultation. Do not photograph a sanctuary as professional development without being asked.

Heritage Month tables that mash a vyshyvanka, a menorah, and a matryoshka into one “Eastern European” booth have already mashed what this brief asks you to keep apart.

sections.heading: War, the State, and the Russian-Door Trap
sections.body:
The political stack is the Holodomor, Soviet surveillance, 1991, 2014, 24 February 2022, Uniting for Ukraine parole, and the later enforcement climate for some arrivals, which is why a DHS badge is not automatically help. For some people, a government form is a thing you survive, and that is not “paranoia” but pattern.

### The badge

The war is current structure for some households: family under fire, mixed marriages, parole that can expire, people who left, and people who have been here for three generations. It is a trap to assume every Ukrainian is a 2022 refugee, and it is also a trap to punish someone for not performing the politics you prefer.

Do not use 2022 as a personality, and do not ask a person to narrate a war for your professional development. Do not collect status you do not need, and do not open the Russian language door as this people.

sections.heading: Work, Markets, and Government
sections.body:
Professional work, trades, small business, public employment, and under-recognized credentials all live here, and a small-business owner and a waiver recipient may be the same extended family. The Compass median household income of about $94,322 (2024 dollars) is an average rather than this kitchen table.

### Work

Book a qualified interpreter, and pay for community work. Do not assign either to staff because of who they are.

### Staff

Take time to introduce yourself and explain the plan, and still give any required notice. The notice still has to exist in the language they read.

Do not count an English eList comment period as reaching this community, since it does not arrive in the language they read.

sections.heading: Health-care and Human-service Encounters
sections.body:
The gates here are language, the patronymic, who is in the room, and the habit of assuming English because the person is white. Book Ukrainian if that is the language, and Russian only if this household asks for Russian, and watch for a child pushed forward as the English speaker. War climate shapes some rooms, while enforcement climate shapes some recent arrivals.

### Language

Confirm the language and still book a qualified interpreter, offer gender match, ask who should hear, and ask how to file the name, rather than making staff the interpreter.

### The meeting

Believe reported pain. Mandated reporting still exists, and so does the duty not to treat a whole people as a risk score, so do not collect status you do not need.

sections.heading: Adjacent Peoples — Do Not Mash
sections.body:
The Russian language door is not this people, so open /ci/russian for a Russian-language request. A Ukrainian family that uses Russian still gets to name their people, which is why you ask, since a Russian interpreter can still be the wrong door.

### Adjacent doors

This is not a Belarusian mash, not Polish as a synonym, and not a “former Soviet” interpreter. It is not Somali and not the African American CI, and it is not “white = no cultural intelligence,” while historic German- and Scandinavian-Minnesota unmarked culture is the European American door, not this one.

Some households are mixed, so ask this household, and never reach for one East-European module or one Slavic interpreter.

sections.heading: Counts, Dated
sections.body:
Minnesota Compass (ACS 2020–2024) describes the Ukrainian cultural community this way: about 22,254 people (give or take 3,082); Twin Cities 71.9%; Greater Minnesota 28.1%; age 17 or younger 28.8%; 65+ 15.2%; foreign-born 31.3%; language other than English (age 5+) 30.0%; English less than “very well” 13.7%; English only 70.0%; high school or higher (25+) 94.5%; bachelor’s or higher 53.2%; median household income about $94,322 (give or take $13,367, in 2024 dollars); poverty 7.7%; owner-occupied 68.0%; average household size 2.46; uninsured 5.3%; and disability 10.9% (give or take 3.1%).

### Counts

Date Compass, because the 2020–2024 five-year estimate includes early 2022 and does not hold the whole post-invasion stream, so you should not invent a 2026 community total. The 2024 one-year ACS counts 19,849 (give or take 3,043) Minnesotans of Ukrainian ancestry and 6,647 (give or take 2,021) born in Ukraine, and the Ukrainian American Community Center told the Legislature in June 2025 that the community was “approximately 25,000.” Counts disagree across ACS vintages and definitions (ancestry vs. birthplace vs. language), which is another reason to date the number you cite.

### What the count is not

A young age structure is not a personality, and an owner rate is not proof the gates closed, since language and child-as-interpreter are gates. White appearance is not English, and a rate is not the person.

sections.heading: Doors and Sources
sections.body:
Start with the Minnesota Compass Ukrainian profile (ACS 2020–2024), and then turn to the Ukrainian Catholic and Orthodox parishes that families name and the civic groups this family names, remembering that CECLC is a door, not the whole community.

### Public doors

Adjacent, and not this page, are the DHS Equal Opportunity and Access LEP resources, where Russian sits among the five, but that list is not this people. Book Ukrainian if that is the language, and Russian only if this household asks for Russian.

### Where to learn more

Use these resources yourself before you ask a Ukrainian colleague to explain, and do not count a BCC to a parish as consultation. Pay partners and report back, and be a guest at a liturgy if invited, remembering that it is not consultation.

sections.heading: How it hits DHS gates — the 40%
sections.body:
Workplace culture and service delivery are both candidates here.

On language: Ukrainian is not Russian, and an interpreter labeled “former Soviet” will not work, so book Ukrainian if that is the language, and Russian only if this household asks for Russian. Still book a qualified interpreter, because a list is not the person and not the dialect. Cyrillic is not optional decoration on a notice that actually has to be read, and you should not use a child.

On names: the pattern is given name, patronymic, family name, and the database that drops the patronymic or “corrects” toward a Russian spelling invents a person.

Do not assume English because the person is white. Ask which language they use.

Hour caps, exception processes, and life-sharing matches made without language are not culturally neutral.

On enforcement and parole climate: some recent arrivals may skip clinic, school, and waiver meetings, which is not noncompliance, so do not collect status you do not need.

On notices and comment: do not count an eList and an English PDF as reaching this community, and record who was reached and what follow-up happened. Greater Minnesota is 28.1 percent, which means a St. Paul meeting is not the whole channel.

On workforce: Ukrainian staff are not the interpreter pool and not the community, because staff are colleagues, not the curriculum, and should not be treated as such.

On the Russian mash: opening /ci/russian because the checkbox or the face looks “Slavic” shuts the person out.

On legislation, funding, and rule: study a channel before you advocate for it. Use this page so that the 40% has a household in it.

sections.heading: A Note on This Guide
sections.body:
This brief is about Vietnamese people — người Việt — as a people with a country, a long literature, and a Minnesota community built after 1975. Kinh are the majority in this state, while Hoa (Chinese-Vietnamese) live in some families, so ask rather than assume. This is not Chinese, it is not Hmong, it is not Karen, and it is not Lao as a synonym, because a shared continent is not a shared culture. A full mosaic of a people is not a stereotype; a stereotype is what happens when this page becomes the person in the lobby.

### Who this is

Vietnamese sits on the DHS CLAS five-language standing written list alongside Hmong, Russian, Somali, and Spanish, but you still book a qualified interpreter, because a list is not the person and not the dialect. Northern, Central, and Southern varieties exist, so put the variety on the interpreter line if it matters in this room.

### Who this is not

Minnesota Compass (ACS 2020–2024) puts Vietnamese ancestry near 32,841 (give or take 3,477), with about 76.8 percent living in the Twin Cities and about 23.2 percent in Greater Minnesota. About 27.4 percent are age 17 or younger and about 8.4 percent are 65+, while about 48.5 percent are foreign-born, which means a large second generation was born here and a large first generation was not. Date the number you use, and remember that a rate is not the person.

The diversity inside this people is the point, so consider a 1975 first-wave Catholic elder, a boat-person who spent years in a camp, a Hoa family, a Buddhist grandmother with an ancestor altar, a U.S.-born nurse, a Greater Minnesota factory household, a college student who uses English with friends and Vietnamese with an elder, and a person who left 1975 politics behind and still shows up at Tết. They share a people, but they do not share a Tuesday.

### How to read this

Always defer to the person in front of you, because this page is a hypothesis that you still have to test on this family.

sections.heading: Origins and the Founding of a People
sections.body:
Vietnamese peoplehood is older than French Indochina, older than 1954, and older than the refugee camp. Vietnam is a country on the eastern mainland of Southeast Asia, with Kinh as the majority people and Hoa, Khmer Krom, and highland minorities inside the Vietnamese state. Minnesota’s community is overwhelmingly Vietnamese (Kinh), with Hoa in some families, so ask rather than assume, and do not lecture a St. Paul family about a taxonomy they did not ask for.

### History for the meeting

Writing in quốc ngữ — the Latin-based script — is the ordinary public literacy, while older scripts and chữ Nôm are history. Many elders read quốc ngữ, but some do not, and the second generation may not read Vietnamese at all.

### What people brought

The 1954 partition after the French war sent a large Catholic stream from north to south, and that fact still sits in Minnesota parish life, though it is not a speech you give the family. 1975 is the foundational event of the diaspora you will meet on this desk, but origins did not begin there.

What people brought with them was language, ancestor obligation, Mahayana Buddhism and Catholicism both, farming and trade skill, and a memory of war — of a state that won and a state that lost. What they met in Minnesota was an English form, one “Asian” checkbox, and often one interpreter labeled “Vietnamese.”

sections.heading: The Geography of the Vietnamese World
sections.body:
Vietnam is north, central, and south, and tones, food, and some vocabulary shift between them. Most of the 1975 and boat-people stream to the United States came out of the south, while later streams include the north, so confirm the variety if it matters in the room. Do not referee Hanoi versus Saigon in a waiver meeting; if they name a place, listen.

### Homeland

The diaspora is global, reaching California (the largest U.S. community), Texas, the Gulf Coast, France, Australia, Canada, and Minnesota. Orange County is not this map, since secondary migration and family reunification built part of what you will meet here.

### Minnesota

In Minnesota the community lives in the Twin Cities — University Avenue / Frogtown in St. Paul, inner-ring suburbs, and other metro pockets — and it holds a real Greater Minnesota share, which Compass puts at 76.8 percent Twin Cities and 23.2 percent Greater Minnesota (ACS 2020–2024). Do not assume University Avenue is the whole, and do not assume the person in front of you has been to Vietnam.

sections.heading: 1975, Boat People, and Later Streams — Foundational Event
sections.body:
If the Secret War and 1975 are the foundational event of Hmong Minnesota, the American War / Vietnam War and 30 April 1975 are the foundational event of Vietnamese Minnesota.

### Foundational events

In April 1975 the Republic of Vietnam collapsed, and first-wave evacuations and airlifts moved people tied to the southern government and to the United States — often more urban, more Catholic, and more already connected. That is a stream rather than a virtue ranking, and most people were not on those planes.

### Who you meet

Boat people followed, in 1978 and the years around it especially, and they faced overcrowded boats, pirates, drowning, and camps in Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, the Philippines, and Hong Kong. Hoa families left under a separate pressure after 1978. Years in camps came first and then resettlement, as church and voluntary-agency sponsors scattered people across the country and family pulled them back together.

Orderly Departure, the Humanitarian Operation path for re-education-camp survivors, the Amerasian Homecoming Act (1987), and later family reunification and ordinary immigration are the later streams. The desk in 2026 does not only meet 1975, because it meets their children — U.S.-born, English-dominant with peers, still translating for parents, and still unable to get the right variety in the lobby.

1975 is literacy for the desk rather than a speech you give the family.

sections.heading: Family
sections.body:
Filial piety — hiếu — is a hypothesis, not a personality. Ask who should speak first, and hear from the person directly. Adult children may be holding a waiver meeting, a factory shift, and a school conference in the same week. Compass puts the average household size at about 2.95, smaller than some neighboring spines, but still not always the nuclear household an English form expects.

### Who is in the household

The person who cares for a disabled adult or a child may be a son, a daughter-in-law, or a sibling rather than the legally recognized caregiver on the checkbox. Hour caps and “natural supports” language can dump unpaid work onto the women in that network and then call it culture.

### Who speaks

The person who speaks in the lobby may be the child with the best English, but that child is not the qualified interpreter, and CLAS still stands. Using a child as the go-between does harm, so book the interpreter and ask who should be in the room.

Women’s labor — shop, salon, factory, professional second generation — sits next to elder obligation, and both can be true in the same room. Minnesota law still stands, so do not skip mandated reporting and call it humility.

sections.heading: Minnesota and Vietnamese History
sections.body:
Minnesota holds a Vietnamese community large enough to put the language on the CLAS five, and large enough that this department will meet it on waivers, child welfare, health care, cash, food, aging, and employment. Compass counts about 32,841 (ACS 2020–2024), and Greater Minnesota is 23.2 percent of that, so do not write this people as a Minneapolis anecdote.

### Places

Think in places rather than a blob: University Avenue and Frogtown in St. Paul; Little Mekong as a public name on a stretch of University Avenue in Frogtown, between Mackubin and Marion streets, not a reservation (its organizers describe an Asian business and cultural corridor, and Visit Saint Paul ties its formation to Hmong settlement, so it is not a Vietnamese district alone); inner-ring suburbs; and Greater Minnesota towns with work and housing. Phở shops and markets are public life, but they are not consultation, and a food-court visit does not make you the expert.

### Partners

Partners include the Vietnamese Community of Minnesota, the Buddhist temples families name, and Catholic parishes with a large Vietnamese stream because of 1954 and 1975. CECLC is a department door rather than the whole community, which is why you pay the partner this household actually uses.

Book a qualified interpreter, and pay for community work. Do not assign either to staff because of who they are. Tết is optional professional development if you are invited, and you attend as a guest, knowing that it does not make you the expert.

sections.heading: Người Việt — the heart of a people
sections.body:
Vietnam is a country with a long history of being in someone else’s war, and forms in Minnesota file Vietnamese people under Asian. Ask plainly whether the person agrees with the plan, and make it easy to say no.

### In this state

1975 sits in the room for some and is a history class for others. First-wave anti-communist politics, later arrivals, U.S.-born children, and Hoa families do not share one Tuesday, so you do not referee, and you do not put “Fall of Saigon” on a case note as color.

In the United States another fact sits on the same desk: many Vietnamese Minnesotans are Asian in a racial order that also holds Chinese, Indian, Korean, and Hmong histories they do not share, and that mash is the gate.

This guide is a working orientation, and because individual variation always supersedes group generalization, always defer to the person in front of you.

sections.heading: Core Concepts
sections.body:
Hiếu is filial piety, held here as a hypothesis, and it means care for parents, an obligation that an English consumer form does not see. Staff do not use it as a guilt tool; if the family names it, you listen.

### Elders

Ask who should be greeted first and who should speak first, and do not use a child as the interpreter.

### Checking for agreement

Before you treat a yes as agreement, ask again, plainly and without embarrassing anyone.

### Ancestors

An altar in a living room — including in some Catholic households — is not a case plan and not a museum, and the death-anniversary giỗ is family time.

### Religion as practice, not a checkbox

Mahayana Buddhism, Catholicism, Cao Đài and Hòa Hảo in some families, and none at all are all present here, so do not make a priest or a monk the case plan unless they asked.

### Work and school

A salon, a shop, and a second-generation degree can be one family’s project, and nail-salon labor is work, not a personality.

1975 is part of the history many families carry. Do not raise it, and do not assume it about the person in the lobby.

sections.heading: Religion
sections.body:
Mahayana Buddhism and Catholicism are the two large public streams in Vietnamese Minnesota, while Cao Đài and Hòa Hảo live in some families, and none is also a Tuesday, so ask. A large Catholic stream exists because 1954 moved northern Catholics south and 1975 moved many of those families again, which is history, not a piety ranking.

### Streams

An ancestor altar in a Catholic household can be true, so do not treat that as a contradiction you need to fix, and do not treat Buddhism as “more Vietnamese” than the parish.

### Practice

The temple and the parish are centers of ritual, mutual aid, and information, but they are not “the community.” Do not BCC one priest or one monk and call it consultation, and do not make clergy the case plan unless this family asked.

Funerals and giỗ gather family, and while you still keep medical and legal time, you name the conflict instead of punishing it. Do not photograph an altar.

sections.heading: Greetings
sections.body:
Ask who to greet first, or follow the household’s lead. Wait to see how the person greets you, and follow their lead.

### Titles

Xin chào is a common hello, and English “hello” is ordinary. Say the name, and since the family name is often the first word in Vietnamese order, do not treat it as optional.

### This room

Let this person’s own greeting guide you, whatever you read on another page.

Ask before any physical contact, and let the person set the limit.

sections.heading: Naming Conventions
sections.body:
The family name comes first in Vietnamese order, and Nguyễn, Trần, Lê, Phạm, Huỳnh / Hoàng, Phan, and Vũ / Võ are common. Nguyễn is common enough that a joke about it shuts the person out, so do not joke, and do not say “too many Nguyens.”

### How to file

U.S. forms reverse the order, which means a person who is Nguyễn Thị Lan in Vietnamese may be Lan Nguyen on a license and Lan Thi Nguyen in another database. Ask which is the family name, how to file it, and how to say it, because the form that guesses will invent a person, and that invented name follows them through MHCP, school, and child welfare.

Given names and middle names (often a generational or gender marker such as Thị or Văn) are not decoration, and tones matter in speech. You do not need to become a linguist; you need to ask and to write down what they say.

Women may or may not take a husband’s family name in U.S. records, so mother and child may not match, but that is not fraud until you have a reason.

sections.heading: Dates of Significance
sections.body:
Tết — Lunar New Year — is the large annual public and family date, and it brings travel, food, elders, red envelopes in some families, and closed shops, so schedule around it when you can. It is not a day off the work, and you attend as a guest if invited, since a calendar click is not community engagement.

### Calendar

30 April 1975 marks the fall of Saigon / the end of the Republic of Vietnam, and in many Vietnamese American rooms this is grief and politics, sometimes marked as Black April. It is not a “Fall of Saigon party,” so you do not put that phrase on a case note, and you do not celebrate reunification at this desk; if they name it, listen.

Giỗ — ancestral death anniversaries — are household dates that will not be on your state calendar, so ask. Hùng Kings commemoration exists in some community public life, which is literacy, not a file.

Do not put “Asian holiday” on a case note.

sections.heading: Education
sections.body:
Compass (ACS 2020–2024) reports that among Vietnamese Minnesotans 25 and older, about 77.0 percent have high school or higher and about 36.1 percent have a bachelor’s or higher, and you should date Compass when you cite it. About 48.5 percent of the community is foreign-born, and a large share of children are U.S.-born and in English-dominant schools, yet the IEP still has to reach the parent who does not read it.

### School and language

A parent who speaks fluent Vietnamese and limited English is not illiterate, and while many elders read quốc ngữ, some do not, which means the English-only form is the gate. Put the variety on the interpreter line if this household needs it.

Second-generation educational mobility is real, and so is a gap that a room that treats everyone the same will call “culture” when it is really language access plus a school that never learned the name. Do not treat a college student in the family as proof the waiver household needs no interpreter.

sections.heading: Etiquette
sections.body:
If you visit a home, look for shoes by the door or ask what the household prefers. If food or drink is offered, accepting a little is fine, and you can still keep to medical and legal timelines.

### In the home

Do not point your feet at an altar or at a person if you are in a household that keeps one. Ask before taking any photograph or touching any religious object, and do not ask anyone to explain their faith or history for your benefit.

### Time
